text: I've never heard of The Fall before, I guess it's my age.
author: Trevor Lord

text: They appear to have released over 30 original albums and a host of compilations.
author: Trevor Lord

text: They formed in 1977, were a bit like punks (but not really), have gone through numerous line-up changes and are led by singer and songwriter Mark E.
author: Trevor Lord

text: It seems he is the lynchpin of the whole project.
author: Trevor Lord

text: The opening track ("Jim's The Fall") features the murmured refrain 'We are the New Fall'.
author: Trevor Lord

text: I don't know why.
author: Trevor Lord

text: Up next is the rumbling rock swagger of "Bourgeois Town".
author: Trevor Lord

text: Mark sounds bemused to be in middle class locale; but it certainly doesn't stop him sounding arrogant and sexy.
author: Trevor Lord

text: 'Crop Dust' is a bleaker and somehow more empty track.
author: Trevor Lord

text: I couldn't really hear the words - there might be something wrong with Mark's liver.
author: Trevor Lord

text: A pounding 'Velveteen' bass line drives "My Ex-Classmates Kids".
author: Trevor Lord

text: This would be good track to drive to, if you own a car.
author: Trevor Lord

text: The next track ("Kick the Can") seems a bit of filler, but all is forgiven by a lovely cover of blue-eyed soul star R.Dean Taylor's "Gotta see Jane".
author: Trevor Lord

text: Apparently the band had a hit in the eighties with his Wigan Casino classic "There's a Ghost in My House".
author: Trevor Lord

text: Next comes the Krautastic (in length at least, it goes on for nearly 10 minutes!) "Ibis Afro Man".
author: Trevor Lord

text: It's a weird and funny track I couldn't help but like.
author: Trevor Lord

text: In fact it seems to be two tracks, which occasionally bump into each other-there's also an extended section of chimp squawking.
author: Trevor Lord

text: "The Acute" and "Hollow Mind" are pleasant enough, quite gentle and ruminative.
author: Trevor Lord

text: (This band's no one trick pony.) The album ends up on the wilfully subjective, very long titled, stop start antics of "Reprise: Jane-Prof Mick-Ey Bastardo".
author: Trevor Lord

text: The old men in the office tell me a lot of the Fall's albums are as good or even better than this one.
author: Trevor Lord

text: Their rhythmic rock and surreal rants have made me one happy bunny.
author: Trevor Lord

text: I'll definitely be spending a few hours in their back catalogue.
author: Trevor Lord

text: Since releasing his debut EP on the Isolate label and his subsequent discovery by Mike Paradinas of Planet-Mu, Winnipeg, Canada based Aaron Funk aka Venetian Snares has quickly become a household name in the underground techno community and its easy to see why.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Within the first two minutes of Doll Doll Doll, its pretty clear that Mr.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Funk isnt just another kid with a laptop looking for a record deal.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Starting off with a simple take on mutant drum and bass, the CD soon veers off into much more experimental territory, most of it dark, dissonant and unbelievably complex - combining the most astonishing collection of rhythms, genres and influences into a record that defies categorisation.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: From the lunatic asylum led free jazz meets off kilter drum and bass of I Rent The Ocean to the demonically vocal gabbercore of Befriend, there is much here to be worried about.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: This is not a record for the timid.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: (Napalm Death fans take note) But, the true genius of this man isnt fully realised until you come across the fourth track on here.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Entitled Dollmaker, it starts from swing jazz which then slowly morphs into something much more sinister.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Fusing full on gabbacore with cellos and distorted synths, Funk takes it one step further, injecting an angry Cannibal Ox-esque hip-hop vocal in the mix.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: The subject matter here is equally dark - most of it focusing on child abuse of some kind of another.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Tracks are entitled Befriend a Childkiller or All The Children Are Dead, a sample from the Jon-Benet Ramsey helpline appears on one track, a darkened voice lurking in the background whispering befriend the childkiller on another.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Like I said: scary stuff.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Its very rare these days that music producers are able to leap from genre to genre while still keeping the overall vision of the source material intact.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Aaron Funk has managed to do exactly that in a way that is darker and nastier than we ever imagined.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Think Naked City's Torture Garden remixed by Squarepusher at twice the speed and you're close.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Make it a lot more cohesive and much more evil and youre there.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Brutally dissonant, mind-blowingly complex and very, very nasty.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Its the kind of release that will have armies of imitators behind it in no time at all.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Watch this man - he will go far and scare the hell out of everyone in his way.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: So far this year has seen solid releases from both Skitz and Mark B & Blade that have done nothing but big things for UK hip hop.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: But it is perhaps this stunning second album from Stockwell born and bred producer come mic destroyer Roots Manuva that has raised the bar for good.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Now, with the release of Run Come Save Me everyone has to jump higher...
author: Christian Hopwood

text: a lot higher.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Primarily this album should be lauded for its degree of musical invention and individual approach to the genre.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Rodney has produced three quarters of the album himself and there are elements here that have subsequently reappeared in the world of R&B.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: On hearing the stuttering, organic funk of that huge, electronic bass line and the relentless, loping rhymes on "Witness (One Hope)"we are reminded of the production on Brandy's "What About" masterminded by the genius of Rodney 'Darkchild' Jerkins.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: There is a playful, anarchic disregard for time signatures as things slip across the bars and are then suddenly pulled back again.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Roots is not afraid to experiment and the results are refreshing and unpredictable.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Not only is he technically adept Roots is also a fearless writer.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Gnashing over minimal keys he confesses on "Stone The Crows" "...as you can tell I'm from a basic stock, shouldn't take these drugs, shouldn't get so p*ssed".
author: Christian Hopwood

text: The raw melancholy of "Sinny Sin Sins" finds Roots refuting the strict religious upbringing imposed by his deacon father.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: "I used to steal collection, I used catch a beating...
author: Christian Hopwood

text: As long as your living under my roof your gonna heed to my interpretation of the truth...
author: Christian Hopwood

text: to this day I fight down their spell".
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Yet, pathos aside, there is a ready wit that is never far from the surface.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: By way of example, his ode to the 'erb "Highest Grade" lifts the hook from Craig David's "Seven Days" to illustrate the sale and daily intake of Stockwell's jolly, green clients.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: He is intelligent, humble but most of all conscious.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: On "Witness" he raps, "I sit here contented with this cheese on toast, I feel the pain of a third world famine".
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Somehow it's hard to imagine any MC from the West Side issuing forth a lactose truth like this but that's Rodney -strictly UK.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Although his debut Brand New Second Hand was an underground success it fell short of the landmark release that UK hip hop had been missing for the last ten years.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: With the completion of album number two, we have here a record that will be artistically and commercially recognised without pandering to the sounds and attitudes of Stateside hip hop.In making this truly individual record Roots Manuva has well and truly done the business.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: It's jazz, Jim, but not as we know it....Flanger's two previous records on Ntone recast early 1970s spacey jazz fusion as the product of a software engineers fantasy.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Blurring the lines between what's been played and what's been digitally generated, Burnt Friedman and Uwe Schmidt's music was playful, eartickling and occasionally ridiculously funky.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Friedman's solo work in particular (check 1999s wonderful Con Ritmo) has been playing with notions of real and cyber musicianship, forcing crisp, funk derived drum patterns into hyperspeed blurs that Jack DeJohnette would be hard pressed to replicate.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Inner Space takes things a bit further by introducing real instruments into the mix, courtesy of a bunch of Latin American rhythm players and Danish soloists.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The resulting brew is warmer and more organic than previous outings; Thomas Hass's tenor and Carsten Skov's vibes provide a harmonic sophistication and coherence lacking in Schmidt and Friedmann's limited keyboard skills, leaving the duo to concentrate on providing texturally rich and rhythmically propulsive backdrops, which is after all what they're best at.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The music here is in a constant state of flux; sonically incredibly rich and marrying warm Zawinul-esque Fender Rhodes piano with digital glitches, dubby atmospherics, intricate layers of percussion and Friedmans trademark drum manipulations.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The second half of "La Dernier Combat" drags the propulsive funk of Herbie Hancocks Thrust into the 21st century with a ferocious slap bass and percussion dialogue topped off by fat analogue synth riffs, while the opening "Outer Space/Inner Space" is possibly the strongest track, mainly due to Hass's probing tenor explorations which dig deep into Friedmann's intricate rhythmic matrix.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Elsewhere the single "Inner Spacesuit" is a clavinet soaked groovathon, while the closing "Himflug" suggests the MJQ as the inhouse band on board a Cuban space station.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Flanger's strongest suit is their refusal to lazily appropriate notions of jazz cool in the manner of many of the so called 'Nu Jazz outfits'.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Theirs is a brave new world where the tenor saxophone and the Powerbook can sit happily alongside each other in a virtual jam session.
author: Peter Marsh

text: (Inner)Space is the Place.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Taking its title from an 11th century Japanese treatise on gardening, Sakuteiki is trumpeter Henriksen's first solo record, and it's a thing of rare and compelling beauty.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Alone on trumpet, harmonium and percussion (often played simultaneously), Henriksen's charged miniatures have the same economy and intensity of expression that is central to much Japanese art; haiku, ink painting and indeed zen gardening, where what is not said, played or drawn is easily as important as that which is.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Henriksen's breathy, sensuous tone and smeared vocal effects are incredibly shakuhachi-like, while his phrases achieve the same sense of restrained, sometimes desolate melancholy that Japanese traditional music can convey, without descending to mere imitation.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Helge Sten's masterful recording (no effects or overdubs throughout) zooms in on detail; spit crackling and bubbling on the mouthpiece, the gentle hiss of escaping breath, valves clicking.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Its almost the aural equivalent of a photo of a familiar object rendered alien by extreme magnification; often unrecognisable as a trumpet, Henriksen's tones are as rich and complex as anything conjured up by electronic means.
author: Peter Marsh

text: On "viewing infinite space", Henriksens trumpet is allowed to wallow in the luxurious natural reverb of the Emmanuel Vigeland Museum to stunning effect, while the warm, recessed throb of a harmonium underpins the aching high register improvisation of "shrine".
author: Peter Marsh

text: Occasionally he shadows his trumpet notes with harmonium tones, sounding like an unplugged take on Jon Hassell's digital harmonisations.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Comparisons with Hassell are inevitable perhaps, but Henriksen has his own voice (and thankfully, none of Hassell's occasionally tiring intellectual baggage).
author: Peter Marsh

text: Each piece seems intimately bound to its title, and stones should never be placed carelessly sums up both the records inspiration and its execution.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Not a note out of place and played with the utmost care, this is musicmaking as natural and essential as breathing.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Here comes yet another French label who are doing something really interesting in the field of new experimental music.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Ive said it before and Ill say it again - 2002 may just well be the year that France firmly establishes itself on the new music scene.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Bathyscaphe are part of the new breed of post-rock band atmospheric instrumentalists like Godspeed You Black Emperor !, Tortoise and Set Fire To Flames, promoting a musical aesthetic that focuses more on actual performance than cute programming tricks.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Hailing from Paris, the band got their start by doing soundtrack work for film directors such as Lionel Delplanque, Georges Zsiga and Dan Salzmann, and have now released a debut full length which takes this soundtrack concept one step further.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: On the aptly titled Road Movie, they have indeed constructed a soundtrack to a film of the imagination.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Kicking off with an ambient bed of guitar drone and feedback, the band soon veer off into several directions at once, embracing atmospheric soundscapes, industrial noise, classical string pieces and some very captivating guitar melodies.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Tracks like the rhythmically challenging but hypnotic Eyelash take the listener through a complex series of plucked guitar harmonics and sliding bass lines before taking the track into more uptempo waters.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Likewise, the band switch gears on Paluxy River, where they ditch the rock element completely in favour of a gorgeous string quartet that morphs from pristine glacial beauty to tension filled dread.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Each of the seven tracks presented here dives into the unknown; there's a wonderful sense of tension and drama that rarely comes across in most music of this genre.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: If you're familiar with the output of labels like Constellation or Temporary Residence, you'll probably have a good idea of what this sounds like.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: For those that arent, Bathyscaphe make a fine introduction to a label thats putting out some excellent experimental music in a country that is absolutely bursting with some really captivating new bands.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Id suggest booking that Eurostar ticket pretty soon...
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Ward 21 are the new boys in town.
author: Denise Boyd

text: Questions surrounding the issue as to whether they would make the grade with their new style of ragga have been answered with the release of their aptly titled debut album Mentally Disturbed.
author: Denise Boyd

text: Named after the infamous psychiatric ward at the University College Hospital in Kingston, Ward 21 could not have chosen a more appropriate title as their crazy approach to production is injecting ragga with a wild energy that the scene just can't get enough off.
author: Denise Boyd

text: Mentally Disturbed boasts an eclectic mix of sounds and genres that are totally original and cannot be found on any other ragga album.
author: Denise Boyd

text: Smash hit "Pain 21st Century" shows Ward 21 at their best with their trade mark digitised sound effects whilst "The Illness" with it's cleverly penned lyrics and sinister back drop provides another stand out moment.
author: Denise Boyd

text: "Anything-A-Anything", sees dancehall star Elephant Man deliver tight lyrics and is a sure-fire hit.
author: Denise Boyd

text: 21, as they refer to themselves, show their production skills at their finest on "Going Going Gone", with it's quick lyrics and flawless timing.
author: Denise Boyd

text: Collaborations with ZumJay, A.R.P, Earthworm Jim, Big Pimp and Mr Wayne Marshall (providing the dulcet tones) complete the line up.
author: Denise Boyd

text: Influenced by many styles of music from Studio One to old skool hip hop these Kingston boys pay homage to crews such as Wrecks 'n' Effects, especially with the track "Wildin' 'n' Freestyling" which will appeal to rap and ragga fans alike.
author: Denise Boyd

text: As a multi-talented collective their versatility and mad studio skills are relatively untapped, and this album is only a taste of things to come.
author: Denise Boyd

text: You may want to stamp this album with 'Parental Guidance Advisable' but your dancehall collection wouldn't be complete without it.
author: Denise Boyd

text: As this group evolves, expect Big Tings!
author: Denise Boyd

text: In a departure from their previous outings, The Altogether showcases eleven short songs; an arena in which the Hartnoll brothers demonstrate a wealth of production values not yet seen in their repertoire.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: The ambient breakbeat pop of the first single !Funny Break (One Is Enough)!
author: Christian Hopwood

text: is a marked contrast to the psuedo-jungle scrape and drone of "Tension".
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Cameo samples from the likes of Tool, Ian Dury, The Cramps and Crass as well as the inclusion, at the request of the fans, of "Doctor?" serves to illustrate both Orbital's punk rock sensibilities and the sense of humour they so readily bring to their live shows.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: That said, their version of Doctor Who is not on a par with the Bon Jovi/Belinda Carlisle mash up of "Halcyon", which sadly was never committed to vinyl.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: This album is proof positive that Orbital have never been a band to rest on their laurels, like their trademark cranial attire...
author: Christian Hopwood

text: they are always looking forward.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Having been a convert to the wonderful ways of Danish electronica since the release of the mind blowing Boredom Is Deep And Mysterious compilation in 1994, Ive made sure that anything even remotely affiliated with Scandinavia makes its way into my CD player.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: As a result, Future 3 and the releases on Denmarks April Records have become a mainstay of my collection for the simple fact that not only do they know a good melody when they hear one but they arent afraid to make experimental music that sings rather than just scrapes, glitches or rumbles by.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Future 3 (aka Anders Remmer, Jesper Skaaning and Thomas Knak) have been involved within the Danish music scene for quite a while now but it wasn't until the release of their full length We Are The Future 3 in 1995 that they caught the ear of various scene stalwarts like Alex Patterson, Mixmaster Morris and even Bjork (band member Thomas Knak was recently asked by the Icelandic wonder woman to produce some of the tracks on Vespertine).
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Subsequently the band soon gained a small but dedicated following in Copenhagen and around the world.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Their third full length release, Like sees the band developing their own take on ambient techno, pushing the limits of modern electronic music as far as it can go.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: But while others like Portishead or Scorn seem to enjoy emphasising dissonance or darkness, Future 3 keep it light and airy with a wonderful childlike innocence and catchy little melodies that seem to stick in your head for weeks at a time.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Lots of their tracks remind me of nursery rhymes played at half their normal speed.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: But for all the synthetic sounds on their releases, the influence here isnt just techno; there are elements of free jazz, trip-hop, ambient and folk music, all thrown together under an umbrella of abstract electronica.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Even the tracks that start out somewhat lo-fi and gritty like A Sound or 1000 break into lush melodies, opening up a unique dynamic musical space between the speakers.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Is it something in the Danish psyche that encourages this type of beautiful music making?
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Is it something in the cafe culture?
author: Olli Siebelt

text: The colourful buildings?
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Who can say.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: What we do know is that Future 3 and April Records have a real knack for releasing some genuinely gorgeous music.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: For those of you that are familiar with the output of Future 3, you will be in familiar territory and may well agree with me that this is by far the best release they've done yet.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: For those of you who dont know them, you should run out and get this CD as fast as you can.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: While you're at it, get all of their releases.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: No, scratch that - just purchase the entire April records back catalogue (especially the bands side projects: Jet, Opiate and Acustic) and see what youve been missing all this time.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Your CD player and your friends will thank you.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: "A gentleman is one who can play the accordion but chooses not to".
author: Andy Puleston

text: Odd that anyone would choose to begin a review of a DJ mix CD with a quote from Oscar Wilde but then not every mix compilation opens the proceedings with Ramirez' squeezebox-tastic "Hablando".
author: Andy Puleston

text: This big, stomping, party tune sets the tone for two CDs of pumpatronic mayhem.
author: Andy Puleston

text: Discone houses most of the tougher cuts.
author: Andy Puleston

text: The brooding bass line of Medicine's acid hook screecher "Junior Aspirin" drives the mix forward in to the dirty funk of Orlando Careca's "I'm A Sex Machine" and on to the industrial thud and plink of Nitzer Ebb's "Join In The Chant".
author: Andy Puleston

text: The second disc proves to be lighter and more progressive although Darren never whimps out on us and keeps the momentum going with some great choices.
author: Andy Puleston

text: The chunky, disco classic "Come In To My Room" by Sandy Rivera, (perhaps best known since Ben Watt's Lazy Dog re-working) lightens the load after the hammering from Slam's swirling "Lifetimes".
author: Andy Puleston

text: Circulation's "Magenta" and Darren's remix of Laurent Garnier's "Man With The Red Face" provide two of the album's outstanding moments.
author: Andy Puleston

text: The former is reminiscent of PFM's approach to drum and bass whilst the latter demonstrates that Darren'sskill on the remix is still highly sought after.
author: Andy Puleston

text: Darren's mixing is very much 'on the fly' and as he says in the sleeve notes, 'I never practice.
author: Andy Puleston

text: It doesn't go - it's like riding a bike.' Unlike the smooth and often lengthy mixes that characterise the sets of say, Sasha, his style is rougher and more organic.
author: Andy Puleston

text: Yet, he never looses the flow and his selection is varied enough to maintain interest at all times.
author: Andy Puleston

text: Everything Emerson has done, be it writing albums with Underworld or travelling the world winding the ones and twos, smacks of credibility and ingenuity.
author: Andy Puleston

text: With a renewed passion for his first love Darren Emerson is ready to take on the world...
author: Andy Puleston

text: well, Singapore at least.
author: Andy Puleston

text: Long may he continue.
author: Andy Puleston

text: Having one of the most magnetic voices in the music business today, doesn't necessarily guarantee you the necessary magazine covers, double platinum record sales or golden industry awards.
author: Keysha Davis

text: If there were one singer who is testimony to this fact, it would be Faith Evans.
author: Keysha Davis

text: More celebrated for partaking in "Ghetto-ised" real life, Soap Opera's than her vocal chords, Faith's new album attempts to tiptoe further away from this notoriety, which in all fairness, expired at least four years ago.
author: Keysha Davis

text: Faithfully is Faith's most ambitious and confident project to date.
author: Keysha Davis

text: By now, you've all seen the video, to "You Gets No Love", a brash, bassy track featuring a svelte looking Ms Evans vocally knocking out, the silly fool, who dared to "play with her emotions".
author: Keysha Davis

text: This is surprisingly hardcore stuff, from a woman who had previously only sung, subtle, love monologues in her trademark jazzy, ethereal style.
author: Keysha Davis

text: The hip-hop influence continues further with opening track " Alone in This World", which borrows a sample from Mobb Deep's " Give Up The Goods".
author: Keysha Davis

text: This moody track provides the perfect accompaniment to Faith's raspy, vocals, as she echoes the bewilderment of a lover gone astray, leaving her to fend for herself in this world.
author: Keysha Davis

text: "Burnin' Up" is probably the main contender for crossover appeal.
author: Keysha Davis

text: Produced by the Neptunes, the latest hit making collective with the Midas touch, this track has all the hallmarks of their previous chart toppers - continuous guitar strumming, plenty beats per minute and a ridiculously repetitive chorus.
author: Keysha Davis

text: Other club friendlies include "Back To Love" which samples "Last Night A DJ Saved My Life" and "Can't Believe" a duet with Carl Thomas.
author: Keysha Davis

text: Old Faith fans that may feel a little neglected due to her new musical direction, need fear not, as a collection of jazzy/blues tunes are also included on this disc.
author: Keysha Davis

text: The simply titled "I Love You" has a summery retro feel to it, with Faith sounding like a young Michael Jackson.
author: Keysha Davis

text: "Brand New Man" is a gospel tinged, woman's anthem which dramatically climaxes with a plea for every woman who has ever been wronged to put her hands up.
author: Keysha Davis

text: Jazz, Gospel, Blues, Hip-Hop - Evans provides all flavours for a variety of listeners on Faithfully.
author: Keysha Davis

text: If this fails to hit the mainstream charts, it will definitely go down as a street classic.
author: Keysha Davis

text: Let's hope this will bury the shroud of negativity that has followed the singer once and for all, and help to focus on one of the most powerful set of vocals in the music industry today.
author: Keysha Davis

text: Following the musical careers of San Diegos Rob Crow and Zach Smith (real name: Armistead Burwell Smith IV) is almost as difficult as keeping track of all the releases on Pete Namlooks Fax label (trust us - its a lot).
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Just as you think you're on top of things, they go and release some other new side project or solo EP, forcing yet another trip to the local record store.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: The two gained notoriety in bands like Heavy Vegetable and Three Mile Pilot and while contributing to separate projects over the last nine or so years, both have established a signature sound so atypical that it could survive a Merzbow remix.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Excelling in layered vocal harmonies floating above complex acoustically driven soundtracks, this new Pinback release follows this trend closely.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Unlike earlier material, the focus is kept clearly on the harmonies, no matter how many odd time signatures that get thrown in.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Think Devo, The Cars, Modest Mouse, Can, Primus and then think of none of them.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: But Pinback arent just another math/post/kraut rock band playing odd compositions for the sake of being terminally hip or to complement their black turtleneck jumpers.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: These guys simply write great catchy indie songs, and as complex as they may be, they do it with no visible pretence or agenda.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Blue Screen Life has enough tricky time signiatures to keep even the most anally retentive musician guessing what comes next, but at the same time, tracks like Prog, Concrete Seconds or the exquisite single Penelope are so pretty and eloquent that they'll be stuck in your head for weeks.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Blue Screen Life is one of the most accessible and melodic releases these two have come up with so far, and long time fans will see a natural progression in the duos output.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: For those of you who are new to the band, this will serve as a great introduction to some of southern Californias most notable talents, whose back catalogue work is certainly worth tracking down and picking up.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: At this rate, I dont think there will be any bands left in San Diego that havent had some musical contribution from one of these guys.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Lets hope they spread their influences far and wide.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: It can only be a good thing.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Since the release of Chocolate Super Highway Michael Franti has been busy.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Working both musically and in activist situations against the death penalty has provided the mainstay of Spearheads third album, Stay Human.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: An imaginary pirate radio broadcast concerned with the impending execution of black activist Sister Fatima provides a platform for the delivery of this meditation on social justice.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Musically, this is a return to the skilful and organic sounding first album, Home.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: The dirty P funk of "Rock The Nation" and the hugely warming and optimistic "Sometimes" and "Do Ya Love" make Stay Human as much a socio-political work as a hymn to the individuality of the soul.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Franti is a poet, philosopher as well as a producer and this collection is his master work; he is six foot six above 'see' level and like the skin on the drum, the harder they hit him the louder he becomes.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Formed in Berlin in 1991, Rene Lamp and Robert Schalinski were working together on short-film projects and decided to expand their scope to include audio and multi-media projects among their repertoire.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: The next thing you know, Column One was born.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: On this highly detailed and wonderfully crafted CD (their fourth), the band have dragged the look and feel of 1950s American science-fiction films deep into their underground laboratory, flicked a few switches and have mutated them into an absolute monster of a release, bringing to life a world of Kraftwerkian rhythms and Forbidden Planet background ambience all cohesively joined by an interesting narrative structure; the tracks ebb and flow into one another not as separate entities but as an entire parable of technology overpowering humanity.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: On tracks like Re-Start To Move, the low-bitrate hip-hop tracks bounce along with a curious intent, just as a determined robot would as it seeks its next human prey, while on MZ4, the mood is much more melancholy, clearly showing the more human side to the mechanical creatures contained therein.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: The band here have clearly done their homework both in terms of studying classic 80s electro as well as the sounds that brought those tracks to life.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Since its heyday on the late 60s, American minimalism has cast a long shadow over the musical landscape; the works of the so called big four (Reich, Glass, Riley and Young) have made themselves felt in the work of bands as diverse as the Velvet Underground, the Orb and Tortoise, to name but three.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Chicagoans Town and Country are a slightly different proposition; instead of just nicking minimalist technique for their own ends, they're expanding on it.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Their delicate, acoustically driven music combines the influences of composers like Gavin Bryars and Morton Feldman with doses of American primitivist folk forms and chamber jazz, but doesn't sound like the mess that often arises from such fusions.
author: Peter Marsh

text: C'mon is their third album and comes on (sorry) like a lost session for Brian Eno's Obscure label.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Quirky, sometimes beautiful and on occasion fearsomely austere in true Feldman stylee, Town and Country's music has the same air of quiet invention that marked early works by Bryars and Michael Nyman (before they achieved respectability), or lesser known figures like Jan Steele and Christopher Hobbs.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Unsurprisingly, all the band members are involved in other projects (usually improvisational), though here they display little interest in notions of technique or expressive playing.
author: Peter Marsh

text: While some pieces such as the opening Going to Kamakura have a meandering, almost improvisational quality, not a note is wasted.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Garden highlights the bands compositional strengths; airy acoustic guitar chords and hand chime figures underpin long bass clarinet and bowed double bass tones which never quite resolve into comfortable harmonies.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The Bells starts similarly, before shifting down a gear into a bleak spell of repetition of a single, crabbed chord from cornet, bass clarinet and double basses.
author: Peter Marsh

text: After what seems like months, the dissonances resolve into lush, open chords in one of those moments of stomach tickling loveliness that come along once in a while.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The closing Bookmobile is powered by an intricate, shifting network of almost hi-life acoustic guitars, hinting at chord shifts that never quite happen.
author: Peter Marsh

text: It's this mesh of tensions, not-quite-resolutions and left turns into the unexpected that make this album such a rewarding listen.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Sounding like it could have been made at any time in the last 25 years or so (and maybe anytime in the next 25 as well), Cmon is worthy of a place on your CD collection, and probably a place in your heart too.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Kicking around their native Odense (thats Denmark by the way), for the past ten years, Limp arent exactly a proper 'band' but rather a collective of musicians already well established on the electronic music scene.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: In the past, these guys have released projects such as Syntaks (Static Caravan), Manual (Morr) and Aerosol (Active Suspension) and all fit into the ambient/electronica category.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: For those who arent familiar with these projects, this collaborative release serves as an excellent introduction to a Danish collective that are doing some really impressive things with ambient guitar work at the moment.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: The band themselves have described themselves to be inspired by intelligent electronica and Chicago post-rock and thats a pretty good summary of whats going on here.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Floating effortlessly between ambient atmospherics and processed guitar, Limp are a musical outfit who are clearly aware of the difference between what constitutes a song rather than just a composition and have come up with a lovely little CD that is equally reminiscent of Mogwai as it is Godspeed You Black Emperor!, The Orb or even early Autechre.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Orion kicks off with Towards, a beautiful opener that builds into a multi-layered piece of sparse guitar chords floating over a shifting rhythm section of soft breakbeats and reversed cymbals.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: From there on in, the disc simply ebbs and flows with a comforting state of warmth throughout the six tracks here.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Perhaps its the analogue instrumentation here that gives this release such a warm resonant feel.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Pieces like the somber Interstellar and the gorgeous title track really see the band show off its true colours, each of the band members playing off against one another without a click track in sight.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: For some odd reason, Denmark has always been sympathetic to the more delicate composer (even Black Metal hero King Diamond had a taste for the melodic!) and Limp slides right in between the childlike melodies of a label like April and the darker guitar based ambience of releases on Euphonious, another excellent Danish label.

text: This inscrutably titled disk features guitarist Cline's new power trio, with Devin Hoff on contrabass and Scott Amendola on drums and percussion (as well as loops, live effects and processing).
author: Bill Tilland

text: There are no singers, and no vocals.
author: Bill Tilland

text: Other guitarists on the scene might trump Cline with a single defining attribute - funkier, flashier, more lyrical, whatever.
author: Bill Tilland

text: But I can't think of anyone right now who covers more musical ground than Cline, or who covers it half as well.
author: Bill Tilland

text: You can hear everyone from Jim Hall to Sonny Sharrock here, depending upon the tune or the passage.
author: Bill Tilland

text: In fact, Cline showcases so many different moods and styles that the initial effect can be a little disorienting.
author: Bill Tilland

text: You have him pegged as one thing, and then he comes at you from a new direction.
author: Bill Tilland

text: However, Cline is not just a musical chameleon.
author: Bill Tilland

text: He always surrounds himself with strong players, and gives them ample opportunity to display their skills.
author: Bill Tilland

text: This trio is fully interactive (no mere time-keepers here), and the two other members maintain a running dialogue with Cline, echoing, reinforcing and commenting on his lines.
author: Bill Tilland

text: Hoff, in particular, often figures prominently on bowed bass.
author: Bill Tilland

text: The solid group dynamic gives the music a continuity and cohesion beneath all the surface variation.
author: Bill Tilland

text: On Instrumentals, Cline himself often favours a thick, somewhat overdriven sound, tending toward dirty or even positively filthy (as on "Lowered Boom," a truly hardcore electric blues).
author: Bill Tilland

text: The opening track, "A Mug like Mine," teases a simple melody line almost to the point of obsession, in much the same way that John Coltrane played with all the possibilities of a simple riff or phrase in his later work.
author: Bill Tilland

text: (On Cline's remake of Coltrane's Interstellar Space with drummer Gregg Bendian, he proved himself to be a superb Coltrane interpreter.) Cline also understands the visceral impact of a good strum, and has added some thrash elements to his musical vocabulary.
author: Bill Tilland

text: (The relentless "Cause for Concern" sounds like a synthesis of Sonic Youth and the Mahavishnu Orchestra).
author: Bill Tilland

text: That having been said, Cline is hardly predictable, and he can certainly play pretty for the people when he has a mind to.
author: Bill Tilland

text: "Lucia," which follows the greasy "Lowered Boom," is so spare and understated as to be well nigh invisible at first, and has a wistful minimalism very reminiscent of Jim Hall.
author: Bill Tilland

text: The CD's closing number, "Slipped Away," is reverbed and ruminative, bringing to mind the work of Ry Cooder and Bill Frisell.
author: Bill Tilland

text: And while "Ghost of the Piñata," is uptempo, Cline's twelve-string chimes and rings with crystalline clarity.
author: Bill Tilland

text: Every track on this CD is a winner, and with a recording as fine as this one, Cline is identifying himself as a major force in the world of electric guitar.
author: Bill Tilland

text: They now present us with a collection of tracks from the masters of the genre - Manchester's A Certain Ratio.
author: Matt Harvey

text: Formed in 1977 the band were, along with Joy Division, the first signings to Tony Wilson's Factory Records.
author: Matt Harvey

text: (All these tracks are culled from their time with the label) On early tracks like 'Flight' you can hear the similarities.
author: Matt Harvey

text: This didn't last long.
author: Matt Harvey

text: While Joy division were of a more Teutonic bent, A Certain Ratio were irresistibly drawn to the Samba and funk of the Americas.
author: Matt Harvey

text: Where else could a punk band with a trumpeter go?
author: Matt Harvey

text: Their first (and probably biggest) hit was a hilarious cover of Banbarra's anti-marriage classic "Shack up".
author: Matt Harvey

text: It became something of a cult track in New York dance clubs and even made it into the lower reaches of the US billboard charts.

text: Alog's 1999 debut release Red Swing Shift is still one of the most rewarding albums of the last few years, and Duck-Rabbit turns out to be a more than worthy successor.
author: Dan Hill

text: It emerged from tours of Red Swing Shift; Dag-Are Haugan and Espen Sommer Eide recorded their after-show improvisations, providing the raw material for this new collection.
author: Dan Hill

text: The title refers to the Gestalt psychology figure of a duck, or a rabbit, depending on how you view it.
author: Dan Hill

text: And this studious pair of Scandinavian David Lynches constantly toy with your perception alright; sounds remain still only for seconds, ducks become rabbits become ducks becoming ...
author: Dan Hill

text: improvised live playing becoming hissing tape loops becoming mannered minimalism becoming Northern European electronica ...
author: Dan Hill

text: As their name suggests, it's both digitAL and analOGue, with Haugan's wheezing analogue equipment conjuring sounds akin to their labelmates' reworkings of Norwegian avant-garde legend Arne Nordheim; other times Eide's laptop munches through found-sound samples, generating flat washes of muted colour.
author: Dan Hill

text: The result is hugely seductive, demanding your attention in gritty arhythmic fits and starts.
author: Dan Hill

text: They neatly avoid any cliched pigeonholes of 'icy Scandinavian electronica' - it's often more in concert with Anti-Pop Consortium's twisted scabrous electro than Biosphere's dazzling northern lights, say.
author: Dan Hill

text: There are less of the sumptuous loops which characterised Red Swing Shift; or rather, they're concealed more.
author: Dan Hill

text: When they do emerge, as on "Fire's For Burning", it's quite lovely, particularly counterposed with what sounds like the irregular hammering of typewriter keys, perhaps lifted from Godard's fingers on Histoire Du Cinema.
author: Dan Hill

text: Alog even breathe new life into the overused Apple Mac voice synthesizer.
author: Dan Hill

text: Here it is really made to sing, as on the heartrending "Violence and Magical Danger".
author: Dan Hill

text: It's never sounded fitter, happier.
author: Dan Hill

text: Haugan and Eide's instrumental skill is all context and arrangement rather than obvious virtuosity, yet both can play.
author: Dan Hill

text: The marvellously-named "As Complicated And As Beautiful As Always" features stunning distortion and feedback, and the album ends with the charming John Fahey-like faux-naive guitar of "Drunk DJ's", departing with quiet Scandinavian grace.
author: Dan Hill

text: Kim Hiorthøy's sublime graphics adorn the cover, another Rune Grammofon gem.
author: Dan Hill

text: This is a label on top of its game, and this is a genuinely beautiful album, confirming Alog as one of modern music's most interesting groups.
author: Dan Hill

text: Developing the sound established on the debut Caretaker release three years ago, A Stairway To Stars is a collection of old ballroom and dance 78rpm records released anywhere between 1920 and 1940 which have been manipulated, slowed down and re-sampled into beautifully creepy ambient pieces which while instantly recognisable, are completely original in both their construction and feel.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: On this superb second release, The Caretaker has taken what may seem to be a pretty rudimentary piece of audio manipulation and has turned it into a wonderfully imaginative concept that is both deliciously spooky and hauntingly beautiful.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Loads of people (eg: Skinny Puppy, Will, Cold Meat Industry, etc..) have tried their hand at stuff like this before, but this goes much further than your typical gothic or darkwave record.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: I cant quite put my finger on exactly what it is, but something really interesting happens when these sources are manipulated like this.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Nuances and timbres come out which tickle the ear drums in a very unique way, giving one not a sense of relief, but one of distinct unease or even dread, especially when listening on headphones.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Tracks like We Cannot Escape The Past and Emptiness really embrace this otherworldly feeling, bringing to life a world of black tie and top hat, mediums and crystal balls.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: It often seems that several ghosts have suddenly entered the room to partake in the listening experience with you.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Yet, while some of it is certainly creepy, there is some astonishing beauty here as well.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Tracks like Robins and Roses and the title track Stairway To The Stars are reversed, re-sampled, and pitch shifted into something so lovely that it would make even Dani from Cradle of Filth crack a smile.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Play it with the lights down low and let the spirits enjoy it with you.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Stairway To The Stars is a truly wonderful little gem that will have you dancing in the haunted ballroom, over and over again.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Now the dust has settled on that controversial remark maybe it's time to once again judge the Chicks on their music rather than their opinions.
author: Chris Jones

text: The brouhaha that followed Natalie'scomment about Dubya probably confirmed many people's deepest fears about the kind of people who listen to homegrown American music.
author: Chris Jones

text: But country music has always been a contradictory beast; lending itself to hijacking by more reactionary elements due to its espousal of 'good old fashioned values', while at its best using traditional skills (of which the Chicks have plenty) to paint a beautifully honest portrait of working class life.
author: Chris Jones

text: Top Of The World is undoubtedly an exercise in capitalising on the Dixie Chicks' stadium-filling status, but hopefully it will draw a line under all this unpleasantness.
author: Chris Jones

text: Ironically last year's Home was the kind of fantastic work that swept away all the above wrongheaded preconceptions and made their crossover appeal even stronger.
author: Chris Jones

text: At the same time it mixed its wry, tearstained tales of shotgun weddings, small town love and ambitions with a dexterity, slickness and humour that ensured they were now a world class act.
author: Chris Jones

text: This record of the following tour, with its proud boast of 'no overdubs' merely confirms what US audiences have known for a while: This trio can really play.
author: Chris Jones

text: Two discs cover all the best points in their small (but perfectly formed) back catalogue.
author: Chris Jones

text: A large smattering of Home is peppered with choice cuts from Fly and Wide Open Spaces.
author: Chris Jones

text: If there's a criticism to be levelled it's that, with a large supporting cast and high production values (five stylists and a pilates yoga instructor?), the Chicks can be too slick.
author: Chris Jones

text: Heartstring-pullers like ''Travellin' Soldier'' or Stevie Nick's ''Landslide'' are dispatched amite hurriedly, with Natalie's voice being a little too strident and the huge venues seeming to dull the impact of Emily and Martie's finer picking.
author: Chris Jones

text: Mind you, the uptempo numbers like ''White Trash Wedding'', ''Goodbye Earl'' or''Hello Mr Heartache'' just brim over with riotous good humour; and the closer ''Sin Wagon'' makes you realise that these girls have enough self-belief and chutzpah to ride out any storm.
author: Chris Jones

text: Make no mistake, they're here to stay...
author: Chris Jones

text: Well, talk about worth the wait.
author: Sue Keogh

text: The Chicks have been involved in a long dispute over royalties with their record label, Sony, which kept them off the stage and out of the recording studio for a year.
author: Sue Keogh

text: They came to an agreement in June, promising them a bigger slice of the pie, which will be a very big slice indeed if Home replicates the success of the last two albums, Fly (1999) and Wide Open Spaces (1998), which have combined sales of 19 million.
author: Sue Keogh

text: The catchy opening track "Long Time Gone" shows them wasting no time in taking a neatly worded sideswipe at today's country music industry, "They sound tired but they don't sound Haggard/ they got money but they don't have Cash/ they have junior but they don't have Hank/ I think, I think, I think the rest is long time gone".
author: Sue Keogh

text: It's easy to sit back and criticise, but the Dixie Chicks take the harder route and lead the "real country" fight back by example, making powerful bluegrass-inspired country music of a standard that everyone else should aspire to.
author: Sue Keogh

text: The songs on Home have come from some very high calibre songwriters.
author: Sue Keogh

text: Treats include the old Fleetwood Mac number and the Chicks' next single, "Landslide", Patty Griffin's "Truth No.
author: Sue Keogh

text: 2", which is great for its rousing bassline and deft key changes, and "Godspeed", the sweet lullaby by Radney Foster with Emmylou Harris contributing additional vocals.
author: Sue Keogh

text: Then there's "Travelin' Soldier", written by Emily Robison's brother-in-law Bruce Robison, which has been stuck in my head since I saw the Chicks perform it at last year's CMA Awards show.
author: Sue Keogh

text: The sad tale of a girl who falls in love with a boy who is never to return from Vietnam, complete with soaring harmonies and drowsy accordion makes for a haunting combination.
author: Sue Keogh

text: High-speed fun is to be found in "White Trash Wedding", one of the songs written by the trio.
author: Sue Keogh

text: "You can't afford no ring/ I shouldn't be wearing white and you can't afford no ring!" hollers Natalie Maines, accompanied by typically blistering performances from band members Emily Robison (banjo) and Martie Maguire (fiddle) and session musicians Bryan Sutton (guitar) and Adam Steffey (mandolin).
author: Sue Keogh

text: Of equal face-slapping velocity is Lil' Jack Slade, written for Natalie's son and featuring the increasingly-ubiquitous mandolin virtuoso Chris Thile.
author: Sue Keogh

text: Album of the year.
author: Sue Keogh

text: A big thank you to BBC Country for this review.
author: Sue Keogh

text: Often seen as forming just another piece in the jigsaw of Robert Wyatt's inspirational post-Soft Machine career, Matching Mole were, in fact, a truly viable quartet of disparate individuals whose musical chops could, when the wind was in the right direction, be most agreeable indeed.
author: Chris Jones

text: Initially formed as a touring vehice for Wyatt's disgruntled solo exit from the Softs, this release ably demonstrates how the band, with extensive touring, had settled into a formidable unit.
author: Chris Jones

text: Smoke Signals captures the band on one of their 1972 European jaunts, moving with ease between free form extemporising and the lazy swirls of Canterbury jazz-noodling.
author: Chris Jones

text: While their first album was initially conceived as a solo piece for Wyatt, by the middle of 1972 the second, Matching Mole's Little Red Record, saw the song writing being shared more democratically.
author: Chris Jones

text: Unfortunately Robert Fripp's authoritarian presence as producer had "reduced (guitarist) Phil Miller to a quivering wreck so that he could barely move his fingers" according to bassist Bill MacCormick, and the album suffered accordingly.
author: Chris Jones

text: This live release shows, at last, what really could have been.
author: Chris Jones

text: "Nan True's Hole" by Miller is a brutal stomp, while keyboardist Dave McCrae's title track is as lovely a homage to the joys of electric piano as has ever been caught on tape.
author: Chris Jones

text: Those expecting the sweet tones of Wyatt's songcraft will be disappointed - only the first album's "Instant Pussy", with its free form scat vocals, features on this set - but his skilful drumming belies former band mate Mike Ratledge's acidic comment that: "he's never enjoyed or accepted working in complex time signatures".
author: Chris Jones

text: Pah and phooey, indeed.
author: Chris Jones

text: The only criticisms are that "March Ides I" owes too much to Miller's idol Fripp and that, at times, the band lapse into the kind of improvisation which wilfully defies tunesmithery as if to merely accentuate their hairy jazz credentials.
author: Chris Jones

text: However, it remains a shame that, soon afterwards, Wyatt found the responsibility of being the band's mouthpiece too much to balance with his love of good times and split what could have been, on this evidence, a truly great part of Rock's avant garde elite.
author: Chris Jones

text: As to the band's name: try saying 'Soft Machine' in French...
author: Chris Jones

text: Despite his long tenure with John Steven's Spontaneous Music Ensemble, one of free improvisation's most important groups, guitarist Roger Smith remains a shadowy figure, under-recorded and rarely seen live.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Working as a guitar tutor by day and sleeping in the evening, Smith improvises by night at home in North London's Wood Green, where these twelve improvisations were recorded in his kitchen (with occasional contributions from the central heating system).
author: Peter Marsh

text: Smith's choice of nylon strung classical guitar marks him out from his steel string totin' contemporaries John Russell and Derek Bailey.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Though there are abstract episodes of string abuse (at one point during "Diminuendo & Crescendo in Green" he sounds as though he might be unwrapping a very sticky toffee that's dropped inside his guitar), for the most part Smith's tone is lustrous, lyrical yet unsentimental as he conjures up dense, knotty arpeggios, resonant harmonics and plangent chords.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Listening to Green Wood is almost like eavesdropping; the intimate documentary recording style admits all the gestural, human noises (breath, guitar rubbing gently against shirt) that classical studio recordings conspire to remove.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Similarly, the longer improvisations are revealing; Smith hovers over an idea, works on it, listens, moves on.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Sometimes he seems to reach an impasse, till he lays back or abruptly switches direction.
author: Peter Marsh

text: He's always present in the moment and unlike Bailey or Russell, his longer pieces seem imbued with a strong sense of narrative.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The shorter, more abstract pieces (Local Twang, Arse Myth, Strange Interlude) are rigorous explorations of extended technique.
author: Peter Marsh

text: In contrast, the gorgeous "Waltz with Heating" is a performance of simple, restrained beauty built around bell like harmonicsand rippling chords.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Derek Bailey once said that maybe the only true free improvisation is solo improvisation.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Green Wood is not necessarily proof of that, but Roger Smith's lucid, honest music couldn't have been arrived at any other way.
author: Peter Marsh

text: "Allo, allo..." It's a crossed line, the other party won't get off the phone and it takes the intervention of the operator to get through to your lover.
author: John Armstrong

text: Sorry, your ex-lover.
author: John Armstrong

text: This is France in the late 50's.
author: John Armstrong

text: We're eavesdropping as a stylish, sophisticated woman makes a final phone call to the man who kept her as a mistress , but who's now moving on, leaving her alone, distraught, and suicidal.
author: John Armstrong

text: It's agonising: there are interruptions, painful pauses, all the emotional picked up an extension somewhere and were riveted by what we heard), we hear dignity turn to despair and desperation as the woman reveals that she's already tried to kill herself.
author: John Armstrong

text: "If you did not love me and were not so awkward, this telephone could easily become a terrible weapon.
author: John Armstrong

text: A weapon that would leave no marks, nor make a noise..." Poulenc's La Voix humaine is a telephonic opera, a monologue with more emotional power than many much larger-scale theatre pieces.
author: John Armstrong

text: It demands everything from a performer, and Felicity Lott is one of the very few non-French sopranos who can pull this off on record - her French is flawless.
author: John Armstrong

text: The orchestra and conductor are the other side of the conversation, and Armin Jordan makes it sound as if he knows exactly what's being said at the other end of the line.
author: John Armstrong

text: Felicity Lott told me recently just how draining La Voix humaine is in performance; a marathon to remember for a start, and it leaves her in tears every time.
author: John Armstrong
