text: Another entrant in the beautifully designed (natch) :rarum series from ECM, Bill Frisell's self-selection is a largely successful retrospective over the varied career of this utterly unique jazz guitarist.
author: Dan Hill

text: Oft-named 'The Clark Kent of the Guitar', in recent times he's been the subject of a few barbs that he's lost the fire in his playing; that he's settled into a comfortable mid-Western Americana.
author: Dan Hill

text: If he has become more like 'The Garrison Keillor of the Guitar', I'm not even sure why this would be considered demeaning (as if we need another Ted Nugent or something).
author: Dan Hill

text: Also, as Frisell mentions in his liner notes here, "some people say (Americana) has come into my playing in recent years.
author: Dan Hill

text: I think it's been there all along." There are recent signs that his work is exploring pastures new again - but for a reminder of what some fans are yearning for, his ECM years provide perfect example of what a fine and varied musician Frisell is.
author: Dan Hill

text: For instance there's certainly evidence of his noisier, expressionistic side, familiar from work on other labels, with Naked City or his trio with Kermit Driscoll and Joey Baron (pictured here with hair!).
author: Dan Hill

text: Exhibit A: "Singsong"'s incredible, sustained call-and-response with Jan Garbarek from the latter's "Wayfarer", a wonderful display of on-the-edge feedback-shaping which would've caused Hendrix to raise an eyebrow.
author: Dan Hill

text: Frisell's delicate supportive phrasing is everywhere, such as colouring for Lee Konitz and Dave Holland (from Kenny Wheeler's delicious "Angel Song") or sculpting an ingenius harmonic understanding with Paul Bley.
author: Dan Hill

text: "Lonesome", from "Lookout For Hope", provides evidence of those Americana roots, and "In Line" and "Introduction" (for Paul Motian) are wondrous solo performances.
author: Dan Hill

text: His many sides are fully represented - though for this writer, some of his finest moments for ECM occur on Eberhard Weber's "Later That Evening" and for Marc Johnson's Bass Desires group, neither represented here.
author: Dan Hill

text: There's little here that the committed Frisellophile won't already have, but experiencing his selection as a coherent collection is a salutary reminder of the value of his playing, and the value of the ECM groups he worked with.
author: Dan Hill

text: Key like-minded performers on these recordings include Garbarek, Paul Motian (with whom he started at ECM and "one of the most important and inspiring relationships in my life" according to Frisell), Joe Lovano, Bley, Wheeler, and not least Driscoll, Baron and Hank Roberts, forming the Bill Frisell Band.
author: Dan Hill

text: Last word, idiosyncratically, goes to the Gavin Bryars piece "Sub Rosa (Dedicated to Bill Frisell)", a 'contemporary classical' piece which Frisell neither appears on nor wrote (though Bryars based his composition on a track from Frisell's "In Line").
author: Dan Hill

text: It's a wonderful choice though, as it suggests both Frisell's signature melodic gift (though refracted through Bryars' prism) and the stately grace of this most humbly inspiring of guitarists.
author: Dan Hill

text: Frisell's an immediately recognisable musician on that most overplayed of instruments, and if anything ":rarum V" reminds us all the benefit of underplaying and restraint - for when Bill Frisell plugs in, he achieves way more contrast, impact, and expression than those who turn their amps up to 11.
author: Dan Hill

text: If you want to study 'Bill Frisell 101' or even 'Introduction to the Modern Jazz Guitar' this term, this collection is perfect.
author: Dan Hill

text: The Thin White One's reissue program progresses onward with these two '70s live artefacts.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: Often dismissed by Bowie critics, they remain his only contemporaneous official live solo albums to date.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: With these releases, the pair are, at last, done full justice; original set orders are restored, the sound is given pin-drop clarity and the picture-stuffed packaging is a joy.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: Recorded over four nights in Philadelphia on 1974's US Diamond Dogs tour, David Live has come in for criticism from Bowie himself, who later famously called the record 'David Bowie is Alive and Well and Living Only in Theory', while adding that the cover shot made him look like he'd 'just stepped out of the grave'.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: Given that sort of support, it's little wonder it's had such bad press.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: Divorcing the music from the spectacle of the shows was hard for critics all those years ago, but 31 years on we are left with a perfect snapshot of the moment where Bowie was absorbing inner city Americana.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: "Sweet Thing" is full of emotional punch, "Knock On Wood" is tremendous fun, as are the louche "Jean Genie" and the nads-out Latino-rock of "Rebel Rebel".
author: Daryl Easlea

text: The addition of the previously unreleased "Space Oddity" - with Bowie singing into a telephone on a cherry picker - highlights the mania of the whole era; the cheer when he appears above the crowd still has the ability to send a shiver.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: From a mere four years later, Stage is also a revelation, and the strange alienation of the old vinyl edition has vanished.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: Touring the big venues again after releasing Low and Heroes, all eyes were on how this new ambient work would be incorporated into his set.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: The original Stage isolated that material, but with the songs now back in their rightful place, there's an easy flow between the songs and the instrumentals.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: Although the original album always sounded cold, here producer Tony Visconti adds considerable warmth; it swaggers away with verve and clarity.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: Hearing Bowie perform the Ziggy Stardust material straight still offers the wow factor that it must have done in 1978.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: The tracks from Low and Heroes are attacked with elan and "Station To Station" still totters along with wobbly majesty.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: "Alabama Song", "Stay" and "Be My Wife" are also restored to their rightful places.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: And, oh, the band...The great overlooked rhythm section of Dennis Davis and George Murray offer a platform for Carlos Alomar's sturdy rhythm guitar and Adrian Belew's stunt guitar work.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: Visconti has done a great job polishing up the silverware with David Live and Stage, and Bowie's voice is truly stunning throughout.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: If you're a newcomer, I wouldn't suggest that these reissues are at the top of your Thin White priority list.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: As a complement to the studio albums, however, they are absolutely invaluable.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: Despite its status as a classic record, Dusty in Memphis had less than auspicious beginnings.
author: Peter Marsh

text: By 1968 La Springfield had scored a string of chart successes with what she called 'big ballady things' and her decision to make an album in Memphis, home of hard edged R 'n' B grooves, was viewed with puzzlement by many.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Teaming up with the crack production/arrangement team of Jerry Wexler, Tom Dowd and Arif Mardin (responsible for Aretha Franklin's Atlantic classics) also proved a bit much initially for Springfield, whose confidence in her vocal abilities was never very high.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Worried that the session musicians would think she was a sham and unnerved by singing in the same vocal booth as used by Wilson Pickett, Dusty's relationship with her producers became strained, with Wexler claiming he never got a note out of her during the initial sessions in Memphis.
author: Peter Marsh

text: You'd never know this from the recorded evidence though.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Springfield unsurprisingly resists any temptation to do an Aretha, instead relying on understatement, timing and delivery rather than vocal firepower.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The songs (all by Brill building denizens) are all top notch, and Springfield's interpretation of them is peerless, almost to the point that it's tempting to slap a preservation order on them to stop any attempts at future covers from the likes of Sharleen Spiteri.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Likewise Mardin's sensitive blend of Bacharach poise and Memphis funk provides the perfect frame for Dusty's blue eyed soul.
author: Peter Marsh

text: 'Son of A Preacher Man' and 'Breakfast in Bed' hum with a potent mix of vulnerability and knowing desire; though both songs are pretty much ingrained in the psyche of anyone of a certain age, they still retain a hefty emotional charge.
author: Peter Marsh

text: On the other hand, Randy Newman's 'I Don't Want to Hear It Anymore' and 'I Can't Make It Alone' must rank amongst the finest ballad performances you're likely to hear, and Springfield even makes the cod psychedelic inanities of Michel Legrand's 'The Windmills of Your Mind" seem almost meaningful.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The cover boasts a sticker proclaiming that this record made it into Rolling Stone's Coolest records of All Time Top 10.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Don't let that put you off; if you have ears, you need this album...
author: Peter Marsh

text: Lurking in a haze somewhere between hip-hop and experimental funk, Boom Bip (aka Bryan Hollon) has been making a very particular kind of noise for a couple of years now.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Having released a few excellent tracks on the notable Mush label, he's now taken a giant step forward and has signed on to Warp Recordsimprint Lex for an album that is as experimental and cutting edge as anything in Warp's back catalogue.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Streets ahead of his previous work, Seed To Sun sees Hollon dipping in and out of a prominent West coast/California psychedelic acid vibe that seems to permeate most of the tracks here.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: From the Beach Boys on muscle relaxants opener "Heads Must Roll", to "Third Sun" which sounds as if a Herbaliser record took heaps of acid and stayed out in the sun too long, there's a real "back to basics" approach to the production on this release.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Instead of following the crowd, Hollon spends a lot of time bathing in the analogue sounds of the 70s rather than the digitally sampled ones of today.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Yes, laid back vibes abound, but there is much to sit up and take notice of.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Check out the superb "Mannequin Hand Trapdoor I Reminder" featuring Dose One, which rivals some of the best stuff coming out on labels like Mush, Anticon and Sound-Ink.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: "The Use Of Unacceptable Colours In Nature" is also a winner - taking the Boom Bip sound into what amounts to instrumental post-rock territory.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: When was the last time you heard a hip-hop record pull that off?
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Hollon is one of those rare composers who can leap genres and styles in a single bound but never lose the artistic integrity of the overall project.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Each one of the 13 tracks included here is as individual as it gets and all are excellent.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Full marks to Boom Bip for an astonishingly complex and sublime release and for Lex for having the courage and taste not only to put it out, but to push the boundaries of hip-hop culture far beyond people's expectations.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: There are onlya select few out there doing this kind of thing right now and with releases like this, we may finally be looking at the next real evolution in hip-hop.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Watch this space.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Make that "Boom Bip".
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Liberally stickered in your local emporium as a 'Best Of', this pumping, testosterone-filled beast of a compilation is, dare I say it, a bit of a sheep in wolf's clothing.
author: Chris Jones

text: Aerosmith were formed in 1970 (gasp) and have released over twenty albums, but what we have here is an anthology of the years spent with Geffen.
author: Chris Jones

text: In other words it's a minute 8 year slice of a band's 31 year career.
author: Chris Jones

text: Admittedly, all of the boy's trademark devices for alienating your neighbours are here - the bluesy sub-Zeppelinesque rifferama of Joe Perry, the yelping 'who let the cat out of the bag?' vocal stylings of Mr Stephen Tyler and, of course, the (ahem) politically correct lyrics.
author: Chris Jones

text: Yet it seems a shame to think that young whippersnappers who wish to annoy Granny this Christmas will be doing so without the full artillery that the Toxic Twins have amassed over the last third of a century.
author: Chris Jones

text: It is well-documented that earning the above nickname was very nearly the ruin of the band, and were it not for the career resuscitating move to Geffen and the hiring of some top drawer producers we wouldn't today be still grinning at their bulgy-trousered antics.
author: Chris Jones

text: That renaissance is all here on view, starting with Done With Mirrors (how apposite) and Permanent Vacation featuring the shouty "Dude Looks Like A Lady".
author: Chris Jones

text: Naturally close attention is paid to the tip-top follow-up album Pump (7 tracks included) which sold squillions and made sure they'd never go away again.
author: Chris Jones

text: From then on, if you don't count the fabulous pairing with Run-D.M.C on the revamped "Walk This Way", the band set the controls to 'stadium-filling autopilot' and proceeded to deliver&well, more of the same.
author: Chris Jones

text: So, it's a real shame that the band's first classic period gems such as the original "Walk This Way", "Back In The Saddle" or even "Draw The Line" are missing, leaving old rockers bereft and young 'uns without a true historical overview.
author: Chris Jones

text: Even worse, the boys left for Columbia before getting to that treacly power-ballad stuff like "I Don't Want To Miss A Thing" - so your girlfriend won't like it either.
author: Chris Jones

text: All in all, nowhere near a best of with a truly puerile cover shot and yet, when young Tyler hits that long screaming note at the start of "Young Lust", well you just can't help grinning one more time...
author: Chris Jones

text: Most of this double CD is really entertaining.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: It's a chronological collection of John Peel sessions starting with the very first Fall session in 1978.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: There are lots and lots of good jokes.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Mark Smith really enjoys himself on the jolly country and western of ''Container Drivers'' or the rollicking fable ''New Face In Hell''.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: ''Hip Priest'' is hilarious, with Mark singing ''he is not...appreciated'' in a ridiculous falsetto.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: He's taking the mickey: out of all singers and out of himself.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: He sings ''Lie Dream Of A Casino Soul'' in the clipped, nervy tones of Noel Coward.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: It reminds you how clever, how witty, how well thought out the song is.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Smith is not a grumpy, incomprehensible ranter.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: You can hear every word, every brilliant detail.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: The music varies.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: The early line up is driven by the powerhouse drumming of Karl Burns and the unique scratchy guitar of Martin Bramah.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Later it can be a bit rough and ready.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: It's held together by Smith's riveting performances; the way he attacks the likes of ''New Puritan'' or ''Deerpark''.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Then suddenly the CD leaps forward nearly twenty years: two sessions recorded in 1995/6.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Smith slurs and rambles and you can't work out what he is saying.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: No amount of aggressive shouting from Brix Smith can disguise the fact that he seems to have lost his ability to focus or edit.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: There are pointless cover versions and unfinished gibberish.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: The only decent track is a not bad cover of Captain Beefheart's ''Beatles Bones 'n' Smoking Stones''.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: It seems perverse to include these later sessions when continuing in chronological order would complete a picture of the Fall at their peak.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: But Smith can be contrary and perverse.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: And is he any more perverse than obsessed Fall fans (like me) who will buy this CD?
author: Nick Reynolds

text: I have a love-hate relationship with The Fall.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Between 1978 and1985 they were the best band in Britain.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: They were unique.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Now, most of the time, they're not very good.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Happy memories leave a bitter taste.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: 'Iain Bostridge sings Benjamin Britten'.
author: John Armstrong

text: That's enough to sell quite a few copies of this set without any further comment, and for some people I'm sure, without having heard a note of the music.
author: John Armstrong

text: But we cannot be so easily swayed, oh no: a little rigour is what we need when faced with this kind of temptation.
author: John Armstrong

text: So, Bostridge is the people's choice for those tenor parts that demand a light-voiced, intelligent, intellectually well-prepared singer.
author: John Armstrong

text: Lieder, English songs, Bach Evangelists, that kind of thing...Britten operas, in those high-lying, usually emotionally tortured vehicles written for the unique instrument of Peter Pears.
author: John Armstrong

text: Thanks to tenors like Robert Tear, Philip Langridge and Anthony Rolfe Johnson (and Jon Vickers in Peter Grimes), there's less need automatically to compare any newcomer in a Britten role to the original; to Pears-o-phobes (and there are many) the roles have been successfully rehabilitated.
author: John Armstrong

text: But to Pears-o-philes (ditto), he's still the man: despite the strange timbre, the precious pronunciation, his was the right voice, and the emotional power of some of his portrayals is unequalled.
author: John Armstrong

text: The sheer malevolence of Pears's Peter Quint still springs undimmed from that 1955 mono recording - but Bostridge is more beguiling, more seductive.
author: John Armstrong

text: The beauty of his calls to Miles from the tower in the First Act convince you that he could cast a spell over the boy.
author: John Armstrong

text: In the final struggle with the Governess for possession of Miles, we feel Peter Quint's own fear, his vulnerability, and in his fading farewell the regret for his loss.
author: John Armstrong

text: But it's the Governess that makes or breaks this Britten opera, and Joan Rodgers is outstanding, vacillating between her duty of care, her fear of the unknown, and her urge to save the children from the spirits that pursue them.
author: John Armstrong

text: Vocally Rodgers is dependably secure, often very beautiful, and always intelligent.
author: John Armstrong

text: You don't miss a syllable, and she delivers a life-sized Governess without ever veering into hysteria.
author: John Armstrong

text: What about the children?
author: John Armstrong

text: As Miles, the young David Hemmings in the original recording is remarkable, reconciling childish innocence with wicked knowledge.
author: John Armstrong

text: For this production Julian Leang was excellent onstage but its harder for him to bring off on record, without his acting skills on show.
author: John Armstrong

text: Even so, it's a moving portrayal that echoes Bostridge's Quint: less pure evil, more amoral compulsion and confusion...as Flora, Caroline Wise is so much better than the adult sopranos sometimes used in the role on record: you can't fake this childlike innocence, and the contrast when Flora turns on her Governess in the second act is really effective.
author: John Armstrong

text: Jane Henschel's Mrs Grose and Vivian Tierney's Miss Jessel are beyond reproach, and last, never least, Daniel Harding, the Mahler Chamber Orchestra, and the recording.
author: John Armstrong

text: Top marks to the lot: well-paced, atmospheric, and detailed: you'll hear new wonders in this score without ever feeling that you've been pulled inappropriately into the pit - the action on stage remains fully in focus, and the various voices off are very well handled.
author: John Armstrong

text: To tell the truth there isn't a dud recording of The Turn of the Screw, they all have claims for your attention.
author: John Armstrong

text: But this newcomer is in many ways the state-of-the-art, 21st century Britten...and I know that many people who went to the Royal Opera House performances that followed this recording are going to want it.
author: John Armstrong

text: This cast worked very well on stage together, and it shows on cd.
author: John Armstrong

text: A new album by Mac Rebennack and what's he gonna do this time?
author: Chris Jones

text: After years of trying popular standards, tributes to Duke Ellington and even the Tom Jones-styled duets nightmare Anutha Zone (which featured a whole cast of youngsters not fit to share the same studio space), The Night Tripper has finally decided to give us a slice of what he was famous for in the first place!
author: Chris Jones

text: Proper funky New Orleans R'n'B, dished up in a swampy setting that would make a zombie dance.
author: Chris Jones

text: Mos' scocious it is too.
author: Chris Jones

text: Backed by his band The Lower 9-11, this album finds Mac in fine voice, whether declaiming the blues on "Imitation Of Love" or serving up the spicy salsa of "Litenin'".
author: Chris Jones

text: The food analogies are apt in this case, with Mac, himself comparing the set to an "etoufee" - a dish which reflects the multi-cultural roots of his home town.
author: Chris Jones

text: God knows, Dr John has played with most of these styles over the years, from Jazz to Boogie, not to mention his guest appearances with luminaries such as Frank Zappa, Van Morrison and even Art Blakey.
author: Chris Jones

text: Overall the feeling is most definitely funky, however.
author: Chris Jones

text: Solidly danceable rhythms pin down work-outs such as "You Swore" and "One 2am Too Many", while he still has time to deliver some of the old Ju ju on "Bruha Bembe".
author: Chris Jones

text: Just feel those hairs on the back of your neck stand to attention!
author: Chris Jones

text: This really is one to compare with his classics like Gris Gris and Desitively Bonaroo.
author: Chris Jones

text: Touring in the UK soon, you'd be crazy to miss the creole confection cooked up by one of the few authentic voices of the Deep South left in the business.
author: Chris Jones

text: It's just the good Doctor doing what he does best.
author: Chris Jones

text: As the man says: " There's only so many bumps on a log, so many grunts in a hog, so many croaks in a frog..." Food for thought, indeed.
author: Chris Jones

text: The annals of classic pop history have been recently sullied by what has come to be almost a genre in its own right - the Duets album: career-boosting "collaborations" wherein old-timers drag younger, hipper names into the studios to wildly variable and often excrutiatingly embarassing ends.
author: Chris Jones

text: Does anyone really believe that Tom Jones hangs out with the Stereophonics?
author: Chris Jones

text: And may the Lord forgive Lulu for her forthcoming addition to the oeuvre.
author: Chris Jones

text: The point being: if you're getting on, you shouldn't have to try and reinvent yourself for a younger audience.
author: Chris Jones

text: Marianne, the grande dame of louche can afford to wait for people to approach her - for the first lady of sixties excess makes the young 'uns look cool by association.
author: Chris Jones

text: This is why Kissin Time, is the embodiment of growing old gracefully.
author: Chris Jones

text: Ms Faithfull DOESN'T CARE whether she's graceful or not; just telling it as she sees it.
author: Chris Jones

text: So who wins the mix'n'match competition to be Marianne's new musical beau?
author: Chris Jones

text: Let's deal with the stragglers first.
author: Chris Jones

text: Dave Stewart is, of course, neither young or particularly cool these days and "Song For Nico", while having all the correct lyrical and cultural tropes turns autobiography into a dull plod.
author: Chris Jones

text: Etienne Daho's contribution to "The Pleasure Song" is suitably smooth in that Gallic cheese way that's so de rigeur.
author: Chris Jones

text: Faithfull gave Jarvis Cocker the job of coming up with a song to match the title "Sliding Through Life On Charm" (a misplaced piece of modesty when you consider work such as Broken English).
author: Chris Jones

text: Alas, all Jarvis could give us is a Pulp-by-numbers remake of "Common People" with a few salty lyrics thrown in to give the effect of risque soul searching.
author: Chris Jones

text: It fails to rise above its dated britpop roots.
author: Chris Jones

text: So who are the winners?
author: Chris Jones

text: Billy Corgan's collaborations show a remarkable sensitivity previously lost in the sub-goth mire of the Smashing Pumpkins.
author: Chris Jones

text: "Wherever I Go" is a slice of glistening pop perfection - stately and deeply affecting.
author: Chris Jones

text: Beck, by Marianne's own admission a genius, comes a close second in the collaboration prize-fight.
author: Chris Jones

text: "Like Being Born" is a plaintive baroque masterpiece, drawing on the filigree folk arrangements that peppered his Mutations album.
author: Chris Jones

text: "Nobody's Fault" from the same album, pales next to the original.
author: Chris Jones

text: Where Beck ultimately fails is in making Ms F sound as though she's a guest on one of HIS albums.
author: Chris Jones

text: The single "Sex With Strangers", with its squelchy beat box mechanics, could easily be an outtake from Midnite Vultures.
author: Chris Jones

text: Which leaves the winner; Blur!
author: Chris Jones

text: Their increasingly avant garde leanings have collided with La Faithfull's cracked vocal musings at a perfect juncture.
author: Chris Jones

text: Krautrock with dub overtones lends itself perfectly to the more obtuse lyrics of the title track.
author: Chris Jones

text: It makes you wish that the whole album had been done with them.
author: Chris Jones

text: Maybe we can hope that she'll repay the favour on their next outing.
author: Chris Jones

text: In the end Marianne Faithfull remains an icon, and far more than the mere uber groupie/muse that the media portrays.
author: Chris Jones

text: Taking the road from Wolverhampton to London, Dave Holland soon found himself an integral part of the capital's free music scene in the middle 1960s.
author: Martin Longley

text: The bassist was discovered by Miles Davis whilst gigging at Ronnie Scott's in 1968, joining the trumpeter's band for three years and launching the main body of a Stateside career.
author: Martin Longley

text: Now, Dave's accent is fully mid-Atlantic and his presence is imbued with that distinctively American larger-than-life glow.
author: Martin Longley

text: This compilation heralds the second wave of ECM's :rarum series, with tracks chosen by the individual artists, not only from their solo output, but often adding collaborative work as sidemen on the same label.
author: Martin Longley

text: The musicians also provide sleeve notes and privileged access to their personal photo archives.
author: Martin Longley

text: Holland's relationship with ECM founder Manfred Eicher spans the label's entire existence, occupying both the personal and professional planes.
author: Martin Longley

text: The bassman/composer has highlighted his work as bandleader, apart from the opening onslaught of the Gateway trio's "How's Never".
author: Martin Longley

text: Their surly jazz-rock gives the genre a clean reputation, Jack DeJohnette making aggressive drum rolls, John Abercrombie spiralling guitar lines with caustic abandon, whilst Holland lays down a pugilistic foundation.
author: Martin Longley

text: Dave started to concentrate on running his quartet and quintet line-ups in the early 1980s, and nearly all of this set comes from the last two decades.
author: Martin Longley

text: Numbers like "You I Love", "Four Winds" and "Homecoming" have become fully embedded as charismatic tunes, and should really have become modern standards by now.
author: Martin Longley

text: The first is a bustling, hyperactive, joint blowing sequence, coming straight out of Ornette, particularly when listening to Steve Coleman's flighty alto unravellings.
author: Martin Longley

text: The second has a slippery, curvaceous melody, with Steve spotlighted once again, this time in a trio setting.
author: Martin Longley

text: The third is the best of all, proudly stomping down the Mingus stairway to heaven.
author: Martin Longley

text: Holland applies the same kind of dynamism to his solo cello work on "Inception", whilst the current quintet's "The Balance" seems positively cool-school by comparison, the players capitalising on their liberal solo space.
author: Martin Longley

text: Cassandra Wilson intones deeply during "Equality", interpreting a poem by Maya Angelou.
author: Martin Longley

text: Kevin Eubanks stands proud on "Nemesis", his surging solo imparting more of a rock-blues feel.
author: Martin Longley

text: "Prime Directive" is another recent piece, involving the quintet's fast interaction, springily negotiating another substantial theme.
author: Martin Longley

text: Holland has followed a wise path in choosing a contrasting spread of settings, the standard of work being as high as might be expected from this towering figure.
author: Martin Longley

text: "I'm born again, found my soul again" proclaims Badly Drawn Boy Damon Gough early on during his new album Have You Fed The Fish?
author: Dan Tallis

text: Indeed, the music found on this recordsounds like it was made by a man who has been re-born and is full of the joys of life.
author: Dan Tallis

text: This feeling is summed up in the title track when Gough sings "You've got to rewind to go forward, there's some good times around the corner".
author: Dan Tallis

text: Obviously he has been doing some life contemplation since his 2000 debut, the Mercury Music Award winning album, The Hour Of Bewilderbeast.
author: Dan Tallis

text: He's in love, has two kids and is generally happy as can be; "I don't know how I could've lived without you, but certainly I know that I'm not about to" ("You Were Right").
author: Dan Tallis

text: But fans of his depressed side will be pleased to know that he still gets a bit down from time to time; "We've got to face the thought of loneliness again...
author: Dan Tallis

text: ("What is it Now?") Jaunty pop is the order of the day here.
author: Dan Tallis

text: "40 Days 40 Fights" and "What Is It Now?" are real foot tappers that raise a smile with their humorous lyrics; "We need a holiday but not today, another day..." The piano is at the heart of his songs.
author: Dan Tallis

text: All the other instruments seem happy to fit around the simple piano beats and rhythms.
author: Dan Tallis

text: Add Gough's distinctive and throaty voice and you have a winning combination.
author: Dan Tallis

text: Gough's vocals manage to be melancholic yet chirpy and amusing whether singing about love or regret, as seen on the wonderfully bittersweet "You Were Right"; "Madonna lived next door and I think she took a shine to me...but I had to turn her down because I was still in love with you".
author: Dan Tallis

text: Gough has something rare in the world of indie rock; he's a superb storyteller who makes life affirming pop music.
author: Dan Tallis

text: You find yourself sitting down and listening intently to his tales and life and love.
author: Dan Tallis

text: "About A Boy" author Nick Hornby recognised this talent and asked Gough to produce the soundtrack to the film earlier this year.
author: Dan Tallis

text: The subsequent album of the same name is possibly the best film soundtrack ever made.
author: Dan Tallis

author: Dan Tallis

text: Like millions of people I bought a copy of Norah Jones' 'Come Away With Me'.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: I was intrigued by Nora's smoky, intimate voice and liked the song "Don't Know Why." However, unlike millions of people, I gave the album away.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Apart from a couple of tracks I found it dull and disappointing.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: 'Feels Like Home' does not make me change my opinion.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Strong melodies or moments of real beauty are few and far between.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Norah's songwriting, with its cliqued images and rhymes, is just not very interesting.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: She needs material which plays against her tendency to slow everything down and relax to the point of dropping off to sleep.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: The occasional moments of drama, like the soulful groove of "In The Morning", all come when she is covering other people's songs.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: It's understandable that so many should turn to Norah's music as a relief from the brutal beats and hysterical textures of modern pop.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: But this album is just too full of tasteful but pedestrian guitar work, dull electric pianos and plodding over-recorded drums.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: It's country soul with all the interesting bits smoothed away.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: There are a couple of highpoints here.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: The duet with Dolly Parton, "Creepin In", is the best track on the album.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Dolly sounds like she's having fun and the results are rather sweet.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Nora has written some words to Duke Ellington's "Melancholia" and performs it solo - one of the few moments where some genuine emotion shows through, helped by someone else's interesting tune.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: There's nothing wrong with quiet reflective music, but when you try and listen actively to Feels Like Home there's little to engage the ear.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Which is a shame, as Nora's voice is rather lovely.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: I'm hoping in future she will take some risks and come up with something a bit more engaging.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: (Though no doubt millions will disagree with me!)
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Having first caught our attention with the wonderfully spacey Sturnin 7" and his captivating "Harmony Twitchell" track on last years Variable Access compilation, Olivier Lamm has been one of our favourite French musicians of late, and we've been anxiously awaiting his debut full length with bated breath.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Finally released this month, Snow Party follows up his trademark sound, living in a strange netherworld between full on glitched out digital noise and more accessible forms of ambient electronic music.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Yet, unlike his previous efforts, Lamm seems to have pulled out all the stops on this one, increasing his musical density ten fold but never forgetting about the actual song.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Olivier Lamm calls this his first 'pop album' and although I think you'll find this is a lot more Autechre than it is Aerosmith, he's not quite wrong.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Like a hyperactive child, he darts back and forth between snippets of the recognisable and the dissonant with incredible ease.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: From looped car alarms and telephone rings to snippets of The Beach Boys and The Flaming Lips, Lamm does know a good melody when he hears one.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Just check out what's going on in "Guitar Innovator": the track kicks off with multiple layers of timestretched noise and glitched samples, when out of nowhere a beautiful ambient piano bed suddenly kicks in.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Just when that is about build to a climax, the piano disappears, only to be replaced by a filtered techno pop song which then kicks back into a classical mode before glitching out into complete abstraction again.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Yet even the more dissonant parts of his music work brilliantly; just listen to the modified acoustic guitar sample on "Mason & Dixon" which has been chopped to bits, but still manages to retain a lovely little melody.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: We've been championing this label for a while now and one of the things we like so much about these French mavericks is their ability to keep their audience guessing, no matter how seemingly recognisable the release.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: While they do put out some of the most experimental glitchy type music that would make people like Autechre and Oval proud, the label has a good ear for releases that work on many different levels, not just the rarified worlds of microsound and glitch.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Snow Party is a captivating and simply joyous work of experimental electronic music which should charm the pants off even the most jaded of experimental techno fans.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Why just listen to laptops crunch when you can hear them sing ?
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Formed in 1996, Spoon have been spending their time carving out a niche in the same underground rock scene as At The Drive In and ...And You Will Know Us By The Trail Of Dead.
author: Daniel Pike

text: You haven't heard of them?
author: Daniel Pike

text: Well, Spoon are less rock and have proved, much to singer-songwriter Britt Daniels' frustration, decidedly more underground than their more famous and less succinctly named fellow Texans.
author: Daniel Pike

text: And yes, that's Texas as in Austin, "down here we like both types of music, country AND western", Texas.
author: Daniel Pike

text: So, all things considered, it is perhaps surprising to find Spoon have crafted an album that sounds so terribly, terribly British.
author: Daniel Pike

text: This, like previous releases, is a distinctly lo-fi post-punk offering.
author: Daniel Pike

text: Elvis Costello (Daniels is an ardent admirer) appears the most dominant influence.
author: Daniel Pike

text: His shadow is most evident on "Someone Something" and stand-out track "Jonathon Fisk".
author: Daniel Pike

text: The latter crunches through vengeful memories of playground bullying, religion and right-wing politics with "atom bombs and blunt razors" thrown in for good measure.
author: Daniel Pike

text: All the stuff of classic Costello.
author: Daniel Pike

text: There are shades of Tim Burgess falsetto on "Something To Look Forward To" and "Stay Don't Go".
author: Daniel Pike

text: The Piano driven "The Way We Get By" is a touch sprightly Badly Drawn Boy and even Britt Daniels' vocal inflections seem affectedly British on opening track "Small Stakes".
author: Daniel Pike

text: "Stay Don't Go" features human beat box which, despite sounding vaguely Rolf Harris, reveals a desire to split from the classic rock mould.
author: Daniel Pike

text: There is an air of tenderness and sincerity about the record, reflected in the sentiment "I will be there when you turn out the light" on "Paper Tiger".
author: Daniel Pike

text: There's also sufficient angst in tracks such as "All The Pretty Girls Go To The City" to satisfy the indie audience's traditional demand for woe.
author: Daniel Pike

text: A total reliance on fuzzed rhythm guitar is averted by recourse to keys and samplers.
author: Daniel Pike

text: All of this marks a departure for Spoon and distinguishes this LP from the efforts of other US White Strokes indie rock outfits.
author: Daniel Pike

text: The mood of Kill The Moonlight is essentially laid back yet the pace is frenetic - twelve tracks in just thirty-four minutes.
author: Daniel Pike

text: The loops and riffs are crude and chunky, as indeed they should be.
author: Daniel Pike

text: Songs are constructed around a strong, coherent melodic core.
author: Daniel Pike

text: The only real anti-climax is the fact that it is all over way too soon.
author: Daniel Pike

text: This band has suffered their fair share of bad luck in the past; they were dropped by their previous label after only four months for example, but with Kill The Moonlight, they have produced an album that really should bring them the success they deserve.
author: Daniel Pike

text: Spoon might at times sound jolly British but they are frightfully good at it.
author: Daniel Pike

text: Charmed I'm sure.
author: Daniel Pike

text: And so we see the return of the latest instalment of the Ragga compilation series.
author: Buki Bakare

text: Now on its 16th CD, Ragga Ragga Ragga 16 serves up an abundance of artist heavyweights, the ultimate cream of the crop.
author: Buki Bakare

text: Yes folks the impressive line up doesn't get much better than this - featuring: Elephant Man, Lexxus, Beenie Man, Capleton and Bounty Killer to name but a few.
author: Buki Bakare

text: First up who better to kick- start the album than the "Energy God" himself.
author: Buki Bakare

text: Leaping straight into "On Line" Elephant Man exemplifies to us in only the way he can, the new dance some are hailing as the official anthem for 2002.
author: Buki Bakare

text: Although I'm not convinced, it is a memorable track, but it's not even close to last year's smash hit dance-floor filler "Log On".
author: Buki Bakare

text: However a possible contender is "Bad Man A Bad Man", which by cleverly using the backing sample of R.
author: Buki Bakare

text: Kelly's "The World's Greatest," provides this track with definite crossover appeal.
author: Buki Bakare

text: So don't be surprised if you catch yourself singing along with it.
author: Buki Bakare

text: It appears that currently the dancehall scene can't get enough of this larger than life lisping DJ.
author: Buki Bakare

text: With four tracks on the compilation, Elephant Man definitely makes his presence felt.
author: Buki Bakare

text: Despite the plucky attempts of Spice to diss him on "Fraid Fi Fly" where she bravely talks of his recent ordeal in the UK, not surprisingly this is short lived as he promptly comes back with "Robbing" and tells her exactly what he thinks of her.
author: Buki Bakare

text: Notable surprising tracks are from Shabba Ranks where he unwittingly takes us down memory lane, and provides us with a subtle reminder as to why he used to be the undisputed champ of Dancehall.
author: Buki Bakare

text: And Harry Toddler - another famed former Scare Dem Crew member with, his instantly enticing track "Drive By" -guaranteed to have you nodding your head by the end of the tune.
author: Buki Bakare

text: A somewhat refreshing change comes in the form of Beenie Man with "Erase your Mind" where we get a breather from the raw, violent and X-rated lyrics often dominating the album.
author: Buki Bakare

text: Despite the all too common pre occupation with violence (and you need only glance at the title tracks "Press Trigger", "Robbing", "Drive By" and "Empty the Clip" to realise they are not singing about picnics!) those looking for something to get the party started and can live with this, need look no further.
author: Buki Bakare

text: With its catchy rhythms and almost hypnotic heavy baselines, you're likely to find it hard to resist shaking a foot or two to this CD.
author: Buki Bakare

text: No doubt several tunes will also serve as a teaching tool, when practising the latest dance craze in Jamaica, although after a while several tracks fall short of distinction and inevitably begin to merge into one another (rest assured your stereo isn't on repeat), despite the DJ's individual trademark style.

text: Having said that if any of you dancehall enthusiasts do not yet have this compilation album in your collection - Shame on you!

author: Martin Longley

text: "Things have never been so swell, I have never felt so well..." Roll up, roll up.
author: Amy McAuliffe

text: Welcome to Nirvana's Greatest Hits, you know the band that changed the face of modern rock music.
author: Amy McAuliffe

text: All your favourites are here, and there's a new track too ("You Know You're Right"), conveniently placed in pole position.
author: Amy McAuliffe

text: Their debut Bleach is criminally under-represented, with only "About A Girl" making an appearance.Then we get "Been A Son" and "Sliver" from the interim sessions prior to Nevermind, before coming across most of the first side of that classic album ("Smells Like Teen Spirit", "Come As You Are", "Lithium" and "In Bloom" all storming songs which remind the listener exactly why Nirvana broke the alt-rock mould).
author: Amy McAuliffe

text: The next section comprises a selection from Nirvana's swan song, In Utero."Heart Shaped Box", "Pennyroyal Tea" and "Rape Me" are still wonderful, visceral songs, but it's "All Apologies" which really tugs at the heartstrings.We finish up with two numbers from the MTV Unplugged session -covers of Leadbelly's "Where Did You Sleep Last Night" and Bowie's "The Man Who Sold The World".The latter makes for particularly difficult listening in retrospect, with Cobain's tortured voice insisting that "we never lost control".Less than six months later he committed suicide.
author: Amy McAuliffe

text: Of course, the main reason most Nirvana fans will buy this record is the only new track on the album, "You Know You're Right".
author: Amy McAuliffe

text: While the initial impact of "Smells Like Teen Spirit" is almost impossible to eclipse (remember where you were the first time you heard that intro and those chords?), for most aficionados of the Seattle Trio it was a veritable shiver-down-the-spine moment when "You Know You're Right" first came on the radio.A rave from the grave.A poignant reminder of what might have been.
author: Amy McAuliffe

text: An almost unbearable sense of bathos.Listening to a dead man snarling out his last gasp of righteous sarcasm.
author: Amy McAuliffe

text: Who these barbed lyrics are directed towards is a matter of debate.The fact that the remaining members of Nirvana have been locked in litigation with Cobain's widow regarding the release of a box set of both old and unreleased material for over two years may be neither here nor there.
author: Amy McAuliffe

text: One can only wonder what the notoriously cynical and anti-corporate Kurt would have made of it all.
author: Amy McAuliffe

text: Faust were always ahead of the game.
author: Chris Jones

text: Like all the greats in the avant rock fraternity, they came complete with weird tales aplenty.
author: Chris Jones

text: Not least being writer/manager/producer Uwe Nettlebeck's success in getting the band carte blanche with Polydor in 1971 (their own studio in Wumme, engineer and a year to come up with an album) and the fact that The Faust Tapes, retailed by a fledgling Virgin label at 49 pence, has to be a contender for the most widely heard piece of musique concrete, excepting the Beatles "Revolution #9".
author: Chris Jones

text: Faust's working methods underpinned a breathtakingly fecund environment where pleasure was found in juxtaposition, distortion and naivety.
author: Chris Jones

text: Remember, these guys coined the term Krautrock, and rarely has improvisation been such an integral part of a band's raison d'etre.
author: Chris Jones

text: Yet don't be misled, none of this comes across as amateurish.
author: Chris Jones

text: It sounds as deliberate as one of Kylie's middle eights and you can't help but be struck by how listenable it all is.
author: Chris Jones

text: So here are 20 reasons why these wayward Teutonic knights of knoise still remain essential.
author: Chris Jones

text: True to form (and similar in construction to the aforementioned Faust Tapes) Patchwork collects material from every Faustian period.
author: Chris Jones

text: In combining snippets from the early Wumme years, the Virgin Manor period and all subsequent projects, long-serving member Hans Joachim Irmler has honoured all criteria for a trip to the planet formerly known as Far Out.
author: Chris Jones

text: Nothing is sacred; everything is divine.
author: Chris Jones

text: No track hangs around for longer than 4 minutes (though somehow you know they're undoubtedly continuing to this day in some parallel dimension).
author: Chris Jones

text: Even a song such as "Duo", squeezing profundity from two chords resists the term minimalist by sounding unequivocally like a Faust recording.
author: Chris Jones

text: Much of this is down to the rough but polished engineering by ex-Deutsche Grammophon engineer Kurt Graupner and his legendary little black boxes.
author: Chris Jones

text: Instrumentation loses definition through studio alchemy to the point where "Ironies" sounds like the original horns tearing the walls of Jericho apart, molecule by molecule.
author: Chris Jones

text: But who can say what's really being played here?
author: Chris Jones

text: Points of recognition only occur in places where old material resurfaces, as on "Stretch Over All Times" which features the old chestnut "It's a Rainy Day Sunshine Girl".
author: Chris Jones

text: All styles are served here.
author: Chris Jones

text: A delicate piano mutates into free jazz territory on "Jassie", yet comparisons are odious.
author: Chris Jones

text: "Nervous" gives Detroit garageland a run for its money but Patchwork is best heard as a fabulous whole.
author: Chris Jones

text: Like some reliable DIY krautrock fix-all, it does exactly what it says on the tin.
author: Chris Jones

text: Patched together from one of musical history's most thrilling cornucopias of taped sound; this Faust is truly a piece of work.
author: Chris Jones

text: The ne plus ultra of baroque music for solo violin is the set of six partitas and sonatas that to most modern violinists is the holy-of-holies, approached with awe, reverence, and sometimes with fear and trepidation.
author: John Armstrong

text: But Bach didn't write the only music for solo violin, and Rachel Podger's new cd reminds us of another prolific composer's contribution to the genre, as well as the differences between the two men.
author: John Armstrong

text: Bach - the cerebral composer, the creator of tortuous fugues, rigorous canons, ingenious chaconnes.
author: John Armstrong

text: Telemann the entertainer, more interested in accessibility (for both performer and listener) than in intellectual satisfaction...yet there's plenty of that to be had in these lovely Fantasias.
author: John Armstrong

text: And they sound like fantasies, conjured out of nowhere as improvisations; ideas tumble after one another almost as though this were a kind of jazz.
author: John Armstrong

text: Telemann was a fine violinist himself, and knew how to make the instrument dance and sing and so does Rachel Podger, who revels in the bagpipe-like drones you sometimes get in the last sections of the Fantasias, reminders of Telemann's love of Polish folk music from his days in Silesia.
author: John Armstrong

text: Perhaps Andrew Manze in his Harmonia Mundi recording from the mid-1990s finds just a touch more freedom in his fantasising, more devil-may-care in the dancing, but Podger's thoughtfulness and clarity, and her easy command of the baroque instrument bring different rewards...not least a reminder that the days are gone when fans of baroque violin music had to suffer for their art, either in ridiculously over-blown performances on modern instruments, or scratchy, technically suspect readings on period violins.
author: John Armstrong

text: Rachel Podger has made my favourite period instrument recording of those great Bach works for solo violin, and this is a lovely companion piece: Bach's friend Telemann showing his expertise and skill both as player and composer in his 12 Fantasias, admittedly relatively humble alongside Bach's awesome vehicles for violinists, but then Telemann would never have wanted them to be compared.
author: John Armstrong

text: His charm, melodic and harmonic gifts and ingenuity are very satisfying in their own right, and in performances like these everyone's a winner.
author: John Armstrong

text: Not just for violinists, by the way: anyone who enjoys baroque music performed with panache should give this a listen.
author: John Armstrong

text: Faust was always a weird lash-up of incongruous experimentation bordering on triumphant success and noble failure, as this welcome 1973 reissue demonstrates.
author: Sid Smith

text: Emphasising feel over instrumental virtuosity, there are times when it threatens to fall apart.Yet this very fragility is also a central part of their enduring charm.
author: Sid Smith

text: "The Sad Skinhead" flirts with ska whilst the happy-clappy square dance of "Giggy Smile" offers a folk-tinged minimalism to their blend of dilettante rock.
author: Sid Smith

text: They stand on firmer ground during the epic groove-driven, "Krautrock", which not only spawned a generic description but whose seeds would later flourish with the likes of The Jesus And Mary Chain and Godspeed You!
author: Sid Smith

text: A bonus CD of contemporary radio sessions, previously unreleased alternate takes and explorations provide a portrait of a sprawling, chaotic but well-respected musical institution that excites and surprises to this day.
author: Sid Smith

text: Discovering Live At The Fillmore East (March 7, 1970): It's About That Time is like chancing across a Spanish galleons-worth of buried treasure.
author: Dan Hill

text: A completely unreleased concert, it's as good as any other recordings Davis and his various shape-shifting units made during his phenomenally creative 1968-1975 period.
author: Dan Hill

text: Which is another way of saying that this is the jazz record of this, and indeed any other year, so it's pretty astonishing that this so-called "Lost Sextet" recording has laid low till now.
author: Dan Hill

text: There's little to add to the scholarly (and not-so-scholarly) body of writing about Miles' genius at this point.
author: Dan Hill

text: This music's now very well known too - comprising the then-imminent Bitches Brew in various embryonic forms, and one earlier track ("Masqualero", from 1962's "Sorcerer").
author: Dan Hill

text: But no matter how familiar you are with this-period Miles, It's About That Time is still shocking - it has the same incredibly raw electricity that, say, Dylan's Albert Hall concert has; far edgier than Bitches Brew turned out to be.
author: Dan Hill

text: It's sometimes as if the band are impatiently and angrily re-inventing the material every few seconds.
author: Dan Hill

text: That over-used cliche about 'telepathic interplay' was surely never more appropriate.
author: Dan Hill

text: The sheer rush of ideas is astonishing.
author: Dan Hill

text: It's almost too good to listen to.
author: Dan Hill

text: In the same way that a weekday edition of the New York Times is said to contain more information than the average person in 17th Century England was likely to encounter in a lifetime, a couple of seconds of this contains enough musical information to frazzle your synapses forever.
author: Dan Hill

text: Each band member plays their ass off.
author: Dan Hill

text: In his last regular gig with Miles, Wayne Shorter, rightly lauded for his nimble peerless grace elsewhere, here sounds a fully paid-up member of the militant Free movement - as fearsome as Malcolm X, Amiri Baraka and Coltrane's Ascension.
author: Dan Hill

text: His screams and squawks spatter the action paintings and irregularly applied sciences emanating from Chick Corea's harshly distorted Fender Rhodes.
author: Dan Hill

text: Dave Holland, often on electric bass, is somehow unspeakably funky and freakily out-there at the same time.
author: Dan Hill

text: Only poor old Airto occasionally gets lost amidst the howls of electricity, struggling to be heard above Jack DeJohnette's surging drums.
author: Dan Hill

text: Well, he's Miles.
author: Dan Hill

text: At the peak of his powers, and combining particularly well with Corea, who's also never sounded more inspirationally inventive.
author: Dan Hill

text: Over 30 years on, this stuff still sounds more sci-fi than pretty much anything since 1970.
author: Dan Hill

text: The group were opening for the Steve Miller Blues Band and Neil Young & Crazy Horse, and it's telling that the gig ends in shrieks of feedback rather than acclaim.
author: Dan Hill

text: A couple of brave, battered souls call for an encore, but this music was heading straight over the heads of the audience, on a collision course with the future.
author: Dan Hill

text: As Miles said, this was "a mother of a band" - amongst his best, which gives an idea of how important a release this is.
author: Dan Hill

text: Jazz album of the year fer sure.
author: Dan Hill

text: Next year too, probably.
author: Dan Hill

text: Depends how good the forthcoming In A Silent Way sessions box is...
author: Dan Hill

text: Throughout his distinguished career, trumpet (and sometimes flugelhorn) player Hubbard has worn many musical hats.
author: Ian R Watson

text: He became best known as a fiery and energetic hard bopper with a string of classic Blue Note albums from the 60s to his name, as well as being a graduate of Art Blakey's Jazz Messengers.
author: Ian R Watson

text: Once the word was out that there was a new kid on the block, his muscular style found its way onto an amazing amount of albums, from Oliver Nelson (Blues And The Abstract Truth) and Herbie Hancock (Maiden Voyage) to John Coltrane (Ascension) and Ornette Coleman (Free Jazz).
author: Ian R Watson

text: Despite an association with Eric Dolphy the avant-garde was never really Freddie's bag.
author: Ian R Watson

text: By the time of this release (1970) his solo material was moving more towards the soul Jazz end of the spectrum.
author: Ian R Watson

text: Despite sidemen usually associated with Miles Davis; (drummer Jack DeJohnette, pianist Herbie Hancock and first call bassist Ron Carter) and that was a ghost that hovered over Hubbard for a long time, this is as far away in approach and sound to the Prince of Darkness that you could get.
author: Ian R Watson

text: After a free trumpet/drums intro "Straight Life" settles into powerful groove that hardly lets up through its 17 minutes, (think supercharged afro-beat).
author: Ian R Watson

text: Where Miles used a less is more aesthetic, Hubbard is exuberant, fearless and clearly at the top of his game.
author: Ian R Watson

text: Tenor player Joe Henderson also plays around the cusp between freedom and melodic ingenuity, while Hancock and guitarist George Benson keep the whole thing cooking and refuse to let the groove flag in any way.
author: Ian R Watson

text: "Mr Clean" lowers the temperature a notch but still provides both a template for acid Jazz (those pop bands too lazy to find their own voices) and enough source material for sample hungry DJs.
author: Ian R Watson

text: This was a time before 'fusion' became a dirty word and Hubbard himself descended into a string of commercially motivated but artistically redundant releases.
author: Ian R Watson

text: Here it's a joy to hear him soar over Hancock's sparkling electric piano.
author: Ian R Watson

text: When he brings out the flugelhorn on "Here's that Rainy Day" Hubbard shows off his romantic side.
author: Ian R Watson

text: Benson and bassist Ron Carter provide a perfect backdrop for Freddies lovelorn ruminations, letting the listener down gently after all the earlier excitement.
author: Ian R Watson

text: Slow Motion is the second album from DavidGray since the lo-fi genius of White Ladder.
author: Jack Smith

text: This time around the drum machine has been replaced with spacious soundscapes of glacial instrumentation, string sections, brass and harmonicas.
author: Jack Smith

text: The songs are layered, polished and occasionally breathtakingly powerful.
author: Jack Smith

text: However, it can take time for his lyrics to cut through the textures.
author: Jack Smith

text: Reassuringly the trademark steady piano chords remain.
author: Jack Smith

text: Gray stands up straight and walks tall.
author: Jack Smith

text: It's still him, just more ornate and less immediate.
author: Jack Smith

text: Nu Jazz - there's a lot of it about.
author: Peter Marsh

text: A few years ago, dance music's relationship with jazz amounted to nicking samples from old Blue Note records in the hope of appropriating some hipster cool.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Things have changed since then, with the likes of St Germain, 4 Hero and Bugge Wesseltoft forging a music where the saxophone and the sampler can (just about) peacefully coexist.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Swinscoe's Cinematic Orchestra are old hands at this game, roping in musicians like Tom Chant (also known for his improv work with the likes of Eddie Prevost) and keyboard whiz John Ellis to add flesh, blood and breath to Swinscoe's digijazz constructions.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Every Day is their second album and seems destined for instant Nu-Jazz credibility - it even has (wait for it) Gilles Peterson sleevenotes.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Every Day kicks off with the single "All that you Give"; cascades of Alice Coltrane-esque harp, followed by (surprise!) an Alice Coltrane string sample, topped off with a deeply soulful vocal from Fontella Bass (of "Rescue Me" and Art Ensemble of Chicago fame).
author: Peter Marsh

text: It certainly pushes all the right cosmic jazz buttons, whereas on the second collaboration with Ms Bass ("Evolution") Swinscoe cuts up her vocal over a downtempo groove into short, repeated phrases that recalls Moby's "borrowing" of blues recordings.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Despite some fine Rhodes soloing by John Ellis and a nice scratch outing from DJ Food's P.C., the track seems constructed rather than played (not surprising when the sleeve lists four different recording locations).
author: Peter Marsh

text: The Orchestra finally head towards escape velocity with 'Man with a Movie Camera'; a slinky, atmospheric slice of fusion driven by Luke Flower's crisply inventive drumming and featuring some fine Tom Chant soprano soloing, which hints at what the band are capable of in a live setting.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Better still is the eleven minute "All Things to All Men"; a cooly minimalist atmospheric funk workout complete with typically off beam rhymes from Roots Manuva (even namechecking the Tardis - cosmic !) and a lovely, kora like Rodhri Davies harp solo.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The closing title track, (complete with a sumptuous Charlie Haden like intro from bassist Phil France) goes nowhere beautifully with gently chattering synths gurgling happily to themselves over Flowers and France's slo-mo grooves and muted kalimba riffing.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Though this is an attractive record, it's mostly all surface; repeated listens don't really reveal anything new and you can't help feeling that this won't be an album you'll be playing much this time next year.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Gilles Peterson's sleevenotes are designed to suggest otherwise; "The Cinematic Orchestra tread the fine line between DJ culture and a week at the Village Vanguard", he writes.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Some might say it's a yawning chasm rather than a fine line, but with Every Day the Cinematic Orchestra are at least building a bridge.
author: Peter Marsh

text: More grit and muscle would be welcome though; how about a live album next time ?
author: Peter Marsh

text: Impulse was (and still is) a jazz label with iconic status.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Browse through any serious jazz record collection and you're bound to come across a cluster of those familiar gatefold sleeves with their orange and black spines.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Though launched in 1961 with no particular stylistic emphasis, the label was bankrolled by a Ray Charles hit.
author: Peter Marsh

text: But to most jazz fansit's inextricably linked with the furious, righteous ecstacies of 'The New Thing', spearheaded by John Coltrane.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Coltrane had been with the label from the start, but by the mid 60s was beginning to act as a talent scout as well as its star attraction.
author: Peter Marsh

text: With the likes of Archie Shepp, Pharoah Sanders and Marion Brown on board, the sleeves were able to boast that 'The New Wave of Jazz is on Impulse!' But it wasn't all screaming tenor solos and thirty minute percussion freak-outs.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Elder statesmen like Count Basie, Paul Gonsalves, Earl Hines, Ben Websterall found homes on Impulse and Khan finds room for them here.
author: Peter Marsh

text: We also get Impulse's greatest hits (Coltrane's "A Love Supreme", Mingus's "Goodbye Pork Pie Hat", Oliver Nelson's "Stolen Moments" etc etc).
author: Peter Marsh

text: Some will grumble about the choice of tracks, but Khan's choice does a great job in giving a flavour of the breadth (and importance) of the label's catalogue.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Thankfully later Impulse signings (like Diana Krall, fer gawdsakes) aren't included, but Khan finishes proceedings neatly and fittingly with a track from Alice Coltrane's wonderful Translinear Light, recorded in 2005.
author: Peter Marsh

text: How do you approach this 22 CD overhaul?
author: Chris Jones

author: Chris Jones

author: Chris Jones

text: There's no denying the confusion that surrounds the world's oldest teenagers 60s catalogue (separate labels in the UK and US with different issues of albums with the same titles etc.), yet will this massive reissue campaign ('A whole new way to get Stoned', indeed) really silence the completists?
author: Chris Jones

text: Probably not, but it's all here - the legendary, and the legendarily bad.
author: Chris Jones

text: Just take your time weighing the pros and cons.
author: Chris Jones

text: It's already been said, but the bias towards the US versions has denied many punters of the ability to truly enjoy these nuggets as they first experienced them way back when.
author: Chris Jones

text: This reviewer's copy of Through The Past Darkly had ''You Better Move On'' on it - and it FITTED; the same goes for High Tide And Green Grass without ''Little Red Rooster''.
author: Chris Jones

text: So we're left with endless duplications and anomalies surrounding the first two or three years.
author: Chris Jones

text: The UK versions of the first two albums (Rolling Stones and Rolling Stones 2) are sacrificed for England's Newest Hit Makers and 12x5.
author: Chris Jones

author: Chris Jones

text: Whole genres and movements arose from these garage blues anthems, and there's yet to be a better version of ''Route 66'' recorded.
author: Chris Jones

text: Following these classics, Jagger and Richards' enforced song writing partnership (which wrested control of the band away from Brian Jones) took no time at all to flourish.
author: Chris Jones

text: Unfortunately the albums don't really reflect this.
author: Chris Jones

text: A skittish search for new experiences in melody and structure leaves Out Of Our Heads and Decembers Children (admittedly made up from EPs) a little patchy.
author: Chris Jones

text: This is entirely forgivable when you remember that pop was still primarily a singles market and only John, Paul, George and Ringo were at the forefront of the move towards albums as coherent collections.
author: Chris Jones

text: But by 1966, the competition (Pet Sounds, Revolver, Freak Out etc.) ensured that Aftermath was a far cry from mere parent-baiting and untapped lust.
author: Chris Jones

text: ''Under My Thumb'', ''Out Of Time'' , ''Stupid Girl'' and ''Doncha Bother Me'' all smack of callow misogyny yet as songs they display a burgeoning sophistication that, by Between The Buttons, could include satire and social commentary (''Yesterday's Papers'') and also saw their blues roots hitting a swaggering stride (''Miss Amanda Jones'') that would bloom two years later with Beggars Banquet.
author: Chris Jones

text: In between sits the great divider, Their Satanic Majesties Request.
author: Chris Jones

text: Cod-psychedelia with its tongue firmly in its cheek, or lost masterpiece?
author: Chris Jones

text: With ''She's A Rainbow'', ''We Love You'' and (possibly their greatest song EVER) ''2000 Light Years From Home'' it's essential to anyone remotely interested in Stones history.
author: Chris Jones

text: Where the Beatles went into detail, Mick and the boys just got weirder.
author: Chris Jones

text: In fact too weird for poor Brian.
author: Chris Jones

text: Satanic Majesties was his swansong and by Beggars his input was minimal.
author: Chris Jones

text: Always more of a Jack Daniels than LSD band, this is the first perfect album by the boys.
author: Chris Jones

text: From the loping groove of ''Sympathy For The Devil'', to the chiming rumble of ''Street Fighting Man'' it's still gritty and in yer face.
author: Chris Jones

text: Even the toilet cover shot and Dickens-meets-Henry VIII banquet scene inside still seem like a glorious f**k you to the world.
author: Chris Jones

text: The Golden Age had begun.
author: Chris Jones

text: 1969's Let It Bleed remains a pinnacle in rock music; Full stop.
author: Chris Jones

text: By now social satire was replaced with drawling tales of lost innocence and darkness made all the scarier by the fact that you knew they weren't just sightseers at the freakshow of the decade's close.
author: Chris Jones

text: Yet the darkness is always flecked with humour (''Live With Me'') and their grasp of American styles (''Country Honk'', ''Love In Vain'') was becoming seamless.
author: Chris Jones

text: The title track's scream of ''Rape, murder, they're just a shot away...'' of course now seems spookily prescient.

author: Chris Jones

Along with all the compilations (High Tide, Through The Past, Flowers, Hot Rocks, More Hot Rocks and The London Years) and the much underrated outtakes collection, Metamorphosis, this is almost too much history to take in one go.
author: Chris Jones

text: However the scrubbed-up sound is remarkable (as is, presumably, the SACD sound also contained herein) and again we're reminded why, 40 years on, these guys can still sell out the local Enormodome.

text: In the stultifying post-war aura of austerity young minds were thrown into turmoil.
author: Chris Jones

text: On one hand convention defined growing up as something messy, to be passed through as quickly as possible; on the other hand something happening in America hinted that there was more to youth than speaking when spoken to.

author: Chris Jones

text: Released in 22 different versions across the globe (the one song common to all being ''Fame'') and accompanied by a remastered DVD, this package is as near perfect as it can be.
author: Chris Jones

text: Disc one takes us from his 1969 career-breaker ''Space Oddity'' up to his first personal crisis (the usual stuff: drugs, occultism, flirtations with right wing imagery) in 1975.

author: Chris Jones

text: With Dr Eno to ease him through the withdrawal in Berlin, we get gems like ''Sound And Vision'' and ''Boys Keep Swinging''.
author: Chris Jones

text: Despite the aberration of ''Under Pressure'' the new methodology held through his last masterpiece Scary Monsters, and then the curse of the 80s fell across Bowie's life.
author: Chris Jones

text: The shiny beast that is Lets Dance had all the seeds of ruin within it.
author: Chris Jones

text: The only trouble was that Dave was shipping so many units that he didn't notice it all going awry.
author: Chris Jones

text: ''Blue Jean'' barely exists, so formulaic is it, and one can't help but think that ''This Is Not America'' was beautiful because of Pat Metheny's measured touch.
