text: At last, Bill Frisell is veering off in a new direction, heading out towards what could best be described as heavy funk for thinking truckers.
author: Martin Longley

text: He's remembering how to crank up his amplifier again, and this disc reels with a satisfying degree of distorted, mangled, steaming, twanging, squealing and grumbling licks.
author: Martin Longley

text: Bill's key collaborator this time is producer Hal Willner, who manages to spread his influence into every nook of the recording studio.
author: Martin Longley

text: Willner's speciality has been to guide wise gatherings of like minds through skewed tributes to maverick composers.
author: Martin Longley

text: He's tackled Kurt Weill, Ennio Morricone, Charlie Mingus and Nino Rota, with the latter project being his first Frisell meeting, back in 1981.
author: Martin Longley

text: Willner has also been reborn as a turntablist, though he's not much of a scratcher.
author: Martin Longley

text: He prefers to infiltrate loops, samples and complete chunks, delving into his extremely obscurist boxes, concentrating on highly rarefied records from the 1950s and '60s.
author: Martin Longley

text: Frisell is using the complete Sex Mob quartet (Steven Bernstein, Briggan Krauss, Tony Scherr, Kenny Wollesen), as well as Curtis Fowlkes (trombone), Don Alias (percussion)and Adam Dorn (synthesisers).
author: Martin Longley

text: The 858 Stings plush out the sound even further, featuring the familiar hands of Jenny Scheinman, Eyvind Kang and Hank Roberts.
author: Martin Longley

text: The striding dance grooves are redolent of the 1960s and '70s, combining mean cracked leather with kitsch polyester sheen.
author: Martin Longley

text: The strings pour on soothing coolant as Frisell remembers his youth, his horn buddies headbutting hard below the belt.
author: Martin Longley

text: There's a direct danceability, but Frisell's tunes are decorated with subversive noises.
author: Martin Longley

text: If this feels too heated, there are five numbers that strip down to gentle duo interaction or have a more opened-up, string-dominated terrain.
author: Martin Longley

text: Creaky pylons and insect chirrups fill the periphery; Frisell is beginning to be unpredictable again...
author: Martin Longley

text: The first taste of the new material, "Hands Around My Throat", was a curious appetiser, a pleasant enough nod towards the electroclash farrago, although not the greatest tune.
author: Pootle

text: If, however, they could afford to leave the formidable b-side, "Scorpio", off the album, what possible delights would messrs Fearless and Holmes offer us this time?
author: Pootle

text: One thing is clear from the first power-chord: there are great tranches of Scorpio Rising that have nothing to do with dance or electronica: DIV are clearly wearing their Rock pants today.
author: Pootle

text: "Leather" is an obvious calling card, opening their account with an absurdly fuzzy bass, balls-out guitar, thrashing drums and radiant keyboards.
author: Pootle

text: "Girls" clarifies the statement of intent, initially laden with Susan Dillane's mellifluous cooing, before careering, unapologetically, into a joyous cacophony, still underpinned by the angelic vocal.
author: Pootle

text: This rough diamond aesthetic becomes a feature of the record; however battered and grubby songs initially sound, you dont have to scratch far beneath the surface for the innate, melodic lustre to appear.
author: Pootle

text: The female voices are generally stacked on a dreamy, ethereal axis - Dillane is joined by the remarkably similar-sounding Dot Allison and the sublime Hope Sandoval.
author: Pootle

text: By contrast, theres a whiff of Dad Rock about the choice of blokes; Liam Gallagher rubbing shoulders with Paul Weller, covering a tune by erstwhile Byrds singer, Gene Clark.
author: Pootle

text: That said, Liam sounds rejuvenated on the albums title track, excited to get his laughing gear round a song worth singing.
author: Pootle

text: To an extent, Scorpio Rising is to DIV what Bow Down To The Exit Sign was to David Holmes, with Liam serving a similar purpose to Bobby Gillespie on the Holmes wig-out, "Sick City".
author: Pootle

text: Both artists are born out of DJ culture and enjoy wildly diverse musical tastes, which isn't to say that this is merely a voguish rediscovery of garage rock.
author: Pootle

text: "Killing Smile" strolls through countrified banjos and a field of strings recorded in India, followed by the minimal and faintly Dr Who-ish "Natja", the nearest thing to electronica as we know it and even that has cellos.
author: Pootle

text: There's nothing here that quite matches the malevolent attack of Iggy Pop confessing "Im a murderer" on "Aisha" (from The Contino Sessions), but "Help Yourself" closes proceedings on a stellar high.
author: Pootle

text: It starts anonymously enough, but builds patiently through 10.5 epic minutes of Hope Sandoval's divine, trouser-melting tones and more Indian strings to a majestic finale.
author: Pootle

text: As the last strains drift out of the speakers and over the horizon, you'd be a brave man to bet on what the next album will sound like.
author: Pootle

text: The first time I saw Derek Bailey play guitar he reminded me of John Lee Hooker.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Of course he doesn't sound anything like John Lee Hooker.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Or perhaps he does, if you removed all of the tunes and all of the rhythm and all of the structure.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: He leaves the listener in a uneasy limbo with no familiar musical landmarks and then punctuates it with brutal climaxes.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Then he plays with a singular violence, torturing the thing, as for example at the end of "Midnight White" here.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: He scratches and scribbles all over it adding feedback to release the tension build up in the preceding twenty four minutes.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: It's raw and compelling.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: I always start to nod my head in rhythm at certain points, even though there is none.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: He usually works well in duos with drummers or percussionists, since he often plays the guitar like a drum.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Here his partner is Susie Ibarra who plays a full kit with a lot of shuffling and banging, and also accentuates the atmosphere of menace with soft cymbal rides and rumbles.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: On "Day Without End" he lets her chatter while adding his trademark weird harmonics that sound like he's playing backwards, then adds some more scrabbling and backwards feedback.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Bailey has grasped the essence of the guitar and pursued it obsessively for thirty years: its a nasty, noise-making machine.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: This album, recorded at a Festival in Norway is probably the closest he's ever come to stadium rock.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: There's more feedback and more drama than usual, some moments that are almost lyrical ("Shine"), some sudden lurches in volume, as well as some rambling passages where nothing much seems to happen.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: How does it make me feel?

text: When Tom Waits released Mule Variations in 1999, it was widely seen as a combination of both old and new Waits.
author: Nigel Smith

text: New Waits meant songs about oddball characters like the Eyeball Kid, growled a la Beefheart through a megaphone and played on a weird-sounding selection of homemade instruments.
author: Nigel Smith

text: The "old" Waits songs harked back to his sozzled barroom days hunched over a knackered piano, singing witty and sentimental stories of barflies and other late night characters.
author: Nigel Smith

text: Dime Store Novel Vol 1 is as good a snapshot of Old Waits as you'll find.
author: Nigel Smith

text: The gig was originally recorded for radio broadcast in a small Denver club called Ebbets Field, in front of what sounds like an audience of two dozen.
author: Nigel Smith

text: Accompanying himself on guitar and piano, Waits rasps through a set that includes such favourites as ''Better Off Without A Wife'' and ''Ol '55''.
author: Nigel Smith

text: It's all interspersed with drunken banter and, by the end, he's taking requests.
author: Nigel Smith

text: Anyone familiar with Tom Waits' early albums will know what's in store.
author: Nigel Smith

text: This is an Edward Hopper painting set to music: drunks, waitresses, sailors and truck drivers all crop up.
author: Nigel Smith

text: The only song here that's not from a Waits album is ''Good Night Loving Trail''.
author: Nigel Smith

text: Written by Utah Phillips, ''the golden voice of the great Southwest'' - it's a mournful ballad about a cook on a wagon train.
author: Nigel Smith

text: Only 24 at the time of this recording, the singer still sounds like he's on two packs of Winstons a day and downed a couple of whiskies before the show.
author: Nigel Smith

text: What's also remarkable, considering his relative youth, is the range of characters he portrays.
author: Nigel Smith

text: On the heartbreaking ''Martha'' Waits imagines himself as an old man looking back on a youthful romance while ''SemiSuite'' sympathises with a stuck-at-home truck driver's wife torn whether to leave her man.
author: Nigel Smith

text: Tom stumbles off stage after 13 songs but the MC announces that he'll be playing again the following night, admission one dollar.

author: Nigel Smith

text: It's a sobering thought that the end of the 1960s saw McCoy Tyner driving a New York cab to pay his rent when only a few years before he'd been a member of one of the greatest jazz groups on the planet, namely John Coltrane's 'classic' quartet.
author: Peter Marsh

text: By1971 however,Tyner was back on track with a deal with Milestone and a subsequent string of albums which saw him team up with post Coltranehorn players like Sonny Fortune and Azar Lawrence, with whom he recorded the classic Enlightenment.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Sama Layuca dates from 1974, and sees Tyner in an octet format, teaming up with Lawrence, old duet partner vibist Bobby Hutcherson, Gary Bartz, John Stubblefield and a monster rhythm section of Buster Williams, Billy Hart and percussionists Mtume and Guilherme Franco.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The results are exhilarating; Tyner's compositions are unsurprisingly modal excursions, topped off with faintly exotic horn themes and driven by insistent,afro-latin rhythms.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Lawrence (on tenor and soprano) and altoist Bartz are clearly at home; Lawrence'sfruity, robusttenor and airy soprano blends Coltrane's fiery yearning with a floating attack worthy of Wayne Shorter, while Bartz is typically wondrous, full of surprise and fire (check his questing solo on the closing "Paradox").Both players provide an abject lesson in getting the mostout of soloing over one or two chords.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Hutcherson was possibly the only vibist around who could survive in the heat generated by such a lineup.
author: Peter Marsh

text: His crystalline voicings are showcased on the two lower key numbers; the impressionistic "Above the Rainbow" (a duet with the leader), and the stately "Desert Cry".
author: Peter Marsh

text: Switching to marimba on the hyperspeed latin groove of "La Cubana", Hutcherson more than holds his own, firing off rhythmically twisty, harmonically probing lines before playing call and response with Franco's cowbells.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Tyner's playing walks his usual line between tough and tender, from the swelling, limpid arpeggios of "Above the Rainbow" to the percussive splash and dark intervals of his solo on "La Cubana".
author: Peter Marsh

text: The expanded lineup holds the pianists's tendency to overcook his solos in check; despite the length of some of the pieces ("Paradox" clocks in at over 16 minutes) this isn't the testosterone fuelled sprawling solofest you might expect.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Solos are kept short and sweet, and the frequent shifts in texture and instrumental combinations keep things interesting.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Most of all it's Tyner's rhythmic sense and his powerhouse left hand that provide the excitement when locking with the irresistible grooves that Williams, Hart, Mtume and Franco whip up.
author: Peter Marsh

text: I bet there were a few sore fingers after this session, but the music here won't leave your ears sore.
author: Peter Marsh

text: In language which would probably have him expelled from a number of university faculties today, Robert Schumann described Schubert's E flat Piano Trio as "spirited, masculine and dramatic" in contrast to his other more "passive, lyrical and feminine" work in the piano, violin and cello genre, the B flat.
author: Matthew Shorter

text: You can just about see what he means in the first two movements.
author: Matthew Shorter

text: The first opens with an assertive gesture of Mozartian simplicity, which, although it subsequently gives way to more gentle material, sets the tone for much of the writing in the movement.
author: Matthew Shorter

text: The Florestan Trio certainly take their cue from this opening, in a reading which occasionally tends towards the martial in its vigour, regularity, and polish.
author: Matthew Shorter

text: The Andante second movement's main theme is a kind of proto-tango, a brooding melody first played by the cello with a wonderfully balletic accompaniment in the piano (the two instruments later swap roles as the piano takes the melody and the violin joins the accompaniment - a trick which often returns throughout the work).
author: Matthew Shorter

text: Here as in the first movement, the players' modesty is almost self-effacing.
author: Matthew Shorter

text: The strings take a particularly polite approach, and I found myself longing for the odd lapse of good taste to carry me out of the atmosphere of the Edwardian drawing room.
author: Matthew Shorter

text: However, the rigid control of tempo and phrasing pays off in the dramatic climax of the Andante, where a series of tremolos reach an enormous passionate crescendo in a weird corner of the late-Schubert harmonic landscape, and the violence is all the more powerful for the restraint which precedes it.
author: Matthew Shorter

text: The Florestan Trio's approach comes into its own in the third movement Scherzo, played with feathery delicacy and real ensemble.
author: Matthew Shorter

text: The relish lacking across some of the sweeping arcs of the first movement abounds in the playful canons which open the Scherzo, and in the fascinating textures of the trio, drawn out beautifully by the sensitivity of the strings, whose spiccato and selective use of vibrato are particularly striking and effective here.
author: Matthew Shorter

text: The structural complexity of the Finale (here presented in alternative versions, with and without the cuts Schubert made before publication) is also shown due respect in this performance.
author: Matthew Shorter

text: The balance throughout the recording is dry and a little austere, but like the careful performance it allows every single detail through, an approach which has distinct advantages in music as multi-layered as this.
author: Matthew Shorter

text: All round, a flawless account, celebrating a Schubert who is as much the son of Haydn and Mozart as the father of Schumann and Brahms.
author: Matthew Shorter

text: Avowedly synthetic / cheesy neo-organ sounds, noise / fluffed chords /upward-bubbling 50s chords; if this is a group they're not listening to each other...well, that's the first minute for you.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Tinkling synthi-piano notes,determinedly chemical bass; for a moment I'm reminded of a busied-up version of the final tracks on Landscape's first album.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: The 'syntheticness' is almost teeth-grating, like the static electric shocks you get from putting on a nylon jumper.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: (Parts 1 & 2)" throws Paul Schutze at a near-bossa rhythm to see what sticks, then collides it with some big band samples resulting in an aural car crash...damn, but there went the kind of guitar synthesizer sound Pat Metheny employed on Offramp; this is fun!
author: Colin Buttimer

text: By the third track ("Blue Ramen #3"), I'm feeling distinctly queasy - why did I drink so much?
author: Colin Buttimer

text: I should know by now - but wait a moment I haven't touched a drop: it's those big clumsy organ chords, the electric piano, the muffled bongos.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: I'm glad it's over quickly otherwise I'd be dashing for the nearest sink.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Track 5 - "Chalky".
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Like the taste of Milk of Magnesia?
author: Colin Buttimer

text: I feel the heartburn coming on already.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: "Chalky" feels like spending time becalmed in an oleaginous ocean, noxious gas clouds occasionally swirling round in the dim light.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Blue Ramen is music for bars on the edges of tanker depots, for all those Airfix kits melted by your big brother and his matches, for all those fans of David Lynch who also happen to have a soft spot for Billy Jenkins, Squarepusher or Four Tet.It's fake jazz, like a counterfeit Gucci watch - bad, where bad means not good for you, choc-full of E numbers, E102, E1194, E1831, E994a, E37 - those are the ones on the pot noodle I'm munching, for starters.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: And if you're going off to the kitchen cupboard to check whether I've quoted the correct chemical constituents, go out and order this album, it might be for you.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: This debut 7 tracker blew us away the moment it hit our CD player.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Maestro Echoplex (from Washington DC) is technically a one man operation, a gifted singer/songwriter named Johnny Fontaine who writes all the music and plays all the instruments.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: On this debut release however, he's teamed up with Ben Azzarra, (drummer for Captiol City Dusters) and banjo player Anthony Broadman to release, quite frankly, one of the strongest debuts we've heard all year.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: These minimally produced sweet and melancholy songs evoke the feel and pace of Will Oldham or Neil Young, yet bring a sensibility that encompasses everything from traditional folk music to indie rock; dark and foreboding on one hand yet spectacularly gorgeous on the other.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Tracks such as the simply wonderful "I Know, I Know" with it's off kilter drum track and modulating Hammond are a joy on headphones, as is the interestingly constructed "'Die Knowing Something' Said Walker Evans.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: (Karen, don't be lonely)" which bounces along with its rather unconventional chord structures and intimate lyrics.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Another surprise here is a version of Shellac's "A Prayer to God" which takes the blistering original and turns it into something much more powerful and personal with nothing but acoustic guitar, Hammond and an analogue bass accompaniment to make its point.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: When you hear Fontaine sing "kill them, kill them, just f**king kill them...", it will certainly make you wonder whom it's directed at (hopefully not you).
author: Olli Siebelt

text: This is a very impressive start to a musical career that looks certain to take off.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Fontaine is taking on a new project called The Amelia Players, which will be a "3-way split concept album of songs for Amelia Earhart, collaborated on by Maestro and his band, Ulf Magnet, and John Lindenbaum." If this release is anything to go by, we're sure that his new project will be just as impressive.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: In the meantime, hunt this glorious release down as soon as you can.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: We'll be keeping a close eye on this one.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: We think you should too.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Though the Chicago Underground Duo occasionally seem to comprise of three members and often swell to become the Chicago Underground Quartet or even the Orchestra, Axis and Alignment just features core members drummer/vibraphonist Chad Taylor and the cornet and electronics of Rob Mazurek.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Though the prospect of a cornet/drums duo may lack obvious appeal, the CUDs approach transcends the limitations of the format.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Taylors ability to play vibes and drums simultaneously helps, (as anyone whos seen them live will tell you), while occasional synthetic basslines from Mazureks powerbook provide a bedrock for the duos interplay.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Powered by Taylors octopoid rhythmic constructions, Mazureks graceful cornet picks out infectious, joyful little riffs ("Lifelines" is virally catchy) or occasional fruity improvs.
author: Peter Marsh

text: On "Two Concepts for the&" he looses off a really touching solo, suffused with equal amounts of fragility, strength and intelligence that Don Cherry would have been proud of.
author: Peter Marsh

text: While Mazureks early recordings showcased his ability as a player of straight bop inflected jazz, since then his concern seems to have been to strip away the extraneous; theres nothing showy or excessive, just a desire to communicate.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Though many of the tracks seem to be unadorned live duo performances, some are spiced up with electronics (Mazurek recently released a solo electronics record) or a spot of post production dub action.
author: Peter Marsh

text: "Memoirs of a Space Traveller" finishes up with a looped acoustic guitar interrogated by Mazureks muted cornet; its this kind of thing that suggests the CUD as a sort of synthesis of the improvisations of the AACM school with the cooly minimalist constructs of the Chicago post rock scene (Mazurek also guests with post rockers Tortoise).
author: Peter Marsh

text: The closing "Noon" hints at prime 70s Miles, with Mazureks cornet morphed and ring modulated into echoed blobs of colour; beautiful, poised stuff.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The only dud is "Average Assumptions &&", whose ham fisted out of tune piano and vibraphone duet suggests an acid crazed Russ Conway jamming with Bobby Hutcherson.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Programme that one out, and youve got 39 minutes or so of absolute heaven.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Following up on their wonderful series of limited edition 7"s and last years impressive evsc1:01 compilation, London based Expanding Records are again hitting all the right notes in terms of releasing quality electronica these days, and with this latest collection of experimental electronic composition, that trend looks certain to continue.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: On this latest from label owner Benge (aka Ben D.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Edwards), we see an interesting approach to songwriting not usually found in this genre.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Instead of simply booting up the computer and throwing a few patches together, Edwards has instead tried something a little more complicated.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: He's constructed these 11 tracks around "Memetics", a concept dealing with the evolution broken down to its basic building blocks (think biological, computer or evolutionary sciences).
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Although it's difficult to say technically exactly how hes integrated this philosophy into practice, the liner notes to the CD do give some clue.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: From what we can gather, each song here seems to have been stripped down into various sound parameters represented by simple vowels and consonants.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: The various combinations of letters were then assigned sounds and then arranged in particular patterns and banks and then triggered in successive, repeating yet constantly evolving steps.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Tracks like "Adam-Age Loneliness", "Urban", "Ajax Goon" and "Pica Unit" all bear astrong resemblance to the current Danish school of electronica; a country that seems to love its music organic and melodious, just as it seems Edwards does.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: The beats here are dubby and minimal, with warm electric piano chords and a general lo-fi ambience of well-being permeating the musical atmosphere.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: It's all a little bit Future 3, a little bit Opiate, a little bit Pole and a little bit Jimi Tenor all rolled into one.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: In other words, Benge plays nice with the other kids.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Listen closely however and you'll spot some interesting touches; a lick of playful jazz sneaking up on you in "Tame/Rude Image", or what could be a mutated kalimba rhythm right out of Africa echoing out on "Eve's Escape Valve".
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Benge keeps the pace snappy and casual throughout yet there's much more than meets the ear here at first listen.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: For those of you who relish the softer side of experimental electronica, or especially if you're into the newer sounds coming out of Scandinavia these days, you'll find this a welcome addition to your collection.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Meme Tunes ultimately is an exercise in comfort that couldn't feel more lovely, and one that gets better and better after repeated listens.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: A very tasty collection of modern electronic music.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Love Travels At Illegal Speeds, Graham Coxon's sixth solo album, is a more relaxed, varied and accessible affair compared to the full-on rock mode of 2004's Happiness In Magazines.
author: Dan Tallis

text: There are still plenty of Coxon's trademark scratchy guitar sounds.
author: Dan Tallis

text: Punk riffs cascade relentlessly, getting faster and faster with each passing song.
author: Dan Tallis

text: "I Can't Look At Your Skin" sounds like late 70s Buzzcocks, only a whole lot better.
author: Dan Tallis

text: But it's with the slower songs that Coxon really comes of age as a songwriter as he tells touching stories of tough love, lust and jealously.
author: Dan Tallis

text: Not to mention imagined affairs ("Don't Let Your Man Know").
author: Dan Tallis

text: While "Just A State Of Mind" is one of several tracks that sound remarkably similar to Blur's 13.
author: Dan Tallis

text: Quirky guitar rhythms, NHS glasses, love soaked ditties.
author: Dan Tallis

text: It's as if Elvis Costello never went away...
author: Dan Tallis

text: So who was Stefano Landi?
author: John Armstrong

text: Well, it depends what you read.
author: John Armstrong

text: To the New Grove Dictionary of Music and Musicians he is 'One of the most important figures in the early history of opera and a leading Roman composer of his day'.
author: John Armstrong

text: But this recording focuses on another, less public side of Landi's art, the more personal books of arias (Libri di Arie).
author: John Armstrong

text: It looks into Landi's 'double life, the reverse side of life at court and its struggle for recognition...so we can discover in Stefano Landi's Libri di Arie pieces that on closer inspection lead the way into a universe all his own.
author: John Armstrong

text: These arias and villanellas, composed by a singer and continuo player, a rhetorician and philosopher, who accompanied his own songs on the harp or the Spanish guitar, constitute a miniature art form of concentrated perfection'.
author: John Armstrong

text: This might sound like special pleading for a minor figure in Italian musical history, but I defy you not to warm to their cause as you listen to this enchanting cd.
author: John Armstrong

text: The liner notes establish a useful human context for Landi's music: Landi was an alto in the papal choir, job-sharing with Grigorio Allegri, and one of the many musical employees of the wealthy and influential Barberini family.
author: John Armstrong

text: This meant he was surrounded by some of the finest artistic talent in Italy all gathered in the Barberini's unheated servants' quarters, all competing for the recognition, attention and exposure that would guarantee them a future.
author: John Armstrong

text: This musical world behind the notes is the hidden universe of the shadows that gives the disc its title: Homo fugit velut umbra - man flees like a shadow - taken from the anonymous title track.
author: John Armstrong

text: After you've heard it, you're hooked; the performers breathe new life into Landi's musical world, with voices that seem to understand every nuance of the things about which they sing.
author: John Armstrong

text: The instrumental accompaniment is improvisatory, earthy and ingenious: lute, theorbo, guitar and harp continuo, plus up to a trio of violins, viola da gamba, a cornet and a gentle sprinkling of percussion.
author: John Armstrong

text: There's imitative entertainment: Augellin (the little songbird) and Canta la cicaletta (the little cicada sings); opera-in-miniature (Quando Rinaldo invitto Armida abbandono); and songs of love disappointed, tortured and betrayed.
author: John Armstrong

text: This is punctuated with instrumental numbers that heighten the beauty of the singing around them.
author: John Armstrong

text: It all feels natural and unforced, yet this is truly sophisticated entertainment.
author: John Armstrong

text: Style triumphs over content in a couple of ways: the cd is so keen on establishing context for the music it forgets to tell us which singers are which.
author: John Armstrong

text: There's such beautiful work from the tenors, Marco Beasley and Stephan van Dyck, it's almost insulting not to attribute the voices to the songs.
author: John Armstrong

text: Also, Landi's arie are taken from a number of sources, and we are not told which works are from where.
author: John Armstrong

text: That apart, congratulations to Christina Pluhar, her singers and L'Arpeggiata, for illuminating the life of a little-known Italian master in such a beautifully rewarding way.
author: John Armstrong

text: The Paris-based label Alpha is a relative newcomer, but this joined-up contextual approach seems to be one of their main goals, as well as using interesting but not necessarily well-established artists and ensembles.
author: John Armstrong

text: I'll be keeping an eye on any future releases of theirs that come my way; this is one of the most pleasurable early music releases I've heard in an age.
author: John Armstrong

text: Most rock and metal fans will have heard of the Murderdolls, if only for the fact that Slipknot sticksman Joey Jordison (unmasked!
author: Amy McAuliffe

text: gasp!) is their guitarist and main songwriter.
author: Amy McAuliffe

text: He is joined by former Frankenstein Drag Queens From The Planet 13 frontman, Wednesday 13, (vocals) and Static X's Tripp Eisen (guitars).
author: Amy McAuliffe

text: Quite an unholy alliance.
author: Amy McAuliffe

text: Beyond The Valley Of The Murderdolls, their debut album, is released by Roadrunner Records, the label responsible for a fair chunk of the big names in Nu-Metal in recent years.
author: Amy McAuliffe

text: All this evidence would suggest artillery-fire drums, brutalist guitars, scary electronic noises, and somewhat po-faced lyrical squealing and grunting.
author: Amy McAuliffe

text: Happily though, it seems that, like their idol Alice Cooper, the Murderdolls have a well-developed sense of humour, and a pierced tongue placed firmly in their cheek.Wednesday 13's vocal delivery recalls the more recent spookily-dressed man in make-up; Marilyn Manson.
author: Amy McAuliffe

text: The guitar sound and chord progressions are pure New York Dolls with the overdrive turned up LOUD, solidly underpinned by a punky & tight rhythm section.The overall result sounds like The Sex Pistols after Johnny Rotten left, only with Casey Chaos on vocals instead of Steve Jones.
author: Amy McAuliffe

text: The most refreshing aspect of Beyond The Valley...
author: Amy McAuliffe

text: is the morbidly anarchic and childish humour displayed in the lyrics.
author: Amy McAuliffe

text: In the shaky days after 9/11, it takes a timely irreverence to release songs with titles such as "Kill Miss America" and "Grave Robbing USA"."Motherf***** I Don't Care" is a brilliant send-up of the whole "no-mom-I-wont-tidy-my-room-maggots-like-you-make-me-sick" school of whiney teenage angst so prevalent in a great deal of Nu-Metal lyricism.
author: Amy McAuliffe

text: There's also a palpable streak of schlock-horror (in the style of the Misfits and The Cramps) which is amusingly evident in "B-Movie Scream Queen" and "Love At First Fright" (a love song dedicated to Regan, the head-turning star of The Exorcist).
author: Amy McAuliffe

text: "Dead In Hollywood" is a deserving single and almost good enough to be mistaken for an Amen tune.
author: Amy McAuliffe

text: While Beyond The Valley...
author: Amy McAuliffe

text: is unlikely to win any prizes for originality, all in all it's an excellent stomp-along rock record.
author: Amy McAuliffe

text: The only niggle is the slightly monotonous nature of the production, but ignore this in favour of the straightouta 1976 guitars and spend a highly enjoyable 45 minutes pogoing around your bedroom.
author: Amy McAuliffe

text: Time has not done much to bridge the gap between those who loved Bird at first sight and those who felt that the big bad soul of Charlie "Yardbird" Parker hadn't even been hinted at in the intense but mythologising movie.
author: Chris Jones

text: Truth be told, your reviewer never felt that Forest Whitaker was the man for the part, but you cannot deny the true jazz buff's zeal that Clint Eastwood brought to the subject.
author: Chris Jones

text: It may be fairer to regard this album as the true monument to Bird and the film as a mere promotional video to tempt you into a place where bebop is most assuredly shouted from the rooftops.
author: Chris Jones

text: This album swings.
author: Chris Jones

text: Shorn of the rough surroundings that Parker's solos often found themselves in, Clint and Lennie Niehaus guessed that sparkling new accompaniment and very intricate sonic laundering would be the only thing to suit a film of this tempestuous life.
author: Chris Jones

text: Only Bird could play Bird.
author: Chris Jones

text: They were right on the money.
author: Chris Jones

text: With a small group composed of not only jazz giants but self-confessed Parker nuts, Niehaus fashioned a fantasists heaven: Parker in stereo!
author: Chris Jones

text: Filtering out all but the crowd noise from a carefully chosen set of live numbers, a group featuring Monty Alexander, Walter Davis Jr., Ron Carter, and John Guerin have re-recorded accompaniment and even solos in appropriate style.
author: Chris Jones

text: The results could have been dreadful, but somehow it works.
author: Chris Jones

text: Of course with Bird himself blowing a mean alto on all the usual suspects, you can't really lose.
author: Chris Jones

text: The opener "Lester Leaps In" is ablaze with nimble-fingered licks and "Ornithology" remains one of Parker's finest moments in whatever guise.
author: Chris Jones

text: Three of the tracks ("Laura", "April In Paris" and "Parker's Mood") allowed the producers to make Parker's dream of working with a large orchestra finally come true, with sumptuous results.
author: Chris Jones

text: Most amazing are the two unheard tracks ("I Can't Believe That You're In Love With Me" and "All Of Me") recorded at Lennie Tristano's home with Kenny Clarke tapping out a rhythm.
author: Chris Jones

text: These home recordings allow Parkers intimate tone to shine out with the added bonus of a sparkling modern backing track that never falls short of the towering standard set decades before.
author: Chris Jones

text: This is one example of a soundtrack that requires no visual accompaniment at all.
author: Chris Jones

text: Trombonist Nils Wogram is pretty much unknown over here but has made a name for himself on the Eurojazz circuit, and this double CD is a fine showcase of his talent as both a player and composer.
author: Peter Marsh

text: CD one is given over to Wogram's sextet, an all brass affair plus drums featuring New York luminaries trumpeter Cong Vu and Chris Speed on tenor and clarinet.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The lack of bass or a chordal instrument allows Wogram to explore a wide range of timbres and voicings for his angular, complex compositions; there are some pretty tricky charts here, flawlessly executed, with plenty of solo space for all concerned.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Wogram favours a heavily vocalised approach to his instrument, growls, muting and split toned multiphonics alternate with literally breathtaking (for him anyway) solo flights.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Steffen Schorn's bass clarinet and baritone saxophone is given a lot of room and quite rightly too, as he's a major find, capable of Jimmy Guiffre style lyricism or ferocious blurtings worthy of Peter Brotzmann.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Wogram's writing has the same kind of relentless intricacy favoured by Steve Coleman, though occasionally he allows himself some space to explore less frenetic pastures such as on "Mayamalaragula" (featuring a gorgeous Speed tenor solo),"Spring Pt 2" and the minimalist riffing of "Ganamurti") with delightful results.
author: Peter Marsh

text: CD2 adds Henning Sieverts' bass and the piano of Simon Nabatov.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Nabatov is a much undersung player, whose mix of overripe classicisms and Cecil Taylor derived rhythmic punch fits in well here.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Drummer Jochen Ruckert is superb throughout; swinging, funkier than a barrelful of monkeys and razor sharp on Wogram's assymetric heads.
author: Peter Marsh

text: His rapport with Sieverts and the soloists (particularly Wogram and Schorn) borders on telepathy.
author: Peter Marsh

text: A name to watch for, certainly, as is Wogram's; if you liked Dave Holland's early outings with Steve Coleman, you'll love this.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Like many of his Chicagoan colleagues, Wadada Leo Smith's work has stretched way beyond 'jazz' to include compositions for string quartet, studies of ethnic musics and free improvisation.
author: Peter Marsh

text: As a trumpeter and composer, he's been responsible for some pretty amazing (and sometimes undervalued) music, from his 70s work with Anthony Braxton to the spiritual classic Divine Love and his Yo!
author: Peter Marsh

text: Miles project with guitarist Henry Kaiser, which paid homage to Miles Davis' electric period.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The Golden Quartet line up was a dream Smith had nurtured for some 30 years till their formation in 2000.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The dreaded word 'supergroup' may be in order here; we have pianist Anthony Davis (whose association with Smith stretches back to the mid 70s and who's no mean composer himself), legendary Art Ensemble of Chicago bassist Malachi Favors Maghostut, and the estimable Jack deJohnette (star drummer for Miles, Keith Jarrett and pretty much everyone else).
author: Peter Marsh

text: Smith, like Roscoe Mitchell, values space and the empathy shown by this band ensures that despite its all star nature, there's plenty of it.
author: Peter Marsh

text: There's no free jazz scramble; instead the music has the coolly passionate feel of Miles's classic quintet in their late, just-going-electric mode.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Think Filles de Kilimanjaro or Water Babies.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Davis sprays ripples of Wurlitzer type electric piano over Favors and DeJohnette's warm, funk tingedswing or lays down plangent, rich chording on acoustic piano.
author: Peter Marsh

text: His composer's ear on alert, Davis achieves a fruity collision of classical form and improv fire.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Smith is on incendiary form; his rich, burnished tone echoes the effortless weight and authority of Miles, particularly on the opening 'Al Madinah'.
author: Peter Marsh

text: His swooning harmon muted tones on the sumptuous ballad 'Piru' are tender, fragile and majestic in equal measure, while his duet with Davis on the episodic,through-composed"Kangaroo's Hollow" is a technical tour de force.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Ideas are tossed round with bewildering speed throughout.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Favors is a towering presence as always; equipped with a warm,honeyed tone on the bass,his stately lines alternately float over or lock with DeJohnette's shifting, airy patterns.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The drummer is predictably brilliant, though the rhythmic shoehorning that dominates the closing "Miles Star in 3 Parts" seems stiff and unwieldy, snuffing out any heat generated by the players.Mostly though,this is exploratory, passionate jazzthat's made with love and skill by four singular talents; a supergroup in the truest sense of the word.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Try These: Henry Threadgill - Everybody's Mouth A Book Chicago Underground Duo - Axis & Alignment
author: Peter Marsh

text: Just when we were beginning to despair of any real vocal talent still left out there in today's market, our favourite V - neck woolly jumper -wearing lads are back to reclaim their throne with their 6th album entitled Full Circle.
author: Buki Bakare

text: Since the early 90s, Boyz II Men have been the original blueprint for male harmony groups worldwide, warranting a steady influx of younger disciples eager to step into the ring.
author: Buki Bakare

text: Though it has to be said very few appear to have come even close to matching the quartets unique vocal range.
author: Buki Bakare

text: After disappointing sales of their last two albums, the award winning Philly four return from a two year hiatus, having left their long-standing label; Motown in favour for Arista.
author: Buki Bakare

text: The Boyz (although I think we can now safely assume they are men), have once again wisely teamed up with their previous winning production formula; LA Reid with Jam and Lewis.
author: Buki Bakare

text: Full Circle sees a return to the familiar signature Boyz II Men sound that we have grown accustomed to; smooth textured ballads accompanied with unmistakable soothing harmonious tones.
author: Buki Bakare

text: With an unwavering effort to complete with the current younger artists they have added a dash of hip-hop flava for good measure.
author: Buki Bakare

text: The outcome however is somewhat dubious, particularly on tracks like "Aint a Thang Wrong" and "Roll wit it".
author: Buki Bakare

text: "Motownphilly" these aint!
author: Buki Bakare

text: However one track where it does seem to work is "Relax Your Mind"; up-tempo but with that chill out vibe, it has all the right ingredients, including Faith Evans.
author: Buki Bakare

text: Noticeable tracks are "The Colour of Love".
author: Buki Bakare

text: Written of course by Babyface, this is classic Boyz II Men drawing you in swiftly and refusing to let you go, and "Oh Well" which demonstrates their exceptional skill of heavenly sounding harmonies, while Shawn sweetly sings of "Maybe tomorrows".
author: Buki Bakare

text: The placid use of strings and percussions on "Thats why I love you" evokes a gentle almost tranquil inner feeling and with Michaels sexy Barritone voice it adds that extra kick, ladies beware!
author: Buki Bakare

text: All in all, this album makes a true return to top form that has been lacking in their previous albums.
author: Buki Bakare

text: A decade on, over 60 million record sales and countless accolades later, our four friends are determined to show us they still remain the cream of the crop when it comes to romantic soul, and although the up-tempo tracks are unlikely to be "Skip proof." Boyz II Men fans and anyone who truly appreciates what constitutes as good quality Rhythm and Blues cannot be disappointed with Full Circle.
author: Buki Bakare

text: Now if we could just get them to leave the pullovers and white socks at home...
author: Buki Bakare

text: This anglo-irish three piece have taken DIY garage punk to the extreme, receiving the well-earned cliche-rich reviews in the music press you'd expect from a band who this time are talented enough to be dubbed the-next-big-thing.
author: Jules Willis

text: Having been dropped by Geffen Records, Andrew Ferris and Jamie Burchell refused to quit, resulting in one of the hardest working stories in album production.
author: Jules Willis

text: Recruiting Jamie's brother Raife on drums, they built their own straight-to-tape Studios in a shed in West Sussex and began recording songs in earnest at weekends over the course of a year.
author: Jules Willis

text: Soon they bought more equipment and booked themselves five weeks straight in their studio in the summer of 2001, resulting in just two backing tracks.
author: Jules Willis

text: But they persevered until early spring 2002 when they finished recording their debut Zero for Conduct.
author: Jules Willis

text: In true punk DIY style, Jamie and Andrew formed their own label Smalltown America and pressed the record.
author: Jules Willis

text: They released their first single from the album "This is not Revolution Rock" through the independent Yogaboy Records set up by Nathan McGough, ex-manager of the Happy Mondays and the rest is media history.
author: Jules Willis

text: The second single "Summer Ends" was released February 2002 and in March Zero for Conduct was re-released on Yogaboy as Smalltown America had already sold out.
author: Jules Willis

text: The mass market appeal of this album lays in the driving optimistic vivacity released as singles but the real mesmerism comes from the gorgeously contemplative "Underground Queen" and the quivering melancholic reverb in "End of the Night".
author: Jules Willis

text: The album genre-hops through its eleven honed tracks from the rhythmically diverse backing to the vengeful grit in Andrew's voice on "What the argument has changed" to melodic US punk lightheartedness with "The boy you love to hate".
author: Jules Willis

text: The glorious Hendrix-esque anthemic intro to "Atom dreams in technicolour" is the final burst of energy before the retrospective acoustic simplicity draws the album to a close with "A miracle of science".
author: Jules Willis

text: This dichotomous debut album of driving rock and soulful yearnings may be titled Zero for Conduct but Jetplane Landing's diverse songwriting talents and sheer determination will have them at the top of the class before the year is out.
author: Jules Willis

text: Smooth Jazz - not everybody's cup of decaf latte perhaps, but there's little doubt that the movement owes a lot to keyboardist Bob James, whose early CTI albums pretty much defined the genre and provided hip hop producers with a whole bunch of breaks and beats (James has also been working with turntablist Rob Swift of late).
author: Peter Marsh

text: Fourplay is probably the smooth jazz group to top the lot, featuring James, guitarist Larry Carlton (formerly of the Crusaders and sessioneer for everyone from Steely Dan to Streisand), bassist Nathan East (usually found with Eric Clapton) and drummer Harvey Mason, whose fatback funk shuffle powered jazz funk classics by Charles Earland and George Benson.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Despite the players undoubted pedigrees, previous Fourplay albums have shown an understandable tendency to play safe; the fussiness of the arrangements and the unnaturally shiny production often yielded superficially attractive music that lacked bite.
author: Peter Marsh

text: (A bit like a decaf latte in fact).
author: Peter Marsh

text: Heartfelt ups the ante though; this time round the band have abandoned their normal working processes in favour of a more collective approach, jamming in the studio then reassembling, editing and buffing up the results.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Tracks like the opening "Galaxia" and "Cafe L'Amour" have an open ended, relaxed propulsion, anchored by Mason's crisp drumming (sometimes bolstered by programmed beats) and East's fat, sharp basslines which are always on the money.
author: Peter Marsh

text: It's easy to forget what a fine soloist James can be (and one with intriguing beginnings - check out his ESP album "Explosions").
author: Peter Marsh

text: He's back on the Fender Rhodes too for some of the time, which lends the music a warm, organic feel reminiscent of early James classics like "Nautilus".
author: Peter Marsh

text: Again, Larry Carlton (who replaced Lee Ritenour a couple of albums ago) is a masterful player whose mix of jazz harmonic sense with a bluesman's bite is never less than impressive, particularly on the collectively composed numbers.
author: Peter Marsh

text: He cuts loose beautifully on "Cafe L'Amour" for a few bars in a manner that could teach John Scofield a few tricks.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Throughout his control and expressivity are always ear catching; his acoustic playing on the Pat Metheny-esque title track is rather lovely too.
author: Peter Marsh

text: A few tracks don't come off; Mason's "Ju Ju" is a bluesy shuffle without much going for it save Carlton's solo, and East's vocal feature "Let's Make Love" is airbrushed soul cliche which seems out of place here.
author: Peter Marsh

text: But for the most part this is a record that's hard not to like, played with craft and affection; next time round can we have a little more rough with the smooth please ?
author: Peter Marsh

text: Recorded in 1979, Fred Frith's first solo album proper after the demise of Henry Cow probably came as a bit of a shock to die hard fans.
author: Peter Marsh

text: With the Cow, Frith's angular, sour melodics had mapped an alternative route for progrock guitar heroics, while his solo guitar recordings suggested our Fred as the missing link between John Cage and Jimi Hendrix.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Gravity however, was Fred's dance record; not the fashionable mutant disco of the early downtown New York scene (where Frith was in the process of setting up stall) but a celebration of rhythm that borrows from folk music, rock and God knows what else.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Not that I could imagine dancing to it, but theres no denying the infectious beauty that Fred and his co-conspirators (drawn from Swedish avant folkies Zamla, Aqsak Maboul and U.S.
author: Peter Marsh

text: progsters the Muffins) create.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Kicking off with a burst of manic laughter, a spot of tap dancing and random percussion overlaid with Frith's distinctive keening violin, Gravity manages to be wildly eclectic yet avoids incoherence.
author: Peter Marsh

text: A few years before World Music became the accepted method for revitalising washed up rock stars careers, Frith had created an album that seems to be from everywhere at once yet from nowhere in particular.
author: Peter Marsh

text: While the tricky metrics of "Hands of the Juggler" and the slurred fiddle gymnastics of "A Career in Real Estate" hint at some half remembered Slavic folk tradition (as did some of Frith's writing for Brechtian industrial doomfolk trio The Art Bears), the supple immediacy of tunes like "Spring Any Day Now" or "Norrgarden Nyvla" sound at once familiar yet like nothing youve heard before or since.
author: Peter Marsh

text: "Crack in the Concrete" prefigures Frith's avant power trio Massacre, with coruscating e-bowed guitar soaring over edgy, dissonant chords and a massed kazoo choir of horns in the distance, though its bumptious rhythms come with a lopsided grin as opposed to furrowed brow intensity.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Likewise Fred's gleeful de/reconstruction of Martha and the Vandellas "Dancing in the Street"; a bizzarely harmonised guitar negotiates the melody over a boiling mass of feedback and tape manipulation (including a recording of Iranian demonstrators celebrating the capture of American hostages), eventually settling into a spare, gorgeous guitar solo over the closing chords.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Even at its most intense, Gravity is a joyful noise.
author: Peter Marsh

text: If you can manage dancing in the time signatures Fred and his mates cook up, you'd better start moving the furniture in anticipation.
author: Peter Marsh

text: A brief snatch of the 13st Puerto Rico Summertime Band closes Year of the Monkey; "ten seconds of the real thing" said Fred in the sleevenotes to the original issue; he shouldn't have been so modest.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Its hard to approach a double CD that tracks a whole songbook, re-cast as orchestral pieces, with anything but a sense of trepidation.
author: Chris Jones

text: And when bassist, co-producer and ex-partner Larry Klein tells you that: "...we have tried to maintain the same challenging spirit of adventure that has always been a part of [Joni's] music...take the time to let these versions of Joni's songs slowly wash over you'', you know that Travelogue isn't going to be an easy ride.
author: Chris Jones

text: You'd be right, too.
author: Chris Jones

text: Mitchell professes to be disgusted with the contemporary music scene and this is a supposed swansong.
author: Chris Jones

text: In summing up her career, this icon of cerebral West Coast songcraft has produced a substantial body of work without one iota of sentimentality.
author: Chris Jones

text: One look at the musicians on offer here - Herbie Hancock, Wayne Shorter, Billy Preston, Billy Blades - gives one a distinct message: this is not music for idiots.
author: Chris Jones

text: This turns out to be both the album's strength and weakness.
author: Chris Jones

text: For all of her heavy friends, Travelogue can make for some heavy going.
author: Chris Jones

text: As on the previous Both Sides Now, Joni pitches her wonderfully matured (as in a fine wine) voice against an orchestra and becomes an interpretive singer; but this time of her own work.
author: Chris Jones

text: From Song To A Seagull all the way to Turbulent Indigo, songs are re-tooled and re-contextualized.
author: Chris Jones

text: In most cases the results take a while to sink in, approaching a cumulative ambience that resists analysis.
author: Chris Jones

text: However, once the finer points are exposed it's plain that there's much to appreciate.
author: Chris Jones

text: Subtle arrangementsframe Mitchell's lyrics in a new light, making more recent work such as ''Sex Kills'' and ''Borderline'' seem even more like the tone poems she's obviously keen to move towards.
author: Chris Jones

text: Her jazz leanings are easily catered for by the stellar cast and one can't help but be impressed by tracks that swing as well as ''Be Cool'' or ''You Dream Flat Tires''.
author: Chris Jones

text: It's when the Mitchell classics are attempted that listener tolerance is put to the test.
author: Chris Jones

text: Songs as historically contextualized as ''Woodstock'' or ''The Circle Game'' would probably be safer in the hands of others.
author: Chris Jones

text: Under her they merely turn from pointillistic snapshots into abstract expressionism.
author: Chris Jones

text: Vast swathes of strings add little to the original impact of the song.
author: Chris Jones

text: As a touchstone of musical intelligence Joni's position is beyond question.
author: Chris Jones

text: However her stance over the last few years has veered towards the specious philosophy that older forms such as jazz or classical equate to more serious vehicles for her dissections of modern America.
author: Chris Jones

text: The fact remains that by the time of Hissing Of The Summer Lawns she was beyond this need for critical validity and, as such, Travelogue often smacks too much of revisionism.
author: Chris Jones

text: That said it's still head and shoulders above anything her contemporaries have offered us recently.
author: Chris Jones

text: And that's something we really should be grateful for.
author: Chris Jones

text: Let's hope it's not the last...
author: Chris Jones

text: Takagi Masakatsu splits his time between video art, installations and music, and over his last 3 cds has perfected a brand of impressionistic, fragile electronica that sits well with the lush, sometimes abstract imagery of his visual work.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Eating compiles pieces recorded between 1996 and 2002, and inhabits the same headspace mapped out by Susumo Yokota or Nobukazu Takemura's Childs View project.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Over 13 short tracks, Masakatsu constructs delicate minimalist soundscapes populated with clicking digital marimbas, soft, spectral shimmers and gentle arpeggiated chords from crystalline electric piano sounds.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Streaks of faltering accordion or (as on the sunkissed Burt Bacharach stylings of 'Fausel") semi-cheesy organ lines wander through; occasionally cloudy, distant beats emerge ("Mihyn").
author: Peter Marsh

text: Some pieces offer a bit more grit; "Angje" builds nagging synthetic rhythms that eventually flower into a muted breakbeat matrix, while the odd "Woei" flirts with a studied discordance.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Elsewhere though, Masakatsu offers seductive ambience that at its least successful borders on twee (as in the dayglo plastic textures of "trot").
author: Peter Marsh

text: Where he scores is in his sensitive deployment of texture and simple yet effective deployment of musical material.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Chords hang unresolved, or faltering rhythms underpin fragmented yet graceful melodies.
author: Peter Marsh

text: For the most part, Masakatsu avoids the glitch, preferring to create subtle discontinuities through big intervallic leaps and occasional rhythmic eccentricites.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Though sounding dissimilar, Masakatsu's work echoes that of Brian Eno's semi-ambient works in that both harbour a slight, intangible sense of threat beneath their still,unbroken surfaces.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Worth a listen.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Scottish duo of Orde Meikle and Stuart McMillan, return this month with Year Zero - their highly awaited follow up to Alien Radio - which is already sending pundits scurrying for their thesauruses for creative superlatives.
author: Jack Smith

text: Slam's reputation is built on a foundation of being one of the dependable, invigorating sources of high-quality dancefloor tackle; the bar has been set high.
author: Jack Smith

text: Yet to their credit Year Zero lives up to the hoopla, mixing and matching influences that range from electro ("Metropolitan Cosmopolitan") to '80s pop (Billie Ray Martin features on synthetic soul of "Bright Lights Fading" - imagine the chanteuse singing along to Kraftwerk's subterranean rhythms).
author: Jack Smith

text: In between the musical spectrum swings from funky grooves to even dub influences: the Princely-sounding "Fast Lane" featuring Envoy's chant-like delivery tones, and the old skool sounding electro-etched "Blow Your Mind" respectively.
author: Jack Smith

text: Accompaniment includes Detroit techno doyenne Anne Saunderson on the upcoming single "Lie To Me" - a slick slice of emotive house, falling somewhere between her pop-tinged Inner City and gospel-orientated Reese Project recordings.
author: Jack Smith

text: But it's the welcome return of fellow Glaswegian, Dot Allison (who's unique tones graced Alien Radio), that steals the show with the haunting simply ethereal "Kill The Pain".
author: Jack Smith

text: The duo's love of warm danceable grooves, with a strong and sometimes leftfield-edge are reflected in the very essence of this conceptual collection, that aptly demonstrates why Slam are firmly ensconced as one of the UK's leading electronic producers.
author: Jack Smith

text: This is a compilation on LTJ Bukem's Good Looking label.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: I've heard of only one of the twelve artists, many of whom have fascinatingly odd names (Greenfly, Bun, Fluff or Hand Polished anyone?).
author: Colin Buttimer

text: A few tasters follow: Things kick off with "Drifting Sun" by Stylin': mellow, repeating figures swoop and soar in the middle air, there's a nice piano solo; this is a track with a good, upbeat feel.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Percussion patterns shift and change until I realise I'm already a couple of minutes into a new track (the cd's mixed down).
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Cadien's "Solaria" comes surfing in on a low tropical wave - pixels visible only if you freezeframe - a cocktail of 808 State circa Pacific State and 4Hero/Two Pages.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Continuing the optimistic feel with a stronger edge, building things up - very nice.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: "Grasshopper" by Sian introduces bongos, wah guitar, electric piano and flute and segues nicely from the previous track; shades of Lonnie Liston Smith's "Expansions", but for the new millennium.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Hand Polished's "Conceptually Confused" has a nice, urgent bass call answered by dips and dashes of electronica maybe from a particularly virulent Warp/Intelligent Listening compilation, snares fizz and flash, this is the sound of speeding through a tunnel, breaking the speed limit.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Phluff's "Fast Movers" feels like we're in an alternate universe where breakbeat broke out in the 60s, loping percussion, soul piano and big strings.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: So, 10 years and more later ­is this where breakbeat is?
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Well no, this is not one of those rare, defining compilations, but it's an indicator of one of the tributaries downstream of the breakbeat delta.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: There's a cool heat here, maybe all that's left of the sonic reverb you get in the jungle, but it's enough to give the listener a sense of space and detail.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Nothing will bite you here, there's nothing fatal like a bludclot art attack but that might sometimes be a good thing.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: There are various flavours here: hiphop, vocal, house etc., however the sense of a drum'n'bass diaspora leads to a sense of cohesion and flow.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: This is Sunday afternoon music for taking it easy after a long slow waking up while you make the breakfast with the sun coming in the window.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: ­ If it's raining, Soul Obsession will make up for it.
author: Colin Buttimer
