text: Last years Invisible Nature was the first album from Surman and DeJohnette in twenty years.
author: John Eyles

text: It was almost entirely improvised, and worked very successfully.
author: John Eyles

text: In contrast to many recent Surman releases, it highlighted his skills as an improviser rather than a composer.
author: John Eyles

text: But with Surman, that distinction soon becomes blurred; as an improviser, he is an instant composer.
author: John Eyles

text: This new release with DeJohnette (recorded live at Robert Wyatt's Meltdown in 2001)makes an intriguing companion piece to Invisible Nature.
author: John Eyles

text: It puts the spotlight on Surman the composer but again re-emphasises the blurring of that distinction.
author: John Eyles

text: Surman's compositional style has remained remarkably consistent for decades now.
author: John Eyles

text: It has a quintessentially English feel, synthesising the influences of folk music and the English classical tradition.
author: John Eyles

text: This piece displays many of Surman's trademarks - deceptive simplicity, lilting lyricism, subtle melodies, and seamless transitions into improvisation.
author: John Eyles

text: It consists of nine movements connected by improvisations that are developments of the written material.
author: John Eyles

text: Surman and DeJohnette are joined by the ten-piece classical ensemble London Brass.
author: John Eyles

text: The ensemble sections are all notated, whereas Surman and DeJohnette effectively improvise throughout.
author: John Eyles

text: But this is not one of those awkward jazz meets classical situations where the classical players need dots to read otherwise they cannot function.
author: John Eyles

text: Surman is experienced in writing for brass through his previous work with The Brass Project and John Warren, but this project integrates him with the brass better than that ever did.
author: John Eyles

text: He plays to the strengths of all the musicians involved here.
author: John Eyles

text: London Brass trombonist Richard Edwards, trumpeter John Barclay and French horn player Richard Bissill all contribute significant improvisations to these bridging passages, debunking the idea that classical players always need the dots.
author: John Eyles

text: Given their track record, it hardly needs saying that Surman and DeJohnette are excellent; to hear Surman's baritone saxophone roar out of the ensemble passage on "Sea Change" and then take off on a solo is simply exhilarating.
author: John Eyles

text: Some three years after their last album, the boys and girls from Oregon are back with another set of long, stoned trawls through the backwaters of American folk, psychedelia and the avant garde.
author: Peter Marsh

text: And I mean long...one track is listed at 45 minutes.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Actually that turns out be a misprint, but still four of the seven tracks exceed the ten minute mark.
author: Peter Marsh

text: And they're the best ones.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Here JOMF drift from spacerock noodling (sounding uncannily like Gong at times) to stoned, mumbled half-songs, generating a forlorn, ragged beauty in the process.
author: Peter Marsh

text: This time around the songs seem to sit better alongside the band's more exploratory tendencies, rather than sounding tacked on.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The closing 'Louder Roared The Sea' is astonishingly lovely; a dense, immersive but ungraspable spacerock ballad.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Since the heady days of Gunther Schuller's Third Stream experiments, many have tried putting jazz and classical musicians together in a darkened room in the hope of magical fusions.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The usual result has been compromised blandness, but The Source and Different Cikadas is exquisite proof that such collaborations can be made in heaven (or at least in Oslo).
author: Peter Marsh

text: The Source are a composing/improvised collective sort of led by saxophonist Trygve Seim, trombonist Øyvind Braekke and drummer Per Oddvar Johansen, who provide all the original compositions here.
author: Peter Marsh

text: They're joined by satellite members bassist Finn Guttormsen and the wonderful trumpeter Arve Henriksen, plus guests Christian Wallumrod on piano and accordionist Frode Haltli.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The 'different Cikadas' alluded to are the Cikada string quartet; ECM regulars and collaborators with Arild Andersen and Annette Peacock.
author: Peter Marsh

text: With a background in new music, the Cikadas are naturally seasoned improvisers, while the Source's composers declare interest in the methods of John Cage, Stockhausen and Xenakis, so there's a definite middle ground waiting to be shared.
author: Peter Marsh

text: As you may have guessed by now, this isn't exactly dinner jazz, but neither is it a dry, difficult academic exercise.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The writing is vibrant, witty and often beautiful.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Throughout the cast of players shifts, giving each piece a distinctive character.
author: Peter Marsh

text: While pieces like the opening "Organismus Vitalis" unite horns and strings in a sweet chunk of graceful minimalism, others rub genres together to create delicious frictions.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The Ligeti plays bop moves of "Fort Jazz" jumpcut between fractured bop lines and delirious pointillistic strings in a way that's ironic but not knowing; this isn't just musical in-joking.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Elsewhere, Henriksen's plaintive trumpet leads Johansen's swooningly lovely "Mmball", or Seim's keening, duduk like soprano floats over glassy, slow moving strings worthy of Arvo Part ("Bhavana").
author: Peter Marsh

text: The harmolodic rough n' tumble of "Uten Forbindelse" leaves the strings behind for cut and thrust avant bebop, with Seim whipping out his claraphone (a tenor sax with bass clarinet mouthpiece).
author: Peter Marsh

text: Braekke's compositions "Saltpastill" and "Sen Kjellertango" are more formalised slices of jazz writing (the latter a nod to the off kilter tango of Astor Piazzola).
author: Peter Marsh

text: But these guys can make it up as they go along just as well as they can write it down; the two free improvisations are stuffed with ideas yet marked by a restraint and a sense of space rarely found in jazz (except maybe on other ECM records).
author: Peter Marsh

text: The closing "Tutti Free" finds the whole 11 piece slowly expanding and contracting as one with a sensitivity and power that's almost unfathomable.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Always hard to second-guess, Kelly Joe Phelps has made an album that's utterly straightforward and yet completely impenetrable.
author: Chris Jones

text: While he's impeccably assured and well-versed in real old-time country blues, his approach to song structure is equally impressionistic.
author: Chris Jones

text: Not a man for the old verse, verse, chorus etc.
author: Chris Jones

text: structure; his songs of rusting broken things and fractured memories are oblique to the point of non-existence.
author: Chris Jones

text: This leaves the listener with one hell of a job to do...
author: Chris Jones

text: Slingshot is, as always, centred around Phelps exemplary acoustic picking, captured live.
author: Chris Jones

text: But this time around he's played this down even more than last year's Beggars Oil EP.
author: Chris Jones

text: As he says in the accompanying press release: 'Earlier on I found myself absorbed by the sound of the guitar...These days my curiosity and passion are piqued by words'.
author: Chris Jones

text: Sure enough, these words approach the condition of poetry, full of memories, snapshots of tiny details and great miniature character studies.
author: Chris Jones

text: Yet they're all delivered with the same authentic smokey voice that signifies 'weary blues'.
author: Chris Jones

text: Without recourse to the CD booklet you'll find they wash over you like wind and rain.
author: Chris Jones

text: And unfortunately it's difficult to pay the weather your full attention.
author: Chris Jones

text: Recorded with two bands -one featuring long-time fan Bill Frisell, the other with three members of Zubot and Dawson -the albumdoes succeed as a piece of warm ensemble playing.
author: Chris Jones

text: Frisell's trademark tones on ''Not So Far To Go'' and ''Cardboard Box Of Batteries'' turn Phelps' ragged tales into softer, more melodic snapshots, while Jesse Zubot's fiddle on ''It's James Now'' lifts the foursquare blues format into a more folk-flavoured realm a little reminiscent of Nickel Creek.
author: Chris Jones

text: It seems needlessly harsh to critique a work with such integrity.
author: Chris Jones

text: But while a live performance by the man is never less than compelling, this studio effort resists repeated attempts to engage the listener.
author: Chris Jones

text: Neither blues testament nor T S Eliot, Phelps runs the risk of our indifference.
author: Chris Jones

text: And that, for a man this talented, would be a crime.
author: Chris Jones

text: This live two-disc set was recorded on the East and West Coasts of the USA.
author: Martin Longley

text: Frisell's repertoire is dominated by standards, some less obvious than others, and peppered with his own dedications to inspirational figures.
author: Martin Longley

text: The guitarist makes a point of refusing to state these melodies obviously, circling around their outskirts and often holding back on their full delivery until the last possible moment.
author: Martin Longley

text: Disc number one might just have the edge, riled up as it is with a tougher mood.
author: Martin Longley

text: Kenny Wollesen drums on both dates, with Viktor Krauss playing bass on this West disc, which was laid down at Yoshi's club, in Oakland, California.
author: Martin Longley

text: Frisell continues exploring the realms of digital effects boxes, though keeping his manipulations well in check, tweaking with a touch of repeat here, covertly mangling into a backwards splice there.
author: Martin Longley

text: "I Heard It Through The Grapevine" is taken at what must be called a lumbering pace, given a very minimalist treatment.
author: Martin Longley

text: Krauss grumbles out a low bassline, and keeps on walking during the slogging and sleazy "Blues For Los Angeles".
author: Martin Longley

text: Here, Frisell delivers some of his most potent soloing in recent memory, cranked up for a brutal flood.
author: Martin Longley

text: "Boubacar" is dedicated to Boubacar Traore, the guitarist with whom Frisell collaborated on The Intercontinentals album.
author: Martin Longley

text: It doesn't employ any of his Malian stylistic tics, but this is no doubt an intentional avoidance.
author: Martin Longley

text: The second disc was recorded at the Village Vanguard in New York, with Tony Scherr on bass.
author: Martin Longley

text: This set is more relaxed, with Frisell exploring a semi-acoustic sound.
author: Martin Longley

text: Its opening numbers are "My Man's Gone Now" and "Days Of Wine And Roses", and the house style is suitably straight-ahead.
author: Martin Longley

text: In fact, rarely has Frisell stood so close to mainline jazz tradition.
author: Martin Longley

text: This makes the wonky turn of the brief "You Can Run" and the extended rolling of "Ron Carter" all the more unusual.
author: Martin Longley

text: Frisell emphasises each micrometer of the melody, ending up with a mimicking of chiming bells, accompanied by groany bass-bowing.
author: Martin Longley

text: The trio surprise again as they suddenly slam into a bone-pulverising interlude, then back to tender sluggishness, as Frisell operates the eternal twang lever on "Goodnight Irene".
author: Martin Longley

text: The guitarist is now entering an unpredictable career phase, where each new album is embarking on a different journey, sometimes delving back to prior concerns, and sometimes looking for new adventures.
author: Martin Longley

text: This is the one where Frisell grabs his axe roughly by the neck, and subjects it to every loving-position in the book, all the while exposed by an obsessive zoom lens, his trio partners leaving him ample space to preen.
author: Martin Longley

text: With his last few ECM albums, Tomasz Stanko has been on a roll, consistently producing jazz of the very highest standard.
author: John Eyles

text: Albums such as Leonia, Litania and From the Green Hill were recorded with a variable cast, including such well-known names as Bobo Stenson, Tony Oxley, John Surman and Terje Rypdal.
author: John Eyles

text: Here, by contrast, Stanko has decided to feature the young Polish rhythm section with whom he has played since 1994 - Marcin Wasilewski on piano, Slawomir Kurkiewicz on bass and Michal Miskiewicz on drums.
author: John Eyles

text: The results are the equal of any of those earlier albums, maintaining their level of creativity and surpassing them in the beauty of the music.
author: John Eyles

text: Even now, after eight years experience with Stanko, the band members are still only in their mid-twenties, but they play together with an ease and understanding of each other that make age irrelevant.
author: John Eyles

text: They know Stanko's music intimately (what Polish jazz musician doesn't?) and their understated playing provides a sympathetic setting for him.
author: John Eyles

text: Stanko's trumpet playing has long attracted comparisons with Miles Davis.
author: John Eyles

text: If anything, those comparisons are more valid than ever here.
author: John Eyles

text: A defining characteristic of Miles' music was his use of space and dramatic pauses; what he chose to leave out was more important than what he chose to put in, both in his own playing and in that of his bands.
author: John Eyles

text: Exactly the same is true of this band's music; it has a beautiful simplicity and economy about it.
author: John Eyles

text: When one isolates the contributions of individuals, they can sound sparse and overly impressionistic; when one listens to the totality, all the pieces fit together and it makes perfect sense, with the whole being far greater than the sum of the parts.
author: John Eyles

text: The album takes the form of an extended composition in thirteen separate parts ("variations"), the longest lasting only just over eight minutes.
author: John Eyles

text: The pieces have a consistency of tempo, sound and mood that gives the album an overarching unity.
author: John Eyles

text: To be fully appreciated, the album needs to be heard in its entirety (but if you need to sample one piece, try "Variation VII").
author: John Eyles

text: Stanko's writing throughout is exquisite - full of melody, soul and allusions to past work.
author: John Eyles

text: In my younger days living in New York, I would spend every Sunday afternoon seeing countless hardcore and punk bands at the all-ages "Matinee" show at CBGB's in New York City.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Cause For Alarm, Snapcase, Shelter, Earth Crisis were regulars and everyone I knew had at least three Victory releases in their record collection at any given time.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Time may have moved on but the Chicago hardcore label has gone from strength to strength: they are now on the road to moving credible heavy music away from the middle class white suburbs of America to a global audience.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Taking Back Sunday are one of these new breed of Victory bands.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Formed in 1999, they attracted attention with a 5 song demo that quickly impressed the emo contingent on the east coast.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Hailing from Amityville, New York, they bring a welcome mix of original styles to an overcrowded playing field.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: The band flirt with an interesting mix of southern Californian post-punk, nu-metal and old school hardcore but "Tell All Your Friends" refuses to be pinned down to just one.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: A constant through the album is their ability to write fantastically catchy songs that are poppy and fun as they are upbeat and emotionally aggressive.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Tracks like the opener "You're So Last Summer", "Timberwolves at New Jersey" and the excellent "You Know How I Do" could easily veer down the path of conventionality but instead hold true to their punk roots.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: It's a lot more All Or Descendents than it is Blink 182 or Sum-41 (what's with the numbers you punk people?) but still retains enough of its own identity to keep the band above the rest.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: The band have already amassed an impressive tour schedule - playing with bands like The Alkaline Trio, At The Drive In and Rival Schools and with songs this good, they look ready to explode and lead the charge for the new school of excellent new music coming out of the US.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: For those of you into the post-punk sound, you need this in your CD collection.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: One to watch in 2002 for sure.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: There's a famous story about critic Richard Williams, who while writing for the Times in the early 1970s was sent a copy of a John Lennon/Yoko Ono album to review.
author: Peter Marsh

text: One side of the album consisted of a single, unmodulated sine tone.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Williams was initially a bit taken aback, but after a few listens began to enjoy what he heard, remarking in his review on how the record drew attention to imperfections in the vinyl, how it made for a deeply meditative experience and so on.
author: Peter Marsh

text: It turned out he'd been sent an engineer's test pressing by mistake, with a reference 1khz sine tone on one side instead of the music.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Though Williams was derided for this, Brian Eno rightly pointed out that his response (though conditioned by the fact that this was a John Lennon record and therefore worthy of attention) was an honest enough one.
author: Peter Marsh

text: John Cage would have been proud of him.
author: Peter Marsh

text: And so it is with this release on the prolific and deeply odd Raster Noton label, though presumably this CD is not a victim of a mix up at the pressing plant.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Carl Michael von Hausswolff, though perhaps not quite as well known as John Lennon has been producing electronic music for around 20 years, and his concern has been often with basic, untreated electronic sound sources, prefiguring the current wave of activity in this ultra-minimalist area spearheaded by the likes of Ryoji Ikeda, Carsten Nicolai and so on.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Recently he has become interested in EVP (Electronic Voice Phenomena), detecting voices from the spirit world buried in radio static or white noise.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Strom maybe a continuation of that interest; whatever, it's 48 minutes of what sounds suspiciously like mains hum, occasionally decorated with blips, slow gaseous hisses and radio static.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Listening under headphones is like sitting in a giant, elderly valve driven radio that can't quite warm up and is tuned permanently at a remote end of the dial where even the Voice of America can't be bothered to broadcast.
author: Peter Marsh

text: At reasonable volume through speakers, the resonant hum is likely to kill any nearby goldfish and can be heard in every room in the house.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Move around while listening and the hum changes to a low, soothing throb or at particularly resonant points in the room, vibrates your skull rather unpleasantly.
author: Peter Marsh

text: But it's when it finally stops that the disc does its work.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The hum's absence is maybe even more powerful than its presence - things sound different, brighter, more vivid, not unlike after your ears have been syringed.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Definitely for the intrepid.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Beth Orton has collaborated with Jim O'Rourke to produce this, her fourth album - and a very grown-up affair it is too.
author: Zoe Street

text: Those who found the lo-fi Daybreaker a bit dreary can take heart because Comfort Of Strangers has a brighter slant altogether.
author: Zoe Street

text: Bleakness is shunned in favour of full-bodied warmth; with harmonies, harmonicas and blissed-out strings throughout.
author: Zoe Street

text: Opening track "Worms" is sweetly upbeat despite love-burnt lyrics -very Aidan Smith.
author: Zoe Street

text: "Shopping Trolley" is a beaut, with joyous crashing drums and pianos supporting Orton's fragile hoots.
author: Zoe Street

text: "Heart Of Soul" is another winner, strident and romantic.
author: Zoe Street

text: "Feral Children" floats along magically though Orton's quavery holler can grate after a while.
author: Zoe Street

text: All in all a very rounded release and a bit of a grower.
author: Zoe Street

text: Ursula Rucker's 2001 debut album Supa Sista wasn't all it could have been.
author: Jack Smith

text: Yes, the verbals kicked and sure, some of the beats rocked, but the sparse, metallic atmospheres and raw, uncompromising nature of the poetics left many feeling cold and even a little alienated.
author: Jack Smith

text: Given Rucker's status as the urban wordsmith of choice for super-melodic acts like Japan's Silent Poets, Germany's Jazzanova, UK's 4 Hero and local Phillie heroes King Britt and The Roots, this austerity came as something of a surprise.
author: Jack Smith

text: Thankfully, Silver Or Lead addresses these issues head on.
author: Jack Smith

text: Instead of hiring a new set of beatmakers, Rucker has commendably re-recruited the same coterie of friends and associates that graced her first outing, commissioning tunes that better compliment her sassy attitude, melody and streetwise head-funk.
author: Jack Smith

text: A showcase of new and unreleased tracks as well as a retrospective of some of her finest moments (most of which have only been previously released on other peoples fulllengths), Silver Or Lead is a more mature and less inhibited record.
author: Jack Smith

text: Cuts like "Time", her philosophical team up with 4 Hero grooves, and the highly personal "Return To Innocence Lost" (which deals with the violent death of her brother) are included here, alongside a continuous flow of swirling soul and melodious thunk supplied by the likes of Rob Yancey, Jazzanova, King Britt, Mysterium and Lil Louie Vega.
author: Jack Smith

text: Within these streams and rivers of sound which take us through Afro-latino, hypnotic hip hop and deep drum & bass, verbal blow after verbal blow is rained upon us as Rucker invests the English language with a rhythm and power all of her own.
author: Jack Smith

text: There's a Septemeber 11 critique on "Release", self-reflection on "Lonely Can Be Sweet", poetic brutality on "What a Woman Must Do" and slavery tales on "Soon".
author: Jack Smith

text: Throughout, Rucker's velvety voice manages to both mollify and add a sinister dimension to the harshness of her subject matter.
author: Jack Smith

text: With her follow up, she has thus created a finely balanced document which is melodic enough to make the hips swing and thought-provoking enough to demand repeated listening.
author: Jack Smith

text: Jimi Hendrix played two shows at Berkeley on 30 May 1970, which have long been both legendary and unreleased.
author: Rob Fawcett

text: Some legendary recordings maintain their fascination only by being unavailable.
author: Rob Fawcett

text: In this case the recordings have been oft-heard in remarkable quality on bootlegs, and the few officially released individual tracks (including ''Johnny B Goode'', and the Rainbow Bridge LP version of ''Hear My Train a Comin''') have been magnificent.
author: Rob Fawcett

text: The weakest point in the set, as so often with gigs from the era, is the start.
author: Rob Fawcett

text: First tracks were often presented as a warm up lap rather than the pyrotechnic rabble-rouser we expect today.
author: Rob Fawcett

text: This opener, an early incarnation of ''Straight Ahead'', is too obviously half-built to achieve much momentum.
author: Rob Fawcett

text: After that, however, there's very little to complain about.
author: Rob Fawcett

text: ''Hey Baby (New Rising Sun)'' is a strong candidate for the best recorded version, studio included (though it's a shocking change of pace when Jimi reverses it at full tilt into the In The West classic ''Lover Man'').
author: Rob Fawcett

text: With Billy Cox on bass, songs like ''Stone Free'' and ''Hey Joe'' are short punchy performances, unlike the epic versions the 68-69 Experience would offer.
author: Rob Fawcett

text: Breathing space is instead given to fresher classics such as ''Machine Gun'' and ''Voodoo Child (Slight Return)''.
author: Rob Fawcett

text: The pace of the show is great, with every song is presented complete and in sequence (many live Hendrix releases, particularly before Experience Hendrix took over his estate, have suffered bizarre editing and re-ordering).
author: Rob Fawcett

text: The sound quality is as good as any live Hendrix, certainly putting the likes of Woodstock and existing Berkeley bootlegs to shame.
author: Rob Fawcett

text: The DVD release of the (shamefully poor) film of this show comes with a bonus 5.1 surround-sound mix of the whole CD album and is a treat if you have the equipment.
author: Rob Fawcett

text: The only disappointment of this release is that only one of the two Berkeley shows has been released.
author: Rob Fawcett

text: The first set is arguably as strong, and was the source for the prior releases of ''Hear My Train'' and ''Johnny B Goode''.
author: Rob Fawcett

text: None the less, this is the strongest newly-released Hendrix material in a long time.
author: Rob Fawcett

text: Homelife are describable in as much as they're a Manchester based collective formed around bassist Paddy Steer and including local heroes like Graham Massey (of 808 State and Bjork fame), Andy Diagram and others too numerous to name, but describing their music is a different matter.
author: Peter Marsh

text: If I was writing a press release for them it'd have to go something like...'imagine Sun Ra, Joe Meek, Brian Wilson, Fela Kuti,, Martin Denny and George Clinton having a scrap in a second hand record shop and you'll be half way there', but it falls way short as a description.
author: Peter Marsh

text: There's nothing calculatedly trendyin Homelife's ramshackle fusions; it all sounds like it just happened by accident, and by some quirk of fate the tape was running to capture it.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Propelled by squelchy analogue synths, eccentric drumming and the tiny bashings of a thousand percussion instruments, Homelife's floating collective produce a richly exotic global fusion without coming across as the usual WOMAD worthies or cynical cultural magpies; bass clarinets jostle with glowing strings, failing drum machines, recorders and the creaky funk of ancient clavinets.It is astrange but potent brew.
author: Peter Marsh

text: As on previous albums (notably the fab Flying Wonders) songs emerge as though someone's actually writing them while they're being played; yet they're often perfect pop songs.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Vocalist Faron Brooks is back to lend his honeyed Nashville twang to the forlorn, wonky disco vibe of "Harder" and the psychedelic tropicalia of "April Sunshine", while the title track's falsetto funk will bore itself into your brain and stay there for ever.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Likewise, the cosmic Toytown-esque fusion of "A Casa" and the rainforest groove of "Windytreehouserollerdisco" carry hooks so sharp you don't feel them going in.
author: Peter Marsh

text: There are reflective moments too; the fragile oriental drift of "Big Tree" or the bizarrelywarped ballad"Strangers".
author: Peter Marsh

text: There's even a hymn of praise to the much maligned banjo, which can't be a bad thing.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Brian Eno once stated that, despite hardly anyone buying this album on its release, everyone that did buy it seemed to have formed a band.
author: Chris Jones

text: Ladies and gentlemen, we are talking about one of the three most influential albums of all time (what are the other two?
author: Chris Jones

text: You work it out, dear reader).
author: Chris Jones

text: Without this slice of plastic there would have been no glam rock, no krautrock and no punk.
author: Chris Jones

text: If Lou and John hadn't decided to ditch their respective careers in order to blur the boundary between pop and avant garde there would have been no Stooges, Can, David Bowie (as we know him) or Roxy Music.
author: Chris Jones

text: Oh, and The Jesus And Mary Chain would have had no career whatsoever.
author: Chris Jones

text: Which is why this deluxe treatment is long overdue and entirely welcome.
author: Chris Jones

text: The tale of how this masterpiece even made it into the racks has long since passed into the realms of legend - Andy Warhol spotting them at a New York club and offering to produce them (i.e.
author: Chris Jones

text: putting up the money).
author: Chris Jones

text: The way he foisted Teutonic femme fatale Nico onto the band and the way she proceeded to set Lou against John (by sleeping with and rejecting them both).
author: Chris Jones

text: The year-long delay before the album made it to the shops (by which time Warhol had lost interest) - It all boils down to one inescapable fact.
author: Chris Jones

text: Even by 1967 this was still frighteningly original music that had as little to do with pop or rock as Frank Zappa's first album, *Freak Out *(which, interestingly enough, was also produced by Tom Wilson).
author: Chris Jones

text: For the very first time a rock band were writing songs that were utterly nihilistic and seemed to come from the very flipside of the psychedelic love-fest that was (if you believed the hype) occurring everywhere else.
author: Chris Jones

text: Here was a group that knew of the depths of perversity to which people could sink and frankly sounded as if they didn't care either.
author: Chris Jones

text: Songs like "Heroin" or "Waiting For The Man" didn't simply hint, they graphically laid out the stories of degradation as if daring you to turn away.
author: Chris Jones

text: It was all wrapped in a musical package that was as stark as its subjects.
author: Chris Jones

text: Reed's oddly scraped 'ostrich' guitar, Cale's droning viola and not least Mo Tucker's almost moronic proto-motorik drumming all added up to a canvas that even when set behind Nico's bored drone couldn't fail to alarm, if all you'd been listening to was the Beatles and their ilk.
author: Chris Jones

text: This release sees the addition, not only of the rare mono mix but the tracks recorded for Nico's first solo outing Chelsea Girls, with the band backing her.
author: Chris Jones

text: Strangely these extras serve to demonstrate, as with tracks such as "Sunday Morning" or "There She Goes Again" that the Velvets could always revert to pop parameters if needed.
author: Chris Jones

text: They just didn't want to.
author: Chris Jones

text: Offerings as extreme as "The Black Angels Death Song" or "European Son" were always going to be the moments that really remained in the minds of those brave enough to experience this album.
author: Chris Jones

text: Not many did and unbelievably it remained a semi-obscurity long after its release, with only rock scribes and musicians enhancing its reputation by word of mouth.
author: Chris Jones

text: Acceptance as a 'classic' hasn't diminished its awesome power to shock and provoke one jot.
author: Chris Jones

text: If you've never heard it, your life will be changed.
author: Chris Jones

text: If you've already got it, it's still an essential purchase.
author: Chris Jones

text: A monument to the evil that men (and women) do.
author: Chris Jones

text: A typically expansive, eclectic and challenging set by England's own saxophone colossus, but this one is special for several reasons.
author: Bill Tilland

text: Firstly, it was conceived as a celebration of Paul Dunmall's fiftieth birthday, with Dunmall writing music for a large jazz group and soliciting the participation of some of his long-time associates, including his three colleagues in the Mujician quartet; Keith Tippett on piano, Paul Rogers on bass and Tony Levin on drums.
author: Bill Tilland

text: Secondly, as Dunmall observes in the CD notes, the drama of the Iraq war inadvertently insinuated itself into the composing process, and while it would be presumptuous to identify this or that musical element as being triggered by Dunmall's reactions to the war, the program does include some overtly spiritual references.
author: Bill Tilland

text: These begin with the CD title and the appropriation of the Hindu word Moksha ("the supreme final liberation of the soul") as part of the bands name.
author: Bill Tilland

text: The first of the three long tracks (which are simply called Parts One, Two and Three) begins with a tamboura-like drone and some sinuous modal blowing from Dunmall, which in the early going evokes the thoughtful meditative lyricism of Charles Lloyd more than the ecstatic intensity of John Coltrane.
author: Bill Tilland

text: However, when the full band enters with a somber legato motif at around the six minute mark, Dunmall quickly heads for the high country, his frenzied flurries punctuated by percussive stabs from Tippett's piano and the rolling boil of drummers Levin and Mark Sanders.
author: Bill Tilland

text: All the classic Coltrane-isms are here in spades the sheets of sound, the hoarse cries, the honks and ecstatic squeals although Dunmall's use of the Coltrane vocabulary has long since transcended imitation, and as he demonstrates here, he is one of the most eloquent and natural energy players on saxophones today.
author: Bill Tilland

text: Part One is Dunmall's feature, but he yields to his bandmates for much of Part Two, which begins as a friendly freeform conversation between the two trombones and then unwinds, so to speak, into a relaxed and relatively conventional post-bop groove featuring Simon Picard (I assume) on tenor and a ringing, almost Gillespie-like trumpet from Gethin Liddington.
author: Bill Tilland

text: Dunmall jumps in briefly, stirring the pot and raising the energy level, but then gives way to a mellow duet between trumpet and tuned percussion.
author: Bill Tilland

text: The high point of this section is Dunmall's extended dialogue with John Adams on electric guitar.
author: Bill Tilland

text: Adams scatters his staccato splinters of sound in colloquy with Dunmall's smears and growls, as Dunmall walks a fine line between shamanistic testifying and a more muscular, gritty swagger that can be traced back to Sonny Rollins.
author: Bill Tilland

text: The section ends almost whimsically with the band fixating upon a repeated bop riff and then finishing with an extended atonal blast.
author: Bill Tilland

text: More surprises await the fortunate listener in the third and final section, starting with Paul Rogers' marvelously melodic upper-register arco bass work and some curious wobbling and squiggling from the two guitars.
author: Bill Tilland

text: Dunmall adds fluttery runs on soprano sax, cushioned by the leisurely meandering of the full band.
author: Bill Tilland

text: The dirge-like theme gradually grows more intense, and when Dunmall switches from soprano back to tenor, individual members of the band begin to break away occasionally with their own flurries and bleats, led by Dunmall's impassioned wailing.
author: Bill Tilland

text: The exhilarating close is very much in the late style of Coltrane's Meditations; a swirling, overwhelming maelstrom of sound which is all at once terrifying and liberating.
author: Bill Tilland

text: When this birthday journey finally ends, some serious musical and emotional ground has been covered.
author: Bill Tilland

text: Over the last 25 years Mike Harding and Jon Wozencroft's Touch imprint has established itself as one of the UK's most worthwhile and challenging labels.
author: Peter Marsh

text: To celebrate their quarter century, they've compiled previously unissued works from the likes of Biosphere, Chris Watson, Philip Jeckand Ryoji Ikedain a typically beautiful package.
author: Peter Marsh

text: As with the label's output in general, there's a lot of variety; from deep listening droneologyto field recordings to lush electronica.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Much of it is staggeringly beautiful, and that seems to be the aesthetic that binds all this disparate stuff together.The sounds of a rusty dredger squealing its way up the River Clyde or the brutal distortotronica of Pan Sonic nestle snugly alongside the Oren Ambarchi's womblike drones or Fennesz's gauzy electro-acoustics.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Some bursts of found sound (from in-flight announcements to news reports to sundry 'field' recordings) appear between tracks, gently (and sometimes not so gently)disorientating the listener.
author: Peter Marsh

text: There's some powerful stuff here; Biosphere's "Spring Fever" is one of the most hallucinatory, dreamlike three minutes and twelve seconds I've had for a long while.
author: Peter Marsh

text: This fantastically moody disc is somehow unclassifiable.
author: Liz Mundler

text: Sometimes jazz, sometimes classical, definitely crossover in the truest sense of the word.
author: Liz Mundler

text: Ukrainian pianist Misha Alperin is the inspiration behind it.
author: Liz Mundler

text: He wrote the work Night in response to a commission from the 25th VossaJazz Festival in Norway (April 1998), and this is a live recording made at that event.
author: Liz Mundler

text: Classically trained, Alperin came late to jazz, but has developed his own very personal style interwoven with folk influences from his musical roots.
author: Liz Mundler

text: The gorgeously mellow velvet-black sound of cellist Anja Lechner suits Alperin's meditative meanderings perfectly.
author: Liz Mundler

text: "Adagio" is particularly stilling, with melodic wanderings complemented by moments of harmonic peace and clarity.
author: Liz Mundler

text: "Tango" is a different story, but told in the same language.
author: Liz Mundler

text: Here a tamed riot of energy meets Alperin's restraining calm, tempered by the understated contributions of Norwegian percussionist Sørensen.
author: Liz Mundler

text: He and his marimba come into their own in "Second Game", where all 3 musicians join together in what begins as a sort of fugue, melds itself into several minutes of harmonically rich Glassian minimalism, and eventually develops into an energetic driving jig-style 6/8 rhythm.
author: Liz Mundler

text: "Night", says Alperin, "is a time of suprises".
author: Liz Mundler

text: And surprises there are, from the vocal contributions from the percussionist, to the startlingly dramatic ending to "Second Game"; "you can walk through a silent village and catch a blast of sound from a bar door suddenly thrown open".
author: Liz Mundler

text: Ah, perhaps that's what it was.
author: Liz Mundler

text: "Heavy Hour" is another track which will wake you up rather than send you to sleep, with tribal rhythms and a twangy-zangy cello sound which even sets your teeth on edge at times.
author: Liz Mundler

text: The title trackhas got to be the most atmospheric: a faintly eerie percussive tick-tock sets the scene, joined by arching, sighing cello phrases and occasional keyboard outbursts.
author: Liz Mundler

text: Some of the harmonic tensions and resolutions reach right into the soul.

text: "It's music for those hours when you don't need to prove anything to the world, when the need for self-presentation subsides".

text: More hardcore improvised abstraction from Konk Pack, whose Big Deep was one of the more impressive improv discs of last year.
author: Peter Marsh

text: While that album was recorded live on tour, Warp Out finds Thomas Lehn, Tim Hodgkinson and Roger Turner in the studio, though this is very much a raw, live and (in)direct recording, as you might expect.
author: Peter Marsh

text: It's a less full on experience as a result, with much use being made of lengthy passages of well...not very much, alternated with occasional hyperspeed dialogue.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Turner is still the pivotal figure in the group; describing him as a drummer is well short of the mark.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Using an arsenal of springs, tools and the kind of stuff you'd find left over from the average car boot sale (plus a tiny 'proper' kit), Turner extracts weirdly funked up beats, skewed African rhythms and occasional depth charge kick drum accents which consistently tickle the ear, while simultaneously sounding like a man methodically dismantling his kit rather than playing it.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Thomas Lehn's analogue synth is all shortwave blips, sawtoothed bursts and alien chattering that sometimes recall the gleeful oscillator fests found on early Faust records.
author: Peter Marsh

text: His constant timbral changes spur Turner into quicksilver dialogue, particularly on the closing "Sach".
author: Peter Marsh

text: Though Hodgkinson is better known as a reeds player and keyboardist through both his improv work and his tenure with avant rockers Henry Cow and the Work, he's taken to the guitar in the last few years (played flat).
author: Peter Marsh

text: His playing is more austere than on Big Deep, rattling off scrapes and stunted scrabbles with occasional distended, detuned bass action.
author: Peter Marsh

text: He's most effective on "White Jem", where his heavily effected avant rockisms recall his old sparring partner Fred Frith's work in Massacre.
author: Peter Marsh

text: What makes Konk Pack special is their ability to generate densely impacted material which doesn't sound like a mess; though the more restrained passages sometimes seem unfocussed, there's plenty of sonic wonderment to keep the intrepid listener's ears firmly pricked.
author: Peter Marsh

text: And so it goes for nearly all of this subdued little (flawed) masterpiece.
author: Chris Jones

text: It's a quiet which stems from confidence and the only times that the band actually approach anything like an upbeat stance, are on the wryly amusing "D Scott Parsley" and the title track which, believe it or not, is a reggae song!
author: Chris Jones

text: Ultimately this is a mood piece.
author: Chris Jones

text: Slow, elegaic and unhurried, it settles like summer dust on the ears and never once presumes to pierce the aura of quiet contemplation.
author: Chris Jones

text: As to its meaning?
author: Chris Jones

text: The abstract wordplay always restricts the listener's total acceptance, and the album's very sameness can let the mind wander a little too much.
author: Chris Jones

text: Yet Wagner's muse will always provide a compelling view and should be treasured for at least daring to steer its own path through the woods.
author: Chris Jones

text: What a confusing thing it is to be a Garth Brooks fan these days.
author: Chris Jones

text: Having sold 100 million albums (that's a lot of rhinestones), the man obviously had a serious identity crisis.
author: Chris Jones

text: Trying out for a baseball team, preparing himself for a film role in the ill-fated The Lamb by actually trying to turn himself into the lead character, Chris Gaines (releasing a fictional greatest hits under the pseudonym) and then hinting that his next album would be his last.
author: Chris Jones

text: Now it seems that he may have been bluffing, or at least attempting to balance his turbulent private life with his career.
author: Chris Jones

text: Certainly The Scarecrow displays no sign of the man - who single-handedly made the concept of a multi-platinum country artist a reality - saying farewell.
author: Chris Jones

text: With its customary mix of power ballads ("Thicker Than Blood"), Merle Haggard influenced honk tonkin' ("Big Money" and the song featured at this year's CMA awards, the George Jones duet "Beer Run") and pop crossovers (Wrapped Up In You"), this album is bound to bring back at least part of the audience who were too confused to buy The Magic Of Christmas.
author: Chris Jones

text: He even finds time to include a vogueish bluegrass version of America's "Don't Cross The River".
author: Chris Jones

text: At the start of the year Brooks had hinted that this would be a fairly dark record, but it seems his mood has lifted - he recently said that: "Somewhere in the spring it popped open.
author: Chris Jones

text: It was happy".
author: Chris Jones

text: In providing us with a set of songs this uplifting and unsurprising he has done exactly what his public demands of him.
author: Chris Jones

text: This is after all what he does best.
author: Chris Jones

text: It would also be a crying shame if his career confusion led to him retiring from live work as plenty of the songs here would really suit his barnstorming live act, particularly his duet with Trisha Yearwood - "Squeeze Me In".
author: Chris Jones

text: So, is everything alright with Mr Brooks now?
author: Chris Jones

text: His mother's death (which inspired " When You Come Back To Me") and the responsibility of fatherhood reportedly weigh heavy on him, and it is these issues which may make it a long wait for those wanting to see the legend in concert again.
author: Chris Jones

text: Yet, with its cover photographs reinforcing the notion of Garth as a born-again cowpoke, it would seem that business is slowly returning to normal.
author: Chris Jones

text: This is one Scarecrow with more than his fair share of brains.
author: Chris Jones

text: Tom Jenkinson's nom de plume is an apt one; whether mashing up drum 'n' bass into hyperspeed mindwarps, infecting two step garage with digital viruses or jazzing it up with his fretless bass, his music pushes the envelope pretty hard.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Beats are squeezed, twisted, mutated and accelerated to the max;in Spinal Tap style, everything seems seemsset set permanently at 11.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Last year's Go Plastic saw Squarepusher back in fully electronic mode, leaving behind the industrialist cyberjazz moves of Music is Rotted One Note.
author: Peter Marsh

text: This new album follows much the same path, though the release of the title track as a single a couple of months ago had critics rummaging through their dictionaries for adequate superlatives.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Over distressed, scratchy beats Jenkinson knits a patchwork of glutinous synth stabs, processed voice and sudden noisestorms with an assurance that recalls his best work (Big Loada, Port Rhombus), but it's not really the leap in the dark we've been led to expect.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Neither is "F-Train", which recycles the usual stop start beats with doomy sci-fi babble narration.
author: Peter Marsh

text: It's difficult to tell whether Tom's tongue is in his cheek or in our ears.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The same goes for "Anstromm-Feck 4", which opens with a challenge; "so you think you're hard do you?..Squarepusher's gonna take your f***ing face off".
author: Peter Marsh

text: I'm afraidTom's usualdrum 'n' bass accelerated to spin cycle speed trick left your humble reviewer's face still attached to the front of his head.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Whereas "Come on My Selector" can still induce sensory overload, this merely irritates.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Things take an upturn with the 10 minute "Mutilation Colony";gorgeous blurred organ chords build till overtaken by a bout of bleak electronics, punctuated by seismic pulses and ending up as an electroacoustic exploration of the properties of cymbals.
author: Peter Marsh

text: It's music charged with possibilities; rigorous yet posessing a sensuality Jenkinson seems at pains to avoid elsewhere.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The album ends with a faithful (yet pointless)rendition of Joy Division's "Love Will Tear us Apart", while the CD comes with a bonus, near bootlegquality recording of the Pusher live in Tokyo.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Both are probably for completists only.
author: Peter Marsh

text: One of Jenkinson's avowed aims is for his music to resist commodification; an admirably punkish attitude, and one that makes a lot of sense, but in much of this album, there's a sense of stasis lurking behind the attitude.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Music that's easy to admire, but hard to love.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Try These: Squarepusher - Go Plastic Autechre - Gantz_Graf Martin Horntveth - Fast Motion
author: Peter Marsh

text: Though the cover and title are more than a little reminiscent of Alanis Morissette or even Tori Amos, Nerina Pallot is a slightly different proposition.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Yes, she's a singer songwriter, and yes, she's obviously listened to a lot of Joni Mitchell, but there's a pure pop sensibility to this record that lifts her out of the 'this year's Tanita Tikaram' category.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Dear Frustrated Superstar draws on elements of trip hop, Crowded House type post-Beatles pop and classic singer songwriter introversion, all topped off with lashings of strings and very little evidence of synths, drum machines or samples.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Doubtless comparisons will be made with Dido, but Pallot comes across more like an anglicised Shawn Colvin, with the potential to be much more than either comparison might suggest.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Quite a few of the songs here immediately jump out as singles (unfortunately "Patience", her current single, isn't really one of them)."Watch out Billie", a warning to a young female would be pop star about the perils of fame, (not dedicated to the current Mrs Chris Evans, surely) is one of those songs that bores itself into your brain and stays there for ever; "If I Know You", "Rainbow" and "Alien" aren't far behind in terms of infectiousness though.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Pallot's voice is, like Colvin's, reminiscent of her heroine Joni Mitchell and even occasionally a less quirky Kate Bush; she gives fine, unaffected performances throughout and enlivens even the less inspired songs with her delivery.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The only problem with the record is that it's too long, though the closer, "My Last Tango", and the subsequent hidden track are two of the album's highlights; a more expansive, acoustic feel predominates here in contrast to the crisply executed pop of the rest of the record.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Definitely a name to watch out for.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Jazz interpretations of pop songs were still a relatively fresh notion when Gordon Beck and chums recorded this set in 1967.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Though much standard jazz repertoire was (and is) based on 30s and 40s pop songs, the advent of rock and roll with its emphasis on foursquare rhythm and unsophisticated harmony meant that few of its tunes were taken up by the jazzers; this was raw material unsuited to the extended harmony of bebop and its cousins.
author: Peter Marsh

text: It's unclear whether Beck was rising to a commercial or an artistic challenge when he arranged this selection of 60s pop toons, but the results justify what must have been a considerable effort.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The leader's piano is crucial in delineating the often highly modified harmonies on tunes like "These Boots were made for Walking" (not the most obvious choice for a jazz rendering).
author: Peter Marsh

text: Beck's splashy chords and octave runs are straight out of the Bill Evans book, but there's an intensity and drive to his solos that is very much his own, and his sound is much brighter, almost bell-like.
author: Peter Marsh

text: He's joined here by John(ny) Mclaughlin in his pre fusion days, bassistJeff Clyneand drummer Tony Oxley.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Oxley played with fellow Yorkshireman Mclaughlin on the latter's seminal Extrapolation a couple of years later and it's clear that the pair were building up a valuable association; Oxley's snare volleys and cymbal torrents are a perfect foil for Mclaughlin's fractured bop lines.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Solos are kept short and sweet, redirecting the focus toward the arrangements rather than displays of individual virtuosity, though the leader's contributions are a bit overcooked at times.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Beck's skills as an arranger are convincing; though he can't do much with the apallingly trite "Up, Up and Away" (a song which would still sound twee in the hands of Motorhead) he manages wonders with many of the other pieces.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The Who's "I Can See for Miles" moves from pensive balladry to ferocious swing - despite Beck's altered chords the melody shines through.
author: Peter Marsh

text: It's best to try and forget the originals if possible and just enjoy this record on its own terms, difficult though it may be with songs like "Good Vibrations".
author: Peter Marsh

text: Despite its obvious Carnaby Street/Julie Christie vibe, Experiments with Pops has a lot of fine moments from some extraordinary musicians and has much more going for it than historical importance.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The Romanian George Enescu was something of an all-round musical genius.
author: Claire Rogers

text: Not only an excellent composer, he was also a first-rate violinist and conductor, and an accomplished pianist and cellist with a formidable musical memory.The three works on this excellent CD span almost 30 years of his career, but each one is as fascinating as the other in its own way, and Adelina Oprean and her brother team up brilliantly to meet each of their challenges.
author: Claire Rogers

text: Adelina Oprean in many ways has the perfect background to tackle these works.
author: Claire Rogers

text: To begin with she's Romanian, which, given the evocative, Romanian folk-inspired element of Enescu's musical make-up, has to be a bonus, and she's also an ex-pupil of Yehudi Menuhin, Enescu's most illustrious and devoted violin pupil.
author: Claire Rogers

text: Enescu's two sonatas take us into fascinatingly different sound-worlds, and sandwiched between them is the enigmatic Sonata 'Torso', one of various works which he left unfinished during his career.
author: Claire Rogers

text: It's the only time this movement has ever been recorded, which is one more reason to go out and buy this CD.
author: Claire Rogers

text: Sonata no.2 is a stunning early work, heavily tinged with Brahmsian sonorities and rhythms.
author: Claire Rogers

text: Oprean captures the mood of the sinuous opening theme of the first movement and the wistful understatement of the Tranquillo slow movement beautifully, as well as playing the more impassioned sections with great command and feeling, before launching deftly into the spirited dance-like finale.
author: Claire Rogers

text: By contrast Sonata no.3 is pure Romanian folk music, but with a difference - there are no real folk tunes here.
author: Claire Rogers

text: Enescu chose instead to write it all himself, annotating the score in incredible detail to explain exactly how each violinistic effect is to be achieved.Menuhin said of these markings that if observed one cannot help but sound like a true gypsy violinist.
author: Claire Rogers

text: But a great technique is also called for, and Oprean manages to negotiate the endless fiendish harmonics of the first two movements with style.Justin Oprean's piano playing hauntingly conjures up the sounds of the cimbalom so closely associated with Romanian folk music, and together they capture brilliantly the contrasting moods of the work, from the mysterious, nocturnal world of the second movement, to the spikier rhythms of the dance-like finale with its almost savage ending.
author: Claire Rogers

text: It's impossible to come away from this music without wondering why on earth Enescu's violin music isn't better known, and well thought-out recordings like this one are hopefully a step in the direction of redressing that balance.
author: Claire Rogers

text: Another Groove Armada album?
author: Christian Hopwood

text: So soon after the last one?
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Yep, Andy and Tom seem to be the embodiment of the old adage about resting and being wicked.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: No sooner have we put Goodbye Country...
author: Christian Hopwood

text: back in its sleeve (or case depending on your format preference) they go and release another record.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: By their own admission the Armada are tired of being labelled 'chill out' and bored of seeing "At The River" appear for the hundredth time on the latest compilation with a picture of a sunset, or ice cube for that matter, on the front of it.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Whether the approach on this new album is a phat, two fingered salute against this is up for debate.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Either way the boys are here to rock!
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Thankfully, the opening number "Purple Haze" is not a cover of the Hendrix classic.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: That said we are treated to a giant guitar riff which according the sleeve notes could well be a Status Quo sample (yes!) over which Red Rat and Nappy Roots get to extol the virtues of their favourite psychoactive.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Similarly "Madder" follows suit with a triumphant speaker bashing, six string crescendo.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Red Rat returns for emcee detail on the awesome "Final Shakedown".
author: Christian Hopwood

text: This is dirty, ragga house at its best and picks up from where "Super Stylin" left off.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: "Groove Armada mash up the place..." Indeed!
author: Christian Hopwood

text: The hands-in-the-air moment is delivered with absolute aplomb in "Easy" with Sunshine Anderson icing the house music cake with her soaring and, dare we say, eye watering vocals.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: The single and title track "Love Box" is classic Groove Armada and is up there with "Chicago", one of Vertigo's most sublime moments.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: The breathy, melancholy synths, Balearic sparkle and surging bass line, like Chicane's "Offshore", create a real end of the summer vibe and bring the record to a close, but not before the bouncy, trumpet sprung, ska-tastic "But I Feel Good".
author: Christian Hopwood

text: As an album Lovebox doesn't hang together as well as Vertigo or Goodbye Country but choon-wise there are still some absolute blinders here.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Given the extensive gigging and touring undertaken by GA over the last twelve months it seems very likely that most of this album has been written with the live arena in mind.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: With their end of 2002 tour nearly upon us, it's sounding like Messrs Cato and Findlay are fully intent on embarking on a nationwide campaign of roof removal.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Try These: Groove Armada - Goodbye Country Hello Nightclub Basement Jaxx - Rooty Chemical Brothers - Come With Us

text: It's difficult third album time for Laura Cantrell, whose first two releases delighted and intoxicated many (including Mr John Peel, to whose memory this album is dedicated).
author: Peter Marsh

text: Now signed to indie label Matador and with a supporting cast that includes members of Calexico, it'd be easy to imagine this record ending up as a trainwreck, derailed by unsympathetic production,ill advised song choices and so on.
author: Peter Marsh

text: And it could so easily have been that way, but hey, everything's ok.From the opening "14th Street" it's clear that Ms Cantrell's ear fora good tune hasn't deserted her.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Written by NYC singer songwriter Emily Spray, it's a dreamy slice of bittersweet pop (more sweet than bitter) that I'll probably never tire of.Cantrell's clear, conversational tone maybe understated, but she can deliver the kind of emotional punch that Kate Rusby can (iewhen you're not expecting it).
author: Peter Marsh

text: This is true for most of this record, and especially so on Cantrell's own "Khaki & Corduroy" and the (almost) title track "Bees".
author: Peter Marsh

text: Both are beautifully wistful, impressionistic observations that attest to her growing strength as a writer.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Even though as ever her choice of covers is exemplary, from Lucinda Williams'"Letters"to Bakersfield boy Wynn Stewart's "Wishful Thinking".
author: Peter Marsh

text: The only slight disappointment is the traditional"Poor Ellen Smith"; Cantrell doesn't really convince singing from the viewpoint of a male murderer.
author: Peter Marsh

text: There again, it might be my lack of imagination that's at fault here...
author: Peter Marsh

text: The guitars may be a bit brasher on occasion and there may be a slightly more expansive (and maybe expensive) approach to production, courtesy of JD Foster, whose credits include Dwight Yoakam, Marc Ribot and Nancy Sinatra.But Cantrell isn't swamped at all; her restraint remains her most powerful weapon.
author: Peter Marsh

text: If "Bees" doesn't bring a lump to your throat, you're much harder than I am.
author: Peter Marsh

text: And with a playing time of just under 39 minutes, you're left wanting much more.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The thing about Lemon Jelly is that they just can't get away from sounding like Lemon Jelly.
author: David Silverman

text: Which I suppose is quite a good thing.
author: David Silverman

text: It's this instantly recognisable mood and swing which captures the ear - allied with trademark breaks and loops dug from dusty records they found at their Grans'.
author: David Silverman

text: They focus on what's important in life and Lost Horizons shines just as brightly as anything they've done previously.
author: David Silverman

text: Fred Deakin and Nick Franglen enjoy life as Lemon Jelly.
author: David Silverman

text: The three elegant 10 EPs that went to create the first album were quietly successful, appearing on numerous TV shows and ads.
author: David Silverman

text: Now, with the energetic single "Space Walk" already reaching the farther echelons of the top 40, it looks like Lost Horizons will be casting its net in the same direction.
author: David Silverman

text: This time, its just got a bit bigger.
author: David Silverman

text: From the smooth horns of opener, "Elements", to the effervescent "The Curse of Ka'Zar", you can tell that Lemon Jelly have definitely got it sussed.
author: David Silverman

text: Weaving a merry dance through tracks like the Charlton Heston narrated "Ramblin' Man" and the children's nursery rhyme of "Nice Weather for Ducks", Lost Horizons is packed full of nifty little samples, beautifully crafted with distant electronica and crisp beats.
author: David Silverman

text: From the sound of trumpet fanfares, to wisened harmonica and flutes, Lemon Jelly have retained their organic roots, and delivered an album which, though weighing in at a mere 8 tracks, is still jolly good.
author: David Silverman

text: Inspired by the Avalanches (or is that the other way round?) and with a sneaky grin flicked at DJ Krush, Lemon Jelly trade somewhere between accessible cut'n'paste and hard-core, coffee table action.
author: David Silverman

text: Lemon Jelly albums reflect an inspired and delicate view of feel good.
author: David Silverman

text: Joined with their graphically designed images adorning the pages of countless magazines and the expensive collectors editions of their records, the boys are gradually turning themselves into a brand.
author: David Silverman

text: Creating beds for radio shows and their prominence on TV and adverts continue to fuel their ever increasing profile.
author: David Silverman

text: This is happy music made for cosy afternoons tucked up on the sofa and if you're looking for something that'll give you a bit of a spring in your step, then you really couldn't do much better.
author: David Silverman

text: Eric Aldea was a member of Lyons based post rockers Bastard, whose collaborators included Chicago luminaries Bundy Brown and Casey Rice, and was previously in industrial hardcore merchants Deity Guns.
author: Peter Marsh

text: His first solo record betrays few of those influences though; compiled from various pieces written for dance company La Baraka, Saturno o Cipolla ?
author: Peter Marsh

text: delivers a warm, organic take on experimental ambient electronics.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Aldeas approach is informed more by the lo-fi layering of industrial types like Zoviet France or the tapeloop outings of Fripp & Eno than by the cut 'n paste glitchscapes beloved by the average bald bloke with a Powerbook, though we do get a bit of digital snap crackle n blip on a couple of pieces.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Elsewhere Aldea delicately weaves together shortwave transmissions, field recordings and acoustic instrumentation with rarely heard skill.
author: Peter Marsh

text: While countless TV advertised ambient compilations may promise to, er, take the listener on a journey, Aldeas gradual unfolding of his pieces seems to do just that.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The thirteen minutes of "02" are especially seductive; opening with a chatter of shortwave crackles and bleeps, an opressive string figure repeats itself to be swept away by a held, suspended chord flecked with bowed double bass harmonics and gurgling synthetics.
author: Peter Marsh

text: A phone goes off somewhere; footsteps are briefly heard.
author: Peter Marsh

text: A gentle synth loop fires up eventually to be overrun by glassy digital tones and telex bleeps which swarm and multiply before abruptly fading.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Here Aldea's manipulation of acoustic space recalls David Toop and Max Eastleys classic Buried Dreams, though is less likely to give you nightmares.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Less successfully, "03" and "04" stray into more conventional electronica territory, with looped sinewave drones, clicks and metallic synthbursts piling up and receding in typical minimal art techno fashion.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The closing trio of pieces save the day though; revolving around mournful, muted strings, alternately decorated with bubbling analogue synth, dolorous cello and distant xylophone figures, they evoke a calm tinted with a vague sense of unease, like seeing a single black cloud in a summer sky.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Immersive, often beautiful and with a slightly ungraspable quality that makes you want to stick it on again as soon as its finished, Saturno o Cipolla ?
author: Peter Marsh

text: may well turn out to be one of the records of the year...
author: Peter Marsh
