text: Anton Webern's music still provokes extreme reactions.
author: John Armstrong

text: In fact the idea of Webern's music is enough to cause a shudder in some people; hearing the name is enough and perish the thought of actually listening to the music.
author: John Armstrong

text: Yet what beauties they miss, and what change.
author: John Armstrong

text: From his early Slow Movement for String Quartet through to the late Op.
author: John Armstrong

text: 28 Quartet over 30 years later you travel from yearning romanticism through Expressionist angst to the atonal 12-note world of Webern's teacher Schonberg, yet with a degree of refinement and crystalline beauty rarely achieved by his master.
author: John Armstrong

text: These new performances from the Artis Quartet of Vienna let you compress this journey into a mere 65 minutes, from first to last.
author: John Armstrong

text: They bring all the warmth those early tonal works cry out for, and somehow manage to carry it through to even the later works, pieces that sometimes receive the coldest of performances from players in awe of Webern's reputation.
author: John Armstrong

text: Maybe it takes a Viennese ensemble to show us that the spirit of Vienna lives in all of this music, not just the obviously romantic early work.
author: John Armstrong

text: It's a pleasure to be reminded that Webern always was a lyrical composer; it's just that he doesn't always get lyrical performances.
author: John Armstrong

text: These from the Artis Quartet ought to win over a few die-hards, assuming of course you can get them to take their fingers out of their ears after hearing the name Webern...
author: John Armstrong

text: If you thought the critics had already exhausted their year's supply of superlatives on Sir Colin Davis's new Berlioz series, then the Trojans proved that the highest praise had been held back.
author: Matt Fernand

text: The acclaim was fully deserved; it's rare enough to get a new recording of this epic opera, but to have it recorded live, and for a second time by perhaps the finest living interpreter of Berlioz, made this really special.
author: Matt Fernand

text: Then add the fact that it's from LSO Live and it's only going to set you back £20.00 (a fiver a disc), and suddenly you can imagine that this remarkable work will find its way into the lives of a whole new audience of potential converts.
author: Matt Fernand

text: About time...and the sales figures so far seem to prove that's exactly what's happening.
author: Matt Fernand

text: So what's so special about the performance?
author: Matt Fernand

text: Try Canadian tenor Ben Heppner, outdoing his fellow countryman Jon Vickers on Sir Colin's first recording of Les Troyens.
author: Matt Fernand

text: The other principals are very fine too; Michelle de Young unexpectedly singing the role of Didon after Olga Borodina fell ill, and Petra Lang as her last-minute replacement, rising to the occasion as a fiery prophetess.
author: Matt Fernand

text: Davis's 1969 recording was the first time Berlioz's Wagnerian epic had been captured complete, but he's lived with this work for another thirty years, and it shows.
author: Matt Fernand

text: And don't forget the LSO's had the same amount of time to grow with Davis, and learn to read his gestures.
author: Matt Fernand

text: The playing is formidable, revelatory, and the big set-pieces have an epic sweep to them.
author: Matt Fernand

text: Yes, even in the Barbican it's possible!
author: Matt Fernand

text: The recording engineers have achieved another minor miracle and made us forget where the four live performances were given.
author: Matt Fernand

text: The audience is spookily silent, and the only indication that this was caught on the wing is the sheer electricity coursing through every bar.
author: Matt Fernand

text: Les Troyens has always deserved this recording, and it might finally bring Berlioz's epic to the audience it deserves.
author: Matt Fernand

text: Owners of the original Colin Davis Trojans for Philips shouldn't fret, but then you probably don't need to: you've already heard the buzz and bought this new recording as well, haven't you?!
author: Matt Fernand

text: Considering that the world's most notorious punks lasted all of 3 years and released only one proper album, it's amazing that a 3 CD set could make it to the shelves at all.
author: Chris Jones

text: But here it is, dripping with snotty attitude, even after 25 years.
author: Chris Jones

text: Don't be fooled, just because John Lydon seems to have swapped irony for greed, this three chord blast still sounds as angry as ever.
author: Chris Jones

text: Of course the usual suspects are here again: the Never Mind The Bollocks tracks, the superb Spunk bootleg demos (step forward and take a bow Chris Spedding!) and the entire legendary Screen On The Green gig.
author: Chris Jones

text: They're all presented in glorious new digital garb and remind some of us of a certain age that simply jumping up and down on the spot was once considered dancing.
author: Chris Jones

text: Let's just not remember what else we did at gigs back then, eh?
author: Chris Jones

text: Added to this are the b-sides, outtakes and cover versions essential to any disciple of the un-fab four.
author: Chris Jones

text: It does the heart good to hear the wondrously dishevelled intro to the Stooges "No Fun", with Rottens snarled "Rrrrright, ere we go naaaooww..." A sociology lecture, indeed.
author: Chris Jones

text: The only sour notes are struck by the inclusion of some completely unrecognizable versions of "The Flowers Of Romance" which bear absolutely no resemblance to the later PIL track and the relentlessly grim closing number from the last gig at the Winterland Ballroom, "Belsen Was A Gas".
author: Chris Jones

text: At least their singer knew that the days of Malcolm McLaren's situationist media provocation were well and truly over.
author: Chris Jones

text: If only the other three had had the sense to walk away.
author: Chris Jones

text: Their later (mis)adventures are thankfully omitted here.
author: Chris Jones

text: So, a tasteful (whoever would have linked that word to the Pistols in 1977?) footnote to this unholy Jubilee and a worthy excuse to fill that gap in your record collection.
author: Chris Jones

text: No doubt the press flurries accompanying the release of this record will be full of references to 'bonkers Icelandic pixie Bjork' or the like, but that would be a severe underestimation of what is after all a singular talent.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Vespertine is Bjork's most personal record, both in that she's had more to do with the music than ever before, and also that it continues with her apparent desire to write songs as confessionals.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Whereas earlier songs like "Human Behaviour" and "Venus as a Boy" were observational, third person affairs, much of her subsequent writing has gravitated towards an intensely intimate self expression.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Pretty much everything on Vespertine is written in the first person, to often quietly devastating emotional effect; there are moments that shock in their honesty, and much that would maybe come across as cliche in someone else's hands.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Like her last album, Homogenic, there's nothing much on the record that's immediate (save perhaps "Hidden Place" or "It's Not Up to You", both which have spine-meltingly gorgeous choruses); this is a record that reveals its secrets slowly.
author: Peter Marsh

text: It's generally a more stripped down affair than previous records; muted beats like footsteps in the snow, whispers, clicks, and sighs open out occasionally into the widescreen lushness of Post and Homogenic; the songs have a mix of fragility and strength which is totally convincing.
author: Peter Marsh

text: As usual, Bjork has chosen her collaborators with much care; UK electronica whiz Herbert, Californian avant laptop duo Matmos, harpist Zeena Parkins, as well as lifting a bit of e.e.
author: Peter Marsh

text: cummings' poetry for "Sun in my Mouth".
author: Peter Marsh

text: There are glacial, slow moving strings, glitchy electronics, blurry atmospherics and even the odd choir lurking in the background, but it's Bjork's singing which steals the show, maybe because it fits so perfectly with the arrangements this time rather than sounding superimposed over them.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Though always an expressive instrument, her voice can still shatter the odd wineglass but here her phrasing seems looser, more plastic, sure enough of itself to sound small and broken at times.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The effect throughout is unapologetically beautiful, totally immersive and often crushingly moving.
author: Peter Marsh

text: It's difficult to pick out highlights from a record that really demands to be listened to in it's entirety, but "Cocoon" and "Undo" stand out (today, anyway).
author: Peter Marsh

text: That Bjork ?

text: When it comes to unstinting devotion to exploring and making available archive material for fan(atics) there can be few labels more committed than Discipline Global Mobile.
author: Chris Jones

text: Only the Grateful Dead with their legendary 'Dick's Picks' series have surpassed Robert Fripp's desire to beat bootleggers at their own game.
author: Chris Jones

text: He's often stated his aim to provide what he sees as a considerable demand for rarities, but has tended to aim product purely at completists.
author: Chris Jones

author: Chris Jones

text: After over 20 soundboard and audience recordings covering all incarnations of the worlds brainiest band have appeared via the online collectors club, this compilation of sorts arrives on high street shelves.
author: Chris Jones

text: Complimenting the recent reissue of the 1971 incarnation's Earthbound (in itself a pseudo bootleg) this wholly new approach will net both casual Crimheads and bona fide nutters alike.
author: Chris Jones

text: For, while one disc consists of highlights from their 71-72 tour - arranged as a virtual gig - the second disc is a different beast.
author: Chris Jones

text: And beast - a word that Fripp himself is prone to use -is the only way to describe this skull-crushing edit of solos from their ultimate manifesto - ''21st Century Schizoid Man'' - entitled ''Schizoid Men (1-11)''.
author: Chris Jones

text: It should be called ''Blowing In C'' for its relentless jazz-tinged attack in one key.
author: Chris Jones

text: Simply put, it's over 50 minutes of almost infinite variety that, due to its sudden termination gives the illusion of continuing to this day.
author: Chris Jones

text: Ian Wallace, in his charming sleeve notes pays homage to original Crimson drummer Mike Giles (''for whom I have nothing but admiration...precise as the Black Watch''), but his freedom around the kit is entirely apt for this looser outfit.
author: Chris Jones

text: This really is as close as they ever got to being funky.
author: Chris Jones

text: The excitement is palpable.
author: Chris Jones

text: Band members yell encouragement as Fripp sets off on a search for God knows what somewhere up at the 17th fret.
author: Chris Jones

author: Chris Jones

text: Poulenc's choral music is unusually taxing for even the finest choirs; the slab-like chords, the strange key changes and awkward intervals are all components of Poulenc's startlingly beautiful textures...yet they bring difficulties for record buyers as well.
author: John Armstrong

text: Some of the most accurate, most perfectly tuned performances available to date have been from the crack British professional choirs, like The Sixteen.
author: John Armstrong

text: Passionate, always musical, often moving...
author: John Armstrong

text: yet somehow just not French enough!
author: John Armstrong

text: There's always a significant difference when you hear French sung by a choir from across the Channel - an added pungency, authentic colouring - but if you pick a French choir for Poulenc you have to accept shaky tuning, less precision, a generally more uncomfortable ride.
author: John Armstrong

text: Ladies and gentlemen, here it is: the happy medium - and in no way does that mean it's a compromise.
author: John Armstrong

text: The Accentus Choir sound as though they've been modelled on the best of British, but they're French with a capital 'rrrrrrrrrrrrrrr', the accent's authentic, and you can feel the depth of their understanding of these texts by Eluard and Apollinaire.
author: John Armstrong

text: Poulenc's choral masterpiece Figure Humaine is a hymn to freedom from occupied France, and it's rarely had anything like this power on record.
author: John Armstrong

text: The lonely chill of Un Soir de Neige is a perfect foil, and lovers of Poulenc or fans of great choral music will be celebrating this cd.
author: John Armstrong

text: Six years...six long years since Time Capsule, an album of angular strings, methodical bass, Rhodes, longform and brief pieces.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Saxophonist Bowden played great solos, but wasn't audible on every track;Time Capsule still comes on like a never-released recording date from an alternative 1973.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: What happened between then and now?
author: Colin Buttimer

text: I heard occasional things, the wonderful 12" collaboration with 4 Hero, much too brief appearances on their Two Pages and Creating Patterns albums (which left me wanting much more).
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Since then he's been playing with the likes of Jessica Lauren and the Herbaliser.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: And now Slightly Askew crashes in (almost literally!).
author: Colin Buttimer

text: The wind arrangement of "Only Angst" comes on like an angry squall when you didn't pack a mac, you're nowhere near any shelter and you're soaked in seconds flat.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Then just to confuse you the rain stops as suddenly as it started, the sun comes out: Bowden's sax is inching and forming shapes as the drums walk him and you along.You're beginning to dry out and along comes another squall.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: You're buffeted by loads of things borne by that wind; organ, trumpet, saxes, piano.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Drums are nervous, metallic, edgy, there's no taking anything for granted; when things quiet down you have to prepare yourself for that cacophonous onslaught returning.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Best not to stand near any steep drops when listening to this one.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: 14 minutes on from pressing the play button and I'm worn out.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: What a way to come back!
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Why's he been away so long?
author: Colin Buttimer

text: "Crockers and Killers" eases up a little bit; there's still those metallic drums, strings weaving in and out, but the bass is more to the fore and married with piano and female voice; the impression is lyrical.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: "Zoo Zoo" is more funky, strident, with gloriously angular (or askew?) string and wind arrangements.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: The first two and a half minutes of "W'p De F' N' Doo" is a duet between Bowden's sax and Tom Gordon's drums until strings, bass and piano join and add a cushioning warmth.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: My first impression of this album was that the sound seemed to be strangely not of this time.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: There's a hell of a lot happening on Slightly Askew's four tracks: many different episodes, musical details; it's not a blowing session, solos are part of a bigger picture and occur where the logic of the music dictates.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: This is jazz where the zz's of the word are the teeth of a saw; at times cutting smoothly, at times rasping through knots.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: This is not polite dinner jazz, thank goodness.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: It's ambitious, thinking music not afraid of expressing feeling.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Chris Bowden is one of the UK's great altoists and composers; Slightly Askew underlines this.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Pleeeeeease don't take so long next time Mr Bowden.

text: Ask an enthusiast about recordings of Mahler's Das Lied von der Erde and you'll end up with a list of classic cds: Kathleen Ferrier, Janet Baker, Klemperer and Bruno Walter.
author: John Armstrong

text: Is it that the contemporary competition just isn't up to scratch, or perhaps that it's such an emotional piece of music that we form a stronger bond with the first recordings we hear?
author: John Armstrong

text: Pierre Boulez has always been the kind of conductor who can challenge your preconceptions in Mahler's music, and his new Song of the Earth deserves a place on your first recording 'pedestal'.
author: John Armstrong

text: He's analytical without sacrificing sentiment; sometimes you feel as though you're way under the skin of the work, getting so much closer to its soul.
author: John Armstrong

text: Make sure there's nothing you have to get done straight after listening to this disc: you'll probably need some space for quiet contemplation.
author: John Armstrong

text: A better title for this CD would be Alchemist, because The Necks have yet again succeeded in turning base metals (i.e.
author: Bill Tilland

text: standard musical ingredients) into gold.
author: Bill Tilland

text: Chemist introduces a slight wrinkle with three tracks of approximately 20 minutes each (instead of the more typical single long track favored by the group), but all the usual elements are here; deep bass ostinati, supple percussive pulse and roiling piano arpeggios (heavy on the sustain pedal).
author: Bill Tilland

text: Still, the little touches and treatments are what elevate a Necks release to a higher level of listening pleasure.
author: Bill Tilland

text: The funky opening "Fatal" adds occasional guitar textures and a distant, soulful organ drone, along with discreet electronic whooshes and small bursts of white noise.
author: Bill Tilland

text: The more minimalist second piece, "Buoyant", begins with randomly generated oscillator beeps, later insinuates the barely perceptible ringing of an alarm bell, and altogether creates a spare but highly charged musical dream state.
author: Bill Tilland

text: "Abillera", the final track, coaxes the sounds of a hammered dulcimer (among other things) out of the piano and plays around with phasing in pleasantly disorienting fashion suggestive of early Steve Reich.
author: Bill Tilland

text: Impeccable ear candy, from start to finish.

text: Tom Waits' last two (simultaneously released) albums contained specifically written pieces for the theatre and found him in a distinctly Brechtian mode.
author: Chris Jones

text: While awesome, one still longed for a return to the classic days of Rain Dogs etc.
author: Chris Jones

text: Thus when it was announced that Real Gone featured the old touring band and a collection of new stand-alone songs excitement ran high.
author: Chris Jones

text: But it seems that this is actually quite a departure...What marks Real Gone as a change of direction for Tom are two things: One is his decision to excise any use of piano or keyboards from the recording process.
author: Chris Jones

text: The second is the use of his own voice.
author: Chris Jones

text: Initial stripped-back home-recordings resulted in Tom using his patent growl as the rhythm track, albeit augmented by drummer Brain Mantia (of Primus).
author: Chris Jones

text: Overdriven and primal, these lolloping grunts and wheezes give the whole album a weirdly steam-driven aesthetic, mirrored in lyrics that highlight the relentless grind of life on the underbelly.
author: Chris Jones

text: Mainly recorded in single takes, the core ensemble of Mantia, Larry Taylor (bass) and Marc Ribot (guitar) swing wild and loose, combining dirty notes with Waits' rasped and shouted lyrics.
author: Chris Jones

text: Additional turntablism by Waits' son Casey adds to the strangely mechanical vibe.
author: Chris Jones

text: Yet it's only the repetitious vibe of men straining under post-industrialism: pile-driven into transgression and misery, but always retaining a gallows humour.
author: Chris Jones

text: Stories of lost love, bitter regret and human life laid waste seem to be the main currency, but Waits and wife Kathleen Brennan's wordplay always narrowly avoids self-parody by use of fantastically impressionistic imagery and wry couplets.
author: Chris Jones

text: Whether it's the resigned calypso shuffle of ''Hoist That Rag'', the processional blues of ''Make It Rain'' ( which contains the priceless line 'I'm not Able, I'm just Cain') or the jazzy shuffle of ''Dead And Lovely'' (a murder ballad sketched in James Ellroy noir shades), Waits comes on, as always, like some socially aware Captain Beefheart, channelling every drunken hobo and down at heel loser that got swept under society's carpet.
author: Chris Jones

text: It's incredible that someone who, these days, is undoubtedly more superannuated than itinerant can still sound this convincing.
author: Chris Jones

text: Only on the hilarious ''Don't Go Into The Barn'' does Tom's brand of louche gothic tip into Nick Cave/Night Of The Hunter southern surrealism territory, and you become concerned that this is grim-by-numbers.
author: Chris Jones

text: But in the company of 14 other instant Waits classics this is a mere niggle.
author: Chris Jones

text: The closing track, ''The Day After Tomorrow'', finally arrives to remind you what a consummate songwriter he is, with its war-weary soldier's letter home a stark reminder of the current world state.
author: Chris Jones

text: Already Real Gone looks like being one of Tom's best...
author: Chris Jones

text: The supremely gifted saxophonist Chris Potter is probably best known for his work with bassist Dave Holland and trumpeter Dave Douglas among others.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Gratitude (which doesn't feature anyone called Dave) is a summation of his influences, with each track dedicated to a saxophone master.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Perhaps the fact that this is his debut for Verve (a classic jazz imprint if ever there was) has something to do with this acknowledgement to jazz tradition, but Potter is undoubtedly sincere in his intentions and has the talent to pull it off.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Though each track has some trace of its dedicatee, Potter hasn't gone for slavish imitation ('tonight Matthew, I'm going to be Lester Young').
author: Peter Marsh

text: Opening with a sweet bluesy blast for John Coltrane, he goes on to adapt a Joe Henderson tune for "Shadow", a lazily funky outing redolent of the tenor player's classic Milestone albums; Kevin Hays' expansive Fender Rhodes is a particularly effective springboard for the leader's tenor explorations.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Potter's most discernible influence is Sonny Rollins; he shares Rollins' rhythmic precision and urgency and consequently his tribute to the great man (a particularly tricky exercise in 15/8) brings out some of his most buoyant, joyful playing.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Likewise "High Noon" (for Eddie Harris") is a lovely slice of langorous, slightly sweaty funk, with drummer Brian Blade (recently heard performing miracles with Wayne Shorter) on top form, chopping bar lengths with surgical precision without sacrificing the groove.
author: Peter Marsh

text: A couple of standards appear too; Potter wisely opts for bass clarinet on "Body and Soul", played as a duet with bassist Scott Colley (dedicated to Coleman Hawkins) and in the process comes up with an original take on ye olde tenor warhorse which doesn't sound like Eric Dolphy - no mean feat.
author: Peter Marsh

text: He switches to alto on "Star Eyes" (unsurprisingly dedicated to Charlie Parker), shoehorns it into 7/4; and it works too, with some desperately exciting seat of the pants interplay between alto and drums.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Not quite a standard is "The Visitor", where Potter takes a trademark Lester Young phrase and bases a composition around it; the results are more Dave Holland than Prez, though there's a tinge of the Porkpie Hat in Potter's generous, sparkling solo.
author: Peter Marsh

text: "Vox Humana" is an impressionistic tone poem for Ornette Coleman, featuring Chinese wood flute and soprano; inspired by Ornette's comment on the saxophone's similarity to the human voice, Potter's playing again evokes Coleman's spirit in some way without sounding much like him.
author: Peter Marsh

text: While Chris Potterisn't out to change the course of jazz history, he doesn't suffer from a Marsalis-like tendency to preserve it in aspic either.
author: Peter Marsh

text: This album is more evidence (if it was needed) of a major talent.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Inspired, beautifully played mainstream jazz, and thoroughly recommended.
author: Peter Marsh

author: Peter Marsh

text: Jim O'Rourke's sizeable discography has covered everything from avant rock to free improvisation to widescreen Americana; his address book includes everyone from Faust to Steve Albini to Fennesz, and recently he's joined up with art punks extraordinaire Sonic Youth.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Though his CV may resemble that of the post modernist genre hopping dabbler, O'Rourke's genuine enthusiasm, expansive knowledge and keen ear has resulted in some fine music as well as the occasional dud.
author: Peter Marsh

text: This album sees Jim boot up his Powerbook in true laptop massive style, though in place of the usual clicks n' cuts beloved of the Mego crowd, he delivers his own individual and heartfelt take on the American minimalist tradition.
author: Peter Marsh

text: On the opening "I'm Happy", O Rourke unleashes piping ostinati sourced from samples of organ, accordion and strings that hypnotically pile up, splinter and regroup into new configurations, sounding much like Steve Reich's Four Organs played underwater on a malfunctioning CD player.
author: Peter Marsh

text: In place of the rigorous addition and subtraction beloved by Reich and his ilk, there's an organic improvisational quality that recalls Terry Riley's solo organ pieces (incidentally these are live recordings, though of course you'd never guess), as eventually Jim's de(con)structive urges crumble the minimal riffery under the weight of pulsing strings and distressed blips.
author: Peter Marsh

text: "I'm Singing" sounds a little like Cluster or Harmonia; a muffled kick drum underpinning swathes of fuzzed guitar melodics emerges from a cloud of sonar bleeps, eventually succumbing to clipped distortions and collapsing in a welter of bells and chimes.
author: Peter Marsh

text: "And a 1,2,3,4" is simply gorgeous; over 21 minutes, a forlorn guitar loop is gradually morphed into a pulsing drone flecked with high oscillations, eventually disappearing in a forest of bleeps and crackles while doleful cello and viola glissandi break the surface.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Like the best of the minimalist canon, O'Rourke's music plays games with time and repetition so that by the end of the piece you're unsure whether 21 seconds, 21 minutes or 21 hours have elapsed.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Unlike so much laptop glitcherama, O'Rourke's digital tools are the means to an end rather than the end itself; this is surprisingly sensual, involving music that doesn't rely on the latest SuperCollider patch for credibility.
author: Peter Marsh

text: If you buy only 25 Jim O'Rourke albums this year, make sure this is one of them.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The fourth in Dolly Parton's series of bluegrass albums is irrepressibly perky.
author: Sue Keogh

text: But whereas the previous three sat folk and country classics next to deliciously unpredictable choices like "Stairway To Heaven" or "I Get A Kick Out Of You", this time there is a consistent theme; peace and protest.
author: Sue Keogh

text: Parton is generous in letting others share the spotlight, from old stalwarts (George Jones, Brenda Lee and even Porter Wagoner and Yusuf Islam) to younger talent (Nickel Creek, Keith Urban and Norah Jones).
author: Sue Keogh

text: And, on the title track, Dollywood regulars The Moscow State Circus.
author: Sue Keogh

text: In places it can all be a bit much, like the syrup-drenched "Imagine".
author: Sue Keogh

text: But a dignified "The Cruel War" and a nimble rendition of "Me And Bobby McGee" with Kris Kristofferson manage to redress the balance.
author: Sue Keogh

text: Belly, American indie band of the 90s, released only 2 albums before splitting up.
author: Lucy Davies

text: But this is a "best of" with a difference: it's more of an introspective view than one geared towards ratings.Included are B sides, radio mixes and live tracksina selection hand-picked by singer and frontwoman Tanya Donelly.
author: Lucy Davies

text: The crowd pleasers are there: "Feed the Tree" and "Gepetto", with sugar spun verses with rollicking trademark choruses, with the bonus of explanations in the sleeve notes.
author: Lucy Davies

text: I'll never listen to the cheery "Full Moon Empty Heart" in the same way now I know that it's about a woman who throws her child and herself out of a window.
author: Lucy Davies

text: But that's the way with Belly; they have a habit of mingling the most cheerful tunes with the most sinister story lines.
author: Lucy Davies

text: We hear Jimi Hendrix and Gram Parsons given the Belly treatment with varying success: Gram's "Hot Burrito #1" fits perfectly, but "Are You Experienced?" is a little unconvincing.
author: Lucy Davies

text: It's enlightening to know that the band's appeal wasn't just in their home country: of the title track, Tanya recounts a moment in Tel Aviv: "I cried onstage (for the first, and, hopefully last time) to hear so many people sing it with me." Of course, there'll be moments of debate between fans: my particular gripe was initially "Judas Mon Coeur": sung in French-and the accent's not great.
author: Lucy Davies

text: This is Tanya's favourite Belly song: would it have made it there at all in any other circumstance?
author: Lucy Davies

text: I changed my mind after a few listens however- it's one of those growers.
author: Lucy Davies

text: And that's the point of this compilation: it's the "best of" from those who know the best, giving an idea of what it was like to be in the band,what was good to play,as well asto listen to, and which songs transcend language and culture.
author: Lucy Davies

text: In early 2000 Starsailor were the most hyped band in the UK; they got top billing as the new Travis Coldplay.
author: Louise Keeble

text: The soulful indie sounds of their debut Love Is Here, released the following year, won them critical acclaim and commercial success.
author: Louise Keeble

text: The single "Alcoholic" reached no.
author: Louise Keeble

text: 10 inthe singles chart.
author: Louise Keeble

text: Cynics however complain that they are bland and depressing.
author: Louise Keeble

text: Does their second release quieten these critics?
author: Louise Keeble

text: Silence Is Easy is captivating.
author: Louise Keeble

text: From the opening track, "Music Was Saved", it's evident that this record is much livelier and more upbeat than its predecessor.
author: Louise Keeble

text: The fresh approach must be partly attributed to a growing maturity.Now they're a successful band they seem happier.
author: Louise Keeble

text: As front man James Walsh sings on current single and title track, "Silence is easy, it just becomes me." Simple lyrics maybe, but you sense that life wasn't always this straightforward for the band.
author: Louise Keeble

text: The group's new found confidence and experimental edge are evident throughout the album.
author: Louise Keeble

text: "Fidelity", "Shark Food" and "Four To The Floor" all have more passion, more get up and go, than anything on Love Is Here.
author: Louise Keeble

text: "Shark Food" uses the simple repetition of the synchronised guitar and chorus to draw the listener in.
author: Louise Keeble

text: After a couple of plays I'm hooked.
author: Louise Keeble

text: The lyrics remind us that they are still an emerging talent; "We are stepping through the door, we're shooting from the heart but if we get it wrong they'll feed us to the sharks." The 'big sound' the band achieve on this record can be attributed to the polished production of legendary producers John Leckie (Stone Roses, Radiohead etc.) and Phil Spector (everyone from The Beatles to The Ramones).
author: Louise Keeble

text: Spector produced the title track and "White Dove" before being inconveniently accused of murder.
author: Louise Keeble

text: Those wanting a second helping of "Love Is Here" will not be disappointed by "Some Of Us" and "Restless Heart" which remind me of The Verve's Urban Hymns.
author: Louise Keeble

text: But Silence Is Easy has so much more to offer on many levels.
author: Louise Keeble

text: If there is any expectation left to be met, it will be to wonder how Starsailor will manage to produce a third album to surpass this fantastic mix of tunes.
author: Louise Keeble

text: The title of Justin's latest, rather reminiscent of Ms Stefani's latest album title, promises much.
author: Lucy Davies

text: The sounds of sex and love in the future.
author: Lucy Davies

text: Hmm, it must sound pretty amazing.
author: Lucy Davies

text: But first, comment must be passed on this album cover!
author: Lucy Davies

text: Is Justin in his Michael Jackson Bad throwback suit smashing up a mirror ball supposed to be smashing up the past and bringing in the future?
author: Lucy Davies

text: Let's hope so.
author: Lucy Davies

text: Initially, it's difficult to listen to the lyrics of the opening tracks and give an objective opinion.
author: Lucy Davies

text: It's like trying to find redeemable qualities about some guy who has zero social skills and stares at women on his own from the corner of a bar.
author: Lucy Davies

text: Only he seems to have found some similarly unreconstructed creepy friends shouting words of encouragement to his clunky chat-up lines, like Timbaland.
author: Lucy Davies

text: By way of example, Prince wannabe track "Sexy Ladies" contains the proud lyrics: 'Just to let you know that I've got sexy laydehs ...all over the floor'.
author: Lucy Davies

text: But it's not all bad!
author: Lucy Davies

text: "Lovestoned" is a great track, with chopping violins, beatboxing, and bongos.
author: Lucy Davies

text: "I Think She Knows", the interlude which follows, is quite beautiful, shimmering, and brilliantly constructed.
author: Lucy Davies

text: "What Goes Around" has a very slight Bollywood flavour, and whilst Justin will never be a profound lyricist, he does do a nice line in falsetto harmonies underlined with flowing violins.
author: Lucy Davies

text: "Losing my Way" is about Bob, a crack addict who doesn't know the colour of his daughter's eyes.
author: Lucy Davies

text: It's a surprising departure with gospel choir kicking in halfway.
author: Lucy Davies

text: I can't decide whether this is brilliant or cheese on toast.
author: Lucy Davies

text: It's difficult to listen to the whole album in one go,sometimes like witnessing the stag night of some young blokes with too much money and very little charm.And the porn photographer bonus track "Pose" could have been executed with humour, but Justin's vanilla character just makes it incredibly icky.
author: Lucy Davies

text: Sure, he's frequently funky, but rarely functional.
author: Lucy Davies

text: Is this the future of sex and love?
author: Lucy Davies

text: If so, it's brutal, defensive, and only sometimes worth negotiating.
author: Lucy Davies

text: It may be stating the obvious to say that Germany has a fine tradition of experimental music, but with a few exceptions (the mighty Workshop, for example) there's been little in the last few years that's hinted at the sounds of surprise that a band like Faust were capable of at their peak.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Hons (pretty much a one man show) bucks the trend here with what the press release calls 'a love story in eight parts'.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Though constructed on a PC and liberally sprinkled with the usual DSP tricks, Ferner Liefen's sound sources are often left to be themselves; a toy piano played against the sound of traffic; a hesitantly melancholic Satie-esque piano alone in a large room peeks through billowing clouds of white noise.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Occasionally fragments of speech or even songs emerge; Gilbert Handler's filtered vocal spins ironic tales of complex emotional detachment over fuzzed out industrial rock n' roll guitar or sparse, dubby electronica; "Im waiting for God to kick sand in my face; this won't be any fun at all", he deadpans.
author: Peter Marsh

text: "Mit Horn" processes a massed fog of trombones over distressed beats into a overripe ten minute slab of perverted jazz techno.
author: Peter Marsh

text: "My Fridge is Empty" imagines Tom Waits trapped in an electroacoustic collage remixed by Pole, while "Shielded With Ease" does the same with an almost motorik groove driven by distorted acoustic guitar chugs.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Here, Hons alludes to the rich Krautrock heritage of Can, Neu!
author: Peter Marsh

text: and the like without descending into imitation.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Ferner Liefen is more of a cinematic experience in the German Horspiel (sound play) tradition than anything else; throughout Hons zooms out, in, dissolves and jumpcuts between different acoustic spaces and environments with consummate skill.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Like a cross between Heiner Goebbels, Faust and Luc Ferrari, Ferner Liefen beguiles, suprises, irritates and seduces.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Worth checking out.
author: Peter Marsh

text: While a star on the Hollywood walk-of-fame may be a bit too much to ask for, I think it's pretty safe to say that it shouldn't be very long now before LA based label Plug Research become the uber-label du jour of Angelino electronic music.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: With recent impressive releases from the likes of DNTEL, Safety Scissors and John Tejada, it seems that with every new release, they simply push the musical envelope one step further from the tired and tested world of dance music, leaving their competition racing to catch up.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Based in Santa Monica, Daedelus started off his career playing double-bass and clarinet before getting corrupted by LA's rave explosion of the early 90s.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: But while many others in LA decided to jump on the cashing in/cheese bandwagon and create some of the most awful "underground" dance music known to mankind (you all know who you are), Daedelus thankfully bucked the trend, dove deep into his studio and has come up with this fiendishly clever and devilishly original little release.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Taking his cues more from people like Nat King Cole, Henry Mancini or Esquivel rather than Fat Boy Slim or Jason Bentley, "Invention" takes big band, 50s sci-fi, downtempo jazz and space age bachelor pad music and mixes everything up in a way that makes you wonder if Arthur Greenslade or Juan Esqivel loved hip-hop and had access to samplers back in their prime - would this be the kind of music they would create?
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Occasionally, there are flirtations with more pure hip-hop oriented territory such as the lightly bouncy "Adventress" with its acoustic bass backing or the vocal based tracks of "Thus The Whirligig" and "Pursed Lips Reply" featuring local MCs Busdriver and Sach.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: These two tracks are both reminiscent of material found on the also excellent Mush label - and not without coincidence, as it's recently been reported that Daedelus will be producing the next "The Weather" album for the avant-hip-hop label.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: What really comes across here is not so much the genre hopping but the attention to detail.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: From the carefully chosen samples to the way the beats are arranged across them, you can really tell that Daedelus and his producer Carlos Nino were coming from the heart, not the chequebook when producing this album.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Full marks to both Daedelus and Plug Research for releasing something as adventurous as this.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Here's hoping we hear more from Daedelus in the near future - something that should please new music fans everywhere.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Poised, once more, to unleash the behemoth that is 'The Rolling Stones on tour' upon the world, it's time to cast an eye over the CVs of Messrs Jagger, Richards, Watts, Wyman and all the other naughty boys that never grew up.
author: Chris Jones

text: 'For the first time ever!' yells the sticker on the cover - but why?
author: Chris Jones

text: Do the racks not groan with innumerable compilations of Richmond's finest?
author: Chris Jones

text: Ah yes, but none have pulled off the trick of spanning those pesky label changes.
author: Chris Jones

text: This time it's the full picture...
author: Chris Jones

text: After (approximately) forty years of dancing with Mr D, the Glimmer Twins and Co.
author: Chris Jones

text: have not only rattled the cages of the establishment but, in refusing (with one famous exception) to go down in a blaze of hell raising glory, have become as much pillars of society (to quote ''Respectable'', shamefully omitted here) as those who sought to silence them.
author: Chris Jones

text: Arise Sir Mick, indeed.
author: Chris Jones

text: So, while Mick Jagger's famous marketing savvy undoubtedly accounts for this collection, it's still important as a reminder of the days when each new release was easily as important as any of the Fab Four's.
author: Chris Jones

text: From the bolshy rhythm guitar intro of ''Street Fighting Man'' the synapses are instantly beaten into a realisation (or re-awakening) that these pasty West London boys virtually wrote the blueprint for hard rock in the 60s and 70s.
author: Chris Jones

text: So much here goes beyond mere R 'n' B.
author: Chris Jones

text: These are archetypes.
author: Chris Jones

text: How many garage-punk bands based their entire careers on the fuzz psych-out of ''Satisfaction''?
author: Chris Jones

text: How many wasted but wasteful wannabes have attempted to emulate the louche pharmaceutical jive of ''Honky Tonk Women'' or ''Tumbling Dice''?
author: Chris Jones

text: Even the paisley nonsense of ''She's A Rainbow'' still echoes on in the work of, say, The Flaming Lips.
author: Chris Jones

text: CD one has (and this is astounding) NO FILLER WHATSOEVER.
author: Chris Jones

text: Every track still shines like a grubby diamond.
author: Chris Jones

text: CD two fares less well - the post-Emotional Rescue era stuff, while efficient, falls into a more lackadaisical groove-driven formula, though stuff like ''Undercover (Of The Night)'' still packs a punch.
author: Chris Jones

text: There's plenty to get your teeth into however: Tracks such as ''Fool To Cry'' and ''It's Only Rock 'n' Roll'', lambasted at the time of release, now sound fresher and more heartfelt than any of today's lame copyists while ''Miss You'' from their last truly great album, Some Girls, proves that when they lost Bill Wyman they lost a vital part of their rhythmic backbone.
author: Chris Jones

text: Four new tracks fare perfectly well, though the closer ''Losin' My Touch'' featuring Richard's groggy vocals actually has the power to tug at the most grizzled of heartstrings.
author: Chris Jones

text: An entire essay could be written on the omissions (''Little Red Rooster'', ''We Love You'', ''Time Is On My Side'' etc.
author: Chris Jones

text: etc.) and while the booklet has a fine selection of photos some kind of Stalinism seems to exist in the Stones camp whereby only one picture of Mick Taylor is included, despite his presence during what many cite as their classic years.
author: Chris Jones

text: But minor gripes aside, this first comprehensive look at all eras of satisfaction-seeking does a mighty fine job.
author: Chris Jones

text: This is a curious album.
author: Liz Mundler

text: For one short studio session back in the '60s, the king of jazz drummers Buddy Rich, and Alla Rakha, the master of the Indian tabla, came together in an early attempt at East-West fusion.
author: Liz Mundler

text: The resulting album was hailed as a 'landmark' and a 'seminal recording' but nevertheless had sunk without trace by the 1980's.
author: Liz Mundler

text: Now re-released in re-mastered and restored form, does it stand the test of time?
author: Liz Mundler

text: As a student in the 1980s, I was given an ancient copy of this disc and wondered at the virtuosity of Alla Rakha.
author: Liz Mundler

text: I also wondered what Buddy Rich was doing as he only obviously features on two of the five tracks.
author: Liz Mundler

text: With this new CD version I realised that he also appears on a third track, minus his shoes and sitting cross-legged playing the dholak (a small hand drum).
author: Liz Mundler

text: It's not that the sound quality of the new release allows such insights, although it is pretty good being re-mastered from the original session tapes, but that the copious sleeve notes explain what's going on in great detail.
author: Liz Mundler

text: The first two minutes of the disc transport you to the Taj Mahal, with sitar and flute introducing a simple theme reminiscent of Indian restaurants everywhere.
author: Liz Mundler

text: In common with the other tracks the melody then stops abruptly to allow the stars to shine.
author: Liz Mundler

text: The following schizophrenic duet sees Rich imitating the tones of the tabla on a snare drum whilst maintaining a different time signature from Rakha.
author: Liz Mundler

text: The third track is fantastic, a battle royal between full drum kit and tabla which still takes my breath away.
author: Liz Mundler

text: The last two tracks are tabla solos with Rakha at the top of his form.
author: Liz Mundler

text: If you want a nice disc of typical Indian music, this one's not for you.
author: Liz Mundler

text: But this re-release, following the deaths of Buddy Rich in 1987 and Alla Rakha last year, offers a unique insight into the early days of fusion.
author: Liz Mundler

text: For many the enduring memory of Jazzy Jeff will be as Will Smith's bumbling sidekick on his hit US TV show.
author: Andy Puleston

text: However, prior to the commissioning of The Fresh Prince of Bel Air it was Mr Smith who rode in the back seat as Jeff's masterful turntable skillsgained them both crowds and a reputation in the early days of their partnership.
author: Andy Puleston

text: Departing Bel Air a household name with 10 million albums and 3 Grammies, Jeff withdrew from the media spotlight to pursue the role of producer returning to Philadelphia to set up A Touch of Jazz.
author: Andy Puleston

text: This full scale production unit houses a team of producers and under his guidance has been responsible for some seminal releases.

author: Andy Puleston

author: Andy Puleston

text: If heaven is Miles Davis' second quintet (and some would say that it is), then this luscious set is indeed aptly named.
author: Peter Marsh

text: It's got seven discs in it, for a start...
author: Peter Marsh

text: The previous sets in Columbia's series have all been centred around particular bands or recording projects.
author: Peter Marsh

text: This one is different, documenting the period of transition between Davis' work with the first great quintet (with Coltrane, Adderley et al) and the second (with Wayne Shorter, Herbie Hancock, Ron Carter and Tony Williams).
author: Peter Marsh

text: Coltrane was (unsurprisingly) a hard act to follow.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Jimmy Heath, Sonny Stitt and Hank Mobley all failed to fit the bill for various reasons (Miles was particularly fond of Heath but the saxophonist's parole officer put a ban on him touring with the band), and the period was marked by what Davis felt were some fairly indifferent recordings and performances.
author: Peter Marsh

text: By the first disc of this set, Davis had settled temporarily on the quintet that cut Seven Steps to Heaven in early 1963 (featured on disc 1 here).
author: Peter Marsh

text: Though the trumpeter's ear had been caught by the talents of both Wayne Shorter and Tony Williams, neither were available.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Bassist Ron Carter was in place however, and the pianist's chair was taken by LA session master Victor Feldman (soon to leave for more lucrative studio work).
author: Peter Marsh

text: George Coleman was the tenor saxophonist, and Frank Butler filled in while Davis waited for Williams to finish his stint with Jackie McLean.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Despite their considerable skills, this band was still very much in the shadow of the Coltrane line-up.
author: Peter Marsh

text: But with the arrival of Hancock and Williams a month later, things shifted up a gear or three.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Live recordings made at Antibes and in particular the Philharmonic Hall gig of February 1964 (all included here) show how.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The set lists drew on a selection of Davis classics plus a few standards.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Though there was still a nod to the hard bop flavours of the Mobley and Heath groups (particularly in the furious pace of "So What"), Hancock's crafty reharmonisations of the material, coupled with Williams' crisp, explosive drumming kept the material in a constant state of flux and fizzing with energy.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Coleman's earthy, precise tenor proved to be a problem for Williams, who craved a more adventurous foil for Davis.
author: Peter Marsh

text: When Coleman left (citing late payments and a lack of gigs), the drummer lobbied for his old bandmate Sam Rivers to take his place.
author: Peter Marsh

text: A live recording from Tokyo seems to be the only document of this short lived line-up.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Though it wasn't an entirely successful one (Rivers' embryonic avant garde approach didn't sit well with Davis), the version of "My Funny Valentine' remains for my money one of the trumpeter's loveliest ballad performances, and Rivers is admirably fearless throughout.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Not long afterwards Davis finally bagged Wayne Shorter, who'd just quit Art Blakey.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The final disc of this set captures the new quintet on a visit to Europe with a broadly unchanged set list.
author: Peter Marsh

text: "Autumn Leaves" is pulled apart and stuck back together with a level of invention and beauty that hints at things to come, and it's fascinating to hear the band tackling tunes they would soon abandon in favour of new self composed material.
author: Peter Marsh

text: There's not a huge amount here that'll be unfamiliar to the Davis collector.
author: Peter Marsh

text: We do get a few alternate takes from the studio sessions and a fairly glorious"Stella by Starlight" on the final disc, but Columbia'slisting of concert announcements among the 'previously unreleased' material is a bit questionable.
author: Peter Marsh

text: But of course, it's all remixed and remastered and (call me superficial), the packaging and annotation counts for a lot.
author: Peter Marsh

text: And of course, the music's pretty good too...a fine investment and an essential companion to the glorious Plugged Nickel set.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Let's get this out of the way: this album will NOT change the world.
author: Chris Jones

text: Its songs fit neatly into the career of the world's most famous lead guitarist.
author: Chris Jones

text: Messages of positive vibrations, ecological warning, vaguely liberal snipes at capitalism (from a millionaire), mystical mumbo-jumbo - it's all here.
author: Chris Jones

text: Unfinished at the time of George's passing, Brainwashed stands as testament to the modest career of a modest man to whom the trappings of stardom really did mean nothing.
author: Chris Jones

text: If you find yourself unmoved by its warmth, sincerity and above all, wisdom not to exceed its boundaries, well, you're a very cold fish indeed.
author: Chris Jones

text: In fact, a fish graces the key song on Brainwashed.
author: Chris Jones

text: ''Pisces Fish'' sets out George's ambitions and dreams as plainly as any song he's ever written.
author: Chris Jones

text: Dispensing with unnecessarily florid couplets he states, ''Rowers gliding on the river, Canadian geese crap along the bank, back wheel of my bike begins to quiver.
author: Chris Jones

text: The chain is wrapped around the crank'', before going on to tell us that he's ''a Pisces fish and the river runs through my soul.'' If it sounds quaint, it isn't.
author: Chris Jones

text: It's a simple song about the simple things that meant more to him than a high public profile.
author: Chris Jones

text: It's worth noting that since 1987s Cloud Nine Harrison had, in effect retreated into a wholly private life filled with gardening and family.
author: Chris Jones

text: Like Lennon before him the world burst in (unbidden, in the form of a crazed assailant), yet he emerged whole, only to be brought down by circumstances beyond his control.
author: Chris Jones

text: In ''Rising Sun'' he talks of being, ''...almost a statistic inside a doctor's case'' and on ''Looking For My Life'' he longs for spiritual solace.
author: Chris Jones

text: Yet this album rarely dwells on personal negativity, despite the circumstances surrounding it.
author: Chris Jones

text: Instead he berates a world gone wrong (''Brainwashed'', ''P2 Vatican Blues (Last Saturday Night)'' and turns in a bunch of lovely, sad, love songs, tinged with regret yet lifted by his trademark slide guitar (''Stuck Inside A Cloud'' and ''Never Get Over You'').
author: Chris Jones

text: And let's not forget the charming ukulele turn on ''Between The Devil And The Deep Blue Sea'' that'll leave a grin on your face.
author: Chris Jones

text: Jeff Lynne has recently apologised for putting a little too much fairy dust on this incomplete set of songs, but he needn't worry.
author: Chris Jones

text: Just as with the Travelling Wilburys, Lynne's production (combined with Jim Keltner's ever-dependable drums) suits Harrison down to the ground.
author: Chris Jones

text: Heaven knows, Lynne spent longer being a Beatle than any of the fab four!
author: Chris Jones

text: This is, without doubt, the way we should remember this dark horse.
author: Chris Jones

text: Released to coincide with the 25th anniversary of the world's most famous man whose middle name was Aaron shuffling off this mortal coil; we are faced once more with the legacy of the King.
author: Chris Jones

text: Jokes about peanut butter sandwiches and fat sweaty guys in white high-collar jumpsuits aside, this is still, despite all that came after (including The Beatles) a collection that sets a benchmark that few will ever approach.
author: Chris Jones

text: The only question is: doesn't everyone already own them?
author: Chris Jones

text: And if not, why not?
author: Chris Jones

text: Like a tin of quick-drying varnish, 30 #1 Hits does exactly what it says on the cover.
author: Chris Jones

text: Starting with his big label debut, ''Heartbreak Hotel'' and ending with his posthumous chart-topper ''Way Down'', you get all the memorable moments, mapping the bequiffed-one's progress from parent-baiting hip-swiveller (''Hound Dog''), through sixties lost-in-hollywood schmaltz merchant (''Wooden Heart'') and comeback kid renaissance man (''In The Ghetto'') to the final Vegas karate surrealism (''The Wonder Of You'').
author: Chris Jones

text: You all know the story, here's the soundtrack.
author: Chris Jones

text: One is struck by the awesome way in which this material has seeped into every part of our lives.
author: Chris Jones

text: Play this album and everybody within hearing range is guaranteed to gasp at some point ''ooh, I love this one''.
author: Chris Jones

text: The fun is in comparing notes on which model's your favourite.
author: Chris Jones

text: If there's any criticism to be levelled, it's that the strict chart-based formula precludes any sign of the glorious Sun sessions that unleashed the Tenessee truck driver upon Western civilisation.
author: Chris Jones

text: Also sadly lacking is any material recorded during his electric '68 comeback special and the inclusion of the pointless ''Little Less Conversation'' remix smacks of heartless opportunism.
author: Chris Jones

text: But hey, that's the way it is...
author: Chris Jones

text: To not have these nuggets of purest pop within reach (in case of emergency) should be considered a crime.
author: Chris Jones

text: From the dirtiest R 'n' B to the weepiest ballads, the Pelvis did it all, and before he hit 43.
author: Chris Jones

text: Icon, avatar, hillbilly and oaf; Elvis may have been all of the above.
author: Chris Jones

text: But musically speaking; he's still taking care of business.
author: Chris Jones

text: After two fine albums on their own imprint (Madwaltz), Manchester's secret weapon Homelife have finally been spotted.
author: Dan Hill

text: Agit-funksters from the big smoke, Ninja Tune, have given them the platform they deserve, and in return Homelife deliver their best yet.
author: Dan Hill

text: After four excellent recordings during the 1990's as part of the Mujician quartet, Dunmall has more recently been fronting an octet, and the last piece on this CD is for sixteen players.

text: Dunmall brings his Mujician mates along for the romp, so the listener is treated not only to Dunmall's fearsome powerhouse tenor sax, but also to Keith Tippett's inside/outside piano wizardry, Tony Levin's percussive thunder and Paul Rogers' nimble, expressive bass.
author: Bill Tilland

text: Dunmall is a democratic leader, so everyone here gets a chance to shine, including the additional members of the Octet, which include second tenor Simon Picard, trombonists Hilary Jeffries and Paul Rutherford, and trumpeter Gethin Liddington.
author: Bill Tilland

text: As with Dunmall's earlier octet recording on Cuneiform, Bebop Stardust, the breadth and depth of music on this recording is truly mind-boggling.

text: In between, though, Parts Two through Five offer a rich compendium of modern jazz, with fine extended soloing from everyone, and a wide dynamic range of shifting duet, trio and quartet combinations, supported by ensemble passages which are sometimes almost Ellingtonian in their sonorities, and sometimes as spiky and weird as vintage Sun Ra.

author: Rob Webb

text: Mott the Hoople turned down ''Drive in Saturday'' as a follow up to ''All the Young Dudes'', which was a shame perhaps, but Bowie's recording is wonderfully atmospheric, and it is difficult to imagine anyone else capturing that languid 'Gee it's hot, let's go to bed' feel in quite the same way.

text: His weary, decadent piano - put to particular good use on the title track -''Aladdin Sane (1913-1938-197?)'' - was one of the album's talking points when it was first released in 1973.
author: Rob Webb

text: It's lost none of its freeform, jazzy sparkle in thirty years and still sounds as Jackson Pollock's blobs might, had they been splattered onto sheet music instead of canvas.

text: Clare Teal's That's the Way It Is inhabits the dark territory of Baz Luhrmann's film "Moulin Rouge".

text: It takes the music of the last century, reshapes it and reflects it back as in a fairground hall of mirrors.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: Clare's voice is smooth and bell-like, but with the suggestion of something dangerous lurking beneath, and her expression is masterful.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: She can be playful and innocent in one chorus and mischievous and threatening in the next.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: "You're My Thrill" is a slow and measured exploration of desire sung with a vibrato which harks back to the first half of last century.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: Clare's similarly languorous delivery of "Speak Low" gives it the intimacy and artifice of travelling theatre, mischief oozing out until the song becomes urgent and threatening.

text: On the other hand, Hoagy Carmichael and Johnny Mercer's "How Little We Know" is an arrangement to synchronised swim to (with the backing singers happy housewives from a 50's hoover ad).

text: Even in this upbeat waltz, though, Clare manages to inject the uneasy feeling that all is not what it seems.

text: Gunter Wand makes no secret of the fact that he thinks Bruckner is the most important symphonist since Beethoven; we don't have to agree with him, but we should certainly listen to what he has to say about a composer he holds in such high regard.
author: John Armstrong

text: You may find yourself learning things about Bruckner you never knew before...for instance Bruckner can dance, and with great dignity as well (Scherzo).
author: John Armstrong

text: That even the most monumental passages of the Eighth Symphony are full of romantic warmth, if you just know how to find it.
author: John Armstrong

text: That the diffident Austrian organist's symphonies are not necessarily analogous to cathedral architecture...they're always compared to monumental stone spaces, where incense hangs heavy in the air, and any sound takes several seconds to decay.
author: John Armstrong

text: Well, Wand has news for us: that's just one way of approaching these works, and it may be a dead-end.
author: John Armstrong

text: He's found a way of making Bruckner's Eighth Symphony communicate more directly, more emotionally.
author: John Armstrong

text: It's not enough here to sit back and be impressed with the structure and the sheer grandeur of the design - Wand demands a human, emotional response, recognition that it's not a heart of stone that keeps this music alive, and if anything the spiritual gains are greater.
author: John Armstrong

text: When it comes to recording Bruckner, I suppose this could still be Karajan's Berlin Philharmonic...but these days it's a younger orchestra.
author: John Armstrong

text: What you get here is the polish, the weight, and the surefooted approach to the longest of phrases familiar from the classic Karajan recordings, plus a new warmth, almost heart-on-sleeve romanticism (try the opening of the Adagio), and a youthful fire that's astonishing from a conductor celebrating his 90th birthday.
author: John Armstrong

text: This new Eighth is more rewarding (and better recorded) than either of Wand's earlier accounts, and it has to be up there with the very best.
author: John Armstrong

text: I usually need a break after one of Bruckner's symphonic epics, but with this new recording I couldn't wait to hear it again, so if you don't mind...
author: John Armstrong

text: Though France was a haven for beboppers like Kenny Clarke and later provided a home for free jazzers like Sunny Murray, Anthony Braxton and the Art Ensemble of Chicago, the French contribution to the jazz oeuvre has been either neglected or negligible (the Hot Club aside), depending on your viewpoint.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Though this re-issue of pianist Henri Renaud's sides for the Saturne label (nothing to do with Sun Ra, by the way) is unlikely to rewrite the history books, it's a strong reminder that though jazz was the sound of Black America, there was much valuable music being made in Europe.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Recorded in 1951 for five rare as hen's teeth picture discs, this group (here in various trio, quartet and sextet formations) did feature two visiting Chicagoans, guitarist Jimmy Gourley and tenorist Sandy Mosse and was originally put together for a festival date.
author: Peter Marsh

text: On a mixture of standards and originals, the sundry lineups display a relaxed, propulsive swing (mainly down to the legendary bassist Pierre Michelot) which provides springboards for some fine solos.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Mosse is very much from the Lester Young school; his blurred tone and urbane, eloquent solos are enjoyable enough, but the star here is Belgian tenorist Bobby Jaspar.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Recorded before his move to the US a few years later (where he played with the likes of Chet Baker, Miles Davis and Kenny Burrell before dying tragically at the age of 37), Jaspar shares Mosse's admiration for Young, but filtered through the airy harmonic interrogations favoured by Warne Marsh.
author: Peter Marsh

text: His playing is a model of poise and taste, with a luscious upper register tone that hits the spot.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Renaud swings hard (easy to see why he was popular with visiting American jazzers in search of a rhythm section), while Gourley's Charlie Christian inspired solos are enjoyably fluid.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The band were obviously enjoying themselves; Mosse and Jaspar's brief exchanges are delightful, and on "Lady Be Bad" quotes from "Dixie" are tossed all over the place with glee by Gourley and Renaud.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The original 1951 picture discs were appalingly bad quality, though engineer Tony Baldwin has done a fantastic digital restoration job in rendering this valuable, unpretentious session listenable; half an hour of Gallic bop at its finest.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Anyone interested in the state of modern jazz will probably have noticed that Norway is producing some of the finest and most adventurous jazz musicians on the planet at the moment, from straight ahead acoustic outfits like Atomic to the nu jazz of Bugge Wesseltoft and Wibutee or the dark electronic improvscapes of Supersilent.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Food unites the lyrical and adventurous saxophony of Iain Ballamy and the highly individual trumpeter Arve Henriksen (whose solo album Sakuteiki was one of the highlights of last year) with the rhythm section of Mats Eilertsen and Thomas Strønen.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Though Ballamy's known primarily as a player who revels in rich harmonic possibilities, he's obviously not afraid of taking chances; Food dispense with chords and tight structures in favour of collective improvisation and electronic shadings.
author: Peter Marsh

text: After two albums which documented the group in a live setting, veggie sees a move to the excellent Rune Grammofon label, complete with a coolly beautiful Kim Hiørthoy sleeve and remixing input from Supersilent's Helge Sten (aka Deathprod).
author: Peter Marsh

text: Unsurprisingly there's more accent on the electronics this time, with samples providing foggy, dreamlike backgrounds for Henriksen's breathy, flute like trumpet and Ballamy's bucolic saxophone (mainly soprano).
author: Peter Marsh

text: Both horn players opt for concise solo statements, uniting for aching, folk like melodies that seem to hang in the air long after they're gone.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The one exception is "pie", where Henriksen's trumpet shines for a few minutes, accompanied by Eilertsen's resonant bass.Meanwhile the rhythm section opt for texture rather than propulsion, offeringtumbling, fractured pulses below the horns and atmospherics.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Strønen's percussive approach is reminiscent of a less hyperactive Tony Oxley, adding bells, the clank of rusted chains and muted depthcharge hits.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The sequenced groove of"chickpea"imagines a chance meeting of krautrock synth pioneers Cluster with Jan Garbarek and AMM in a scrapyard, while on the final 'mushroom' Strønen reluctantly takes upa slow, truculentbeat under Henriksen's throatsinging.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Sten's role is crucial; his skill at the board drops Ballamy's lines in pools of luxurious reverb or draws instruments and samples out of the mix to give an almost tangible depth and shape to the soundfield.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The studio as the fifth member of the quartet, in fact.The effect is immersive in the way that Eno's On Land or Miles Davis' "He Loved Him Madly" are.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Deep listening makes veggie a hypnotic, sometimes deeply beautiful record.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Food for the ears, indeed.
author: Peter Marsh
