author: Peter Marsh

text: I don't like records which include dogs barking.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: It's like the artist is saying "Hey, look at me, I'm so weird, I can do anything - so here's a dog!" There's a dog barking on this album.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: There's also a lot of startling and impressive guitar work.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Bob Drake can really play: country picking, Beefheart style action painting ("Rtuuf"), Derek Bailey abstraction and noise.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Once you get past the disjointed rhythms and the ferocious technique, things can start to sound a bit ordinary.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: For example, the gibbering Spanish which appears to be thrown in at random; it's irritating.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: But there are some good tracks here.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: "Ten For A Dime" rises to an alarming climax of mellotron and sinister vocals, like a prog rock band reaching the end of its collective tether.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: The best song is the most conventional but also the strangest.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: "Griffin" is straightforward.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Well, as straightforward as an erotic dream of a statue of a Griffin could be.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: It's rather good, and leaves you wondering whether Bob is really just a sweetie, albeit one you wouldn't want to meet in a dark alley.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: It's followed by an instrumental "Pechan and Willy" which is a subtle and successful development of tune and weird.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Similarly "In Case The Insulator Fails", a country ballad gone off the rails.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: In contrast "Building With Bones - OrA Thing" is a thirteen minute long free-form distorted improv drum wig out.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: It sounds like it comes from a completely different album.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: And things then trail off with an inaudible piano piece and some more distorted Spanish.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: I like this, but against my better judgement.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Bob has invited me into his strange world.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: But is he going to extremes just to impress me, or because it's the only way his music must be made?
author: Nick Reynolds

text: It's the people that look normal that you've really got to watch out for...
author: Nick Reynolds

text: For what it's worth, a zooid is "an organic cell capable of spontaneous movement independent of the parent organism." And that's as good an explanation as any of Threadgill's oblique, intricate compositional methodology.
author: Bill Tilland

text: Measured against his simultaneous release of Everybodys Mouth's a Book (with the Make a Move quintet), the styles and textures of this session are decidedly more exotic, with instrumentation that includes tuba, oud and cello.
author: Bill Tilland

text: The tuba provides foursquare, marching-band/Dixieland resonance, the oud lends tart, percussive bite, and the bowed cello contributes some highbrow ambience.
author: Bill Tilland

text: Threadgill used two (!) tubas in an earlier group, Very Very Circus, often combining them with two electric guitars for some delightfully ragged harmolodic funk.
author: Bill Tilland

text: Zooid is not necessarily an evolution, but the playing has more discipline and clarity, with Threadgill's prominent use of flute (on three of the seven tracks) creating an aura of chamber jazz sophistication.
author: Bill Tilland

text: Yet even at its most genteel, the music on this CD is no snoozefest.
author: Bill Tilland

text: The single ballad features Threadgill's flute and Liberty Ellman's excellent acoustic guitar, but it is much closer to Ravel or Debussy than to generic mood jazz.
author: Bill Tilland

text: And overall, Zooid's rhythmic underpinning is quietly insistent, with drums, tuba and oud (and sometimes the pizzicato cello) all pushing the music forward vigorously, while Threadgill and Ellman skitter in and out of the mix.
author: Bill Tilland

text: Threadgill's alto is a special treat in an acoustic setting, where he's not competing with multiple electric guitars and a thick wall of sound.
author: Bill Tilland

text: He's a playa, make no mistake -- incisive, fiery and technically impeccable.
author: Bill Tilland

text: His solos are seldom more than three minutes long, but he squeezes more into three minutes than most saxophonists could play in ten.
author: Bill Tilland

text: Jose Davila is also a strong presence on tuba.
author: Bill Tilland

text: He conducts frequent forays into trombone and even French horn territory, and on one extended solo, throws in some multiphonics for good measure.
author: Bill Tilland

text: This is today's jazz, for the hip, thoughtful jazz fan who looks to jazz for more than museum pieces and/or bachelor pad makeout music.
author: Bill Tilland

text: This compilation, produced to accompany Michelle Mercer's biography of the same title, maps Wayne Shorter's remarkable career asa composer and interpreter with great precision.
author: Lara Bellini

text: It details how profound an evolution jazz has undergone over Shorter's lifespan, to an extent where it's impossible to disentangle his progression as a saxophonist from that of the genre itself.
author: Lara Bellini

text: Shorter is said to have played a substantial role in selecting the 22 tracks.
author: Lara Bellini

text: To speculate about the extent of his involvement with the anthology is unavoidable: Shorter belongs to an era of great performers who would allow their emotional range to play a structural role in the makeup of their jazz DNA.
author: Lara Bellini

text: For them, bravura and virtuosity are nothing without a story to tell.
author: Lara Bellini

text: As such, a compilation like this almost immediately translates into biography.
author: Lara Bellini

text: It goes from Shorter's early solo records, his collaborations with Miles (in so doingrevealing his formidable originality as a composer, spanning from Speak No Evil to Bitches Brew), to the genius of the early Weather Report - where his inimitable sound reaches one of its many creativepeaks.
author: Lara Bellini

text: And then beyond, with the absorption of a fusion-implemented Brazilian vocabulary (eg: the collaboration with Milton Nascimento in Native Dancer).
author: Lara Bellini

text: From there, the anthology follows Shorter's ingenuity as an innovator spreading over many a crossover experiment (Steely Dan; Joni Mitchell), including the more divisive ones (the overflowing synthesisers that plagued the Eighties).
author: Lara Bellini

text: But even then, Shorter's class is not to be overlooked.
author: Lara Bellini

text: And thus to the present day: the formidable acousticquartet and the recent collaboration with Herbie Hancock.
author: Lara Bellini

text: The only two remarkableomissions from this double-cd collection are the seminal Juju and Night Dreamer: regrettably no material from either is featured (presumably due to licensing limitations).
author: Lara Bellini

text: Last but not least, the choice of "Footprints" as title track pays homage to Miles the mentor, the man without whom all this wouldn't have happened as it did.
author: Lara Bellini

text: Miles' last words to Shorter were for his genius 'to be more exposed'.
author: Lara Bellini

text: Hence this compilation, one guesses.
author: Lara Bellini

text: Yet again, the Shorter story is thereto amaze us.
author: Lara Bellini

text: A different kettle of fish to Trout Mask Replica's avant-glory days, Unconditionally Guaranteed, (1974) alienated many die-hard fans with its unashamedly commercial overtones.
author: Sid Smith

text: Nevertheless "On The My-O- My" and "Full Moon, Hot Sun" retain the expected grit and gravel beloved of the Beefheart thrum.
author: Sid Smith

text: Following the mass defection of his regular band, Beefheart toured with a hastily convened pick-up group.
author: Sid Smith

text: Previously unreleased, Live In Drury Lane '74, shows Don and his so-called Tragic Band were actually anything but.
author: Sid Smith

text: With "Bluejeans And Moonbeams" (also 1974), Van Vliet's voice has never been recorded as sympathetically, revealing him to be a consummate balladeer.
author: Sid Smith

text: Don't believe the received wisdom; it's isn't half as bad as they reckon.
author: Sid Smith

text: Lacking the extraneous filler that mars the later recordings, the strangulated Yosemite-Sam-on-helium vocals of 1980's Zappa-infected Shiny Beast (Bat Chain Puller), is a joyful collision of odd-metered out-thereness.
author: Sid Smith

text: Though the wordplay might be more inclined to arch than acerbic, combined with the high-flying marimba, trombone and rattling slide guitar combo, it's still more than capable of putting hairs on your chest and probably represents his last truly great moment as a recording artist.
author: Sid Smith

text: Notwithstanding momentary flashes of agitated brilliance, Doc At The Radar Station (1980) and Ice Cream For Crow (1982) stumble alarmingly into self-parody.
author: Sid Smith

text: Past his best, they vindicate Van Vliet's instinct to become a full-time painter.
author: Sid Smith

text: This admirable reissue series, with its crisp sound and Mike Barnes' excellent fact-packed sleevenotes decoding the Beefheart mythos, is only let down by its cursory design and packaging.
author: Sid Smith

text: First hearing of this album stirred memories of George Russell's Electronic Sonata For Souls Loved By Nature (1969): Both feature an acoustic jazz group, piano-driven, set within an electronic context.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Here the pianist is Matthew Shipp and instead of Russell's tape composition, DJ Spooky supplies laptop, turntables, treatments, bass, etc.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Optometry comes with liner notes and the track titles are...
author: Colin Buttimer

text: The opening "Ibid, desmarches, ibid" delivers traffic sounds out of which a snare-heavy, rolling, tripping rhythm appears, a double bass starts to play a catchy figure, piano chords drive things along.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: There's an intense, muscular quality to Shipp's playing, a McCoy Tyner-like emphasis.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: "Reactive Switching Strategies for the Control of Uninhabited Air" has the bass up in the mix, there's a circular piano figure and clickety percussion; things are accessible, near-catchy; laptop loops may be in play.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Again those heavy, dramatic chords with the bass figures pushing patterns through.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: In "Variation Cybernetique: Rhythmic Pataphysic (part I)" repeated piano clusters played fast almost recall Philip Glass, reverberating off each eardrum, long violin notes, glass-like percussion, gong.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Captivating, beautiful stuff.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: "Periphique" is a beautiful piece of work: the percussion is all brushes and ride cymbal, there's bowed double bass and Joe McPhee plays trumpet.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: This penultimate track starts with a feeling of aimlessness, of wandering in a wide-open, darkened landscape where the sky is all too big and we're all too small.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: With "It's a mad, mad, mad world", the final track, a confused certainty returns; there are a couple of jokey/ironic vocal samples and some more straightahead playing.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: This initially surprised me by appearing to belie the music that had gone before it, to represent an unexpected loss of confidence.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: On further thought it's perhaps understandable in light of "Periphique"s sense of loss/lostness.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: All in all, Optometry is a big, serious-sounding piece of work.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: The overall impression of this reviewer is of an earnest, driven endeavour which finds itself in a place it didn't expect to be.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Although Optometry sounds like an essay in possibilities, a sonic prototype which is unlikely to go into production, it bears repeated listening and throws many sonic jewels before our ears.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: As we're constantly reminded by a certain TV advert, the world's favourite word is 'OK'.Not bad.All right.
author: Matt Fernand

text: The same could be said for much of the world's music.You buy it and it sort of fills a silence and it's OK.
author: Matt Fernand

text: Then along comes a gem like Simian's We Are Your Friends and you realise OK simply isn't good enough.
author: Matt Fernand

text: This is what you really wanted - a solid set of songs, engagingly delivered, with a depth and texture that mean you can keep playing and playing it.
author: Matt Fernand

text: There's no one stand-out classic on this album.
author: Matt Fernand

text: But there are no low points either.It simply storms along in a way that you wish 20 other albums you own would.
author: Matt Fernand

text: The top line is the timeless bit.The vocal on "The Way I Live", for example, has enough sneer and swagger to give the snottiest indie singer a tough time in a bratfight.
author: Matt Fernand

text: The softer deliveries, like "Sunshine", are in the English psychedelic tradition and you've heard those harmonies a million times before because they just work.
author: Matt Fernand

text: The music, however, is squelchy, springy, loopy 21st century now.Most of the grooves are of the strut-tastic sort that go straight to your shoulders, which is cool because you're an Indie fan and you can't dance.
author: Matt Fernand

text: On the other hand, if you want to turn your Converse into Seven League Boots, slap on "Big Black Gun", crank it up and get stomping.
author: Matt Fernand

text: You'll be striding a mile a go before the second chorus.
author: Matt Fernand

text: This is not the classic album you find yourself reaching for whenever you're stuck for a listen.
author: Matt Fernand

text: No, this is the one that you find in the tray when you open the CD player, think "great", close it and press play.
author: Matt Fernand

text: Is that OK for you?

text: Long term, prime exponent of the New York Slam poetry scene, Ursula Rucker has spent the last seven years working with some of the finest downtempo outfits including Silent Poets and The Roots.
author: Andy Puleston

text: Whilst her talents have embellished their work from 1994 onwards, it is former musical partners 4Hero, Alexkid and King Britt who have returned the gesture and collaborated with her on this beautiful fusion of hip hop, nu-jazz and soul.
author: Andy Puleston

text: Inspired by the social commentary of black female writers Zora Neale Hurston and Sonia Sanchez, Ursula Rucker has made it her mission to elevate the mind of hip hop and purify the art form.
author: Andy Puleston

text: Like her previous work Supa Sista fixes Ursula's attentions firmly on the issues of sexuality, technology, women's rights, politics, education, evolution and spirituality.
author: Andy Puleston

text: Unlike so many working in the business she is an engaged woman who knows the true power of words.
author: Andy Puleston

text: Levelling criticism at some of her male contemporaries for the effects that the violence and machismo in their lyrics has on the young, she purrs, "...
author: Andy Puleston

text: formidable minds pay the price for your microphone mistakes.
author: Andy Puleston

text: Change or be changed.
author: Andy Puleston

text: Break the chains, don't be slaves".
author: Andy Puleston

text: Lazy beats with sweet soul soaked in Rhodes piano and double bass punctuation provide a wonderful, musical contrast to the often gritty subject matter.
author: Andy Puleston

text: "Philadelphia Child" combines the city's trademark strings with tabla percussion whilst "What???" extends the variety to subtle drum and bass rhythms all of which compliment Ursula's vocals.
author: Andy Puleston

text: Charged with 'she-lectricity', hers is a silken delivery that, like Michael Franti's, demonstrates that a quiet word in the ear can speak volumes above the microphone rant.
author: Andy Puleston

text: Ursula is one that would like to see hip hop become more responsible and more original.
author: Andy Puleston

text: This is a woman who is both a poet and performer with important things to say and with her smoky, seductive lyricism it is all too easy to listen and absorb.
author: Andy Puleston

text: Most people will remember Brian James as the guitarist who made the first Damned album such an adrenaline-packed ride of noise that they could never replicate.
author: Chris Jones

text: Many more remember him as the proto-goth messiah co-piloting the Lords Of The New Church through the 80s.
author: Chris Jones

text: However James, between the demise of the Lords and their reformation last year, was far from idle, as this double set reveals.
author: Chris Jones

text: His one proper eponymous solo album, is here combined with Ready To Crack: tracks produced by Stones legend, the late Jimmy Miller under the name of The Dripping Lips.
author: Chris Jones

text: Three tracks (including the growling "Push Push") had appeared on the film soundtrack to Abracadabra and had aroused Miller's interest.
author: Chris Jones

text: The results, recorded with the same line-up, didn't come to light for another five years but Burning Airlines have done a fine job in re-releasing them with a commentary from James himself.
author: Chris Jones

text: Both albums subscribe to the punk doctrine that James helped give birth to.
author: Chris Jones

text: While obviously owing a huge amount to Miller-period Stones ("Slow It Down" from Brain James is a fine example), BJ's Wayne Kramer-esque arpeggios give the whole thing a razor edge that never fails to get the body moving.
author: Chris Jones

text: It's a far more stripped-down approach than the Lords more lush dark textures and, as such, suits James no-nonsense approach to vocals as on "Becoming A Nuisance" and "Powerful", the opener on Ready To Crack.
author: Chris Jones

text: Yet this isn't merely a collection of three chord knockabouts.
author: Chris Jones

text: "Such A Lot Of Stars" is a charmingly melodic ballad that tugs at the heartstrings while "Popeyed" is a gloriously strange piece of guitar tomfoolery which shows that James is craftsman in this game we call Rock 'N' Roll.
author: Chris Jones

text: All in all this collection provides a valuable document of a talent that, even in slower times and with very little critical encouragement, strives to make a great rocking noise.
author: Chris Jones

text: It keeps the flame that was lit in 1976 well and truly alive, and for that we should all be grateful.
author: Chris Jones

text: The first solo album from the Mojave 3 and former Slowdive singer starts with the uptempo Seasons.
author: Niky Daley

text: Nature is clearly a subject close to the writer's heart and the singer-surfer-songwriter mixed and recorded some of the album in his home-town Cornwall.
author: Niky Daley

text: The negative and positive ions from the sea osmose into a chilled and flowing album that reflects the soothing power of the big outdoors.
author: Niky Daley

text: Instrumentation is mainly acoustic, although Nick Holton is credited with 'funny noises' which appear on a couple of tracks.
author: Niky Daley

text: The subtle effect on Halstead's voice in Two Stones In My Pocket is reminiscent of Chris O'Connor's in the Primitive Radio God's Standing Outside A Broken: the result is a track every bit as powerful.
author: Niky Daley

text: Melancholy is woven throughout but the restrained trumpet brings it to the fore in Driving With Bert.
author: Niky Daley

text: Elsewhere it takes on a mariachi tone, but here wails in unison with the sentiments "music for your head, love is for your pain".
author: Niky Daley

text: Halstead has often been compared to Nick Drake, and his response to Drake's Northern Sky in terms of lyrical beauty is Hi-Lo And Inbetween.
author: Niky Daley

text: Both use a piano driven melody, but lyrically where Drake had found "magic as crazy as this", Halstead's desire remains unrealised.
author: Niky Daley

text: On other tracks Halstead takes on a more Dylanesque tone, and the waltzy Martha's Mantra wouldn't have sounded out of place on a Simon & Garfunkel record.
author: Niky Daley

text: The album echoes a road movie in sound and lyrical content that is further reinforced by its title Sleeping On Roads.
author: Niky Daley

text: The characters contained are either in limbo or on quests: "But heaven is the place that's open , when all the bars in town are closed, heaven is the place, I never find".
author: Niky Daley

text: If this search produces such ethereally melodic songs full of intense longing, let's hope he doesn't find what he's looking for too soon.
author: Niky Daley

text: The press release insists these three utterly marvellous electro knob-twiddlers hail from deepest darkest Michigan, but I'm not so sure.
author: Peter Davis

text: Seconds into the opener "Still Love In The Midwest" I'm convinced their Chevy spends a lot more time on the M42 than it does on Route 66.
author: Peter Davis

text: With its darkly funky echoes of 1980's New Order guitar licks and aggressively cheesy 808 handclaps, this just has to have something to do with Manchester doesn't it?
author: Peter Davis

text: Fear not, kids, Midwest Product are not from any place like you, as rapidly becomes clear on the superb "Clicks And Crackers", which as well as doing exactly what it says on the tin, sounds like Air playing space jazz on the moon with Adrian Sherwood.
author: Peter Davis

text: And boy can they play; despite being card-carrying bleepmongers, Chad Pratts live drumming has an effortless swing that's guaranteed to get your booty moving, as American audiences have been finding out on the Ghostly International tour this summer.
author: Peter Davis

text: Midwest Product manage that rare thing, a shimmeringly sucessful fusion of atmospheric high-end electronica and live instruments, without either sounding tacked on.
author: Peter Davis

text: But just when you think you've got these boys all worked out, along comes "Alternator".
author: Peter Davis

text: One of the finest of a very fine bunch indeed, this stunningly beautiful ambient groove could chill the socks off the angriest of Republican Guards.
author: Peter Davis

text: Warp Records listen up...
author: Peter Davis

text: Hold on, is that a sheep?
author: Peter Davis

text: Well, yes actually.
author: Peter Davis

text: Our four legged friends provide unexpected backing vocals on "Beardman In The City" to almost devastatingly strange effect while that slinkiest of grooves just keeps on getting better; who needs vocoders anyway?
author: Peter Davis

text: Things get a little darker with the late night road trips of "Lethal Cop (Kurt Russell)" and "A Genuine Display", in what is surely a wilfully mischevious attempt to make the outrageously cheesy opening to the left-field pop of "Vitamin" sound even more unsettling.
author: Peter Davis

text: The club night would be, er, interesting.
author: Peter Davis

text: Don't say I didn't warn you.
author: Peter Davis

text: The LP (do the kids still call them that?) draws to a close with "Clarity", a perfectly blissful fusion of acoustic guitar, laid-back funky drums and stylish electronica that leaves you in no doubt you've just been listening to one of the best albums of 2002.
author: Peter Davis

text: Catch them now, and feel very smug and terribly terribly knowledgeable in a few months time.
author: Peter Davis

text: Midwest Product: Because you're worth it.
author: Peter Davis

text: Over the last half a century Lol Coxhill's saxophone has appeared in a bewildering variety of contexts alongside the likes of (to name but a few) Rufus Thomas, Chris Macregor, Kevin Ayers, Alexis Korner, Derek Bailey, Anthony Braxton and the Damned.
author: Peter Marsh

text: To compile Spectral Soprano, Coxhill and producer Steve Beresford have trawled through the archives (going as far back as 1954) and collected a range of collaborations and solo works which cover free improvisation, straightahead jazz, R&B and much else that is unclassifiable.
author: Peter Marsh

text: What does unite Coxhill's contributions to these disparate (and indeed sometimes desperate) pieces is a deep love of melody, which is evident as much in the free improvisations as it is in the Lester Young-esque tenor of "Autumn in New York", "Perdido" and "Out of Nowhere", all recorded at 50s jam sessions.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Whether playing over jazz changes, electronics or (for example) drummer Roger Turner's unholy amalgam of Kenny Clarke, Tony Williams and a breakers yard, Coxhill's playing (mostly on soprano, of course) seems utterly convincing in any context; capable of lovely, soaring melodic lines, spluttering atonalities or acerbic sarcasm.
author: Peter Marsh

text: His solo improvisation "Strictly Legal" is remarkable, taking a long, unfolding series of lines for a walk which imply some inaudible accompanist's chords.
author: Peter Marsh

text: On the group improvisations his approach ranges from the lyrical (with bassist Dave Green and altoist Bruce Turner) to playful (with Veryan Weston) to rhapsodic (with Steve Miller).
author: Peter Marsh

text: One of the loveliest things on the record is his 1973 duet with Miller's electric piano included 'to remind hippies that I once travelled with an echo unit', according to the sleevenotes.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The Coxhill sense of humour is also well in evidence, as on the English Translation of Althea and Donna's "Uptown Top Ranking" or the overripe vocal delivery of "Embraceable You", which segues into a meticulous deconstruction of Charlie Parkers "Quasimodo" (played brilliantly and with love by Coxhill and pianist Veryan Weston).
author: Peter Marsh

text: This kind of approach is a breath of fresh air in an area of music that can take itself a bit too seriously; much like a good joke, Coxhill's playing is founded on notions of timing, cirumstance and quick thinking.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The man is a national treasure, and Spectral Soprano is crammed full of fine examples of his work in progress.
author: Peter Marsh

text: From Radiohead to the Red Hot Chili Peppers; not a day goes by without some young musical whippersnapper admitting that prog rock's not such a bad thing.
author: Chris Jones

text: But before we all rush out and start buying err...Rush, let us examine what semioticians would refer to as a 'key text': The music of Yes.
author: Chris Jones

text: The Word Is Live gives us an alternative chronological overview.
author: Chris Jones

text: That's three discs of mainly unreleased live versions of their classic work.
author: Chris Jones

text: Like musical Marmite, Yes divides the masses...but if you have a musical bone in your body you'll be hard-pushed to not find something of worth here.
author: Chris Jones

text: Beginners will be drawn in by Jon Anderson's frankly angelic voice (just don't ask what he's on about), whereas hardcore fans will melt over Steve Howe's edgy guitar dynamics, Chris Squire's in-yer-face bass and Bill Bruford's whipchord snare.
author: Chris Jones

text: All in all it's a cherry-picked primer on one of rock's most distinctive b(r)ands.
author: Chris Jones

text: Go on...be brave.
author: Chris Jones

text: A long time veteran of the 4-Track home studio, Bill Callahan (aka Smog) has been releasing his own kind of unique homespun rock for a little more than ten years now.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: While this in itself is nothing new, hes amassed an incredible amount of both support and material for his music.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Callahans songs have never been the kind that you would ever play at a party, unless you wanted to drive everyone to drink rather quicker than usual, of course.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: But still despite being a pretty melancholy and self-obsessed kind of character, the guy writes some absolutely amazing songs.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Just released on Domino here in the UK, Rain On Lens sees Callahan teaming up with other scene stalwarts Rick Rizzo (Eleventh Dream Day) and Pat Samson (US Maple) to create another wonderfully gloomy acoustic indie rock meets alt-country type album.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Recorded at Electrical Audio and Acme Studios in Chicago, the birthplace of Smog, the tracks are heavy and thick, plodding along like an overweight jogger on an incredibly hot day.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Bettina Richards from Thrill Jockey records once described one of her favourite bands as back-porch minimalism and that term would be pretty appropriate here.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Ive heard this sort of thing before on other Drag City releases, but theres just something about Smog that makes them sit above the rest.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: His songs touch on the raw nerve of melancholy - a soundscape that paints a picture of deserted warehouses, darkened skies and rural Americana as seen through the rainy windscreen of a rather large automobile.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Fans of Will Oldham or Jim O Rourke will be in familiar territory here, while for the rest of you - we suggest picking up a copy of this and just letting it sink into you.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Like those tobacco stains on your nice button down shirt you wore to the pub last night.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Its the kind of release thats been there all along, its just that you dont notice it straight away.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Quality, if not melancholy stuff.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: "Oh my", you're thinking, "a cd of 20th century music for solo trombone and orchestra?!
author: Andrew McGregor

text: McGregor's lost it (again); what on earth makes him think this is of any interest to most record buyers?" Fair point...but it's Christian Lindberg, see, the best thing that's ever happened to the trombone.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: The man can actually fill concert halls for his solo recitals all over the world, and if you don't think that's astonishing, just ask yourself if any other trombonist alive could do it; in fact just ask yourself if you can think of the name of another solo trombonist.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Yes, he's that good.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: And that means not only does Lindberg make marvellous sounds with his 'bone, but sometimes people write him marvellous music for it as well.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: I'm not sure I'd include his own piece on the disc though, the title track Mandrake in the Corner.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: I'm not sure I'd have put it first on the cd either; while there's nothing actually objectionable about it, there's nothing particularly memorable, and I don't need to hear it again.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: The Danish composer Axel Jorgensen's Suite from 1926 has some lovely, long melodic phrases that give Lindberg plenty of time to win us over with his lustrous tone, and it's hard not to warm to its romantic charms.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Egil Hovland's Concerto from the early 70's is a technical tour de force, with humour and a Bernstein-ian jauntiness to the finale...but it's the last work on the cd that left me grinning all over my face.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Jan Sandstrom's name might be familiar; Lindberg fans know him as the man behind that notorious Motorbike Concerto, and this is another brilliant and colourful showpiece for Lindberg.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Cantos de la Mancha takes the form of five scenes from the life of Don Quixote, and the trombonist has to sing, stamp, laugh and shout his way through the score, as well as playing some of the slickest trombone parts I've heard in a while.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: It's an astonishing display, colourful, humorous, brash, beautiful, and even at times genuinely moving.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Lindberg's a lucky man having a vehicle like this in his garage.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: "The trombone slide shall be your lance and with it you will fight windmills" the composer told him.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: This time he wins.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Should this cd have been made at all?
author: John Armstrong

text: When a composer is unhappy with a work and alters it himself, have we any right to ignore his wishes?
author: John Armstrong

text: Vaughan Williams actually revised the London Symphony three times, pruning it, removing material...about 20 minutes of music in all.
author: John Armstrong

text: And when you hear it restored, the symphony has changed...looser, yes, but more mysterious.
author: John Armstrong

text: You can understand why some of the composer's friends were sorry he'd cut the symphony, and it's good to have a chance to hear the original 1913 version for the first time - but you couldn't recommend it if the performance wasn't up to scratch.
author: John Armstrong

text: It is: Hickox and the London Symphony Orchestra have come up with a recording that you can cheerfully measure against most others in the catalogue, before you consider its unique extra charms!
author: John Armstrong

text: Richard Hickox told me recently that if it wasn't for Vaughan Williams' insecurities about the length of the original London Symphony, he'd never have removed what turned out to be some of the most startling and original sections of the piece.
author: John Armstrong

text: Permission was given just for this one recording, no public performances, but Ursula Vaughan Williams has been so delighted by the recording, and the enthusiasm with which it's been received, that there will now be a concert.
author: John Armstrong

text: Hickox also told me about the astonishment of the players at the recording session, when they'd played through what's a very familiar work and suddenly turned a page to find some completely new sounds and ideas...it's changed the way they, and everyone who's listened to the recording with such delight, think of this favourite British symphony.
author: John Armstrong

text: We loved it anyway, but it's better than we all thought, and no wonder Gramophone Magazine has made it Record of the Year, 2001.
author: John Armstrong

text: A Little Deeper is the acclaimed debut album from North London's finest Ms Dynamite aka Naomi McLean Daley who initially grabbed the nations attention as the bolshi MC on the Sticky produced Booo!
author: Emmy Perry

text: Expect a sixty-minute introduction into the life and strife of this gifted twenty two year old.
author: Emmy Perry

text: A smooth head nodding ride through heartbreak care of tracks "Sick n Tired", "Now You Want My Love", bad relationships "Gotta Let You Know" and a plethora of warning messages against the pitfalls of today's social ills typified by acapella "Watch Over Them".
author: Emmy Perry

text: There's even an ode to her baby brother.
author: Emmy Perry

text: Essentially, Dynamite wants you to learn from her mistakes and the mistakes of others to be the best that you can be.
author: Emmy Perry

text: Sentiments that on occasion come across as slightly preachy.
author: Emmy Perry

text: What the album isn't is a repeat of Booo!
author: Emmy Perry

text: (check out her limited release garage album A Little Darker for that) In search of world domination, Dynamite has decided somewhat wisely to broaden her appeal beyond the UK garage scene.
author: Emmy Perry

text: Hence why generous production credit is down to Salaam Remi, best known as the guy behind the sound of the Fugees multi-platinum release, The Score.
author: Emmy Perry

text: The 'there is something for everyone' attitude is stamped all over this debut effort with slow R&B numbers "All I Ever" rubbing shoulders alongside hip hop flavas "Get Up Stand Up" and electro influenced "Krazy Krush" each held together with the recurring undercurrent of dancehall.
author: Emmy Perry

text: Stand out tunes include singles "It Takes More" and "Dy-Na-Mi-Tee" plus Latin tinged "Put Him Out", reggae duet "Seed Will Grow" featuring Kymani Marley and title track "A Little Deeper".
author: Emmy Perry

text: Jamaican music legend Barrington Levy features on a classy rendition of "Too Experienced".
author: Emmy Perry

text: Vocally, whilst a unique talent, Dynamite's Lauryn Hill meets Nelly Furtado tone has definite room for growth but this album shows she can indeed dig deep and has brought out a genre bending, personal musical journey that is likely to be a prelude for greater things yet to come.
author: Emmy Perry

text: This is the sound of today's troubled urban multi-cultural British youth, slickly packaged to appeal to the masses.
author: Emmy Perry

text: Russ Jones (Future World Funk DJ) and Felix Buxton (half of Basement Jaxx), have assembled this unstable blend, both providing some bonus remixes of their own.
author: Martin Longley

text: When Gilles Peterson levitated the entire 2005 Big Chill gathering with N.O.H.A.'s "Balkan Hot Step", we knew that lolloping gypsy village brass had finally gone overground.As well asfusioneers like DJ Shantel and Balkan Beat Box, the authentic veterans are represented by Romania's Fanfare Ciocarlia and the Macedonian Kocani Orkestar, the latter tussling with novelty electronicist Senor Coconut.
author: Martin Longley

text: Sometimes, the marching programmed beats can be a touch insistent, but the wild wedding band vitality always remains untamed.
author: Martin Longley

text: A waddling sousaphone can easily deliver the lowest possible bassline, invariably topped by swarming brass hyperactivity.
author: Martin Longley

text: The Acid Mothers Temple discography seems to be expanding weekly with limited edition vinyl and CD-Rs cropping up on obscure labels all over the place.
author: Peter Marsh

text: When you record live and have a band that's pretty much incapable of playing anything under 20 minutes long, there's a lot to release.
author: Peter Marsh

text: No-one's complaining though, as guitarist Makoto Kawabata and friends seem to be on a roll at the moment in their quest to unite the drive of psychedelically fuelled rock with a deeper, more spiritual aesthetic.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The sprawling 40 minute title track is based on an Occitanian folk tune, and the unearthly acoustic opening with its overtone singing sounds like something that might have made its way on to a Werner Herzog soundtrack.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Indeed once the guitars come in and the band stoke up their mighty drone, the effect is that of an amped up Popul Vuh, the German band who soundtracked many Herzog films.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Ashra Tempel or Amon Duul are other reference points.
author: Peter Marsh

text: At times, it's impossible to believe that this wasn't recorded in Berlin in 1972, such is the authenticity of the enterprise.
author: Peter Marsh

text: But Kawabata's crew aren't merely K-tel Krautrockers; La Novia shows a deep respect for the traditional folk form and integrates it completely with the long forays into deep space that the leader's fuzz "Bon Voyage au LSD", though a mere 17 and a half minutes long makes up for in intensity what it lacks in length, building up from a stark montage of synth cries and guitar shrieks to a bludgeoning trainwreck of a riff.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Likely to send even your Granny on a trip to the outer regions of the known universe, this record should be handled with care.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Try These: Kawabata Makota and the Mothers of Invasion - Hot Rattlesnakes Neu!
author: Peter Marsh

text: King Crimson - Earthbound, Thrak, USA
author: Peter Marsh

text: A new Levellers album.
author: Nikki Smith

text: A chance for those who were students in the early 90s to relive the days when they believed there really was only "One Way" of life.
author: Nikki Smith

text: But will this new album be able excite us now that we've all grown up and become the business exec/accountants that we used to love to hate?
author: Nikki Smith

text: I wondered whether the Levellers were attempting to get people like me to dust down their tie-dyes and head off in a camper van, or whether they're attempting to attract a new generation of middle class hippies.
author: Nikki Smith

text: Lets examine the evidence...
author: Nikki Smith

text: To take the album at face value, it's not half bad.
author: Nikki Smith

text: "Four Winds" is a catchy opener and no doubt you'll be singing along to the chorus in no time.
author: Nikki Smith

text: However, vocalist Mark Chadwick sums up the over-riding sentiment in "Falling From The Tree" when he sings 'I just can't get back to where I've been'.
author: Nikki Smith

text: Much as it pains me to say it, he's probably right.
author: Nikki Smith

text: Energy levels amongst the songwriters have clearly declined over the years as there are far more ballads on the album than anticipated.
author: Nikki Smith

text: But the Levellers prove they can still pen an upbeat tune.
author: Nikki Smith

text: "Pretty Target" starts with a guitar riff that's bordering on indie; just add a violin and were back to Levelling the Land again.
author: Nikki Smith

text: 'I won't let you down' coos Mark.
author: Nikki Smith

text: And they don't.
author: Nikki Smith

text: After all, this is what the Levellers do best.
author: Nikki Smith

text: In "Wild As Angels" a certain recurring theme becames evident in the lyrics.
author: Nikki Smith

text: It seems that the Levellers realise they've grown older too.
author: Nikki Smith

text: 'With heavy wings I can recall the freedom flown'.
author: Nikki Smith

text: I know how he feels!
author: Nikki Smith

text: This track saves the album though and revives memories of how vibrant and energetic the Levellers are as a live band.
author: Nikki Smith

text: Overall Green Blade Rising is one long plea for the stable base of Levellers fans to keep the faith.
author: Nikki Smith

text: In "Wake The World" they claim 'You were brave when you were young.
author: Nikki Smith

text: Would you ever believe it could all come undone?' The answer is no, but then I never believed I'd have to work for a living either.
author: Nikki Smith

text: They finally lay themselves bare as they 'take a look around to see who's still listening'.
author: Nikki Smith

text: We are still listening, but only just.
author: Nikki Smith

text: File this under one for posterity and let the next generation decide.
author: Nikki Smith

text: Try These: Richard Ashcroft - Human Conditions David Gray - A New Day At Midnight
author: Nikki Smith

text: The patent and copyright on the cd's back cover is 2000.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: It's released by Thirsty Ear, but it's not a part of the Blue Series.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: The six titles look a bit of a ragbag (a 2nd piece, a version 4).
author: Colin Buttimer

text: The distributor claims it's a companion piece to Masses, but there's not actually much evidence of that.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: The typography on the front cover looks like somebody did it with a felt tip pen on a barmat and the image doesn't appear to bear relation to anything much.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Oh and remember - the cd's called Oddities.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Must be a hodgepodge, outtakes affair; something you might spot, lift out of the cd racks because you like Spring Heel Jack's stuff, but then maybe think better of and put back.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: "Root" starts off with guitar figures heard through and increasingly submerged by layers of near-orchestral and electronic sound like a stormtide engulfs a beach.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: "The Road to the Western Lands" appears to employ exactly the same recording of William Burroughs as used by Bill Laswell for his Material album Seven Souls.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Spring Heel Jack eschew the rhythmic patterns of the Material production in favour of a sympathetically eery ambience threaded with saxophone notes, stately piano chords and occasional vibes in a sympathetic treatment.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: "Trouble" continues the dark atmosphere with what sounds like threatening fireworkson a dark night.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: This almost 12 minute track sounds like a parallel to Eno's On Land where musical instruments are used to produce non-musical ambience, though in this case the result is generally a lot noisier, with the exception of an interlude of almost humorous lightness towards the end.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: "Shine a Light" (a Jason Pierce composition) is a beatless, beatific humalong of a melody.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: "2nd Piece for LaMonte Young" is a rich tectonic movement which begins groaning and shrieking and ends in a high beautiful place in the rafters, tones singing, long slow sirens sounding.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: "Piece for Six Turntables, version 4" is a BBC Festival Commission, clocking in at over 16 minutes.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: This (as with the preceding pieces) betrays a strong sense of severe drama recalling orchestral modernism.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: John Coxon's guitarwork here is graphic, tactile.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Oddities reveals a rich, dark seam of possibilities.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: It's dark, gorgeous music which makes me wonder how deep this seam penetrates; is there more, or is this it?
author: Colin Buttimer

text: It's difficult but accessible music (if that's not too much of an oxymoron for you).
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Don't pass this one by.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Lazy journalism dictates that all reviews of a new Beck album must make reference to the fact that he is a 'post-modern Prince' and that his lyrics tend to be 'surreal wordplay with a hip hop edge'.
author: Chris Jones

text: Well, scratch all that because, compared to his last release - the sexy funk pot-pourri, Midnite Vultures -this is about as straightforward as he's ever been.
author: Chris Jones

text: If Midnite Vultures was his seduction album, Sea Change is his bitter break-up opus.
author: Chris Jones

text: Yes, someone has broken Beck's heart and, for better or worse, we're invited along for the ride.
author: Chris Jones

text: Always invested with the ability to skip genres, Mr Hansen returns to the melancholy folk template last seen on Mutations tracks such as ''Nobody's Fault But My Own'', but existential angst is replaced by desolate tales of despair and loss.
author: Chris Jones

text: Anyone fond of the white suit-wearing, body popping art terrorist will be disappointed.
author: Chris Jones

text: Maturity, it seems, has taken its toll on our boy, but the stripped back honesty of his approach, with acoustic guitars tastefully picked throughout, perfectly suits the subject matter.
author: Chris Jones

text: The song titles tell the whole story; ''Lost Cause'' (''I'm tired of fighting, fighting for a lost cause''), ''Lonesome Tears'' (''Oh they ruin me every time'') and ''Already Dead (''Days turn to sand'') while the exquisite production, courtesy of Nigel Godrich, perfectly captures the desert-dry keening of crushed dreams.
author: Chris Jones

text: After this and OK Computer Godrich's must be the only number to ring if you wish your album to be as maudlin as a Sunday round at Morrissey's gaff .
author: Chris Jones

text: Sea Change displays a cohesiveness that, again, defies expectations from the magpie kid.
author: Chris Jones

text: Only the somewhat sullen and perfunctory guitar trashing sequence at the end of ''Sunday Sun'' threatens the ambience.
author: Chris Jones

text: However, the rewards are plenty for the stout-hearted, with minute attention to detail in subtle instrumentation (check Jason Faulkner's tasty licks on the mogadon hip hop of ''Paper Tiger'') and arrangements.
author: Chris Jones

text: Beck's own dad, David Campbell (a veteran of the LA studio scene from Jackson Browne to, gulp, Aerosmith), provides strings that keep the hairs on your neck erect at all times; especially on the Nick Drake homage ''Round The Bend'' and the aforementioned ''Paper Tiger''.
author: Chris Jones

text: Again and again, Beck's words reflect the cynicism born of betrayal and longing.
author: Chris Jones

text: Desert imagery becomes a metaphor forwashed-up, strung-out weariness.
author: Chris Jones

text: Yet, on the ironically-titled opener ''The Golden Age'', it also serves as a space where care can be sloughed off: ''Let the desert wind cool your aching head.
author: Chris Jones

text: Let the weight of the world drift away instead.
author: Chris Jones

text: These days I barely get by.
author: Chris Jones

text: I don't even try''.
author: Chris Jones

text: The whole album-as-catharsis exercise leaves the listener exhausted but undeniably moved.
author: Chris Jones

text: Its slightly self-pitying tone means that it falls some way short of being Beck's Blood On The Tracks, but taken as a whole this is as finely-crafted and achingly beautiful as anything you''ll hear this year.
author: Chris Jones

text: Bruised, but most definitely unbowed.
author: Chris Jones

text: This is tenor saxophonist Ned Otter's first album as a leader.
author: John Eyles

text: Prior to this, he served a long apprenticeship with George Coleman, including membership of Coleman's Octet and featuring on their album Danger High Voltage (another release on Two and Four).
author: John Eyles

text: For So Little Time, Coleman repays the favour, joining Otter's band for three of the album's eight tracks.
author: John Eyles

text: The band also includes two other long-term associates of Coleman's, Harold Mabern on piano and Billy Higgins on drums (in one of his last sessions before his death last May), plus relative newcomers Tom Kirkpatrick on trumpet and Daniel Vitale on bass.
author: John Eyles

text: The music is classic post-bop of the kind that could have been recorded any time in the past forty years.
author: John Eyles

text: It wouldn't have sounded out of place on Blue Note in the sixties (it even has Rudy Van Gelder as the recording engineer).
author: John Eyles

text: All of the tracks, including five Otter originals, put the focus primarily on the soloists.
author: John Eyles

text: Every member acquits himself well, although Mabern and Higgins jointly manage to steal the limelight, adding drive and panache to the band.
author: John Eyles

text: Otter reveals his true class by matching Coleman admirably.
author: John Eyles

text: On "The Right To Know", Coleman lays down a fine solo, only to have it bettered by a rapid-fire tour-de-force from Otter.
author: John Eyles

text: By comparison, Kirkpatrick rather suffers by being recorded too far back in the mix.
author: John Eyles

text: Otter is featured at length on the ballad "Funny", which showcases his exquisitely mellow tone and impeccably timed phrasing.
author: John Eyles

text: This album will not set the world alight, but it does contain some excellent playing and will supply many long hours of listening pleasure.
author: John Eyles

text: A debut to be proud of.
author: John Eyles

text: The biggest girl group in the world return with the follow up to their 1999, nine million copy selling Fanmail and it's hot...
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Since signing to LaFace in 1991 TLC have ridden the rock 'n' roll rollercoaster all the way.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: From their humble beginnings in Atlanta to the incredible breakthrough album that was CrazySexyCool there followed record company fall outs, rumours about break ups and bankruptcy.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Not to mention their phenomenal record sales and countless MTV, Soul Train, Billboard and Grammy awards.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Unfortunately, the incredible highs have been tempered with the most unbearable of lows.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: The loss of Lisa 'Lefteye' Lopes in a car accident earlier this year sent a shock wave through the music world, one that still mourns the loss of agenuine talent.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Regrettably, she joins Biggie Smalls, Tupac Shakur, Aaliyah, and Jam Master Jay who, for one reason or another, have been taken prematurely.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Kicking off with a drum and bass intro 3D progresses through an uncompromising take on the R&B sound.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: "Quickie" and "Girl Talk" are upfront party jams propelled by bare faced cheek and female power while the sweet, acoustic soul of "Turntable" provides a welcome contrast with its beautiful harmonies.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Pharrell Williams and Chad Hugo team up with the girls on vocals and studio desk duties on "In Your Arms Tonight".
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Although softer than most of the Neptunes productions this pops, dips and surges on the electro tip that has become their trademark style.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: "Dirty Dirty" is a real high point with Missy Elliot and Timbaland taking the lead on the writing and production.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: These two are making the most forward thinking music that is above and beyond anything else being made at the moment and we love them for it.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Quite what the future holds for the band remains to be seen as they have announced recently that they will not be looking for a replacement to make the trio complete.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: If 3D is the last record TLC will have gone out on a high, either way Lisa would have loved it.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Still crazy, still sexy, still cool.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Imagine Kate Bush taking you by the hand, leading you deep into the Slovakian countryside and showering you with pine cones.
author: Fiona Talkington

text: Well, when you listen to Sui Vesan's debut album this wild fantasy virtually comes to life.
author: Fiona Talkington

text: At the moment Sui's name is little known outside her native Slovakia, but there's a sort of buzz going on at the moment, a little ripple in the music business, that suggests we're going to be hearing more from her.
author: Fiona Talkington

text: And that's a good thing!
author: Fiona Talkington

text: She's been likened to to Bjork and Tracy Chapman.
author: Fiona Talkington

text: For me it's her combination of the sweeping wildness of Kate Bush, the unpredictability of Iva Bittova, and the dramatic, haunting nature of Norwegian singer Sidsel Endresen which makes this a dead cert for one of my albums of the year.
author: Fiona Talkington

text: The first track "Makoienka" ("Poppy"), is enticing enough, though later, when you realise what she can do without the security blanket of a guitar, even this seems fairly run of the mill.
author: Fiona Talkington

text: "Beh po kamienkoch" ("Run on the Pebbles") is a glorious explosion of Sui's exploitation of the natural rhythms of the Slovakian language and her own curious and very attractive onomatopaeic sounds.
author: Fiona Talkington

text: She uses poppy heads, seeds and bark for percussion and she really does give the feeling that she's out in the open air whooping and calling across the fields in a frenzy of vocal exploration!
author: Fiona Talkington

text: "Malinka som hviezdy pasiem" ("Small as I am, I graze stars") unleashes an Eartha Kitt feel to her voice.
author: Fiona Talkington

text: You are sitting in the front row of a smoky jazz club looking straight into her eyes.
author: Fiona Talkington

text: "I am tiny and am shepherding the stars" she sings.
author: Fiona Talkington

text: "I dance with them until I shiver...
author: Fiona Talkington

text: Hair will be tangled, but I'm just a human".
author: Fiona Talkington

text: And how easily she slips from Eartha Kitt into an almost Lapland joik with hints of Mari Boine.
author: Fiona Talkington

text: There is no doubt that Sui Vesan has a voice of her own and confidence in the presentation of her music.
author: Fiona Talkington

text: Marks out of 10?
author: Fiona Talkington

text: Whatever 10 is in Slovakian.
author: Fiona Talkington
