text: Kandia is one of Mali's best known Griots, or "praise singers".
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Her voice is thick, gritty and powerful, with a big, broad range.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: On the softer songs she is warm andsoothing.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: And when she lifts up her voice and starts testifying as on "Sanougnaoule" or "Ibalan" or most of the tracks here, it cuts through the air and electrifies your senses.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: She's been doing this all her life (Griots are a caste you are born into, with the tradition handed down through the generations) although this is only her second album.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: But the Griot tradition of West Africa goes back thousands of years.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: A Griot is a combination of a singer, poet, historian, and community leader, the custodian of a particular peoples oral tradition.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: They're a central part of their communities, binding them together with songs and chants that offer inspiration and consolation to deal with life's struggles and setbacks.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: For example, "Ibalan" literally translates as "Try Hard".
author: Nick Reynolds

text: The first track "San Barana" opens with stunning guitar from Djelimady Tounkara.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: This sets the standard for a very high quality album.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: The performances are great, the recording is excellent, even the CD sleeve is lovely.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: There's plenty of instrumental colour, jolly balafon playing, flute and vocal chorus.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Kandia's own group of musicians provide her with assured backing and some unusual instruments, like violin and accordion provide even more variety.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: A wah wah pedal and a double bass add a reallyfunky edge to "Tchegniba".
author: Nick Reynolds

text: There's excellent sax on "Mbensera" played by Nicholas Gueret, which pays tribute to her Kouate griot ancestors.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: This is conscious music, preaching sometimes but always sympathetic and never judgmental, as on "Mortalite".
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Even if you don't understand a word of it, it's life affirming and joyful.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: It pulses with integrity and passion, and exudes a deep, reassuring strength.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Your spirits are lifted up.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: You feel in a better mood to face the day and to try a little bit harder.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Is bossa nova supposed to be this sad?
author: Nick Reynolds

text: I thought it was supposed to keep things light and low key, cool and relaxed, in a culture where theres too much sun to over exert yourself.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: But this remarkable album reinterprets Antonio Jobims songs in a quietly radical way.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: It points up his similarities to classical composers like Debussy and Chopin.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: But it also brings out a bittersweet sadness at the heart of his music.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Its the deep, dark keening sound of the cello, the twilight voicings of the piano and the perfect, pure pitch of Paula Morelenbaums creamy voice.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Its a cliche, but in this case its true: it makes the hair on the back of your neck stand on end.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Sometimes the combination is almost too rich, too sobbing, too dramatic, almost too beautiful.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: "Imagina", a duet with Ed Motta pulses with quietly suppressed longing, At times its surprisingly intense and maybe too much (over 71 minutes) to take at one sitting.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Perhaps the emotion expressed here is in part a requiem for Jobim, the inventor of bossa, who died from cancer in his fifties.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Paula and Jacques Morelenbaum were both long time Jobim collaborators, and the album was partly recorded at his home in Rio De Janeiro, with Sakamoto sitting at Jobims own piano.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Sakamoto was in a bossa nova group when a teenager, and his playing here seems thoroughly assured and emotionally sophisticated.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Some of the material has never been played before, while songs like "Bonita" and "Fotografia" are more familiar.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: "Imagina", a duet with Ed Motta pulses with quietly suppressed longing, "Chanson Pour Michelle" featuring piano and cello alone is one of many highlights.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: This is chamber music of great beauty, which should appeal to both classical music lovers and fans of bossa nova.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Its a lovely album.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Just dont play it too loud if youve just split up with someone.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Yes, it's that time of year when both the grizzled veterans and bright young things of the UK jazz scene start making space on their mantlepieces in anticipation ofa BBC Jazz Award.
author: Gordon Miles

text: And again, here's the soundtrack album, featuring all the hopeful nominees.
author: Gordon Miles

text: If nothing else, this compilation shows what a broad church the British jazz scene is (some might say it's too broad, particularly if there's room in it for Jools Holland).There's everything here from classy takes on the American Songbook to punk-tinged fusion, straightahead hard bop and even a spot of free improv.
author: Gordon Miles

text: Names include the familiar (John Taylor, Clare Teal, Alan Barnes, er, Jools Holland) and the less so (Polly Gibbons, Fulborn Teversham, Ronnie Rae).
author: Gordon Miles

text: Of course, even those blessed with ultra-catholic taste are unlikely to love everything here.But if you want an intelligently compiled snapshot of the state of British Jazz in 2006, this is the album for you...
author: Gordon Miles

text: Blessed with the most confusing name in music today (try telling your friends you like him, without soliciting gales of laughter), young Ryan is currently a song writing fool.
author: Chris Jones

text: A year on from his classic Heartbreaker he gives us this 70 plus minute epic (also available in a limited edition with a CD of 5 extra tracks) and has, by all accounts, just completed its follow-up Pink Hearts.
author: Chris Jones

text: His live shows are witness to this prolific urge, as he dips into his ever-present notebook to play "one I wrote, just yesterday".
author: Chris Jones

text: In fact, recently a man attacked him on stage, enraged that he stopped the show to pen a new song!
author: Chris Jones

text: His life, it seems, is a constant source of inspiration.
author: Chris Jones

text: Adams often attracts the odious tag of "Alt Country" for his Americana-soaked musings, but while songs such as "When The Stars Go Blue" contain a folksy integrity inherited from his old band Whiskeytown, the overall feel of this mighty work is that of plain old Rock.
author: Chris Jones

text: The plaintive lilt of "Wild Flowers" and "Answering Bell" hark back to previous work, but his muse seems to be undergoing a transformation on the raucous "Tina Toledo's Walkin' Blues".
author: Chris Jones

text: It's pure Sticky Fingers-era Stones with its slide guitar and Jagger swagger.
author: Chris Jones

text: Backed by band that includes Stephen Still's son Chris, much of this 16-song opus rocks with an intensity that reflects his relocation to the faster environs of LA.
author: Chris Jones

text: The subject matter is still that of broken relationships but, whereas before the sense was of an unremitting resignation, now a lighter note leavens the confessionals.
author: Chris Jones

text: He's just enjoying life a little more, as he says on the hypercharged opener "New York New York" - "And love don't play any games with me anymore, like she did before.
author: Chris Jones

text: The world won't wait, so I better shake that thing right out there through the door." The lazy melancholy is still there, but mixed with an offbeat humour as on the touching "Sylvia Plath".
author: Chris Jones

text: The only problem is quality control - an editor is undoubtedly needed for this boy with the blues.
author: Chris Jones

text: Yet that doesn't stop Gold being one of the most uplifting of this year's releases.
author: Chris Jones

text: HIM have been a low key, almost shadowy presence on the much hyped Chicago music scene in the six years or so they've been active.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Put together in 1995 as a solo project by sometime June of 44, Rex and Codeine drummer Doug Scharin, HIM have put out an album a year with all the typical Chicago ingredients; a bit of dub, a bit of jazz, a drop of ethnological forgery; they've even had a few Tortoise members on board at one time, but haven't seemed to garner the same recognition as their peers.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Which is a shame, as Scharin is one of the most individual and powerful drummers around and can create the kind of loose limbed, multidirectional propulsion that Tortoise can only hint at.
author: Peter Marsh

text: So, what are they doing on the Jazz page then ?
author: Peter Marsh

text: New Features follows on from last year's Points of Departure, which played down the dub inflected studio treatments of earlier records in favour of a more live, open ended group feel, but this time around the group is more expanded, the arrangements are tighter, the overall sound is softer and more melodic.
author: Peter Marsh

text: And it sounds like, er, jazz...
author: Peter Marsh

text: As on Points, long time Scharin associate Fred Erskine's precise, economical bass playing locks with the leader's Sly Dunbar-meets-Tony Allen drumming to create slinky, infectious grooves which will provoke involuntary booty shaking in the most inert of listeners.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Langorous horns, ticking guitars and muted keyboards have been added, sketching out long, graceful arcs of melody over the bubbling rhythms.
author: Peter Marsh

text: It's exciting, dynamic stuff, with a freshness that belies its influences and displaying a refreshing lack of irony.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Unfortunately alto saxophonist Carlos Cennano doesn't really have either the tone, the ideas or technique to convince as a soloist, and (as on Points) Scharin gives him an amount of space that's in inverse proportion to his abilities.
author: Peter Marsh

text: While he's not as bad as say, Van Morrison, and his playing does work as texture when Scharin gets busy with the dub, it's tempting to wonder what someone like Henry Threadgill could do over the tumbling, skittering rhythms of the otherwise brilliant 17 minute "In Transition''.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Still, everyone else turns in fine solos and group playing, and repeated listenings reveal a wealth of detail due to Scharin's undoubted skills at the desk, which gives the music here a lush, expansive feel.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The more traditionally dub inclined fare of "Clouds" is a joy; graceful, echo soaked trumpet emerges through, well, clouds of delayed guitars over Erskine's restrained, deep in the pocket bassline, while "Were Once" has the warm, oceanic groove of Can's Future Days fused with the drift of Miles Davis' "He Loved Him Madly".
author: Peter Marsh

text: The only clanger is the closing "Sea Level", an attempt at mid 70s Miles funk brutality which fails to convince despite some fine drumming.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Scharin has certainly got it in him to make a great record; this isn't quite it, but he's on the way.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Boy, is this hard to explain!
author: Andrew McGregor

text: The Hilliard Ensemble vocalising while Christoph Poppen plays Bach's most famous work for solo violin...surely some mistake?
author: Andrew McGregor

text: You see, it's all down to the sharp eye and keen ear of German musicologist Helga Thoene.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: She specialises in seeing the hidden messages in baroque music that our superficial 21st century approach misses, and her theory is that Bach's D minor Partita for solo violin is full of hidden references to death, riddled with quotations from his own chorales.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: I've played the piece and never noticed anything like that&but then I wasn't looking, was I?
author: Andrew McGregor

text: I won't go into details, it's mind-boggling enough when you read the notes, and that's the best place to direct you if you're interested in finding out more.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: But how have Helga Thoene's analyses been made flesh by our performers, you're asking?
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Well, the chorales, performed gently and very beautifully by the Hilliards, alternate with the individual movements of the D minor Partita, allowing us to investigate the associations with our own ears, or at least to luxuriate in an imaginatively mixed recital of Bach at his most affecting.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: And so it goes - until we reach the great Chaconne.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Thoene's thesis is that this movement represented a memorial to Bach's wife, Maria Barbara, who died while he was away from home.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: He returned to find not only that she'd died, but she'd actually been buried a week before his return; it's hard to imagine how this must have affected him.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: So, says the Professor, the Chaconne is a 'tombeau' for Maria Barbara Bach, and here, as Poppen plays one of the greatest movements for violin ever composed, the Hilliards sing the chorale quotations, showing how they fit alongside the solo line.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: It must have been extremely difficult to make this work in performance, but the result is extraordinary, turning the Chaconne into a memorial, and an expression of faith in the resurrection of the dead and life everlasting.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: You may not want to play this every time you think of the D minor Partita, but it's deeply affecting, and beautifully realised' ECM's been intelligent enough to give us a number of possibilities, recording two versions of the Chaconne, with and without voices, so if you want you can programme Christoph Poppen's performance of the Partita with no vocal interventions at all.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: But I bet you won't want to after you've heard them together.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: It's probably not adding much to the sum total of human knowledge to say that Dave Holland's current band are one of the most accomplished and exciting acoustic jazzoutfits on the planet.In fact, they're so good it's quite difficult to know what to write about them anymore;you almost wish they'd put a foot wrong occasionally.
author: Peter Marsh

text: No such luck.
author: Peter Marsh

text: This record was made partly as a response to public demand and from a need to document the band's stretched out, exploratorylive sets.Consequently there's little here that clocks in at less than 15 minutes or so.
author: Peter Marsh

text: While that may seem a bit excessive, what we have here is a band that seems incapable of being dull.
author: Peter Marsh

text: While it's Holland's band in name, writing credits and solo opportunities are spread evenly.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The front line of sax, vibes and trombone may strike some as unconventional, but to say it works would be a bit of an understatement; more than sum of their parts, indeed.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Holland and drummer Billy Kilson inject even the most obscure time signatures with irresistible elan anda deep, funky precision.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Kilson is unstoppable, sending the crowd into ecstacies with furious, timestretching eruptions that somehow always end precisely where they should, while the bassist gives his usual mix of flawless timekeeping and wiry, muscular lyricism.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Steve Nelson adds extra percussive flair with urgent marimba ripples, or supports and comments with sweetly ringing vibes chords.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Robin Eubanks simply has to be one of the most agile, expressive and precise trombonists around today, while Chris Potter's facility on soprano, tenor and alto connects with all sorts of saxophone traditions; one moment he's in garrulous Sonny Rollins mode, the next he's darting around with the quizzical grace of Wayne Shorter.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The same goes for the music; all kinds of jazz traditions are hinted at, from Mingus to M-Base.Despite being forever tagged as Miles Davis' discovery, Holland, like Jarrett, Hancock, Zawinul et al, has made his own place in jazz history, and this band is as state of the art as it gets.Unmissable.
author: Peter Marsh

text: 24-year-old Mileece has had a remarkable life.
author: Marcus Scott

text: When she was growing up, her parents ran a recording studio in Covent Garden, and started an early music video company.
author: Marcus Scott

text: Later her father became a director of television programmes such as Fraggle Rock and Countdown, whilst her mum ran a record label.
author: Marcus Scott

text: In early life she lived in various parts of the world including "The crystal garden" where she encountered counter-culture figures such as Timothy Leary and Charles Lucy - the inventor of the Lucytune microtonal scale.
author: Marcus Scott

text: After this, she moved to a large house full of animals in rural France to escape and learn about classical music.
author: Marcus Scott

text: On top of this, her grandfather Max Matthews programmed the first computer generated song, "Daisy, Daisy"which was cynically referenced in Kubricks "2001, A Space Odyssey", sung by the Hal computer as it loses control of its senses.
author: Marcus Scott

text: Well that's her life so far, and Formations is her stunning debut album, a charming suite of gentle tones that manages to sound natural, intimate and sunnydespite utilising the rigorous theories and practice of up-to-the minute electronic composition.
author: Marcus Scott

text: There are no hooks, choruses and sometimes little in the way of melody, but it's an example of an album that I could imagine anyone enjoying.
author: Marcus Scott

text: This music was composed using generative musical computer languages, something that inMileece's words "allows for structures to generate autonomously, the same as a plant or any living thing would".This is beautifully illustrated in track one, "aube" which actually sounds like the musical equivalent of cell division, as delicate tones chime out at seemingly random intervals but constantly keep an internal form and harmonic relationship.
author: Marcus Scott

text: The title tracksounds more like the familiar music of modern minimalist composition.
author: Marcus Scott

text: Repetitive motifs grow out of seemingly random clusters of notes, building up then dropping down in order to regroup, just as it seems the music is getting cluttered.
author: Marcus Scott

text: In this track, Mileece's strong grasp of psycho-acoustics is evident as her sparse music sometimes creates difference-tones (two notes together simultaneously creating another audible tone).
author: Marcus Scott

text: With the addition of a simple bass guitar accompaniment and a melody that sounds like a traditional fiddle reel trying to work itself out,"fern" creates a sound reminiscent of a more advanced, stripped down Tortoise, whilst"nightfall" adds simple cello and voice to the sine tones to create a warm lullaby.
author: Marcus Scott

text: If you are looking for an album of astonishing paradoxes; artificial yet natural, simple yet advanced, harmonic and ordered but random, then look no further than this outstanding release.
author: Marcus Scott

text: Beautiful, real musical science.
author: Marcus Scott

text: Try These: Takagi Masakatsu - Eating Polmo Polpo - The Science of Breath Ogurusu Norihide - Humour
author: Marcus Scott

text: Although Ogurusu Norihide is described in his press release as one of the "leading purveyors of minimal pop", I'm pretty certain this collection of title-less, vocal-less musical sketches isn't going to worry your average pop idol too much.
author: Marcus Scott

text: The fact is, Norihide (who is currently studying to be a Shinto priest) doesn't give away many clues; perhaps making the tracks on this album only identifiable by their lengths goes someway to allow the audience to find their own meaning in his music.
author: Marcus Scott

text: One meaning you can read into the music comes through in the gentle melding of the organic/acoustic world and the digital world.
author: Marcus Scott

text: It's easy to see the nature worship of Ogurusu'sShinto faithliving side by side with his super modern native city of Tokyo as an easy comparison to the methods and sound of his music.
author: Marcus Scott

text: Humour compiles Norihide's own self released eps study and I.
author: Marcus Scott

text: The album features an array of tracks mostly played on either the acoustic guitar or on the piano.
author: Marcus Scott

text: There are also two tracks of pure abstract electronics and one played on a dry sounding hand drum.
author: Marcus Scott

text: The electronic side of the album (aside from the two purely digital tracks) consists of very subtle manipulations, or barely-there rhythmic accompaniment.
author: Marcus Scott

text: Over three of the folky acoustic guitar tracks, it's the deceptively simple touches of backwards loops, delays and layering which bring the tracks to life, along with the use of subtle, quiet digital drums that manage to sound organic; like blocks of wood or metal on metal.
author: Marcus Scott

text: However it's track four, a simple guitar melody against a background of chirping crickets which fall in and out of time and pitch with the music in the foreground, and track eight which employs the use of dramatic silences as two chords are slowly repeated, which show the artist at his most thoughtful and creative.
author: Marcus Scott

text: The overall minimalism of this album reveals both its best and worst qualities; whilst some of it works, as Ive just described, it also reveals the problem that as a collection it comes across as a series of unfinished sketches.
author: Marcus Scott

text: This problem is most obvious in the piano pieces, which sound much like someone practising.
author: Marcus Scott

text: Furthermore, the solo drum piece which although is given a little deft electronic manipulation is still as exciting as any other seven and a half minute drum solo you can think of.
author: Marcus Scott

text: The two electronic tracks are fine but they seem out of place, as if they were added to show off the musicians skill; unfortunately this is unnecessary and they detract rather than add to the cohesion and feel of the album as a whole work.
author: Marcus Scott

text: In parts this is an enjoyable album, andNorihide has some finely honed skills.
author: Marcus Scott

text: However a more careful selection and a little more work could have made it a great deal more special.
author: Marcus Scott

text: Starsailor assert their rock credentials with moody third album On The Outside.
author: Jack Smith

text: Recorded in LA with producer Rob Schnapf (Beck, Elliott Smith) this release proves the band are still capable of well crafted, affecting songs.
author: Jack Smith

text: "Counterfeit Life", for example, rails against materialism with commendable disdain as singer James Walsh denounces corporate glory above a distorted guitar riff.
author: Jack Smith

text: Less introspective than previous albums, opening track "In The Crossfire" is typically upbeat, bursting from the speakers with remarkable bombast, all ringing guitars, pounding drums, and the occasional operatic whoop.
author: Jack Smith

text: But there's still the odd ballad too, "Jeremiah" being an ode to a murdered youth.
author: Jack Smith

text: Elements of U2 are peppered throughout, in the image of the red-filled skies of "In My Blood" and in the stirring progressions that drive "Faith Hope Love".
author: Jack Smith

text: But the band's earnest sentiments are scuppered somewhat when you notice that Walsh's vocals sound like Robbie Williams.
author: Jack Smith

text: Still, On The Outside remains well worth a listen.
author: Jack Smith

text: Prior to his late 50's stints with Gerry Mulligan and the Jimmy Guiffre 3, valve trombonist Bob Brookmeyer had been a key member of Stan Getzs 1953 lineup, so this little known 1961 session marked a reunion of sorts.
author: Peter Marsh

text: By this point in his career Getz's tenor playing was displaying less of an obvious debt to Lester Young, and his tone had developed the luxurious breathiness that would mark his most famous work.
author: Peter Marsh

text: As if in a direct riposte to the emergent avant garde scene (which he distrusted intensely), Getz seemed to be looking back to the luscious, quivering vibrato of Ben Webster on this sets two ballads, though his solos retain Youngs devotion to unbroken melodic line.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Theres an edge that comes through on occasion, as on the end of "Thump Thump Thump"; while trading fours with drummer Roy Haynes, Getz squeezes out an extraordinary high register phrase followed by bluesy slurs which seem at odds with his usual studied cool.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Brookmeyers tenure with Giuffre and guitarist Jim Hall had quietly revolutionised jazz, though there were (at the time) few adherents to their highly improvised chamber music.
author: Peter Marsh

text: On this date his highly mobile solos are peppered with the kind of vocal effects that were to become the common currency of new thing players like Grachan Moncur and Roswell Rudd.
author: Peter Marsh

text: A nod of the head to the brash novelties of New Orleans brass players perhaps, but Brookmeyer's not interested in novelties or entirely new vocabularies.
author: Peter Marsh

text: He's a craftsman, not a revolutionary, and throughout his carefully wrought improvisations are testament to that.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Certainly his rapport with the tenor player is a joy; the two handle the poised intricacies of the two uptempo Brookmeyer tunes ("Minuet" and "Thump Thump Thump" ) as one voice, and elsewhere fashion gracefully sublime counterpoint passages.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The valve trombone (not really a popular instrument) has a darker, less brash tone than the common or garden variety; Brookmeyers precision and timbral range shines on his gorgeous "Who Could Care" (maybe an ironic companion to Jerome Kern's "I Should Care").
author: Peter Marsh

text: The rhythm section were one of Getz's usual units; Haynes is as intelligent and dynamic as usual, while pianist Steve Kuhn (best known for his ECM dates) is restrained, supportive and precise, as befits Brookmeyers arrangements.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Credit is due to Verve for putting this one out (and doing a fine job of the packaging too); lovers of Getz should snap it up right away, while anyone interested in well crafted jazz will find plenty to keep them happy.
author: Peter Marsh

text: It appears that many of those who have faced the challenge of reviewing this album are in agreement that word count is a real bind.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: There is just too much to say.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: In fact, a small book could, and probably will, be written examining what The Streets has achieved with the execution of Original Pirate Material.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: It could be argued that not since Never Mind The Bollocks...
author: Christian Hopwood

text: has there been a record that has said as much about being young and living in the UK.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Moreover, what makes this album even more remarkable is that it is the work of a one unassuming 22 year old, namely Mike Skinner.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Despite an early passion for hip hop and house Mike was never embroiled in the London's pirate radio scene, in fact he was working in Australia when the UK garage cemented its position in the mainstream.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Perhaps it is this cultural and geographical distance that has kept Skinner's musical slate clean and allowed him to forge this unique 'high rise' style.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Ska, dub, house, drum and bass, hip hop and UK garage have all been thrown in to The Streets' sampler for processing and rearrangement.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: When combined with his vocal delivery the results are mesmerising - not quite hip hop, not quite an MC and not quite slam poetry but somewhere in between.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: He's engaged, enlightened and writes with a degree of insight that is humorous, heart-wrenching, humbling and worthy of so much more than this little review.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: By his own admission Original Pirate Material is the "day in the life of a geezer" yet amongst the bitter sweet, inner city anecdotes of drugs, violence, playing computer games, trips to the garage and going clubbing, Mike's best punches are pulled when he is at his most sensitive.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: In "Weak Become Heroes" he muses "It's easy, no one blames you, it's that world out there that's f**ked!...
author: Christian Hopwood

text: you're no less of a person and if God exists he still loves you, just remember that".
author: Christian Hopwood

text: In "Has It Come To This" he announces, "The music's a gift from the man on high, the lord and his children".
author: Christian Hopwood

text: More of these gems are revealed with successive listens and it is clear as the title in "Let's Push Things Forward" suggests Mike is on a mission.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: In the years to come if you're ever asked what it was like being young at the start of the twenty first century you could do a lot worse than dig this album out of your collection provided, of course, you've taken it out of your CD player.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: This 2CD set follows swiftly in the wake of the equally captivating first volume.
author: Martin Longley

text: Here, the time period covered goes back even further, spanning 1956 to 1982.
author: Martin Longley

text: The first volume concentrated on eight West African countries, but this second selection is an entirely Congolese mixture of rumba roots and early soukous.
author: Martin Longley

text: The compilation's positive intentions are immediately apparent, with the opening twelve minute "Co-operation" between Franco and Sam Mangwana: an odyssey of shimmering guitars, sweet vocal interplay and joyous horn stabs, topped off by a juicy saxophone solo.
author: Martin Longley

text: Nyboma provides the second song, weaving his own web of gleaming interaction.
author: Martin Longley

text: Tiny details, like the tightly-strummed rhythm guitar part, rise to the surface as the listener dances.
author: Martin Longley

text: The whole Zairean area was rife with feedback from Cuba, setting up an Afro-Caribbean dialogue that had been bouncing backwards and forwards over the decades.
author: Martin Longley

text: The singer Jospeh Kabasele founded his African Jazz band three years before Franco's O.K.
author: Martin Longley

text: Jazz became the other giant dynasty of Zairean music.
author: Martin Longley

text: Tracks 3 and 4 are by Kabasele, maintaining the scintillating vibrations, before Franco's duet with the accordionist Camille Feruzi diverts the path completely.
author: Martin Longley

text: There will be several such dalliances before the compilation's over, as Docteur Nico floats off on pedal steel guitar, Le Likembe Geant pluck their electrified thumb pianos and Feruzi returns for a couple of his own accordion pieces.
author: Martin Longley

text: Franco and (visiting Cameroonian) Manu Dibango are caught at the very start of their careers, and the second disc delves back even further into quaint recording history.
author: Martin Longley

text: Tabu Ley Rochereau's warm vocal proximity pulls in the listener on "Aon-Aon", and the now London-based Mose Fan Fan's "Pele Odija" offers a rare opportunity to hear what this guitarist was doing thirty years ago.
author: Martin Longley

text: Already partially unleashed on vinyl earlier this year under the name of Metaphormosis, this timely CD release fills in a sizeable hole in the enigmatic career of the mighty Fripp and pals and their part in the creation of the Crimson King.
author: Chris Jones

text: Mainly consisting of demos recorded at the titular address, this document is amazing for two reasons.
author: Chris Jones

text: Firstly, as the splendid sleeve notes demonstrate, this was far more than a couple of mikes fed into a Revox set-up.
author: Chris Jones

text: The sound quality of these pieces is a testament to the precision of artists forced to work under primitive conditions while developing a profile which their first album (The Cheerful Insanity Of Giles, Giles And Fripp) - with it's bland production - failed to deliver.
author: Chris Jones

text: Secondly, with its addition of key players such as Ian MacDonald on wind instruments and Pete Sinfield, this shows how a year of hard work away from the limelight could turn a jokey little trio into a powerful musical unit, ready to take on the post psychedelic music scene.
author: Chris Jones

text: It is fascinating to finally hear all of the tracks that featured the criminally underrated Judy Dyble, the original vocalist with Fairport Convention.
author: Chris Jones

text: Committed King Crimson fans will already be familiar with her rendition of "I Talk To The Wind", but on the evidence of the other material on offer here, she should have stayed for longer than the mere two or three months it took to record them.
author: Chris Jones

text: "Drop In" by Fripp, which became a Crimson live staple the following year, makes its first appearance here as does a re-versioned "Suite No.
author: Chris Jones

text: 1" which should dispel any notion that the Wimborne wonder was anything less than a young genius of the fretboard.
author: Chris Jones

text: Lush harmonies, assured, jazzy instrumentation and a sense of humour (check out those Pythonesque photos!), all wrapped up with most scholarly and amusing sleeve notes from Pete Giles.
author: Chris Jones

text: This is both a lovingly prepared historical document and a well-prepared argument in favour of a band who have, for too long, languished in the shadows as a mere precursor to greater things.
author: Chris Jones

text: Why don't you just drop in?
author: Chris Jones

text: Fresh from winning the Mobo awards best reggae act 2002, Sean Paul unleashes the follow up to his first album Stage One with an album entitled Dutty Rock (Dutty is the Jamaican slang for Dirty, for those who dont know.) Sean Paul Henriques (more commonly known as Sean Paul) began his career as a songwriter but has since found greater success as a performer.
author: Darren 'Shaq-D' Springer

text: His major breakthrough came with the dancehall hit "Infiltrate", which competed with Beenie Man's international smash hit "Who Am I", and was based on the same rhythm.
author: Darren 'Shaq-D' Springer

text: Sean's style is reminiscent of established DJs Super Cat and Spragga Benz.
author: Darren 'Shaq-D' Springer

text: Aware of these comparisons he has tried to nurture his own unique style and his clear and concise delivery has made a huge impact on the international audience.
author: Darren 'Shaq-D' Springer

text: Dutty rock commences with a comical intro in which Sean Paul is rehearsing with a British rock band called 'Advanced Alternative' who have misinterpreted the meaning of 'Dutty Rock'.
author: Darren 'Shaq-D' Springer

text: From this point onwards Sean gives us his interpretation of 'Dutty Rock'.
author: Darren 'Shaq-D' Springer

text: "Shout (Street Respect)" is the first track on the album, it cleverly uses the current popular trend of mixing dancehall, R&B and hindi music.
author: Darren 'Shaq-D' Springer

text: The album features two tracks which are already considered to be dancehall smashes; these are "Gimme The Light" and "Can You Do The Work" featuring Ce'cile.
author: Darren 'Shaq-D' Springer

text: "Im Still In Love With You" which was originally sung by Alton Ellis is another tune which is currently doing the rounds on the dancehall circuit.
author: Darren 'Shaq-D' Springer

text: The increasingly popular Neptunes have collaborated with Sean Paul and Fahrenheit to give you "Bubble"; this is a mellow dancehall groove which uses a Hindi beat (the constant drum used in this track is known as the 'Tabla').
author: Darren 'Shaq-D' Springer

text: The album peaks when Sean Paul joins forces with Busta Rhymes for the 'Pass The Dro-Voisier' remix of "Gimme The Light".
author: Darren 'Shaq-D' Springer

text: This remix is a remake of the 2002 dancehall floor filler; the lyrics are completely re-worked in-order to go toe to toe with Busta Rhymes, who handles the dancehall crossover with ease.
author: Darren 'Shaq-D' Springer

text: Dutty Rock demonstrates Sean Pauls versatility, from dancehall to R&B to hip hop, (he even performs one track in English and then in Spanish).
author: Darren 'Shaq-D' Springer

text: The album is a must have for anyone who consider themselves to be a dancehall fan.
author: Darren 'Shaq-D' Springer

text: It's going to blow up baby.
author: Darren 'Shaq-D' Springer

text: Mudhoney practically invented grunge when they formed in 1988, signing to and then defining the Sub Pop label.
author: Jules Willis

text: Since then they have ambled through the transatlantic rock scene with mixed reviews for the past fourteen (yes, that long!) years.
author: Jules Willis

text: Since We've Become Translucent is their eighth studio album and their first in four years since their last 1998 offering Tomorrow Hit Today.
author: Jules Willis

text: The album is characterised by the departure of bass player Matt Luckin who left in 1999 after ten years with the band and the arrival of ex-Lubricated Goat, Guy Maddison.
author: Jules Willis

text: His introduction and fluid bass style marks a watershed in Mudhoney's history and a spirited change in direction.
author: Jules Willis

text: Often more psychedelic than their contemporary grunge counterparts, Mudhoney re-emerge at the right time given the garage revival of the moment.
author: Jules Willis

text: Nevertheless they retain a more melodic, less raw experimental sound.
author: Jules Willis

text: They offer a logical, listenable alternative to the lo-fi norm.
author: Jules Willis

text: It's an expansive, polished album recorded three songs at a time in three different studio locations with three different engineers.
author: Jules Willis

text: This gives the album a sonic variety and the band the opportunity to diversify, yet retains singer Mark Arms trademark strong, rasping vocals, rendering each song unique.
author: Jules Willis

text: The energetic "Inside Job" is the anomaly having been recorded with Jack Endino in 2000 with MC5's Wayne Kramer on bass pre-Maddison.
author: Jules Willis

text: The outstanding tortured vocal of the swirling rock classic "In the Winners Circle" has it's roots somewhere back in the late sixties or early seventies, while "Where the Flavour Is" features a horn section.
author: Jules Willis

text: The imposing, discordant "Crooked and Wide" precedes the stunning first single "Sonic Infusion"; a Zeppelin-esque epic outburst lasting nearly eight minutes.
author: Jules Willis

text: An impressive return to form invigorated by new blood in the form of Maddison and engineers from Egg, Gravelvoice, Jupiter and Private Radio, that should be received as one of Mudhoneys finest.
author: Jules Willis

text: The lyric from the prophetically titled "Our Time Is Now" rings true for the transmuted, redefined Mudhoney: 'Given two lousy choices, we chose neither'.
author: Jules Willis

text: Go your own way.
author: Jules Willis

text: Viktoria Mullova plays Mozart: that's already enough to get my attention.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: As anyone who's heard her Bach - solo and concertos - can attest, this is a supremely stylish fiddle-player, possessed of a powerful modern technique, but who's always ready to put it at the service of the music rather than imposing her personality on everything she plays.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Maybe that's why Mullova has her undeserved ice-queen reputation; we're not used to hearing players of her provenance and prowess placing themselves quietly in the hands of the composer, without the emotional histrionics and interpretative licence taken by some of her peers.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Ok, so I'm already interested...but then you see that this is Mullova with the Orchestra of the Age of Enlightenment: period instruments.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: There's no conductor; she directs them herself...and she's strung her Strad with gut, and plays it with a classical bow.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Now I'm fascinated.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: But Mullova's going to be compared to the real specialists, the people who've made solo performance on period violins their life's work, your Standages and Huggets, and there are bound to be significant differences.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: The giveaways are usually found in the right hand; the 21st century violinist often finds it difficult to moderate the power and pressure that's been drilled into them for decades - they can sometimes sound really rough.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Not Mullova; while she doesn't have the quicksilver sound and instinctive mastery of the classical bow, and perhaps not quite the full range of tone colours that gut strings can deliver in the hands of a seasoned period instrumentalist, she's fluent, warm, and surprisingly gentle.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Mullova's is one of the great techniques amongst modern players, and obviously that total security is as enjoyable in Mozart as Tchaikovsky or Shostakovich...perhaps even making too light of the cadenzas, newly written by Mullova and Ottavio Dantone.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Maybe there's a touch more vibrato at times than you'd expect, especially in the slow movements, yet Mullova also revels in the sound of her gut-strung violin, employing open strings to good effect.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: The OAE is on top form, obviously enjoying this outing, with a superstar soloist meeting them on their own terms - the finales really dance, and there's an infectious enthusiasm about the whole disc that's refreshing.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Several big names are going back to gut at the moment, but of the violinists Viktoria Mullova's making the best job of it on this evidence.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: I'd cheerfully, nay, enthusiastically recommend this to her fan-base and anyone interested in period instrument performance.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Word is, the next Mullova project is the Beethoven and Mendelssohn Concertos with John Eliot Gardiner.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Bring it on...
author: Andrew McGregor

text: A man works night shifts while his wife works regular hours.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: They never see each other so their marriage breaks down.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: A simple, sad tale.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: And not the sort of thing you'd expect to hear from the larynx of Mark E Smith, leader of the Fall.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Smith has often been (mis)represented as a ranting anger monger.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: But this new compilation shows he can be tender as well as abrasive.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: The Fall racks in record shops are clogged with shoddy compilations.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: In their quarter century of existence they've released a minimum of an album a year.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: They change labels more often than most bands change their underwear.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: This offers a field day for unscrupulous record companies to chop it all up and keep repackaging it.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: But this one is better than most.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: It has excellent art work and good, detailed sleeve notes.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: And the period surveyed (1990 - 1992, three albums for Fontana records), is one of the group's most interesting.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Smith's ex wife Brix had just left the band.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: They moved in a conventional, accessible direction: orthodox pop rock with an unorthodox sensibility.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: There are verses and choruses, and the songs are tightly edited, and rarely ramble.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: "High Tension Line" and "Hilary" have great hooks, funny lyrics and a vaguely sixties feel.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: There's quiet, reflective material like the touching "Bill Is Dead", "Gentleman's Agreement" and "Shiftwork" and pretty electronica ("The Mixer").
author: Nick Reynolds

text: The Fall as easy listening?
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Well, perhaps meditative listening.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: And there are two of the Fall's greatest.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: "Free Range" is a fractured portrait of war and anarchy; Nostradamus proclaiming over a great garage band riff.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: "Blood Outta Stone" is a dark, polished gem: a bleak, sad pop song, immaculately played, produced and sung.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: There are always quibbles: no "Edinburgh Man"?
author: Nick Reynolds

text: No "Arms Control Poseur"?
author: Nick Reynolds

text: No "Life Just Bounces"?
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Why include the dull "Littlest Rebel" and "Immortality"?
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Here, Smith showed signs, perhaps misleading signs, of growing old gracefully.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: If you can't get "Extricate", the best album from these years, this will do.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Not quite sensical.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Everything shorn, smoothed, streamlined into a form that narrowly resists apprehension.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: After so many years.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: They f*** back.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Instruments swim along in the slipstream.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: This is the sound of a sleek new car cutting you up and leaving you way behind in a trail of anger and dust.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: "This one's dedicated to the children of love...
author: Colin Buttimer

text: the children of God..." Abi's impassioned delivery on "Fly Your Kite" lies uncomfortably across synthetic, over-compressed beats.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Dub rises to the surface on "Paternoster": vocals echo and break apart, only to return reassembled into new shapes.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Funk, breakbeat, dub and now a new shape, messy and unpredictable, never knowing whether the beat will rocksteady out or break up in static...
author: Colin Buttimer

text: "Gets Things Strait" lays vocals from Patrice Bart-Williams over and around the reprised melody of a Flanger track which ultimately feels like an entirely new creation.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: "Looks like the whole world is falling apart, a small scratch to remind you of the next track." The revisit gets revisited later in a dub version which brings everything together into a rickety, wheezing falling-apartness.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: His Name Is Alive join Friedman on the eighth track "Someday My Blues Will Cover the Earth" which signals the end of the vocal element of the album.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Four instrumentals bring up the rear leaving a strange impression after the expressiveness of the singers - like when a band carries on playing after their vocalist has taken a bow and left the stage.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: "Consider A Bigger Wallet" is an instrumental version of "Fly Your Kite".Minus the vocals it's clear how melodic the track (and by extension the whole album) is.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: There's a moment when the breakbeat rhythm seamlessly eases into reggae before almost immediately returning to the plucked, strummed, echoing, horn-sectioned whole, and you realise how rich this sound is, how detailed and how effortless sounding.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: What seemed initially to be straightahead and smooth is revealed to be complex, detailed and a real work of art(ifice?) Burnt Friedman appears to have put aside his penchant for shapeshifting games and jazz, but perhaps it's still lurking there deep down under the mellifluous tones and guest vocals.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Can't Cool is a heavier, more richly melodic sound than his previous music.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: After a long silence a voice intones, "44 degrees Centigrade in the shade".
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Is that Burnt Friedman lurking there in the shadows?
author: Colin Buttimer

text: He's a moving target tracing an unpredictable musical odyssey, impossible to nail down in one place.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: What will be his next missive from the other side of irony?
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Ah laughing Lenny, how we've missed your eloquent sadness and weary baritone.
author: Chris Jones

text: Back from the Buddhist retreat on Mount Baldy (no, really) after seven years of quiet contemplation, Mr Cohen returns with a new name (Jikan - given by his Buddhist teacher) and the latest news from the front line of the emotional wars.
author: Chris Jones

text: The news is much the same as it was way back then.
author: Chris Jones

text: Love is a mystery and all we can do is reflect on that enigma.
author: Chris Jones

text: Leonard is, after all the master of bearing those battle scars with dignity.
author: Chris Jones

text: So, if the more things change, the more they stay the same, why do we need Ten New Songs by the original bedsit bard?
author: Chris Jones

text: Over to the man, himself.
author: Chris Jones

text: Oh, lothario Lenny, the loquacious ladies man, how the girls love that smoky voice.
author: Chris Jones

text: At 67 the tones remain world-worn.
author: Chris Jones

text: Indeed, Cohen is the finest example of a man who has grown into his public persona as time has passed, but the accompanying sound seems startlingly contemporary.
author: Chris Jones

text: The elements remain the same as his previous few albums - the soft nylon strings of a lone guitar replaced by digital keyboards and perfectly poised female backing vocals (provided by writing and performing partner Sharon Robinson).
author: Chris Jones

text: Yet the thing that always marks his work is the sense of removal from the North American singer songwriter tradition.
author: Chris Jones

text: The murmuring simplicity owes far more to the European chanson and, as a result, always appears far more personal.
author: Chris Jones

text: Torn from the pages of Leonard's heart and served up with startling honesty.
author: Chris Jones

text: This man has loved and lost plenty.
author: Chris Jones

text: So, lilting Lenny serves us a diet of sex, love and ageing.
author: Chris Jones

text: Songs such as "A Thousand Kisses Deep" show that, Zen training or not, the carnal is still uppermost in the troubadour's mind: "Confined to sex, we pressed against the limits of the sea&I blessed our remnant fleet - and then consented to be wrecked, a Thousand Kisses Deep." Indeed, it's somehow heartening to hear how the man who epitomises intellectual philandering is still compelled to chronicle his conquests and defeats.
author: Chris Jones

text: "You Have Loved Enough", "Here It Is", "Love Itself", all concern themselves with the eternal questions surrounding the bonding of male and female and, despite the autobiographical shell, achieve a moving universality.
author: Chris Jones

text: And that is why we need Ten New Songs from lovelorn Lenny.
author: Chris Jones

text: "A sip of wine, a cigarette, and then it's time to go...
author: Chris Jones

text: " Until the next time.
author: Chris Jones

text: Dave Holland has worked with such diverse figures as Miles Davis, Stan Getz, Derek Bailey and Anthony Braxton, in the process earning a reputation as one of the finest jazz bassists of his generation, at home equally with standards, post bop grooves and free improvisation.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Since the early 80s he's led his own quintet, recording several superb albums for ECM of accessibly melodic yet muscular jazz, and winning possibly every jazz award known to man.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Not for Nothin' is the second recording by this version of the quintet and is possibly the best group album of the lot, surpassing even Seeds of Time.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Dave had better start clearing some more space on his mantelpiece...
author: Peter Marsh

text: Like Charlie Mingus, Holland can get very big sounds out of a small group.
author: Peter Marsh

text: His band is totally in command of its resources, aware of its influences but not imitating them, and at the same time unhindered by any quest for novelty (no turntablists in evidence here).
author: Peter Marsh

text: Holland and drummer Billy Kilson negotiate complex time signatures effortlessly and what's more they make them groove; check the oily polyrhythmic funk of 'Global Citizen' for the evidence.
author: Peter Marsh

text: They're also highly responsive, never overplaying, but able to turn the heat up under the soloists when required, as on 'Shifting Sands' and the M-Base meets Miles polymetrics of "What Goes Around", where Kilson's torrential snare hits provoke trombonist Robin Eubanks into a fiery solo smeared with multiphonic growls.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Eubanks (a long time Holland collaborator) is on astounding form and is ridiculously agile; his long, detailed solos on "Lost and Found" must have left him unable to talk for a few hours.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Critically lauded saxophonist Chris Potter combines the rhythmic ebullience of Sonny Rollins with the weightless lyricism of Wayne Shorter on alto or tenor; though he's more restrained than on earlier solo outings, his solo on "What Goes Around" is an intense, sustained flurry of ideas.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Steve Wilson's vibes are deep in the rhythm section's pocket, riffing or firing off spare, hanging chords.
author: Peter Marsh

text: His own "Go Fly a Kite" is lovely, reminiscent of some of Carla Bley's writing for Gary Burton and inspiring some beautiful alto playing from Potter.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Holland's own playing is predictably great, ranging from bluesy ruminations to freebop scrabble, and his ensemble playing is sensitive, supportive and suggestive as ever.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Propulsive, exciting and very satisfying.
author: Peter Marsh

text: If I hear a better jazz record this year, I'll be very lucky...
author: Peter Marsh

text: Syd Barrett is probably more talked about than listened to these days, though he remains a seminal influence on British indie psychedelia and countless of wannabe Pipers at the Gates of Dawn.
author: Peter Marsh

text: This compilation brings together most of the material from his two official Harvest albums, *The Madcap Laughs* and *Barrett*, plus a few tracks from the outtakes collection *Opel*.
author: Peter Marsh

text: There's little of the acid fuelled guitar abuse that drove Barrett's contribution to Pink Floyd's first album, and whereas Barrett-penned Floyd singles like "See Emily Play" and "Arnold Layne" had been superbly assured slices of Brit psychedelia, here the songs are looser and more exploratory.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Barrett (along with Ray Davies and Robert Wyatt) was one of the first singers to give English rock a uniquely un-American voice, and his lyrics here owe much to a literary tradition that takes in Edward Lear, William Blake and Hilaire Belloc.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Surrealism, pastoral whimsy and a strain of bedsit melancholia run through many of the songs here, and again a peculiarly English obsession with wordplay (see "Octopus" for details).
author: Peter Marsh

text: Though some of the performances (particularly those drawn from *Opel*) show evidence of Syd's well documented instability, the songs themselves are sharply honed and transcend their sometimes erratic delivery.
author: Peter Marsh

text: "Baby Lemonade" and "Gigolo Aunt" are as catchy as Legionnaire's disease and show that Syd's talent for writing great pop songs hadn't died with the Floyd's "Apples and Oranges", while "Dominoes" is exquisitely melancholic.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Completists will want this set for the previously unavailable "Bob Dylan Blues" (appropriate in the year of Bob's 60th birthday and containing the immortal lines; 'I've got the Bob Dylan Blues My hair and my hat's in a mess But I don't give a damn about that'), and for others it's a good place to start.
author: Peter Marsh

text: They might have received enough praise already, but when the music is this good, you've just got to give them even more.
author: David Silverman

text: "Space Walk" is the first single to be taken form Lemon Jelly's long awaitedsecond album, Lost Horizons, and shines just as brightly as anything they've done previously.
author: David Silverman

text: Inspired by the Apollo space missions, "Space Walk" uses spoken word samples taken from the first moon landing in 1969 and melts them effortlessly into a warm, organic groove as low slung as your belt-less jeans.
author: David Silverman

text: With layers of wistful guitar arpeggios and tinkly water drop pianos, "Space Walk" should also cheer up a few ad men looking for the music to their next car-driving-down-long-winding-road advert.
author: David Silverman

text: There's nothing particularly new or revolutionary here, but its all done with an infectious enthusiasm and summery gusto that makes "Space Walk" almost impossible to dislike.
author: David Silverman

text: However, part of the Lemon Jelly signature seems to be that omni-present, arpeggiated acoustic guitar which is there on virtually everything they write these days much more so than on any of the tunes from the 3 EPs that together formed the first album.
author: David Silverman

text: On the flip, "Return to Patagonia" is crammed full of nifty little samples and, as such, is probably more suited to the more discerning cut 'n' paste fetishists out there.
author: David Silverman

text: Its also great to hear something where the presence of a sultry saxophone doesn't necessarily equate to cheesy-lounge jazz and Lemon Jelly pull this off effortlessly with the help of oh-so-funky double bass and subtle string samples.
author: David Silverman

text: Set against a backdrop of light, airy breaks, they create a gentle and contagious rhythm that should come with a Warning: Smooth sign on the packet.
author: David Silverman

text: There's a sleek production throughout that matches up to the expensive, leather bound sleeve which, I assume, will make sure it wont slip off your coffee table.
author: David Silverman

text: Lemon Jelly are still impressively unclassifiable, never take the easy route and always aspire to make music which is much more than the sum of its parts.
author: David Silverman

text: This is arty, melancholic and gentle - and just a taste of what to expect from the forthcoming long-player.
author: David Silverman

text: Well worth investigating.
author: David Silverman

text: 'It's not my body that plays the drums, it's my arms and legs,' says afrobeat masterdrummer Tony Allen in the liner notes to this well-thought out compilation.
author: John Armstrong

text: Most Nigerian music fans will be aware of Tony's work with Fela Kuti's band over the years,but only the true fan will have the rare solo material presented here.
author: John Armstrong

text: Perhaps the most defining work showcased is taken from his early period with Africa 70: Jealousy (1975), Progress (1977); and No Accommodation with Lagos (1979).
author: John Armstrong

text: 1979's ' No Discrimination' and 'Ariya' show all the Afrobeat trademarks: politically involved lyrics, stabbing horn sections, and Allen's preternaturally co-ordinated four-beat drumming.
author: John Armstrong

text: Such was Allen's sheer physical stamina that when he left Fela's band in 1977, Kuti needed four drummers to replace him for live performances.
author: John Armstrong

text: After No Accommodation,Allen formed the Mighty Irokos in Lagos.
author: John Armstrong

text: The band made a living in the clubs but recording opportunities were few and far between, so 1984 saw Tony emigrating to Europe.
author: John Armstrong

text: The first solo fruit was the excellent N.E.P.A.
author: John Armstrong

text: EP from 1984: the title track is included in this selection.
author: John Armstrong

text: In 1989 there followed an uneven French recording, Afrobeat Express, which relied too heavily on the synthesised sounds of 80s pop and dance to advance Allen's own musical path significantly.
author: John Armstrong

text: But a good half of the music presented here is culled from Tony's most recent period: the three albums that he's recorded between 1999 and today.
author: John Armstrong

text: And here, with the resources of an obviously empathetic and young production team, Allen's sound is subtly updated.
author: John Armstrong

text: It embraces the world of hip hop and dj beats: 'Asiko', 'Get Together' and 'Kindness' all sit seamlessly alongside the wider genre of dance music.
author: John Armstrong

text: This is essential if Nigerian music is to move forward decisively once more, as it did all those years ago from highlife to afrobeat.
author: John Armstrong

text: 70 minutes of music as good as this for a mid-price albummakes it a must-buy for newcomers to Nigerian music: there's 20-odd years of history implicit in its rhythms.
author: John Armstrong

text: When The Strokes first emerged critics and public pounced on their debut as the start of a new rock golden age.
author: Jaime Gill

text: The sequel, the underwhelming and repetitive Room On Fire, led many to realise they had over-estimated the New Yorkers.
author: Jaime Gill

text: If the brilliant lead single "Juicebox" seemed to indicate Julian Casablancas was broadening his musical horizons, it's misleading.
author: Jaime Gill

text: First Impressions Of Earth is, with the odd exception, very much Strokes business as usual.
author: Jaime Gill

text: However, the opening three tracks show the band at their best.
author: Jaime Gill

text: "You Only Live Once" is a brash and winning opener, sounding as vibrant as a lost Blondie classic.
author: Jaime Gill

text: Nick Valensi provides thrilling guitar work throughout.
author: Jaime Gill

text: It's Casablancas singing and songwriting that let's the side down, and with fourteen songs he gives himself a lot of space to disappoint.
author: Jaime Gill

text: If this undeniably talented band are to repay that initial excitement, their fourth album is going to have to offer a great deal more consistency and invention than on display here.
author: Jaime Gill

text: Each David Bowie album from Black Tie White Noise onwards has been greeted with a huge puff of publicity but very little aftertaste.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: This is as much our fault as his.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: In our long-established immediacy culture, unless you are repeatedly whacked around the head by something, it evaporates.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: The complex and distant music Bowie has produced over the past ten years often demands the one thing we don't have in abundance today: time.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: To underline the importance of his recent oeuvre, Bowie played Heathen in a block, as if to say; this is really special, bear with it.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: With that in mind, I'm delighted to report that his 25th studio album, Reality is among his very best works, and this is being written not in the exhilarating judgement-numb of a long-in-advance copy.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: This is after living with it.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: Its rock music, for sure; it travels along similar lines to Heathen and Hours..., but it has a real freshness and accessibility and, in this era of ever-extending CDs, it's a proper album; clocking in at under 50 minutes.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: Working with Tony Visconti again has certainly given energy to Bowie and working in Visconti's small studio in New York brings the work a real freshness and intimacy.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: With his regular players Sterling Campbell, Gail Ann Dorsey and Mike Garson; and with Visconti playing his economical and often underrated bass, there is a beautiful lustre to the sound which manages to embrace innovation in a most organic manner.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: 'New Killer Star', freely referencing his own 'TVC 15', is an effortless overture that plays to the highlights of the Visconti/Bowie partnership.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: 'She'll Drive A Big Car' is a perfect embodiment of Bowie's new spirit; full of subtle kinks and nuances which actually finds it recapping Young Americans in terms of that records emotional drive.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: The backing vocals on 'Looking For Water' equal the strengths of the Berlin-era recordings and the strings-rich cover of 'Try Some, Buy Some' is a fitting tribute to its author, George Harrison.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: 'Fall Dog Bombs The Moon' is a fantastic voyage through Bowie's Burroughsian box of tricks and 'Bring Me The Disco King' first mentioned at the time of Black Tie White Noise is a extraordinary closer, its refrain evoking both Chic's 'Dance Dance Dance (Yowsah, Yowsah, Yowsah)' and Joy Divison's 'Transmission'; a woozy, off-kilter jazz homage, with long term Bowie pianist Garson referencing his best work.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: So, Reality is a proper album, with a beginning, a middle and an end.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: It's direct, warm, emotional honest, even and the surfeit of pleasingly deceptive musical simplicity allows the irony of the central concept - that there is no such thing as reality anymore - an opportunity to filter through.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: It's also rather lively and convincing.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: With Earthling, its David Bowie's best album since Scary Monsters.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: The king of experimental drum and bass cut-ups is back with more recycled timestretched madness.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Taking a darker and more complex approach to song writing this time, he's managed to push beat manipulation to it's furthest coherent limits all without sacrificing the overall integrity of a 'song'.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: For all it's 250+bpm madness, there remains some lovely melodic touches - especially on tracks like "I Wish You Could Talk" and "My Red Hot Car".
author: Olli Siebelt

text: However, for all the dextrous and filtered wonder on this album, there is a rather disturbing trend with Mr.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Jenkinson's work as of late.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: As you begin comparing his releases, you notice it's often the same loops used over and over again - the differences between them only in how they are arranged.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: "Bonneville Occident", for example, could easily be a remix of "Come On My Selector".
author: Olli Siebelt

text: This is a stunning record, and one that comes totally from left field.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Spring Heel Jack (aka Ashley Wales and John Coxon) have been most closely associated with the 90's drum n' bass scene, though their remit was always much wider.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Elements of free jazz squall were surfacing on early 12"s like Casino, while last year's underrated Disappeared saw the duo placing John Surman's horn playing over sandblasted ambient electronica as well as fashioning a tribute to the late Lester Bowie.
author: Peter Marsh

text: However, nothing there signalled the quantum leap forwards (or even sideways) that is Masses; Wales and Coxon have hooked up with some of the cream of the New York free jazz scene (William Parker, Matthew Shipp, Roy Campbell, Daniel Carter) as well as the ubiquitous Evan Parker, to create a mix of impassioned free jazz and electronics that is utterly seamless.
author: Peter Marsh

text: From the opening "Chorale" where Shipp's bittersweet piano picks its way gingerly through dirty swathes of guitar noise and a beautiful sampled trumpet figure, Masses seeks to confound expectations and head deep into uncharted territory.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Daniel Carter's alto winds through a sampled doublebass/handclap figure; Roy Cambell's luminous harmon muted trumpet etches out parched, lyrical lines over a choir of bowed basses.
author: Peter Marsh

text: "Salt" is a monstrous looped groove which features Parker's patented bubble n' squeak soprano, while Berne is on blistering form on "Red Worm", his baritone blurting and screaming over a repeated guitar drone.
author: Peter Marsh

text: There are many moments of unearthly beauty; Carter's flute and Berne's alto duet over Parker's resonant bass and unearthly electroacoustic creaks on "Interlude 2", while the closing "Coda" loops steam driven synth chords under Campbell's cackling foghorn trumpet and a cracked gypsy violin.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Despite occasional obvious electronic manipulations the feel is live and almost lo-fi, with SHJ doing for free jazz what Teo Macero did for electric Miles Davis.
author: Peter Marsh

text: It's dense, exhilarating stuff which contrives to sound utterly alien and familiar all at once.
author: Peter Marsh

text: If you want to know where jazz's cutting edge is, you need this record.
author: Peter Marsh

text: In some ways Albert Sammons was the great British violinist of the early 20th century.
author: John Armstrong

text: He began earning his living in theatre orchestras and hotel bands, before Thomas Beecham made him leader of his Beecham Orchestra in 1908, and a solo career beckoned.
author: John Armstrong

text: Sammons first played the Elgar Concerto in 1914, and this recording from 15 years later is the first complete reading on disc.
author: John Armstrong

text: People who know this performance (many of them violinists) tend to rave about it, and in this new transfer from Mark Obert-Thorn it's easier than ever to hear why.
author: John Armstrong

text: Sammons is such a modern-sounding violinist, with a full, firm tone, passionate vibrato, fluid fingerwork, and an effortless technique which makes light of the toughest moments in this concerto.
author: John Armstrong

text: Remember that this would have been recorded in complete takes, and the all-but flawless intonation and confident interpretation is still more impressive.
author: John Armstrong

text: So, if Sammons's recording is so good, why isn't it better known...in fact if he was such a fine violinist, why isn't his name as familiar as others of his generation?
author: John Armstrong

text: Several reasons; firstly Sammons hated foreign travel, so international tours were out and a reputation with the general public abroad was unlikely to follow.
author: John Armstrong

text: The Elgar recording was never issued in the US, so while the Delius Concerto (written for Sammons) that's also on this new transfer was a favourite of Isaac Stern's, he probably never heard the Elgar.
author: John Armstrong

text: Sammons played the Concerto many times with Elgar conducting, but as they worked for different labels that partnership would never be heard on disc; instead Elgar went on to make the recording that was effectively to eclipse Sammons's, with the young Yehudi Menuhin.
author: John Armstrong

text: As Tully Potter writes in the notes for this Naxos transfer, it was a marketing coup for EMI, the world-famous 16-year-old prodigy paired with the great composer - it was bound to sell, and it still does, such is the affection it inspires.
author: John Armstrong

text: But is it as good as Sammons and Sir Henry Wood recorded three years earlier?
author: John Armstrong

text: Well, I've always preferred the Sammons, but I wouldn't go as far as Potter in his notes; Menuhin and Elgar were hardly a 'marketing gimmick'.
author: John Armstrong

text: There are many beautiful things in the recording as many of us have recognised for years, as there are in more than a handful of more recent interpretations in far better recorded sound.
author: John Armstrong

text: But there'll always be something special about both the Menuhin and the Sammons recordings, and one reason to prefer Sammons is Sir Henry Wood, who manages to make Elgar's reading of his own Concerto sound almost self-indulgent.
author: John Armstrong

text: Wood is clear-eyed and unsentimental, noble and true - he leaves the heart-on-sleeve romanticism to the soloist, and the contrast works superbly.
author: John Armstrong

text: You also end up with a very brisk reading, minutes faster than most others, beaten to the tape only by Heifetz and Sargent...which by the way, is another of my favourites.
author: John Armstrong

text: Too fast for some, but Heifetz is technically on another plane - and anyway, the Elgar Concerto grows in stature when it's not over-sentimentalised.
author: John Armstrong

text: If you're curious you really should investigate this Naxos Historical cd, and at their usual super-budget price you'll still have change for your bus fare home, as they used to say.
author: John Armstrong

text: It's a great performance, and to my ears this is the best transfer it's had to date, with none of the over-processing, pseudo-stereo or bad edits that have marred previous efforts.
author: John Armstrong

text: Take Potter's passion with a pinch of salt, but revel in the music-making of one of the greatest British violinists, heard more clearly than ever.
author: John Armstrong

text: The years just fall away.
author: John Armstrong

text: It's no surprise that men comfortably in their 40's haven't created another hi-energy stomping dance-athon or mega-pop album.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: After a career spanning 18 years the Pet Shop Boys have decided to try something a bit different.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: Out with the big production, dancey sounds and mid song theatrical melodrama of tracks like "Go West" and "New York City Boy", in with a more guitar based songwriting and melancholic, mature sound.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: Release starts off quite solidly with recent single "Home and Dry" and the sing-along, lighter waving in the air, end-of-the night song "I'll Get Along" but then takes a terrible turn at "Birthday Boy".
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: Strangely inspired by Michael Owen's birthday and Jesus, the track is a wishy-washy ballad with dodgy guitar solo (albeit from top former Smiths guitarist Johnny Marr) and bleak and moody soundscape which borders on uncomfortable listening.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: "Tell it like it is," Neil Tennant emplores on the next track "London".
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: OK then, it's another gawd awful song.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: One of the joys of the Pet Shop Boys was their wit and ironic sense of humour but this is sadly missing on much of Release.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: What was once often fun and entertaining has been replaced with sober tales of woe and heartache, which is fine& if you want to be left feeling depressed!
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: There are a few breaths of fresh air on the album though - "The Samurai In Autumn" is a great track (primarily thanks to it's lack of many lyrics offers a break of Neil's voice for a little while) where the band venture briefly back into chilled, yet euphoric dance production.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: "The Night I Fell in Love", with it's tongue in cheek lyrics about a boy fan's one night stand with Eminem, also raises a brief smile but not enough to forget the remainder of the album's sins.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: With an established career spanning so long, taking such a change of direction and become an ageing rock band is bound to be a gamble but this is one that failed to pay off.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: Bland and uninspiring - file it under, 'music your parents might like'.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: This is a very sad album.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: It's like listening to two people you love arguing in the next room.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: The Libertines, Britain's best new band, fall apart in front of your ears.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: "Can't Stand Me Now" is a great start and a perfect example of why they were so refreshing.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Carl Barat and Pete Doherty were a classic song writing team, whose contrasting styles (and voices) complemented each other brilliantly.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Tracks like the exhilarating thrash punk of "Arbeit Macht Frei" and the astute social observation of "Campaign Of Hate" shows just how much we need them.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: They deserve an award just for keeping the English language alive.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: When did you last hear the phrase 'the cut of my jib' in a song?
author: Nick Reynolds

text: The music is much the same as the first album: raw, scratchy, bare bones guitar and a hyperactive rhythm section.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: The Clash's Mick Jones doesn't really produce, he just records what's there.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: It's all about the songs, the strength of the tunes and their unique vision of British life.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Pete Doherty's personal difficulties have been well documented.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: He sounds like a man who knows something's wrong but is struggling to put it right.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: His vocal on "Don't Be Shy" is loose and incoherent.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Like three or four other songs, it rambles and grinds to a halt, as though it hasn't been finished properly.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Pete lashes out angrily on "The Saga" at the vultures feeding on his situation and denies he has any problems.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: It's a fantastic song, but he does have problems.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Carl obviously cares deeply for his best friend.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: But by the end of the album you feel he has given up.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: The final track, "What Became Of The Likely Lads?", is heartbreaking.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Carl gently chides Pete one more time, they reflect on their shared dreams and wonder how it all went wrong.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: There doesn't seem to be any way back.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: This is a compelling, voyeuristic listen.
author: Nick Reynolds
