text: Time to set the mood, dim the lights and bring out the chilled wine because our favourite stateside crooner is back with his third album entitled Life Goes On.
author: Buki Bakare

text: The Chicago-bred artist returns laden with more smooth and sexy tales of love and romance.
author: Buki Bakare

text: With his charming storytelling style and silky vocal cords, you'd be forgiven for dismissing him as just another ballad singer.
author: Buki Bakare

text: But don't get it twisted Donell Jones is not your average run-of-the-mill soul singer belting out those sensual grooves we know so well.
author: Buki Bakare

text: Apart from being an accomplished songwriter and producer, he stands slightly distanced from his peers, due to his innate ability to "keep it street" and produces an attractive cocktail made of raw hip-hop flavour mixed with heartfelt soul.
author: Buki Bakare

text: This album dishes up a balanced diet of mid tempo cruising in-your-car joints, alongside those dangerously suave seductive ballads; echoing the perfect 21st century life soundtrack.
author: Buki Bakare

text: He provides a greater sense of musical sophistication with the apparent use of strings and live percussions, marking a refreshing change stylistically that is likely to appeal to the fans.
author: Buki Bakare

text: The first track released is "You Know That I Love You"; an ode to his long time girlfriend.
author: Buki Bakare

text: It's an instant, summertime track, enticing you with its subtle soothing keyboard intro, a sure-fire way to draw the ladies in.
author: Buki Bakare

text: However as first singles go it's not quite on level of the superb 1999 chartbuster "You Know What's Up." Another cruise-control track is "Put Me Down"where an impatient Mr Jones seems a little eager to take things to "that next level" (hmm enough said).
author: Buki Bakare

text: Lyrically speaking the most noticeable track is "Life Goes On" where a pensive Donell sings of the consequences of imprisonment on his relationship.
author: Buki Bakare

text: Other notable tracks include, "Guilty By Suspicion" and "Girls Friend" both comprise of that discernible Jones vocal trademark signature.
author: Buki Bakare

text: After winning an American music award for his 1999 sophomore album Where I Wanna Be, our mellow ghetto poet is out to prove that he can take us even further with Life Goes On.
author: Buki Bakare

text: However, I'm not entirely convinced this is the one to do it.
author: Buki Bakare

text: With the exception of "Girls Friend" it starts to falter towards the end of the album, and you can't help thinking you've eaten all your dessert before you've had the main meal.
author: Buki Bakare

text: Nevertheless, for the sweet toothed amongst us its still a worthy album to have in your collection.
author: Buki Bakare

text: No doubt dedicated R&B fans will be at the record store as you read this.
author: Buki Bakare

text: Like many other notable Japanese bands (Merzbow, Ruins, etc..), Xinlisupreme arent afraid to inject a little dissonance into their music.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: A three piece group from Japan, they've been making quite, er...a noise for themselves over the past two years and seem to get better and better with every release.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: It is somewhat difficult to explain what Xinlisupreme actually is, or sounds like.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: What we can say is that instead of letting the concept of noise, feedback, etc needlessly carry them away (like so many others; you know who you are), the band take matters into their own hands and boldly shape and craft theirs into a melting pot of dissonance based ideas.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: From the industrial tribal beats of the opener "Murder License" to "Sakae" which runs from full on Neubaten-esque sheet metal mayhem to raucous feedback, the seven tracks here embrace the listener into a tightly scripted and perfectly choreographed exercise in intense music making that never fails to impress.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: This is about unleashed power, about unbridled energy, the sucker punch that hits you out of nowhere.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: It's Lee Ranaldo in Sonic Youth on overdrive, it's My Bloody Valentine on a bad day, it's Merzbow on a good day, yet it's none of these things.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: It is simply Xinlisupreme.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Even on the album's quieter moments.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: like the pristine ambient and glacial beauty of "I.T.D.O.O.M" and the exquisite piano minimalism of "Nameless Song", the band never once explode into an ambient noise improv free-for-all.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: There is a method to their madness, as is shown by their cover of an American flag surrounded by smeared blood.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: We get the message but to truly understand the idea, we need to dig a little deeper.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: When it comes to music like this, there are many out there (especially in the bands hometown of Japan) who do it rather well.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Yet, what puts Xinlisupreme almost in a class of their own, is their incredible ability to bring their secret and complex world out one listen at a time, rather than simply throw it all out there at once.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Who knew dissonance could be so complex and so much fun?
author: Olli Siebelt

text: For those about to grind, we salute you.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: It would appear that there is no one genre big enough to contain the artistic prowess of Adam F.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Not content with setting a new standard in drum and bass with his 1998 album Colours, the all conquering producer has turned all the knobs and flipped all the switches in his studio so that they point to hip hop.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Anyone present at Adam's DJ appearances will have heard him regularly dropping rap in to his drum and bass sets as well as using effects and jingles to personalise his turntable delivery.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Cultivating an interest in film scores such as The Mission and Batman beyond the confines of the DJ box has also affected his approach to music making.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: It is the fusion of these two schools of thinking that are responsible for this masterful release and left many of hip hop's upper echelons reeling only to declare Adam F as the new Dr Dre.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Kaos owes much to A&R guru Kim Spikes for its all star cast.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Having worked on the last Busta Rhymes album she was in a strong position to present Adam's ideas directly to the artists without having to negotiate the usual record company grind.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Having recorded the introduction and backing track for what was to become "Smash Somethin'" using a full orchestra and choir, Redman was easily won over once he realised the voices, which easily dwarf the Hallelujah chorus, were singing his name!
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Without reservation the opening revels in its' histrionics and won't fail to raise a smile at the absolute shamelessness of it all.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Following that, LL Cool J, De La Soul, Guru, M.O.P.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: and CNN were won over in gradual succession, and so Kaos took shape.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: The sheer audacity of this album, its unabashed confidence and sense of drama is jaw dropping.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: It's like Tim Burton meets Dr Dre for a block party in the post-apocalypse year 3000.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Adam F has delivered such a fresh and hyped take on the hip hop sound that it would be fair to say that this album reaches miles above the years' rap releases.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: The slick R&B female vocals of Lil Mo on "Where's My...", the dirty acid jam of LL Cool J's "Greatest Of All Time" as well as Beenie Man's dancehall flow on "Dirty Harry's Revenge" illustrate both Mr F's versatility and intuition.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: So, how large is this album?
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Imagine Westwood sporting a ten gallon Stetson, a top an Indian elephant at the summit of Everest booming "Nothin' but big things, baby!!!" and you're almost there.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Acerbic art rockers in post-punk clothing, Wire's reductionist manifesto, Pink Flag, challenged prevailing pop wisdom that what can't be said in three minutes isn't worth saying.
author: Sid Smith

text: Nearly thirty years after its release their stark survey of the 1977 landscape remains taut and decidedly bracing.
author: Sid Smith

text: More Barrett-era Pink Floyd than Pink Flag, Chairs Missing (1978) still shows their aesthetic rigour undiminished.Witty, gritty, dysfunctional classics ("Outdoor Miner" and "I Am The Fly") benefit from producer Mike Thorne's interventions and make this glorious avant-pop coup the most satisfying of the three reissues.
author: Sid Smith

text: Nevertheless, 154 (1979) offers an ominous space where the ever-caustic guitar hooks and doom-laden minor chords are bench-pressed into dark matter to be hurled into a black hole of reverb.
author: Sid Smith

text: On the fearsomely uncompromising "A Touching Display" their famous brevity is stretched into nearly seven minutes of thrilling, overwrought rock.
author: Sid Smith

text: Bold and direct, they don't make them like this anymore.
author: Sid Smith

text: Known to his bank manager as Keith Fullerton Whitman, Hrvatski has produced his first full length album for Mike Paradinas' Planet-Mu label.
author: Marcus Scott

text: Here's an artist with a scholarly understanding of sound and an ear for dissecting breaks like a musical scientist; thankfully he's also one with a slightly twisted, trashy sense of humour.
author: Marcus Scott

text: On this mixed selection the gloves come off, as Hrvatski gives his own twist to virtually every strand of contemporary electronic music, remarkably keeping it fairly cohesive over the albums length.
author: Marcus Scott

text: Overall it does suffer a little froma virtuosity and unwillingness to stick to the subject, much like a very clever but bored school kid.He also occasionally covers areas betterhandledby Aphex Twin, but it still left me wanting more.
author: Marcus Scott

text: The albumkicks off with "vatstep dsp", which does a jungle-ragga thing over Prince Jammy's famous sleng teng bassline with a silly Macintosh "vocalwriter" voice doing the toasting, before drifting through track two into an autumnal folk meets Fennesz take on the Rolling Stones' "Painted Black".
author: Marcus Scott

text: It's notable that Hrvatski is something of a break connoisseur; "ewc4"shoots in with a death metal guitar and 'amen' break rush before the combination is edited down to a metronomic tattoo, like a kind of instant gratification Steve Reich, which gently dissolves into soft Rhodes tones.
author: Marcus Scott

text: It's the second half of the album which displays a deeper more thoughtful side; "Anesthetise thineself" is made from discrete field recordings as an abstract counterpoint to some gentle Labradford-like minor key instrumentation.
author: Marcus Scott

text: It's as if the melodies are trying to express the longing buried in the abstracted momentsfrozen inthe field recordings.
author: Marcus Scott

text: "Carrots" cleverly fuses folksy guitar and oboe into a take no prisoners hoover rave bassline, making the combination oddly more emotive.
author: Marcus Scott

text: The album finishes with a jaunty math rock cover of swedish band "trad gras och steners" tegenborg.
author: Marcus Scott

text: It feels a little out of place, somehow betraying the confident emotional expression of the previous few tracks.
author: Marcus Scott

text: However, the ending of a minutes worth of held organ and guitar chords reminiscent of Terry Riley is violently cut off just as your can happily indulge your ears, it could be pointing in a future direction.
author: Marcus Scott

text: Maybe next time he'll allow some indulgence for a little longer.
author: Marcus Scott

text: She burst into the big time three years ago with perhaps the only good song of her career, "Genie in a Bottle".
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: Hot on the heels of Britney Spears and Jessica Simpson - teenage, female, innocent and blonde - she rode on the crest of teen success filling the charts.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: 2002 and the sweet innocence is long gone.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: Last years' "Lady Marmalade" collaboration gave a good indication that Christina Aguilera is keen to distance herself from her teenybopper peers and show the world that she is a real diva.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: However, it's easy to forget her vocal talents when she makes a habit of hitting the headlines as the butt (literally) of Eminem's jokes or for her freaky dress sense.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: From start to finish Stripped is as full-on bold and over the top as most of Christina's outfits.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: Although recent single "Dirrty", featuring Redman, might have misled some into expecting a sleek and sleazy R&B album, much of this seems to be an exercise in stretching the vocal chords to weak backing tracks.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: The album intro kicks off with an obvious attempt to put the record straight on preconceptions of herself, "sorry you can't define me, sorry I broke the mold".
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: Lacking the class of Destiny's Child or Aaliyah, it's true; there is no-one else like Aguilera around at the moment but then, who would want to follow in those footsteps?
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: "Can't Hold Us Down" brings in the assistance of Lil Kim to add a bit of edge but does little to deviate from the monotony of tracks like "Underappreciated" and the hilarious "Fighter".
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: Things become slightly more interesting in "Make Over", where recent Pink tunesmith Linda Perry has been roped in to bring out the Courtney Love in Christina.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: Here, the rough, rock vocals make a pleasant change from the gymnastic warbling and sultry panting that plagues the rest of the album.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: The success is then spoilt by "Cruz", a big Michael Bolton cringe worthy rock ballad, and thus the agony of Stripped continues.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: It's the sign of a bad album when the sense of peace that falls as the CD finishes is the most fulfilling feeling of the last hour and ten minutes of your life.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: This, unfortunately, is one of those albums.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: Winning Days is the second album from Australia's wildest exports, famous for both their exhausting live shows and mind-bending off-stage antics.
author: Lisa Haines

text: With reports of shattered guitars, groupie mayhem and determined substance abuse, this new offering comes as something of a surprise.
author: Lisa Haines

text: It's a more melodious follow-up to their debut Highly Evolved, though the winning formula of nervous energy and shuddering crescendos remains firmly in place.
author: Lisa Haines

text: The Vines have furthered their trademark fusion of Nirvana and John Lennon by adding layers of harmony.
author: Lisa Haines

text: A technique that manifests itself on "Evil Town" and "TV Pro" where grinding guitars meld seamlessly into moments of psychedelic whimsy.
author: Lisa Haines

text: But while "Animal Machine" and "Evil Town" emulate Nirvana's grunge infernos, the sunny disposition streaming through this album is unmistakeable.
author: Lisa Haines

text: In fact, the resolute chirpiness of "Ride" and "She's Got Something to Say" is more akin to Supergrass than Sgt Pepper.
author: Lisa Haines

text: Comparisons with The Beach Boys will be inevitable once people hear the seductive harmonies on "Winning Days" and "Rainfall".
author: Lisa Haines

text: And such parallels are well deserved; singer/songwriter Craig Nicholls has a remarkably versatile voice.
author: Lisa Haines

text: Plus there's a touchstone here for fans of the recently-departed Elliott Smith.
author: Lisa Haines

text: Elements of his lyrical style are sprinkled across the whole album, most notably on wistful folk-number "Autumn Shade II".
author: Lisa Haines

text: This influence may be due in part to the fact that Smith's erstwhile producer Robert Schnapf (also of Beck and Guided By Voices fame) is back on board.
author: Lisa Haines

text: Winning Days was recorded in the hallowed grounds of Woodstock's famous Bearsville Studios.
author: Lisa Haines

text: After listening to these tunes it's somewhat tempting to imagine that after a long day thrashing about indoors The Vines hastened to the tranquil woodlands outside to sit dreaming up harmonies under the stars, a cold beer in hand.
author: Lisa Haines

text: The result is startling, a truly unique effort that leap frogs gaily between tortured ecstasy and furious abandon.
author: Lisa Haines

text: Listen to it now!
author: Lisa Haines

text: 'No Direction Home' - Martin Scorsese's revelatory documentary of the boy from Hibbing's 10-year journey from Woody Guthrie acolyte to wigged-out electric 'Judas' -may well prove to be one of the most important rock docs ever made.
author: Chris Jones

text: This, volume seven of the Bootleg Series, not only reflects this beautifully but fills a much-needed gap in the Dylan market.
author: Chris Jones

text: For, while none of the out-takes and demos will come as a revelation to Dylanologists, it IS the first chronological overview of his early years and goes some way in demonstrating (to those that weren't there) why Bob was raised to the status of cultural icon.
author: Chris Jones

text: And why he balked....
author: Chris Jones

text: Starting with home recordings made in 1956, disc one charts the transformation from juvenile blues copyist to fully-fledged people's poet.
author: Chris Jones

text: Which is, of course, exactly what he didn't want.
author: Chris Jones

text: His vague Carnegie Hall explanation of "A Hard Rain..." is that '...something's gonna happen' is a far cry from railing against the A bomb.
author: Chris Jones

text: What did happen was his retreat from the politically correct world of Joan Baez, Pete Seeger et al into a modern maelstrom of electricity, volume and dazzlingly oblique wordplay.
author: Chris Jones

text: By Disc two, with its recorded 'betrayal' at Newport(a blistering "Maggie's Farm")the transformation is startling.
author: Chris Jones

text: Mike Bloomfield's scorching licksturn "Tombstone Blues" from literary surrealism into proto-psychedelia.
author: Chris Jones

text: By the closing cut (the only previously released track - the Manchester 1966 version of "Like A Rolling Stone") you feel like you've travelled as far as Bob had in one short decade.
author: Chris Jones

text: Every step is worth it...
author: Chris Jones

author: Dan Tallis

text: The Tipperary born singer is sexy, she has a superb sultry voice and on her debut album, Night On My Side, she's got some great pop songs.
author: Dan Tallis

text: However, there is a lot more to this album than throwaway pop.
author: Dan Tallis

text: The album opens with the dreamy intro "Day One" that quickly enchants you with its soothing melody but before you know it you're given a wake up call with recent single "Hanging Around".
author: Dan Tallis

text: Full of juicy guitar riffs and a great chorus its a cool n' catchy pop song.
author: Dan Tallis

text: And so, after the first two tracks, you're given a clear idea of what to expect for the rest of the album.
author: Dan Tallis

text: There are the softly spoken acoustic guitar songs that can transfix you with their beauty, as with "Over and Over" and "Ran For Miles" and there are the indie rock songs like "Tear in my Side" that will force your head to nod, your legs to tap and your mouth to smile.
author: Dan Tallis

text: There is, of course, the exception to the rule; "Whata Day" is guitar free.
author: Dan Tallis

text: In their place are various cool electronic beats and synthesised vocals that echo around your head.
author: Dan Tallis

text: Listening to Night On My Side you can tell that Hayes hasn't quite decided what works and what doesn't; she's prepared to make mistakes and to take chances which, inevitably, results in a few misses.
author: Dan Tallis

text: "I Wanna Stay", for example, meanders aimlessly leaving you cold.
author: Dan Tallis

text: But Hayes has something that Kylie's never had: superb song-writing skills.
author: Dan Tallis

text: Her lyrics are intelligent and often unusual, as in "My God": 'My God, hope you're on call, because I may be in danger of crashing before I get to fall.
author: Dan Tallis

text: Lets cry boy while the neighbours have their backs turned.
author: Dan Tallis

text: I'm having trouble believing anything you say'.
author: Dan Tallis

text: All in all an excellent debut, full to the brim with potential for even greater things next time.
author: Dan Tallis

text: This second album on Evan Parker's Psi label is a bit of a shock in a couple of ways.
author: Peter Marsh

text: ThoughDudek's name will be familiar to any fan of European Free Jazz as a member of the Globe Unity Orchestra and veteran of sessions with Tony Oxley, Peter Brotzmann.Misha Mengelberg etc, surprisingly this is his first outing as sole leader, at the age of 63.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Secondly, this is an album of tastefully executed, tuneful modern jazz that would be worthy of a label like Enja or ECM (not to decry Mr Parker's rather excellent imprint).
author: Peter Marsh

text: Dudek's partners are seasoned Britjazzersguitarist John Paricelli, bassist Chris Laurence and drummer Tony Levin.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Three tunes by trumpeter Kenny Wheeler (also a Globe Unity veteran) open the record.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Dudek's airy yet precise phrasing seems ideally suited to Wheeler's compositional style, particularly the winding, aching melody of "Phrase Three" and the mournful "Ma Bel".
author: Peter Marsh

text: Though the influence of late John Coltrane made itself felt in Dudek's freer playing, here it's an earlier Coltrane, still steeped in Lester Young and Sonny Rollins, that filters through.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Dudek marries Coltrane's full, emotive tone with the weightless grace of Wayne Shorter; his unaccompanied solo on ye olde tenor player's chestnut "Body and Soul" is a tour de force; he then locks horn(s) with Levin's polyrhythmic assault to provide the albums most fiery moments.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The tricky bop pileups of George Coleman's "By George" is an ideal vehicle for some nimble, gently oblique tenor, while Jimmy Rowles's "The Peacocks" features the leader's sweet toned soprano, plus a finely articulated guitar solo from John Paricelli.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Paricelli's delayed, swelling chords recall early Bill Frisell, though his soloing eschews quirky fusion stylings for a sparkling, vibrant melodicism.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The much undersung Laurence is one of the UK's great bassists; whether with bow in hand or with fingers, he propels, comment and suggests throughout,yet is as unobtrusive as the ground you walk on.
author: Peter Marsh

text: His solo on "Ma Bel" is a thoughtful, melodic jewel, which is a pretty good way to sum up the whole album.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Much credit goes to Evan Parker and Emanem boss Martin Davidson for putting this one out.More please...
author: Peter Marsh

text: If that title sounds like a Trout Mask Replica-style surrealist statement, in typical Emanem fashion, the reality is both more prosaic and more logical.
author: John Eyles

text: This album originates from live recordings made at The Worm in Rotterdam, an organ interlude from the Red Rose Club (a bit of a cheat, eh?) and L'Archiduc in Brussels.
author: John Eyles

text: Nonetheless, that title does conjure up images worthy of the humour of Coxhill and Weston.
author: John Eyles

text: The pair have been performing together for a quarter of a century, their earliest gigs predating their first recorded encounter on the fine Digswell Duets.
author: John Eyles

text: Each is an experienced and accomplished duo player, and these encounters are testimony to the wealth of experience that each brings.
author: John Eyles

text: The long opening piece, "The First Duet of Worms", demonstrates the duo's strengths.
author: John Eyles

text: Funny as they are on occasion, they can establish and sustain a serious mood, and do so here.
author: John Eyles

text: Weston is as technically impressive as ever, a restless source of ideas.
author: John Eyles

text: Coxhill maintains a dialogue not only with the piano but also a call-and-response dialogue with himself, reacting to his own rather melancholy melodic fragments.
author: John Eyles

text: "The Second Duet of Worms" (historical pun, anyone?) is shorter, more upbeat, and makes a good contrast with the opener.
author: John Eyles

text: "Organ Interlude" is exactly that, a playful eight minutes, in which Weston extracts an impressive array of sounds from the chamber organ, with apposite responses from Coxhill.
author: John Eyles

text: It is something of a novelty piece, but does not outstay its welcome.
author: John Eyles

text: The two duos from Brussels mirror those from Rotterdam (they were recorded the day after them, in March 2001), giving a pleasing symmetry to the album.
author: John Eyles

text: At the start of the first, Weston's rippling backdrop gives the piece a romantic setting that evolves but is never lost.
author: John Eyles

text: In the second, Coxhill takes control early, with some quiet but sustained, high pitched blowing.
author: John Eyles

text: From that opening, which introduces a deliberate, funereal tempo, the piece slowly unfolds and picks up.
author: John Eyles

text: By the end, without any forced changes of gear along the way, we narrowly avoid a full blown climax of "Secret Love"!
author: John Eyles

text: This is, quite simply, an object lesson in duo improvising, from two masters of the art.
author: John Eyles

text: With the recent successful Mutek festival in Montreal and several key releases by labels like Suction, Constellation and Mille Plateaux, this year could see Canada really coming on to the world stage full on in terms of new underground and electronic music.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: And if this release is anything to go by - 2002 looks to be very promising indeed.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Polmo Polpo is the musical output of one Sandro Perri, who also happens to run the Toronto based Audi Sensa label.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Taking a major influence from labels like Basic Channel or Mille Plateaux, Perri operates in a strange netherworld between avant-dub and more post-rock influences.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Yet, unlike many others, he captures enough few twists and turns along way to showcase a true mark of respect rather than blatant thievery.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: The Science Of Breath is a compilation of material Polmo Polpo have released over the past two years on Audi Sensa plus four brand new tracks especially recorded for this release.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Like other new music entities like Apartment B and Carpark, there seems to be a slight rock influence to some of the tracks, something it seems is deeply rooted in Canadian music these days.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: They like their guitars, but never resort to being constrained by the conformity of the rock, indie or "post-rock" genres.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Throughout this 8 track CD, various textures are mixed and experimented with but always rooted in a deep, murky dub sound, constantly keeping the music in a state of musical fog; it's asound that easily separates him from most other musicians currently operating out of Canada.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: For example, "Oarca" resembles the sound of sheet metal blowing in a hurricane while a 4/4 techno track can be heard in the distant rumble.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: "Acqua" takes on the Basic Channel sound full on and transplants it to a hot sweaty summer night in Brasil.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: "Rottura" on the other hand, mixes sampled processed guitar loops over a dark pan-delay, eventually echoing (quite literally) the work of Mike Ink's Gas project.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Where Perri really outdoes himself however, is on the closing "Riva", which sneaks up on you quietly before kicking in to a deep dubby and scratchy track - a dark 4/4 rhythm accentuated by a gorgeous slide guitar like sample and incredibly sexy sub-bass line that acts like a snake, darting in and out of the rhythm bed.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: This track just begs to be played on a huge sound system.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Lurking in a twilight world somewhere between dusk and dark, between rhythm and texture, this is ambience at its most sultry, its most luxurious.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: The Science of Breath is a winner in every sense.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Thank the Lord for chronic fatigue syndrome.
author: Chris Jones

text: For were it not for Dan Berridge's bout with this illness we wouldnt have ever been lucky enough to receive the gift of his first marvellous album Compassion, recorded at his parents house while recovering from the aforementioned malady.
author: Chris Jones

text: Its intriguing patchwork of samples and strings has slowly but surely won over an audience old enough to spot the source material, and young enough not to feel too precious about the magpie tendencies.
author: Chris Jones

text: Two years on Dan and new accomplice, singer Richard Palmer bring us MK2 of the Project's development.
author: Chris Jones

text: This album is a different beast.
author: Chris Jones

text: Whereas Compassion had you constantly surprised by the DJ Shadow-style juxtaposition of disparate genres (Rachmaninov meets Spirit, Eno vs the Mahavishnu Orchestra etc.) The Vessel is composed of actual songs and features real instruments accompanying Palmer's bizarrely treated vocals.
author: Chris Jones

text: It's less an exquisite corpse and more of a complete body of work.
author: Chris Jones

text: In fact, The Vessel has such a homogenous sound that highlights are harder to find.
author: Chris Jones

text: Samples tend to be more ambient than integral here.
author: Chris Jones

text: Scratchy string tracks and floating electronica underneath the almost-female vocals can't help but remind one of the heydays of Bristolian trip hop (though, in fairness, Berridge is from Bristol).
author: Chris Jones

text: "Sufi" could be a sweeter version of Portishead.
author: Chris Jones

text: However while lyrics often fall short of anything memorable, Berridge's exemplary production always draws the heart back in.
author: Chris Jones

text: The use of Paulette Browns' imploring gospel on "Darkling" is certainly tear-inducing and there's no denying the aching loveliness of "Angel Heart"'s chord sequence.
author: Chris Jones

text: Yet too often the mind drifts away from the material.
author: Chris Jones

text: It's too nebulous, too formulaic in its loveliness.
author: Chris Jones

text: Even the band's own website make use of fluffy terms such as 'a diverse collection of moody filmic washes'.
author: Chris Jones

text: Such vagaries are too often the curse of modern chill-out music.
author: Chris Jones

text: So it's a step sideways for Dan and his crew.
author: Chris Jones

text: There's no denying the sense of time-biding here.
author: Chris Jones

text: He even reworks "For The One" from Compassion AGAIN, and fails to make any improvement.
author: Chris Jones

text: But hope isn't banished entirely.
author: Chris Jones

text: The final track, "Manifesto" easily matches and surpasses previous work.
author: Chris Jones

text: It's a simple return to the mix 'n' match, jazzy sampling Berridge is so good at, and its final clipped female voice could possibly be the most chilling thing you'll hear all year.
author: Chris Jones

text: Sometimes you can have too much of a good thing.
author: Chris Jones

text: Fairport Convention are unassailably the greatest folk rock band ever formed, with past alumni including legendary names within both folk and rock: Sandy Denny, Richard Thompson, Ashley Hutchings and a host of others.
author: Chris Jones

text: A Pete Frame-style family tree comes with this enormous set to really demonstrate the labyrinthine history that's being archived here and along with the huge book (that's book not booklet, note) it all forms a collection to make completists spontaneously combust with delight.
author: Chris Jones

text: And yet, like fifteen helpings of chocolate cake in a row it can get a bit much.
author: Chris Jones

text: For while the remarkable voice of Ms Denny or the wild guitar of Thompson never fails to thrill, the post-heyday material can pall quite seriously.
author: Chris Jones

text: Buyer beware, there's five hours of this stuff and your CD programming button may be needed...
author: Chris Jones

text: Historically, Fairport have needed this amount of attention for years.
author: Chris Jones

text: Their rapid transformation from (frankly not bad) Jefferson Airplane clones to leading advocates of all things rustic and traditional is here told in a stunning patchwork of rehearsals, outtakes, live tapes and radio sessions.
author: Chris Jones

text: These go all the way from their jazzy debut "If I Had A Ribbon Bow" to tracks recorded at the institution that constitutes the yearly Cropredy reunion festival.
author: Chris Jones

text: The problem lies with the organisation of this box.
author: Chris Jones

text: In a brave attempt to break away from a chronological format the four discs have been grouped by theme.
author: Chris Jones

text: So we get a first disc which moves timewise, but the others are grouped as rarities, epic historical songs and a selection of their classic repertoire.
author: Chris Jones

text: Thus "Walk Awhile" from 1970 will sit next to "John Gaudie" recorded in 1998, and comparison isn't necessarily a good thing.
author: Chris Jones

text: Lest this review seem churlish, it must be noted that a good two thirds of this box are from the pre-1972 era.
author: Chris Jones

text: While a lot of this stuff approaches roughest bootleg quality ("A Sailors Life" recorded live, appropriately enough, in Southampton) it shines out as incredibly adventurous.
author: Chris Jones

text: It was this period that saw the band forging new music by drawing on a rich heritage in much the same way that the Band were doing in America.
author: Chris Jones

text: This band saw no problem in mixing jazz with folk and psychedelia on such gems as "Autopsy".
author: Chris Jones

text: And when such archaeology unearths tracks as good as these it becomes clear that 1969's landmark Liege And Lief didn't just materialise out of thin air, but was the result of a unit inspired by each other's musical prowess and inquisitiveness.
author: Chris Jones

text: Fairport these days often seem like a bunch of rural pub bores intent on mulling over past glories while permanently trapped in an anodyne aural comfort-zone.
author: Chris Jones

text: Yet who could deny that in their first five years they created a legacy so rich and varied that it's no surprise that it continues to support the ultimate cottage industry.
author: Chris Jones

text: Congratulations must go to Free Reed for setting this material loose on the world, but let's make it a double album next time shall we?
author: Chris Jones

text: It's not often you find Keith Jarrett on the same album as Usted Fatah Ali-Khan.
author: Liz Mundler

text: Or indeed the delightfully named Rogers Covey-Crump.
author: Liz Mundler

text: The unifying force behind these and a whole host of other musicians from extremely diverse backgrounds is the amazing Norwegian saxophonist Jan Garbarek.
author: Liz Mundler

text: It's not just his technical ability that amazes, although he may well be the finest saxophonist you'll ever hear.
author: Liz Mundler

text: It's the breadth of that talent, the vast imagination, the sheer all-embracingness of his musicality that astounds, impresses and haunts.
author: Liz Mundler

text: This double album is a retrospective compilation drawn from a number of Garbarek's albums recorded over the last 30 years.
author: Liz Mundler

text: It is Garbarek's own celebration of the wealth of collaborations and musical partnerships that his career has embraced.
author: Liz Mundler

text: Through this selection of tracks he charts his own musical progress, stands back and finds a perspective, maps out the warp and weft of his own music by tracing some of the influences.
author: Liz Mundler

text: Jan Garbarek's music always has a direct emotional impact.
author: Liz Mundler

text: His range of tone is incredible.
author: Liz Mundler

text: From limpid torrents to dreamy mists, jarring jagged edges to ice-cool curves, he can tingle your spine one minute, jar your nerves the next, and then melt your heart.
author: Liz Mundler

text: This disc runs the gamut of all of these and more.
author: Liz Mundler

text: The tabla, the oud, the double bass and the ethereal voices of the Hilliard Ensemble (including the aforementioned Covey-Crump) feature on this disc, and with all of them Garbarek blends superbly without losing the individuality of his sound.
author: Liz Mundler

text: Everyone will have their own favourite track (there are 24 to choose from).
author: Liz Mundler

text: Mine's "My Song", recorded with Keith Jarrett back in 77.It has a freshness about it, an air of mellow optimism.
author: Liz Mundler

text: Jarrett's playing is gentle, almost offhand, with gorgeous clarity, and Garbarek's saxophone weaves around the piano and percussion like a spider weaving a web.
author: Liz Mundler

text: A close second would be the last track on the album, "Parce Mihi Domine" (by Christobal de Morales) from the chart-topping album Officium, recorded with the Hilliard Ensemble in 1993.
author: Liz Mundler

text: There's something about the way the saxophone soars above the four male voices, the church acoustic, the meditative, sacred feel to the music that lends an air of calmness and tranquillity.
author: Liz Mundler

text: Its an unlikely combination, but it works.
author: Liz Mundler

text: I start to listen to this music for the first time tired and a bit depressed at the onset of another London autumn with its chill and rain.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Outside my window the rain is beating down, the leaves are being blown from the trees, but I close my eyes with Dead Hollywood Stars in my headphones and suddenly it's a hot Mexican/Spanish/American afternoon where the heat haze obscures the distance and a multitude of experiences await.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Junctions employs found sound as signifier in the best filmic tradition: cicadas, threatening drones, Bollywood strings, Cooder-esque guitar drenched in reverb implying great (American) distances, a horse neighing, gritty noises, and so on.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: There's lots of things going on, but the detail isn't fussy at all, just necessary to the setting of a particular scene.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Synthetic sounds associated with IDM or D'n'B (bass waves, washes) are placed in a different context and the consequent mix of acoustic and synthetic is highly enjoyable.Rhythm tracks are used sparingly, and when they are the template is electronica-derived.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: The sonic world of Junctions is luxurious, like a book whose first page you've just read and you know you're going to enjoy the rest of.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Lavishness is a large part what this music seems to be about: in the same way you'd enjoy savouring a Thali, here the constituent parts await your delectation, adding up to a satisfying whole, a nice full belly.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: John Zorn's Spillane, FSOL's Lifeforms, Fourtet's first album, Ry Cooder's Paris, Texas.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: New invisible soundtracks are emerging constantly -this is one of the (much) better ones.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: There are three photographs on the cover of the cd: mountains covered in cacti with a vivid blue sky above, railway tracks and shadowcast, old wooden doors.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: There is nobody visible in these images: they are scenes waiting for you to step into, out of rainy London or wherever you are.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Try These: Asa-Chang & Junray - Jun Ray Song Chang Hazard - Wind Casino vs Japan - Whole Numbers Play the Basics
author: Colin Buttimer

text: This is the first time since, ooh, 1978's *London Town *that a Paul McCartney album been genuinely awaited.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: That's not to say the listener hasn't been surprised and delighted by the contents of many of his records since then.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: When they have been good (*Flaming Pie*, *Flowers In The Dirt*), they have bordered on exemplary; when they have been less good (*Press To Play*, *Off The Ground*) they have bordered on the execrable.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: But, throughout, there is always something there to remind us of Pauly's shimmering majesty.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: Now, we all know McCartney doesn't need to work, but his endless drive to be cutting edge makes him all the more endearing.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: He's Paul bloody McCartney, after all.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: 2001's *Driving Rain *was a fine rock album despite it's awful sleeve.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: What truly killed it was mixing eulogies to his recently deceased wife with ones to his new partner.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: It felt a little, er, hasty.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: And he'd forgot, in the main, to pack the tunes.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: Oh, and 9/11 happened on its release date too.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: No wonder it only spent a solitary week in the chart.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: Since then, McCartney has reconnected with his live audience and has gone back to playing virtually everything himself in the studio.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: In working with Radiohead/Beck producer Nigel Godrich, McCartney actually sounds somewhat stretched.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: So what does it sound like?
author: Daryl Easlea

text: Very, very good.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: He still finds it essential to play the chart game hence opener "Fine Line", the weakest track on the 14-track collection.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: But "Riding To Vanity Fair", "Too Much Rain", "Anyway" and "How Kind Of You" are full of subtle nuances, killer hooks and sweet surprises.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: They really do rank among his very best work.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: And "Jenny Wren" nods to "Blackbird" too.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: *Chaos and Creation In The Backyard *is a better album than anyone could reasonably expect from a 63-year-old who helped remould not just world popular music but world popular culture, as well.
author: Daryl Easlea

text: Two years after her last album, Kissin Time, and fresh from her recent appearance in William Burroughs' stage musical The Black Rider, Marianne Faithfull returns with Before the Poison.
author: Rob Webb

text: On Kissin Time it was Beck and Billy Corgan, amongst others, who shared the songwriting and playing duties.
author: Rob Webb

text: This time her fellow passengers, more suited perhaps to her nicotine-stained voice and brooding style, are Nick Cave and PJ Harvey (and their respective bands), with one track each from Damon Albarn and American composer Jon Brion.
author: Rob Webb

text: Nick Cave's three songs, co-produced with Hal Wilner, are by far the strongest here.
author: Rob Webb

text: The haunting "There is a Ghost" and "Crazy Love", the latter bearing no relation at all to the lazy Van Morrison tune of the same name, feature members of the Bad Seeds plus Cave on tinkling piano.
author: Rob Webb

text: They evoke rainy European boulevards and Proustian moments: classic Cave and a perfect match for Faithfull's measured vocals.
author: Rob Webb

text: The third Cave composition, "Desperanto", crackles like pylons in a thunderstorm.
author: Rob Webb

text: Faithfull raps over a howling sax and wailing Hammond, while the Bad Seeds chant (from the neighbouring room, it seems) lines by Jim Morrison.
author: Rob Webb

text: Yes, it's that odd.
author: Rob Webb

text: Other than Faithfull's slowburn drawl, there is little in Harvey's contributions - especially "The Mystery of Love" and the oblique "In the Factory" - to distinguish them from Harvey's own recordings: good news, if you like Polly Harvey's work.
author: Rob Webb

text: "My Friends Have" is built around a typically taut Harvey riff and throbs along in a punky kind of way.
author: Rob Webb

text: The languid "Before the Poison", another Faithfull/Harvey co-write, is an odd choice for the title track.
author: Rob Webb

text: Heavy on the minor chords, Damon Albarn's ballad, "Last Song", resembles Coldplay or Radiohead, with a nod towards the mordant Jacques Brel.
author: Rob Webb

text: Musically speaking, how much further has the former-Blur frontman travelled than his Britpop rivals?
author: Rob Webb

text: Closing the album on an unsettling note is Jon Brion's nursery-lullaby "City of Quartz", played on a variety of obscure instruments, such as the "paintbrush" guitar, toy piano and "fake glockenspeil".
author: Rob Webb

text: It's apparently about the fall of Babylon, although it may well be inspired by the Mike Davies book of the same name, which portrays a dystopic Los Angeles.
author: Rob Webb

text: If a film is ever made of Davies' City of Quartz, here's the perfect soundtrack.
author: Rob Webb

text: Before the Poison is a career high for Ms Faithfull and a timely release in the wake of acclaimed new albums from Cave and Harvey.
author: Rob Webb

text: There are times when someone decides that an album deserves plaudits, laurel wreaths and all round backslapping because it's an auspicious debut recorded without the help of some guy with a ponytail in a big office.
author: Chris Jones

text: Well, far be it for BBCi Music to pooh-pooh such laudatory behaviour but surely history tells us that you can count your chickens far too early?
author: Chris Jones

text: Whither Roni Size these days?
author: Chris Jones

text: The real joy to be found in a hand-tooled album like this is imagining what its siblings could turn out to be like if its creators are just left to get on with it.
author: Chris Jones

text: And what a funky little curio this album is?
author: Chris Jones

text: Blessed with a running time polite enough to not overstay its welcome, it cuts a meandering swathe through a whole plethora of styles.
author: Chris Jones

text: The overall vibe is one of laid back summer ambience sprinkled with surreal lyrics that hint at a some definite herbal assistance.
author: Chris Jones

text: Songs such as the breezy opener "Punchbag" with its swaying horns and the reggae charmer "No Trophy" both display an easy dynamic while retaining a sense of the absurd.
author: Chris Jones

text: "Angryman" is all Curtis Mayfield meets latter-day Beck and contains the central message of the album: that of tolerance and the triumph of kindness over anger.
author: Chris Jones

text: It's as if the Mexican-style masked wrestlers on the rather lovely cover are actually fighting for love's redemption.
author: Chris Jones

text: The Central American theme hits a somewhat sticky path with their cover of Os Mutantes' "A Minha Menina".
author: Chris Jones

text: Used extensively as the wonky good-time background music to a thousand TV clips this summer it's undoubtedly effective and known to millions, but adds absolutely nothing to the sacrosanct original.
author: Chris Jones

text: By the close, however, Bees have regained any lost ground by allowing us to share in the blissed-out piano stumble of "Zia" - one of those tracks so deceptively simple as to make you wonder why you didn't think of it first.
author: Chris Jones

text: Its only drawback is that it's so good that it will endlessly crop up on innumerable The Best Chilled Out Jazz Bliss Ambient Album Of All Time-type compilations.
author: Chris Jones

text: The loving message of the closing track "Sky Holds The Sun" acts as some kind of mantra/epilogue with the couplet about wanting to hold the one you love like?
author: Chris Jones

text: well, the sky holds the sun, leaving one with a sense that everything will be alright.
author: Chris Jones

text: At this stage the rather obvious debt to Beck and, especially, the Beta Band is a little too obvious, and the stylistic mixture still hints at a lack of purpose.
author: Chris Jones

text: But the fact remains that this IS an exemplary album, recorded by two blokes in a shed in the Isle of Wight that, at times, has the power to become sublime.
author: Chris Jones

text: To kill the goose who lays the golden eggs with hyperbole would be a crying shame.
author: Chris Jones

text: We need as many off-the-wall homegrown efforts as we can get these days and it's certainly more interesting than watching another bunch of testosterone-fuelled heroes attempting to breath life into rock's bloated corpse.
author: Chris Jones

text: Forget the Hives - concentrate on the Bees instead.
author: Chris Jones

text: After a three-year absence we see the return of our favourite Wolverhampton lass, armed and ready with her third album entitled: Who I Am, our Bev is taking no prisoners.
author: Buki Bakare

text: This 2 time MOBO award winner is proudly announcing just exactly who she is!
author: Buki Bakare

text: Probably the most underrated soul/ R&B artist born and bred from these shores, and equipped with a voice that is effortlessly up to par with that of our American cousins, her passionate vocals are so powerful and energetic that even the most hardened rock fan would have to sit up and take notice.
author: Buki Bakare

text: Anyone who has ever had the opportunity to see Ms Knight live will know exactly what I'm talking about.
author: Buki Bakare

text: Determined to break out of that tiresome, specialist mode that many British r&b female artists fall prey to, where ill-fated members often endure a somewhat short- term shelf life, Who I Am marks a significant change in direction for this tenacious 28-year-old singer, signifying her own personal growth as a true artist and developing songwriter.
author: Buki Bakare

text: (Knight co- wrote all the tracks on the album).
author: Buki Bakare

text: With an impressive line up of industry heavyweights including writer: James Poyser (previously worked with the likes of Jill Scott, Lauryn Hill and Erykah Badu), and producers Dodge, Mike Spencer and D'influence.
author: Buki Bakare

text: This album sees an eclectic hybrid of musical influences, from her first single released: "Get Up," the feisty self-empowered dancehall track guaranteed to work up a sweat on any dance floor, to "Best Seller Mystery," a track with more than a sprinkle of the blues added to it.
author: Buki Bakare

text: Not to mention her current (and finally first) top ten hit "Shoulda Woulda Coulda" with a distinct twinge of Country and Western, the acoustics adding the finishing touch.
author: Buki Bakare

text: Noticeable tracks include "Beautiful Contradiction" a soothing soulful duet with Musiq Soulchild that washes over you like a warm shower, along with the piano keys on the poignant "Gold" accompanied with heartfelt lyrics, gift wrapped to us in that notable trademark voice.
author: Buki Bakare

text: On this her most personal work to date, she takes us on a intimate journey where she bares her soul with such raw honesty that you get the distinct impression a healing process is taking place.
author: Buki Bakare

text: Although devoted fans expecting a return to the up-tempo, feel- good factor tracks from her previous album Prodigal Sista may be a little disappointed at first, due to the slower paced, more classy soulful feel, but stick with her, press "Rewind" and I guarantee you'll be glad you did.
author: Buki Bakare

text: Great Australian dance acts have been few and far between over the years but with the release of their debut album The Avalanches look set to redress the situation.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: A Badly Drawn Boy remix and one of their members coming runner up in the DMC Championships would lead us to believe that this band are not short on talent.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: However, even a cursory listen to their album Since I Left You brings with it the realisation that gold has been struck.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Ploughing a wide furrow, this record draws on a history of influences from hip hop, funk, soul, and big beat.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: The filter disco of "A Different Feeling" contrast nicely against the lazy breaks and John Barry-esque horns of "Frontier Psychiatrist".
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Whilst their clever sampling of Madonna's "Holiday" on "Stay Another Season" compliments the sweet pop of their, Radio 1 A listed, first single "Since I Left You" undoubtedly making this the soundtrack to the summer of 2001.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: This accomplished debut and a forthcoming tour in the UK make The Avalanches one to watch this year.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Taking time out from 'putting jazz back in the hands of hip hoppers', 4hero's Marc Mac follows in Kenny Dope's footsteps to put together the second chapter of Brazilika, a compilation of remixes of Brazilian music from the Far Out record label.
author: Lara Bellini

text: The music comes from across the decades,but the album opens and closes with tracks from Milton Nascimento's 1980 ballet 'Ultimo Trem' -which helps give the mix a cohesive feel.
author: Lara Bellini

text: Also featured are four classic Azymuth tracks - they're the most featured band here - as well as more recent Faro acts such as Joyce and Sabrina Malheiros (the daughter of Azymuth bass player Alex Malheiros).
author: Lara Bellini

text: The remixes of are top quality, which is what you'd expect from the likes of Incongnito, Osunlade and, of course, 4hero.
author: Lara Bellini

text: The infectious Brazilian rhythms sit comfortably with reassuringly hypnotic broken beats, giving off none of that 're-mix for the sake of it' vibe.All in all,a very stylish offering indeed.
author: Lara Bellini

text: Though probably not as well known as other West Coast members of the Cool School, ex Stan Kenton star Lennie Niehaus's string of 50s dates for the Contemporary label are gems of compositional and improvisational flair.
author: Peter Marsh

text: This 1956 Sextet session followed various experiments with strings, Octets and more conventional lineups; following Gerry Mulligan's lead, Niehaus dispenses with piano, relying on lush, complex counterpoint from baritone, tenor, trumpet and his own alto.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The sound Niehaus gets from his band is much greater than the sum of its parts, thanks to intelligent, sensitive horn charts that (in true Cool School style) substitute subtlety for bluster.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Niehaus's alto is firmly in post Charlie Parker mode, though Parker's urgency is replaced with relaxed, behind the beat phrasing (reminiscent of Lee Konitz) and a woody, almost clarinet like tone.
author: Peter Marsh

text: This combination of languid, expressive playing and agility is best heardon Niehaus originals like "Knee Deep" and "Take It from Me", where his fleet lines suggest a gentle subversion of bop cliche.
author: Peter Marsh

text: A young Jimmy Guiffre is on baritone duty, occasionally adding some bluesy grit, particularly on "Take it From Me"; here too trumpeter Stu Williamson contributes an agile valve trombone excursion.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Tenorist Bill Perkins is a less memorable soloist (firmly in Lester Young mode), but the supple, translucent ensemble horns are a joy throughout (check the opening to "Three of a Kind" for evidence).
author: Peter Marsh

text: Perkins does contribute some lovely flute to "Ill Wind", which features some of Niehaus's finest arranging (and soloing).
author: Peter Marsh

text: Longtime Niehaus associate Shelly Manne is his usual quietly inventive self, while bassist Buddy Clark is solid and lyrical by turns.
author: Peter Marsh

text: An unashamedly enjoyable record and proof that though Niehaus's more recent achievements as favoured composer for his old airforce buddy Clint Eastwood (Bird, The Unforgiven) have earned him much success, his contribution to Cool School jazz was no less important.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Actions was recorded live in 1971 at Donaueschingen and features the "New Eternal Rhythm Orchestra" (especially assembled for this project to perform under the direction of Krystzof Penderecki and Don Cherry).
author: Ian R Watson

text: The Orchestra were a veritable who's who of the then emerging European Free Jazz scene; Peter Brotzmann, Willem Breuker, Paul Rutherford and Han Bennink, plus Terje Rypdal, Kenny Wheeler and Tomasz Stanko are all in evidence.
author: Ian R Watson

text: These must have been very heady days indeed when 'serious composers' like Stockhausen and Penderecki could find a common ground with jazz players like those above.
author: Ian R Watson

text: For whatever reasons the Classical composers were finding that their interests and working methods (structured improvisation, graphic scores, conduction and gesture as composition) were overlapping with like-minded musicians from an altogether different area, that of free jazz.
author: Ian R Watson

text: Meanwhile Don Cherry had come out from under the shadow of his mentor Ornette Coleman to spearhead the influence of the new found freedom (particularly in Scandinavia), whilst at the same time letting different folk musics seep into his musical DNA.
author: Ian R Watson

text: So it should be little surprise to hear echoes of Turkish folk and classical Indian rhythms on Cherry's pieces ("Sita Rama Encores") interspersed with explosive passages of 'energy' playing.
author: Ian R Watson

text: The Penderecki piece ("Actions for Free Jazz Orchestra") explores the balance between composition and improvisation in a less playful yet no less meaningful way.
author: Ian R Watson

text: Drones and extended techniques such as overblowing (which explore a concern with timbre) sit alongside brass chords which hang in the air as well as 4/4 walking bass.
author: Ian R Watson

text: Apparently influenced by the Original Globe Unity Orchestra piece of 1967, "Actions" often sounds more overtly 'jazz' than that group; there are episodes that showcase the explosive playing of guitarist Terje Rypdal and saxophonist Brotzmann that will make your hair stand on end.
author: Ian R Watson

text: Sadly Cherry has passed on, and Penderecki's promised further pieces for the group didn't materialise.
author: Ian R Watson

text: That said, the combustible influences that shaped both pieces are still relevant today and find echoes in the work of Butch Morris and myriad others.
author: Ian R Watson

text: Oh, I've almost forgotten to say, (amongst all this talk of structure and influence) this is still damn fine music of any stripe that can be enjoyed without any prior knowledge of its participants whatsoever.
author: Ian R Watson

text: Heady days indeed.
author: Ian R Watson

text: It's been six years since he last released a new album and a lot has happened since.
author: Adam Smith

text: The Spice Girls have been and gone, Destiny's Child have become the hottest R&B act around, UK Garage and Nu-Metal have both arrived.
author: Adam Smith

text: His 80s colleague Madonna has gone from dwindling sales in the mid-90s to become more credible, successful and respected than ever.
author: Adam Smith

text: So where does that leave Jackson?
author: Adam Smith

text: His answer is the sixteen track - and 77 minute - Invincible.
author: Adam Smith

text: Those expecting a 'Ray of Light' kind of re-invention - forget it.
author: Adam Smith

text: This is Michael Jackson as we've come to expect him.
author: Adam Smith

text: The album is a mixture of upbeat tracks with his usual yelps - when he does actually sing his voice is still amazing.
author: Adam Smith

text: The best of these are '2000 Watts', 'Whatever Happens' and 'Threatened'.
author: Adam Smith

text: The ballads which make up most of this album cover his usual concerns - his privacy, children and falling in love.
author: Adam Smith

text: Some of them are good, but the others are pure Disney like 'The Lost Children' or 'Speechless'.
author: Adam Smith

text: If you are a big Michael Jackson fan and like what he does there is plenty here to keep you happy.
author: Adam Smith

text: However, if you are just curious to see whether the hype, the wait or the money has been worth the wait - you might just find that there isn't enough here which is fresh or original.
author: Adam Smith

text: It's not a great album and it's not a bad album.
author: Adam Smith

text: It's just not very thrilling.
author: Adam Smith

text: Well, you've probably already read in the press of how Heathen is a return to form due to the reunion with the producer most closely linked to Bowie; Tony Visconti.
author: Chris Jones

text: Such idle banter holds no water in these parts.
author: Chris Jones

text: To put it bluntly, David Bowie's return to form began way back in about 1993 when he ditched faux rock band Tin Machine.
author: Chris Jones

text: Each album since has displayed the same eclectic, questing vibe that made him the world's favourite (and most commercial) art rocker back in the day.
author: Chris Jones

text: Heathen isn't a return to form.
author: Chris Jones

text: It's a continuation of all the marvellous things that we love about the man, and how many other 55 year-old rock stars can you say that about?
author: Chris Jones

text: From the bubbling electronic undertow of the introduction to the first track "Sunday" one knows that this is sonically satisfying fare.
author: Chris Jones

text: Visconti's strengthisn't asmooth unifying approach that, say, Ken Scott brought to Hunky Dory, but an ability to stretch the artist and point them in new directions.
author: Chris Jones

text: As he said recently of guiding the mercurial Dame: "I'm one of the few people - possibly including Brian Eno - who can keep up with him, switch genres and roles very quickly.
author: Chris Jones

text: We have no holds barred." Genres certainly get switched here.
author: Chris Jones

text: Comparisons are odious, but the aforementioned "Sunday" and "I Would Be Your Slave" exist in the wild melodramatic spaces that Scott Walker used to inhabit before he became so scary.
author: Chris Jones

text: Two cover versions; the Pixies' "Cactus" and Neil Young's lost classic "Ive Been Waiting For You" (with Foo Fighter Dave Grohl providing suitable six-stringed mayhem) both prove that DB's not losing his love of noise (or a good song).
author: Chris Jones

text: This is backed up by the first single "Slow Burn" which features some ridiculously truculent axe work from Pete Townshend.
author: Chris Jones

text: And that voice?...from emotive rumble to idiosyncratic yodel, the pipes are as distinctive as ever.
author: Chris Jones

text: Moods also mix in varying degrees.
author: Chris Jones

text: "Slow Burn"s opening couplet: "Here shall we live in this terrible town, where the price for our eyes shall squeeze them tight like a fist" is incredibly forceful in its misery.
author: Chris Jones

text: However his follow-up to Hunky Dory's "Kooks", "Everyone Says Hi" is the chirpiest thing the man has done in years.
author: Chris Jones

text: In fact the overall feeling is of celebration and reconciliation despite the overall theme being that of the desolation of living in a Godless century.
author: Chris Jones

text: His shiny speed-thrill rendition of The Legendary Stardust Cowboy's "Gemini Spacecraft" is truly a return to the sci fi optimism of his earliest days.
author: Chris Jones

text: With the man himself back in the UK soon to curate the Meltdown Festival on London's South Bank, dusting off the stage threads once more, and with Ziggy celebrating its 30th anniversary, this couldn't be a more serendipitous release.
author: Chris Jones

text: It bursts with a positively rude health.
author: Chris Jones

text: Everyone has at least one Bowie album they hold dear to their hearts.
author: Chris Jones

text: This could be the one for you...
author: Chris Jones

text: OK, I admit it.
author: Chris Jones

text: It's taken me a long time to review this album BECAUSE IT SCARES ME.
author: Chris Jones

text: How long has it taken me to quell my shaking hand in order that I can warn you, dear listener, about this incredible disc?
author: Chris Jones

text: Mr Drake has fashioned something almost indefinable in its creepiness.
author: Chris Jones

text: Let's look at the evidence: The self-designed cover with gloomy engravings of dark abandoned houses and empty rooms, the disconcerting dedications to "Britain's most famous Ghost Hunter" and a mysterious "HPL" (that couldn't be...could it?), titles like "The Shocking Efflorescence" and "Fearsome Heads (I & II), and, finally, the album's very title.
author: Chris Jones

text: Apparently it is based on a real mailbox which "if you open on certain nights you'll see something inside you wish you hadn't." Listener, enter at your peril, for what we have here is possibly the strangest and most morbidly amusing little morsel for many a year.
author: Chris Jones

text: Twenty seven vignettes that are all played and sung by Bob himself (apart from some acompanying gravel-shovelling and er...dogs) re-define the term renaissance man.
author: Chris Jones

text: Bob is an engineer, musician and member of experimentalists 5UU.
author: Chris Jones

text: As label boss Chris Cutler states on the ReR web site, "People that work this hard are becoming an endangered species".
author: Chris Jones

text: The level of playing is absurdly high and Drake's guitar technique alone deserves an essay to extol its subtleties (as on "The Wig Screamed Murder"): Kind of Zoot Horn Rollo meets Woody Guthrie in Arkham asylum.
author: Chris Jones

text: Tunings are elastic.
author: Chris Jones

text: Ghostly choruses wail.
author: Chris Jones

text: Harmoniums drone menacingly and a whole kitchen of ironwear seems to clank and squeak as punctuation to the dreadful tales of indescribable horror which (in true HPL fashion) fill you with an unnameable dread.
author: Chris Jones

text: The lyrics are, at once, shocking and hilarious.
author: Chris Jones

text: This little snippet comes from "The Tragic Seance": "Something unexpected and equally uninvited materialised itself amongst them, with unspeakable appetites.
author: Chris Jones

text: And unfortunately for them, it was very hungry." Edward Gorey on acid?
author: Chris Jones

text: You're getting close.
author: Chris Jones

text: But be careful, dear listener, not to get too close, for you may never be quite the same again...
author: Chris Jones

text: For most British music fans, the word Gospel conjures up images of Aretha Franklin and Sam Cooke emerging from the churches of black America to invent soul.
author: Alwyn Turner

text: But that was 50 years ago, and for those who may have lost touch with subsequent developments, this double-CD provides a helpful round-up of the current state of play.
author: Alwyn Turner

text: And the tradition clearly remains active if a little confused.
author: Alwyn Turner

text: The superstars of the movement, sisterly duo Mary Mary, top and tail the collection: their US hit "Shackles (Praise You)" is a solid piece of R'n'B but, like many of the tracks, is indistinguishable from mainstream pop-soul.
author: Alwyn Turner

text: Programmed rhythms and over-production all but drown out the messages of hope and praise, and even when the messages do appear, they're often bland rather than inspirational:'Keep the faith, stay positive, stay away from the negative' urges hip-hop artist Seven.
author: Alwyn Turner

text: Standout track is dancehall reggae singer Chevelle Franklyn (as heard on Shabba Ranks' "Mr Loverman"), whose "Salvation" is both infectious and devotional - would that the rest of the album had such depth.
author: Alwyn Turner

text: On one side of the UK Garage coin there is the classically trained MJ Cole trading in sweet vocals, pianos and pizzicato strings, on the flip there is Oxide and Neutrino, the dynamic duo spawned from the massive, London based So Solid crew.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: For those above the underground these guys blasted in to the mainstream last year with the release of the chart topping, Casualty sampling 'Bound 4 Da Reload' - a tune which pricked up the ears and raised the eyebrows of many in equal measure.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: However, this subsequent release is proof positive that Oxide and Neutrino are no one trick pony; in fact, Execute is perhaps the definitive UK garage album so far.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Sure, there have been great singles but nothing to date has nailed the sound and the attitude in one.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Reminiscent of punk and the early days of jungle, this is a deep and dangerous collection with a sense of humour made for the people and by the people that love it.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Just goes to show, you don't need much more than drums, bass, a mic and nuff love.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Watch their space.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Of the many significant improvised music ensembles formed in the late 60s and early 70s (AMM, Globe Unity Orchestra, ICP, The London Jazz Composers' Orchestra, SME, to name a few), Iskra 1903 was one of the least recorded and (with the benefit of 20/20 hindsight) one of the more important.
author: John Eyles

text: Formed by Paul Rutherford in 1970, and originally consisting of Rutherford, Barry Guy and Derek Bailey, the trio had no drummer, in contrast to all those listed above in which the drummer was a key figure.
author: John Eyles

text: This removed any expectations of a conventional rhythm or pulse, allowing the listener to focus on the individual voicings and their interactions, a giant leap at the time.
author: John Eyles

text: Emanem has been a primary source of Iskra 1903 recordings; the triple CD Chapter One (Emanem 4301) documented their earliest work from 1970 to 1972, and Buzz Soundtrack is an important complement to it.
author: John Eyles

text: Recorded early in the trio's existence, it is the soundtrack to a long forgotten film by Michael Grigsby, a friend of Rutherford's.
author: John Eyles

text: The trio played while viewing the film, providing a soundtrack to complement the events they saw on screen.
author: John Eyles

text: Across the twenty-one tracks (which play continuously, without gaps) there are trio, duo and solo pieces.
author: John Eyles

text: Unlike most improvised music, the players are not primarily reacting to each other's playing but to the stimulus of the film.
author: John Eyles

text: However, this music definitely stands alone, not needing any visuals to enhance it.
author: John Eyles

text: Similar in character to the trio's earliest work on Chapter One, the defining qualities on show are subtlety, restraint, patience and sensitivity.
author: John Eyles

text: The music is allowed to evolve slowly without any of the players forcing the issue.
author: John Eyles

text: All three sublimate individual ego to the greater totality, content to leave each other ample space in which to create, without the need to constantly assert themselves.
author: John Eyles

text: If one recognises parallels between improv and conversation, this music is not idle chatter or a heated argument; it is a polite, formal debate.
author: John Eyles

text: Given that it is over thirty years old, Buzz Soundtrack sounds remarkably contemporary; the understatement and restraint displayed are reminiscent of the work of New London Silence players such as Mark Wastell and Rhodri Davies.
author: John Eyles

text: This welcome release can stand on its merits; it is of far more than historical interest.
author: John Eyles

text: Judging by the amount of releases were getting in here every week, it seems that the world of contemporary laptop electronica is getting to be a pretty crowded place these days.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: As such, its getting progressively more difficult to separate the wheat from the chaff, so to speak.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Luckily, there are labels like Temporary Residence who make our lives a little bit easier by putting out the kind of releases that make you sit up in your chair and take notice from the minute you hit the play button.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Sybarite's Placement Issues is exactly that kind of record.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Having released several tasty singles on labels such as Emanate and Static Caravan, Xian Hawkins (a former member of psychedelic electronic outfit Silver Apples) has been delving deep into moody cut and paste electronica for about three years now, and this album is a collection of previously released and generally hard to find singles.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Although some of these were released as far back as 1999, they sounds as fresh and up to date as any out this week.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Taking his cue from people like Isan and Fridge, Hawkins has constructed a fabulous world in which traditional rock elements and modern electronica are thrown into the laptop blender to emerge as a tasty cocktail, going down smoothly but with just enough bite to keep it interesting over repeated listens.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Hawkins manages to keep his live elements perfectly in sync with the loops scattered around each track, no matter how complex it all gets.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: The results are fantastic - kind of like a live band jamming over a laptop thats been kicked around too much, its hard disc glitching every time a new track or bassline comes in.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Especially lovely are the multi-layered rhythms of "Second Cities" and "Unforced Force Of The Truth", which reminds one a lot of Telefon Tel Aviv or Sea and Cake.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Hawkins has a deep love of melody and refuses to let it slide to the background, no matter how dissonant the surrounding mix gets.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: We like that.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: We like that a lot.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Having just signed to 4AD, we're expecting great things from Hawkins in the near future.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Go out, get this now and say you were there before everyone else.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: A winner in every respect.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Even though Zero 7 have enlisted the abilities of the Australian born vocalist and writer, there is a bigger and better reason to be excited about Sia Furler, namely her debut album Healing Is Difficult.
author: Andy Puleston

text: This combination of R&B, two step and jazz flavours provides a backdrop for one of the most exciting voices to have emerged in recent years.
author: Andy Puleston

text: Prior to the album's release "Taken For Granted" crashed the charts last year at number 10 and "Little Man" had the overhaul from UK garage star Wookie and sold 10,000 white labels to the dance music underground.
author: Andy Puleston

text: With the full showcase now available, Sia has pulled a handbrake turn and skidded neatly in to the space marked 'this year's diva'.
author: Andy Puleston

text: The title of this album is not without good reason as Sia's past has been a trying one with the tragic loss of a partner and subsequent grieving providing the basis and catalyst for much of the writing.
author: Andy Puleston

text: From the outset we are exposed to a brutal honesty as the opening track, "Fear" confesses, 'And sometimes I worry my boyfriend will die, my first love is already dead.
author: Andy Puleston

text: You see fear is only holding us back'.
author: Andy Puleston

text: Complementary to this, the hip hop beats of "Taken For Granted" have been layered over Prokofiev's 'Romeo and Juliet' - whether this choice reflects a darker irony and further mediatation on the subject only adds to the track's mystique and appeal.
author: Andy Puleston

text: However bold, her sensitivity never descends to self-depreciation or pity, in fact, it is tempered with a well developed sense of humour - a natural extension of her playful nature.
author: Andy Puleston

text: By way of an illustration, she arrived on stage to perform "Destiny" at the recent Zero 7 show to a rapturous applause, took the mic and in the thickest of Australian twangs exclaimed, 'I probably shouldn't talk, should I?
author: Andy Puleston

text: It'll spoil the illusion!' Mindset aside, it is the delivery that singles Sia out.
author: Andy Puleston

text: Her range and versatility across the album mark her as being both natural and at ease in a jazz mode, "Drink To Get Drunk", as well as down tempo in the seductive R&B ballad "Blow It All Away".
author: Andy Puleston

text: That said, the soaring vocal power on the exceptional "Judge Me" proves she can belt it out with the best of them.
author: Andy Puleston

text: Sexy, soulful and masterful, she is without question a kick ass singer!
author: Andy Puleston

text: It's not really a question of drawing parallels with other vocalists rather that in years to come it is others that will be compared to her.
author: Andy Puleston

text: The road has been long with too many winding turns to mention but Sia is finally here.
author: Andy Puleston

text: Intelligent, moving and funny which begs the question, 'What does the girl do for an encore?'.
author: Andy Puleston

text: Do not deprive yourself of this little gem.
author: Andy Puleston

text: Long thought buried somewhere under the M3 along with prints of the full version of the film, this release represents a truly wondrous piece of archaeology.
author: Chris Jones

text: In most cases any film labelled 'cult' tends to use the label as a get-out clause for some wobbly production that had something to do with Russ Meyer.
author: Chris Jones

text: The Wicker Man was always much more than this.
author: Chris Jones

text: From, probably, the last period when British cinema was prepared to show more than gritty portraits of life 'up north' or sappy feelgood nonsense about Hugh Grant living in a ridiculously large apartment in London, The Wicker Man dared to combine a genuinely creepy story line about provincial paganism with a simply stunning collection of songs.
author: Chris Jones

text: Despite its trouble with the distributors the film has now been rightly placed in the pantheon of great celluloid, and its soundtrack deserves the same accolades.
author: Chris Jones

text: Ironically the saviour of this sonic scariness was the other ubermensch of cult movies, Roger Corman.
author: Chris Jones
