text: Found within his private collection of film prints, Paul Giovanni's songs reside neatly against a portrait of the idyllic community of Summerisle whose adherence to an older order attracts the unwanted attentions of uptight Presbyterian policeman Edward Woodward.
author: Chris Jones

text: American Giovanni collected a fine bunch of sessioneers under the banner of Magnet and conjured up some surprisingly authentic-sounding folk numbers.
author: Chris Jones

text: The lilting (how come folk is always lilting?) melodies of numbers like ''Corn Rigs'', ''Gently Johnny'' and ''Willow's Song'' are stuffed with a vaguely sinister eroticism, reflecting Woodward's unease as he scratches the tranquil surface of the island community to discover its sinister secret (you know, the usual: child sacrifice, fertility rituals, Britt Ekland rubbing up against a wall etc.).
author: Chris Jones

text: Christopher Lee (the Laird of Summerisle and, himself, a vocalist on the bawdy ''The Tinker Of Rye'') described this album as:''...quite extraordinary, it is probably the best music I've ever heard in a film''.
author: Chris Jones

text: He's not far short of the truth.
author: Chris Jones

text: Maybe it takes a foreigner to get to the dark heart of much of our indigenous music, but it's a darkness suffused with beauty.
author: Chris Jones

text: Coupled to the original incidental music - complete with snippets of dialogue, including Woodward's terrified shriek as the full weight of realisation hits him !
author: Chris Jones

text: - this is a vital document of a time when the UK could still produce classic cinema.
author: Chris Jones

text: It's also a really fine album.
author: Chris Jones

text: If you love everything that's weird and wonderful about early violin music, these recordings are for you.
author: Claire Rogers

text: Andrew Manze is surely the most knowledgeable and talented baroque violinist around today, and in his hands what he describes as Biber's "unpredictability" and constant musical inventiveness magically spring to life.
author: Claire Rogers

text: It's a real meeting of minds.
author: Claire Rogers

text: Biber was something of a 17th century Paganini, a formidably talented and innovative violinist.
author: Claire Rogers

text: He seems to have been even more highly valued as a composer in his day though, and it's thanks to the extraordinary music he wrote for the violin that we can build up a vivid picture of the heights to which he took the art of violin playing at that time.
author: Claire Rogers

text: The sad fact that much of Biber's music is still oddly overlooked makes this excellent 2-CD set by Romanesca a welcome treat, particularly as it features all eight of Biber's violin sonatas from 1681 recorded in their entirety for the first time.
author: Claire Rogers

text: The notes, as well as the ideas, flow like water in these kaleidoscopic works, but also show that Biber was capable of music of great beauty and reflection as well as virtuosity.
author: Claire Rogers

text: For out and out eccentricity, though, the Sonata Representativa wins hands down, with its incredible creature impersonations (including an amazing violinistic impression of a cat meouwing) and a Musketeer's March which Manze and company capture with an abandoned mixture of Eastern exoticism and more than a hint of blue grass!
author: Claire Rogers

text: Manze rounds off this lovely recording with Biber's towering polyphonic Passacaglia for solo violin - a more serious note which seems a fitting tribute to the enduring musicianship of John Toll who died last summer.
author: Claire Rogers

text: All in all, these CDs offer a wonderful trip around the world of Baroque music and ideas, in all their diversity, and are a real treasure.
author: Claire Rogers

text: She was one of the great American sopranos, yet Leontyne Price had to wait to make her solo recital debut at Carnegie Hall on 28th February 1965.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: She was far from unknown in the hall: she'd actually appeared there in concert more than eighteen times since the mid-50s, and by the mid-60s she was a busy and very popular singer at the Metropolitan Opera in New York, but in some ways this was a return to her roots, the kind of recital programme Price would have sung before operatic fame overtook her.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Just one thing had changed - the audience.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Carnegie Hall was packed out with fans, and by the time we get to the encores they're howling with enthusiasm; it sounds as though they've been imported from the local sports stadium.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Which could be very off-putting, if this weren't such a fine recital, and if the recording hadn't captured the atmosphere so well - there's such a huge sense of occasion.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Price's Handel arias are performed straight, no chaser - current singers with a sense of period style would approve.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: The Brahms Zigeunerlieder benefit from the freshness of the voice, still lithe and flexible, silvery with a hint of cream...almost a junior Jessye Norman, but with turn-on-a-sixpence handling.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Then for me the high point of the recital: the four Poulenc melodies are deliciously handled, the Barber songs are breathtakingly beautiful without ever falling over the line into sentimentality, and they segue into the Lee Hoiby songs as though this was the way they were originally written.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: The noise levels increase significantly for the four spirituals, Price in fiery form and the audience responding to her simple sincerity.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: By the time you reach the encores, Price can do anything she wants; we're all in the palm of her hand, and she's enjoying herself.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: It's a long, tiring recital, but there are few signs of frailty in this magnificent voice, and David Garvey's piano playing is only occasionally too matter-of-fact for the occasion.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: But why Leontyne Price Re-discovered?
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Well, only the Brahms songs have been released on disc before, but when you've heard the rest of this recital, it beggars belief that RCA sat on it for thirty-seven years.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: At least they've relented now, and if there has been electronic intervention or editing, you're never made aware of it.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Instead you get a top-price ticket to a concert I bet is still talked about by those who were there.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Go on, join them - all recitals should be this rewarding.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Hundred Reasons first emerged into the popular consciousness in 2000, that fruitful time when rock music started to be really good again.
author: Kate Lawrence

text: Even then they were a cut above the rest.
author: Kate Lawrence

text: Whilst they didn't capitalise on the uprising of rock at the time, (you'll still find the band playing Clubs rather than Arenas) this means they retained a certain credibility.
author: Kate Lawrence

text: And they managed to neatly dismiss the lazy emo-rock labelling that they clearly didn't welcome.
author: Kate Lawrence

text: This second album sees them settle into their style, resulting in a consistently polished album of good hearted, anthemic rock.
author: Kate Lawrence

text: You might long for the slightly raw edginess that originally made them stand out from the crowd, but Hundred Reasons know what their fans love and this album presents us with an unadulterated selection of uplifting riffs and crunching rock.
author: Kate Lawrence

text: Sturdy opener "Savanna" is about as moody as it gets; pointless whining clearly isn't an option with these boys.
author: Kate Lawrence

text: The album does sometimes err towards the mainstream a little more than perhaps hoped.
author: Kate Lawrence

text: A prime example of this is "Stories With Unhappy Endings" which sounds suspiciously like a watered down Jimmy Eat World which is disappointing given the more petulant promise of HR's debut album.
author: Kate Lawrence

text: Perhaps this is due to the overbearing influence of American producer Dave Sardy.
author: Kate Lawrence

text: However, there are some really great anthems on Shatterproof Is Not A Challenge - "Harmony", whilst appearing plaintive (if not slightly repetitive) from the comfort of your lounge, will no doubt prove to be a fantastic live rabble-rouser.
author: Kate Lawrence

text: "Truth Without Elegance" is another stand out track which builds up to a roaring chorus that tests Colin Doran's vocals to their limit.
author: Kate Lawrence

text: The album is accomplished without being pretentious and cathartic without bitterness - in short, it's good old shouty rock music.
author: Kate Lawrence

text: Whilst it will never be considered cutting edge, you have to ask whether it needs to be.
author: Kate Lawrence

text: With bands like Hundred Reasons providing the kids with music of this quality, we can hope that the currentrock revival will remain more than just a fad.
author: Kate Lawrence

text: Zero Tolerance is the latest collection of songs featuring one singular rhythm track, with a total of 20 artists all delivering their own unique interpretations.
author: Keysha Davis

text: The album provides the perfect forum for established artists to go head-to-head with their peers, and also serves as a great training ground for the younger guns to flex their lyrical skills by partaking on the same arena as the big boys.
author: Keysha Davis

text: The rhythm track in question comes complete with a classical music intro, and then delves into a drum machine driven melody.
author: Keysha Davis

text: A carefully selected line-up ensures a hybrid of sounds that range from the socially conscious and comedic to the hyper sexed, and vocally aggressive.
author: Keysha Davis

text: First off on the mark is an artist that at some point has encapsulated all of the above - Capleton, with a track entitled "Push Wood".
author: Keysha Davis

text: In what appears to be quite a tepid contribution from the self-proclaimed Fireman, we are invited to play privy to his superior lovemaking skills and physical prowess.
author: Keysha Davis

text: True fans may be slightly disappointed due to the stellar performances usually associated with this artist, but there are plenty of worthwhile substitutes including sound-alike Kulcha Knox.
author: Keysha Davis

text: Knox embellishes on the continual theme of police brutality in the simply titled "Police".
author: Keysha Davis

text: Urging the nation to uprise and thwart the establishment, the passion inherent is signified by the verbal lashings and violent sentiments echoed throughout the track.
author: Keysha Davis

text: In a similar vein Sizzla's "Empty The Clip" attacks the government for social injustice (particularly the uneven distribution of wealth), and deeply seeped corruption.
author: Keysha Davis

text: Assuming the role of lyrical maverick, Sizzla runs rife by threatening to eradicate the guilty parties through rapid gunfire hence the track-title.
author: Keysha Davis

text: Vocal assassinations aside, the comic relief comes courtesy of Lexxus with a track entitled "Lord Mi Body".
author: Keysha Davis

text: Exposing a female victim of having delusions of grandeur, Lexxus hilariously breaks down all the lies and seems particularly miffed about said female's greatest untruth - pretending to have a top-notch body (shock, horror)!
author: Keysha Davis

text: "&Talk bout she tight and her body set right, but her belly well flabby flabby".
author: Keysha Davis

text: For further humour listen to Merciless & Pickney's "Mi nah Tek Nuh Talk", and Merciless' "Come Here".
author: Keysha Davis

text: Natural Black and Singer J hold it down on the vocal tip with "Young Black & Beautiful", and "Princess For Life" respectively.
author: Keysha Davis

text: Having such a multitude of songs on one rhythm track makes it virtually impossible to prevent the inevitable task of fast forwarding.
author: Keysha Davis

text: So in all frankness there are a few which pails into insignificance leaving the obvious choices to shine.
author: Keysha Davis

text: However, to maintain the interest of a listener on this particular format is a challenge within itself that the album manages to achieve.
author: Keysha Davis

text: After a lengthy hiatus, Ashcroft returns with his third album.
author: Chris Jones

text: contains songs written over six years showcasing Ashcroft's sneeringly cocksure voice in fine, mature form.
author: Chris Jones

text: But has he got anything to say?
author: Chris Jones

text: He's undoubtedly right in his assumption that he was the template for swaggering Northern vocalists.
author: Chris Jones

text: Yet the anthemic quality of many of the tracks leaves you thinking of another northern testosterone-filled crooner: Robbie Williams.
author: Chris Jones

text: Single, "Break The Night With Colour" has all the tropes of his moving, yet vapid stadium-fillers.
author: Chris Jones

text: "Sweet Brother Malcolm" and "World Keeps Turning" hint at depth, but it's too cliche-ridden to attain classic status.
author: Chris Jones

text: This is Verve-lite (the best track, "Music Is Power", is built around a Curtis Mayfield sample) - it's full of sound and fury, but not really saying much.
author: Chris Jones

text: "I could put together the greatest rock 'n roll band you ever heard," boasted the legendary Miles Davis in the end of 1969.
author: Paul Tingen

text: The then 43-year old Davis already had an impressive pedigree behind him as one of the great innovators in jazz, but at the time this must have sounded like a claim too far.
author: Paul Tingen

text: This 5-CD boxed set documents Davis's search for "the best rock 'n roll band you ever heard" during February-June 1970.
author: Paul Tingen

text: Featuring now famous jazz musicians like Chick Corea, Herbie Hancock, Keith Jarrett, Dave Holland, Wayne Shorter, Airto Moreira, Billy Cobham, and John McLaughlin, it illustrates both the pitfalls and the highlights of Davis's quest.
author: Paul Tingen

text: The pitfalls come in the form of tracks that would better have stayed in Columbia's vaults.
author: Paul Tingen

text: Oddities like "Johnny Bratton," "Archie Moore," "Sugar Ray," "Ali," and "Little High People," sound like shapeless ramblings of clueless jazz musicians.
author: Paul Tingen

text: They illustrate the words of Davis's producer at the time, Teo Macero: "the musicians didn't know what the hell they were doing." Mercifully, the highlights are very good.
author: Paul Tingen

text: One could question whether we really need six takes of "Willie Nelson," but especially on the earlier versions a storm is kicked up by John McLaughlin's heavily distorted and Hendrix-influenced electric guitar, Corea's weirdness on ring modulator, and Davis's own majestic trumpet playing.The leader'sunadulterated blues playing on "Go Ahead John," here showcased without the strange edits and effects on the originally released version, is also a sheer delight.
author: Paul Tingen

text: However good this material in its own right, it wasn't yet great rock 'n roll.
author: Paul Tingen

text: Davis needed one more ace in his pack, and this came in the form of bassist Michael Henderson, who at the time played with Stevie Wonder.
author: Paul Tingen

text: Together with Billy Cobham on drums, Henderson drives the boogie groove of "Right Off" to astonishing heights, and he sets the James Brown bass riff used on "Yesternow" in concrete.
author: Paul Tingen

text: On top, both Davis and McLaughlin excel with some of the best playing of their career.
author: Paul Tingen

text: Teo Macero rightly called this music (recorded on April 7, 1970) "dynamite" and in 1971 he compiled most of "Right Off" and "Yesternow" on Miles's A Tribute to Jack Johnson LP.
author: Paul Tingen

text: This set offers some precious extra material from this April session, and also traces Davis' next steps in May and June with music that had little to do with rock 'n roll; the ever-changing trumpeter was already on to new challenges.
author: Paul Tingen

text: Yet to create, if only for one day, the "best rock 'n roll band you ever heard," was a remarkable and historic achievement.
author: Paul Tingen

text: The Complete Jack Johnson Sessions is a fitting testament.
author: Paul Tingen

text: Triumphant performances at this year's Big Chill and Shepherds Bush Empire combined with the nomination of Simple Things in this year's Mercury Music Prize are shaping the perfect summer for Zero 7.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Combining the musical heritage of Ray Charles and Quincy Jones with the last ten years of house and electronica, Zero 7's blend of spacious, soulful jazz/funk is without doubt one of the finest releases of the year.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Prior to the album's release in April they attracted the attention of Gilles Peterson, amongst others, who enlisted their skills to remix Terry Callier's "Love Theme From Spartacus" and in addition, producer and friend Nigel Godrich asked them to remix "Climbing Up The Walls" for Radiohead.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Faith in their abilities has been rewarded with a record that will force many to reassess the bench mark in British music.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Unlike the fifteen piece (yes, it does take that many musicians to recreate the sound) band employed for their stunning live show, Zero 7 are principally a duo, namely Sam Hardaker and Henry Binns.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: From North London, both studied sound engineering and sharpened their production skills before making the decision to break out on their own.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: In piecing the record together Sam and Henry have pulled together some exceptional vocal talent, providing diversity to the recording as well as the live outing.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Mozez, who on tracks "I Have Seen" and "Simple Things" demonstrates a sweet, soul delivery that will please fans of Marvin Gaye and Maxwell alike.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: The distinctive, dulcet tones of Australian born Sia Furler embellish the lush instrumentation of "Distractions" with more husk than a wheat field whilst the vocal partnership with the sublime and as yet unsigned Sophie Barker on "Destiny" soar on a summer thermal to new heights.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Characterised by Rhodes piano, sweeping strings and gentle, parping brass their music is way beyond the monikers of 'chill out' or 'ambient', it is soul food from the lounge room at the end of the universe.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Ignore any comparisons you might read or hear about this band, whatever they are they won't do Zero 7 any justice, the only thing that will is your undivided attention.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: A must have.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Roots Manuva( AKA Rodney Smith) is supremely talented but - just like you or I - he has no special gift for getting through life.
author: Ruth Jamieson

text: His talent is for expressing himself, turning pain and bewilderment into poetry.
author: Ruth Jamieson

text: As such, he's British hip hop's answer to Kurt Cobain, and his lyrics are the genius ramblings of a justified and righteous loony.
author: Ruth Jamieson

text: Slow steppa "Mind 2 Motion", as the title suggests, concerns itself with turning good intentions into good actions.
author: Ruth Jamieson

text: Or, to be more precise, reconciling good intentions with bad behaviour.
author: Ruth Jamieson

text: The guilt creeps in further on "Colossal Insight", to the sound of a twisted fairground, complete with haunted fruit machines: 'Gracious Lord/My Mega Almighty/I know that I been slightly outta your path& I know I should cut down on this drinking/too many late nights and wayward thinking.' "Too Cold" sees him corrupted by money, which makes 'civilised men start to act gunny gunny'.
author: Ruth Jamieson

text: Added to these internal struggles are external worries.
author: Ruth Jamieson

text: Smith speaks of injustice on "A Haunting" and his suspicion of the powers that be on nasty bass-ridden grime anthem "Chin High": 'Government man keep fighting down the weed/While they boost up the booze, the Prozac and methadone.' All this pressure seems to be affecting his mental health.
author: Ruth Jamieson

text: The dub-heavy, acid-slashed horror film soundtrack of the title track is paranoia sonic-ified.
author: Ruth Jamieson

text: His guilt and confusion is starting to get the better of him; 'Voodoo in the hills and I'm running from ghosties' he declares.
author: Ruth Jamieson

text: Young black males have a higher instance of mental illness than any other social group, but its rarely discussed in young black music.
author: Ruth Jamieson

text: Smith is not so afraid and speaks of trips to the 'farms of the funny.' Awfully Deep may be an astounding hybrid of calypso, drum 'n' bass, breakbeat, electro, grime and hip hop, all heavily flavoured with dub.
author: Ruth Jamieson

text: But, once its overlaid with Smith's rhymes, it's pure blues and soul.
author: Ruth Jamieson

text: Bon Jovi's massive fan base have had to wait two long years for this, Bon Jovi's first release since 2000's Crush.
author: Morwenna Fisher

text: Bounce shouldn't disappoint their die hard fans as the band doesn't stray far from their trademark sound that made them famous the world over.
author: Morwenna Fisher

text: They stick to the winning recipe; a healthy mixture of rock anthems and sultry ballads that's sure to get the guys 'n' girls playing air guitar to every song.
author: Morwenna Fisher

text: From the opening heavy drum beat of the first song "Undivided" to the final guitar solo of the last track "Open All Night" this is unmistakably Bon Jovi; radio-friendly hard rock.
author: Morwenna Fisher

text: This first song is lyrically the weakest song on the album with Jovi's repeated chorus: 'one for love, one for truth...' It is quite a dark and uninspiring opening track which sets the tone for an album that is influenced by the events of September 11th.
author: Morwenna Fisher

text: Thankfully, the next track and recent single, "Everyday", is much more of a pop rock song with its unusual opening bars, slightly offbeat drumming and catchy chorus.
author: Morwenna Fisher

text: It's set to become another of their anthems, easily sitting alongside such legends as "Wanted Dead or Alive" and "Keep The Faith".
author: Morwenna Fisher

text: "Everyday", "Love Me Back to Life" and "Bounce" are all upbeat, loud tracks with superb power chords, a big drumbeat and Jovi's unmistakable vocals that ooze good clean American fun.
author: Morwenna Fisher

text: You won't be able to stop your feet tapping and your hands playing imaginary drums.
author: Morwenna Fisher

text: However, the rest of the album is more mellow and reflective compared to their previous albums.
author: Morwenna Fisher

text: Gone are the wild celebratory songs that can be heard on Crush and Keep the Faith and in their place there is a bleaker, even sombre sound.
author: Morwenna Fisher

text: The ballads here, "You Had Me From Hello" and "All About Lovin' You", don't quite hit the mark and are not in the same league as classics "Always" and "Bed of Roses".
author: Morwenna Fisher

text: All in all Bounce is an album every Bon Jovi fan should have in their collection, the cover and booklet are pretty fantastic for a start.
author: Morwenna Fisher

text: They haven't broken down any barriers here, but they have once again successfully bridged the gap between heavy metal and stadium rock.
author: Morwenna Fisher

text: Try These: Queens Of The Stone Age - Songs For The Deaf Vex Red - Start With A Strong And Persistant Desire
author: Morwenna Fisher

text: For his latest release as Biosphere, Geir Jenssen has based the bulk of this album on "the orchestral works of Claude Debussy" - an interesting choice, given how David Toop argued for Debussy's status as the forefather of modern ambient music in his seminal book, "Ocean Of Sound", and that Biosphere is one of the few projects still flying the ambient flag with any purpose.
author: Dan Hill

text: Seemingly sampling miniscule sections from vinyl recordings (as far as I can tell), there are no melodic quotes from the composer's work.
author: Dan Hill

text: Shenzhou is a deeply ambient album, barely containing any traditional melody at all (quoted or not).
author: Dan Hill

text: There is a sense of Debussy's liquid, impressionistic approach in the timbre and harmony, but as with other Biosphere recordings, the overwhelming mood is Northern Scandinavian, rather than Javanese Gamelan (In "Ocean of Sound", Janssen said, "I feel at my most creative when the sun is gone" - two or three months of the year in Tromso, his home town).
author: Dan Hill

text: This results in an intriguingly mismatched experiment which works on its own terms, but ultimately raises as many questions as answers.
author: Dan Hill

text: Jenssen deals in fragments, looped and smeared across the mix, but more smoothly integrated, working in waves, pulses, and electrical fields rather than splashes of paint - a modern take on delicate, abstract expression.
author: Dan Hill

text: Compared to other pre-eminent purveyors of ambient, say Susumu Yokota or Paul Schutze, Jenssen's music employs fewer dynamics, and there's little sense of an individual voice to provide contrast ; the entire album drifts past in an engaging diaphanous waltz, but without leaving much of a mark...Only on "A Path Leading To The High Grass" do we get a sense of percussion; and on "Bose Eisenstein Condensation", tumbling motes of piano provide a more clearly delineated sense of space within the music.
author: Dan Hill

text: Both catch the ear amidst the rest of the album's "tints".
author: Dan Hill

text: It's a lovely work and no mistake; a beautifully-crafted series of gently undulating backdrops and scenes which will appeal to most discerning listeners to contemporary music: classical, ambient, whatever.
author: Dan Hill

text: It's just ...
author: Dan Hill

text: if you draw from Debussy, you're raising the bar a bit.
author: Dan Hill

text: Try These: Hazard - Wind 310 - Downtown & Brooklyn Only The Caretaker - A Stairway to Stars
author: Dan Hill

text: It's hard not to feel a surge of deja vu when first listening to this latest waxing from the overlord of lounge lizards.
author: Chris Jones

text: Not a nostalgia for the old days but a warmth that comes from knowing that old heroes have still GOT IT.
author: Chris Jones

text: Now in his sixth decade the smouldering Geordie puts so many contemporaries to shame (Neil Young take note) with an album that grows richer with every listen.
author: Chris Jones

text: Even in Roxy Music's heyday Mr Ferry was cleverly carving out a solo niche for himself.
author: Chris Jones

text: Covers albums such as These Foolish Things and Another Time Another Place (you remember, the one with Bryan poised in a tuxedo by a Bel Air swimming pool a la Bogart, sealing his place as roue supreme) allowed him to plunder the past while throwing new light on old chestnuts.
author: Chris Jones

text: Frantic manages this trick particularly well with two songs by Dylan.
author: Chris Jones

text: The opener "It's All Over Now Baby Blue" is almost obscenely ballsy with BF's harmonica (a muscular sonic signifier throughout) slotting into the mix alongside Chris Spedding's magnificent guitar histrionics.
author: Chris Jones

text: With "Don't Think Twice" he somehow manages to turn Zimmerman into a fitting accompaniment to cocktail hour.
author: Chris Jones

text: Even more bizarre is his brilliant reconstruction of Leadbelly's murder ballad "Goodnight Irene" as a cajun lament.
author: Chris Jones

text: Who would have thought it?
author: Chris Jones

text: But this is no simple rehash of ancient ground.
author: Chris Jones

text: The new stuff outnumbers the old and there's no denying the quality on offer.
author: Chris Jones

text: One thing which always marked Ferry as more than just a well-dressed glam has-been (apart from his undeniable way with a tune) was his willingness to experiment and tracks like "Goddess of Love" with its skittering electronics and intimate whispers show that the creative heart is still beating strongly.
author: Chris Jones

text: Who else would preface a song like "Fool For Love" with Mary Nelson's sumptuous recital of "Ja Nun Hons Pris" (written by Richard Coeur De Lion, medieval trivia buffs)?
author: Chris Jones

text: It matters not one jot that old lags like Spedding, the great Paul Thompson and producer Rhett Davies are along for the ride.
author: Chris Jones

text: Ferry, by now, knows exactly what he wants and who can deliver it.
author: Chris Jones

text: With the nuts and bolts firmly in place he displays an ease and poise that men half his age strain to achieve.
author: Chris Jones

text: "San Simeon" even manages to mention cocktails without one hint of cliche.
author: Chris Jones

text: Most delightful however is the closing duet with Brian Eno, "I Thought".
author: Chris Jones

text: Reprising their collaboration on Mamouna this sums up the value of this whole album.
author: Chris Jones

text: Its (seemingly) childish simplicity, with cheap cha-cha beatbox rhythm and wobbly guitar, is both disarming and strangely poignant.
author: Chris Jones

text: It recalls the halcyon days of both men's early solo efforts and reminds us how only the true masters can make it look so easy.
author: Chris Jones

text: Indie guitarist solo albums are a rare thing.
author: Ian Wade

text: Seldom much cop, and often overlooked by journalists who are only interested in their previous incarnation and who have probably already sold their copy of the album.
author: Ian Wade

text: Stone Roser John Squire, ex-Smith Johnny Marr and still-Radiohead Jonny Greenwood are worthy of your attention.
author: Ian Wade

text: Greenwood's Bodysong soundtrack is a particularly good listen, maybe because he didn't sing on it.
author: Ian Wade

text: But, in a field of few, Graham Coxon's solo catalogue towers above them.
author: Ian Wade

text: Having released three albums prior to leaving Blur, this is Coxon's second release since going permanently solo.
author: Ian Wade

text: Though not without a few charms, it's fair to say his previous solo efforts only appealed to the most hardcore of Blur fans.
author: Ian Wade

text: His music swings schizophrenically from crackly folk odes recorded in a bucket to shouty bluegrass metal which sounds like it was recorded in a shed.
author: Ian Wade

text: Happiness In Magazines, however, is something of a relief.
author: Ian Wade

text: On the funky blues of "Hopeless Friend" and "Bottom Bunk" he sounds like your funny best mate.
author: Ian Wade

text: Other highlights include the punkin' buzz of opener "Spectacular" and the equally glorious radio-rawk of "Freakin' Out".
author: Ian Wade

text: While the cinematic "Are You Ready" sounds like The Shadows feat.
author: Ian Wade

text: Ennio Morricone and is a thing of genuine beauty.
author: Ian Wade

text: Nearly every tune is milkman-friendly hummable.
author: Ian Wade

text: The only exception being the daft comically angry hectoring of "People Of The Earth" which harks back to his solo past.
author: Ian Wade

text: A bit of a pop genius on the sly, Coxon claims that the songs pleaded with him to be recorded properly this time, and he's done them proud.
author: Ian Wade

text: Producer Stephen Street, the man who had a hand in the first five Blur albums, has done wonders here, reflecting a more upbeat and happier Coxon, making this a joy to listen to.
author: Ian Wade

text: Whatever his real reasons for leaving Blur, on Happiness In Magazines, Coxon has shown he most certainly doesn't ever need to go back.
author: Ian Wade

text: Japanese pianist Satoko Fujii is a busy woman, with 14 CDs under her belt in the last 5 years ranging from her Orchestra project to trios and duos with the likes of Mark Dresser, Mats Gustaffson and Taysuya Yoshida from avant rock outfit Ruins.
author: Peter Marsh

text: This is her second duet album with her husband, trumpeter Natsuki Tamura (maybe it's the only time they get to see each other).
author: Peter Marsh

text: Their last CD (on the estimable Leo label), How Many ?
author: Peter Marsh

text: was an intriguing release.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Like Arve Henriksen, Tamura's vocalised trumpet often resembled a shakuhachi (wooden Japanese flute) or (more fancifully) the gentle soughing of wind through trees.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Occasionally he would let loose a volley of fat, brassy tones or gurglings, while Fujii's piano wandered from delicate impressionistic colours through to knotty, dense clusters of notes or ominous low register rumblings.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Clouds offers more of the same, but with a less diffuse, more focussed aesthetic at work.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Each of the tracks is named after a different cloud type.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Appropriately, the opening "Cirrus" is a sparse, wispy essay with Tamura's bruised lyricism following the twists and turns of Fujii's piano, which travels from Paul Bley like restraint to pointillistic episodes of prepared piano percussives.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The 16 minute "Cumulonimbus" (the fat cotton wool ones, for the meteorogically challenged) pits grainy smears of trumpet over piano clunks, then opens out into a sumptuous dialogue between thoughtful, lovely chording and a full toned exursion from Tamura.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Eventually Fujii builds minimal, pulsing figure which open into a detailed solo of quiet joy, subsiding into abstract inside-the-piano scrapes, joined by Tamura's slap tongued percussives and hisses.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Like its subject matter, this is music that's forever on the move, morphing, dissolving and regrouping into new shapes.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Throughout the interplay is exquisite; Fujii and Tamura offer unsentimental beauty, space, silence and humour.
author: Peter Marsh

text: "Stratus" offers the duo's most impressionistic playing, while "Altocumulus" is a restless series of abstract miniatures.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Tamura alludes to players like Lester Bowie and Leo Smith, but sounds very little like either; he's a major (and pretty under-recorded) voice on the instrument.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Fujii is a superb colourist and a strong, sensitive partner.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Proof that improvised music can be emotionally engaging as well as ear tickling, Fujii and Tamura give us six clouds, all with a solid silver lining.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Worth your time.
author: Peter Marsh

text: 20 year old flamenco singer Estrella Morente is (quite literally in her native tongue) a star.
author: Peter Marsh

text: And a star with impeccable flamenco connections too; her father and musical mentor is legendary singer Enrique Morente, her accompanists include veteran guitarist Manolo Sanlucar as well as new flamenco stars Ketama, and to cap it all she's married to a matador.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Though Morente senior is famed for his crossover projects (his band Lagjarta Nick were named after a song by Bauhaus), My Songs and a Poem is very much in the tradition, free of electric instruments and studio tricks; some tracks were even recorded in a cave in Granada.
author: Peter Marsh

text: While on the opening "Cockles" Morente's vocal gymnastics are suffused with the emotive Gypsy howl that's become the norm on recent flamenco, in the main her singing adopts the subtle lilt of 1940s cantadores like the late Pastora Pavon.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Even at her most incantory, as on "Pilgrims", there's a sweet rasp to her voice that catches the ear, and an incredible rhythmic confidence that belies her age.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Though there's a nod to recent flamenco fusions on "Moguer" (written by Morente senior) with a jazzy, restrained ballad that brings out an even more lyrical side to Estrella's vocal conception, much of the music here seems to come straight from the wellspring of flamenco tradition, full of passion, grace and fire.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The ancient sounding "Alcazaba" (in praise of the Alhambra Palace) is heart stoppingly lovely, with a measured, yearning accompaniment from Sanlucar (previously guitarist for Pavon).
author: Peter Marsh

text: Probably the best song about a building you'll hear all year.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Throughout the various guitarists are unobtrusive, sensitive but capable of dazzling improvisational fire and a rhythmic sensibility that rivals Indian music in its complexity and strangeness (to Western ears); Morente is there to respond to anything thrown at her and vice versa.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Their dialectic is a reminder that flamenco is foremost an improvisational music, and in the hands of Morente and her collaborators remains a living, breathing tradition.
author: Peter Marsh

text: A beautifully assured and compelling debut.
author: Peter Marsh

text: In a world obsessed with the minutiae of D-list 'stars' and their tragi-comic dysfunctionalism, who needs another autobiographical album whinging about the hardships of success?
author: Chris Jones

text: Luckily Mike Skinner, the man who is The Streets, has a more perceptive and honest eye than most.
author: Chris Jones

text: Filled with tales of self-loathing, drug abuse and the creative wasteland of fame, you might expect *The Hardest Way...
author: Chris Jones

text: *to be devoid of laughs.
author: Chris Jones

text: Not a chance; songs like "When You Wasn't Famous" (don't snort coke in front of the camera phones, starlets!), and "Memento Mori" (the best retail therapy song, ever) show Mike can still find comedy among the chaos.
author: Chris Jones

text: His serious points - particularly on "Two Nations" and "Never Went To Church" - seem a little at odds with the very (self-imposed) disposable nature of his work, and his Eminem-style use of nursery rhyme tunes can pall over a whole album.
author: Chris Jones

text: Yet at 39 minutes Skinner's already learned that less is more.
author: Chris Jones

text: And that honesty is still the best policy in the fight against mediocrity.
author: Chris Jones

text: This compilation serves as a comprehensive musical history lesson into the foundation of dancehall music.
author: Darren 'Shaq-D' Springer

text: The release of this double whammy collection could not be better timed as it coincides with Jamaica celebrating its 40th Independence.
author: Darren 'Shaq-D' Springer

text: For anyone who started listening and collecting dancehall music from the late eighties to the present time, this album will surely fill some of the missing gaps you may have in your collection, the only problem will be convincing your peers that you have the original vinyl, because the standard crackles have been removed from the tracks.
author: Darren 'Shaq-D' Springer

text: Featured on this album we have greats like Barrington Levy, John Holt, Clint Eastwood and Nicodemus to name a few.
author: Darren 'Shaq-D' Springer

text: Highlights include General Echo's "Bathroom Sex", in which he uses a lyrical comedy style, and Ranking Dread's 1981 No 1 classic smash, "Fattie Boom Boom".
author: Darren 'Shaq-D' Springer

text: To all of you dancehall sound clash fans; we have the original "Gunman" by legendary Michael Prophet.
author: Darren 'Shaq-D' Springer

text: Gunman has been cut on special by all of the biggest sounds on the planet and used to win clashes from year to year, some specials have paired Michael with the likes of Beenie Man and Bounty Killer, which increases the chances of winning the sound clashes (i.e.

text: An office favourite around here for almost a month now, this new full length from Ulrich Schnauss hasn't left our stereo pretty much since since the day it arrived, and with good reason.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Infusing the emotional intensity of classical compositions from J.S.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Bach or Ludwig Van Beethoven with the electronic warmth of Richard James or Global Communication's more ambient work, Ulrich Schnauss has created a bit of a minor masterpiece with this six track album of unprecedented beauty.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Hailing from Berlin, this 24 year old composer has been releasing a few records here and there over the past few years.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Pushing out drum and bass under the names of Ethereal 77 and View To The Future, his output so far has been notable enough, but hindsight really can't really prepare you for the lushness of this new release.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Simply put: Far Away Trains Passing By is elegant, simple and beautifully refined ambient techno.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: These melodies aim straight for the heart and capture it, embracing you in a dance of pure bliss that will have you spinning around the room like a whirling dervish.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: One of the things that's so immediate is that Schnauss's creations ebb and flow without a single glitch or DSP effect in sight.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: The production here harkens back to the pre-glitch days of IDM or experimental electronica; a time when people composed tracks rather than simply tweaked them.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Still - it would be folly to say that this is dancefloor friendy.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: The beats here are pretty thin on the ground, and while they offer just enough quantization and swing to give just the right amount of momentum, they simply pale in comparison to the lush orchestrations and tonality of the melodies.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Schnauss it seems, it simply incapable of writing ugly songs.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Our German friend may not have the catchiest or trendiest of names, but rest assured, if the man keeps pumping out albums like this, he may very well be crowned king of the IDM scene in 2002.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Quite frankly, this is one of the most stunningly beautiful releases of the year and now that I've finally got my review copy back from the greedy vultures here in the office, this baby is staying right where it belongs: In my office stereo.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: If only more musicians would be doing stuff like this, the world would certainly seem a much brighter place.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Without question, one of the most impressive releases we've heard in quite a while.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Over the past few years, Brad Mehldau's grandly titled Art of the Trio records have gained him a reputation as a thoughtful, lyrical pianist who (like Bill Evans) draws as much from classical tradition as jazz.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Largo is quite a different kettle of fish though, resulting from Mehldau's collaboration with producer Jon Brion, whose CV includes work for Fiona Apple and Aimee Mann among others.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Unused to spending much time on a record, Mehldau was shocked to discover he and Brion had 6 days in the studio.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Not much for the average rock album, but a lifetime for a realtime improviser.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Brion goes for the studio as instrument approach, treating the piano either physically or electronically and adding splashes of colour from horns, electronics and guitars using a cast of players including Mehldau's usual trio of Jorge Rossy and Larry Grenadier, as well as session vet Jim Keltner and Beck's bassist Justin Meldal-Jonson.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Mehldau more than rises to the challenge; on "Dropjes" and "Free Willie" (both studio jams edited and reconstructed Teo Macero style) he unleashes solo flights of sparkling brilliance, while Brion's treatments twist new sonorities from the Steinway.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Similarly, "You're Vibing Me" (featuring Mehldau on vibes) and "Alvarado" offer expansive, almost psychedelic takes on the piano trio format.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The opening "When It Rains" is simply beautiful, somewhere between Bill Evans and the wide open spaces of Bill Frisell's Americana.
author: Peter Marsh

text: At other times though, Mehldau appears a bit hemmed in; the lifeless funk thud of "Dusty McNugget" fails to inspire anyone much, while the grim sub metal antics of "Sabbath" go nowhere slowly.
author: Peter Marsh

text: If there's irony here, it's buried deep.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Similarly, the covers of "Dear Prudence" and "Mother Nature's Son" (here coupled with Jobim's "Wave") only begin to work once the tune is a distant memory.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Maybe there should be kind of legislation to stop jazzers touching Beatles tunes (maybe Kenneth Clarke could do it as a private member's bill).
author: Peter Marsh

text: That doesn't extend to Mehldau's rework of Radiohead's "Paranoid Android".
author: Peter Marsh

text: Mehldau's covered the Oxford prog existentialists before and here transforms the tune into a mini suite, opening with an extended episode of edgy gamelan funk before picking out the aching melody in Satie-esque fashion over a brooding backdrop of horns.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Lovely, though whether Radiohead fans will think so is a moot point.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Brion and Mehldau are certainly unafraid of experiment, and that can only be a good thing.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Even if occasionally the results are a curate's egg, it's one well worth tucking into.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Joe McPhee's childhood instrument was the trumpet (which he took up at the age of eight) but his earliest recordings in the late 1960's featured his work on tenor sax.
author: Bill Tilland

text: Over the years, McPhee has become adept on alto and soprano saxes, value trombone, flugelhorn, pocket trumpet, cornet, and various clarinets.
author: Bill Tilland

text: And the operative word is 'adept', as McPhee is highly fluent on all his instruments.
author: Bill Tilland

text: Even though his playing can wander far 'outside', and is at times replete with key clicks, multiphonics and other extended techniques, critics just as often have lauded McPhee for his gorgeous touch and tone.
author: Bill Tilland

text: This CD is a recording of a 1997 radio broadcast for WPKN, Bridgeport, Connecticut, consisting of duets between McPhee and Joe Giardullo.
author: Bill Tilland

text: It would be easy to make assumptions here, e.g.
author: Bill Tilland

text: four year old, low-budget jazz radio broadcast + small independent label = forgettable result.
author: Bill Tilland

text: But McPhee never gives less than his best, and Specific Gravity is yet another worthy addition to McPhee's splendid body of work.
author: Bill Tilland

text: McPhee plays alto clarinet, soprano sax, valve trombone and electronics, while Giardullo plays flute, bass clarinet, soprano sax and electronics.
author: Bill Tilland

text: It's not always easy to tell who is playing what, but the flute and trombone are giveaways, and it appears that McPhee's sound is spatially oriented to the right, while Giardullo is on the left.
author: Bill Tilland

text: The long opening track, "A Priori" is a bit of a showcase for the two musicians.
author: Bill Tilland

text: The piece starts with some electronic loops from Giardullo's soprano, together with a subtle electronic pulse, to which McPhee adds his valve trombone.
author: Bill Tilland

text: Giardullo moves from bass clarinet to a sweetly ethereal, electronically enhanced flute, while McPhee joins in with an equally lyrical alto clarinet.
author: Bill Tilland

text: The tranquility is slowly dispersed by some strident but passionate soprano blowing by McPhee , following this with some growling, multiphonic vocalizations on trombone, sounding for all the world like a one-man digeridoo duet.
author: Bill Tilland

text: This description of the music makes it sound fragmented and episodic, but it all flows together quite effortlessly and unselfconsciously.
author: Bill Tilland

text: With McPhee, it's the heady mixture of outside and inside, of experimentation and tradition, and of technique and imagination, which gives his music its character.
author: Bill Tilland

text: It's as if he's telling the listener -- "hey, open your ears....it's all music, and it's all good." The second shorter title piece is a vehicle for Giardullo, who displays an impressive circular breathing technique on bass clarinet, maintaining an ostinato pattern in the lower register while setting harmonic figures against it.
author: Bill Tilland

text: The third and fourth pieces reveal just how solidly McPhee is locked into the jazz tradition; the first is a breathtakingly poignant rendition of John Coltrane's "After the Rain," for two sopranos (this piece alone is worth the outlay for the CD), while the final selection, "Sienna," begins with Giardullo on flute, and then features a series of bluesy, swinging vamps from McPhee on trombone, which wouldn't be out of place on a Count Basie date.
author: Bill Tilland

text: Clearly, McPhee can do it all - and with style, wit, passion and grace.
author: Bill Tilland

text: Christmas is upon us once more and again we are flooded with a tide of Greatest Hits and Best Of's, some more dubious in their claims than others.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: Gabrielle's Greatest Hits collection 'Dreams Can Come True' does just what it says on the tin.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: Crammed with an impressive track record of 11 Top 10 singles (including 2 No.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: 1's) and a further 5 that landed comfortably in the Top 30; as the lady herself comments, "Not bad for a little girl from Hackney".
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: Since her '93 'Dreams' debut, Gabrielle has notched up an impressive portfolio of sophisticated and soulful pop, carving a niche for herself as an accessible pop diva.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: Her voice has always held a distinctive strength over many of her peers, the slightly nasal, unusual tone gives her a unique star quality that carries her through even her weaker songwriting moments.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: 'Dreams Can Come True' is a chronological journey through Gabrielle's career to date.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: Spanning four albums, this collection is an autobiography of her life over the past decade.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: She is an artist who is sincere and openly emotive in her lyrics.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: Combined with the radio-friendly sound that has made tracks like the self-fulfilling 'Rise', and the Gladys Knight sounding 'Give Me Just A little More Time' so familiar, Gabrielle's success lies in her audience's ability to relate to her simple tales of emotion.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: Although maybe too mushy for some, to the casual fan, by dispensing with the sometimes bland and uninspired filling of previous albums, 'Dreams Can Come True' provides the listener with the chance to hear the cream of Gabrielle's output.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: The highlight has to be the Bacharach cover of 'Walk on By' - Dionne Warwick version classic it's not, but still a respectable performance.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: Bringing us right up to date with the Bridget Jones' Diary endorsed 'Out Of Reach' and recent hit 'Don't need the Sun To Shine (to make me smile), this really is the ultimate collection for any fan.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: In 1993, Cassandra Wilson released Blue Light 'Til Dawn, the album that redefined her career and made her a commercial success.
author: John Eyles

text: Its blend of pop covers (Van Morrison, Joni Mitchell), delta blues and original compositions, combined with a stripped-down instrumentation, gave it a mass appeal rare in jazz.
author: John Eyles

text: The formula was repeated on 1995's New Moon Daughter with more risks (yes, "Last Train To Clarksville") and success.
author: John Eyles

text: It also led to Wilson getting flak from purists, unhappy that some of the songs were not worthy of a jazz artist.
author: John Eyles

text: (Pah!) We must count Wilson's last album - the Miles Davis tribute Travelling Miles - as a one-off special project, so Belly of the Sun is the third part of the trilogy.
author: John Eyles

text: This was originally intended to be an entirely blues-based record, and the recording was largely made in the train depot in Clarksdale, Mississippi, to achieve a suitable ambience.
author: John Eyles

text: Some of the most memorable tracks from those earlier Wilson albums are by Robert Johnson, and it's fair to say that she's effectively re-invented Johnson's music.
author: John Eyles

text: Her voice has a husky-toned lower register that's a perfect vehicle to convey its emotions and nuances, but also makes the blues sexier than you'd believe possible, (witness her 1993 version of "Come On In My Kitchen").
author: John Eyles

text: On the finished version of this album, though, there are only three blues tracks; an effective reading of Mississippi Fred McDowell's "You Gotta Move" (best known to many in The Rolling Stones version), a rather hurried, throwaway version of Johnson's "Hot Tamales" and an atmospheric "Darkness on the Delta" with solo accompaniment from the veteran Mississippi pianist Boogaloo Ames.
author: John Eyles

text: Instead of more blues, what we do get here is another eclectic selection, including "The Weight", "Wichita Lineman", and Dylan's "Shelter from the Storm.
author: John Eyles

text: Such well-known songs are often the first to grab attention on Wilson albums.
author: John Eyles

text: But experience has shown that her own compositions (of which there are four here) stand the test of time.
author: John Eyles

text: They are perfectly matched to her voice, she sings them with great personal feeling and intimacy, and they age well (an obvious candidate here is "Justice").
author: John Eyles

text: I hope that this album does complete the trilogy.
author: John Eyles

text: While it is good, and will satisfy Wilson's fans, it suggests that this format is getting mined to exhaustion.
author: John Eyles

text: Looking to the future, Wilson should build on the trilogy's strengths, maybe by making that all blues album, maybe by recording a songbook album (I'd nominate Van Morrison), or an album solely of her own compositions.
author: John Eyles

text: With her talent, the sky's the limit.
author: John Eyles

text: For now though, Belly of the Sun is good enough.
author: John Eyles

text: There's been an embarassment of riches for the hardcore John Martyn fan of late, and whaddya know, here's some more.
author: Peter Marsh

text: In Session contains all the songs our John recorded for the Bob Harris and John Peel shows between 1973 and 1978, and though some of these performances are available elsewhere, this is an essential purchase for the committed fan.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Though consistency was (and is) never one of Martyn's strong points, it would seem that he did make a bit more of an effort when he was in front of a BBC microphone, judging by this set of performances.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Most are solo; four tracks add the peerless double bass of Mr Danny Thompson, though annoyingly he's barely audible (what were the engineers thinking?).
author: Peter Marsh

text: Martyn's tendency to improvise means that even his most straightahead acoustic songs (like "May You Never" or "Spencer The Rover") have new life breathed into them every time he sings them.
author: Peter Marsh

text: From the 1973 sessions "I'd Rather be The Devil" and "Outside In" (both mysteriously retitled here) take things further out with some typically cosmic guitar explorations; you get the sense that at this point in Martyn's career, each performance was as much about self discovery as anything else.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The set closes with the glorious "Small Hours", which sounds like it was recorded yesterday afternoon rather than nearly 30 years ago.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Essential stuff from probably the most fruitful period in Martyn's career.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The summer's glut of media fuss over 'chill out' music being the new black and the coolest thing ever (hey, I saw that 30 page article on the art of chilling and that commercial hawking a compilation CD that's made of ice) can be attributed to the likes Groove Armada et al.
author: Andy Puleston

text: They have raised the profile of down tempo way above and beyond the computer bleeps and swishes with a mixture of astute sampling and great musicianship.
author: Andy Puleston

text: Come on, be honest - three albums down and a shed load of great tunes, they are all over it like a rash.
author: Andy Puleston

text: Confident enough in their own ideas, Groove Armada are a band that make merit through what they leave out of their music as opposed to how much they can cram in.
author: Andy Puleston

text: In short, with Andy Cato and Tom Finlay, less is more.
author: Andy Puleston

text: Subtle instrumentation and smooth production keep Goodbye Night (Hello Nightclub) engrossing, regardless of whether they're aiming for the dance floor or the sofa.
author: Andy Puleston

text: The first single "Super Stylin'" is reggae-house at it's finest.
author: Andy Puleston

text: So what if it's been done before?
author: Andy Puleston

text: The hook and vocals are fantastic and let's face it any track whose bass line is big enough to bowl over a bungalow has got to be worth the gamble with the speaker cones.
author: Andy Puleston

text: The four to the floor chunk of "Fogma" and "Healing" is yet further demonstration that Groove Armada can cut it 'up' as well as 'down'.
author: Andy Puleston

text: The breaks and old skool electro funk of "Raisin' The Stakes" is proof positive of how well they can lend themselves to a sound that is largely being forged by prominent others.
author: Andy Puleston

text: For obvious reasons the furore over UK hip hop seldom includes Groove Armada yet whilst the likes of Mark B and Blade, Skitz and Roots Manuva fly the flag, the Armada have made some great breakbeats.
author: Andy Puleston

text: Whilst "Sun Toucher" featuring the gifted Jeru Tha Damaja, "Raisin The Stakes" and "Whatever Whenever" from Vertigo have featured US based artist, musically their approach and contribution should not be ignored.
author: Andy Puleston

text: Like the others before it, this record eases in and out of styles gracefully.
author: Andy Puleston

text: The heartfelt string arrangements of "Edge Hill" take the vibe of "At The River" and sail it down stream only for it to be picked up by Andy's cheeky trombone parp and a brief reprise of one of Vertigo's finest moments and a firm reminder that Groove Armada have done it again.
author: Andy Puleston

text: Sometimes perfection is a real bore.
author: Chris Jones

text: In an age where karaoke puppets and corporate niche marketing have rubbed any rough edges from our aural diet, it comes as quite a shock to hear stuff like this.
author: Chris Jones

text: For, while most of this material stems from a timeframe and genre that prided itself on its musical ability, it's by no means a smooth and unchallenging ride.
author: Chris Jones

text: Even Richard Madeley's favourite band, the Moody Blues (who provide the title track to this anthology) sound edgy and mysterious to modern ears.
author: Chris Jones

text: And yet it all fell under the banner of the mighty Decca label.
author: Chris Jones

text: By late 1967 something was happening, and (to paraphrase Dylan) it wasn't just Mr Jones who didn't know what it was.
author: Chris Jones

text: Major labels were faced by an audience who now wanted something considerably more challenging than three minutes of the Hollies singing about bus stops.
author: Chris Jones

text: Those pesky Beatles had opened Pandora's musical box and it wasn't unreasonable to ask for at least three time signature changes in the space of one song.
author: Chris Jones

text: Lyrics about women selling tea!
author: Chris Jones

text: Scary chord changes!
author: Chris Jones

text: Folk music played on electrical instruments!
author: Chris Jones

text: Blues played backwards!
author: Chris Jones

text: It was all legal tender in them days and Decca wanted a piece of the action.
author: Chris Jones

text: Signing acts left, right and centre to their subsidiary, Deram, the label inadvertently set loose some of the strangest music known to man.
author: Chris Jones

text: It's all here...
author: Chris Jones

text: To be fair most of this music's fascination lies in its position somewhere between psychedelia and progressive.
author: Chris Jones

text: It's some evolutionary stop-gap, like a musical sabre-toothed mongoose and, on the whole, clumsy and not a little pretentious.
author: Chris Jones

text: Let's face it, there's a reason why you've probably never heard of Human Beast, Clark-Hutchinson or Aardvark.
author: Chris Jones

text: But for every Keef Hartley obscurity there's a lost gem waiting to blow your mind.
author: Chris Jones

text: Revel in the jazz exotica of the Johnny Almond Music Machine (featuring a fledgling Alan White).
author: Chris Jones

text: Be dazzled by the young Robert Fripp on Giles, Giles and Fripp's ''Suite No.1''.
author: Chris Jones

text: Realise why the folksy intricacy of Mellow Candle has won them cult status.
author: Chris Jones

text: To lump it all under prog or underground seems utterly pointless; Ten Years After's blues owes just as much to Wes Montgomery as to Freddie King, while the Canterbury sounds of Egg, Khan and Caravan juggle complexity with a self-deprecating homeliness (and how many modern bands even bother to sing with an English accent these days?).
author: Chris Jones

text: 3 CDs may seem daunting, yet such is the passion and vaulting ambition (9 times out of 10 falling charmingly short of ability) that you merely wish that major labels could still be this adventurous.
author: Chris Jones

text: Those days are long gone but, thanks to this fine compilation, far from forgotten.
author: Chris Jones

text: In a year in which many of the highlights have had more than a whiff of emperor's new clothes about them, it falls to Wilco to squeeze under the wire for an 'album of the year' contender.
author: Chris Jones

text: Kicking Television is glorious.
author: Chris Jones

text: Capping ten years of re-invention re-tooling and rehab, it's significant that Jeff Tweedy chose now to document his band's live sound; for newcomers Nels Cline and Pat Sansone make this the best Wilco yet.
author: Chris Jones

text: This double disc set, drawn from four nights in Chicago, shows a band deeply in love with the process of simply making music.
author: Chris Jones

text: Impressively stretching from innocent ballads to noise terror (often simultaneously as on ''Via Chicago'') The album's title is also strangely appropriate: Tweedy and Cline could easily be the new Verlaine and Lloyd.
author: Chris Jones

text: Alt country is no longer their playground; they make Wilco music and it's much, much better than watching television...
author: Chris Jones

text: Richard Lainhart was seduced by the possibilities of sound at an early age after hitting the low E string on a bass guitar.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Since then, with a background that encompasses electroacoustic composition and jazz vibraphone, he's evolved a singular vision as a composer, performer and engineer of darkly seductive minimalism; this 2 CD set compiles six pieces from 1975 to 1989.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The first three pieces here subject various sound sources to similar treatments; long tones are stacked upon one another, filtered and pitch shifted to provide rich, glassy drones.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The harmonies are loose, ambiguous; sometimes sunny, major tonalities peek through to be subverted by dense note clusters that flirt with dissonance.Though the music has the unlocked, semi improvisational quality of some of Brian Eno's or Robert Fripp's work, Lainhart's background suggests a more rigorous compositional approach rooted in the minimal dronescapes of Pauline Olivieros, Alvin Lucier or even Tony Conrad.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The results are very much Lainhart's own; "Bronze Cloud Disk" (for bowed tam tam) coaxes subtle harmonics into a glacial mass of gently shifting drones centred round a single note.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Listened to at low volume, it purrs away innocently enough; up close under headphones, it's a different animal, intense, metallic and a bit scary.
author: Peter Marsh

text: "Two Mirrors Face Another" uses the pure sinetones of bowed Japanese temple bells; again at volume it's a bit unforgiving, the tones almost too pure to engage.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The later title track and "Staring at the Moon" use an algorithmic sequencing package to generate semi improvisational soundscapes, joined by vibes on the latter piece.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Though the harmonic devices remain pretty much unchanged, the softer, recessed electronic textures and a greater use of silence offer a deep listening experience that rivals the best flotation tank.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The ear is invited to zoom in on small details, registering tiny perceptual changes, picking up on faint sonic vapour trails as they drift out of audibility.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The closing "Walking Slowly Backwards" is a quietly virtuoso performance for solo vibes; Lainhart draws long drones with the bow while coaxing gentle rolling swells with the mallets.
author: Peter Marsh

text: This piece has some of the crystalline beauty of Harold Budd's Pavilion of Dreams, shot through with a darker, chromatic hue.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Rewarding, engaging music that's worth your time.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Crazy name, crazy career...
author: Chris Jones

text: Mr Nichols is the product of a Wyoming, Missouri and Texas upbringing that involved a diet of Bluegrass festivals, Hank Williams, Merle Haggard, Charlie Rich and...err, Jimmy Cliff.
author: Chris Jones

text: If you've ever wondered why no one ever dares to combine southern soul, dub reggae, folk and country well, wonder no more, dear reader.
author: Chris Jones

text: Jeb's here to show you the way.
author: Chris Jones

text: Whereas Nichols' first two albums Lover's Knot and Just What Time It Is were reggae inflected concoctions, his approach has become more sparse and relaxed, as if in response to his new rural home in the Welsh mountains (the album was recorded in his barn - how country is that?).
author: Chris Jones

text: Easy Now is an album of acoustic instruments layered over vaguely hip hop beats and peppered with Al Green licks, each track as easy and laid back as a porch swing in August.
author: Chris Jones

text: A more relaxed and assured piece of work has yet to appear this year.
author: Chris Jones

text: As Nichols himself says, "We wanted to make a very immediate, emotional record, the kind of records that are very rarely made these days, non-cynical, no irony, nothing clever." This is why this album succeeds where other alt.
author: Chris Jones

text: Country mavericks like Lambchop often fail.
author: Chris Jones

text: Kurt Wagner's combination of Curtis Mayfield, Phil Spector and George Jones often comes across as a little too calculated and post-modern.
author: Chris Jones

text: Jeb's sunny use of everything from Willie Mitchell to Adrian Sherwood (with whom he shared a flat!) springs from a purer love and appreciation.
author: Chris Jones

text: These are not songs filled with surreal invocations but just paeans to love, life and the simple pleasures that make it all worthwhile ("Better Than Beautiful").
author: Chris Jones

text: Nichols wants to show us a life that, for all its imperfections, is full of small wonders.
author: Chris Jones

text: Tracks such as "Mostly Bittersweet" ("Aint got a roof, I got a starry crown' I'm not bitter, no, no, these days I'm mostly bittersweet") and the optimistically resigned story of a failed relationship, "Not The Only Man" can't help but fill the listener with wholesome warmth.
author: Chris Jones

text: The natural world makes a constantly recurring theme (listen to the birdsong on "A Little Love") and the fusion of classic soul stylings with Nichols' country twang of a voice never falters in its mission to move the heart as well as the feet.
author: Chris Jones

text: Easy Now won't set the world on fire, but it'll keep the homefires smouldering, and that's more than enough for now.
author: Chris Jones

text: In the late 60s, British jazz was in a state of flux, pulling itself into strange new shapes influenced by the U.S.
author: Peter Marsh

text: avant garde, European improvisation and rock and giving birth to bands such as Keith Tippett's Centipede, Nucleus, and Trevor Watts' Amalgam.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Alto saxophonist Watts was the driving force behind the legendary Spontaneous Music Ensemble, alongside drummer John Stevens.
author: Peter Marsh

text: While that outfit took post Coltrane jazz further out into the spiky landscapes of what was later to be called 'free improvisation', Amalgam operated in more melodic, less cerebral territory over their thirteen year history.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The 1969 debutPrayer for Peace originally appeared as a double album on the Transatlantic label (home to Brit folkies Pentangle) and featured the trio of Watts, bassist Jeff Clyne plus the now sadly departed Stevens on drums.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Though you might expect flat out full on free jazz blowout from such a line up, Prayer for Peace is for the most part a warm, soulful thing, full of space, light and shade.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Watts's fruity alto stylingscarry amagisterial weight derived from Coltrane coupled with some of Albert Ayler's quivering vibrato, though his preference for clear, unbroken melodic line recalls Ornette Coleman.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The absence of a chordal instrument isn't felt, partly due to Eddie Offord's lushly atmospheric recording but mostly due to Clyne, whose fat, melodic lines provide warm, unflagging support throughout.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The opening "Tales of Sadness" is a beautiful essay in controlled group improvisation; Clyne and Stevens opt for pulse rather than time under Watts's spare but lovely theme, with Steven's skittering snare decelerating and accelerating.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Eventually the rhythm section hits a splashy, restless groove as the alto heads off into abstracted, chopped up phrases.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Three takes of "Judy's Smile" show both the trio's differing approaches to the same material and their ability to generate a fearsome amount of swing.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Throughout there's a constant three way exchange - these guys have big ears, always on the listen.
author: Peter Marsh

text: For the closing title track Clyne is replaced by Barry Guy, whose warm, buzzing arco bass makes the ideal foil for Watts's plaintive Ayleresque melody.
author: Peter Marsh

text: To close, bass and alto circle each other, firing off high pitched harmonics into the ether.Lovely, empathic musicmaking from a fascinating era in Britjazz history.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Try These: Elton Dean/Alan Skidmore - El Skid Chris Mcgregor's Brotherhood of Breath - Travelling Somewhere Guy, Riley, Wachsmann - Improvisations 1977-79
author: Peter Marsh

text: Producer/percussionist Trilok Gurtu has spent the fifteen-odd years since the release of his first solo album Usfret exploring the potential of collaborations between musicians from the Indian, jazz and African traditions.
author: Neil Bennun

text: Over the years he's moved from an energetic avant-garde approach to make gentler, more accessible music.
author: Neil Bennun

text: Remembrance features musicians of the quality of the sarangi player Ustad Sultan Khan, the flute of Ronu Majumdar, the tabla player Zakir Hussain and the vocalist Shankar Mahadevan.
author: Neil Bennun

text: Trilok's mother Shoba Gurtu makes her first recording with her son since Usfret.
author: Neil Bennun

text: With this cast list, it's no surprise that the most successful pieces on Remembrance are those most grounded in the classical Indian tradition.
author: Neil Bennun

text: The album's opening track 'Brindavan Dance' is a potentially off-putting percussion and programming workout, dated and somewhat unattractive.
author: Neil Bennun

text: But on 'Expression Of Love' we hear Shankar Mahadevan and Shoba Gurtu combine over gentle santoor, Sultan Khan's shocking sarangi and Trilok's syncopated trap drums to powerful and atmospheric effect.
author: Neil Bennun

text: Although nothing at all like a traditional raga, except perhaps in the passages of impossibly fast extended harmony, it's simultaneously forward-looking and rooted in tradition, combining an unusual arrangement, sophisticated production and extraordinary musicianship.
author: Neil Bennun

text: 'Witness to Marriage' follows, with an affecting Bollywood string arrangement and African vocal sample building into something of an epic of insistent funk and north Indian percussion.
author: Neil Bennun

text: The light, but enchanting 'Our Heritage' showcases Majumdar's flute.
author: Neil Bennun

text: Trilok syncopates trap drums beneath the flute and a rolling synthesiser sequence, giving the tune his rhythmic trademark.
author: Neil Bennun

text: It's quickly obvious that the arrangements and the studiocraft here are grounded in pop territory, for all the album's glorious musicianship.
author: Neil Bennun

text: 'Greetings', where Zakir Hussain does his 10,000-fingered tabla thing over synth bass and distracting sequenced synthesiser, exemplifies this.
author: Neil Bennun

text: Where Remembrance really comes to life, as it does on 'Evening In India', simply harmonium, vocal and percussion, it's really quite splendid.
author: Neil Bennun

author: Neil Bennun

text: I didnt want to say it but there it is.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: After waiting what seems like ages after Richards previous work of Miami-bass meets Depeche Mode on acid genius, Windowlicker, we have finally been able to get our greedy hands on some new Aphex Twin material.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: So whats it like?
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Well, Druqks sounds exactly like a mix tape made from various unreleased Caustic Window, Richard D.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: James and Ambient Works 2 sessions with a few new John Cage-esque pieces of minimal piano thrown in for good measure.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Therein lies the problem, you see, as there is very little new and or overly exciting on this record.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: True, there are some amazing moments - Mt Saint Michel + Saint Michaels Mount is inspired, but then again, the first two minutes could easily just have been released on the last Squarepusher CD.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: 56 Cymru Beats again, is technically impressive - but again could have easily been released in 1994.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Being nostalgic is one thing but was that Stakker Humanoid sample really necessary...again?
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Druqks simply copies and pastes its loops and ideas from previous releases and rehashes them into something weve heard a million times before, albeit in a slightly different sequence.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: It isnt until we come to disc two that we see some of the more interesting material come to light.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Here we find treated pianos and bells submerged in an 8 voice chorus but just as it starts to draw you in, it stops.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: It seems like hes run out of ideas a minute and a half into it and has to revert to remixing his old hardcore tracks to get the momentum flowing again.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Its not until the last track Nanou 2 that we begin to hear James true colours come out and see what kind of mind blowing beauty hes capable of creating.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: I think Druqks probably would have worked better as two separate releases with a lot more time and effort put into it.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Dont get me wrong, I love Richard's work as much as the next guy, but for the all too brief moments of joy and beauty on this release, there is still far too much laziness for the truly awe-inspiring work to shine through.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: He's still on top...but for how much longer remains to be seen.
author: Olli Siebelt
