text: One can only imagine Mike's chagrin at performing Robert's early, full vocal version of the erotic song, "Instant Pussy".
author: Chris Jones

text: However, this is music of a wholly original hue.
author: Chris Jones

text: As an overview of a band rapidly expanding its horizons (and line-up, as we get the full seven-piece with brass section stuff as well) it's well-nigh unbeatable.
author: Chris Jones

text: Beginners may well be scared by the intricacies and oddly emotionless explorations contained herein.
author: Chris Jones

text: But perseverance is recommended.
author: Chris Jones

text: You won't be sorry...
author: Chris Jones

text: Without being too elitist about it, when the name of Andrew Lloyd Webber crops up anywhere near a project it's a fairly safe bet that its going to be a crowd-pleasingly anodyne collection of saccharine-sweet tunes; i.e.
author: Chris Jones

text: not really too challenging.
author: Chris Jones

text: The man may have single-handedly saved the West End with his string of tourist trapping musical fripperies but hey, money isn't everything.
author: Chris Jones

text: If you caught the recent furore surrounding the premiere of Bombay Dreams you may have been fooled into thinking that this is ALW's project alone.
author: Chris Jones

text: So it comes as a pleasant surprise when it turns out that the music was, in fact, written by classically-trained musical polymath A R Rahman.
author: Chris Jones

text: Until you actually hear it however...
author: Chris Jones

text: Based on Meera Syal's book of the same name and with lyrics written by Don Black, Bombay Dreams seems hell-bent on transferring Mr Lloyd Webbers formula to the sphere of world music.
author: Chris Jones

text: Quite obviously, a soundtrack album devoid of the stunning dance routines and cod-Bollywood stage sets that convey the story is bound to be somewhat contextually adrift, but in this case the gap could be measured in light years.
author: Chris Jones

text: At least with Rodgers and Hammerstein or Leonard Bernstein the songs were strong enough to stand alone.
author: Chris Jones

text: Rahman's string arrangements are sumptuously Asiatic, to be sure, and the production fuses east with west in often seamlessly post-modern fashion.
author: Chris Jones

text: Breakbeats meet pounding drums.
author: Chris Jones

text: Sweeping string sections underpin bubbling synths and at times on songs such as "Ooh La La" (top title, by the way) the sensuous mix becomes almost exotic enough to fool the listener.
author: Chris Jones

text: Yet, this being a musical, these soundscapes cannot come without vocals.
author: Chris Jones

text: Bolted onto the sparkling music are performances that never seem to know to which continent they belong.
author: Chris Jones

text: Stage school karaoke clashes with bhangra and the results are not pretty.
author: Chris Jones

text: Maybe it's because they have to deliver lyrics that sometimes defy description.
author: Chris Jones

text: "Contradictions, city of extremes, anything is possible in Bombay dreams.
author: Chris Jones

text: Some live and die in debt, others making millions on the internet." No, really...
author: Chris Jones

text: Worst offender here is the single sung by star Preeya Kalidas, "Shakalaka Baby".
author: Chris Jones

text: In a shameless attempt to appeal to the supposed 30 second attention of under 25s a vaguely garage rhythm accompanies pearls of wisdom such as: "Saw your face and the damage was done, you weaved (sic) a spell that took me over.
author: Chris Jones

text: I found a bolt right out of the sun, I'd love to send it supernova".
author: Chris Jones

text: And so it goes.
author: Chris Jones

text: The real disappointment is that someone with as much talent as Rahman seemed unable to break the free of his producer's spell and produce something that really did translate the glamour of Bollywood onto a West End stage.
author: Chris Jones

text: In fact a vast amount of talent seems to have been wasted in giving us just another one for the tourists.
author: Chris Jones

text: For a band renowned for creating classic clubbing anthems ("Insomnia", "God Is A DJ", "Salva Mea" and "Take The Long Way Home"), Faithless are a band who have suffered from the 'mixed bag' syndrome when it comes to writing albums.
author: Jack Smith

text: Their long players,with the exception of Reverence,have never quite lived up to the genius of their house hits.
author: Jack Smith

text: However, the fourth album No Roots, manages to go that one step further and gather song writing, gravitas and production under the same roof.
author: Jack Smith

text: Hit single "Mass Destruction" is a fine example of this as Maxi Jazz chooses to hit us with the highly-charged lyrics: "Whether long range weapon or suicide bomb a wicked mind is a weapon of mass destruction".
author: Jack Smith

text: This catchy, sign-o-the-times anthemembodies the mood of the whole album as the band combine ambient beats with a self-assessing philosophical perspective on the world today.
author: Jack Smith

text: As ever,Rollo and co.have made a concerted effort to expand the dance boundaries.
author: Jack Smith

text: This time they have done it by attempting to ensure each track spills over into the next.
author: Jack Smith

text: "I Want More: Part 1 and 2" are juxtaposed superbly, with the former oozing affecting eloquence while the second half morphs into the album's tub thumping dance anthem.
author: Jack Smith

text: The songs here are short and tightly focussed and thankfully, we are spared the drawn out monotonous melodies that often befall the progressive house genre.
author: Jack Smith

text: The fact that there are 15 songs on this record means the level of dynamism and interest is intact which, given that the entire album is in the key of C, is remarkable!
author: Jack Smith

text: The title track is the pick of the bunch with Dido's angelic tones and Maxi'sspoken wordrolling into a perfect combination.
author: Jack Smith

text: The song reflects the sad beauty that made "One Step Too Far" such a strong track.
author: Jack Smith

text: It also makes you wonder why Dido doesn't stick to what she's good at, singing dance anthems instead of hollow love songs for housewives.
author: Jack Smith

text: Whilst depressing at times it is a clear that the band, like so few others in dance music have a conscience and the intelligence to inject some meaning into their music.
author: Jack Smith

text: This, in the end, is the record's greatest strength.
author: Jack Smith

text: In an age where political descent in the world of commercial music is akin to career suicide Faithless should be applauded for their conviction.
author: Jack Smith

text: After years and YEARS of legal wrangling and bad blood the first professional recordings made by a spotty bunch of Shepherds Bush mods, originally called the High Numbers, get the release they deserve.
author: Chris Jones

text: Producer Shel Talmy, in the extensive sleeve notes, still sounds as thrilled to be talking about this legendary debut as he must have been the first time he walked into that church hall to watch the newly re-christened Who rehearse in 1965.
author: Chris Jones

text: At last those Talmy masters see the light of day and a vital piece of rock's jigsaw has been restored: in meatier, beatier, bigger and yes, bouncier digital stereo.
author: Chris Jones

text: With an entire extra disc of A-sides, instrumental/A Capella versions, EP tracks, B-sides and mono mixes you get the entire picture of a cocky and (in the songwriter's case) irascible bunch of young turks determined to be the centre of attention.
author: Chris Jones

text: What made this identikit R'n'B combo more interesting than most was the fact that the aforementioned scribe had a compellingly maudlin and detached view of the mechanised mating game played by his peer group.
author: Chris Jones

text: Songs like ''The Kids Are Alright'' - with its defeated realisation that the author can't, or won't keep up with the peer pressure, even if it means losing the girl, push Daltrey's already mature vocals to new levels of expression.
author: Chris Jones

text: ''A Legal Matter'' refuses to get tied down in domesticity; it's just too damn young.
author: Chris Jones

text: ''I Can't Explain'''s just got all confused about those funny feelings it's having, especially when it's around girls.
author: Chris Jones

text: Even ''My Generation'' with its still unbelievably irresistible explosion out of your speakers has its braggadocio undermined by the singer's stuttered delivery.
author: Chris Jones

text: LikeLennon, Ray Davies and later, Syd Barrett, being an integral part of the 60s also meant being able to see through the gloss of swingin' London.
author: Chris Jones

text: But enough about Townshend and Daltrey: what of the other half?
author: Chris Jones

text: Sadly the departed portion of the group was more than equal to the task of taking the lead.
author: Chris Jones

text: How many classic singles can you name with a bass solo taking the place of the guitar?
author: Chris Jones

text: Entwistle the Ox's bass is indeed bovine in its presence and strength while Moon's drums remain hyperactive but drop-dead precise at all times (listen to his time-keeping on the instrumental version of the title track).
author: Chris Jones

text: It only makes you miss them more.
author: Chris Jones

text: The covers draw on Daltrey's good taste by sticking close to the James Brown/West London R'n'B scene axis.
author: Chris Jones

text: ''Please, Please'' is especially convincing though ''Shout And Shimmy'' with its hilarious mock 'shindig' crowd (Townshend hopelessly heckling with ''yeah man, gimme some more'') makes Lulu look hard.
author: Chris Jones

text: Thousands of words have been expended over the years on why this has to rate as one of the best debut albums of all time.
author: Chris Jones

text: Some go even further by declaring it to be the ONE.
author: Chris Jones

text: To someone who joined the ride a decade too late to hear it the first time round, it still sounds like one of the most vital and important reasons to love rock 'n' roll.
author: Chris Jones

text: Intelligent but naive, flawed and yet perfect - they're still talkin' 'bout your generation.
author: Chris Jones

text: Time to listen again...
author: Chris Jones

text: Peter Gabriel is one of the greatest soul singers that the UK never produced.
author: Chris Jones

text: Much has been written about his leaving the safety of that most English of institutions, Genesis; about his bankruptcy in the name of world music; his championing of the anti-apartheid movement.
author: Chris Jones

text: But why doesn't anyone mention the voice?
author: Chris Jones

text: To listen to this remastered collection that charts the first 12 years of his solo career you're struck by the sheer emotive soulfulness of the larynx, and from one still young.
author: Chris Jones

text: It's easy to forget that, in 1977 when his first album was released, he was only 26, despite being thought of at the time as some kind of fossil by the burgeoning punk scene.
author: Chris Jones

text: Shaking The Tree confirms two distinct facts.
author: Chris Jones

text: One: On a good day Gabriel was a really good singles artist (this album is chock full of great ditties), and two: for an artist intent on breaking new ground he became as rooted to the eighties as Duran Duran.
author: Chris Jones

text: The career path has been erratic.
author: Chris Jones

text: The first album, produced by Bob Ezrin came with an odd sheen of American AOR; the second album (supposedly part of Robert Fripp's MOR trilogy and not even represented here) was just plain odd.
author: Chris Jones

text: By album number three he began to hit pay dirt, both commercially and artistically.
author: Chris Jones

text: "Games Without Frontiers" and "Biko" still sound great, though "Family Snapshot" suffers from too much cod psychology (parental divorce led Lee Harvey Oswald to rub out JFK).
author: Chris Jones

text: By the following year's 4 he was trying too hard.
author: Chris Jones

text: Just listen to the rather naff synth stabs and over-produced drums on "Shock The Monkey".
author: Chris Jones

text: Tracks from the really big follow-up So have aged gracefully due in no small part to the aforementioned voice.
author: Chris Jones

text: "Don't Give Up" could so easily have seemed a mawkish attempt at heart-string pulling were it not for the superbly impassioned delivery from Gabriel (for a demonstration of how not to do it try Willie Nelson and Sinead O'Connor's attempt).
author: Chris Jones

text: "Big Time" and "Sledgehammer" are funny, funky standards his throat was surely designed for, and "Mercy Street" still has the power to reduce this reviewer to tears.
author: Chris Jones

text: Gabriel's one abiding fault was his reluctance to stand still long enough to capitalise on such strengths, but this is still a timely reminder of the power of the voice.
author: Chris Jones

text: A plain white cover with black writing contains a CD with eight numbered (but unnamed) tracks ranging between 1:04 and 10:05 in length.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Tiny clicks, almost not there, precede and then accompany acoustic piano chords sounded regularly until they become almost hypnotic.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Small changes maintain engagement.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: (Thoughts on first listening: there's nothing there, just obvious things: what could possibly be interesting about this music?) Simple elements - strummed acoustic guitar, muffled beatbox, acoustic piano, organ, occasional electronics - are arranged to create an elegant anonymity which allows the listener to listen in their own way.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: (Thoughts on second listening: melodies begin to blossom, details emerge, warm sunlight floods a pale room.) There is something approaching silence in this music: the implication of negative space above and around each piece.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Some tracks hover between songform and ambience, at times the balance tips toward the latter.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Throughout there is a sparing, subtle, opaque quality to the music.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Diverse feelings are evoked by employing limited materials organised into minimal structures.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Norihide appears at times intent on expressing sentiment with as great a clarity as possible, while at one and the same time providing a clear, uncluttered space for its contemplation.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: (Thoughts on third listening: listening to this out loud in a room is best, not in headphones -that way the music inhabits the environment, it creates a space in your soul).
author: Colin Buttimer

text: I am grateful for this luminous music.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: What a long strange trip it's been for the world's favourite android.
author: Chris Jones

text: For a brief span the world belonged to Gary Numan.
author: Chris Jones

text: Then, as the alienated electronic wastelands of Numanoid imagination fell from favour, Gary found himself floundering with little more than a pilot's license and a small but fiercely loyal fan base to support him.
author: Chris Jones

text: Nowadays the hard times are well and truly over and he has a much larger and still intensely loyal legion of metal/goth/industrial fans.
author: Chris Jones

text: What's more he can now count among them such credible luminaries as Beck, Marilyn Manson, Liam Howlett and Damon Albarn and his back catalogue (in sample form) is now helping other acts such as Basement Jaxx, Armand Van Helden and the Sugababes achieve their own chart goals.
author: Chris Jones

text: Let's face it, Electroclash and bootleg culture is about as hip as you can get in 2002.
author: Chris Jones

text: Who'd have thought it?
author: Chris Jones

text: It is, however, important to note that this new found credibility is not necessarily the most important thing on Gary's mind.
author: Chris Jones

text: Many times he has stated his desire to move on, and it's the ability to continue creating music that speaks to a newer, younger audience that's paramount.
author: Chris Jones

text: At least half of this collection does exactly that.
author: Chris Jones

text: If ever there was a career of two halves this is it, though both have their merits.
author: Chris Jones

text: Firstly this is a 'best of' not a hits collection and being assembled by a fan of Numan's it gives a more balanced view than the usual record company bandwagon-jumping.
author: Chris Jones

text: Tracks are not chronological but sequenced thoughtfully to allow a sense of Numan the complete artist and while new layers of technology and sophistication now layer his compositions there emerges an odd continuity.
author: Chris Jones

text: Admittedly lyrics have become more assured with experience; compare the bleak sci fi musings of "Are 'Friends' Electric?" or "Remember, I Was Vapour" with the darker and quasi-religious strain running through "My Jesus" and "Dominion Day".
author: Chris Jones

text: Yet the gradual reinvention of Numan as industrial father-figure to Trent Reznor and his ilk has done nothing to remove the essential Numanoid quality of his best work.
author: Chris Jones

text: Instead, he's merely removed the more derivative strains of his early work ("Complex" is pure Eno, while ""She's Got Claws", one of the few examples of Gary in decline, is akin to Japan meeting Bowie in a new romantic karaoke bar) and arrived at a musical landscape that is, most assuredly, 100 percent Numan.
author: Chris Jones

text: Despite his adoption by Kerrang!
author: Chris Jones

text: readers, Gary's music still retains a canny eye for a brooding synth riff ("Pure") and the voice has lost its young plaintive edge to become a much more emotive tool.
author: Chris Jones

text: Witness the improved reworkings of "My Shadow In Vain" and "Everyday I Die".
author: Chris Jones

text: With a new album due next year, this new, improved model of Numan seems intent on building even further on his second coming and paying no lip service whatsoever to paltry nostalgia.
author: Chris Jones

text: It may not be everyone's cup of motor oil, but such dogged individuality deserves to prosper long into the 21st century.
author: Chris Jones

text: Manics fans are more likely than most to morosely ask, "What's the point?" Over two decades they have looked to Manics albums for answers, or at least refinements on the question.
author: Daniel Pike

text: Now, a Best Of compilation and the question is turned upon the release itself.
author: Daniel Pike

text: Just what is the point?
author: Daniel Pike

text: Two possible motivations: to spread the music and message of six albums to a wider audience; to exploit commercial profitability.
author: Daniel Pike

text: The integrity of the first motivation appears shaky.
author: Daniel Pike

text: You see, Forever Delayed is dominated by the Manics most popular, already well known, MOR output.
author: Daniel Pike

text: But the Manics have political consciousness!
author: Daniel Pike

text: Surely cash cow milking can't be their motive?
author: Daniel Pike

text: Yes, it always seems to jar that anti-capitalist posturing can sell so well.
author: Daniel Pike

text: The album's keystones are the hits of the Everything Must Go and This My Truth...
author: Daniel Pike

text: era ('A Design For Life', 'Australia', 'Kevin Carter', 'If You Tolerate This'...).
author: Daniel Pike

text: The complementary free new tracks, 'There By The Grace Of God' and 'Door To The River', continue in the Manics Lite vein.
author: Daniel Pike

text: Soft rock anthemic guitar epics from the early albums ('La Tristesse Durera', 'From Despair To Where', 'Little Baby Nothing') and a couple of upbeat punky numbers ('You Love Us', 'Motown Junk') complete the palette.
author: Daniel Pike

text: All safe stuff.
author: Daniel Pike

text: Only one track, 'Faster', is taken from the stark, harrowing The Holy Bible - the only Manics album to truly stretch the rock paradigm.
author: Daniel Pike

text: That said, anyone who has witnessed the pub-emptying impact of songs with the bleak solemnity of The Holy Bible's 'The Intense Humming Of Evil' will perhaps understand, if not forgive, this compilation's timidity.
author: Daniel Pike

text: There is nothing here for the archetypal Manics fan, except perhaps the excellent, rare, and poignant, cover of 'Suicide Is Painless'.
author: Daniel Pike

text: For others, if you like to get your rock soft and your political protestations abstract or mute, you'll find Forever Delayed quite painless too.
author: Daniel Pike

text: Firstly - it is hard, of course, to approach any new product from the estimable Macca without making reference to his new main squeeze (one track is called "Heather" for goodness sake, and she gets a name check in the sleeve notes) and herein lies the problem.
author: Chris Jones

text: An awful lot of this, Sir P's 28th album or so, is devoted to the transition between old and new loves, and when folk fret about the proper amount of time spent since Linda's demise and his renewed passion, it may have more to do with how it actually affects his output rather than whether it offends our sense of propriety.
author: Chris Jones

text: Nobody would deny the great man a little company, but there's nothing fires a great songwriter more than a touch of misery.
author: Chris Jones

text: The fact is that he sounds so, well, jolly contented, and perhaps a bit of lonely yearning would have made the material a little more challenging and rewarding.
author: Chris Jones

text: Let's face it, we haven't really had the chance to listen to a lonely Paul McCartney since about 1965.
author: Chris Jones

text: Considered by afficianados as the third part of a trilogy to mark the end of his life with the world's most famous vegetarian, this album is, by no means, pointless, overly sentimental or even dated.
author: Chris Jones

text: By using a bunch of fresh young American musicians and allowing some of the material to stretch out into more experimental jamming territory ("Spinning On An Axis" and the 10 minute plus "Rinse The Raindrops"), Mr Thumbs-Aloft has injected a raw urgency into his sound which really does hark back to Band On The Run days.
author: Chris Jones

text: However, in attempting to keep his sound as contemporary as possible he also falls into the strange trap of often sounding rather similar to the legions of those heavily influenced by him.
author: Chris Jones

text: Whisper it, but parts of this album sound like Crowded House.
author: Chris Jones

text: No one can deny the true worth of a man who, even when rich as Croesus and in no need of validation, still feels the need to create and comment on the world around him (the album finishes with "Freedom", his response to September 11th).
author: Chris Jones

text: Yet, McCartney's cardinal fault was always a tendency to slip into cosiness and songs such as "Magic" and "I Do" serve as little more than snapshots into his own happy little world, rather than resonate with the universality of his greatest moments - though let's hope he doesn't stop trying.
author: Chris Jones

text: Dabrye main man Tadd Mullinix has been wowing crowds and DJs alike in his hometown of Detroit for a little while now, gaining notoriety for not only his excellent ragga/jungle releases under his SK-1 moniker, but for his elegantly crafted modern electronica crafted under his own name.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Signing to the stylishly adventurous US based Ghostly International label about a year ago, this new release sees a new side project and a new sound for 2002.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: On this first of three planned releases under the name of Dabrye, Mullinix has abandoned his glitchy layered sound for a stripped down, funk fuelled ten track odyssey that will get you shaking your thing on your living room table before the first track is even over.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: We guarantee it.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Effortlessly blending instrumental hip-hop, 8-bit analogue and beds of ambient synths, One/Three bounces and swings along with all the swagger of a drunken pimp yet has all the grace and poise of a ballet dancer.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: From the gorgeously evolving saxophone sample on The Lish to the cut up vocoder loop on Smoking The Edge, you can read the influences here like you were reading off the ingredients list to making a fantastic gourmet cake: 80s electro, old-school hip-hop, abstract techno and of course good old fashioned Detroit funk.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Mullinix has brilliantly captured his influences and has thrown them into a kaleidoscopic playground of sound, where they all seem to be having a really good time together.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Interestingly enough, Mullinix says his main influences are people like Terry Riley, Gavin Bryars and Phillip Glass.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Perhaps its these influences (along with the fact that hes a classically trained cellist) that makes his beats so hauntingly gorgeous.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Either way - hes doing something right and I suspect well be hearing a lot more from the boy before the year is out.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: One/Three is easily one of our favourite releases of the year thus far on one of the most promising labels coming from the US today.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: If you like your beats with a dash of class, do not miss this.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: An essential purchase of the highest order.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Intensive Care opens with Robbie shouting, cocksure and desperate, "Here I stand victorious, the only man to make you come".
author: Lucy Davies

text: The sixth album from Williams is overwhelming in its pureness of personality.
author: Lucy Davies

text: It couldn't come from anyone else, dysfunctional, showy, telling stories about women he doesn't understand, relationships he can't function in, paranoia and isolation, all with a strangely positive and exciting spin.
author: Lucy Davies

text: Williams is putting more self reflection and understanding in his music than ever before, and he's a rich seam of material.
author: Lucy Davies

text: As you would expect, he's not short of the hi-budget surrounding support of cellos, gospel choirs, and brass.
author: Lucy Davies

text: But it would be unwise not to mention his writing partner in the unlikely and credible shape of Stephen Duffy: surely the reason behind the new honesty and eloquence, and more interesting and inventive songs that convincingly capture about 50 different genres.
author: Lucy Davies

text: Gloriously imperfect, the personality makes the album, and it's his best yet: almost worth the 80 million.
author: Lucy Davies

text: Romanian expatriate vocalist Sanda Weigl has quite a personal history.
author: Bill Tilland

text: She first learned gypsy songs as a child and found early success as a child star on Romanian national television.
author: Bill Tilland

text: Later she was a rock singer in East Berlin, and was tossed into prison for protesting against the communist regime.
author: Bill Tilland

text: In the 1990s she moved to New York and recently began performing again.
author: Bill Tilland

text: This album is a collaboration with a number of downtown NYC's finest, including pianist Anthony Coleman, guitarist Marc Ribot, and the peerless Glen Velez on hand percussion.
author: Bill Tilland

text: To call Weigl's voice "powerful" would be an understatement.
author: Bill Tilland

text: She has an impressive vocal range.
author: Bill Tilland

text: Her range, timbre and declamatory style makes for an intriguing presentation of passion and even sexuality that is a synthesis of male and female.
author: Bill Tilland

text: She adopts a male persona in at least four of the songs.
author: Bill Tilland

text: For example "Cintec din Oas," which presents the "desperate cries of a man rejected and betrayed by all the women in the world".
author: Bill Tilland

text: Her interpretations are dramatic, even theatrical, but never "over the top".
author: Bill Tilland

text: A comparison with Diamanda Galas might have some resonance, but Weigl's purpose is not to shock, but rather to communicate the vibrant life force inherent in the music.
author: Bill Tilland

text: Which she does admirably, with an energy and panache that speaks of her intimate familiarity with the material.
author: Bill Tilland

text: Much credit is due also to Anthony Coleman's sensitive arrangements.
author: Bill Tilland

text: The opening track, "Trenule masina mica," pretty much consists of Weigl's voice and Velez' accompaniment on hand drums, but Coleman slips in an almost imperceptible drone halfway through the piece, and then a soft, skeletal piano counterpoint for a few stanzas.
author: Bill Tilland

text: It's very simple, but also hauntingly effective.
author: Bill Tilland

text: The traditional Romanian cimbalom (dulcimer or zither) is the sole accompaniment on the dramatic and stately "Cine iubeste si lasa." The table-thumping "Ciulenadra, described as "possibly the most popular song in Romania", is at the other end of the scale.
author: Bill Tilland

text: A full ensemble goes full tilt, starting with a small string section, accordion and then swooping trombones and a squealing clarinet, as the pace of the piece doubles and then doubles again before ending in a wild frenzy.
author: Bill Tilland

text: Always though, it comes back to Weigl's extraordinary voice.
author: Bill Tilland

text: And if you're a fan of vocal ethnic music of any sort, that's something you don't want to miss.
author: Bill Tilland

text: Try These: Sui Vesan - Sui Various - Rough Guide to Hungarian Music
author: Bill Tilland

text: The second album from Portland based quintet Fontanelle is aptly named; their first album had critics scratching their heads searching for some way to describe their instrumental meanderings, and thisone's likely to do the same.
author: Peter Marsh

text: So here goes...
author: Peter Marsh

text: Style Drift is a blend of plastic funk, improvisation and textural exploration, dominated by soft, occasionally cheesy analogue keyboards laid over slippery live grooves and spiced with bursts of propulsive guitar riffs.
author: Peter Marsh

text: It's attractive music, with the massed keyboards occasionally recalling the warm bubbling electric pianos of Keith Jarrett or Herbie Hancock with Miles Davis, the pastel drift of Cluster's Hans Joachim Roedelius' solo work or even Robert Wyatt's "The End of an Ear" .
author: Peter Marsh

text: Even when more abrasive digital sounding textures are employed, there's a muted, organic quality to them (best heard on the mournful "James Going").
author: Peter Marsh

text: Though Fontanelle can get funky (in a repressed post-rock kind of way), there's a looseness to the playing which veers between being engaging and frustrating.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Some of it's just messy ("Red Light, Green Light") and suffers from a lack of commitment; they hit a groove then seem unwilling or unable to take it anywhere much.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The problem is that the band (save perhaps drummer Mat Morgan) don't have the chops to carry off any extended improvisation; but there remains an intriguing trade off between note playing and dubby, spacey soundscaping which at its best makes Style Drift a seductive, transporting proposition.
author: Peter Marsh

text: It's almost as if Fontanelle are attempting to play something like Bitches Brew, but much as A Certain Ratio and the Pop Group (who tried the same thing with Brownian Funk as their template) they're failing and in the process discovering something precious of their own.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Try These: Sand - Still Born Alive Chicago Underground Duo - Axis & Alignment Limp - Orion
author: Peter Marsh

text: From the tender beginnings of a Take That number 38 'hit' - complete with lycra shorts and 'interesting' dance routines - Robbie Williams has worked his way into the hearts and onto the bedroom walls of the nation.
author: Talia Kraines

text: After 13 years we now have this, his greatest hits album, cataloguing his journey from the teenage heartbreak of leaving Take That through to the Robbie we know so well.
author: Talia Kraines

text: After 5 studio albums, this compilation isn't going to hold any surprises.
author: Talia Kraines

text: It's worth noting that Robbie isn't one of those artists where the singles are great but the rest of the album isn't much cop.
author: Talia Kraines

text: While Sing When You're Winning probably clocks in as the weakest of the albums, each one is a great listen in itself, and this compilation is perhaps somewhat weaker for containing singles only, missing strong album tracks like I've Been Expecting You's fiery "Karma Killer" and Life Through A Lens' romping "Ego A Go Go".
author: Talia Kraines

text: We start not quite at the very beginning.
author: Talia Kraines

text: The first solo single, a cover of the 1990 George Michael classic "Freedom", seems to have been erased from Robbie history; it's never performed live and gets completely overlooked on this album.
author: Talia Kraines

text: Instead, we kick off with the first single from LTAL, the laddish "Old Before I Die".Also missed out are "South Of The Border", his only non-top 10 single, and the sickly "Somethin' Stupid".
author: Talia Kraines

text: The now classic (and somewhat overrated) "Angels" is promoted out of chronological order to track two and will undoubtedly be a highlight of the album for many.
author: Talia Kraines

text: For me, however, it's the other ballads that are the stand-out tracks; from the summer soaring of "Eternity" to the break-up pain of "Sexed Up", it's these soft rock ballads that are consistently great.
author: Talia Kraines

text: As is seemingly now the fashion (check out the forthcoming Britney and Kylie releases), this compilation also contains two new tracks.
author: Talia Kraines

text: We'll all know by now the opinion-dividing "Radio", which, Robbie tells us, is the start of a new era in his music.
author: Talia Kraines

text: New song number two, "Misunderstood", taken from the second Bridget Jones movie, sees Robbie return to familiar power-ballad territory.
author: Talia Kraines

text: In a few weeks it'll no doubt be populating radio station playlists everywhere and will be impossible to escape.
author: Talia Kraines

text: It's been a rocky 13 years, but towering above the personality, the drugs, the girls and the drink, it's the quality of the music that will surely stand as Robbie's legacy.
author: Talia Kraines

text: It's impossible to write about Robbie Williams' music without looking at the bigger picture.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: Self-proclaimed King of Light Entertainment, his every move is documented in the press and he's now the most expensive man in pop thanks to his new £80 million record deal.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: Robbie is more than just a singer.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: He's an all round entertainer and the closest thing to a superstar this country has produced in the past 10 years.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: As if to hammer the point home, Robbie's return to the limelight after a years break "Feel"is one of his greatest singles ever.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: Just as "Angels" starts to lose its magic as the ultimate lighter in the air, tear in the eye moment at any Robbie performance, he comes up with another majestic blinder.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: With "Feel" so early in the album, it's easy to lose momentum initially with the remaining tracks, but given a few listens Escapology reveals all the dark emotion, showmanship and tongue-in-cheek arrogance that gives Robbie his charm.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: The Guy Chambers song writing partnership has once again delivered the goods, maturing Robbie's style confidently with a new found rawness and live feel.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: It may be raw, but Robbie certainly hasn't lost his accessibility.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: "Monsoon" nods acknowledging to Queen, all strutting guitars and Freddie vocals and "Handsome Man" is perhaps a final homage to his own self parody.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: All the wry humour and ego is still there, but with lyrics like, "I'm going to milk it 'til it turns to cheese" and enough stadium rock to get any crowd bouncing, it can't help but raise a smile.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: "Come Undone", surely a future single release is another highlight, as is "Me and My Monkey", with its trumpets, Spanish guitar and daft lyrics.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: The surprise of the album though is Robbie's first solo writing credit.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: "Nan's Song" is a beautiful strings and acoustic guitar song number and a fitting conclusion to his best album yet.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: Cynics may scorn at Robbie; he's got it all and he isn't afraid to acknowledge it.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: The thing to remember though is that we should forgive him, because he's Robbie and he's great.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: Try These: Will Young - From Now On Natalie Imbruglia - White Lilies Island
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: If you need any further proof that Europe (and particularly Norway) is the place where all the interesting stuff is happening, look no further than this record.
author: Peter Marsh

text: A Livingroom Hush is the debut from Norwegian collective Jaga Jazzist, now given a wider release by Ninja Tune.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The album's already picked up critical praise (even from the NME!) with one memorable quote describing it as 'Charlie Mingus with Aphex Twin up his arse'.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Though this is an interesting (if unsavoury) notion, the album is far from the kind of confrontational experience it suggests.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Jaga Jazzist bolt together elements of electronica, formal jazz writing and the wide open spaces of dub and post rock into a lush, listenable stew that's very much their own.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Unlike some of their contemporaries, there aren't any specific references to jazz tradition; you won't find any Alice Coltrane samples here.
author: Peter Marsh

text: In fact they're as likely to remind you of Soft Machine or John Barry as much as Herbie Hancock.
author: Peter Marsh

text: This pluralist approach is laid out on the opening "Animal Chin" as flute and vibes patterns swirl over lurching breakbeats and churning bass, and the luscious glide of "Going Down", where luminous horns carve out aching melodic lines.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Often the cool beauty of the brass arrangements is reminiscent of Gil Evans or Oliver Nelson, and the short, sweet solos of Lars Horntveth, Jorgen Munkeby and Mathias Eick offer the same mix of introspection and inquisitiveness that you might find on a late 60s Blue Note date.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Nothing stays still for very long; "Airborne" kicks off as spacey jazz ballad peppered with digital crackle n' pop before morphing into a slinky Hancockian bass clarinet riff, joined by intricate countermelodies from strings and horns as the tenor takes over.
author: Peter Marsh

text: All in under 6 minutes.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Elsewhere you get space age bachelor pad music ("Lithuania"), breakbeat cheesetronica mashup ("Midget") or queasy abstract ambience ("Cinematic").
author: Peter Marsh

text: Jaga Jazzist's grasp of dynamics and structure(whether achieved in real time or through digital cut-up) puts them apart from the usual jazztronica suspects.
author: Peter Marsh

text: It's the mix of 21st century texture, intelligent jazz writing and improvisational concision that makes this one of the most enjoyable records of this (or any other) year.
author: Peter Marsh

text: In the UK the young 10-piece Norwegian drum 'n' jazz collective from Tonsberg have sprung, seemingly fully-formed, out of nowhere.
author: Chris Jones

text: Nothing, of course, could be further from the truth.
author: Chris Jones

text: Now, on the 10th anniversary of its release, Smalltown Supersound make available their rare Norway-only mini album, Magazine.
author: Chris Jones

text: It's a welcome addition to their small but perfectly formed catalogue, and proves that core members - brothers Lars and Martin Horntveth - have always had these wonderful catchy, serpentine tunes running around their brains.
author: Chris Jones

text: It's also a testament to the Scandinavian tradition of getting jazz into the bloodstream when the kids are barely out of nappies.
author: Chris Jones

text: While this debut lays bare its influences much more transparently, it remains a scarily assured piece of work from what were essentially teenagers.
author: Chris Jones

text: The aforementioned influences include early Mothers of Invention (in the jolly horn groupings) and, even more impressively, classic period Gil Evans: something that still holds sway over Lars Horntveth, as shown on his latest solo outing, Pooka.
author: Chris Jones

text: But added to this is the band's irrepressible way with a melody and d 'n' b dynamics - allegedly arrived at by merely hearing a description of what the genre sounded like!
author: Chris Jones

text: Of course, none of this would work without Jaga Jazzist'samazing and unorthodox blend of instrumentation.
author: Chris Jones

text: "Jaga Ist Zu Hause" soars out of the speakers on wings of steel guitar, punctuated by clusters of woodwind and propelled by Martin's imaginatively hyperactive drums.
author: Chris Jones

text: "Plym"'s delicate acoustic stirrings feature some of the most heart-rending chords ever plucked and builds to a wildly megalomaniac storm of noise.
author: Chris Jones

text: But it's "Swedish Takeaway" that indicates what fine straight jazzers these boys were before settling on a more recognizable sound.
author: Chris Jones

text: Recorded at Oslo's legendary Club Bla, it's a naggingly lovely two chord vamp that's as infectious as it is free, with some very fine trumpet soloing.
author: Chris Jones

text: With a couple of remixes and the unusually vocal "Seems To Me", this release still sees itself as much a product of the indie scene as the more monumental heritage of Miles and Coltrane, and that's why Jaga continue to amaze.
author: Chris Jones

text: Like many of their fellow countrymen, they refuse to recognize the boundaries.
author: Chris Jones

text: Allegedly their next album throws prog rock into the mix.
author: Chris Jones

text: Rest assured, this should be a very good thing indeed...
author: Chris Jones

text: In 1972, 60s-style beat combo The Way We Live songwriter, guitarist and vocalist Jim Milne and drummer and bassist Steve Clayton dived into the bubbling progressive-rock pot and resurfaced with multi-track still in hand, as Tractor.
author: Kathy Narayan

text: The Way We Live were newly signed to John Peel and Clive Selwood's Dandelion label for the album, A Candle For Judith (cover photograph by none other than the Hairy Cornflake, Dave Lee Travis).
author: Kathy Narayan

text: Dandelion were unhappy, however, and asked the duo to re-record the album at London's Spot studios - where Cream had cut their first album.
author: Kathy Narayan

text: It was Peel who suggested the name change, after he saw a tractor drive by his kitchen window.
author: Kathy Narayan

text: So, A Candle For Judith was repackaged and re-released in 1972 as Tractor by Tractor.
author: Kathy Narayan

text: The album received much airplay, climbing to number 19 on Kid Jensen's Hot Heavy 20 on Radio Luxembourg and number 30 in Virgin Records' chart.
author: Kathy Narayan

text: Tractor, an original of which is highly collectable, has since been reissued twice and now makes a 30th anniversary appearance, this time with six bonus tracks.
author: Kathy Narayan

text: It's an unpredictable and, at times, downright creepy affair.
author: Kathy Narayan

text: The weighty bass of the opener, ''All Ends Up'', pulls you straight down, before galloping drums and close harmonies lift and unsettle, leaving you with a feeling of vulnerability.
author: Kathy Narayan

text: Then that heavy, distorted bass kicks in again.
author: Kathy Narayan

text: We're on an emotional roller-coaster here, passing through the haunted house more than once!
author: Kathy Narayan

text: The rest of the album unravels more melodically: Clayton's clattering cross-rhythms fill in cleverly around Milne's vocals.
author: Kathy Narayan

text: The production is basic and angry, with echoes of Zeppelin and Hawkwind, but the real beauty of Tractor is that, even with all this going on, they still deliver that mystical vibe.
author: Kathy Narayan

text: Four of the six bonus tracks were recorded in 1973, as the label was on the verge of folding.
author: Kathy Narayan

text: ''Dandelion suggested we have a final fling in the studio'', recalls Milne.
author: Kathy Narayan

text: ''So, we took loads of songs with us, enough for another album, but work was very slow.'' There's also a live performance recorded at Glastonbury 2002 and a track featuring Hawkwind's Nik Turner on sax and flute.
author: Kathy Narayan

text: They're somewhat lighter than the rest of the album.
author: Kathy Narayan

text: Without them, Tractor could leave you feeling a little anxious and exhausted.
author: Kathy Narayan

text: This is prog rock at its most jagged.
author: Kathy Narayan

text: Try These: Pink Fairies - Neverneverland Pink Floyd - Echoes Yes - In A Word
author: Kathy Narayan

text: Fans of Hitch-Hiker's Guide to the Galaxy may remember that the designer of the planet Earth (Slartibartfarst) was rather pleased with his work on Norway, particularly the fjords.
author: Peter Marsh

text: he must have put something in the water too, judging from the incredibly fertile nature of its music scene.
author: Peter Marsh

text: This lot are just one manifestation of it.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Jaga Jazzists's debut A Living Room Hush (which got a UK release last year) won the hearts of many who probably wouldn't be seen dead in the Jazz section of your local Megatower CD emporium.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Fusing 21st century electronica with airy horn parts and succint, considered solos, it was a joyful, intricate noise stuffed full of stop-start dynamics.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Clever stuff, and all the more impressive when you see them doing it live.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The recipe stays pretty much the same for The Stix; interlocking brass, flutes and bass clarinet patterns thread their way through piles of shredded, hyperactive beats.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Again, the melodic writing owes much to a rarified strain of jazz rock rather than anything else; Soft Machine or Frank Zappa's Grand Wazoo spring to mind.
author: Peter Marsh

text: With a sound as distinctive and fully formed as this, it'd be unrealistic to expect too much change this time around, but there are subtle shifts in emphasis.
author: Peter Marsh

text: There's less improvisation; all the effort seems to have gone into creating even more detailed writing.Some pieces are almost geometric in their construction but there's always a sucker punch round the corner; Jaga Jazzist can beguile with lovely, translucent melodies then give you a swift kick up the behind.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Summery acoustic guitars jostle with squirts of digital noise, arcing horns and what sounds like a solo played on a giant kazoo shoved through a fuzz pedal.
author: Peter Marsh

text: It's all charged with a nervy, hyperactive energy that'll have the more mobile amongst us cutting a rug on the living room floor.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Luminously, predictably brilliant.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Shy FX and T Power have achieved far reaching success in the drum and bass field.
author: Will Sansom

text: They've reworked R&B and latin riffs, to the same extent that Adam F reinvented the treatment of a junglist hip-hop beat.
author: Will Sansom

text: These two London based pioneers have studied the old school with distinction.
author: Will Sansom

text: Now graduated, Shy FX and T Power are schooling the Top 40 chart with works from Set it Off to mass popular acclaim.
author: Will Sansom

text: Tracks like "Don't Give a Damn" - stay true to OG drum and bass production values and are in keeping with the breakthrough rolling Metalheadz sound of yesteryear.
author: Will Sansom

text: The additional vocals provided by Fallacy and Di have transformed these looped beats into a bonofide Top 40 smash.
author: Will Sansom

text: Set it Off is not short of guesting artists.
author: Will Sansom

text: Coree Richards appears on "Love The Way" addin' a Keith Sweat mackin style to the proceedings.
author: Will Sansom

text: Charmaine's sweet soul harmonies give "Run Along" the essence of Full Cycle's early Music Box numbers and include the same sharp cut beats that can't fail to work the dance floor.
author: Will Sansom

text: On the other hand, not everything that Shy FX and T-Power set off here is likely to blow up large on the popular music scene.
author: Will Sansom

text: "Nature" sees Jamaica's Elephant Man working ruff junglist moves to bring a whole new meaning to the term when Nature calls.
author: Will Sansom

text: Exotic birds are all over this one, by the sounds of things.
author: Will Sansom

text: Luckily in the case of "Don't Wanna Know" a lush vocal from the magnificent Di saves the track from becoming a mental happy hardcore salsa frenzy and transforms it into a definite crowd pleaser.
author: Will Sansom

text: The album is an audio cocktail with a Mexican tequila twist.
author: Will Sansom

text: It's a diverse mixture of lyrical flavas suitable to wet anyone's palette.
author: Will Sansom

text: These two recognised engineers are set to educate the masses with a host of British vocal talent.
author: Will Sansom

text: You can't deny that their popularity and success has guaranteed their place in today's musical curriculum.
author: Will Sansom

text: Try These: Aphrodite - Aftershock Future Engineers - Technetium
author: Will Sansom

text: Transcription - arranging a piece of existing music for a different instrument - has a long and illustrious history.
author: Paul Cutts

text: In an age before recorded music, transcriptions enabled music lovers to more easily access orchestral and operatic repertoire and virtuosos to display their wit and ferocious keyboard talent.
author: Paul Cutts

text: Bach metamorphosed simple hymn tunes into complex chorale preludes for organ; Liszt realised Schubert songs, among a multitude of other composers works, as florid fantasies.
author: Paul Cutts

text: The great Russian composer-pianist Sergei Rachmaninov made a small but significant contribution to the genre and it's his take on the art that compatriot Vladimir Ashkenazy celebrates on this new recording.
author: Paul Cutts

text: Rachmaninov's highly distinctive and chromatic voice is clear in all the arrangements - from the glittering transformation of Schubert's song 'Wohin?' to his famous transcription of Rimsky-Korsakov's Flight of the Bumblebee (which can sting the fingers of the most dextrous pianist).
author: Paul Cutts

text: Ashkenazy - a long-time champion of Rachmaninov's music - rattles it all off with a technical ease that borders on prestidigitatious.
author: Paul Cutts

text: But there's also an innate sympathy with the musical language that means these sometimes over-gilded musical lilies (often too saccharine for many) never lose their intelligent fragrance.
author: Paul Cutts

text: The reworking of Tchaikovsky's Lullaby embodies all that's best in the art of transcription - it's both a loving homage and a distinctly personal poetic statement.
author: Paul Cutts

text: It's not music that will be to everyone's tastes.
author: Paul Cutts

text: But as an illustration of creative imagination and virtuosic keyboardism, this Decca disc is as good as it gets.
author: Paul Cutts

text: This wonderful newcd isn't supposed to exist.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: When Sony began their Ligeti Edition in the 1990s, their ambition to record definitive performances of one of the most interesting, influential and consistently entertaining avant-garde composers was widely acclaimed, and the results were spectacularly good.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: So when Sony quietly pulled the plug on the series after eight volumes there were sighs of despair.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: In the current climate in classical music, who was likely to pick up the baton and run with it to the finish-line?
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Cue Teldec, which back in 1999 was still an independent label operating under the giant Warner umbrella.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Teldec picked up where Sony left off, and planned the five remaining volumes that would complete what was now 'The Ligeti Project'.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Two volumes in, and Warner's effectively shut down Teldec as a separate record label, and we all expected the Ligeti Project to come to a premature end again.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Well, it hasn't; here's Volume III - and the best news is that the last two volumes are already in the can, so unless some Warner Music executive has a rush of blood to the head, this project will be completed.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: < > Volume III of the Teldec Ligeti Project shows us why the series is so important.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: For instance, Clocks and Clouds from 1973 for twelve female voices and orchestra, which uses an article on the philosophy of science to generate poetic images, a seductive soundworld where the exactly determined rhythms melt into pools of complex chords and microtonal intervals.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Anyone who thrilled to Ligeti's Lux aeterna in the movie '2001: A Space Odyssey' will find much to admire and entrance in Clocks and Clouds...
author: Andrew McGregor

text: how come this is a WORLD PREMIERE RECORDING?!
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Sorry, didn't mean to shout...but that's why this series is so important.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: A score like this from a composer as vital to contemporary music as Ligeti has to be recorded.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: That it's taken so long is scandalous.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: The other premiere is a much more recent work: Sippal, dobbal, nadihegeduvel (With Pipes, Drums, Fiddles), a cycle of seven Hungarian songs from 2000 - music as playful and profound as the poems that inspired it.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: The Violin and Cello Concertos have both been recorded several times before, but that doesn't detract from the importance of these versions.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Sigfried Palm was the dedicatee of the Cello Concerto, and his unique authority combined with the commitment of the ASKO/Schonberg Ensemble and their director Reinbert de Leeuw (rehearsing and recording in the presence of the composer) makes for a memorable account of this shimmering 60s score.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: The Violin Concerto, though, belongs with the song-cycle among Ligeti's later works, and again micro-intervals are a vital part of the sound: horns play only natural harmonics, and two of the orchestral string players are scordatura (open strings in non-standard tunings), giving Ligeti an unusual range of chordal textures to play with.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: The woodwind players are sometimes asked to play ocarinas, those strange lemon-shaped clay whistles with simple finger-holes all over them.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Its a lovely sound, and so's the solo part, warmly expressive in Frank Peter Zimmerman's hands.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: A superb recording, and fascinating sounds from a contemporary composer who never sounds quite like anyone else, and also writes good notes about his own music.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: If only all cds of contemporary composers were this interesting, and necessary...
author: Andrew McGregor

text: In 1958, Thelonious Monk's appearance at the Newport Festival finally alerted a world beyond the demi-monde of beatniks and jazz cognoscenti to his unique abilities.
author: Glenn Rice

text: By 1962 his glory days were over.
author: Glenn Rice

text: Still, Monk remained an inimitable pianist.
author: Glenn Rice

text: His 50's albums for Prestige were great by ordinary standards, displaying flashes of his compositional genius.
author: Glenn Rice

text: But the iconoclastic fire that forged his legacy of innovation had infrequently risen above a steadily glowing ember since the 40s, when works like "Mysterioso", "Round Midnight" and "In Walked Bud" had struck like weird electric cattle prods at the spine of a bewildered musical establishment.
author: Glenn Rice

text: By 1962 Monk had spent twenty years not so much ahead of the curve of jazz as at angles to it.
author: Glenn Rice

text: Approbation flowered too late to prevent his questioning the sense of working so hard in the face of scant recognition, and so the latter stage of his career commenced.
author: Glenn Rice

text: Its beginning can be traced roughly to this album, here reissued with 27 minutes of alternate takes.
author: Glenn Rice

text: Entering the studio for his first Columbia session, it's tempting to wonder if Monk found irony in recollections of the composition lessons that he'd once given to now all-conquering new labelmate Miles Davis when they were alchemists together at the crucible of long-gone bebop.
author: Glenn Rice

text: Monk's skew-wiff timing and harmony saddled him with a serial hanging-on-to-sidemen snafu.
author: Glenn Rice

text: Lately, intuitive bassist John Ore, deceptively loose-sounding drummer Frankie Dunlop and equal parts funky and angular tenor man Charlie Rouse had hung tough over months of club dates, and their broken-in sympatico thwacks all the often chestnutty tunes of "Monk's Dream" bang in the centre pocket.
author: Glenn Rice

text: The magic works best on devilish riff-fest "Bye-Ya".
author: Glenn Rice

text: Listening now to Monk parley "Body & Soul", "Just a Gigolo" or "Sweet & Lovely", it almost seems funny he was considered a radical modernist.
author: Glenn Rice

text: Straight-up blues underpins almost all; pointedly amateurish technique regularly recalls original model James P.
author: Glenn Rice

text: Then, Thelonious himself; aching, spring-day romanticism of fleeting substitutions in ballads.
author: Glenn Rice

text: Blanging, wide, not-quite-dissonant chord interjections, as if a chord were some exotic beetle to be turned over just long enough to see how many legs it had before throwing it down.
author: Glenn Rice

text: Monk's unique contribution to music, and "Monks Dream" itself, is founded on these motifs, which purely expressed his madcap, avuncular presence and which he would never attempt to expand upon again after this record.
author: Glenn Rice

text: Studio Confessions is the groundbreaking third album from maverick Peven Everett.
author: Joy Dunbar

text: Before this enduring album hit the streets, Peven had released an amazing 12 critically acclaimed singles including timeless deep house classics like "Watch Them Come" and the Roy Davis Jr collaboration and UK Garage smash "Gabriel", that inspired the two-step movement.
author: Joy Dunbar

text: The celebrated, 27-year-old underground artist from Illinois turned down a place at Berkley School of Music to go touring with jazz legends Betty Carter, Wynton Marsalis and Branford Marsalis.
author: Joy Dunbar

text: The multi-talented performer plays an array of instruments including piano, guitar, bass, trumpet and saxophone.
author: Joy Dunbar

text: Studio Confessions is difficult to classify as it flirts with every possible musical genre from jazz to soul, house to hip-hop and Latino to funk.
author: Joy Dunbar

text: It has a worldly, organic and evolved sound that can be quite complex and dynamic in structure.
author: Joy Dunbar

text: The album was written, arranged, performed, produced and mixed by Peven himself, it takes you on a modern music journey full of discovery.
author: Joy Dunbar

text: The voyage starts with "World Love"which highlights Peven's ability to sing the most sensual love songs with soothing and inspiring orchestral threads.
author: Joy Dunbar

text: He proves he is in the same ilk as other great soul singers like Barry White and Marvin Gaye.
author: Joy Dunbar

text: "Testin Me" is a catchy, commercially tinged pleading love song that fulfils the artists aim to get people dancing.
author: Joy Dunbar

text: The last track, "Sankofa" takes you back to the 70s with a phat-and-funky instrumental jam, which goes against the ethos of the rest of the album but shows that Peven is a non-conformist in every sense of the word.
author: Joy Dunbar

text: In a time where Peven's contemporaries are going towards the left, this album is going back to basics but still retains its innovative appeal.
author: Joy Dunbar

text: The biggest disappointment on the CD is that it does not feature the truly astounding "Gabriel".
author: Joy Dunbar

text: However, Studio Confessions takes you on a unique 40 minute journey from one of the most understated, energised and passionate singers around.
author: Joy Dunbar

text: It is a voyage you and your music system will enjoy taking again and again.
author: Joy Dunbar

text: Try These: Donell Jones - Life Goes On Gerald Levert - The G Spot Curtis Mayfield - Superfly
author: Joy Dunbar

text: Following the recent frenzy of commercially successful French talent (ie: Daft Punk, Air, Cassius, etc..), it seems a new wave of Gallic sound seems to be taking shape and this time, it's the experimental avant-garde who seem to have the upper hand.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: From the streets of Paris to outlying towns like Larnod or Strasbourg, countless record labels and musicians are popping up releasing homespun glitchy bedroom techno.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: They can't seem to get enough of it, it seems.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: On this release the newly combined force of Aspic and Optical Sound Records have embraced modern electronica, albeit with a unique twist that only the French seem to be able to pull off.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Likening the band to "pop freak losers who don't have any money to buy equipment and who'd rather be making music without instruments", .tape come to the techno table with a press release that would make most PR people blush.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Thankfully though they've more in common with peers like Darky, Ultra Milkmaids, o.lamm and Rainier Lericolais, rather than certain aging rock bands who shall remain anonymous.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Utilizing a wide range of instruments and sounds, .tape operate in a world of micro ideas, fragments and mini-songs.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Found sounds, guitars, vibraphones, 8-bit synths and analogue drum machines are brushed vigorously with cut and paste pyrotechnics, exploding aurally with a pretty pop rather than colourful starburst.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: The aptly named "My Life As Comedy" takes what sounds like an old-school 8-bit Nintendo game theme and re-structures it into something approaching manic Japanese techno pop.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: "Bm song preludic" is a damaged post-rock mix accentuated with acoustic guitar and cello.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: The opening "point" reminds one of Tortoise.There are also some lovely remixes included here by Missing Person, Sweet Trip and Kunstner5 as well, allowing for further exploration into .tape's sound.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Straddling the line between experimental laptop techno and good old fashioned indie-rock, .tape have come up with a debut CD that should win over fans of both camps.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Theres some great melodies here and the promise of great things to come.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: If you're into Chicago post-rock or anything approaching it, Flying over Banugues should tickle your lo-fi aesthetics with a feather of abstract electronica.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: A very promising debut, indeed.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Try These: o.lamm - snow party Fontanelle - Style Drift Limp - Orion
author: Olli Siebelt

text: As one third of vocal group LeVert, who enjoyed moderate success in the 80s with their crossover hit Casanova; Gerald Levert has since become the most high-profile member of the singing outfit.
author: Keysha Davis

text: Gerald has always maintained a core army of R&B fans who marvel at his offering of authentic soul, which lies in the tradition of the great warblers of our time including Teddy Pendergrass and Marvin Gaye.
author: Keysha Davis

text: His latest CD The G Spot is a highly confident disc, which marries the worlds of classic and contemporary R&B in a way that only a seasoned pro can.
author: Keysha Davis

text: Kicking off with the dynamic "Too Much Room", Gerald teams up with Mystikal to produce a 3 minute fun feast.
author: Keysha Davis

text: Mystikal is on fire when he yelps "Shake what ya mama gave ya/ I see by the way you move you can take it/ Hips dont lie...".
author: Keysha Davis

text: Ok, so it will hardly qualify for an Ivor Novello songwriting award, but within a club-orientated context, its absolutely perfect.
author: Keysha Davis

text: The vibe alters from hereby onwards as Levert slips into the more familiar role of churning out mid-tempo numbers.
author: Keysha Davis

text: "Since You Aint Around", "Funny" and "Wildin Me Out" are nice sounding ditties, but its the Marvin Gaye inspired "The Top Of My Head" which stands out both for its nostalgic quality and heartfelt delivery.
author: Keysha Davis

text: Jazz fans will want to check out "Oh What A Night" a collaboration with musical giant Roy Ayers.
author: Keysha Davis

text: Its a pleasant enough track, with strings, cymbols and harmonies in the right places.
author: Keysha Davis

text: But it can hardly be classified as groundbreaking - a word weve become accustomed to associating with one of the most influential players in contemporary jazz.
author: Keysha Davis

text: Hardcore Levert fans needn't fear, as there are more than a few traditional love songs laced throughout the CD such as "Catchin Feelin" and "Backbone".
author: Keysha Davis

text: But its the dire "The G Spot" which provides the only low spot on the record.
author: Keysha Davis

text: Succumbing to all the cliches associated with this genre such as erotic groans, whispered interludes of dont stops and faux climaxes - its apparent that this lover man needs to draw upon more imaginative ways to seduce the listener at times.
author: Keysha Davis

text: Overall The G-Spot is an enjoyable CD, which proves that Gerald Levert can compete against the new guns.
author: Keysha Davis

text: Core fans will be duly satisfied, whilst new fans will be enchanted by the powerful vocals, capable songwriting, and tuneful melodies throughout the disc.
author: Keysha Davis

text: Ladytron's debut album 604 cut through the lumbering, bloated, chart pap and introspective indie whinging when it was released in late 2001.
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: The harsh, spoken vocals of Bulgarian vixen Mira Aroyo mirrored the emotive lobotomy of Neil Tennant, while her sugarspun double, Helen Marnie, wandered as if trapped within the audio beat-box prison of stylised hand claps, space zaps and synth-jazz of Daniel Hunt and Reuben Wu.
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: The follow up, Light & Magic, draws back the curtains to shed a little light on the many tributaries that float the Ladytron boat.
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: This is a fascinating exercise in music-by-numbers.
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: Only now, as the marketing gimmick that was Electroclash is worn down to a blunt stub, can we fully appreciate where they sit.
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: Current single "Seventeen" mirrors the catchy and immediate pop sensibilities of their previous singles "Playgirl" and "Paco".
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: It takes the framework of verse-chorus-repeat supported by a thumping, staccato heartbeat.
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: It's a pliable formula that might have come from the back-bedrooms of Glaswegian punk-pop outfit Bis or Air's moonbase hideway.
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: Or, God forbid, it could have been dumbed down by a BPM or two to suit the sample cannibals, Sugababes.
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: Back, back I say!
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: "Fire" betrays a consistent fondness for some Eastern European fantasy state, a sort of techno-Prussia in which 100ft statues of Kraftwerk look down upon our precocious usurpers.
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: Helen slips into the flayed skin of a new-look leatherette Madonna for an insidious rendition of "Evil".
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: Instrumental tracks are too often used as padding, but the grandiose "Turn It On" filters the very essence of the band's audio beam, splitting it into a divergent sum of parts.
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: The vocoder chorus traces a direct link to core Electro and the likes of Newtrament, while it's but a blob of solder to make a connection with early Hip-Hop stylings.
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: As the album progresses, so a third dimension of beeps and troughs appears together with haunting commentary and fearsome barked commands.

author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: Many things were begotten by the New York class of 76 bands: Talking Heads gave us art-rock; the Ramones gave us freedom from anything using more than three chords and lasting more than two and a half minutes; Johnny Thunders gave us a template for Guns 'n' Roses (cheers Johnny) and Television gave us mind-bending guitars and bleating poetry.
author: Chris Jones

text: But what of Blondie?
author: Chris Jones

text: Always with an eye firmly superglued to the prize, they were often reviled for their ability to mould their perfect pop into chart-ravishing hits.
author: Chris Jones

text: Plus, they had a blonde singer with an appeal beyond the geeky new wave set, so they couldn't be taken seriously, could they?
author: Chris Jones

text: Wrong, and wrong again.
author: Chris Jones

text: History has, again proven that these boys (and girl) in skinny ties were one tough, pioneering bunch.
author: Chris Jones

text: Here's the proof.
author: Chris Jones

text: Superceding previous hits collections due to their reformation (and subsequent #1 with ''Maria''), this collection brings us up to date.
author: Chris Jones

text: Despite the undoubted quality of the recent material, Blondie's place in the pop pantheon was assured by about 1980.
author: Chris Jones

text: How many other bands could fill an entire album with nothing BUT hits (including 7 #1s)?
author: Chris Jones

text: OK, the early singles from the first album (''Rip Her To Shreds'' and ''X Offender'') weren't really hits but check out the quality.
author: Chris Jones

text: It's clear that Chris Stein, Clem Burke, Jimmy Destri and co.
author: Chris Jones

text: knew exactly what they were doing from the word go.
author: Chris Jones

text: You know the score, from the tumbling naivety of ''Denis'', to the widescreen bluster of ''Atomic'' or ''Union City Blue'', they couldn't put a stiletto wrong.
author: Chris Jones

text: There's the proto-rap of ''Rapture'' (bad pun, great single), the disco heaven of ''Heart Of Glass'' and the purest pop of ''Sunday Girl''.
author: Chris Jones

text: In all this chart-worrying action it's also worth remembering that they culled these nuggets from albums that never even approached shabby.
author: Chris Jones

text: Parallel Lines still stands as an artistic whole that's as valid and era-defining as Marquee Moon or Remain In Light.
author: Chris Jones

text: So, no arguments - Blondie were, in modern parlance, the bomb.
author: Chris Jones

text: Musical chops, sharp suits and a singer whose iconic resonance has yet to fade.
author: Chris Jones

text: Yet again, they're gonna be your number one...
author: Chris Jones

text: The Red Hot Chili Peppers are renowned for their unique brand of funk-rap-punk-rock (reader, please feel free to add your own descriptors, according to taste and pretension.
author: Daniel Pike

text: Neo and fusion are always good.
author: Daniel Pike

text: Eclecticism is, apparently, passe).
author: Daniel Pike

text: But, with By The Way, the Californian foursome have made things much simpler for all concerned by releasing what is essentially a straight-forward rock album.
author: Daniel Pike

text: Ok, so there may be some notional rap, funk, and a sniff of punkishness (punk not really being achievable in half measures).
author: Daniel Pike

text: But it is a rock sound, with balladic verses and powerful harmonised choruses, that wins through.
author: Daniel Pike

text: This marks a definite continuation of the successes of their previous release, 1999's Californication.
author: Daniel Pike

text: The strutting of old is replaced by a melancholy if ennobled air, pervasive in "Universally Speaking", "Dosed" and "I Could Die For You".
author: Daniel Pike

text: The radio-friendly "Zephyr Song" with such lyrics as "In this perfect weather, we'll find a place together..." is even a little twee.
author: Daniel Pike

text: Although a rock album, By The Way is far from one dimensional.
author: Daniel Pike

text: The energetic, "Can't Stop" and "On Mercury" cut to a ska feel while "Don't Forget Me" proves slow and gritty.
author: Daniel Pike

text: The boisterous "Cabron" features arpeggiated guitars which brings to mind images of somewhere strangely medieval and Spanish.
author: Daniel Pike

text: The Chilis have seen their fair share of life's stress and tragedy.
author: Daniel Pike

text: "Venice Queen" is dedicated to Kiedis' recently departed friend and drugs councillor Gloria Scott.
author: Daniel Pike

text: His break up with long-time girlfriend Yohanna Logan perhaps further influenced the album's plaintive sound.
author: Daniel Pike

text: "Sex-god" posturing aside, The Chilis have always harboured a gentler, emotional side.
author: Daniel Pike

text: It is with By The Way that a band famous for performing in no more than a "modesty sock" have finally reached maturity and managed to truly lay themselves bare.
author: Daniel Pike

text: Fans of Baaba Maal's souped-up contemporary Senegalese music step this way.
author: Neil Bennun

text: Suuf's 'Debbo Hande' is a resolutely forward-looking debut.
author: Neil Bennun

text: It features twitchy studio-crafted rhythms, instrumentalists from Europe and West Africa, impassioned vocals and conscious lyrics sung in Peulh, Wolof and French.
author: Neil Bennun

text: This combination is supposedly patented by the Senegalese superstar Baaba Maal in his collaborations with producer Simon Emmerson.
author: Neil Bennun

text: For Baaba Maal, read the singers Djiby Guisse (of Les Freres Guisse) and the comparatively less-known Biram Seck.
author: Neil Bennun

text: Their voices are forceful and supple, and they're joined by the sweet-voiced Hady Guisse.
author: Neil Bennun

text: For Simon Emmerson, read the Bristol-based producer Simon Sleath, Real World alumnus and all-round studio don.
author: Neil Bennun

text: The album features contributions from the future-blues guitarist Justin Adams, pianist Sarah Class, percussionist Aliou Guisse of Les Freres Guisse and the bassist Dembel Diop.
author: Neil Bennun

text: And it's a genuinely collaborative affair, although the emphasis is certainly weighted towards Senegal.
author: Neil Bennun

text: There are nods to mbalax, the sound of urban Senegal ('Fit'), and more reflective folk music ('Sakou Kham').
author: Neil Bennun

text: But the textures and production make categorisations tricky.
author: Neil Bennun

text: This is exemplified on 'Debbo Afrika' ('African Woman') with its funky chicken-scratch guitar riff syncopating with African lute and dubby drums.
author: Neil Bennun

text: 'Xarit', is a gorgeously sad lament sung by Hady Guisse.
author: Neil Bennun

text: A quite beautiful piano silvers the West African instrumentation.
author: Neil Bennun

text: "I wrote your name on my heart and it will neither wash out nor die," Guisse sings, and it certainly sounds like he means it.
author: Neil Bennun

text: The lyrics are certainly worth a mention.
author: Neil Bennun

text: 'Debbo Hande' ('Modern Woman'), a duet sung by Hady and Djiby Guisse, a spectacular mix of syncopated folk rhythms and programming, features the line: "Let's wake up and go to work...
author: Neil Bennun

text: Man I hear your voice, but I'm afraid to go near." Subtle, articulate and ambiguous, it makes an apposite title song for a rewarding album.
author: Neil Bennun
