text: The success of Red Hot Chili Peppers begins when an unknown guitarist, John Fruciante, joined the band in 1988.
author: Jack Smith

text: The release of Mothers Milk helped break the group in America with their cover of the Stevie Wonder classic "Higher Ground".
author: Jack Smith

text: They soon became regulars on MTV and in the early 90s, as the underground moved into the mainstream, the Chili Peppers, like Nirvana, REM and Sonic Youth, benefited from this shift of music.
author: Jack Smith

text: After the release of Blood Sugar Sex Magik the Chili Peppers became one of the worlds biggest bands.
author: Jack Smith

text: The album spawned hits such as "Give It Away", "Under The Bridge" and "Suck My Kiss".
author: Jack Smith

text: Their sound was noisy and funky and grungy and to many fans this album was seen as their high point.
author: Jack Smith

text: Many believe that they have never been able to recapture that magic.
author: Jack Smith

text: But bands that stay stagnant and create the same sound album after album only end up like Oasis.
author: Jack Smith

text: At the height of their success guitarist John Frusciante left and Dave Navaro was recruited as replacement.
author: Jack Smith

text: One Hot Minute was the sound of the band trying to recapture the sound of Blood Sugar Sex Magic and is seen as a low point in their career.
author: Jack Smith

text: Only "My Friends" appears from that period and for a while the world almost forgot about the Chili Peppers.
author: Jack Smith

text: Then Dave left the band and John returned and in 1999 the band released Californication.
author: Jack Smith

text: The sound was softer and more melodic, yet they still retained that sound that made them, well them.
author: Jack Smith

text: "Scar Tissue", "Otherside" and "Californication" were without doubt Chili Pepper songs, but taken to a different place.
author: Jack Smith

text: Some thought they had sold out.
author: Jack Smith

text: But they hadn't sold out, they were evolving.
author: Jack Smith

text: When By the Way was released last year the sound of the band had shifted further away form the bass lines of Flea to the guitar melodies of John.
author: Jack Smith

text: The album was based on The Smiths and Neu!
author: Jack Smith

text: instead of Gang of Four and Bad Brains.
author: Jack Smith

text: The Chili Peppers have become a band famous for strong, anthemic songs rather than the punk-funk sounds characteristic of their early sound.
author: Jack Smith

text: Personally I'm disappointed in the song selection as it favours Blood Sugar Sex Magic and Californication rather than being a well-balanced and truly representative sample from their back-catalogue.
author: Jack Smith

text: But as a hits compilation rather than a retrospective CD, it does what it says on the tin, and is an enjoyable listen in spite of the obvious track selections.
author: Jack Smith

text: With Stadium Arcadium freshly plonked atop the UK chart, the Red Hot Chili Peppers are now confirmed as card-carrying Rock Gods.
author: Zoe Street

text: This two-disc intergalactic triumph (titled 'Jupiter' and 'Mars'), glows with Rick Rubin's shiny clean production.
author: Zoe Street

text: "Dani California" and the jerkily melodic "Tell Me Baby" see the Chilis at their best even if the grown-up band have replaced raunch with romance, mixing gritty funk with acoustic janglings and even choir-boy wailings.
author: Zoe Street

text: "She's Only 18" winks at their willy-ruled lyrics of yore: Anthony Kiedis may be about 92 now but he can still sing about undies, even if his body fluid fixation a la Blood Sugar Sex Magik has faded.
author: Zoe Street

text: "Wet Sand" rockets from balladry to sing-along stadium rock, while "Hey" boasts too much dinner-jazz strumming to really grab.
author: Zoe Street

text: But amid theprog like melee of sounds Flea's bass-thuddery still rules.
author: Zoe Street

text: A multi-faceted must.
author: Zoe Street

text: Paul Rogers should be well known to anyone with even a passing interest in British free jazz.
author: Peter Marsh

text: His ability to swing hard, sing sweetly and get down, dirty and abstract has made him bassist of choice for top improvisers like Evan Parker, John Stevens and Keith Tippett.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Listen is his second solo bass record and features two sessions recorded ten years apart, from 1989 and 99.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Solo bass records are, it should be said, an acquired taste.
author: Peter Marsh

text: There's an old joke about a marriage guidance counsellor who manages to get uncommunicative couples talking to each other in his sessions by playing Charlie Mingus records, in the belief that no-one can keep quiet during a bass solo.
author: Peter Marsh

text: No-one told the audiences here though, who let out barely a cough as Rogers negotiates his way through these stunning performances.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Rogers' vocabulary is huge and his facility pretty incredible.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The 38 minute Listen 99 opens with a blistering display of pizzicato playing before moving though soft harmonic ripples, bowed drones and episodes of scratchy abstraction, returning to just fingers and strings for lengthy, sometimes bluesy solos where he worries away at little phrases, repeating, embellishing and eventually dismantling them before moving on.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Occasionally he plays whistles, cymbals and drums for extra colouration (part 3 of the 99 gig is pure texture), but it's the note based stuff (reminiscent of Barre Phillips at times and undoubtedly drawing from 'jazz' harmony) that really sticks.
author: Peter Marsh

text: His tone is rich, punchy and resonant, and the lovely recording gives the bass a warm, physical presence that still has ambience.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The 19 minute solo from '89 is more in classic free improv mode.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Though there are some sweet moments, there's a much more episodic feel than the later material, which has a beautifully rounded shape to its structure, almost compositional in its precision and economy.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Aside from its potential for therapeutic use as discussed above, Listen is a tour de force of the first order; highly recommended to any fan of solo bass, but for those who simply enjoy hearing a master improviser at work, there's much to savour here.
author: Peter Marsh

author: Peter Marsh

text: Two master guitarists from Africa and Cuba combine to create an album which is a fluid and welcome treat.
author: Maud Hand

text: It would seem the most natural thing in the world for the cultures of Africa and Cuba to combine forces musically.
author: Maud Hand

text: African artists are undoubtedly influenced by Afro-Cuban rhythms - Ricardo Lemvo, Africando and Youssou nDour come to mind.
author: Maud Hand

text: And Cuba's musical heritage is firmly rooted in Africa.
author: Maud Hand

text: Yet its a rarity for musicians from both continents to collaborate.
author: Maud Hand

text: Papa Noel grew up in the Congo, listening to Cuban records on his mothers phonograph.
author: Maud Hand

text: He took up the guitar as a teenager and was part of the emerging rumba scene in that country of the late 50s.
author: Maud Hand

text: He's now recognised as one of Africa's finest, having played with legends like Franco and T.P.O.K.
author: Maud Hand

text: Papi Oviedo, is a master of the Cuban tres, a mini-guitar with three sets of double strings.A veteran of the Cuban big band circuit having played with Elio Reves orquestra for 15 years, most recently he's been delighting world audiences on tour with Buena Vista Social Club's Omara Portuondo.
author: Maud Hand

text: And it's the guitar work which is truly astounding on this album, particularly on the second track, "Kin Havane", where each master guitar solo washes over you like the waves along Havana's Malecon.
author: Maud Hand

text: Then theres the high soulful sound of Papa Noel's voice which would soften the hardest heart, particularly on the plaintive "Juliana".
author: Maud Hand

text: Again, the solo guitar sequence which opens this love song is simply superb.
author: Maud Hand

text: Right from the opening title track, "Bana Congo", the African backing vocals set an earthy tone and pace.
author: Maud Hand

text: The song pays tribute to Papa Noel's country and culture.
author: Maud Hand

text: The flourishes from the horn and rhythm sections are contained by the distinctive chorus which deftly opens up for the guitars of Papa and Papi.
author: Maud Hand

text: Theres a subtle energy to Bana Congo which uplifts rather than over-exerts.
author: Maud Hand

text: Not for these sixty-somethings the sweat of soukous or timba.
author: Maud Hand

text: Rather the tender yet up-tempo rhythms of rumba and son.
author: Maud Hand

text: With songs sung in Spanish, French and Lingala and excellent sleeve notes, this album truly celebrates the Afro-Cuban connection.
author: Maud Hand

text: If most British listeners have an image at all of Spanish choral music, it will be of Renaissance masters such as Victoria and Lobo, who brought a special fervour to the seamless 16th-century contrapuntal style.
author: Matthew Shorter

text: So neglected is 19th-century Spanish choral music that the majority of recordings on this disc, recently selected by Gramophone as a Critics' Choice CD of the year, are world premieres.
author: Matthew Shorter

text: The Coro Cervantes - Britain's only professional group devoted to Hispanic classical repertoire - and their director Carlos Fernandez Aransay are clearly on a mission of discovery and recovery.
author: Matthew Shorter

text: Their zeal shines forth in these performances, whose passion is balanced by finely-nuanced direction and precise ensemble.
author: Matthew Shorter

text: The excitement of discovery is especially palpable in the first four tracks of the disc, which in their awestruck polyphony capture something of the spirit and technique of the Renaissance greats, from the numinous opening of Albeniz's a capella psalm setting to Vicente Goioechea's impassioned Christus Factus est, via some splendid organ fanfares in Granados' Salve Regina and a perfect minute-long sliver of a motet by Falla.
author: Matthew Shorter

text: The appearance of great names such as Albeniz, Granados, Falla and Sor in the unfamiliar guise of sacred choral music is one of the best surprises of the collection.
author: Matthew Shorter

text: At just under 80 minutes and with 19 tracks this disc is good value, though such a rich feast demands a lot of the musical digestion.
author: Matthew Shorter

text: Every work but one is in Latin, and the acoustic and organ of Exeter College chapel, Oxford make for a somewhat uniform texture - albeit wonderfully mellow and full-bodied across a well-balanced recording.
author: Matthew Shorter

text: But thoughtful programming is very helpful here, with a capella numbers and those with organ accompaniment alternating to vary the texture, and several works featuring a solo part peppered throughout.
author: Matthew Shorter

text: There's also a range of idiom and mood, from the sublime intimacy of the more modern opening numbers to the light-hearted and operatic, by way of Francisco Barbieri's dramatic word-painting and Pedrell's densely syllabic settings.
author: Matthew Shorter

text: If at times the quality of the music seem uneven, this is probably a fair reflection of a period in which Spanish church music seems to have been under attack from all sides, as first Napoleonic invaders and later the Spanish government itself seized church assets, closed music chapels and finally banned lay musicians from performing in churches.
author: Matthew Shorter

text: Hardly surprising that the choral tradition became somewhat impoverished as a result - which makes the care and attention that have clearly gone into assembling what is generally a very strong collection all the more impressive.
author: Matthew Shorter

text: Lucie de Lammermoor?
author: Annabel Caulton

text: Surely some mistake...
author: Annabel Caulton

text: But no, this is Donizetti's version of Walter Scott's novel dressed up for the Paris Opera in 1839.
author: Annabel Caulton

text: Dressed down, rather: this isn't just Lucia di Lammermoor translated into French - Donizetti's been at it with a pruning knife, and we've even lost the role of Alisa (Lucia's maid)...so our tragic heroine is utterly alone, adrift on a sea of testosterone.
author: Annabel Caulton

text: Donizetti specialists are automatically interested; for the rest of us it's the casting of the leads that's the draw: Roberto Alagna as Edgard, without the wife at his side for a change...and Natalie Dessay sings Lucie, a part irrecoverably owned by either Joan Sutherland or Maria Callas, depending which school of opera fanatic you happen across in the foyer.
author: Annabel Caulton

text: The funny thing is I don't want to compare Dessay to either of them: this Lucie is such a different animal, utterly believable as the naive, beautiful girl whose forced marriage to a much older man tips her over the edge into one of the most famous mad scenes in opera.
author: Annabel Caulton

text: Dessay's voice is a wonder: crystal clear, devastatingly accurate, and with a remarkable power and flexibility...no hint of strain even at the outer limits.
author: Annabel Caulton

text: Which brings us to Roberto Alagna, who's tended to heave himself at his last few roles on record, with the strain all too evident.
author: Annabel Caulton

text: This is an altogether happier result: an ardent, impassioned performance, and for once the sense of struggle adds to the weight of the character.
author: Annabel Caulton

text: There are no weak links in this cast, and Ludovic Tezier is outstanding as Lucie's scheming older brother, Henri Ashton.
author: Annabel Caulton

text: Evalino Pido supports his singers sensitively, sustains the dramatic tension, and the Lyon Opera forces never flag.
author: Annabel Caulton

text: It's an outstanding recording aswell, warm, detailed, and with a velvety bass that packs quite a punch in the climaxes.
author: Annabel Caulton

text: You may not think you need to hear Donizetti's masterpiece in French, but you really should hear Dessay making sense of the title role in a way I've never heard before, and worth the price of admission on her own.
author: Annabel Caulton

text: There's a certain grace about Patty Griffin that sets her apart from fellow coffee-house singer-songwriters like Eliza Gilkyson, Lucy Kaplansky and Catie Curtis.
author: Sue Keogh

text: It could be in her delicate, melodic picking, the poetry of her lyrics or her yearning vocal; whatever it is, there were fisticuffs between Led Zeppelin bassist John Paul Jones and Daniel Lanois over who would produce her 1996 debut Living With Ghosts (she eventually released the demo version instead).
author: Sue Keogh

text: Quickly taken to the heart of the wider country and Americana community, her songs have been taken on by Reba McEntire, Emmylou Harris, Buddy and Julie Miller and the Dixie Chicks, who chose two for their all-killer-no-filler album Home.
author: Sue Keogh

text: Her last album,1000 Kisses shunned the rock sound of 2000's Flaming Red - on which she had built such a firm fanbase - for something altogether more gentle.
author: Sue Keogh

text: Produced again by Craig Ross, Impossible Dream continues with the acoustic mood.
author: Sue Keogh

text: Nostalgia is in plentiful supply, from the woman taking one last look around before fleeing town in ''Useless Desires'', to the echoing piano and Emmlyou Harris drifting harmonies in ''Kite Song'' adding weight to the childish memories already hanging heavy in the air.
author: Sue Keogh

text: An old man mulling over a life of opportunities wasted is to be found in ''Top of The World''; here Griffin's breathy vocal and Lisa Germano's violin offer a more subtle and intimate atmosphere than in Natalie Maine's version on Home.
author: Sue Keogh

text: The semi-autobiographical ''Florida''tells of two girls cheerfully heading down to the Sunshine State, only to become faces in the crowd.
author: Sue Keogh

text: With simple words she hones in on that feeling of isolation; 'Isn't it hard sometimes, isn't it lonely?/ how I still hang around here/ and there's nothing to hold me'.
author: Sue Keogh

text: It's a grower, this album.
author: Sue Keogh

text: But to ease you in gently, the UK version includes some great live versions of old tracks ''Chief'', ''Rain'' and ''Truth #2'', recorded in Nashville's Ryman Auditorium.
author: Sue Keogh

text: Just the thing to get you in the mood for her live performances in the UK this summer.
author: Sue Keogh

text: In the case of global superstars like Shania Twain it's often easy to forget how long it takes to promote your latest album - for the world is a BIG place.
author: Chris Jones

text: While the album Up!
author: Chris Jones

text: came out in November 2002 the juggernaut that is Shania and her touring band have been plugging it ever since.
author: Chris Jones

text: Fans in the UK who missed her Hyde Park gig last summer will get the chance to see the show in February 2004, but in the meantime they can (p)re-live the experience with this glossy document of an open air gig in Chicago from this year's US leg of the tour.
author: Chris Jones

text: With the obligatory 5.1 surround sound mix and pin sharp visuals, DVD is fast becoming the place to experience any band in a live context (short of being in the front row) and Shania's utilised the advantages to the max.
author: Chris Jones

text: The question remains; just how country is this really?
author: Chris Jones

text: Her band are honed to perfection and the string section always provide the requisite hoedown feel; yet the enormous line-up (four guitarists anyone?) and tub-thumping drummer (in irritatingly wacky goggles) provide power that's more readily associated with stadium rockers.
author: Chris Jones

text: Of course, if you're playing a stadium this is only to be expected.
author: Chris Jones

text: But one can't help hesitating slightly at the spectacle that's born of multi-million predecessors such as Garth Brooks.
author: Chris Jones

text: Shania may wish to rock this country (as she does on the last track) but the spectre of husband Mutt Lange's production leaves the whole thing sounding more like Def Leppard than Dolly Parton.
author: Chris Jones

text: The performances are photocopy-perfect (almost too much so in the vocal department; one suspects a fair amount of post-production) but the live setting and crowd ambience make it a far from sterile experience.
author: Chris Jones

text: Shania works the crowd in her inimitable style - even duetting with some cutesy little kids plucked from the audience on ''I'm Gonna Get You Good'' and there's no denying the pop power of material like ''Man!
author: Chris Jones

text: I Feel Like A Woman!'' And ''Nah!'' (doesn't she ever tire of those exclamation marks?).
author: Chris Jones

text: Overall, you know exactly what you're getting with Ms Twain, and for her fans this is bound to be a very good thing indeed.
author: Chris Jones

text: Can the rest of us just have a little more country next time around?
author: Chris Jones

text: Big Brovaz is a homegrown UK hip-hop outfit and they've just broken through to the big time.
author: Will Sansom

text: They're a tight act whose perseverance has paid off and now they've proven themselves in commercial circles.
author: Will Sansom

text: They broadcast a creed which looks at both sides of anti-social and materialistic behaviour, as well as the importance of honesty in relationships.
author: Will Sansom

text: This is refreshing, this is the Gospel according to Big Brovaz.
author: Will Sansom

text: The calm and collected messages delivered on this album can tend to sound out of place in the hip hop arena.
author: Will Sansom

text: Yet Lauryn Hill has already successfully broken musical stereotypes with caring rhyme and reason.
author: Will Sansom

text: There is no reason why others shouldn't follow a good example.
author: Will Sansom

text: Having said this, the Brovaz' male contingent definitely play off the ladies' harmonious tones and melodies.
author: Will Sansom

text: "Don't Matter" is filled with plenty of cheeky banter from the boys' corner.
author: Will Sansom

text: "Nu Flow" is a cracker of a party track which starts this LP off to an energetic yet laid-back start.
author: Will Sansom

text: It is easy to find similarities between the Big Brovaz bouncin beats and Outkast's spoken fluidity.
author: Will Sansom

text: However, their supportive and positive attitudes link them more closely with acts like City High and of course the original hip-hop music aficionados The Fugees.
author: Will Sansom

text: Another stand-out number comes in the from of "Find a Way".
author: Will Sansom

text: The Brovaz bring to light the problems associated with a far from affluent existence.
author: Will Sansom

text: Filled with feeling, it takes a popular Busta Rhymes type beat and the soul of a Mary J.
author: Will Sansom

text: Blige style vocal.
author: Will Sansom

text: The result is emotionally fuelled.
author: Will Sansom

text: These guys give off enough energy to keep 'em rolling well beyond this album.
author: Will Sansom

text: Hip-hop has been embraced by wider audiences throughout its evolution.
author: Will Sansom

text: So it's perfectly natural that modern production will incorporate quality blends of R&B, soul and garage with positive results.
author: Will Sansom

text: If you like the bumpin' beats and don't care much for rowdy hip hop banter then you'll feel at home here.
author: Will Sansom

text: Nu Flow is definitely best described as the his and hers of hip-hop albums.
author: Will Sansom

text: Having adhered to the Alison Krauss 'shhh, not so loud!' approach to production for their excellent first two albums, young prog-bluegrass trio Nickel Creek are now under the guidance of Good Charlotte and Queens Of The Stone Age producer Eric Valentine.Andthey'reclearly enjoying the chance to clatter around a bit more.
author: Sue Keogh

text: It's like they've found their dark side.
author: Sue Keogh

text: Fiddle player and squeaky clean vocalist Sara Watkins now has a much more assertive edge, and the lyrics have gone beyond putting one's lover on a pedestal to something altogether more scathing; "I hope you meet someone your height so you can see eye to eye/ With someone as small as you" ("Somebody More Like You").Sounds like someone upset Sean Watkins before he wrote that song.
author: Sue Keogh

text: Why Should The Fire Die is one of those albums which grows on you, revealing more light and shade with each listen.
author: Sue Keogh

text: But what shines through immediately is the sheer musical brilliance, found in the careful harmonies of the title track or the intricacy of the arrangements on "Helena" and "Eveline".
author: Sue Keogh

text: Seeing mandolinist Chris Thile and his cohorts perform live is something you do with an open mouth, and while it's always difficult to capture that energy on a studio recording, the instrumentals certainly give you a flavour of the fun they'll be having on the road this year; "First And Last Waltz" is smooth and dreamy, "Stumptown" is a merry little jig, and "Scotch And Chocolate" is just reel-y good, ho ho ho.
author: Sue Keogh

text: All the songs are written by the band, with the exception of Dylan favourite "Tomorrow Is A Long Time" and a co-write with Jayhawk Gary Louris on "Jealous Of The Moon" (think Soul Asylum).
author: Sue Keogh

text: Considering the artists they've worked with lately from Dolly Parton and John Paul Jones to the LA Philharmonic, this timid choice of collaborator is a missed opportunity to be really adventurous and at the same time grab the column inches they so rightfully deserve.
author: Sue Keogh

text: Outlaws And Angels is the third in a series of live specials produced for American television.
author: Sue Keogh

text: Like its predecessors, Stars and Guitars (2002) and Live And Kickin (2003), it sees Nelson teaming up with some country pals - this time it's Merle Haggard, Toby Keith, Lucinda Williams and Lee Ann Womack, with whom he recently won a Grammy for "Mendocino County Line" - and making unusual pairings with artists outside the genre.
author: Sue Keogh

text: Gracing the intimate surroundings of the Wiltern LG auditorium in Los Angeles are Kid Rock (who IS this guy?
author: Sue Keogh

text: Does his Mum sponsor him five bucks for every time he gets on stage at a country gig?), Al Green, Toots Hibbert, Keith Richards, Jerry Lee Lewis and allegedly Bob Dylan, who's there in the press release but conspicuous by his absence on the album itself.
author: Sue Keogh

text: Perhaps he got scared.
author: Sue Keogh

text: Because, like the first two albums in the series, it's just a big ol' mess.
author: Sue Keogh

text: Everyone has cottoned on to Nelson's trademark style of straying from the beat, to the point that no one is in time with anyone else.
author: Sue Keogh

text: The sound is muggy, the performances unrehearsed, and they whip through the whole thing so quickly you'd think the bar was about to close.It probably looked great on t'telly; who wouldn't want to see what Jerry Lee Lewis, Keith Richard and Merle Haggard do with the rock'n'roll classic "Whole Lotta Shaking Going On"?
author: Sue Keogh

text: But with only your ears to rely on, one can't help but spot all the flaws.
author: Sue Keogh

text: The one which looked most promising on paper, "Will You Still Love Me Tomorrow?" finds Nelson needing to clear this throat and Carole King's voice wobbling uncontrollably, with the result that all the subtlety and delicacy of the original is knocked sideways.
author: Sue Keogh

text: Even the old Outlaws classic "Pancho And Lefty", which these guys have been playing for nearly thirty years now, manages to get screwed up by everyone coming in on the wrong beat and Haggard's electric guitar solos going all over the place; it's up to young honorary Outlaw Toby Keith to save the day with an authoritative vocal.
author: Sue Keogh

text: The whole thing ends with the gospel favourite "I'll Fly Away", which was delivered with great precision recently by Alison Krauss and Gillian Welch on the O Brother, Where At Thou?
author: Sue Keogh

text: soundtrack but is performed here in that forgivably sloppy end-of-night everyone-get-on-stage kind of way.
author: Sue Keogh

text: Top marks for barnstormin' atmosphere, but it sure don't sound great in your CD player.
author: Sue Keogh

text: The country superstar's first album since 2002's desperately commercial Cry sees her taking a more downhome turn; the prominence of the mandolins and steel, the 'I'm just Jenny from the block' style protestations in "Mississippi Girl" and even her new brunette look, for which she quite literally went back to her roots, ho ho.
author: Sue Keogh

text: She's one of those rare artists from whom you actually want to hear more power ballads, and here the duet with husband Tim McGraw "Like We Never Loved At All" is on a par with previous gems like "Breathe" and "There You'll Be".
author: Sue Keogh

text: But it's far from schmaltzy.
author: Sue Keogh

text: The complex relationships featured in the three Lori McKenna songs, the light-hearted "Sunshine And Summertime" and the shotgun wedding humour of "Dearly Beloved" help make Fireflies one of the most enjoyable albums of Hill's 12 year career.
author: Sue Keogh

text: Shania Twain is a much better pop singer than country singer.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Her early material, placed at the end of this compilation, is pretty average 'new country'.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: The songs are routine, the production flat.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Shania warbles and gabbles as though her mind is elsewhere.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: On the hits from the multi-platinum Come On Over, Shania and her producer Robert Mutt Lange raise their game.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Lange has a vision of perfect pop music: bright, shiny, technology driven, stuffed with hooks.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Every note and detail is obsessively placed for maximum impact.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: When the songs are great, the effect is stunning.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: "Still The One" is wonderful, romantic, sweet; the perfect wedding song.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: I played it at my own wedding.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: I Feel Like A Woman" is the sound of a thousand Saturday nights in clubs all over the Western World.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: "From This Moment On" features a beautiful melody, a power ballad with real power.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: "Honey I'm Home" is Def Leppard for the working woman; "Love Gets Me Every Time" is infectiously cheerful.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: But when the songs are less than first class they can sound cloying and too fussy.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: "I'm Gonna Get Ya!" is impressive but "Up!" sounds thrown together.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: There are too many exclamation marks -"Kerching!" is a bizarre mistake.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Shania attacks greed and consumerism to a backing track that's part Bollywood, part Coolio's "Gangsta's Paradise".
author: Nick Reynolds

text: It's a bit odd coming from someone who's prepared to stick a horrible disco beat on "That Don't Impress Me Much" in order to sell more copies.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Shania's best is as good as the classic adult pop of the Carpenters, the epic productions of Trevor Horn or even the twinkling machine music of Kraftwerk.But Richard Carpenter would never have gone near something as tasteless as "Kerching!".
author: Nick Reynolds

text: This CD is a good Christmas present for Shania Twain fans.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: For students of pop music, there are many examples of how to do it right here.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: And how to do it wrong.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: "Auntie Dorothy", as several generations of appreciative southern African fans call this warm and charismatic singer, was born in Bulawayo.
author: John Armstrong

text: Although technically Zimbabwean, many Bulawayans feel they have more in common with their Zulu neighbours just a few miles away in South Africa.
author: John Armstrong

text: Many of Dorothy's most celebrated songs are in Ndebele, a language much closer to Kwazulu than to Zimbabwe'smajority tongue, Shona.
author: John Armstrong

text: Consequently, this excellent introduction to her work will sound immediately familiar to fans of Dorothy's much better-known South African contemporary, Miriam Makeba.
author: John Armstrong

text: Mariams career moves brought her much greater exposure than the equally gifted Masuka.
author: John Armstrong

text: The collection wisely concentrates on Masuka's exceptional talents as a songwriter.
author: John Armstrong

text: She recorded her very first song (also the first on this compilation) 'Nonstokolo', in 1953 whilst a schoolgirl.
author: John Armstrong

text: An immediate hit, she followed it up with 'Iyo Pata Pata', later recorded and made world-famous by Makeba.
author: John Armstrong

text: Other tunes that you'll subliminally 'recognise', even if you're unaware of having heard them before, are 'Nhingirikiri', 'Teya Teya', and 'Ufikizolo'.
author: John Armstrong

text: They all have that easy-rolling swing tempo that is the hallmark of early marabi jazz and penny-whistle jive.
author: John Armstrong

text: A great collection and good value, too: 20 good cuts and no filler, with liner notes that draw on recent interviews with the lady herself rather than just rehashing old album sleevenotes.
author: John Armstrong

text: One minor reservation: some of her most artistically successful work appeared on the album 'Ingalo', recorded for Zimbabwe's Starplate label in about 1987.
author: John Armstrong

text: Perhaps due to the current difficulties in Zimbabwe, it simply wasn't possible to license any of that material.
author: John Armstrong

text: But if you like what you hear on this record, search out the Starplate albumin the secondhand shops.
author: John Armstrong

text: And now let's have a long-overdue collection from the third great female singer of that era and locality, Dolly Rathebe....
author: John Armstrong

text: It's refreshing to see Martine McCutcheon tackling Broadway standards and songs from the shows.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: She has professed her love of Barbra Streisand and Liza Minnelli, and must be applauded for having the courage to tackle this material.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: The Broadway tradition still survives because many of the songs are of the highest quality.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: You need a big voice and a big personality to sing them.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Theatre acting, particularly musicals, requires the artiste to start over the top and then go further over.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Whereas television, Martine's forte so far, works best when underplayed.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: So it's a surprise that this album works best on the more theatrical, uptempo songs.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: On anything where she has to play a character, say "Nobody Does It Like Me" or "Diamonds Are A Girl's Best Friend", she manages to be warm, entertaining and even swings a little.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: "Lady is a Tramp" is one of the album's highpoints and she tackles "Don't Rain On My Parade" very well.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: On the ballads she is less convincing although she does manage to deliver a pretty good version of a pretty awful song in "Can You Feel The Love Tonight".
author: Nick Reynolds

text: But the selection of songs is patchy, poorly sequenced and does not always play to Martine's strengths.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: "The Winner Takes It All" is spoilt by a lumbering arrangement.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: And, as usual, this CD is far too long, and ends with unappealing versions of "What I Did For Love" and "White Christmas".
author: Nick Reynolds

text: So in the end Musicality is frustrating.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Better care in the choice of songs might have resulted in more of an artistic success, although perhaps less of a commercial one.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: But, if she chooses, Martine will have a good career ahead of her in musical theatre.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: She's not quite a diva yet, but give her time...
author: Nick Reynolds

text: He's back again with his third solo album Higher Level.
author: Darren 'Shaq-D' Springer

text: Yes, I'm talking about none other than the 'Energy God'; Jamaica's undisputed No.1 and MOBO award nominee Elephant Man.
author: Darren 'Shaq-D' Springer

text: Even from looking at the cover, it's obvious that Elephant Man has not lost any of his originality - the bright yellow locks are still intact.
author: Darren 'Shaq-D' Springer

text: His unique vocal style is displayed in one of this year's massive hits "Tall Up Tall Up".Produced by Stone Love (Jamaica's leading sound system), Elephant Man shows his diversity with a combination of classical singing and his usual dancehall lisp DJ style.
author: Darren 'Shaq-D' Springer

text: This can only be described as 'Elephant Man featuring Elephant Man'.
author: Darren 'Shaq-D' Springer

text: Higher Level also includes Elephant Man's main hits of the year: "Look", "On Line", "Approach", "Do Yuh Ting", "Elephant Message" and the explosive "Bad Man A Bad Man" which is a re-version of R.
author: Darren 'Shaq-D' Springer

text: Kelly's World's Greatest (another Stone Love production.) Fresh tracks include "Give Her It Good" (from the Diwali rhythm), "Egyptian Dance", "Low Mi Name", and "Party Like This" featuring Jagwa.This track has a nice soulful feel and if released as a single,could do well on the international scene.
author: Darren 'Shaq-D' Springer

text: Destined for big things due to its crossover appeal is "Run For Your Life" featuring newcomer Jarvis Church.This tells the deadly story of a star struck fan who takes things to a higher level (excuse the pun).
author: Darren 'Shaq-D' Springer

text: 'Run for your life, she cut you with a knife' is a warning to all Jamaican celebrities.
author: Darren 'Shaq-D' Springer

text: Elephant Man hasn't failed us with Higher Level; it is a befitting follow up to last year's massiveLog On.
author: Darren 'Shaq-D' Springer

text: Limber up for the inevitable dance crazes that will surely emerge as this album blows up.
author: Darren 'Shaq-D' Springer

text: It's packed with hits and oozes energy, and in the words of the man himself, "You No".
author: Darren 'Shaq-D' Springer

text: Yusa is a singer and a songwriter from Cuba, born in the celebrated Buena Vista district of Havana.
author: Neil Bennun

text: The Buena Vista Social Club, however, this certainly isn't.
author: Neil Bennun

text: It isn't that she actively shies away from Cuba's much-feted musical heritage on this debut CD.
author: Neil Bennun

text: It's more that she draws her influences from all over the American continent and wears them proudly to produce bright, soulful, contemporary Cuban music with intelligent arrangements, excellent lyrics and an international flavour.
author: Neil Bennun

text: Like a vocally dexterous Tracy Chapman with a large jazz collection, her songs display a definite melancholic tinge, nicely leavened by her Brazilian and Cuban influences.
author: Neil Bennun

text: 'Cuestion de Angulo' (A Question of Angle) is a good case in point.
author: Neil Bennun

text: It begins with unaccompanied acoustic guitar reminiscent of Joni Mitchell until a salsa clave rhythm strikes up over a bossa nova shuffle.
author: Neil Bennun

text: "I let the impertinence of that silence loose into the street", she sings, before the tune plays out with a choral arrangement like classic Airto Moriera (think advertisements featuring Ronaldo or Roberto Carlos shown in the ad breaks of the World Cup).
author: Neil Bennun

text: She displays a yen for striking organic funk music ('Involucion', complete with nifty strings, harmonies and a rap in rapid-fire Spanish) and sweet latin soul ('Tienta Paredes').
author: Neil Bennun

text: And she has a splendid facility for reworking more traditional latin music forms in songs like 'A las Doce' and 'La Partida', incorporating elements of Cuban vocal music and bossa nova with choirs and high-velocity acoustic guitar.
author: Neil Bennun

text: The horn arrangements are striking, the sound modern and soulful.
author: Neil Bennun

text: Others like Lenine and Chico Cesar have revitalised traditional Brazilian musics by incorporating funk and soul influences into forro and maractu.
author: Neil Bennun

text: Similarly, Yusa has shaken up son and filin to make something distinctively Cuban but proudly international.
author: Neil Bennun

text: An excellent, sophisticated, debut.
author: Neil Bennun

text: Imagine that Ed Harcourt's debut album is a bottle of wine, found by chance in a cool, undisturbed place.
author: Annabel Caulton

text: The caveat on the label is'Here be Monsters'.
author: Annabel Caulton

text: Don't say you haven't been warned.
author: Annabel Caulton

text: Uncorked; the first hints of mellow fruitiness dance from the bottle.
author: Annabel Caulton

text: A dark, velveteen residue lingers at the bottom, cloaking something decidedly more sinister.
author: Annabel Caulton

text: In much the same way, this collection of songs -some finely polished versions of earlier tinkerings from the Maplewood EP - can ease you towards divine intoxication.
author: Annabel Caulton

text: With a voice that sounds like it's been refined through years of excess and a cacophony of words and instrumentation that play like a musical zoo crawling with creatures from Maurice Sendak's 'Where the Wild Things Are', Harcourt breaks us in gently with the first track, the rhythmically soothing "Something in my Eye".
author: Annabel Caulton

text: "God Protect your Soul", is made of meaner stuff, laden with low, off key notes, Mariachi style trumpets and piano keys tumbling with waterfall abandon.
author: Annabel Caulton

text: It's not all brooding insolence though, there are glorious, uplifting love songs that pluck playfully at your heartstrings."Shanghai", "Apple of my Eye" and "She fell into my Arms" make your soul swoop and incorporate a heady cocktail of musical instruments including banjos, vibraphones, trombones and harmonicas.
author: Annabel Caulton

text: He mixes pure pop and grungy rock with odd, quirky experimentation.
author: Annabel Caulton

text: The solo trumpet on "Beneath The Heart Of Darkness", played over a swirly, backward loop is apparently inspired by a dodgy boiler.
author: Annabel Caulton

text: Starting with a cranky rhythm and lulling grace it descends into the sound of a madman's mind, buzzing with bees.
author: Annabel Caulton

text: The songfinally reaches a psychotic crescendo and falling into a pacified calm.
author: Annabel Caulton

text: It's not surprising to hear that Ed drafted in producers Dave Fridmann (Mercury Rev) and Gil Norton (Pixies and Throwing Muses among others) to add their edge.
author: Annabel Caulton

text: Or that his influences include Tom Waits, Chet Baker and more recently Perry Farrell of Jane's Addiction fame.
author: Annabel Caulton

text: He mingles well with Beth Orton and Neil Finn and sits comfortably on the wine rack with the Eels and Elliot Smith.
author: Annabel Caulton

text: So, pull up an armchair, uncork the bottle and get deliriously drunk with Ed Harcourt and his monsters.
author: Annabel Caulton

text: Ed Harcourt escorted me home the other night.
author: Richard Banks

text: Not personally, you understand, but via my headphones, on the last northbound tube.
author: Richard Banks

text: When you're feeling tired, emotional and woozy, there are few songwriters that proffer a musical hug like Ed.
author: Richard Banks

text: There's just something about his melodic blend of romance and melodrama that's innately comforting.
author: Richard Banks

text: The album in question that night was his second, From Every Sphere, one of my favourite records of 2003.
author: Richard Banks

text: Since then, he's been frolicking in Swedish snow, touring the US with REM and, most importantly, falling in love.
author: Richard Banks

text: Strangers is the end product of an eventful year, it would seem, and Ed's talent certainly hasn't waned.
author: Richard Banks

text: Listening to Mr.
author: Richard Banks

text: Harcourt is an acutely intimate experience, like catching up one-on-one with an old friend.
author: Richard Banks

text: His lyrics are consistently charming and personable ("My parents named me Ed, I tried my hardest to smile" he sings on "Born In The 70s").
author: Richard Banks

text: His vocal production is faultless and his ability to captivate the listener unfailing (see the beautiful, organ-drenched "Something To Live For").
author: Richard Banks

text: What is most striking about his writing on Strangers, however, is the apparent sincerity of his sentiment.
author: Richard Banks

text: It's certainly his most candid record to date.
author: Richard Banks

text: When he sings "my heart is on its sleeve" in lead single "This One's For You" he really means it; it's a gorgeous, drunken ode to new love along the lines of Badly Drawn Boy's "Pissing In The Wind" with wistful horns that tug at the heart strings.
author: Richard Banks

text: Elsewhere, Ed shows he can be dramatic as well as delicate.
author: Richard Banks

text: "The Storm Is Coming" and "Let Love Not Weigh Me Down" are rousing, dizzying epics that would sit happily in a Jeff Buckley songbook, whilst "The Music Box" tells a poignant wartime tale.
author: Richard Banks

text: The record benefits from a richness of sound throughout and is graced with a healthy variety of instruments, played mainly by Ed himself (and presumably that includes the playful kazoo on the title track).
author: Richard Banks

text: Although the tail end of the album doesn't quite reach the standard set by the bulk of the songs on offer here, Strangers is further proof that Ed Harcourt is one of the UKs finest songwriters.
author: Richard Banks

text: As you might expect, John Peel's contribution to the excellent Fabriclive series is not like the others.It's not perfect.
author: Matt Fernand

text: It's not even really that great when you pick it apart but it's got soul, imagination and style.
author: Matt Fernand

text: And in these days when rumours persist that certain DJs are more likely to be in Ibiza having their eyebrows flossed while a personal assistant produces their mix CDs, Peel's weak spots here are forgivable.
author: Matt Fernand

text: This isn't strictly a mix CD.
author: Matt Fernand

text: It's more a collection of curiosities and classics with some added football commentary.
author: Matt Fernand

text: It's not really 100% Peel either.Someone has smartened it up with a computer so that all the tunes come in at the right speed.
author: Matt Fernand

text: If it was the real Peel we would get three seconds of something we heard 5 minutes ago, followed by a long apology and then the thing he actually meant to play.
author: Matt Fernand

text: If the skills aren't John's, then the choices certainly are.Nobody else would have segued the lumpy jump up of MC Det's "Hipsteppin'" into the classic girl-band sound of the Velvelettes "Needle in a Haystack".
author: Matt Fernand

text: Likewise running the mighty, ramshackle racket of The Fall's "Mr Pharmacist" into the twisted techno of Smith and Selway's "15.5 Remake" reminds you why he's been 40 years in the business.Because he's the goddam MAN!!
author: Matt Fernand

text: The feel of this thing is more like a compilation tape your mate made you, and that includes a few tunes that only an owner could love.
author: Matt Fernand

text: So alongside classics like Joy Division's"Love Will Tear Us Apart" and the inevitable closer, "Teenage Kicks", there comes the lame doo-wop of The Capris' "There's a Moon Out Tonight" and the equally forgettable R'n'B of Act 1's "Tom the Peeper".
author: Matt Fernand

text: But somehow they just sort of add to the charm.
author: Matt Fernand

text: Now that's another thing mix CD's don't have.
author: Matt Fernand

text: Hank Jones (elder brother of Elvin and Thad) is one of the elder statesmen of Jazz piano.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Like fellow Detroit school player Tommy Flanagan, Jones' style is marked by an unfussy, straightahead approach derived from stride playing,delivered with a deceptively light touch.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Unfairly, his reputation as an accompanist (mainly due to 5 years with Ella Fitzgerald) has always outshone that of his abilities as a soloist, despite a fine string of trio dates that stretches from the 50s to today.
author: Peter Marsh

text: This set pairs up two Jones sessions, Rockin in Rhythm and Lazy Afternoon from 1977 and 1989 respectively.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The earlier set sees Jones in relaxed, playful form and marks a rare dalliance with Fender Rhodes piano on a few tunes.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Like Bill Evans, he doesn't sound comfortable with the thicker sonorities of the electric instrument, though on "My Ship" Jones' delicacy shines brightly.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The title track is admirably despatched (as is a bouncy "Bags' Groove"), with the wonderful Ray Brown and drummer Jimmie Smith in supple, propulsive form throughout.
author: Peter Marsh

text: If Rockin' in Rhythm is meat n' potatoes stuff, then Lazy Afternoon is definitely the gravy.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Pairing Jones' then regular trio of Dave Holland and Keith Copeland with Ken Peplowski on half the tracks, it's agem of a session.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Peplowski's airy revivalist alto and clarinet (both drawing heavily from Benny Goodman) fit neatly with the leader's classy swing.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The lovely title track has a whiff of Ellington in its carefully paced atmospherics, with discreet touches of celeste colouring the long shadows cast by Peplowski's doleful clarinet.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Beautiful, resonant stuff.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Holland's presence may surprise those used to hearing him in more adventurous settings, but he seems quite at home.
author: Peter Marsh

text: As usual he's inventive and alert, turning out fine solos (especially on J.J.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Johnson's poignant "Lament").
author: Peter Marsh

text: Copeland's a bit heavy handed at times; some of his breaks sound as though they've been beamed in from a different session entirely.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Despite this slight reservation, it's hard not to be captivated by this warmhearted, engaging set.
author: Peter Marsh

text: German guitarist Rupp plays acoustic instruments exclusively on this solo CD, and initially, his work might bring to mind another underground favourite, Steffen Basho-Junghans.
author: Bill Tilland

text: Indeed, common points of reference do exist.
author: Bill Tilland

text: Basho-Junghans favors hypnotic, repetitive chords, loaded with overtones and harmonics.
author: Bill Tilland

text: Rupp follows that formula on one piece ("#7"), where a single chord is struck rhythmically and repeatedly, creating a buzzing, amorphous cloud of overtones.
author: Bill Tilland

text: But in general Scree dazzles with jagged runs of dissonant note clusters and chords, often suggesting a species of turbocharged, wayward flamenco and "outside" classical guitar, mixed with a some elements of traditional Chinese music (particularly for the pipa, an ancient four-stringed lute).
author: Bill Tilland

text: Rupp played an electric Fender Stratocaster on his debut recording, Life Science, but his intensity on this CD clearly doesn't suffer as a result of unplugging.
author: Bill Tilland

text: In fact, hearing all of this energy electrified might be way too much of a good thing.
author: Bill Tilland

text: "Scree" is defined as "a mass of debris comprising loose fragments of rock," and the twelve pieces on this recording do conjure up, in terms of notes, a great many small hard, inter-related objects with a dangerous latent energy.
author: Bill Tilland

text: The swarming, smothering sound of Rupp's rippling arpeggios, lightning runs and staccato chords is perhaps symbolic of some inexorable force, e.g., a tumbling avalanche of musical scree, although the force is not always in motion, and the music sometimes slips into a more reflective mode.
author: Bill Tilland

text: In fact, once Rupp's amazing tour de force digital dexterity has served its notice on the first several pieces, the silences between the notes gradually become more prominent, giving the listener a chance to take a breath and assimilate the ebb and flow of the music.
author: Bill Tilland

text: Some later tracks actually invite a kind of contemplation, with the frequent use of microtones, harmonics and string damping giving some of the more subdued pieces an austere Zen Buddhist quality.
author: Bill Tilland

text: All in all, Rupp offers up an exciting, challenging CD, highly musical in the broadest sense, and a must for anyone who likes to hear an acoustic guitar pushed to its physical and aesthetic limits.
author: Bill Tilland

text: Lost in Revelry, The Mendoza Lines' fourth album, is a rich multi-textured corker of a record, full of rare beauty and wit.
author: Nick Unwin

text: What's more it marvellously confounds the pigeonhole brigade by shifting effortlessly between sweet lonesome country and quirky 90s alt mellowness.
author: Nick Unwin

text: There is a wonderful mix of country roots and the mid-1990s indie world of Belly and The Breeders.
author: Nick Unwin

text: Formed in 1996 in Athens, Georgia - alsoREM's hometown- the band members appear to share a love of classic songwriters such as Bob Dylan and Elvis Costello.
author: Nick Unwin

text: The former is a blatant influence in the opening track, the swaggering "A Damn Good Disguise" and later in the meandering "The Queen Of England".
author: Nick Unwin

text: This country/indie vibe - an odd mix at the best of times - flows seamlessly together throughout the record and is a testament to the song-writing ability and musicianship of McArdle, Bracy, Hoffman et al.
author: Nick Unwin

text: This is encapsulated superbly in the manic duet on "Mistakes Were Made" sung by the gravely Hoffman and the sugar-sweet McArdle.
author: Nick Unwin

text: Indeed McArdle seems equally at home in either style.
author: Nick Unwin

text: In the desperate "I'm That" McArdle even manages to incorporate an almost Twin Peaks-esque dreamy melancholy and finishes with mournful beauty on the closing track "The Way Of The Weak".
author: Nick Unwin

text: Indeed, McArdle's saccharine voice, aligned with a liberal sprinkling of slide guitars, serve almost to mask the albums deep malevolence, maybe reflecting the band's recent move to the mean streets of Brooklyn.
author: Nick Unwin

text: Most songs cover a dazzling array of seriously messed-up human relationships and a variety of lost and lonesome souls.
author: Nick Unwin

text: The darkly witty, casually caustic wordplay of the album is illustrated during "It'll Be The Same Without You" where the rhythm almost lulls the listener into missing the deeply cutting lyrics: "Rest assured someone will quickly take your place and it will be the same without you".
author: Nick Unwin

text: Despite so many familiar touches, Lost In Revelry oozes originality.
author: Nick Unwin

text: If you're into quality song-writing and love being lulled into a false sense of security then you'd do well to add this album to your Xmas list.
author: Nick Unwin

text: Fortune, The Mendoza Line's fifth offering, sees the country crooners from Georgia return with a record filled with emotion.
author: Damian Jones

text: Joy, loss, pain and wit are all thrown effortlessly together to serve up an infectious album filled with intoxicating melodies.
author: Damian Jones

text: Since their last record, the band have been scouring the earth's plains and a life on the road has clearly influenced their new record.
author: Damian Jones

text: This is particularly evident on the stomping melody "Before I Hit The Wall".
author: Damian Jones

text: The upbeat lyric: "I want a big car with a kicking stereo - one that can go anywhere I wanna go", encapsulates the euphoric feeling of running away without a care in the world.
author: Damian Jones

text: This catchy country number, filled with killer hooks, is arguably one of the album's finest tracks.
author: Damian Jones

text: Equally as good is the heart wrenching "Let's Not Talk About It", a haunting, painful ballad lost in eerie chords and lifeless vocals.
author: Damian Jones

text: "Fellow Travelers" (correct spelling), is tinged with the same sad country vibe.
author: Damian Jones

text: The woozy backing vocals: "Wash it away, wash it away", give the song a real bluesy edge.
author: Damian Jones

text: But it's not all pain and misery.
author: Damian Jones

text: The album also contains a few detailed narratives; "It's A Long Line (But It Moves Quickly)" and a touch of wit; "An Architect's Eye".
author: Damian Jones

text: Naturally Bracy, Hoffman and McArdle mix up the vocal duties throughout.
author: Damian Jones

text: But at times McArdle's voice becomes grating, particularly on the dull final track "Throw It In the Fire" and the forgettable "Faithful Brother (Scourge Of The Land)".
author: Damian Jones

text: The same goes for the guys at times too.
author: Damian Jones

text: "Metro Pictures" dreary vocals fail to spark the imagination and doesn't match the more upbeat tracks like "Tiny Motions" and the witty "Road To Insolvency".
author: Damian Jones

text: Still this doesn't put too many dents in what is on the whole a creditable fifth record.
author: Damian Jones

text: Fortune still sounds damn good compared to the identikit indie crooners kicking about at the moment.
author: Damian Jones

text: Once upon a time there lived an extremely gifted pop princess who possessed beauty, poise and a set of vocals that would make the clouds smile.
author: Keysha Davis

text: Critics were perplexed by this seemingly perfect specimen, and swiftly termed her bland and banal.
author: Keysha Davis

text: However, a bad-boy husband, 120 million album sales, and rumours of a dubious lifestyle ensured that Whitney Houston never leaves the headlines.
author: Keysha Davis

text: With one of the most exceptional voices in contemporary music, her latest album, aptly titled Just Whitney sees the diva return to her former glory with a combination of high-voltage ballads and smooth-liqueur R&B.
author: Keysha Davis

text: 'Love That Man' sounds suspiciously like an ode to her much criticised hubby.
author: Keysha Davis

text: Here Whitney comes across as soulful and sincere as she ooohs and aaahs in the right places.
author: Keysha Davis

text: The mid-tempo track harks back to 80s soul with its simple bass line, and unfussy production.
author: Keysha Davis

text: 'One Of Those Days' also has a slight retro feel to it, cleverly sampling the Isley Brothers' Between the Sheets.
author: Keysha Davis

text: Modern day women will be able to relate to this one, as Whitney croons about the need to withdraw from the pressures of day-to-day living for a spot of girlie pampering.
author: Keysha Davis

text: Whitney has been experiencing her own fair share of pressure-cooker environments recently.
author: Keysha Davis

text: For evidence, look no further than 'Whatchulookinat', an assertive, defiant statement against her critics.
author: Keysha Davis

text: The gentle vocals, which appeared on previous tracks, have now been replaced by an authoritative Whitney stating: 'Unashamed by the life that I lead, the choices I've made, the things I have done, my belief in the one'.
author: Keysha Davis

text: The most welcomed return on Just Whitney is the incorporation of big love ballads; with the melancholic "On My Own" providing one of the album's highlights.
author: Keysha Davis

text: The big-band orchestral feel to this track provides the perfect platform for Whitney to deliver vocally.
author: Keysha Davis

text: Climaxing with one of those highly sustained notes sung in an octave that only the likes of Mariah, Celine and Aretha are capable of, she renders this track truly awesome.
author: Keysha Davis

text: The moral of this story is always stick to what you do best.
author: Keysha Davis

text: Whitney's return to big ballads will hopefully ensure that this pop princess will be able to lead the rest of her life like a cliched fairy tale - happily ever after.
author: Keysha Davis

text: Long before the likes of J-Lo and Britney Spears hypnotised the world with their frequently photographed rumps and midriffs, Toni Braxton spearheaded the cluster of desirable females with a knockout combination of seductive looks, silky vocal tones and an inclination towards dresses which seemed to be produced during a cloth shortage.
author: Keysha Davis

text: But image aside, Braxton's career CV can't be laughed at.
author: Keysha Davis

text: With six Grammys, seven American Music Awards and a total of 25 million worldwide album sales, record company bosses will be relying upon her to deliver the goods with her latest offering.
author: Keysha Davis

text: More Than A Woman is a diverse blend of danceable club numbers, trademark Braxton ballads and experimental tracks which borrow from the genres of rock and jazz.
author: Keysha Davis

text: First off is the feisty "Let Me Show You The Way (Out)".
author: Keysha Davis

text: A new woman's anthem for 2003?
author: Keysha Davis

text: I truly think so.
author: Keysha Davis

text: Over a hammering hip-hop bassline, angry incessant piano chords and Braxton's calm but commanding vocals lies a telling tale of infidelity, which sets the theme for the majority of the album.
author: Keysha Davis

text: Nothing demonstrates this so magically as "Hit The Freeway".
author: Keysha Davis

text: What at first sounds like a quintessential Neptunes track - melodic synthesiser, staged handclaps and funky drum patterns - later transpires into an impressive slice of pop R&B.
author: Keysha Davis

text: The chorus: "Farewell my lonely one, nothing else here can be done, I don't ever wanna see you again" is eagerly contagious.
author: Keysha Davis

text: Revenge has never sounded sweeter.
author: Keysha Davis

text: For your dosage of classic love songs, turn to the elegant "Always".
author: Keysha Davis

text: Harking back to the Toni of yesteryear,this is a tenderly honed R&B ballad with rich, multi-layered vocals, which add balance to the edgier, street-orientated tracks.
author: Keysha Davis

text: The album's surprise comes courtesy of Braxton's hubby, Keri Lewis who produced the standout track "Lies, Lies, Lies".
author: Keysha Davis

text: The most notable element on this record is the usage of live instrumentation.
author: Keysha Davis

text: Toni's vocals also provide an interesting mix, as her gravelly tones are pit against an electric guitar.
author: Keysha Davis

text: There's no doubt that More Than A Woman will sell bucket-loads.
author: Keysha Davis

text: At age 34 Braxton is in a great position to serve both middle-of-the-road listeners with her high-powered ballads, as well the comrades of the streets with her attitude-ridden take on modern day living.
author: Keysha Davis

text: Few rock supergroup line-ups in recent years have had fans slavering in anticipation as much as Audioslave, the band which emerged from the ashes of Rage Against The Machine's acrimonious split with singer Zak La Rocha.
author: Amy McAuliffe

text: The notion of Soundgarden's Chris Cornell stepping into La Rochas Fair Trade moccasins may have raised a few eyebrows.
author: Amy McAuliffe

text: But it will put a smile on the faces of those who have been itching to hear Cornell put his redoubtable talents to good use again.
author: Amy McAuliffe

text: All too often in the case of supergroups, the resulting whole is less than the sum of its parts.In this respect, Audioslave have defied convention, producing a record that sounds both classic and fresh, and more importantly, like a going concern rather than an exercise in necrophilia.
author: Amy McAuliffe

text: As one would expect from anything touched by the mighty hand of producer Rick Rubin, it's a tattooed-to-the-bone rock record.Sure, there are dim echoes of RATM and Soungarden, but if comparisons are to be made with anyone, it's 70s rock greats that spring to mind.
author: Amy McAuliffe

text: Opening track "Cochise" thrusts and grooves its way down a road well-trodden by the likes of Led Zeppelin and Black Sabbath.
author: Amy McAuliffe

text: This sets the tone for the rest of the album; heavy, powerful riffage over rumbling bass lines and thumping colossal drums.Subsequent tracks such as "Gasoline" and "Shadow On The Sun" continue to mine a similar vein, the latter climaxing spectacularly in a tempest of throbbing guitars and broken-glass vocals.
author: Amy McAuliffe

text: Guitarist Tom Morello is on scorching form, discharging killer riffs like a magazine of bullets, while Chris Cornell proves effortlessly that he is without question one of the finest rock singers ever, capable of both sexually-charged crooning and feral blasts of vocal rage.You rate Kurt?
author: Amy McAuliffe

text: Cornell wrote the book.
author: Amy McAuliffe

text: Although the heaviness tails off a little by the time we get to "Getaway Car", this is a looser, freer record than anything RATM ever did.
author: Amy McAuliffe

text: It's almost as if Tom, Timmy and Brad are just happy to rock out without having to worry about the righteousness of the lyrics.
author: Amy McAuliffe

text: Cornell sticks to well-worn Jesus-Christ-Pose musings such as "Nail in my hand / From my Creator" ("Show Me How To Live").
author: Amy McAuliffe

text: This is an excellent debut.
author: Amy McAuliffe

text: So turn that stereo up to eleven, close your eyes, and pray for some live dates soon...
author: Amy McAuliffe

text: Samira Said is one of the most popular contemporary singers in the Middle East.
author: Garth Cartwright

text: Yet she is largely unknown in the West.
author: Garth Cartwright

text: That looks about to change with Samira's nomination for a BBC Radio 3 World Music Award and with the release in the UK of this excellent new album.
author: Garth Cartwright

text: Samira's originally from Morocco but don't expect to hear elemental Berber trance music (as championed by The Master Musicians Of Jajouka) or tough gnawa grooves.
author: Garth Cartwright

text: Samira has long been based in Cairo, Egypt, and Cairo is to Middle Eastern pop what Bombay is to Indian film.
author: Garth Cartwright

text: Youm Wara Youm finds Samira retaining her Arabic roots while effectively blending many contemporary Western pop elements.
author: Garth Cartwright

text: On the title track Samira duets with Cheb Mami across a pulsing electronic beat while Arabic strings dance around their vocals.
author: Garth Cartwright

text: "La Binna Kilm" is epic Arabic pop with strings coiling behind Samira.
author: Garth Cartwright

text: "Kol El Awkaaj" has a muted chorus of 'yeah yeah yeah' and bouncy beats to show Samira can compete with Kylie on the dance floor.
author: Garth Cartwright

text: "Abeltak Leith" is my favourite track: beautiful forests of violins fill the air while Samira gently wails over a very subtle rhythm.
author: Garth Cartwright

text: "Min Youmi" is certain to be a hit in the discos of Cairo and Beirut with its fast beat and massed vocal chorus.
author: Garth Cartwright

text: Tasty oud playing too!
author: Garth Cartwright

text: "Kan Mali" starts off with menacing, almost soundtrack atmospherics then blasts off into a hard house beat with Samira's gutteral Arabic phrasing ripping across the rhythm.
author: Garth Cartwright

text: The arrangements are constantly interesting, and the mix of Arabic and Western styles never feels forced.
author: Garth Cartwright

text: The amount of space between voice, string instruments and beats helps you appreciate how potent a vocalist Samira can be.
author: Garth Cartwright

text: If you love rai, you'll like this.
author: Garth Cartwright

text: The trombone is reputedly the instrument that best imitates the human voice, with personal styles on it being as individual as players own voices.
author: John Eyles

text: Yves Robert is a virtuoso player with a very personal sound.
author: John Eyles

text: Largely avoiding the swoops and slurs that can make the instrument an ideal comedy foil, he instead produces a sound that is plaintive and vulnerable, at its best as affecting as Miles' Harmon-muted trumpet.
author: John Eyles

text: This album's subtitle "48 de tendresse" is well chosen.
author: John Eyles

text: On this, his debut album as leader on ECM, Robert's melodic compositions are ideally suited to his own sound and that of his trio.
author: John Eyles

text: Typical are the album's three separate versions of Robert's title composition, a funereally paced piece that perfectly sets the tone; melancholy and brooding yet strangely optimistic.
author: John Eyles

text: Robert is joined by Vincent Courtois on cello and Cyril Atef on drums in a chamber jazz group of the highest order.
author: John Eyles

text: Courtois sometimes takes on the role of a conventional bassist, but more often acts as a melodic foil for Robert.
author: John Eyles

text: The trombone and cello frequently play lines that intertwine and blend together, at times becoming inseparable.
author: John Eyles

text: By way of contrast, Atef provides an understated punctuation of sounds, full of micro detail.
author: John Eyles

text: The longest track here, "La Tendresse", encapsulates all of the above qualities and more.
author: John Eyles

text: In particular, it allows Robert the time and space to give a bravura demonstration of the range of his playing, from slow and mournful through to quickfire staccato, never losing that wonderful tone.
author: John Eyles

text: He shares the spotlight with Courtois, whose slowly evolving sustained phrases underpin the trombone.
author: John Eyles

text: The piece is engaging throughout, and its seventeen-minute duration flies by.
author: John Eyles

text: In that, it typifies this beautiful sounding album.
author: John Eyles

text: It's hard to think of more than a handful of films with instantly hummable scores: Jaws, the Bond movies, The Good, The Bad and The Ugly, but Mr.
author: Fenella Fudge

text: Jones sure drew the long straw!
author: Fenella Fudge

text: The seven rising notes of the main Raiders theme turn us all into "Name That Tune" contestants in seconds.
author: Fenella Fudge

text: On this CD John Williams' magnificent scores are given the Czechoslovakian once-over by the City of Prague Philharmonic Orchestra, tightly conducted by Nic Raine.
author: Fenella Fudge

text: If you like your film scores big, this ones XXL, instantly transporting you to the tangled jungles of South America on hair-raising adventures.
author: Fenella Fudge

text: The undertones of mystery and suspense suffused with mortal danger and a hefty dollop of derring-do make this one of the most perfect scores ever written.
author: Fenella Fudge

text: From "The Raiders March" which first introduces us to that unforgettable Indiana Jones melody, to the melancholic "Marion's Theme" the adventurer lurking in even the most resolute couch potato must surely be stirred.
author: Fenella Fudge

text: The CD covers all of Indiana Jones' three epics and the expert evocations never let up.
author: Fenella Fudge

text: If you remember the underground chase in The Temple of Doom, Track 10 ("The Mine Car Chase") will have you on the edge of your seat all over again.
author: Fenella Fudge

text: The best all-round sound capturing the original films' feel comes in track 7, simply called "Raiders of the Lost Ark".
author: Fenella Fudge

text: It'll transport you back to the first time you saw this magical film, a rarity in an era when Hollywood moguls had foolishly assumed the era of the boys-own-adventure-flick was long past, and a time when cinemas were being demolished at an alarming rate.
author: Fenella Fudge

text: This score, like the film it so brilliantly and exuberantly illustrates, is John Williams at his dramatic and comic best, a style often copied but never bettered.
author: Fenella Fudge

text: And this is a glorious tribute.
author: Fenella Fudge

text: While the fact that Pearl Jam are still together fourteen years after the release of their seminal debut album Ten is remarkable enough, this, their eighth studio album, provides ample evidence that they still have a marked determination to continue preaching their message.
author: Dan Tallis

text: The record opens in angry style with Vedder snarling over furious guitars that don't relent until the end of the fifth track.
author: Dan Tallis

text: You'd be forgiven for thinking you'd stumbled across the latest batch of angst-fuelled, punk-loving teenagers rather than the Seattle grunge veterans.
author: Dan Tallis

text: They rage against George Bush, the Iraq war and American apathy while guitarists Stone Gossard and Mike McCready serve up aggressive rock solo after solo.
author: Dan Tallis

text: However the ballads that dominated previous albums are evident here too, though they sound unnervingly similar to Bruce Springsteen's acoustic work.
author: Dan Tallis

text: Their most accomplished album in years closes in epic style with the seven minute long "Inside Job" - proving the band care little about writing three minute pop songs these days.
author: Dan Tallis

text: Long may their crusade continue.
author: Dan Tallis

text: If ever a band stood for innovation rather than imitation then Pearl Jam are it.
author: Catherine Chambers

text: Riot Act is the seventh album from the Seattle five-piece and the strongest indication yet of a band refusing to compromise their direction regardless of commercial pressures or musical trends.
author: Catherine Chambers

text: Certainly, with the current climate favouring nu-grunge outfits such as Nickleback and Puddle of Mudd, now would be as good a time as ever for the Seattle band to return to the fray and deliver an album of anthemic-styled grunge.
author: Catherine Chambers

text: Considering the decline in previous album sales, some might argue it would be the most sensible thing to do.
author: Catherine Chambers

text: However, Pearl Jam have rejected this route.
author: Catherine Chambers

text: Instead, Riot Act is an album full of rustic melodies and angular guitars, a record that is more Neil Young than Nirvana.
author: Catherine Chambers

text: While it may seem a brave move it hardly comes as a surprise.
author: Catherine Chambers

text: Ever since 96's No Code, their career path erred towards a semi-acoustic trajectory.
author: Catherine Chambers

text: 2000's Binaural straddled a laid-back experimental palette that left anyone pining for the Pearl Jam of old sorely disappointed.
author: Catherine Chambers

text: Riot Act explores this direction even further.
author: Catherine Chambers

text: The first single to be taken from the album, "I am Mine", is as near as Pearl Jam have come to touch balladry.
author: Catherine Chambers

text: Refined guitars, complete with concluding modest solo, produce a soothing, yet simultaneously achingly vulnerable song; albeit one that is so middle of the road you can almost see the white markings.
author: Catherine Chambers

text: Although maturity has served Pearl Jam well, this record is far from representative of a band growing old gracefully.
author: Catherine Chambers

text: Check out the unsettling opener "Can't Keep" and the strident dynamism of "Save You".
author: Catherine Chambers

text: These tracks are perfect slices of unreconstructed rock; evidence that Pearl Jam never lost the art of penning memorable tunes.
author: Catherine Chambers

text: Riot Act reaffirms Pearl Jam's place in rock: not so much grunge survivors as experimental rock flag-wavers.
author: Catherine Chambers

text: Eleven years on from their epochal debut Ten, an album that paved the way for the Seattle grunge scene, Pearl Jam may well have finally have laid the ghost of their past to rest.
author: Catherine Chambers

text: Despite losing a member since their last full-length offering, the S Club collective seem as determined as ever to stay at the peak of pop greatness and with Seeing Double they do exactly that.
author: Ruth Mitchell

text: They have wasted few moments on sentimentality and have crammed their fourth album full of funkier, sassier tunes, that cover everything from cool garage grooves to sweet seductive Latin melodies.
author: Ruth Mitchell

text: With a more immediate and mature sound, Seeing Double opens with the infectious disco-tinged first single "Alive", and it's this hip-swaying slice of dance-pop that sets the pace for nearly all of the sixty-one minutes.
author: Ruth Mitchell

text: On the very first listen there is an instant temptation to turn up the stereo and clear a big plot of dancing space.
author: Ruth Mitchell

text: Standout track "Love Ain't Gonna Wait For You" is a rippling, rolling anthem with a fresh and dynamic sound, but is still reminiscent of the polished S Club of yesteryear.
author: Ruth Mitchell

text: It's quickly followed by "Bittersweet", which slinks and slithers along with a hot R&B hook that gives those Destiny Child girls a real run for their money.
author: Ruth Mitchell

text: "Gangsta Love" continues the faster and more furious momentum and kicks off with drum&bass inspired beats before spiralling into a ferociously catchy silky, smooth pop tune.
author: Ruth Mitchell

text: It's this alongside the two-step driven rhythm of "Who Do You Think You Are?" that are the most accomplished examples of the revamped six-piece's stab at more diversity.
author: Ruth Mitchell

text: Unfortunately it's the ballads that are the weaker aspect of this otherwise energetic album.
author: Ruth Mitchell

text: "Straight From The Heart", where as usual Jo takes the lead, slows down the pace and includes pleasant but unadventurousharmonies from the rest of the gang.
author: Ruth Mitchell

text: "The Greatest" and "In Too Deep" follow in a similar vein, and despite being more mid-tempo affairs with bubbling basslines, they fail to pack much of a punch.
author: Ruth Mitchell

text: Coming in at an all-too-long sixteen tracks, perhaps Jo, Rachel, Bradley, Tina, Hannah and Jon should have stuck to the more grown-up sensibilities of quality over quantity.
author: Ruth Mitchell

text: Nevertheless it'll still get you bopping!
author: Ruth Mitchell

text: The biggest ever pop act in the UK return with their fifth album called Turnaround.
author: Jack Smith

text: The title Westlife chose is lost on us because this seems like more of the same from the puppy-dog-eyed five piece.
author: Jack Smith

text: The no-risk chart-topper "Mandy" kicks off proceedings.
author: Jack Smith

text: The song first hit the charts, as "Brandy", 32 years ago before Barry Manilow renamed it "Mandy" and took it to No.
author: Jack Smith

text: The rest of the album is generally full of similarly down-tempo croon-fests.
author: Jack Smith

text: Thankfully, the balladeering is interspersed with upbeat tracks like "Hey Whatever", "Turn Around" and "Thank You" - just in case you feel like nodding off.
author: Jack Smith

text: Now we like a decent ballad as much as the next popster, but it seems like these songs have been around in one form or another over the last couple of albums.
author: Jack Smith

text: For example the band put a twist on the old classic "When A Man Loves A Woman" by reversioning the song, getting some new lyricsand calling it "When A Woman Loves A Man".
author: Jack Smith

text: And there's a cover of the Mr Big favourite "To Be With You".
author: Jack Smith

text: So, if the fact that the best songs here are other people's doesn't put you off ("Mandy", "To Be With You"), then you're probably going to find something you like.
author: Jack Smith

text: Meanwhile, we're with Simon Cowell on this one.
author: Jack Smith

text: Review courtesy of TOTP
author: Jack Smith

text: With Christmas fast approaching, Westlife return to give fans the customary stocking filler.Allow Us To Be Frank is a silky tribute to a bygone era frequented by the movers and shakers of the Las Vegas music scene.Westlife have been winning big in recent years and with this album they seem to be cashing in the chips they've acquired during their rise to mega stardom.
author: Roger Kerrison

text: This is their first return since the exit of Brian McFadden to pursue a solo career/star in Sugar Puffs commercials.Whilst McFadden is attempting to launch his solo career amidst the all-too-public break-up of his marriage, the remaining members of the band have produced an album which portrays their wholesome, charming, sugar coated image.
author: Roger Kerrison

text: The album will no doubt introduce a whole new generation to the music which in its heyday was the pop of modern times.
author: Roger Kerrison
