text: Recorded with a 60-piece orchestra in the not-so-smoky lounge culture of Wembley, North London, Allow Us To Be Frank replicates the originals almost exactly;note for note, swing for swing, croon for croon.
author: Roger Kerrison

text: Alas, Westlife aren't a match for the original Rat Pack.Frank Sinatra, Dean Martin, Sammy Davies Jnr et al were charismatic playboys and serial philanderers who would raise hell in Hollywood and Vegas alike.
author: Roger Kerrison

text: In fact, they courted tabloid controversy, but then this was always part of their appeal.
author: Roger Kerrison

text: Conversely, Westlife are a marketing man's dream and owe their success more to their clean cut image.
author: Roger Kerrison

text: No gambles have been taken with the selection of songs chosen, either.
author: Roger Kerrison

text: All the classics are in situ; "That's Life" and "Ain't That A Kick In The Head" supply the rousing big band sound, whilst "Fly Me To The Moon", "When I Fall In Love" and "Moon River" provide the more wallowing love songs.
author: Roger Kerrison

text: The catchy big band swing will no doubt get Granny dancing on Christmas Day after one too many helpings of sherry trifle, but it's doubtful that this album will appeal to the band's core teenage audience.
author: Roger Kerrison

text: Westlife really should have stuck instead of twisting.
author: Roger Kerrison

text: If it's the Rat Pack you want, put your money on Frank, Dean and Sammy.
author: Roger Kerrison

text: Only Westlife could stretch the definition of greatest hits to its full potential.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: For four years now the band has stolen the hearts of our nation's youth, clocking up a record-breaking eleven number 1 singles and 3 multi-million selling albums along the way.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: With recent single "Unbreakable" topping up this total, there seems no end in sight for the unprecedented success of these Irish boys.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: Unbreakable (the album) is a chronological showcase of their career to date.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: From debut "Swear It Again" and the karaoke-favourite "Flying Without Wings" to the Cliff Richard cover and forthcoming single "Miss You Nights", the Westlife formula is blatant.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: They know how to ham it up for the ladies and are masters of the sentimental power ballad, smouldering sincerity and well-rehearsed harmonies.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: Maybe it's just that they offer a change in tempo to the staple of the bands' fodder but Westlife sound at their best when they loosen their hips and rock out a bit.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: "World Of Our Own" is a stormer of a pop song and goes at least some way to excusing their more painful moments, such as "What Makes A Man" and the weedy "My Love".
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: "When You're Looking Like That" (despite sounding like the illegitimate child of A1 and Boyzone) gives fans the chance to stop sobbing into their Nicky pillows and tap their feet for a moment.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: Westlife however know their place in pop and the 6 new tracks featured here all show a lean further and further towards more grown up songs as their audience matures and the lure of the US market beckons.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: Greatest Hits have a habit of being a final nail in the coffin for many a band before them (remember Steps and Five?), but there still seems to be enough steam in Westlife's engine to keep them going for a while yet.
author: Jacqueline Hodges

text: Given the mediocre quality of his previous albums, most people had given up on ole Snoop ever finding his way back to the top dogg position.
author: Buki Bakare

text: That is until now.
author: Buki Bakare

text: With his 6th album, the Professor of G-ology is back in true form.
author: Buki Bakare

text: The first album to be released on his Doggystyle label, Snoop D-O Double Gizzle is wasting no time in stating his position; as head honcho, he's commanding respect.
author: Buki Bakare

text: He's put down the joint and stepped to the mic; delivering a well- balanced album that includes soulful melodies, head banging beats and a welcome return to that 70s funk influence which compliments his West Coast lazy drawl so well.
author: Buki Bakare

text: With his newly acquired freedom from No Limit, the lanky Long Beach rapper has certainly done his homework and enlisted a roster of heavyweight producers; Neptunes, (yes, them again!) DJ Premier, Hi Tek, Fredwreck and Just Blaze.
author: Buki Bakare

text: The first single "From the Chuuch to Da Palace" proves Snoop's still got that bark.
author: Buki Bakare

text: It's infectious, if somewhat repetitive,featuring the standard Neptunes sound all the way.
author: Buki Bakare

text: Another head nodder has got to be the Premier produced: "The One and Only." It's classic east coast flava, equipped with the right scratches and breakbeats.
author: Buki Bakare

text: The album features eleven guest appearances from, Ludacris, Pharrell Williams, Redman, Charlie Wilson and others.
author: Buki Bakare

text: The more noticeabletracks are the intoxicating flutedriven "Lollipop" with Nate Dogg and Jay Z and the quirky "Batman and Robin" with Lady of Rage.
author: Buki Bakare

text: Snoop'strademark Gangsta-meets-Pimp style is ever present but with a difference.
author: Buki Bakare

text: Are we seeing a more mature reflective and sensitive side of Snoop with tracks like "I Miss that Bitch" (hmmm) and the soulful "I Believe in You" featuring Latoiya Williams?
author: Buki Bakare

text: Here the soothing piano keys compliment her soft vocals.
author: Buki Bakare

text: However he still "keeps it gangsta" with his diss track; "Pimp Slappd" when he responds to Suge Knights taunts.
author: Buki Bakare

text: Although not on the same par as the classic "Doggystyle", if one album can catapult him back on top of his game this has got to be it!
author: Buki Bakare

text: Snoop fans will no doubt be rejoicing and those of you who thought Mr Broadus would never cut it without the assistance of the almighty Dre need to think again.
author: Buki Bakare

text: After a decade in the game, It would appear an old Dogg can still learn new tricks!
author: Buki Bakare

text: Snoop Dogg's reinvention is probably one of the more startling of modern times.
author: Adam Webb

text: Bursting onto the scene ten years ago, he was the self-styled OG; the baddest hound in the pound, with a killers drawl and a real life murder rap.
author: Adam Webb

text: 'Kick this evil bastard out' screamed the tabloids when he visited the UK.
author: Adam Webb

text: Ten years on and Snoop is an MTV parody pimp - your loveable fur-coated friend, who, though he might misbehave occasionally, is more likely to sidle up, rest his nose on your lap and shizzle your nizzle.
author: Adam Webb

text: In other words, he's more Droopy than the Hound of the Baskervilles.
author: Adam Webb

text: Even his trademark misogyny has been toned down.
author: Adam Webb

text: 'Just leave her, don't hit her', he counsels here, on what he introduces as 'another nine-inch dick classic', "I'm Threw Witchu".
author: Adam Webb

text: OK, it's hardly Andrea Dworkin, but it's a start.
author: Adam Webb

text: And, with the preposterously titled R&G (Rhythm & Gangsta): The Masterpiece, he's probably produced the essential Snoop Dogg album.
author: Adam Webb

text: Built on the best beats money can buy, smooth-as-silk G-funk and that low-slung Dogg delivery it could easily be subtitled 'The Best Lapdancing Soundtrack Album In The World...Ever.' Much of the acclaim can be laid at The Neptunes' door.
author: Adam Webb

text: Pharrell Williams and Chad Hugo co-produce five tracks here, including the awesome "Drop It Like It's Hot".
author: Adam Webb

text: Combining the sleek minimalism of Jeru The Damaja's "Come Clean" with a futuristic "Buffalo Girls", it's one of the singles of 2004.
author: Adam Webb

text: Elsewhere, Justin Timberlake pops up for what sounds like a Justified outtake on "Signs", joining a roll call of big hitters that includes 50 Cent, Nelly, Lil Jon, Bootsy Collins, and The Gap Band's Charlie Wilson.
author: Adam Webb

text: But it's Snoop who dominates.
author: Adam Webb

text: His sleazy demeanour might lack the cold-eyed instinct of old, but he remains one of hip-hops most distinctive voices.
author: Adam Webb

text: And even if he outstays his welcome here by at least half an hour, R&G is, if not a masterpiece, then certainly entertaining and occasionally mind-blowing.
author: Adam Webb

text: Top Dogg, still.
author: Adam Webb

text: Rod has long refused to let musical credibility stand in the way of kitsch, and has passed from the position of vital artist to the status of karaoke favourite.
author: Mick Fitzsimmons

text: It's therefore apt to find him singing this selection of standards from the pen of such luminaries as Gershwin and Cole Porter.
author: Mick Fitzsimmons

text: According to the sleeve notes, this was a labour of love for Rod.
author: Mick Fitzsimmons

text: Apparently he can be regularly heard whistling these songs while hanging around studios and photo shoots.
author: Mick Fitzsimmons

text: Unfortunately, his private passion doesn't translate to a fiery performance.
author: Mick Fitzsimmons

text: It's a bit like listening outside Rod's bathroom door as he soaks that famous rooster cut beneath the shower.
author: Mick Fitzsimmons

text: Rod's greatest asset, his famed leathery rasp, is muted throughout.
author: Mick Fitzsimmons

text: In any case, it's better suited to noisy rave-ups and sentimental lighter wavers than smooth standards.
author: Mick Fitzsimmons

text: The bland arrangements certainly don't help, but it must be said, Rod just ain't much of a crooner.
author: Mick Fitzsimmons

text: His performance may be pitch-perfect, his phrasing spot on, but lacks any real sense of passion or adventure, the very things Rod used to have in abundance.
author: Mick Fitzsimmons

text: As an interpreter of songs Stewart has often proved peerless.
author: Mick Fitzsimmons

text: But his version of "These Foolish Things" is oddly respectable whereas Bryan Ferry's version injected new blood into tired veins.
author: Mick Fitzsimmons

text: And since when was a respectable Rod desirable?
author: Mick Fitzsimmons

text: Still, its hard to mess up with standards such as these.
author: Mick Fitzsimmons

text: Great songs always shine through, with the title track a case in point.
author: Mick Fitzsimmons

text: But it would have been nice if Rod had dug a bit deeper into them.
author: Mick Fitzsimmons

text: If you're a fan of Rod's glory years in the early 70s then you may be nonplussed by this album.
author: Mick Fitzsimmons

text: In the context of Rod's career arc, however, it makes perfect sense.
author: Mick Fitzsimmons

text: Perfectly inoffensive background music, but ill suited to closer scrutiny.
author: Mick Fitzsimmons

text: Fans of pop prodigy and all round whiz kid Todd Rundgren will already be aware of The Nazz's place in their hero's history.
author: Chris Jones

text: Formed in 1967 in Philadelphia, they were not originally Todd's band but quickly fell under the vision of the intense young anglophile.
author: Chris Jones

text: At a time when the happening synapse-melting sounds emanating from the West Coast, such as the Grateful Dead or Jefferson Airplane, were seeing bands across the US throw away the three-minute template, the Nazz were going against the grain.
author: Chris Jones

text: With Rundgren taking the songwriting and production reins, the four-piece managed three albums in a short two years.
author: Chris Jones

text: In fact all the material was recorded in their first year and by the time of their second album (Nazz Nazz) Todd, and bassist Carsen Van Osten had actually left.
author: Chris Jones

text: Their first opus (Nazz) was a template of concise songcraft heavily influenced by Todd's heroes; the Who, the Small Faces and the Kinks, yet Rundgren's desire to make the follow-up a double album (with the working title of Fungo Bat) ran foul of both bandmates and record company executives.
author: Chris Jones

text: With Rundgren pursuing his muse alone, frustrated by short-sightedness and musical shortcomings, a third album (with hastily re-recorded vocals) compiled from unfinished work was the last the world would ever see of The Nazz.
author: Chris Jones

text: All three albums have been compiled here (along with rarities etc.) to give a complete picture of the sublime pop dynamics of this underrated outfit, and as a testament to the vision of Rundgren.
author: Chris Jones

text: Sixties hipsters will already know their punchy original single ''Open My Eyes'' (immortalised by Lenny Kaye on his seminal Nuggets compilation, and also a b-side to Todd's later-reworked ''Hello Its Me''), yet there's a wealth of other gems to choose from.
author: Chris Jones

text: The sound not only draws on the aforementioned British invasion vibe but also dares to combine it with Beach Boys' harmonies, Philly soul funkiness (check the Archie Bell and the Drells spoof opener ''Loosen Up'') and Laura Nyro's winsomeness.
author: Chris Jones

text: In the end, Todd's burgeoning sophistication was always going to be far more than this garage band could handle.
author: Chris Jones

text: Let's not forget that in a matter of a year or two he was producing his own double albums - and playing everything on them as well!
author: Chris Jones

text: Yet, this is no mere footnote to greater things to come.
author: Chris Jones

text: Rundgren and Van Osten, along with Robert 'Stewkey' Antoni and Thom Mooney were a bona fide pop phenomenon and, as a band, deserve to be remembered as more than just Todd's springboard to fame.
author: Chris Jones

text: If psych-pop with a twist is your bag, baby, this compilation is definitely where it's at...
author: Chris Jones

text: 'Through one of those paradoxes so characteristic of musical history, Vivaldi's output still remains largely unknown'.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: That's how the notes for this new recording begin...surely they cannot be serious: have they never heard of The Four Seasons?
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Well, that's precisely the point; the success of a small number of concertos has completely eclipsed the rest of Vivaldi's music with the result that he is now a prisoner of his own image as an instrumental composer.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: That may be pushing it, but how many Vivaldi operas can you name for instance?
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Thought so...and Vivaldi himself reckoned he'd written ninety-four of them.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Which may also be a bit of an exaggeration, it turns out and anyway, he had an almost Rossini-like attitude to recycling: about forty percent of this opera comes from other pieces.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: But isn't it about time someone got off their backsides and started mapping Vivaldi's vast, neglected operatic hinterland on disc?
author: Andrew McGregor

text: It's a perfect project for Alessandrini and Concerto Italiano, whose series of Vivaldi recordings for Opus 111 has already been stimulating and refreshing.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: It would take me almost as long to explain what happens in L'Olimpiade as it would to listen to it; it's a pig to precis; basically the Ancient Greek Olympics are being held, and two great friends are entering the overall contest for top athlete, both in love with women they're forbidden from meeting.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: The father of one of the women is in charge of the games, and he's offering his daughter's hand to the victor, which means the two friends are effectively competing for the same woman, who one already loves, and the other is about to fall for in a big way.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Look, as an opera it's never going to outsell Tosca, but there's some beautiful music here, and fine performances.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Try Licida's Act 1 aria Mentre dormi for starters, superbly sung by Sara Mingardo...in a trousers role.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Yes, all four of our leads are sung by women, and it does get a bit confusing.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: But Alessandrini only relaxes his grip on the score to allow the most beautiful passages breathing space, and the playing is brilliant.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: 'Opere teatrali vol.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: 1' this says on the sleeve.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Looks like they'll be in the studio for some time...
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Try These: Gluck: Alceste Lalande: Music for the Sun King Stefano Landi: Homo fugit velut umbra
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Within seconds, slippery turntable chatter and tight horn section twists announce how much Barcelona collective Ojos De Brujo have developed their signature sound even further, sharply arranging the tumble of cross-cultural elements that all fall within the bounds of what must still be called flamenco.
author: Martin Longley

text: Emphatic acoustic guitar strumming, fast handclaps and booming cajon (a percussive sitting-box) still form the music's heart.
author: Martin Longley

text: But it's a small step from the staccato rush of Marina's traditionally-derived vocals to the accelerated couplet-gush of guest rapper Faada Freddy, from Senegal's Daara J.
author: Martin Longley

text: Even as hip hop, reggae, Indian pop and even heavy metal grinding make their mark, flamenco's wellspring is never diluted.
author: Martin Longley

text: Instead, its fluids are thickened, and the music courses forward, superbly modernised and sleekly integrated with these variegated intruders.
author: Martin Longley

text: From the moment it starts, there's no doubt that this an album of now.
author: Charlie Gillett

text: Energetic, assertive and joyful, it does what you want a record to do: it changes the mood and makes life seem full of possibilities.
author: Charlie Gillett

text: Reaching back to flamenco and rumba, grabbing handfuls of hip hop, dub and modern-sounding drum licks and bass lines (but not drum-and-bass!), the group makes forward-looking music that could definitely have been made only in Spain and probably only in Barcelona.
author: Charlie Gillett

text: Usually, the most interesting popular music has been made far from the cities where the major international record companies have been based.For the twenty years from 1952 to 1972, the American South was the best place to make adventurous records.
author: Charlie Gillett

text: For the next thirty it could have been Kinshasa in Zaire or the capital cities of Guinea, Mali or Senegal.Right now, some of the most creative locations are bordering the Mediterranean: Marseilles, Naples, Istanbul, Cairo, and especially Barcelona.
author: Charlie Gillett

text: It's not a matter of simply moving to the right place and expecting the magic to rub off; you have to be based there, be part of the culture, and be able to absorb some of what is flying through the air around you.
author: Charlie Gillett

text: Ojos de Brujo is the band in the right place at the right time.Although the group (whose name means "Eyes of the Wizard") previously made a good debut album, Vengue, it featured the lead vocals of Dani, leader of another Barcelona group, Macaco, and it did not have the distinctiveness of Bari, which is in many ways a new beginning.
author: Charlie Gillett

text: The vocals are now shared between Marina La Canillas and Lucy, and it is their interplay that gives the album its character.First time through, the song that particularly jumped out was 'Nalta', its strong flamenco elements updated without being softened or processed.But with each play, the inventiveness of the groups style and the consistency of the material become more apparent.
author: Charlie Gillett

text: Try a sample.If you like one track, you're going to like it all.Its not often a reviewer can be so confident.
author: Charlie Gillett

text: With her self-penned songs stamping a bovver-boot over the vagaries of adolescent angst, this tomboy of teen rock kicked into the chart two years ago, providing a refreshing alternative to the bubbling broth of confectionary pop.
author: Annabel Leathes

text: So, has the 19-year-old matured from the punk pixie doing time in the skate park and finding things just oh-so complicated?
author: Annabel Leathes

text: Well, the stock loaded guitar riffs, ambling piano melodies and brooding vocals suggest that Avril is desperate to ditch the mantle of youth and be taken seriously as an artiste.
author: Annabel Leathes

text: But this is where she goes wrong.
author: Annabel Leathes

text: We enter the world of dating with Avril and what a gloomy, dire place it is.
author: Annabel Leathes

text: Too many tracks, such as 'Take Me Away' and 'My Happy Ending', pivot on the pain and despair of relationships going off the boil and, despite the stadium-rousing choruses, her whiney vocals and trite lyrics imply that madam is merely having a strop rather than wearing the hair shirt of Alanis Morrissette-style suffering.
author: Annabel Leathes

text: 'Don't Tell Me' turns all coy with the finger-wagging warning to her boyfriend, "Did I not tell you that I'm not like that girl, the one who gives it all away".
author: Annabel Leathes

text: So it's with relief that 'He Wasn't' leaps out with all the plucky cheek of old-skool Avril.
author: Annabel Leathes

text: A punchy chorus harks back to the kohl-lined rock chicks of yesteryear but possesses enough contemporary verve to set it up alongside the best of Busted.
author: Annabel Leathes

text: Similarly, the final track on the album, 'I Always Get What I Want' delivers a healthy slap in the face of authority, smacks heavily of Transvision Vamp and suggests that Avril isn't quite ready to grow up.
author: Annabel Leathes

text: The combined writing efforts of band mate, Evan Taubenfeld, ex Evanescence guitarist Ben Moody and the watchful eye of Linkin Park producer Da Gilmore infuse the album with a nu-metal edge that might levitate this release from the ashes of forgettable rock but until Avril learns to take herself a little less seriously and manage a glimmer of a smile, she will continue to sound like a petulant teenager having a strop.
author: Annabel Leathes

text: Midival Punditz, the first Indian electronica band to sign to an international label, have recreated the sound of Asian ambience and trance in a melting of Indian classical and contemporary club music.
author: Faye Burton

text: The musical partnership of Gaurav Raina and Tapan Raj dates back to childhood, a friendship which helps explain the ease with which their talents gel on the album.
author: Faye Burton

text: Veterans of the New Delhi club scene, the Punditz set up their own studio in 1997, gaining instant respect from the Asian Massive group of DJs, including Talvin Singh and becoming part of Tabla Beat Science.
author: Faye Burton

text: Fusing folk and electronica can appear premeditated: a mix of too many sounds and not enough subtlety.
author: Faye Burton

text: But not here.
author: Faye Burton

text: This is masterfully produced, each sound meticulously placed with heart and soul, for maximum impact.
author: Faye Burton

text: The album creates equal space for past and present, East and West, but it's the Punditz first love for Indian classical music which creates its depth and beauty.
author: Faye Burton

text: 'Fabric', is recognisable from the "Monsoon Wedding" soundtrack, and builds looping electronica upon a ghazal sung by 50s star, Heera Devi Misra.
author: Faye Burton

text: The propulsive rhythm of 'Extasis' is far more trance orientated, mixing intelligent drum 'n' bass with soaring santur laden raga.
author: Faye Burton

text: The wholly ambient 'Night' stands out as a vast work, the space between ancient and digital culture radiating soulful sound.
author: Faye Burton

text: With track titles including 'Forest Dream' and 'Far From Home', this is music to take you far away to extraordinary worlds!
author: Faye Burton

text: Its intrigue lies in the fact that not one track remains the same, but constantly evolves on each listening.
author: Faye Burton

text: Closing the album, 'Dark Age' is an extraordinary piece of music, lost in the snake like travels of Shailendar's bansuri flute, dark beats and haunting semi-classical vocals, it opens itself up to constant exploration.
author: Faye Burton

text: This album lacks for not a single beat and the sounds of tabla, sarangi and synth are heightened to the max.
author: Faye Burton

text: The experience is over all too quickly: put it on repeat and take the trip over and over again!
author: Faye Burton

text: Who is the highest-selling female recording artist ever?
author: Morag Reavley

text: It's not Madonna, Celine Dion or, bless her, Dolly Parton.
author: Morag Reavley

text: Nope, with 47 gold albums in a 40-year career, Barbra Streisand shows them all a clean pair of heels in the diva stakes.
author: Morag Reavley

text: Only Elvis has sold more records.
author: Morag Reavley

text: Not bad for an actress who sings, as she once described herself.
author: Morag Reavley

text: La Barbra's 57th album, "Duets', is a collection of 17 duet hits and two new tracks.
author: Morag Reavley

text: Given that there is very little previously unheard here, does this album illustrate anything more than the impossibly glamorous contents of Streisand's address book?
author: Morag Reavley

text: Even the most faithful Streisand acolyte must be delighted by the range of songs and singers assembled.
author: Morag Reavley

text: There is 70s disco with the high priests of glitterball: Donna Summer and Barry Gibb.
author: Morag Reavley

text: Streisand and Michael Crawford engage in a 'who-can-hold-the-note-longest' competition in Lloyd-Webber's "The Music of the Night".
author: Morag Reavley

text: (The winner, of course, is Streisand.) And there are chart hits in the form of 1978's wistful "You Don't Bring Me Flowers" with Neil Diamond, and the 1998 epic "Tell Him" with Celine Dion.
author: Morag Reavley

text: Two new tracks bookend the previously-released pieces.
author: Morag Reavley

text: "I Won't Be The One To Let Go" with Barry Manilow is a soaring, feel-good ballad.
author: Morag Reavley

text: "All I Know Of Love" with young baritone Josh Groban brings the album to a stately close and shows that Barbra can still hold her own yet another new generation.
author: Morag Reavley

text: Best of all are two gems from the start of Streisand's career.
author: Morag Reavley

text: The Witch is Dead", sung with a deadpan Harold Arlen, the Wizard of Oz soundtrack composer, is witty, jazzy, almost avant-garde in its syncopation.
author: Morag Reavley

text: It would barely be recognised in Munchkinland.
author: Morag Reavley

text: Backed up against it is an exquisite duet with Judy Garland, recorded live in 1963 on The Judy Garland Show.
author: Morag Reavley

text: "Get Happy / Happy Days Are Here Again" counterpoints two classic songs, with Streisand's pure, youthful notes pirouetting around Garland's throaty, unbearably melancholy voice.
author: Morag Reavley

text: Getting a duet with Streisand is an essential step on the path to musical superstardom.
author: Morag Reavley

text: Robbie Williams must be hoping that his phone rings very soon.
author: Morag Reavley

text: Musical snobs over the age of 21 are likely to be highly suspicious of Avril Lavigne.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: She's only 17, she's pretty, she's sold a zillion albums already, she talks a lot about keeping it real: she must be rubbish, right?
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Avril's current single 'Sk8ter Boi' is brilliant.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: It's a classic high energy pop song with crunchy guitars and a great hook.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Its tale of a snobby girl who rejects the loser who becomes a grunge superstar while she turns into a single mum is as slick and clever as an episode of Buffy.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: It bowls you over with its energy and sticks in your mind.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: It's one of the best tracks on this uneven debut album.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: 'Losing Grip', the opening track, is another absolute cracker.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: When the guitar and the scratching cuts in at maximum volume and Avril starts wailing about some boy who did her wrong, I'm with her all the way: it seems real enough, exciting enough to me.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: And in the quiet bits her voice has the purity of a folk singer.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: 'Complicated' you already know about: a classic radio friendly pop song that lodges in your head.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: And 'I'm With You' is a sweet and rather touching power ballad, and must be the next single.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: But about half the album plays far too safe: not enough raw guitar, too many weak songs.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Every one needs to be a potential single and some aren't.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: 'My World' contains some horrible rapping that even an eleven year old would find embarrassing.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Lyrics like "Sometimes I get so weird I even freak myself out" are pretty naive.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: But these are the mistakes of someone still learning.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: I'd take 'Losing Grip' over the supposedly more adult but actually more self indulgent angst rock of Tori Amos or Alanis Morrissette.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: There's nothing better than anger combined with a great pop hook.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: More quality control, more grit and Avril will build her current success into a long, bright future.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: This re-released CD has a wonderfully atmospheric picture on the front cover, a slightly blurry black & white photo of Steve Lacy and Thelonious Monk playing at Jazz Gallery, NYC in 1960.
author: John Eyles

text: Cecil Taylor originally turned Lacy on to Monk, and Lacy recorded his first version of a Monk song while in Taylor's quartet.
author: John Eyles

text: Ever since, throughout his massive discography, Lacy has repeatedly returned to the compositions of Monk.
author: John Eyles

text: From his earliest group albums such as Reflections, Evidence and School Days, through solo recordings like Only Monk and More Monk, to the recent Monk's Dream - a period of well over forty years - Lacy has established himself as the greatest Monk interpreter, bar none.
author: John Eyles

text: In the process, Lacy has kept Monk's compositions in the spotlight and immeasurably enhanced Monk's reputation as a composer.
author: John Eyles

text: We See dates from 1992, and is one of the essential Lacy discs.
author: John Eyles

text: It features his regular quartet of the time (Steve Potts/Jean-Jacques Avenel/John Betsch) plus Hans Kennel on trumpet and Sonhando Estwick on vibes, an unusual instrumentation for Lacy.
author: John Eyles

text: From the opening notes of "We See" itself, played on the vibes, the sound is very different to most Lacy (and most Monk).
author: John Eyles

text: The use of the vibes is inspired.
author: John Eyles

text: Their lighter, brighter tone helps Lacy to reinvent the music, important on a piece such as "Evidence" that he has recorded many times.
author: John Eyles

text: Across the eleven tracks here, there is great variety of sound, with the full sextet used only sparingly.
author: John Eyles

text: Avenel plays "Eronel" completely as a solo bass piece, a fine display of fluent, melodic playing.
author: John Eyles

text: Lacy uses "Reflections" and "Monks Mood" as solo showcases for his own playing.
author: John Eyles

text: And "Shuffle Boil" and "Thelonious" are both performed by the trio of Lacy, Avenel and Betsch.
author: John Eyles

text: On these tracks, Lacy is in the spotlight and shows his mastery of Monk's music.
author: John Eyles

text: He makes it sound flowing and effortless, as natural as breathing; in other hands it frequently sounds just the opposite.
author: John Eyles

text: Above all of those, though, I would choose "Ruby My Dear", performed as a duo by Lacy and Potts, both playing soprano sax.
author: John Eyles

text: The two lines weave around each other, Lacy and Potts displaying an intuitive knowledge of each others playing based on their decades together.
author: John Eyles

text: Lacy's own "Hanky-Panky" closes the album and fits seamlessly into the programme, having some of Monk's left-field logic.
author: John Eyles

text: As a tribute, it is as fitting as everything that has gone before.
author: John Eyles

text: A man is playing acoustic guitar.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: He is disturbed by an insect.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: It gets trapped inside his guitar.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Some of the time he tries to shake it out, sometimes he makes his playing fit with the insect's buzzing.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Guitarist Arturo Parra originally comes from Colombia, so it's hardly surprising that there's a strong Latin flavour to his style.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: He's now based in Canada, regularly collaborating with electroacoustic composers, people who make sound sculptures out of electronic noise.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: This CD brings together five such pieces.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Arturo weaves his guitar through bass drones, occasional surges and waves of noise, sinister echo effects, low level rumbles, creaks and plops.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: He's an accomplished player, and combines fluid runs and riffs with the occasional bit of fret board abuse and scrabbling.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: On "La basilique Fantome" he syncopates his music with the rythmn of a hand saw.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: At one point in "Soledad" he battles with a malevolent washing machine in a wind tunnel.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: I'd be a bit more impressed if he had improvised his parts live on hearing these pieces for the very first time.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: But the sleeve implies that he listened to them a great deal before writing his sections.This does contribute to the feeling that sometimes this is a bit of an academic, slightly bloodless exercise.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: It's almost too considered and thought out in places.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Occasionally you long for Parra to go for it and really wig out.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: The flimsy, irritating cardboard sleeve and rather pretentious sleeve notes don't help.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: The closing piece "Lenvers du temps" which starts with a creaky door that turns into a mechanical guillotine, is slick and almost lyrical.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Indeed, compared to a lot of the sounds you'll find under the experimental banner this CD could almost be classified as easy listening.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: So, if your idea of easy listening is a guitar jamming with a mutant cross between a fire alarm and a fax machine, look no further...
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Not so long ago, electronic music was the province of those lucky enough to be able to gain access into the squeaky clean labs of IRCAM or similar institutions, where large, impossibly expensive boxes festooned with dials and flashing lights awaited the bidding of the composer.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Now that a similar level of wizardry is achievable with just the aid of a laptop, and contemporary electronica made in bedrooms all over the world enjoys cutting edge status, it's tempting to wonder what the point of 'classical' electronic music actually is.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Records like this one may be the answer...
author: Peter Marsh

text: A graduate of Jonty Harrison's B.E.A.S.T.
author: Peter Marsh

text: project, Natasha Barrett's approach is highly rigorous, borne of compositional rather than improvisational process.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Though on paper her methods can seem alittle dry, her music is posessed of an overtly sensual and often awesome power that rivals anything else you're likely to hear.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Her 'acousmatic' techniques transform field recordings, percussion and voices into restless soundscapes that conjure up strange geographies buffetted by even stranger meteorological phenomena, cosmic forces on a massive scale or hallucinatory rainforests straight out of J.G Ballard.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Barrett's structural precision gives her pieces a strong sense of narrative as well as place.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Tiny sonic fictions unravel throughout; footsteps recede over glassy, gong like tones.
author: Peter Marsh

text: A door is opened, a cat enters, draws near, purrs and eats from a bowl seemingly placed in your left ear.
author: Peter Marsh

text: You're dragged through dense undergrowth packed with insects, or sat in a dripping cave listening to distant machines devouring the landscape.
author: Peter Marsh

text: But most of all it's her control of timbre that catches the ear again and again.
author: Peter Marsh

text: At times during the opening "Three Fictions" the immersion factor almost sent me into some deep alpha state, or the abstract sweep of millions of tiny oscillations produced such strange sensations in the small of my back I had to take my headphones off to catch my breath.
author: Peter Marsh

text: One of Barrett's interests is in manipulating the listener's perception of time, and it's something she does with consummate ease.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Lush, disturbing and beautiful all at once, Isostasie at once connects with the rich and strange concoctions of classic musique concrete,coupled witha timeless quality lacking in the ephemeral world of contemporary electronica.
author: Peter Marsh

text: It would be a little disengenuous, when talking of Will Oldham, to say his latest album takes an unexpected turn.
author: Chris Jones

text: His entire career has consisted of a series of bogus identities adopted to confound any expectations about his next direction.
author: Chris Jones

text: Nevertheless, if someone had suggested that, after last year's marvellous Master And Everyone he would re-record a bunch of songs from his Palace period with some crack Nashville cats you'd probably have been right to scoff.
author: Chris Jones

text: But he has, and the results are somewhat confusing.
author: Chris Jones

text: One aspect of Oldham's appeal was always his stoically lo-fi stance.
author: Chris Jones

text: Albums filled with his old-time biblical analogies and secular obsessions have been recorded in bedrooms and kitchens with barely a nod to modern recording techniques.
author: Chris Jones

text: Here we get that stuff smothered in the cream of Nashville players such as Hargus 'Pig' Robbins (legendary keyboard player on everything from George Jones' ''White Lightning'' to Dylan's Blonde On Blonde) and violinist Stuart Duncan.
author: Chris Jones

text: Had Will's faltering larynx been removed from the mix this could be mistaken for some mainstream countrypolitan release from the early 70s.
author: Chris Jones

text: However there's no escaping Oldham's darker viewpoint and Greatest Palace Music is unavoidably a deeply schizophrenic album.
author: Chris Jones

text: This doesn't mean that it's any kind of failure.
author: Chris Jones

text: It just becomes harder to engage with when you suspect that some kind of wry self-parody could be happening before your ears, but you're not quite sure why.
author: Chris Jones

text: The strident pedal steel and Robbins' jaunty piano work urge Oldham's songs into a bizarrely jolly place.
author: Chris Jones

text: Listen to the singalong of ''I Am A Cinematographer'' or his duck impersonation on ''I Send My Love to You''!
author: Chris Jones

text: Even the garish cover (all tropical fauvism) screams 'happy' at you.
author: Chris Jones

text: However on his gloomier tracks the band easily matches the mood, resulting in some genuinely affecting moments.
author: Chris Jones

text: ''Agnes Queen Of Sorrows'' and ''Riding'' are gorgeously maudlin folk gems that stand with his greatest work while ''West Palm Beach'' uses the soft backing to lift its lovely melodic chorus to new heights.
author: Chris Jones

text: Ultimately though, this is an album that is musically so easy on the ear as to be strangely easy to ignore.
author: Chris Jones

text: One longs for less to distract you from his unique world-view and wonderfully idiosyncratic voice.
author: Chris Jones

text: As a detour it's mighty fine, but as Neil Young famously did after the mellow Harvest, you cant wait for him to grow tired of the middle of the road and head back towards the ditch...
author: Chris Jones

text: The voices in Will Oldham's head that speak to us via his Bonnie 'Prince' Billy incarnation are not peaceful ones.
author: Chris Jones

text: This is an album of universal questions, asked on a personal level.
author: Chris Jones

text: What role does traditional love hold in the modern world?
author: Chris Jones

text: How does one reconcile the undeniable evil in us all?
author: Chris Jones

text: Heavy stuff - but all these questions relate to Oldham alone.
author: Chris Jones

text: The outsider looking in.
author: Chris Jones

text: It's a long decade since, as a post-rock contemporary of fellow Louisville legends Slint, Oldham( along with sibling Paul as Palace/Palace Brothers/Palace Sound) started searching for a new American music.
author: Chris Jones

text: With an exponentially decreasing brouhaha, successive releases have shorn slick production values until he reached the zen-like clarity of Bonnie 'Prince' Billy.
author: Chris Jones

text: Last album, Ease Down The Road was a far jauntier trip, but this time it's all ambient foot-tapping, sighing electronica and hushed harmonies.
author: Chris Jones

text: This is hardly suprising as Master And Everyone was produced by Lambchop's Mark Nevers, whose Is a Woman had the same whispered vibe.
author: Chris Jones

text: This gorgeous album however replaces Kurt Wagner's pantheistic joy in small things with a more carnal slant on life's mysteries.
author: Chris Jones

text: ''Let your unloved parts be loved'' he mutters in the opener, ''The Way''.
author: Chris Jones

text: Previous reviews of Bonnie 'Prince' Billy seem to have downplayed his influence on master magpie, Beck, yet it's this track that proves the fact irrefutably.
author: Chris Jones

text: Like Beck he's not frightened of mixing bluegrass religiosity, slacker nonchalance or even English folk rock.
author: Chris Jones

text: Duetting with Nashville professional Marty Slayton on several tracks, they summon the ghost of Sandy Denny.
author: Chris Jones

text: The title track even resembles a stripped down reel.
author: Chris Jones

text: Yet it's the ambivalent lyrics that draw you in - balancing tender love songs (''Ain't You Wealthy, Ain't You Wise?'') with explorations of biblical evil, only to deflate the whole enterprise with a song like ''Maundering'' (it means talking drivel - look it up).
author: Chris Jones

text: It tells you straight that he's just a very flawed man, on the lookout for redemption - and with a tendency to ramble.
author: Chris Jones

text: In the end it's all about infidelity and indifference.
author: Chris Jones

text: Even a song called ''Joy And Jubilee'' hardly convinces you that this is a happy world to visit.
author: Chris Jones

text: As American gothic goes, this is far more compelling and convincing than, say, Nick Cave's cartoon baptisms of fire.
author: Chris Jones

text: Finally, the key track seems to be ''Wolf Among Wolves'', with its plea to let Oldham/Billy be loved for what he really is.
author: Chris Jones

text: The biggest question seems to be; if we are evil, why can't we accept it?
author: Chris Jones

text: This is a peaceful album, but it contains very little peace.
author: Chris Jones

text: With its themes of murder, celebrity and media manipulation, its dark sexuality and bone deep cynicism, 'Chicago' is a musical that seems very contemporary.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: It's been so successful that Hollywood has now given it the big budget treatment, with accompanying soundtrack.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: And much of John Kander and Fred Ebb's score is so strong that it stands up even without pictures.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: "And All That Jazz" and "Razzle Dazzle" are great songs, witty showbiz standards.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Set pieces like "Cell Block Tango", are delivered with so much oomph that they remain compelling.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Catherine Zeta-Jones and Renee Zellweger as the two leading bad girls get all the best material, throws themselves into it and are pretty entertaining.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: And rap star Queen Latifah excels as Mama Moreton in her showcase "When You're Good To Mama".
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Her rap version of "Cell Block Tango" with Lil Kim and Macy Gray is not bad either.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: But Richard Gere as shyster lawyer Billy Flynn seems merely irritating rather than genuinely vile and doesn't have much of a vocal presence.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: And the less said about the obligatory pop song tacked on the end of the album, a useless effort by Anastasia called "Love Is A Crime" (ugh!), the better.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Soundtrack albums are by their nature incomplete.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: If you love the film so much you must have a souvenir this will do.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: But the real problem is that 'Chicago' itself is so relentlessly bleak that it can get a bit samey and one note.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Without the razzle dazzle of hot babes to punch it home, it needs better performances and a deeper, more interesting interpretation than this to produce a really satisfying album.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Schuller is one of those musical eccentrics who inhabit the Pacific Northwest region of the U.S.
author: Bill Tilland

text: in substantial numbers, drawing upon the area's peculiar convergence of styles, cultures and sensibilities.
author: Bill Tilland

text: The influences on this CD (as much as they can be untangled) are noise metal, dark ambient, industrial, Asian and world music, Native American and traditional folk - with rock and jazz more or less assumed.
author: Bill Tilland

text: Subtitled the History of Misery Series, Volume One, from The Library of World Misery, this is predictably not a barrel of laughs, although the dominant mood is perhaps a kind of madcap gallows humour, i.e., "you gotta laugh to keep from cryin'." The opening track, "another hanging," is a disturbed (and disturbing) dreamscape built around a stumbling but mesmerizing piano etude (as played by a not-very-precocious child during a daily practice), with an additional languid motif on electric guitar, and squalling figures from Eyvind Kang's violin.
author: Bill Tilland

text: This gently warped lyricism is soon displaced by "electric candyland," which is filled with distorted rumbling and overdriven guitar noises ranging from howls to sci-fi lab pulses and whines.
author: Bill Tilland

text: One can almost see Igor emerging from the chemical fog, ready to do his master's bidding.
author: Bill Tilland

text: Without any transition at all, the listener is transported to some sort of faux Japanese court, where an artless, on-and-off-key male falsetto voice babbles inscrutable syllables over a repetitive organ riff.
author: Bill Tilland

text: Then it's back to electronic static (with some crazed laughter) in "vanilla sufi," which evolves into another insistent, hypnotic pattern from Schuller's strummed zither, along with Bill Horist's rhythm guitar and some deep, thumping ritual percussion.And so it goes, for the entire ten selections on the CD, with one improbable musical scenario mutating into another.
author: Bill Tilland

text: On one level, it would be easy to dismiss Lesser Angel of Failure as artless and crude.
author: Bill Tilland

text: Indeed, the entire CD contains precious little evidence of any instrumental (or vocal) expertise.
author: Bill Tilland

text: But that criticism would miss the point; the extraordinary impact of this music comes from the unlikely juxtapositions and configurations which force the mind (and ear) onto rutted, weed-infested roads leading to strange, unimaginable destinations.
author: Bill Tilland

text: Some tracks have a vaguely programmatic quality, e.g., "another hanging" sounds sad, disconnected and quietly unsettling, while "civil war bukakke" (a ragged march) has qualities of mindless, even obscene futility.
author: Bill Tilland

text: Other pieces, though, such as "camel dragged to death" and "bulimian rhapsody," provide no obvious literal associations between titles and music, which is probably a very good thing (!).
author: Bill Tilland

text: Clearly, Schuller's work contains an element of parody, but most of his work is far too convincing, intense and unsettling to be dismissed (or appreciated) as some sort of ironic, po-mo diversion.
author: Bill Tilland

text: You may hate this CD, or you may love it.
author: Bill Tilland

text: It may just leave you scratching your head and muttering to yourself.
author: Bill Tilland

text: But in a world of cookie-cutter, rubber stamp music, it surely stands out.
author: Bill Tilland

text: Humphrey Lyttleton's favourite vocalist is renowned for her devotion to the Great American Songbook and for her wonderful way with a ballad.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: For her new album 'The Boy Next Door', the tempo is still relaxed and the delivery languid, but there are some new kids on the block.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: Stacey's still clutching the Songbook in one hand, but in the other she's brandishing music associated with the likes of Chet Baker, Paul Simon and James Taylor.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: Stacey draws consonants out like bubblegum in 'The Best is Yet to Come', her voice smooth but with that serrated edge that keeps you entranced, and David Newton contributes a tiny but perfectly-conceived piano solo on this and on the title track.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: Both are simple but beautiful vehicles for Stacey's Christmas-bauble vocals and impeccable timing.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: 'Makin' Whoopee' sees Stacey and the band getting low down and bluesy.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: Imagine Carrie from 'Sex and the City' as a jazz singer, and that's Stacey on 'Makin' Whoopee'.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: She's completely in control, with a demure, half-hidden sexiness that shines through in her diction and delivery.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: Stacey's musicians happily succumb to her lead - the rhythm section hangs back behind the beat and Stacey's husband Jim Tomlinson provides gentle support on the sax (but only when the lady permits it).
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: 'Ooh-Shoo-Be-Doo-Bee' is infused with the same pert sexiness, but here it becomes mock theatrical as David, Jim and recording engineer Curtis Schwartz add tongue-in-cheek backing vocals and tons of swing behind Stacey's luscious phrasing.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: Keeping the band focused on accompaniment and not on solos works to give the tightly-structured performances that we've come to expect.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: Nothing can ruffle her cool, in-control exterior.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: You can almost hear her relaxed smile in 'Tis Autumn' and in 'I Get Along Without You Very Well' she's jettisoned Chet Baker's air of mild despair and adopted stoical acceptance instead.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: It's questionable whether Stacey adds anything to 'You've Got a Friend' - where even her vibrato is reminiscent of Carole King's - or to "Bookends" by Paul Simon.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: Both are covers, not reworks.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: Burt Bacharach's 'What the World Needs Now', though, demands playing and replaying.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: David Newton's piano sits well behind the lyric, allowing it freedom and movement, and Stacey's breathy, perfectly-timed vocals give David the space to stretch his fingers out just a little.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: At 16 tracks you certainly get your money's worth from this album, and there are no interruptions from long or inaccessible instrumental solos.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: If that's how you like your jazz, you'll love The Boy Next Door.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: Ms Kent's stepping out beyond the Great American songbook and there's no stopping her now.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: Now that Stacey Kent's hit the 200,000 mark in sales, it seems like a good time to whip out a collection like this.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Taken from her first three Candid albums (plus a collaboration with tenor player Jim Tomlinson and one unreleased track), it's ample demonstration of the qualities that have made her one of the most popular mainstream singers around.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Kent has the knack of giving straight, unadorned readings of well worn standards witha freshness that's rare and sweet.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Much like Peggy Lee, she doesn't reinvent on a grand scale or dazzle with vocal pyrotechnics but draws you in with the clarity of her delivery.
author: Peter Marsh

text: It's subtle, unforced stuff; she can be cute without cloying, sassy without being smug and handles ballads with an assured delicacy and depth.
author: Peter Marsh

text: What could easily become cliche is never in danger of being so; check the joyful treatment of "In The Still of the Night", "It's Delovely" or the poise of the hushed, Bill Evans-esque "You Go To My Head".
author: Peter Marsh

text: Tomlinson's tenor displays similar qualities; with a breathy tone reminiscent ofZoot Sims or Al Cohn,he elaborates on the Lester Young school with an easy grace (best heard on the delicious bossa-tinged take on "East of the Sun, West of the Moon").
author: Peter Marsh

text: Able support is given by pianists David Newton and John Pearce, guitarist Colin Oxley and rhythm sections that include the wonderful Dave Green on bass.
author: Peter Marsh

text: (Though a slap on the wrist should go to Candid for not crediting Guy Barker's sparkling trumpet on Ellington's "I'm Just a Lucky So and So").
author: Peter Marsh

text: All in all, a fine introduction to the work of one of the best interpreters of the Great American Songbook around.
author: Peter Marsh

text: If someone told you that the main songwriter of a second-league band who haven't had a top 20 hit in over twenty years had decided to unleash 13 (!) albums of home demos on the world, you'd probably be a little underwhelmed.
author: Chris Jones

text: That is until you discovered that the 'second-league band' was the criminally undervalued XTC, and the songwriter is Andy Partridge; a man who, like Robert Wyatt, is fast becoming a paragon of that rare breed, 'The Great English Eccentric'.
author: Chris Jones

text: For this is no ordinary writer, and these are no ordinary demos.
author: Chris Jones

text: Admittedly these sets are no starting point for anyone wishing for an introduction to the popsy-turvey world of Swindon's finest, but for dedicated Partridge-fanciers this is a real treat.
author: Chris Jones

text: Mr P demonstrates the lure of salvage by adopting a 'warts 'n' all' approach to these collected snippets.
author: Chris Jones

text: However,for a musician with this amount of skill and experience most songs have a studio sheen that far-surpasses a 'drum machine and a four track' set-up.
author: Chris Jones

text: Most tracks fall into one of three areas: instrumental noodles (such as the lovely Mellotron-based ''Ridgeway Path'' on volume 2 or fifties sci-fi guitar twangathon ''Space Wray'' on volume 1); nascent XTC gems in either solo versions or studio rough cuts (''Merely A Man'', ''Miniature Sun'', ''Complicated Game'', ''Then She Appeared'' etc); and songs that remained Patridge's alone, such as his work for film soundtrack A Bug's Life (ultimately rejected in favour of Randy Newman.
author: Chris Jones

text: Were they mad?).
author: Chris Jones

text: As always with Andy, humour is never far away.
author: Chris Jones

text: Check the jolly studio banter (and hilarious Robert Smith impersonation) on ''That Wag''.
author: Chris Jones

text: Likewise, his wordplay is relentless and turns the sleevenotes into a genuinely warm, and humbly informative document of his mind's inner workings.
author: Chris Jones

text: As a man whose own crippling stagefright curtailed a live career, he's never less than candid about his feelings at the time of composition (cf: ''Ship Trapped In The Ice'') and this turns a potentially self-indulgent exercise into a fascinating glimpse into one of the late 20th century's greatest pop brains.
author: Chris Jones

text: Two volumes in, and it's already looking like a memorable ride...who cares if it's slightly fuzzy?
author: Chris Jones

text: Salsa superstar alert.
author: Neil Bennun

text: David Alvarez from Manzanillo, Cuba, takes the slick contemporary salsa of South America and re-injects a healthy dose of tempered anarchy, Cuban style.
author: Neil Bennun

text: The result is a pan-Carribean style successfully designed to induce havoc on dancefloors.
author: Neil Bennun

text: It blazes; superb musicianship, tongue-in-cheek eroticism and a positively unearthly quantity of energy are the order of the day.
author: Neil Bennun

text: Alvarez reclaims for Cuba a quantity of the cutting edge, not to mention the commerciality, normally considered the exclusive province of the Columbians and Venezuelans.
author: Neil Bennun

text: He achieves this while maintaining an unmistakably Cuban flavour in the music.
author: Neil Bennun

text: He has a life-long addiction to the greats of bolero and son such as Beny More, Blanca Rosa and Trio Matamaros, a grounding in more traditional Cuban forms such as tres, and he very clearly likes to party.
author: Neil Bennun

text: The colours are bright, the music uptempo and the lyrics consistently engaging here.
author: Neil Bennun

text: Alvarez's voice, with its force, lack of pretension and gentle vibrato is instantly familiar.
author: Neil Bennun

text: The vocal harmonies and arrangements, showcased to splendid effect on Oscar Olivera's 'Mi Velorio' and his amusing reworking of 'Que Rico Vacilon', here an emotive pean to a slippery Argentinian woman, show some genuine innovation.
author: Neil Bennun

text: Although the emphasis is overwhelmingly weighted towards salsa, Alvarez successfully co-opts instruments from all over the Latin and Caribbean musical world.
author: Neil Bennun

text: Theres a hint of tango on on 'Que Rico Vacilon' and bright guitar runs somewhere between calypso and west African pop on 'El Beso', while the clever, understated use of samplers and synthesisers demonstrate a forward-looking approach.
author: Neil Bennun

text: For a splendid arranger and genuine lyrical talent possessed of a curiously moving voice, this is something of a breakthrough album.
author: Neil Bennun

text: Pretty much state of the art for contemporary salsa.
author: Neil Bennun

text: I love this album - I've listened to it dozens of times, which makes writing about it rather difficult: there's so much there that's good.
author: Lucy Davies

text: Star*Bodixa are a relatively new, unheard of band, but it shouldn't be so.
author: Lucy Davies

text: From Leeds, they were formed by Anna and Emily, who have been writing songs together from childhood.
author: Lucy Davies

text: They seem to have been dogged by bad luck ever since -whilst soundchecking for a showcase gig,armed robbers invaded the venue, and on the way to another, a lorry crashed into their car (true!).
author: Lucy Davies

text: Despite this,Star*Bodixa have created a strong, self assured debut, full of great moments.
author: Lucy Davies

text: So, I'll try to list some of the many highlights of And They Danced on Glass: Their lyricsdeal with conflicting emotions and irregular subjects.
author: Lucy Davies

text: 'Mr Trebus' is about a man who lives in North London, documented on John Peel's TV programme,Life of Grime.
author: Lucy Davies

text: He wouldn't throw anything away in his house, until he was living in about 2 square feet of real space.
author: Lucy Davies

text: There's a mixture of pity as he is doomed to fail against the authorities; and repulsion as the reality of the stink and decay sets in.
author: Lucy Davies

text: Instrumentation and arrangements are inventive throughout - take 'Balloon Song', which ends in a four-part close gospel style harmony, and the accordion break in 'Film Song' takes on a new, French, Amelie style dimension.
author: Lucy Davies

text: Gorgeous chords and melodies are played with real control and energy - everything seems to be there for a purpose.
author: Lucy Davies

text: 'Give Me Rain' is as powerful as Doves' 'The Pounding'.
author: Lucy Davies

text: 'Universe' and 'Fairytailed' are uplifting and energetic pop songs, that aren't afraid to be pretty.
author: Lucy Davies

text: Beautiful words sum up the world and lodge themselves in your head - 'Universe':"I wish the universe was smaller, then I could look it in the eye".
author: Lucy Davies

text: It may be naff in print, but not the way that Anna sings it.
author: Lucy Davies

text: If this album isn't in your record shop, get in there and order it.
author: Lucy Davies

text: It's time we had an alternative to Nu Punk that we can actually dance to and think about, and this is it.
author: Lucy Davies

text: 2003 should be the year for Star Bodixa.
author: Lucy Davies

text: Hugh Hopper's best known as a member of the 'classic' lineup of Soft Machine, whose early 70s albumsdisplayed a sometimes whimsical, very English mix of jazz, psychedelia and rock.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Hopper's approach to the bass guitar lay somewhere between John Entwistle and Charlie Mingus, capable of sweetly melodic lines or vicious bursts of thick fuzz; it's still one of the most recognisable sounds in English music.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Since the heady days of prog,Hopper's been involved with a bewildering range of projects, from Soft Machine spin offsfeaturing various Canterbury scene alumni to his own seminal tapeloop driven 1984, to more recent hookups with Kramer, American singer Lisa Klossner and art rockers Caveman Shoestore.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Hopper's said that his primary concern has always been with texture and sure enough,Jazzloops drips with atmosphere.
author: Peter Marsh

text: It appears to be an assemblage gathered from rehearsal tapes and studio jams, reconstructed and added to by Hopper's bass, guitar and samples (I presume it's a Jimmy Garrison sample underpinning "Garrisoi").
author: Peter Marsh

text: The saxes of Elton Dean, Gong man Didier Malherbe and the underrated Simon Picard (often heard with Trevor Watts) pick their way in lyrical, post- Coltrane style through grainy loops of bass and drum grooves (old mucker John Marshall appears to be the propulsion unit behind the one legged swing of "L4", which comes on like a fragment of an old Henry Cowsession).
author: Peter Marsh

text: Though occasionally the bassist treats us to a taste of his fuzz pedal, for the most part it's the (mainly soprano) saxes that do the talking; Pierre-Oliver Govin whips out a particularly incandescent display on the closing "nigepo" and Didier Malherbe (I think) is responsible for the muezzin calls of the ethno-ambient "sfrankl".
author: Peter Marsh

text: In a blindfold test, most of us might think this was some hot new post rock/postfusion outfit out of Chicago or Norway, paying homage to mid 70s Miles in lo-fi fashion.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The truth is that Hopper's been a past master of this kind of thing for over 30 yearsand is still hard at it.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Electronic performance duo Furt (aka Richard Barrett and Paul Obermayer) have been quietly dismantling the boundaries between improvisation and composition for some 16 years now.
author: Hannah Skrinar

text: Barrett is a composer of dense, knotty works (often termed 'New Complexity') while Obermayer works in free improv trio Bark!
author: Hannah Skrinar

text: Defektkicks off with "Plint", the most 'difficult' and rhythmically disjointed piece of the four.
author: Hannah Skrinar

text: Derived from one of the duo'slive performances, it's a sparse, slow-moving mix of Cageian prepared piano sounds, which at one point becomes a mesmerizing duet between left and right speakers.
author: Hannah Skrinar

text: By contrast "Gute Nacht" is dominated by warmer textures and a comforting drone background reminiscent of the Orb's "Little Fluffy Clouds", over which is superimposed a flickering rush of processed sounds.
author: Hannah Skrinar

text: Brief classical music interjections (all presumably from Schubert) seem to have been carefully selected so as to make them very hard to identify, and although this might not be to everyone's taste, all in all this is a highly enjoyable 5 minutes.
author: Hannah Skrinar

text: The most derivative piece on the disc is the anti-Fascist "Volksmusik", which begins with a marching band loop reminiscent of Charles Ives, minus the crunchy harmonies, and features the voice of Charlie Chaplin (taken, I imagine from The Great Dictator), as a sort of camp cross between Hitler and Basil Fawlty.
author: Hannah Skrinar

text: Full of dark undertones, and complete with a long, drawn-out orchestral climax (shades of Wagner or Strauss; hard to tell which exactly), it's both humorous and disturbing at once; a gripping combination.
author: Hannah Skrinar

text: The best is kept till last though.
author: Hannah Skrinar

text: As soon as the 45-minute masterpiece that is "Ultimatum" begins to unfold, the listener is transported into asonic world that could come from another galaxy.
author: Hannah Skrinar

text: Superbly crafted and incredibly inventive, "Ultimatum" (dedicated to Stockhausen) holds the attention with ease.
author: Hannah Skrinar

text: It's music that has the formal rightness of a late Beethoven quartet, yet rhythm is its least important element.
author: Hannah Skrinar

text: Although the pace varies often, the piece never sounds segmented.
author: Hannah Skrinar

text: It's in every respect a great piece of music, and alone is worth buying this CD for.
author: Hannah Skrinar

text: On the whole, Defekt is a varied disc which stands repeated listening; a strangely therapeutic and superb musical experience.
author: Hannah Skrinar

text: Richard Barrett and Paul Obermayer balance themselves between the two disciplines of electroacoustic composition and free improvisation.
author: Martin Longley

text: Their attitude towards sampling is 'hands-on', even though their music could easily be the result of pre-meditation.
author: Martin Longley

text: This album consists of just two extended pieces.
author: Martin Longley

text: "Mice" nearly touches forty minutes, and was crafted in the electronic music studios of Durham University in June 2004.
author: Martin Longley

text: An immediate chatter begins, and it never really shuts up.
author: Martin Longley

text: Furt admire density.
author: Martin Longley

text: Their samplers behave like busy hives, communally sucking in, chewing, swallowing, then regurgitating in a persistent shower of sound.
author: Martin Longley

text: Much of the matter is generated by old-fashioned acoustic instruments, granulated into a fresh existence.
author: Martin Longley

text: Wood, metal, plastic.
author: Martin Longley

text: These might be the materials.
author: Martin Longley

text: Scrunch, bleep, scuttle, mash, whoosh, scrape.
author: Martin Longley

text: There is a good deal of spatial swooping and scooting.
author: Martin Longley

text: Furt's fast attack is maintained throughout, dynamic in the extreme.
author: Martin Longley

text: They are terminally hyperactive.
author: Martin Longley

text: Toy voices are wrenched out, but some of these lend an unwelcome academic feel, possibly sourced from suspect tutored tonsils.
author: Martin Longley

text: Many of the sounds are string-generated: a babble of bowed, flicked and plucked nylon or steel.
author: Martin Longley

text: A repetitive thrum develops, with splurges of laser stuttergun.
author: Martin Longley

text: A series of silent pauses heighten the tension.
author: Martin Longley

text: "Sad Fantasy" is shorter.
author: Martin Longley

text: Just under thirty-two minutes.
author: Martin Longley

text: It was recorded live at London's Conway Hall, during the 2002 Freedom Of The City festival of improvised music.
author: Martin Longley

text: Perhaps because of real-time pressure, Its sonic range seems more limited.
author: Martin Longley

text: Much of the initial source material springs from the innards of a piano, possibly recorded earlier in the day, and almost certainly self-generated.
author: Martin Longley

text: These makings are stretched, warped and looped, although remaining mostly recognisable.
author: Martin Longley

text: As the piece develops, its rate is even faster than that of the studio work, the duo doubtless ruffled up by the presence of an audience.
author: Martin Longley

text: What sounds like some kind of reed instrument is slowed down and sped up to extremes, then a garbled voice is matched with pervasive crackling.
author: Martin Longley

text: A complex rhythmic pattern develops towards the climax, looped and repeated into unpredictable structures.
author: Martin Longley

text: Barrett and Obermayer sustain an intense atmosphere of busy resourcefulness, filling their long developments with an impressively contrasting range of sound.
author: Martin Longley

text: Their experimentation never loses its vital lust for visceral thrills.
author: Martin Longley

text: Furt's only fear is the silence, used so sparingly on this disc.
author: Martin Longley

text: Godskitchen has become something of a global club phenomenon over the past decade along with the likes of Cream and Ministry Of Sound.
author: Damian Jones

text: Going by this latest triple CD, filled with banging 40 trance tunes, it is easy to see why.
author: Damian Jones

text: Capturing three perfect clubbing moments in one night (11 pm, 1 am and 3am), Direct avoids the typical run-of-the-mill cheesy trance anthems and concentrates on a solid mix of mostly unknown dance floor fillers.
author: Damian Jones

text: Hybrid's dark groover "Gravastar" sets the tone superbly kicking in with an eerie slapping bass.
author: Damian Jones

text: Despite the fact Push's tranced up remix of Moby's "In This World" is a million miles away from the little man's moody album version, this dressed up dance offering is still sure to go down well in the clubs as will the uplifting "Wandering Star" by Seraque.
author: Damian Jones

text: Dutch trancer DJ Tiesto puts his magic touch to the Paul Oakenfold favourite "Flesh" by Jan Johnston, injecting this dance classic with a much harder, darker edge.
author: Damian Jones

text: CD 2 cranks the mood up a gear drawing in big name mix-meisters such as Junkie XL (famous for the No 1 Elvis hit "A Little Less Conversation"), Tiesto and Oakie.
author: Damian Jones

text: Bar the slightly cheesy lyrics, Tiesto's remix of "Tears From The Moon" by Conjure One is a perfect club anthem, oozing a thumping bass over shimmering vocals.
author: Damian Jones

text: Armin Van Buuren's euphoric "The Sound Of Goodbye" and Cygnus X's dreamy "Positron 2002" are by far two of the strongest tracks on this triple CD.
author: Damian Jones

text: Its just a shame Tiesto and Junkie XLs monotonous effort "Obsession" is such a let down.
author: Damian Jones

text: CD 3 makes up for this mere blip though, lifting the tempo up another notch with a selection of hard dance floor stompers.
author: Damian Jones

text: The pounding "Brazil" by Boca and the gothic sound of Umek's "Gatex" along with 100 mile an hour mover "Modifier" by Pale X reflect the mood of a truly accomplished trance album.
author: Damian Jones

text: Piano Creeps is a gem of a record.
author: Dan Tallis

text: Simple yet beautiful, these 12, mainly instrumental songs glisten and shimmer with mysterious charm.
author: Dan Tallis

text: They dazzle the listener with eerie piano rhythms and simple guitar and violin led compositions.
author: Dan Tallis

text: Mary Lorson& Billy Cote were the songwriting pair behind Madder Rose, the New York indie band that received critical acclaim for '93's Bring It Down and '94's Panic On.
author: Dan Tallis

text: They even sold a few copies.
author: Dan Tallis

text: A gradual dive into obscurity followed with the low key release of the bands final album Tragic Magic in '97.
author: Dan Tallis

text: However, Lorson and Cote never really stopped working together with Cote contributing to Lorson's Saint Low project.
author: Dan Tallis

text: Piano Creeps is the first release under this guise and it stands out as their best work in years.
author: Dan Tallis

text: The album opens with "E Guitar".
author: Dan Tallis

text: A basic, unnervingly addictive drumbeat fills the background while a three chord guitar rhythm dominates the foreground.
author: Dan Tallis

text: The song doesn't really develop but when the song closes after four minutes you're left not unsatisfied.
author: Dan Tallis

text: "Dig A Hole" features violins blended seamlessly with a deep bass beat.
author: Dan Tallis

text: Muffled, distorted voices cry desperately throughout the song.
author: Dan Tallis

text: The listener feels as if stuck in a recurring dream where the voices fail to give explanation or resolution.
author: Dan Tallis

text: "World's Fair" is a particularly enchanting song where the guitars are more prominent.
author: Dan Tallis

text: The music sways like a candle flame flickering in the breeze; it can fade, almost dying altogether, then it suddenly soars high and true.
author: Dan Tallis

text: It's not until track 7, "See The Stars", that we hear the first vocal performance.
author: Dan Tallis

text: Even then they consist of a repeated chorus that merely serves to accompany the instruments.
author: Dan Tallis

text: Lorson explains the lack of vocals succinctly: "Billy and I really enjoy the freedom of the instrumental format, since there is no requirement to 'get to the chorus' or stick to the songwriting roadmap".
author: Dan Tallis

text: As the album title suggests the record is held together by simple recurring piano rhythms and beats.
author: Dan Tallis

text: Often eerie and ghostly, but always captivating, these songs simply demand your attention.
author: Dan Tallis

text: I was forced to stop whatever it was I was doing and listen; a very rewarding and pleasant experience.
author: Dan Tallis

text: Free improvisers are a funny bunch.
author: Peter Marsh

text: There are those who like to argue endlessly over the aesthetics and politics of the music, while others prefer to let their instruments (ahem) do the talking.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Those in the former camp may think that Clive Bell and Mike Adcock's use of ethnic instruments in their improvisations raises all sorts of extra thorny issues of cultural authenticity and so on.
author: Peter Marsh

text: With musiclike this though, such arguments are pushed aside pretty conclusively.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Bell and Adcock played together in Accordions Go Crazy, a slightly peculiar avant ceilidh outfit whose polkas and waltzes were bookended by free improvisations.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Here they revel in the strange, sometimes raw timbres of reed instruments such as the khene (Thai mouth organ), shakuhachi (Japanese flute) and the decidedly non-ethnic (and rather scary) stereo goathorn coupled with accordions and prepared piano to create 12 vibrant, delicate miniatures.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Bell's been doing this kind of thing for years; while having cornered the (admittedly small) market as a session musician offering such exotica in the studio and on stage, his other endeavours have includedimprov outfit British Summer Timeas well as being a member of Jah Wobble's ethnodub outfit Deep Space.
author: Peter Marsh

text: His command of these obscure and unwieldy wind instruments results in a rich palette of whoops, breathy lyricism and throaty, buzzing rasps that pick their way through Adcock's shifting clouds of accordion drone or fragile prepared piano.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Sometimes the duo hint at the immersive deep listening droneology of Pauline Oliveros or the limpid expressionism of Toru Takemitsu; at other times traces of traditional musics appear, but shot through with an improviser's taste for the unexpected (this is the only record I'm aware of that features a duet between shakuhachi and sticky backed tape, which is probably enough to recommend it to some of us).
author: Peter Marsh

text: Much of it is beautiful, but (as you may have guessed) it's not the pan global mush you might encounter playing in your local health food shop.
author: Peter Marsh

text: This is honest, open, resonant music, sympathetically recorded.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Sleep It Off could charm the birds from the trees, and might just do the same for you.
author: Peter Marsh

text: It's strange but deeply satisfying to be able to say that the reputation of [Arnold Bax](http://www.bbc.co.uk/music/artists/9138c4da-1959-445c-8ac8-ba917ec84b3a)'s Symphonies is probably secure, thanks to the efforts of conductors like Vernon Handley, Bryden Thomson and David Lloyd-Jones; Bax's tone poems are even better bedded-in now.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: But the rehabilitation is hardly complete, as this new Naxos release reminds us.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: So we know the pleasures of Bax's orchestral music, the intense colour of the scores; how does his chamber music compare?
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Inevitably a string quartet offers fewer colours to play with, yet while you listen to the String Quartet No.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: 3 you never feel impoverished.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: The intensity, the warmth, the sheer lyrical beauty of the work is quite staggering at times, and the playing of the Maggini Quartet is stunning, from the hushed whispers of the third movement's Trio, to the rhythmic unanimity of all four performers in the Scherzo proper, with its unsettling harmonic insecurity and nervous tics and twitches...
author: Andrew McGregor

text: or the robust exuberance of the finale, with its unexpectedly powerful ending.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: The melodic ideas pour from Bax's pen, a rich profusion that seems to stem from a summer spent in England, and memories of his beloved Ireland: 'the coming of spring in beautiful Kenmare'...and if there are shadows, then they're not the shadows of war; the Third Quartet dates from 1936, written for the Griller Quartet.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: The Magginis have already made a superb recording of the first two Bax quartets for Naxos, and this fine recording completes the picture: warmth and detail, intimacy yet beautifully captured ambience.
author: Andrew McGregor
