text: Add the other two works, earlier Bax expressing in more straightforward terms his love-affair with Ireland; observe that none of this heart-warming music is otherwise available on CD, and clock the price: £4.99.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: How can you possibly resist?
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Whither Ryland Cooder?
author: Chris Jones

text: The world's foremost slide guitarist, uber-sessioneer and general guardian of music with authenticity has, for the last few years, subsumed his profile under projects that threw the spotlight onto musicians that the Western world had yet to 'discover'.
author: Chris Jones

text: The Buena Vista Social Club and Ali Farka Toure etc.
author: Chris Jones

text: all benefited from from Ry's commitment to educating, enlightening and entertaining.
author: Chris Jones

text: But where's the man that made Into The Purple Valley, Chicken Skin Music or Paris, Texas?
author: Chris Jones

text: Well, Mambo Sinuendo doesn't exactly redress the balance, but he's back in full electric form, and world music this ain't.
author: Chris Jones

text: Cooder's not the first to attempt to conjure up his childhood years in the form of musical nostalgia.
author: Chris Jones

text: Many artists from Billy Joel to Neil Young have recalled their post-war years, emerging at the cusp of jazz's transformation into rock 'n' roll.
author: Chris Jones

text: Donald Fagen's Nightfly erred on the side of smooth sophistication with its evocation of 50s optimism, but Mambo Sinuendo remains closer to Tom Verlaine's underrated Warm And Cool, with retro-reverbed guitars and whammy bar whooziness.
author: Chris Jones

text: Joining forces with Manuel Galban, former member of Cuba's premier vocal group of the 50s and 60s, Los Zafiros, Mambo...
author: Chris Jones

text: plays homage to the Perez Prado school of cha-cha rock 'n' roll (there's a delightfully cheesy version of Prado's ''Patricia'' here).
author: Chris Jones

text: Sinuous rhythmscourtesy of old pal Jim Keltner, collide with girly choruses -all Duane Eddy holidaying in Havana.
author: Chris Jones

text: Remember the seedy Cuban club Fredo took Michael to in The Godfather Part 2?
author: Chris Jones

text: This is the soundtrack.
author: Chris Jones

text: Galban's grit and twang (one track is even called ''Los Twangueros'' A result of Ry's inability to find a suitably descriptive term in Spanish!) is more than matched by Cooder's trademark growl, especially on "Monte A Dentro".
author: Chris Jones

text: It's a welcome return to a sound unheard since Get Rhythm and perfectly showcased in such a warm and humorously danceable setting.
author: Chris Jones

text: However it's the penultimate track, a slow extemporised version of the jazz standard ''Secret Love'' that really stands out here.
author: Chris Jones

text: Cooder's twitches, flourishes and tentative pickings all put one in mind of the only other man to approach the guitar with such a breadth of vision- Marc Ribot.
author: Chris Jones

text: So he's still in love with Castro's Caribbean hideaway and this is an exquisite tropical jewel of an album.
author: Chris Jones

text: In these uncertain times he's a lucky man to have been granted a special dispensation (courtesy of Bill Clinton) to visit Cuba at all.
author: Chris Jones

text: But maybe the signs are here that he's turning his eyes homeward at last.
author: Chris Jones

text: Not before time...
author: Chris Jones

text: Formed in 1995 by two drum and bass pioneers, E-Z Rollers cohorts Jay and Alex have risen steadily through the dance music ranks.
author: David Silverman

text: For their production work, the pair enlisted the help of sometime studio friend and associate Kelly Richards.
author: David Silverman

text: Their first long-player together, Dimensions Of Sound, arrived in 1996 and its gentle, jazz influenced hooks, solid beats and melodic keys were wonderfully enhanced by Kelly's exquisite vocals.
author: David Silverman

text: The benchmark was thus set.
author: David Silverman

text: The crew kept their hand in over the next few months with various 12s before unleashing their second album, Weekend World, in 1998.
author: David Silverman

text: This saw a brief excursion into the UK charts with "Walk This Land" which reached an astonishing No.18 in the UK charts after being used for the British flick, Lock, Stock and Two Smoking Barrels.
author: David Silverman

text: Still ahead of the pack after all this time, they have produced their most accomplished LP to date.
author: David Silverman

text: Packed with anthemic tunes such as the forthcoming single "Back To Love", and the hip-hop groove "You'll Never Know", this album stretches right across musical genres, from the breaks inspired "Take It EZ" to the dancehall-style flavas of "Lady Jam".
author: David Silverman

text: Always open minded and well known for serving a huge assortment of different sonic delicacies from a number of different platters, Titles of the Unexpected sees them search deeper within their inner self.
author: David Silverman

text: With the enrolment of hip-hop beatbox legend Doug E Fresh and soul diva Sharon Brown, the sonic adventure is complete.
author: David Silverman

text: This album has got to rock dancefloors all over the country.
author: David Silverman

text: The EZs roll with high tempo d & b and mid-tempo breaks with a collection of tracks full of fervour and flair.
author: David Silverman

text: And yet, unlike many of their predecessors, they seem to be having a very good time doing it.
author: David Silverman

text: Any artist doing their third album must be doing something right and maybe this is the reason why they've come so far.
author: David Silverman

text: This is a superb representation of where drum and bass is today.
author: David Silverman

text: It's hard to believe that it's been ten years since Germany's Basic Channel label crossed the threshold between deep techno and dirty dub.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Since then, the techno community has come a long way and regularly enjoys bathing in scratchy rhythm beds and deep minimal basslines brought to us from the back streets of Berlin.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: From New York to Tokyo to Auckland, there have been many who have embraced this sound, with notable success.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: More recently however, the Canadians have gotten in on the act - First with Toronto's Audi Sensa imprint, and now Montreal's own Deadbeat is leading the charge.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Deadbeat is one Scott Montheit, a key player in Montreal's new music scene for almost a decade now.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Getting his start with labels like Revolver and Hautec, he recently signed up to the excellent ~scape label for this debut full length.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: The fact that a German label has released a record like this is no mistake.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Bringing the patented King Tubby/Lee Perry sound ten steps further down the road, Wild Life Documentaries sees Montheit layering ambient beds of granular noise over skanking beats, offering the best bang for the buck the further the tracks progress.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: But rather than simply dive into the effects processors like the Basic Channel crew, Montheit keeps his style firmly grounded in the old school of dub.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Its a sound half rooted in the analogue low end of yesterday and the razor sharp digital dynamics of today.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Although it's a linear listen, there are a few twists and turns along the way.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: "A Dub For Akufen", (a track meant originally as a collaboration between the two artists) bounces and along like a dub filled dustball, gathering speed and size as it rolls down a steep hill.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: "Organ In The Attic" takes an old Hammond B3 and throws it straight into the dub blender at half speed creating a wonderfully thick and chunky sound, as does the aptly titled "To Berlin With Love", where we see Deadbeat crank out a heavy almost four-to-the-floor beat with some fantastic rhythm samples thrown in.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Germany, or at least certain factions within Berlin's techno scene, would indeed be proud.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: While perhaps not as groundbreaking as some of the other music coming out of Montreal these days, Deadbeat is nevertheless an excellent exercise in dubbed out techno that fans of the style should consider an essential purchase.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: A very cool release for you crazy dubheads out there.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Howard Shore won an Oscar for scoring the first part of The Lord of the Rings trilogy.
author: Morag Reavley

text: In 'The Two Towers', the difficult middle part of the Middle-earth saga, he further develops his weird aural landscape.
author: Morag Reavley

text: As before, he has created a full-blown orchestral score of Wagnerian proportions, each character and realm with its own musical identity.
author: Morag Reavley

text: With the fellowship now splintered into three, the score of the second part becomes more complex than the first, weaving between the plot strands with different musical themes.
author: Morag Reavley

text: Leitmotifs are picked up from the first soundtrack, for example, the perky Hobbit anthem in "Samwise the Brave", and new ones developed as the groups diverge.
author: Morag Reavley

text: The music is mercifully far from airy-fairy.
author: Morag Reavley

text: It begins with the fulminant "Foundations of Stone", all serried choirs and pounding percussion.
author: Morag Reavley

text: The dark elements invoked in the earlier score now dominate as the struggle of Frodo and friends becomes more intense.
author: Morag Reavley

text: But the endless succession of unresolved crescendos and the ever-escalating sense of doom get a bit much.
author: Morag Reavley

text: Elizabeth Fraser (of Cocteau Twins fame), Sheila Chandra and Isabel Bayrakdarian provide banshee accompaniment so high that it approaches ultrasound.
author: Morag Reavley

text: The closing track, "Gollum's Song", is an instant winner.Performed by Iceland's latest singing elf Emiliana Torrini (and originally intended for Bjork), this elegy is tormented, twisty, infinitely strange.
author: Morag Reavley

text: An Icelander singing in English sounds far more otherworldly than the choirs singing in Old English and Tolkiens made-up Sindarin.
author: Morag Reavley

text: Fine qualities aside, the soundtrack is ultimately marred by the partial nature of its form.
author: Morag Reavley

text: Driven by the visuals, not its own logic, it is a series of musical vignettes rather than an organic whole.
author: Morag Reavley

text: And since Shore has conceived the score for all three films as a single orchestral whole, the music of the middle section by definition lacks resolution.
author: Morag Reavley

text: Die-hard fans of Tolkien (are there any other kind?) will cherish this album as a painstaking musical description of the Middle-earth mythology.
author: Morag Reavley

text: The rest may admire its ambition and the haunting set pieces, but without a deep knowledge of the film or books they will inevitably find it...
author: Morag Reavley

text: If the soundtrack from A History of Violence reminds you a bit of the Lord of the Rings' music, its not surprising.
author: Morag Reavley

text: Both scores are for films exploring the nature of good and evil, and both were penned by Howard Shore, Hollywood's most Wagnerian composer.
author: Morag Reavley

text: But unfortunately the new score lacks both the epic sweep of the Rings' soundtracks and the memorable experimentalism of Shore's earlier Cronenberg outings (The Fly, eXistenZ, Naked Lunch).
author: Morag Reavley

text: On the positive side, there is Shore's scrupulous instrumental characterisation, with a troubling French horn and a pure alto flute representing the moral struggle within the mysterious main character.
author: Morag Reavley

text: And there are some beautifully polished individual scenes.
author: Morag Reavley

text: But overall Shore's music sounds deeply conventional, without the benefits convention confers.
author: Morag Reavley

text: There is no strong theme to hold the score together, and a lamentable lack of pace or variation.
author: Morag Reavley

text: Ultimately this is less 'dark and brooding' than 'dull and boring'.
author: Morag Reavley

text: Send on the hobbits, please.
author: Morag Reavley

text: Assembled in an en-suite at the Mount Olympus Motel for Square Peg Monsters of Rock, it came to pass that three of the mightiest warrior-musicians did meet.
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: Curt Kirkwood (guitar and vocals, ex-Meat Puppets), Krist Novoselic (bass and vocals, ex-Nirvana) and Bug Gaugh (drums, ex-Sublime) emerged blinking into the light.
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: Thus began Eyes Adrift.
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: Free from the burdensome shadows that threatened to eclipse them, in the wake of the success and tragic deaths of former band members, they have produced a powerful but melancholic album.
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: Their pedigree is a mongrel mix of country punk, angst rock and Stateside ska.
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: However, this, their debut offering, favours the accomplished philosophy of Kirkwood's plectrum.
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: Occasionally the pace quickens, edging toward the open vein that bleeds still from the corpse of Nirvana.
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: "Alaska" and "Telescopes" bookend a largely mellow debut with a gutteral, chop and change lyricism reminiscent of Cobain's former delivery.
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: Such baggage and weight of talent might easily have resulted in some horrendous fusion-dish.
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: Yet the dough holds shape, rising to resemble vintage REM.
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: The Edward Munch Scream-like form of Michael Stipe hovers greedily over "Sleight of Hand", "Slow Race", and "What I Said" and are all the better for it.
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: Surprisingly, Novoselic adopts lead larynx for "Inquiring Minds" (a peculiar, even contradictory, attack against media fascination in the Jon-Bennet Ramsey murder case), "Dottie Dawn & Julie Jewel" (unsullied bluegrass riffs), and "Pasted" (fifteen minutes of grizzled muck-slinging at an uncaring music industry).
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: His flawed, apologetic vocals add a refreshing sense of naivety, escaping the chains that bind the trio to past incarnations in favour of a garage rehearsal session after school.
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: It's a momentary respite, as the album as a whole resonates with a sonorous, elegiac quality.
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: Of being old beyond their years, suspended within 'a time that doesn't pass...sand, frozen in the hourglass' ("Solid").
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: A new super-group who renounce the jock-posturing of recent successors, and raise a glass instead to what has been, and what has yet to be.
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: Last year, Emanem released Trombolenium (1986-1995), an impressive series of snapshots of Paul Rutherford's improvised trombone solos.
author: John Eyles

text: In the sleeve notes of that album, Emanem boss Martin Davidson welcomed Rutherford's recovery from his serious illness of 2001 and also said it might be time for a new solo record.
author: John Eyles

text: Well, here it is.
author: John Eyles

text: It records Rutherford's appearance at the Empty Bottle Festival in Chicago, in which he performed solo and in a septet.
author: John Eyles

text: Even more than with his recent contribution to Amassed by Spring Heel Jack, it confirms that Rutherford is in fine fettle.
author: John Eyles

text: The solo track here, "Bottling Up", lasts for over half an hour.
author: John Eyles

text: In that time, at his own pace, Rutherford demonstrates his strengths; a variety of tones (not least his beautiful, vulnerable, human tone), his use of the full range of his instrument, his lucid, flowing phrases, his focus, his energy.
author: John Eyles

text: As Spring Heel Jack's Ashley Walessaid of Rutherford's solo playing recently, "He is playing beautiful notes, notes you recognise, sequences you recognise.
author: John Eyles

text: Some of it sounds like Vaughan Williams".
author: John Eyles

text: Rutherford's sense of occasion and sense of humour also shine through as he quotes a phrase from "Strangers in the Night" (no, I didnt believe it either!) - maybe there was some essence of Sinatra in the Chicago air that night...
author: John Eyles

text: In the septet, Rutherford is joined by Chicagoans Jeb Bishop (trombone), Fred Lonberg Holm (cello and electronics) & Kent Kessler (double bass), Swedes Mats Gustafsson (tenor sax) and Kjell Nordeson (percussion), plus Britain's own Lol Coxhill (soprano sax) - remarkably, only on his second visit to the USA.
author: John Eyles

text: The first of three septet pieces, "Loliloquy", is a showcase for Coxhill.
author: John Eyles

text: It slowly gathers momentum and has a melancholy air to it until an unaccompanied solo feature for Lol midway through.
author: John Eyles

text: But it's the final three minutes of the piece that really kickstart the septet and set the pulses racing, as all seven players engage in a bout of full-tilt all-out blowing - the kind of stuff that gets people hooked on improvisation (or, yes, totally alienates others!) On the other two septet pieces, "Blue Bottle" and "Bottle Out" (typical Emanem titles), Rutherford himself is more prominent, but the level of intensity and whole group interaction is consistently maintained.
author: John Eyles

text: It may be unfair to single out particular players, but Gustafsson's raw, throaty tenor and Lonberg-Holm's use of electronics and distortion both grab the attention.
author: John Eyles

text: In a rare moment of levity for the normally rather serious Emanem label, Martin Davidson's sleevenotes for this album describe it as 'great honky European improvised music'.
author: Peter Marsh

text: And he's not wrong either.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Trombonist Paul Rutherford is one of the founding fathers of that tradition alongside figures like Derek Bailey, Evan Parker, John Stevens and so on.
author: Peter Marsh

text: While he's most famed for the pointillist artprov of bands like Iskra 1903 or the stark meanderings of his pioneering solo records, this trio was put together to give reign to Rutherford's jazzier leanings (that's free jazz in case you hadn't guessed...).
author: Peter Marsh

text: 'Gheim' was recorded in 1983 and the first half of this CD originally appeared on the wonderful Ogun label.
author: Peter Marsh

text: It captures the trio of Rutherford, bassist Paul Rogers and drummer Nigel Morris live at the Bracknell festival in front of an enthusiastic crowd, who even clap after the solos just like they would at a proper jazz gig (now that wouldn't happen at an Iskra 1903 performance...).
author: Peter Marsh

text: Inevitably, there's something of the festival vibe about the music here.
author: Peter Marsh

text: It's high energy stuff, but it changes shape throughout with bewildering ease and fluidity, from freebop polyrhythmic pummelling to spidery ballad forms to spacey textural exploration.
author: Peter Marsh

text: This is also one of those recordings that makes you stop and think 'wait a minute - how did they get there?' This was one of Paul Rogers' first recordings, though you'd never guess that from the assured confidence of his performance.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The range of his playing is incredible; he serves up guttural scrapes with the bow, rich, melodic chordings and deeply swinging funkiness.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Two thirds into "Gheim Pt 1", he sets up an impossibly fast tumbling ostinato, sustains it for a good three or four minutes and then launches into a beautiful solo passage complete with Monk quotes.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Bet he had blisters that night.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The little known Morris matches Rogers' every move with an equal or opposite reaction, sometimes breaking off to follow his own path for a while before returning to active engagement with his bandmates.
author: Peter Marsh

text: It's thrilling, engaging, beautiful stuff, and the audience evidently love it with a passion that makes you wonder why this kind of music is so marginalised.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The rest of the CD is drawn from studio recordings which see the trio in a more textural mode.
author: Peter Marsh

text: There's a lot going on, but there's a flatness to the proceedings that makes it hard going compared to the glorious flights of the Bracknell gig.
author: Peter Marsh

text: But for that set alone, highly recommended.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Pram are probably one ot the UK's most individual bands, and maybe even one of its best kept secrets.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Over ten years and seven or so albums they've spun strange tales of mermaids, chrysalids, childhood, love and owls, framed by a strangely archaic music stuffed with theremins, trumpets, tinkly keyboards, shimmering, fragile guitars and warm, dubby basslines anchored to loping, gently chaotic rhythms.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Rosie Cuckston's lyrics are dreamlike observations, mixing imaginary landscapes ("Penny Arcade") with fragmentary recollections of childhood or thoughts on the inadequacy of language, all delivered in a sweetly dispassionate, very English tone.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Dark Island is another small step; things change slowly in Pramworld.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Maybe the arrangements are slightly more detailed; maybe it's a more intimate record.
author: Peter Marsh

text: It's hard to tell yet; Pram reveal their secrets slowly too.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The 10 tracks here are like Joseph Cornell's boxes; crammed with seemingly disparate elements that together create something new, resonant but elusive.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Rosie's tales mix sharp observation with sudden dark, personal confessions; 'We both wear paper hats and there's a jelly shaped like a rabbit on a plate' ("Paper Hats"); or from the hushed, melancholic "Goodbye"; 'In my dreams the graverobbers fill their pockets up with goods'.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The band's gift for warm, delicate strangeness recalls the aquatic ballads of Robert Wyatt, and like Wyatt or late 70s post punk experimentalists such as The Raincoats, structures seem fluid, quiet surprise never far away.
author: Peter Marsh

text: It's not a contrived strangeness either; unlike the sometimes calculated quirkiness employed by others, Pram's music suspends disbelief as they draw you into their intricate little world.
author: Peter Marsh

text: It's a place worth visiting.
author: Peter Marsh

text: We've been waiting so long for this, it's hard to believe it has actually arrived: a truly distinctive hip hop record made by Africans based in the UK.
author: Charlie Gillett

text: JJC- Johnny Just Come - is the term given to newcomers from Nigeria by the people who've been here for a while, and Fela Kuti had a song of this title.
author: Charlie Gillett

text: I don't know much about the rapper JJC except that hes a member of the Big Brovaz posse, and he has his own global hip hop show on the BBC digital radio channel, 1Xtra.
author: Charlie Gillett

text: What he establishes with this album is that he has wide tastes, a unique vision and a mischievous sense of humour.
author: Charlie Gillett

text: What more do you need?
author: Charlie Gillett

text: "Finally, after many obstacles, it's a miracle, I've made the album now", says JJC in the intro, and he then helpfully lists the ingredients that he has brought together: hip hop, R&B, soca, salsa, garage, mixed with African flavours.
author: Charlie Gillett

text: And we're off into the exhilarating surging rhythms of the title track "Atide".
author: Charlie Gillett

text: A salsa piano figure threads through the infectious chorus sung by a female vocal group led by guest vocalist Cherise, as JJC talks his way through the lyric, exhorting his people to come together, to feel good in each other's company.
author: Charlie Gillett

text: It's an anthem for a very different idea of Nigeria than the one we've been reading about in the papers recently.
author: Charlie Gillett

text: "Gbao" admonishes Nigerians in London who mimic Jamaicans, while also making fun of the conmen who come up with schemes for us to share in illegally siphoned government funds.
author: Charlie Gillett

text: "Malemicita" is a very ingenious salsa-meets-highlife-meets hip hop, with a catchy chorus that could put the song on pop charts worldwide.
author: Charlie Gillett

text: Where hip hop is so often the vehicle for an egocentric bully, nasty to women and threatening to other men, the good natured banter of this album conveys the opposite spirit of collaboration and inter-dependence.
author: Charlie Gillett

text: All in all, a great party album that will play in any situation.
author: Charlie Gillett

text: Cops Hate our Love is the idiosyncratic but strangely brilliant album from Toah Dynamic.
author: Marcus Scott

text: The band have an 'everything and the kitchen sink' attitude to making musicthat's refreshing to hear.
author: Marcus Scott

text: They have the same attitude to genres too, casually mixing English folk, old school hip hop and so on, creating a strange, unique hybrid.
author: Marcus Scott

text: Before listening, it's worth considering that some of the bandssolo projects have ranged from Kid Acne's collaboration with hip hop head Req, to Supreme Vagabond Craftsman's utterly bizarre medieval folk.
author: Marcus Scott

text: As if that weren't enough,, their drummer plays with speed metal band Bolt Thrower.
author: Marcus Scott

text: Lyrically, Toah Dynamic occupy a bizarre and hysterical world of their own, full of strange tales of acid trips, paying kids to fight forM& Ms, and lions, tigers and bears.
author: Marcus Scott

text: It's all delivered by various vocalists in a style reminiscent of the Fall's Mark E Smith or on occasions Shaun Ryder.
author: Marcus Scott

text: The albumkicks off with"Rave Radio".
author: Marcus Scott

text: Like Mantronix or early Boogie Down Productions on strange drugs, its hammered 808 stabs and off kilter samplers providing the only moment of relative familiarity on the album.
author: Marcus Scott

text: It's closely followed by "Billy Jean Kickout"; imagine the theme tune to Different Strokes loosely interpretedbynorthern farmers raised on hip hop and bad milk, complete with twanging banjo, scratching and buried drums.
author: Marcus Scott

text: "Lions tigers and bears" is all folk guitar, recorder and accordion with incoherent glitchy vocals, while"Drug Songs for the Irish" recalls Parliament and the Happy Mondays jamming with broken equipment.
author: Marcus Scott

text: The quite beautiful instrumental"Ghosts in Petrol" offers some respite from the towering oddness of the vocals, with pretty strings, guitar, minimal drums and xylophone.
author: Marcus Scott

text: The album ends with "Pentecostal Quids In", which features an uncanny impersonation of Sting (singing"Don't Stand so Close to Me").
author: Marcus Scott

text: Overall, Toah Dynamic must be applauded for their single minded madness.
author: Marcus Scott

text: Their music is in the spirit of British post punk bands who did their own thing, like 23 Skidoo, 400 Blows or A Certain Ratio, although it certainly doesn't sound like any of them.
author: Marcus Scott

text: In the currently retro musical climate it's good to hear a band taking wisdom from the past without descending into mere imitation.
author: Marcus Scott

text: If there's anyone on the planet who could produce an album that could conceivably appeal to both lovers of free improvisation and country music (a tall order, let's be honest), it's Eugene Chadbourne.
author: Peter Marsh

text: And by criminy, if the man responsible for Country Music in the World of Islam ain't been and gone and done it.
author: Peter Marsh

text: An Afternoon in Austin (subtitled Country Music for Harmolodic Souls)was made at the same time as the second chapter of Chadbourne's Doug Sahm tribute, which also featured Susan Alcorn's pedal steel.
author: Peter Marsh

text: It's a mix of free improv and typically wayward Chadbourne takes on tunes by Merle Haggard, Mickey Newbury and Loretta Lynn (one of the good doctor's original notions was a covers project of tunes by Lynn and Sun Ra).
author: Peter Marsh

text: Alcorn more than rises to the challenge; she's a beautiful player, capable of sweet, longing lines (as on the 11 minute drift of Haggard's doleful "If we Make it Through December" which slowly ravels and unravels itself into a strange dialogue of faltering melodies) or ghostly resonances.
author: Peter Marsh

text: She's got big ears, as they say in jazz; capable of following the skewed logic of Chadbourne's acoustic guitar or banjo with precision and imagination.
author: Peter Marsh

text: As usual, Eugene's sense of humour is in full effect (check the avant hoedown of "Sugene")yet he never sounds like he's disrespecting his sources; having fun with them maybe, which ain't no bad thing.
author: Peter Marsh

text: On the vocal tunes, his nasal singing seems to flirt with parody, but it's hard to tell.
author: Peter Marsh

text: But of course this is the man who played Albert Ayler tunes on a banjo,and second guessing him is a pointless task.
author: Peter Marsh

text: As ever his guitar playing is unpredictable, sometimes irritating even, but never dull, and he is capable of breathtakingly lovely bursts of melody.
author: Peter Marsh

text: He certainly remains one of the great avant guitar heroes (for want of a better phrase).
author: Peter Marsh

text: To borrow Brian Eno's description of the output of Miles Davis, there's very little self censorship in Chadbourne's release policy.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The huge mountain of self produced stuff he's put out makes it hard to get a grip on what he does, which I suspect is just the way he wants it.
author: Peter Marsh

text: An Afternoon in Austin won't offer much enlightenment on that score, but who cares.
author: Peter Marsh

text: 'Oriental Landscapes' is a subtle showcase for percussionist Evelyn Glennie's skills, and the first piece, Chen Yi's Percussion Concerto tackles the obvious problem head on.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: She talks in the notes about combining Eastern sounds and folk music with Western art music: 'If you just put them together...then it sounds artificial.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: But if you can merge them in your blood, then they sound natural together'.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: For the first two minutes there's the astonishing range of sounds made by a collection of traditional Chinese gongs, and when the orchestra enters it feels effortlessly oriental.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Then there's the reciting style of the voice in the second movement, startling for westerners unfamiliar with Beijing Opera.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: The percussionist is also supposed to supply the vocals, but I can't believe this is Evelyn Glennie!
author: Andrew McGregor

text: If it isn't, the singer should surely be credited somewhere in the packaging?
author: Andrew McGregor

text: After Chen's concerto ends (with the sounds of a traditional fight scene from Beijing Opera), Thea Musgrave's Journey through a Japanese Landscape could sound like pure pastiche.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: But of course it doesn't, and Musgrave doesn't try to imitate eastern instruments.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Her concerto for marimba and winds is a kind of 'Four Seasons' based on Japanese haiku, and the marimba has the perfect range of woody colours and effects to evoke the autumnal fog or the wintry winds and swirling snows of the last movement.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Chen Yi's husband, Zhou Long doesn't bother imitating eastern instruments either; he uses the real thing.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Out of Tang Court is, Zhou says, an attempt to give a new lease of life to the music of the Tang Dynasty by stretching the Chinese instruments westward, and the Western instruments eastward to achieve a common ground.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: The sounds of the erhu and sheng are eerily beautiful against the symphony orchestra, evoking a timeless, ceremonial atmosphere against which the outbursts of percussion feel peremptory, even ill-mannered.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: And them we come to the prolific American, Alan Hovhaness, who died in 2000.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: I suspected his Fantasy on Japanese Woodprints might sound tame alongside the other works, but I needn't have worried.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Hovhaness turned his back on the west in the mid-40s and spent twenty years travelling the east, and this is his love-poem to Japan.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: He doesn't need real Japanese instruments because he can make a symphony orchestra imitate them - startlingly good impressions of the hichiriki and the sho although it probably helps that this is the Singapore Symphony Orchestra, who are bound to have a better idea of the sounds of gagaku, Japan's ancient court music, than their western counterparts.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Yes, Hovhaness is closest to imitation, but it's so beautifully crafted (and performed) he pulls it off; he didn't spend all that time in Japan without perfecting the accent.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Glennie is superb, and somehow self-effacing; you never feel that her performance is screaming 'soloist!' at you...and the recording helps, beautifully balanced.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: A Brit and American in Japan, a Chinese couple now in the States, a western-style symphony orchestra in Singapore, and a Scottish soloist...it needed Swedish diplomacy to stitch this coalition together, and it works surprisingly well.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: First off, this is not an album for your jazz snob.
author: Matt Harvey

text: If your idea of a good time is listening to John Coltrane's Live In Seattle, standing on your head while twirling a beret on your toes, don't bother to listen to this.
author: Matt Harvey

text: And please don't bore the rest of us by telling us Jamie Cullum isn't proper Jazz (you're right, but who cares!).
author: Matt Harvey

text: Telling Tales is Jamie's third album, and the album is littered with collaborations from the international music scene, including Guy Chambers, Dan The Automator and Ed Harcourt.
author: Matt Harvey

text: And the results are pleasingly varied (in an undemanding sort of way), from the introspective ballads like "London Skies" to the jazzy big beat of "Get Your Own Way".
author: Matt Harvey

text: This is the perfect music to listen to while driving through the English countryside on a clear autumnal morning, and none the worse for that.
author: Matt Harvey

text: Twentysomething is the first fruit of Jamie Cullum's recent signing to Universal and he's filled it with melodic and witty standards, show tunes, Cullum brothers originals, and the occasional off-the-waller.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: On Twentysomething, Jamie's vocal sound is warmer, softer, less crisp than on his debut Pointless Nostalgic, because producer Stuart Levine has chosen to record in analogue, not digital format.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: He's recorded live, too, which leaves some of Jamie's piano solos sounding rough and ready, but gives the performances the power of a live show.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: Whether the songs are swingers or heartstring pullers, Jamie has the timing and conviction to get the best out of them.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: "I Get A Kick Out of You" is fast, spontaneous and vibrant; simulated cocaine-snorts and a dominant, no-nonsense delivery boot it into the modern day.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: On "Old Devil Moon", strings snake around Jamie's vocals, but introspection quickly gives way to big band swing with the backing of the distinguished horns of Mark Nightingale, Martin Shaw and Alan Barnes.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: The Hendrix classic "Wind Cries Mary" becomes an upbeat Van Morrison-like blues in Jamie's hands, but the familiar 3-note riff remains and Sebastiaan de Krom peps up the rock groove with drum rolls to keep up the momentum.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: Truer to the original is Jeff Buckleys sublime "Lover, You Should Have Come Over", with Jeff's high-pitched vocals replaced by a voice tending towards the gravel of Joe Cocker.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: Running through the album as through a stick of rock are Geoff Gascoyne's sophisticated arrangements.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: He makes "Singin' In the Rain" fresh and exciting, giving it a chilled-out feel with funky Rhodes piano.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: Geoff's bassline comes straight from the tune, surprising when it appears under the chorus, and the whole works a treat with Jamie's low tones pitched against the airy backings.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: Only "I Could Have Danced All Night" lacks some cohesion, with instrumentation mutating from trio to string quartet to electric guitar, with a persistentfunk bassline jarring against the melody.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: This is still great, though, Jamie thumping on the piano and humming and singing up a storm.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: Jamie tweaks a heartstring or two with "Blame It On My Youth".
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: He parallels Chet Baker's version, evoking powerlessness through vocal simplicity, sensitivity, and a paucity of instrumentation.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: Bob Dorough's "But For Now" is a great ballad, too, springing out of a Billy Joel-like piano accompaniment.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: A post-hangover rasped vocal and mournful cello give the finishing touches to a poignant and witty classic.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: He may have a million pound record deal now, but Jamie hasn't sold out.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: Resisting the temptation to lavish the cash on major changes, he's continued to invest wisely in great musicians and tasty arrangements.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: As the saying goes: if you ain't broke and it ain't broke, don't fix it.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: With female jazz singers in the ascendant, it's encouraging to see the men refusing to be eclipsed.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: Rising star Jamie Cullum's vocal sound starts at Sinatra, puts its foot down at Harry Connick Jr., and veers past Kurt Elling.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: Also the keyboard player in rock band Taxi, Jamie's used to playing the piano with whichever limb is free - and he takes this refreshing irreverence into his jazz debut.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: The material is mostly very familiar (Gershwin is well-represented) but Jamie isn't aiming for sepia-coloured portraits of the music.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: The pieces he's chosen, like video shorts, tell a story in each track - with Jamie cast as the modern-day hero and his band creating an urban backdrop.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: So, while Diana Krall's "Devil May Care" is a fireside version, Jamie's is the roadside one, given pace and edge by a fine set of horns arranged by Geoff Gascoyne.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: Sparks fly as drummer Sebastiaan de Krom works up the excitement in a piano trio version of "You're Nobody Till Somebody Loves You"; even in this format Jamieprojects as though he's with a big band, while Gascoyne's bass assumes a near-vocal quality.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: Not old enough to have lived the jazz life yet,Jamie's rough-edged sound is embryonic, but the combination of spiky and haphazard piano with his insinuating vocals is a winner.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: Assaults on the piano, melodramatic pauses and exasperated sighs bring Monk's "Well You Needn't" to life, too, with humour and gritty excitement.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: Ben Castle goes all gruff and boppish on tenor here, in contrast to his sweet handling of the weepy "In the Wee Small Hours", where he builds a simple and beautiful solo from nowhere.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: Strangely, the contemporary songs come across more nostalgically than the old-timers.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: The title track and Radiohead's "High and Dry" have you staring into space and reminiscing, both featuring stripped-down trio and an intense, passionate vocal.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: The album ends on an ironic note with "I Want to Be a Popstar" - its premise being that jazz is an elevated music played by real musicians, and pop (especially the manufactured kind) is faking it.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: With Jamie already a semi-pop star with Gareth Gates-through-a-hedge looks, and tenorman Ben Castle leader of the big band on Pop Idol, the irony and energy in this track more than make up for its uninspiring melody.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: Pointless Nostalgic trades sepia for cibachrome, finding vibrant expression in the old songs and nostalgia in the new.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: Jamie's irreverent approach to jazz and his association with some of the finest British jazz musicians should find him favour with jazz and rock fans alike.
author: Kathryn Shackleton

text: Following on from the success of the new classic soul artists like Erykah Badu, Jill Scott, Angie Stoneet al, Hil St.
author: Greg Boraman

text: Soul (pronounced Hil Street Soul)come back with their second album Copasetik & Cool, and a quality collection it is too.
author: Greg Boraman

text: Fronted by vocalist, Zambian born Hilary Mwelwa, this latest release displays the usual rootsy and mildly retro template forged by those above artists but mixes it up with a subtle but undeniably British sensibility.
author: Greg Boraman

text: With highly renowned producer Victor Redwood-Smith supplementing Hilary's own song writing skills, Hil St.
author: Greg Boraman

text: Soul manages to mix the retro influences with a very fresh sound that should appeal to old soul-boys and younger beat-heads alike.
author: Greg Boraman

text: The mix of acoustic instrumentation along with the particularly solid drum programming manages to encapsulate the last 30 years of soul music without sacrificing too much to the past or present.
author: Greg Boraman

text: Hilary's voice has a unique quality that sets her apart from her contemporaries, without any particular influences coming to the fore; if she sounds like anyone, Randy Crawford is the only singer that she bears even the slightest resemblance to vocally (She also shares an equally dazzling smile).
author: Greg Boraman

text: The British feel of this outfit is perfectly illustrated in the lyrics and song titles: "All that (and a bag o' chips)" is a sentiment that could only originate within UK shores.
author: Greg Boraman

text: The musical highlights are many including a brilliantly executed cover version of The Isleys' "For the Love of You" which manages to sweep along without making the listener hark back to the original, and that's a rare feat.
author: Greg Boraman

text: Melodically, the track "Pieces" is the highpoint of the album, an instantly catchy track with touching lyrics that seem borne of real experience rather than the usual well-worn love song cliches.
author: Greg Boraman

text: On the strength of this collection, Hil St.
author: Greg Boraman

text: Soul deserve to move on to greater commercial success and credibility.
author: Greg Boraman

text: It's rare in the soul arena for UK based acts to genuinely give the Americans a run for their money, but Hil St Soul seem on track to do just that.
author: Greg Boraman

text: In the late 70s Fleetwood Mac's Rumours was one of those albums that was impossible to avoid, and was proof that having messy relationships with other members of your band and writing catchy songs about them could make you very popular.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Its follow up, Tusk, was a different story; a critical and relatively commercial flop (though yielding a couple of hits), its four sides were dominated by guitarist Lindsey Buckingham's increasingly eccentric musical vision.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Often miles away from the lush West Coast sheen of its predecessor, it's an album that doesn't even merit cult status; neither has it been reasessed and hailed a lost masterpiece.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Well, not yet anyway.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Which makes it all the more strange that the (admittedly slightly eccentric) Camper Van Beethoven should have chosen to cover the entire album.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Recorded in 1987 and conceived on a whim, the project was a source of irritation to the band themselves.
author: Peter Marsh

text: After a few days, some members realised it was quite a silly idea perhaps left as such, and the project collapsed.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Half finished, some tracks remained as sketches, others recorded later by individual band members.
author: Peter Marsh

text: So a decade and a half later, here are those tapes, cleaned up and reassembled.
author: Peter Marsh

text: While you couldn't call this a labour of love, neither is it a demolition job.
author: Peter Marsh

text: While some tracks (particularly the Stevie Nicks and Christine McVie tunes) are often cruel deconstructions, there's a sense that the Beethovens warmed to some of their material.
author: Peter Marsh

text: For the most part, the original is reconfigured to fit the band's gift for skewed, country and western tinged psychedelia.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Sometimes this works beautifully, as on "Save Me A Place", "That's All For Everyone" and "Tusk" (which is actually a bit straighter than the original).
author: Peter Marsh

text: It's also extremely funny, as when the vocal for "Sisters of the Moon" is provided by a Mac of the Apple rather than Fleetwood variety, which at the end of the song starts quoting Shakespeare and Spinal Tap.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Or there's the insertion of a few lines from the B-52's "Rock Lobster" into "Not That Funny".
author: Peter Marsh

text: The last thing we hear is one of the band murmuring "ah, that was a bad idea".
author: Peter Marsh

text: Not so, chaps...
author: Peter Marsh

text: Whilst writing this review I was reminded of the scene in Monty Python's Life of Brian where the Judean People's Front...
author: Christian Hopwood

text: sorry, the People's Front of Judea are sat in their headquarters condemning the Roman Empire.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Somewhat combatively John Cleese asks "And what have they ever given us in return?!" Well, in addition to the sanitation, medicine, education, wine, public order, irrigation, roads, a fresh water system and public health, the Italians are now responsible for giving us some decent house music.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: But, Man Music Technology, the debut album from producer Stephano Fontano, is more than just house music.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: It's electro, it's hip hop, it's funk and it's breaks all rolled into a futuristic disco soundtrack for 2003.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Like the man says, "It's the old school with the new school".
author: Christian Hopwood

text: And it's ace!
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Having been influenced from an early age by the imported sounds of Chicago house, Detroit techno and hip hop, Stephano got in to DJing from an early age.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: His father bought him his first pair of Technics as a reward for passing his sound engineering diploma.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: The next decade was spent revising Italy's dubious relationship with dance music, obsessing over turntablism and breaking a few bones as a professional skater.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: The results are a thrilling excursion of squelched synths, funky ass b lines, loping beats and some great vocals.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: "Da Symphony" is guilty on all counts with its Memphis brass stabs, bumping bass and soulful lilts, as is last years' single "Bizarre Mind" for that matter.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Both are full force disctro house moments.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Other highlights come in the form of the Della Reese-Lett sampling bedtime story "If Everybody In The World Loved Everybody In The World" and the funk-fuelled, hip hop jam "Way of Life" featuring Digital Underground on mic detail.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Italy's enthusiasm for house music has never been an issue yet it has never had a seminal release, one that would establish itself as a player on the international music scene.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Occupying the parking space between Daft Punk, Basement Jaxx and Metro Area, Man Music Technology manages to embrace dance music's history with both authority and humour.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: 1 Giant Leap is a multi-media project dreamt up by Jamie Renton (Faithless) and original Take That producer, Duncan Bridgeman.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: They journeyed to 25 countries armed with a digital audio video camera and laptop, capturing sound, images and spoken word from some of the world's most influential artists.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: The result is some magician-like mixes and a seamless and clever production.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: The CD cuts down the music to the core and starts with the wonderful soaring vocals of Senegalese legend, Baaba Maal.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Braided Hair and My Culture have both been hit singles and the latter features Robbie Williams and Maxi Jazz.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Neither has a particularly strong infusion of world sounds.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: The driving rhythms of the percussion and guitar do, however, set the tone for much of the music.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: The Way You Dream begins with beautiful wailing from 65 year old Indian vocalist, Asha Bhosle, soon interrupted by a trademark REM guitar line and Michael Stipe at his passionate best.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: The vocal interplay continues with seriously mellow Indian percussion grooves, some sublime kora and then the inspired addition of drum and bass.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: It adds up to 8 minutes of something quite special, a marriage of sounds made in heaven.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: This track is in my desert island top ten.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Daphne features Romu Majumadar, the Mahotella Queens and Eddie Reader.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: The ethnic mix of vocals and rhythms works a treat while each artist remains faithful to their original style.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: However, I had a nagging feeling that the CD was watered down and over-produced for western consumption.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Would it really have detracted if the big keyboard synth sounds had been toned down to a minimum?
author: Christian Hopwood

text: If a bit more courage had been used with the arrangements?
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Ironically that nagging feeling was washed away completely after viewing the DVD.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: There are extended intros where the artists have more solos and are brought to the fore.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: The percussive and rhythmic grooves are developed further.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: The whole experience brings the diversity of the world together in 155 minutes of stunningly rich and colourful imagery.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: Comments from the R3 Awards for World Music clearly show that the DVD has had a profound effect on a wide range of people.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: The DVD is truly superb and more than deserves its two Grammy nominations.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: To be really successful, a future CD should represent the artists in the raw and in a more stripped down way.
author: Christian Hopwood

text: All hail the king!
author: Morag Reavley

text: With five Academy Awards and over 40 Oscar nominations, John Williams is a member of cinema's elite.
author: Morag Reavley

text: No one has contributed more to modernfilm music.
author: Morag Reavley

text: This gargantuan four-CD collection marks the fortieth annivesary of Williams' film career.
author: Morag Reavley

text: The tracks are arranged generically rather than chronologically.
author: Morag Reavley

text: Williams' work for Steven Spielberg fills the first two discs; the fourth features blockbusters written for other directors, including a romp through the Star Wars series.
author: Morag Reavley

text: Overworked as the big numbers have become, they are far from worn out.
author: Morag Reavley

text: The music from Jaws, The Empire Strikes Back and Indiana Jones still startles in the fullness of its sound and simplicity of its structure.
author: Morag Reavley

text: Not all the music is familiar.
author: Morag Reavley

text: The third disc gathers music from early and less well known films, starting with a suite from the 1966 movie The Rare Breed - the complete soundtrack of which has never been released.
author: Morag Reavley

text: Other less familiar work includes a florid, romantic suite from Jane Eyre, pastiche-Western music from 1972's The Cowboys and the end titles from Alfred Hitchcock's last film, Family Plot.
author: Morag Reavley

text: Such a heterogeneous collection reveals interesting sub-themes.
author: Morag Reavley

text: There's a folksy strand evident in the harmonica of Williams' first Spielberg collaboration, 1974's Sugarland Express, and the fiddle music of Schindler's List.
author: Morag Reavley

text: Tracks from Dracula and The Witches of Eastwick reveal a darker, Gothic strain.
author: Morag Reavley

text: And there's an interesting cluster of choral pieces, from the pseudo-African chorus of Amistad to the Borodin-esque "Duel Of The Fates" from The Phantom Menace.
author: Morag Reavley

text: Williams isn't slowing down.
author: Morag Reavley

text: Tracks from Catch Me If You Can and AI show he's still at the top of his game.
author: Morag Reavley

text: "Hedwigs Theme" ,from the first Harry Potter film, is already a classic; its magical, ring-a-roses melody miraculously avoiding sentimentality.
author: Morag Reavley

text: These are renditions by the City of Prague Philharmonic, not original recordings.
author: Morag Reavley

text: The reinterpretation rightly treats the music as living, complex works.
author: Morag Reavley

text: Despite its girth, this collection merely samples Williams' oeuvre - it cannot convey the depth of individual scores.
author: Morag Reavley

text: What it does proclaim is the astonishing variety and sheer quality of his achievement; here's to the next 40 years.

text: When I review a cd I try to listen with as much concentration as I can.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: I don't scrutinise the cover or liner notes or track titles or record companyPR material until after at least a couple of listens.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: I'm explaining this because this cd comes with fairly lengthy liner notes which establish a particular context somewhat different from the one I experienced initially.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: There's also common ground though, more of which later.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: All of the 8 tracks are called "Chase through".
author: Colin Buttimer

text: "Chase through number one" sounds like a large factory workfloor, perhaps one not on this planet - interesting how the more automated manufacturing becomes, the more electronica appears to present the sound of the factory for listening at leisure - the hammering of tools, the worrying of voices, the seething, sighing of breathing...
author: Colin Buttimer

text: The second "Chase through" comes on like the sound of air currents blowing through a subspace engine cowling with the ultimate chill of vacuum metres away - at times I'm reminded of Rutger Hauers death speech in Bladerunner: 'Attack ships on fire off the shoulder of Orion.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: I watched c-beams glitter in the dark near the Tannhauser gate...' By track three spacecraft are docking, elements careening off each other (sounds at some distance from any televisual/filmic imaginings)...
author: Colin Buttimer

text: There are momentary voices, long decayed until they're an integral part of the circuits, abstracted almost entirely out of humanity.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Jonathan Marshall's liner notes explain that the groups intent is to establish a discourse about contemporary non places, specifically the attempts made by the corporate world to normalise the experience of long distance travel from airport departure lounge to aeroplane cabin via muzak, standardisation, etc.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Well I wasn't that far off with subspace engine cowlings and vacuums, only a few miles at most...
author: Colin Buttimer

text: The secondCD of video material does reinforce the text, but for me doesn't do much to open up any new possibilities.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Chases Through Non-place occupies an almost environmental sonic area, occasionally invaded by rhythms which seem to extrude themselves up out of deep sonic strata, at other times they appear like detritus sparked unwillingly into shortlived animation.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Back in the 80s, drummer Paul Motian's association with guitarist Bill Frisell and tenor saxophonist Joe Lovano led to a great run of recordings for the ECM and JMT labels in a variety of guises, including collaborations with Charlie Haden, Paul Bley and others.
author: Peter Marsh

text: For some it was the trio of guitar, drums and tenor that made the most impact, and certainly as a live band they had very few equals.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Motian provides all the material for this long awaited reunion,apart from one Monk tune ("Dreamland") and the Jerome Kern ballad that gives the album its title.
author: Peter Marsh

text: It's on this latter track (ie in the context of a familiar tune)where Motian's rhythmic approach is best highlighted.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Rarely (if ever) does the drummer play time; or if he does, it's set so obliquely against everything else that, even at its most emphatic, the music has an unlocked, floatyquality about it.
author: Peter Marsh

text: His own compositions are mostly fragmented, mournful affairs, stuffed with bursts of folkish melodies and oblique twists, and they provide much for Lovano and Frisell to chew on in their improvisations.
author: Peter Marsh

text: While nowadays the guitarist seems content to recede into the background a little further with each new venture he gets involved in, this trio has always been one of the best showcases for his playing.
author: Peter Marsh

text: While he's maybe not as forthright as he was on earlier records, all the signifiers are there; Jim Hall's chamber jazz stylings, little slivers of the blues and Nashville twang, topped off with adiscreet use of electronics.
author: Peter Marsh

text: He's a supreme colourist and his solos can still dazzle; it's good to know he can still do it.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Lovano remains one of the greatest tenor players around; his phenomenal technique allows him to roam the upper ranges of his instrument without much audible effort.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Notes seem to flow from the bell rather than being squeezed, and Lovano seasons everything he does with liberal (yet equal amounts) of soul and intellect as he curls his tenor round Frisell's spectral chording.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The only slight bugbear here is that the album is too long and unbalanced.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Though a couple of pieces (notably "The Riot Act") kick up a bit more dust, their placement towards the end of the album is too late to work effectively as contrast to thecrepescular ballads that have gone before.
author: Peter Marsh

text: But I'm nitpicking -at its best this is incomparably lovelymusic, made one of the most empathic units of recent times.
author: Peter Marsh

text: This is Paul Motian's second recording for ECM since his return to the label in 2005 after a long absence.
author: Bill Tilland

text: Garden of Eden is a typical Motian date; highly nuanced and thoughtful, combining bop tunes, Broadway standards and his somewhat abstract originals in a pleasing package which is both stimulating and easy on the ears.
author: Bill Tilland

text: After his tenure with Bill Evans, Motian seldom used a piano in his own groups, and the group assembled for this session consists of two saxophones, three guitars, electric bass and drums.
author: Bill Tilland

text: The fourteen relatively short pieces (including gorgeous renditions of Mingus's "Pithecanthropus Erectus" and "Goodbye Pork Pie Hat") are fluid, lyrical conversations between various combinations of guitars, saxophones and bass, all of which coil sinuously around a theme, approaching it from various perspectives, while Motian lays down a foundation of rhythmic colours.
author: Bill Tilland

text: Elegant, mature work from a jazz master.
author: Bill Tilland

text: Pity John Williams writing his umpteenth Star Wars score.Although with all those royalties rolling in, pity is perhaps not quite the right word.
author: Morag Reavley

text: Burdened with a legacy of his own making, Williams' technique for the three prequel scores has been to embroider the films' existing musical mythology, retro-fitting familiar motifs from the older scores while attempting to devise distinctive new themes.
author: Morag Reavley

text: So, much of this soundtrack is a case of deja ecoute, a self-referential riffing on nostalgic sequences.
author: Morag Reavley

author: Morag Reavley

text: The opening and closing medleys areas statley as aGalactic galleon, as festive as the Last Night of the Proms.

text: Drummer Motian has assembled a heavyweight line-up for this album of standard ballads (originally released in 1989).
author: Ian Latham

text: Joe Lovano is the real star of the session, providing further evidence of his ascent to tenor man of the moment.
author: Ian Latham

text: Guitarist Bill Frisell provides the most stylistically distinctive contribution to the band, preventing it from becoming a run of the mill bebop album.
author: Ian Latham

text: Charlie Haden and Motian (as ever) provide impeccable, unobtrusive backing.
author: Ian Latham

text: Although Motian is the leader of the session, he only really pushes himself into the foreground on the first track where he provides the intro and coda and takes the first solo.
author: Ian Latham

text: Lovano's solo on this fast tempo version of "Liza" is masterful bebop playing.He manages to pull off the trick of sounding speedy, muscular and really driving the band, but at the same time making it all sound effortless.
author: Ian Latham

text: Up next, Frisell takes a different approach, leaving more space and moving away from pure bebop language.
author: Ian Latham

text: Haden drops out for a delicate but luscious rendition of "Somewhere Over The Rainbow", a real highlight of the album.
author: Ian Latham

text: Frisell's pedal steel style harmonic accompaniment creates an ideal backdrop for Lovano's thoughtful and lyrical ballad playing.
author: Ian Latham

text: He tastefully controls his attack with the volume pedal to fade invoicings which avoid the obvious chord changes.
author: Ian Latham

text: Frisell leaves Lovano all the space to waft through the rich harmonies with his light, fluffy tone; deep and rich in the lower register and beautifully fragile in the upper.
author: Ian Latham

text: Motian's input here is so sparse and restrained, he's barely there.
author: Ian Latham

text: Its exactly this sort of thoughtful, musical playing that his reputation is built on.
author: Ian Latham

text: "What Is This Thing Called Love" opens in trio format with Frisell's oblique, understated interpretation of the melody and characteristically weird chords.
author: Ian Latham

text: Lovano enters for the first solo which once again showcases his silky fluency as he weaves long expressive lines through the harmony.
author: Ian Latham

text: Haden's singing bass takes the next chorus while unfortunately failing to find any worthwhile melodic interest.
author: Ian Latham

text: Lovano plays the head on the way out.
author: Ian Latham

text: It's the kind of ending that leaves you wanting more.
author: Ian Latham

text: This is essentially an album for connoisseurs, probably too subtle to appeal to anyone but the hardcore jazz fanatic.
author: Ian Latham

text: Having said that, there's nothing threatening or raucous here that would offend anyone's sensibilities.
author: Ian Latham

text: Trouble is, I suspect, most people outside of the jazz cognoscenti would find the album's mood of autumnal introspection a tad dreary.
author: Ian Latham

text: However, it's the chemistry between Lovano's immersion in jazz language and Frisell's style (which finds more of its influences outside jazz) that make this album.
author: Ian Latham

text: It's great to have Paul Motian on Broadway, but it's Lovano's name that's in lights.
author: Ian Latham

text: Unlike some of the musicians who've been the subject of ECM's :rarum collections, Paul Motian's output for the label doesn't really provide any definite overview of his career, which has taken in stints with Keith Jarrett, Lennie Tristano, Bill Evans, Paul Bley and, er, Arlo Guthrie.
author: Peter Marsh

text: In Motian's case you'd probably need a box set (at the very least) for that job.
author: Peter Marsh

text: It was ECM's Manfred Eicher who persuaded the drummer to try his hand at composition, and this set documents his various outings as bandleader.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Through his debut for the label featured Jarrett, subsequent albums were piano-less.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Maybe this was a consequence of a desire to break away from his associations with great ivory tinklers (see above); plus Motian's first instrument was the guitar, which may explain his adoption of players like the underrated Paul Metzke and the overrated Bill Frisell.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Motian's writing is sparsely pretty; folky almost, with echoes of Jarrett, Ornette Coleman and Monk.
author: Peter Marsh

text: His melodies sidle up to you and breathe gently in your ear, much like early Carla Bley.
author: Peter Marsh

text: "Folk Song For Rosie" is a fine example, with Charles Brackeen's luscious soprano wrapping itself around Motian's gently meandering tune.
author: Peter Marsh

text: In later groups Joe Lovano's blurry tenor would give the drummer's themes a magisterial weight coupled with a sly playfulness; with the longstanding trio of Frisell and Lovano, Motian's music maybe found its ideal interpreters, but the early records have a sweetly astringent feel to them.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Motian's drumming refuses to restrict itself to mere timekeeping.
author: Peter Marsh

text: His slightly awkward snare figures punctuate and accelerate, shadowing the contours of the melody at every turn.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Without a bass (as in the trio or the hushed melancholia of the Paul Bley group) the kit takes on melodic duties too, as Motian restricts himself to occasional, hushed cymbal caresses or faint wisps of brushed snare.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Motian's body of work outside ECM is just as impressive, but this album is a timely reminder of the pleasures of his early music and in particular the magical, poised interplay he shared with Bley, Frisell and Lovano.
author: Peter Marsh

text: John Williams, Steven Spielberg's musical collaborator on 20 films is the man responsible for works as seminal as the ET flying theme, the menacing Jaws bars and the Star Wars music.
author: Morag Reavley

text: Fresh from scores for AI and Minority Report, Williams produces something altogether lighter for Spielberg's 1960s tale of a baby-faced codologist, Catch Me If You Can.
author: Morag Reavley

text: Reflecting the aspirational times in which the film is set, Williams has put together a progressive jazz score which is classy, catchy and consummately professional.
author: Morag Reavley

text: The eponymous title-track is a slippery little number, sax and bass chasing each other in helter-skelter pursuit.
author: Morag Reavley

text: The melodic repertoire is incredibly simple.
author: Morag Reavley

text: Only a few musical themes of five notes or less lay the scores foundations, and make for more of the irresistibly memorable theme tunes of which Williams is the maestro.
author: Morag Reavley

text: In our post-September 11 era, the idea of a conman posing as a pilot, doctor or lawyer has disturbing resonances.
author: Morag Reavley

text: But the soundtrack, like the film, lingers on the light-hearted, with that classic Hollywood leitmotif the feel-good glockenspiel riff making inevitable appearances.
author: Morag Reavley

text: Only in pieces about the relationship between Frank Abagnale Jr.
author: Morag Reavley

text: does a hint of something unhappier emerge.

text: In "Recollections" and "Father and Son", a morose, rambling sax gestures at chasms beneath the mellow surface.
author: Morag Reavley

text: Retro-tracks selected for the album capture the period's cheesy brand of glamour.
author: Morag Reavley

text: There are the usual, overworked cliches such as Sinatra inviting us to fly with him and Nat King Cole's chestnuts on an open fire.
author: Morag Reavley

text: But gems such as Judy Garland's "Embraceable You" and the original, wistful "Girl from Ipanema" still have a lot of life left and it is a joy to hear them here.
author: Morag Reavley

author: Morag Reavley

text: At last...after the Brahms, Dvorak, Schubert and Schumann Piano Trios, the Florestans finally take a deep breath, sit down together and tackle Beethoven's legacy.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: And yes, we're to have them all: 'The Complete Music for Piano Trio 1' this tells us reassuringly on the cover.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: From the triumphant opening fanfare of the Ghost Trio you know it's been worth the wait.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: There's such unanimity of purpose here, three minds united in their common musical goal, and yet able to realise it without surrendering their individual character.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Violinist Anthony Marwood seems incapable of playing a sourly tuned note, and in the opening of Beethoven's ghostly Largo he's matched perfectly by cellist Richard Lester in the chilly opening phrases, drained of colour until they slowly add vibrato and warmth.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Susan Tomes is the core of the trio, if not the key to it; perfectly balanced with the two string players, never overcrowding them or shouting them down.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Even when she's at her busiest, say at the start of the Ghost's Finale, Tomes never drowns the other voices, and her beautifully articulated runs are exact but effervescent, fizzing with life and energy.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: As in the Florestans' earlier recordings there's no distortion, no ugly bulges or individual eccentricities to learn to tolerate - everything has the ring of truth about it, and it's easy to feel that you're hearing the authentic voice of the composer throughout, and not the voices of the interpreters.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: The recording's superb, analytical but warm with the instruments close enough, yet in a nicely captured acoustic.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: If what I've described has you worrying that these performances might be characterless, then banish the thought - there's character in spades, but in performances you really could play every day without tiring of the individual personalities at work (as is sometimes the case with the so-called power-trios of the past).
author: Andrew McGregor

text: For quite a while it's been difficult to recommend the core piano trio repertoire on record without having recourse to the Beaux Arts Trio, or a venerable classic such as Stern-Rose-Istomin.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: The Florestans are changing that with this sequence of Hyperion recordings; buy this now, and wait impatiently for Beethoven Volume 2.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Now entering his 31st year as a solo artist, and still garnering the same old 'Britain's best kept secret/cult' remarks in the press -but why?
author: Chris Jones

text: To everyone in the know (and this is probably a lot more people than you'd think) RT is, without a shadow of a doubt, one of the greatest British post-war songwriters.
author: Chris Jones

text: Not only this, he is the master of a guitar style that is as influential and as distinctive as that of, say, Hank Marvin or Steve Howe.
author: Chris Jones

text: And not just in the folk idiom either - without Thompson there would be no Tom Verlaine for starters...Now he returns with another text ripped from the pages of suffering and heartache, but more importantly, the guitar is aflame once more.
author: Chris Jones

text: This album marks a far more stripped down approach than of late.
author: Chris Jones

text: Backed only by Danny Thompson's fleet-footed bass and solid drums courtesy of Michael Jerome, Thompson shows he's not lost the ability to evoke the bleaker side of the human condition.
author: Chris Jones

text: While the album's title implies the necessary resilience needed to forget one's woes and carry on with the game of life, the songs themselves speak of a life filled with lost loves (''I've Got No Right To Have It All''), bitter regrets (''A Love You Can't Survive'') and people of untrustworthy motives (''Pearly Jim'', ''I'll Tag Along'').
author: Chris Jones

text: Inexplicably split into two halves: 'The Haunted Keepsake' and 'The Pilgrim's Fancy', this collection of ''Unguents, fig leaves and tourniquets for the soul'' may come with a standard 'olde worlde' folk sleeve but is full of Thompson's skill in taking a contemporary subject matter and placing it within a story-telling tradition.
author: Chris Jones

text: The aforementioned ''A Love You Can't Survive'' is a standard tale of misfortune and twisted fate, but concerns a coke smuggler and the first half's songs are peppered with some of the spikiest six-string mayhem for a good while.
author: Chris Jones

text: Yet songs such as ''Jealous Words'' could come from any of the last two thousand years.
author: Chris Jones

text: It's this timeless quality that allows Thompson to float above the crowd and stake his claim as a true British classic.
author: Chris Jones

text: He may be working on the West Coast these days and his muse may still reside in Middle England, but Richard Thompson remains a world-beater.
author: Chris Jones

text: South African singer Miriam Makeba's life history is almost a history of post-war South Africa itself.
author: John Armstrong

text: But her recent material on Polydor, 'Sing Me A Song', 'Eyes On Tomorrow', 'The Legend Lives On' and others, are a little middle of the road for the true African music fan.
author: John Armstrong

text: So this compilation of her early Gallo and Syliphone material is a welcome palate-cleanser, and a reminder of her extraordinary versatility.
author: John Armstrong

text: She was chosen at 20 to be the female voice with S.A.'s leading vocal group of that time, the ManhattanBrothers.
author: John Armstrong

text: The release four years later of 'Pata Pata' brought her to the attention of a wider African audience.
author: John Armstrong

text: 1959 was the year that saw Makeba's real international breakthrough: including a visit to perform in the States; and a Grammy Award for the album An Evening With Harry Belafonte.
author: John Armstrong

text: In 1961, after comments she made about the Sharpeville Massacre, Miriam's passport was revoked.
author: John Armstrong

text: Middle America's love affair with her ended abruptly when she married Black Power leader Stokeley Carmichael.
author: John Armstrong

text: They fled to Guinee-Conakry on the West African Coast, where Miriam lived and recorded with the Syliphone record company.
author: John Armstrong

text: Paul Simon's invitation in 1987 to appear on Gracelands resuscitated her career.
author: John Armstrong

text: In 1990, Makeba returned to a post-apartheid South Africa, and continues to this day to tour the world almost constantly with her 8-member band.
author: John Armstrong

text: Ah, yes, the music.
author: John Armstrong

text: She moves from rough-hewn shebeen-style marabi with its New Orleans clarinet and guitar inflections ('Orlando') through Christian gospel -drenched pieces ('Live Humble'), to the Sarah Vaughan-like sophistication of 'Back Of The Moon'.
author: John Armstrong

text: 'Pata Pata' is there, of course, as is her first-ever studio session from 1952 with the Manhattan Brothers ('Laku Tshone 'Ilanga').
author: John Armstrong

text: But this reviewer's favourite material is from her 1975 Syliphone album Miriam Makeba And Her Guinea Quintet, represented here by 'Teya Teya', 'Milele' and others.
author: John Armstrong

text: At 24 tracks and mid-price, this is great value, with informative liner notes and individual comments on each track, and an excellent companion to the recent Best Of Dorothy Masuka collection.

text: Its an impressive achievement when your career has been so fruitful that an entire box-set can be made up of your rarities, but then this is Richard Thompson, the archetypal folk troubadour.
author: Chris Long

text: Dipping into live performances, demos and long-forgotten tapes, the 90-odd tracks take in his entire career from his days with Fairport Convention, through the years with former wife Linda, to his solo work.
author: Chris Long

text: There's several beautiful surprises in here, not least a fuzzed-up take on Plastic Bertrand's "Ca Plane Pour Moi", and a live medley of Who songs, which give more than enough to satisfy even the most die-hard Thompsonite.

text: Yes, she can warble away in her melancholic fashion but the positioning of the nutty priestess smacks of a lack of adventure or risk taking.

text: Massive Attack used to be adept at bringing lesser known vocalists in to the mainstream and making them shine.
author: Andy Puleston

text: Miss O'Connor may need the work but listening to her pine for the slaughtered children on the hugely self indulgent "A Prayer For England" is tiresome whilst the debut single "Special Cases" does little to redeem these felonies.
author: Andy Puleston

text: Production-wise 100th Window is solid and occasionally sublime.
author: Andy Puleston

text: The drum/bass relationships are all expertly executed and the tracks are mixed beautifully, "Butterfly Caught" in particular.
author: Andy Puleston

text: But that means jack when you feel nothing whilst waiting for the record to play out.
