text: There simply aren't enough hooks, melodies or songs here to make this memorable.
author: Andy Puleston

text: The prior outing Mezzanine had a brooding, cinematic edge that did much to fire the imagination, Protection had the emotive title track, "Karmacoma" and "Weather Storm" amongst its finery.
author: Andy Puleston

text: And Blue Lines was...
author: Andy Puleston

text: This takes itself so seriously you can feel the furrows of worry.

author: Andy Puleston

text: This is lazy music making, to be avoided at all costs.
author: Andy Puleston

text: After a three-year hiatus, Massive Attack's sole survivor, Robert '3D' Del Naja has skimmed the cream off their four albums for Collected, a medley of musical mastery.
author: Jack Smith

text: This 'Best Of' launches with 1991's "Safe From Harm", featuring Shara Nelson's emotionally-charged delivery which pulls on the heart-strings and sets the quality bar for the next 13 songs.
author: Jack Smith

text: The band unfurl their armoury of chilled beats, dub-drenched basslines, shimmering vocals and brooding strings, reminding you of just how influential the Bristol trio have been on down-tempo music in the UK.
author: Jack Smith

text: With gems including "Teardrop", "Inertia Creeps", "Protection" and "Unfinished Sympathy", Collected is an ear-pricking panorama of the '90s.
author: Jack Smith

text: A hint at the band's future direction comes with the bonus track "Live With Me", which boasts the soulful talents of Terry Callier.
author: Jack Smith

text: This is a compilation to cherish - one where you can leave the skip button untouched.
author: Jack Smith

text: Firstly, let's clear up some of the confusion around this album.
author: Morag Reavley

text: Unleashed, Massive Attack's first venture into film soundtracks, appeared at the end of 2004 in the guise of Danny the Dog, as the film was to be titled before waking up to the fact that this might offend audiences in China.
author: Morag Reavley

text: It's now repackaged for release with the film in late summer 2005.
author: Morag Reavley

text: But don't let all that put you off: Unleashed is a fresh and remarkably listenable soundtrack.
author: Morag Reavley

text: A martial arts thriller scripted by Luc Besson, the film tells the story of Danny (Jet Li), a feral gladiatorial fighter treated like a dog by mobster Bart, played by Bob Hoskins.
author: Morag Reavley

text: A chance encounter with Morgan Freeman's blind piano tuner Sam, begins Danny's tentative process of humanisation through his music.
author: Morag Reavley

text: As you'd expect, Massive Attack excel in creating a droogish urban soundscape full of eerie spaces and layers of saturated, ambient noise.
author: Morag Reavley

text: There are plenty of thrills, from the pumping technorush of "Atta Boy" to the gristly funk of "Simple Rules".
author: Morag Reavley

text: Another stand-out track is "One Thought at a Time," which features ahypnotic sixties rock guitar riff.
author: Morag Reavley

text: But this score has another, more reflective dimension, shaped by haunting dub and ambient sound.
author: Morag Reavley

text: Sam's redemptive music is represented by the piano which is his trade, and by child-like plucked strings.
author: Morag Reavley

text: "Sam" and "Two Rocks and a Cup of Water" are magical pizzicato lullabies, intricate and tender, but with a razor-edged sweetness that manages not to be sentimental.
author: Morag Reavley

text: Even without the film's visuals the soundtrack functions well.
author: Morag Reavley

text: Chronologically arranged, tracks are short, byte-sized pieces, swerving seamlessly into each other to create a surprisingly integrated whole.
author: Morag Reavley

text: Best of all, it sounds truly contemporary and devoid of the usual soundtrack cliches.
author: Morag Reavley

text: Vivid and compelling, Unleashedoffers ample evidence that - should the charms of Bristol ever wear off - Massive Attack's next destination might well be Hollywood.
author: Morag Reavley

text: Tunnel Vision is New York trumpeter Jim Cifelli's third album with his Nonet.
author: Ian Latham

text: It's a typical offering from today's jazz college trained musician; technically competent but lacking key ingredients found in the best jazz -namely personality, identity, taste and soul.
author: Ian Latham

text: The ensemble is shown in its best light on the opening "Go".
author: Ian Latham

text: It's a carefully constructed composition; the rhythm section phrases fit neatly with the horn parts, alternating between the tension of an ostinato bass figure and the release of the walking bass.
author: Ian Latham

text: The horn voicings are bright and pleasing, the playingtight and confident.
author: Ian Latham

text: Cifelli (on trumpet) takes the first solo which tastefully emerges from the head, settling into a few choruses of standard bop fare before returning to an ensemble interlude.
author: Ian Latham

text: Joel Frahm follows with a hard hitting Michael Brecker style tenor solo, before guitarist Pete McCann takes over.
author: Ian Latham

text: The band negotiate an intricate ensemble passage before returning to the head.
author: Ian Latham

text: I'm certain this chart would get a good grade in college.
author: Ian Latham

text: For all the sophistication of compositional technique, the tune itself is unmemorable and(crucially)lacks soul.
author: Ian Latham

text: Cifelli never manages to say anything really worthwhile in his soloing and stylistically he's completely without an individual voice.
author: Ian Latham

text: Frahm is at a similar level.
author: Ian Latham

text: For sure he can play, but he's yet another Brecker clone content to reel out his idols licks verbatim...
author: Ian Latham

text: The ensemble phrasing is tight but there's not a hint of the sophisticated collective phrasing found in the best ensemble jazz, whether it be Gil Evans or Count Basie.
author: Ian Latham

text: Here, the horn section always sits square on the beat.
author: Ian Latham

text: It's about as straight as jazz ever gets.
author: Ian Latham

text: Weaker still are the arrangements of established jazz classics.
author: Ian Latham

text: The Nonet's versions of Wayne Shorter's "Fee Fi Fo Fum" and "Speak No Evil" and the standard "What is This Thing Called Love" are quite simply tasteless.
author: Ian Latham

text: The latter is so weak it really isn't clear whether the arrangement is attempting to parody something or whether it's just a failed attempt at writing progressive harmony.
author: Ian Latham

text: This album neatly exemplifies the weakness of todays jazz education in the US.
author: Ian Latham

text: Yes, they can train people to play in tune, to play in time, to sound impressive.
author: Ian Latham

text: But there are more important qualities that the colleges seem unable to nurture.
author: Ian Latham

text: Jazz is an art form which places a premium on individualism and the ability to express human emotions and feelings.
author: Ian Latham

text: The jazz education system may be an unfair target, but Cifelli and his Nonet (despite their technical accomplishment) somehow miss the point of what great jazz is all about.
author: Ian Latham

text: Tunnel Vision indeed.
author: Ian Latham

text: Short pieces of acoustic piano, tracks and traces of other sounds left as marks of dust and scratches upon the instrument's case, like a persistent emotional residue.

text: A family get together to play some music.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: All the brothers and their father are skilled jazz players.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Probably the most interesting is the brother who plays the sax.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: He seems both the most fluent and the most searching, and his composition "Cain and Abel" is the most aggressive and spiky thing they play.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: The father composes most of the material; pleasant, cool midtempo post bop that sound like it comes from the late fifties.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: They also have a crack at some standards, and the trombonist has a pretty solo on "Sultry Serenade".
author: Nick Reynolds

text: So far, so unremarkable.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: But this is not just any family.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: It's the Marsalis men, the most controversial band of brothers in jazz.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: If you've read this far, you probably have an opinion about them.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: You either see them as bright new stars and protectors of the music's heritage or, particularly in the case of Wynton, as purveyors of a reactionary view of jazz that seeks to rewrite its history in rather narrow minded way.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: But you have to see this album for what it is: a relaxed, blowing session, a live concert to mark Ellis Marsalis' retirement from teaching.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Everyone sounds like they're enjoying themselves, and celebrating their father.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: But their limitations are shown on the version of "St James Infirmary", one of the most covered pieces in jazz and blues.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: It's a deeply bleak, sad, and relevant song.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: But guest star Harry Connick Jr sings it and throws it away as a party piece, with Wynton growling away on a rather intrusive muted trumpet.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: You find yourself thinking "I know you're just having fun...
author: Nick Reynolds

text: but is this what this song's really about?
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Isn't this approach trivialising it just a little?" There's nothing jazz fans like better than a good argument.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: And this album is not going to settle any.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: If you're looking for innovation, you're not going to find it here.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: A perfectly pleasant listen then, but after afew spins, this CD starts to sound less like a celebration than a boring (and just a little smug) family get together...
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Having produced his finest album in a decade, and made it a double one at that, Nick Cave can be forgiven for putting his feet up and reaping the rewards of a compilation of cast-off tracks.
author: Chris Long

text: Who could deny him that?
author: Chris Long

text: Only thing is, he's on record as saying that this is his favourite Bad Seeds album.
author: Chris Long

text: It's quite a claim to make.
author: Chris Long

text: It could be simple bravado.
author: Chris Long

text: Three discs of tunes that have been previously housed on flip-sides, flexi-discs and studio floors doesn't make the most enticing prospect, but Cave's output is never as simple as one album full of tunes at a time, and it's of little surprise to find that this is a compilation of rare gems and flashing wonders that many an artist would have been happy to include first time around.
author: Chris Long

text: Covering every corner of his 21 year, post-Birthday Party career, it stands not only as a tribute to a man whose talent is yet to dull, but also as a lesson in progression.
author: Chris Long

text: All the tracks are unmistakably Bad Seeds fare - even the occasional cover versions that rear up between the originals - and they deal with their emotion, their ire and their fire, their love and their pain in so many ways that the onslaught is quitedizzying.
author: Chris Long

text: Acoustic versions of harrowing fearsome turns like "Deanna" and "The Mercy Seat" sit alongside soundtrack works for Wim Wenders films.
author: Chris Long

text: The Bad Seeds' first b-side, "The Moon Is In The Gutter", casually lolls before recent works "She's Leaving You" and "Under This Moon".
author: Chris Long

text: Duets with Shane MacGowan (a truly shambolic desolation of "What A Wonderful World") and the original "Where The Wild Roses Grow", complete with drummer Blixa Bargeld's very un-Kylie-like counterfoil, create sparks before the weighty work-through that is "O'Malley's Bar" (Parts 1, 2, 3 and Reprise).
author: Chris Long

text: This is a treasure trove for the inner sanctum, a lover's tick-list of how darkness can sound so sweet, and while it may become a touch trying at times (particularly in the covers of traditional song "King Kong Kitchee Kitchee Ki-Mi-O" and Leonard Cohen's "Tower Of Song"), the sheer weight of splendour on offer rolls over any problem moments like a tide across the wrinkled sand.
author: Chris Long

text: If these are his cast-offs, it's little wonder that Nick Cave has remained intoxicatingly essential for over two decades.
author: Chris Long

text: The flowers that dominate the cover of this record are neither common or English (going by my limited botanical expertise).
author: Peter Marsh

text: Looking more like they've escaped from a 50s sci-fi film or at the very least some forgotten corner of Kew Gardens, they loom out of a desolate, possibly English landscape.
author: Peter Marsh

text: It's a strangely compelling image, tinged with an odd beauty and potential malevolence, a mix of the natural and the...well, unnatural.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Much the same could be said of Martin Archer's music, which here continues on the same paths he traced with 2001's Winter Pilgrim Arriving.
author: Peter Marsh

text: As before, Archer's brand of Anglicana combines trace elements of Canterbury scene rock, free improvisation, electronica and wistful folkishness.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The inner sleeve carries a short piece of text, a frozen snapshot of England, 1968; a reassuring world of cups of tea, rollups, organ solos, football scores on the radio, Reggae Chartbuster albums.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Though written in the present tense, it knowingly predicts a future of software and shopping malls; so where (or when) are we?
author: Peter Marsh

text: It's subtle dislocations like these that are the lifeblood for Archer's music.
author: Peter Marsh

text: (As Captain Beefheart once remarked, "The past sure is tense").
author: Peter Marsh

text: The opening "I'm yr Huckleberry" pits a reedy, fuzzed Mike Ratledge keyboard sound over gentle synth bubbles, later interrupted by meandering fuzz bass and distant, lovely horn parts.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Maybe if the Orb remixed Soft Machine's Third they'd come up with something like this.
author: Peter Marsh

text: "Trash White Tonal" and "Down the Road" are equally seductive; on the former, double bass and trombone ghost their way through a cloud of gently gurgling synths, while the latter sounds like John Martyn and Richard Thompson jamming with Brian Eno.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Elsewhere, more abrasive saxophony (handled by Archer and longtime colleague Charlie Collins) recalls the kind of post AACM improv that characterised Archer's earlier work.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The episodic 17 minute "Mall Bunnies" is reminiscent of the intricate detail of his Wild Pathway Favourites, though with bonus carcrash guitar bursts and chattering electronics.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Possibly the album's best moment is Archer's beautiful rework of Nick Drake's "Know" (his second cover from Pink Moon).
author: Peter Marsh

text: Drake's plaintive melody rises and falls into dense, scything drones reminiscent of Faust at their best.
author: Peter Marsh

text: English but in no way common, Archer's complex, gorgeous music demands a wider audience.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Nocturama, Nick Cave's twelfth studio album with the Bad Seeds, is a far cry from 2001's No More Shall We Part, but is just as impressive.
author: Dan Tallis

text: Cave is the king of passionate, darkly beautiful pop songs and Nocturama's ten mesmerizing tracks maintain his position on the throne.
author: Dan Tallis

text: There's more emotion in each word that Cave sings than can be found in a whole pack of pop idols.
author: Dan Tallis

text: The album's first track, "Wonderful Life", builds layer by layer, winding around a fluid bassline.
author: Dan Tallis

text: The song centers around the chorus "It's a wonderful life, if you can find it".
author: Dan Tallis

text: Cave's deep, sad voice seems skeptical that anyone but the lucky few can achieve anything near happiness.
author: Dan Tallis

text: The musicians create a hauntingly beautiful sound which perfectly accompanies Caves lamenting vocals.
author: Dan Tallis

text: From the Birthday Party's demise in the early eighties and The Bad Seeds rising from the ashes in 1983 Nick Cave and his band have toyed with an esoteric melodrama understood only by those who see beauty in sadness.
author: Dan Tallis

text: Some 20 years later, Nocturama sees Cave come of age.
author: Dan Tallis

text: Songs like, "Dead Man In My Bed", which can be seen as a blistering return to their thrashy rock 'n' roll days, with Cave as the preacher of fire and brimstone.
author: Dan Tallis

text: There are also songs that feature the familiar Bad Seeds themes of love and death but here the winning motif seems to be an uneasy acknowledgement of the presence of love.
author: Dan Tallis

text: "Rock of Gibraltar" celebrates the bittersweet endurance of love against the odds but, typically, is still tainted by the possibility of betrayal.
author: Dan Tallis

text: He has the freedom and confidence for the epic final track "Babe, I'm On Fire" to contain 43 verses and to last for 15 emotionally charged minutes.
author: Dan Tallis

text: Here, the incredibly talented Bad Seeds are all given a chance to run riot with their various instruments.
author: Dan Tallis

text: Guitars, drums, violin and percussion all vie for attention while Cave's strained vocals struggle, but ultimately succeed, in keeping pace with his wild musicians.
author: Dan Tallis

text: Simply a fantastic and enthralling end to a superb album.
author: Dan Tallis

text: Fact: Hell is For Heroes are a great British hope for 2003 and it isn't an exaggeration to state that The Neon Handshake is one of the most eagerly awaited debuts from a British band.
author: Catherine Chambers

text: Recorded over a year ago, the decision was made to hold off its release until the band felt ready.
author: Catherine Chambers

text: But as anyone who has heard the singles "Night Vision", "I Can Climb Mountains" and "You Drove Me To It", will vouch, it is well worth the wait.
author: Catherine Chambers

text: To understand the significance of The Neon Handshake it's necessary to go back to the beginning of the Hell Is For Heroes history.
author: Catherine Chambers

text: It starts with the sad denouement of their precursor, exuberant pop-punkers Symposium, whose promising future was cut short thanks to record label hassles.
author: Catherine Chambers

text: As the band members went their separate ways, it seemed as if UK homegrown talent had taken another kick in the teeth.
author: Catherine Chambers

text: Guitarist Will McGonagle and drummer Joe Birch then went on to form Hell is For Heroes.
author: Catherine Chambers

text: Shouldering expectations heavier than that faced by a 'new' band, the London quintet concentrated on honing their sound and blowing crowds away with stunning live sets rather than rush a release.
author: Catherine Chambers

text: As it happens, it turned out to be the right decision.
author: Catherine Chambers

text: Listening to the climactic, empowering riffs that run amok through its pulsating forty-two minutes, The Neon Handshake is a rush of blood to the head.
author: Catherine Chambers

text: It's the feeling of a band that has seen the shit come down and survived, kicking and screaming, to tell the tale.
author: Catherine Chambers

text: From the breathless chuggery of "You Drove Me To It" to the driving riffage of "Out Of Sight", Hell is For Heroes have a seemingly endless stockpile of slamming riffs that are intense without suffocating.
author: Catherine Chambers

text: HIFH's statement is simple enough: you can accomplish anything if you put your mind to it.
author: Catherine Chambers

text: Look no further than the spirited optimism of "I Can Climb Mountains", a chest-beating anthem of Herculean proportions.
author: Catherine Chambers

text: Brimming with confidence, The Neon Handshake isn't just the most inspired, upbeat record you'll hear this year, it's one of the best British rock albums to ever hit the shelves.
author: Catherine Chambers

text: Previously New Yorkers Black Dice have had a fearsome reputation as purveyors of extreme sonic assault.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: But the mood here is much more relaxed than the previous album Beaches and Canyons.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Simple guitar figures weave away gently while a variety of machines burp, belch, twitter, shriek and talk to each other.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: The sounds they use are very raw, but are given lots of space to breathe.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: You feel that what you are hearing is natural, organic.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: The track "Creature" is well named.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Its like listening to the heartbeat of some huge, mythical amphibian, while you lounge on the bottom of the sea bed, while "Skeleton" features some gentle shamanic chanting.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Their use of stereo is simple but very effective.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Sounds and textures bounce from extreme right to extreme left, setting up a call and response effect.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Natural percussion (they use a conventional kit, no drum machines), and pulses are put in the middle.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: It's the kind of balance you would use for a rock band: bass and drums in the middle, guitars on the left and right.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: As a familiar sonic picture, it doesn't mess with your head.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: The distorted bass frequencies and gritty trebly loops do that.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Its only on the two final tracks "Schwip Schwap" and "Night Flight" that things get nasty, where the machines start to fight each other with dirty, explosive bursts of sound.

text: "Night Flight" sounds like angry seagulls circling overhead.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Whatever their mood, Black Dice always sound like themselves and no one else.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: On balance I just prefer Beaches And Canyons, simply because I like extreme noise.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: But this is a thoroughly enjoyable and even relaxing listen.

author: Nick Reynolds

text: They listen hard to each other: there's a group gestalt going on.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: There's a great sense of dynamics and light and shade, with fragments of melody and quiet moments among the mayhem.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: "Things Will Never Be The Same" rises to an alarming climax of intense moaning and metallic loops.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: "The Dream Is Going Down" starts out like one of Pere Ubu's more extreme sonic experiments pushed into overdrive before switching into overlapping rising guitar drones.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: It ends with a rather jolly, bubbling hoedown section with enthusiastic tambourine.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: The closing "Big Drop" is as close as Black Dice get to conventional rock music.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: A 16 minute long guitar freak out with glimpses of thrash metal and Sonic Youth, whooping and hollering and (gasp) some conventional pounding drums.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Just when you think it's gone it returns for a galloping finale a bit like "Ghost Riders In The Sky".
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Well, only a bit like it...
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Egg heads, noise addicts and pain freaks alike will clutch this to their hearts.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: But this is a classic crossover record.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: If you occasionally try something more extreme, you'll find much to startle and impress you.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Black Dice have a great name, and they've made a great album.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: I rarely listen to an album once and fall immediately in love with it but that's what happened when I heard Richard Hawley's first solo album.
author: Niky Daley

text: So it was with trepidation that I listened to Lowedges; I was dubious that anything could match his previous effort Late Night Final.
author: Niky Daley

text: It begins with indie-sounding drums that are true to Hawley's roots; he was formerly a member of indie-heads The Longpigs.
author: Niky Daley

text: His distinctive voice resonates like polished grit over a combination of searing strings, hawaiian lap steels, mellotrons and even enchanted lyres.
author: Niky Daley

text: The depth and testosterone of his vocals also stop his sentimental lyrics from sounding cloying.
author: Niky Daley

text: All the tracks are driven by strong melodies and are mainly at a mid-tempo pace that keeps the album moving along nicely, until you get to the fourth track that is.
author: Niky Daley

text: There is only one thing wrong with "The Only Road"; it is too bloody good and I can't get past the track asIhave to keep playing it again and again.
author: Niky Daley

text: Despite it being the longest on the album, (almost 6 minutes), I just wish it would never end.
author: Niky Daley

text: With an enchanting melody and chords that sit alongside luscious lyrics, strong images are conjured up: "I water flowers in the rain, I dance beneath your silver flames".
author: Niky Daley

text: I'm not entirely sure what he's really going on about here but I'm so blissed out by this point I hardly care.
author: Niky Daley

text: Just about anyone who has a heart will identify with the pain and suffering of love that Hawley is referencing but despite being "crippled by the sound of love" the sado-masochist pleads "please keep me in your heart".
author: Niky Daley

text: However do get past this track as although for me it doesn't get any better, there are still plenty more gems to be had such as the catchy "The Motorcycle Song" and the instrumental "Danny".
author: Niky Daley

text: Lowedges (an area of his native Sheffield) doesn't break any new ground or push any musical boundaries but this is melodic songwriting at its best and a pleasure to listen to so keep 'em coming Richard.
author: Niky Daley

text: After all, when you get it so right why change a thing?
author: Niky Daley

text: New York based experimentalists Black Dice have lost a drummer and released a new album.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Their previous releases have each introduced fresh textures to their sound.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Here they are revisiting old ideas not introducing new ones.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: But this is their most accessible and concise album to date, and a good starting point for new listeners.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: The grubby, wordless vocals, basic drumming and general sonic mayhem heard on the classic "Beaches and Canyons" are combined with the squelching, distorted keyboards and gentle guitar figures of "Creature Comforts".
author: Nick Reynolds

text: The mood is jolly and swinging throughout.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: It kicks off with the loping one legged rhythm of "Snarly Yow" which soon develops into a series of electronic pulses on frequencies only dogs can hear.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Machines fart and splurt in a rather rude way in the first half of "Smiling Off".
author: Nick Reynolds

text: The second half sounds like The Residents playing "The Lion Sleeps Tonight" during an air raid.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Similarly the tribal yelping, pounding drum and cheerful guitar of the final track "Motorcycle" sets up a kind of polka to end the album on a dancing, happy note.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: The one genuinely new moment is the frustratingly brief and very gentle keyboard loop of "ABA".
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Some of the textures are still extreme.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: I'd advise you to turn your headphones down during the relentless electric distortion of "Twins" (iPods make you deaf you know).
author: Nick Reynolds

text: But for Black Dice this is a pretty relaxed and warm session.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Black Dice are a rock band who write songs.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: They just use sounds and noises rather than conventional instruments to do it.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: And only a rock band would design the bizarre cover art, a picture of a naked human bottom.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Can they develop what they do further, or is this the point where they start to run out of ideas?
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Until we find out "Broken Ear Record"remains top entertainment from my favourite new band.
author: Nick Reynolds

text: Zwan is Billy Corgan's new band.
author: Dan Tallis

text: The ex-Smashing Pumpkin has produced an album full of bright and breezy pop songs that are full of the joys of life.
author: Dan Tallis

text: This is a back to basics record that will satisfy Pumpkin heads and should bring on board a whole new legion of fans.
author: Dan Tallis

text: Billy Corgan finally brought The Smashing Pumpkins to an end in 2000.
author: Dan Tallis

text: The final couple of years of their illustrious career had been fraught with death, drug abuse and, with their last studio album Machina / The Machines Of God, critical and commercial failure.
author: Dan Tallis

text: To form Zwan Corgan called upon old friends Slint / Tortoise guitarist Dave Pajo, Skunk guitarist Matt Sweeney, A Perfect Circle bassist Paz Lenchantin and fellow Pumpkin drummer Jimmy Chamberlain.
author: Dan Tallis

text: Together they've got the enthusiasm, excitement and vitality that all new bands possess.
author: Dan Tallis

text: Combine that with years of experience and the invaluable ability to produce radio friendly pop songs and you have a winning team.
author: Dan Tallis

text: The 14 tracks on Mary Star of the Sea do sound like Smashing Pumpkins songs.
author: Dan Tallis

text: Corgans nasal voice is instantly recognisable but it is the guitars that sound most familiar; sonic noises and guitar riffs that soar.
author: Dan Tallis

text: As with classic Pumpkins albums, this record features heavy rock anthems ("Ride A Black Swan"), followed by more peaceful ballads ("Heartsong").
author: Dan Tallis

text: The album is jam packed full of great songs.
author: Dan Tallis

text: "El Sol" is a beautiful indie track, "Yeah" is just plain cool and "Jesus I / Mary of the Sea" is a fantastic 14 minute epic roller coaster ride!
author: Dan Tallis

text: If you disliked the doom and gloom that was so characteristic of the Pumpkins later albums you have nothing to fear.
author: Dan Tallis

text: Mary Star of the Sea is full of fun and simple happiness, even love.
author: Dan Tallis

text: 'There is no place I could be without you...I feel love' sings Corgan in the superb "Honestly".
author: Dan Tallis

text: You can sense the enjoyment the band had in making these bouncy pop songs.
author: Dan Tallis

text: Beware; you won't be able to wipe the smile of your face.
author: Dan Tallis

text: Is it better or worse than The Smashing Pumpkins?
author: Dan Tallis

text: Who cares, it sounds great and that's good enough for me.
author: Dan Tallis

text: What is going on?
author: Andrew McGregor

text: There's so much Messiaen being added to (and returning to) the catalogue at the moment, I wonder whether we'll look back at the last couple of years and see that this was either some kind of golden period for Messiaen recordings, or that there was a genuine reassessment of his music underway at least by a generation of performers, interpreters and record labels.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: It's altogether harder to know how the regular record buyer is reacting to these riches without knowing the sales figures for each new release.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Myung-Whun Chung has already played a significant part in this process (whatever it turns out to be!), and hard-on-the-heels of his DG recording of La Transfiguration, here's the late Messiaen orchestral epic that outdoes the Turangalila Symphony in its breadth and colour.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: 'From the Canyons to the Stars' was intended to mark the bicentennial of the United States in 1976, and Messiaen's music links the land itself, the canyons of Utah - whose colourful layers reach back in geological time - with the stars sparkling in the clear-blue desert sky, their light emanating from long ago and far away.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: A sense of colour then, natural majesty, a palette of every shade of red and rich orange-brown; a timeless quality that reaches far back in time and human history...also a direct analogy with the American flag: the stars in the night sky and the geological stripes of the canyons.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: The variety of sounds is staggering, especially when you consider the forces Messiaen was using here; a standard symphonic wind section, to be sure, but only 13 solo strings, a wind-machine, thundersheet and the newly invented 'geophone' -lead shot rotated in a large flat drum to make a sound somewhere between water lapping on a beach, and shifting sands - plus a major percussion section.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: This isn't the orchestra of Turangalila, a mere 44 performers, yet the impact they're able to make through the kaleidoscope of colours and the subtle use of chamber-sized ensembles is immense - sometimes this feels like Messiaen's biggest orchestral work.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Did I mention the birds?
author: Andrew McGregor

text: They're a vital part of the soundscape, almost another set of instruments again - the Mockingbird, the Wood Thrush, the White-Browed Robin - set against the 'Interstellar Call' of Jean-Jacques Justafre, whose solo horn-playing is superb.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Special praise also for pianist Roger Muraro, who's a fine impersonator of winged wildlife.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: This is a score that requires a shockingly high standard of virtuosity from every player, and gets it - the French Radio players are thrilling to listen to, Chung is Messiaen's devoted disciple, and he knows just how to frame his soloists, unleash the exotic colours and pace the whole piece as it sprawls over two CDs.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Actually, durations of 48 and 45 minutes mean that there was at least another three-quarters of an hour to play with, and Esa-Pekka Salonen's Sony recording is much more generously filled.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: But...this new one feels warmer, more affectionate, and has a demonstration-class recording to win you over, one of those miraculous mixes where you hear every last detail, yet the engineers have still managed to give each instrument its own acoustic halo without separating it unrealistically from the ensemble as a whole.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Time stands still when you immerse yourself in this remarkable new recording.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Messiaen always was better at eternity than almost anyone else.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Go on, lose yourself in the canyons of Utah under a star-filled azure sky.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: It was a busy week for Portuguese pianist Artur Pizarro.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Not only did he release his first disc of what you might call 'serious' solo piano music; he also began his ambitiousyear-long concert cycle of all Beethoven's 32 Piano Sonatas at St John's, Smith Square in London.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: This cd pulls together four of Beethoven's best-known sonatas: the Pathetique, the Moonlight, the Tempest, and the Appassionata.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: There's no shortage of recordings of these piano sonatas, so what makes Pizarro stand out from the crowd?
author: Andrew McGregor

text: It's curious, but however well you think you know these sonatas, the freshness and incisiveness of Pizarro's playing somehow takes you unawares.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: From the almost unfeasibly grave Grave introduction to the Pathetique to the torrential outbursts in the finale of the Appassionata, Pizarro shows how well he understands Beethoven - a man prone to fits of temper, depression, and passion - a man with his heart on his sleeve.Pizarro manages to combine these romantic emotional extremes with unusual clarity, bringing out lines that can often be marred and mushed by foggy sustain pedalling.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: The combination of this almost forensic precision and the warm woody tones of the Bluthner piano Pizarro plays here makes for compulsive listening, and guarantees you'll hear something new and exciting in these performances.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: So, Beethoven's four best-loved sonatas - a canny marketing ploy on Pizarro's part?
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Well, if it is, who can blame him - it's hard to get noticed in this game, especially when you're up against the likes of Emil Gilels, Wilhelm Kempff, and Alfred Brendel, to name just a few.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: But Pizarro definitely has something special to offer.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: He has said that he strives to get to the heart of Beethoven's music, to cut through the veneer, to enable us to hear it as if we'd never heard it before.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: And in this I think he has succeeded - if you don't already know Beethoven's Piano Sonatas, this is a great place to start - and if you do, you won't be disappointed...
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Try These: Mikhail Pletnev: Live at Carnegie Hall Murray Perahia: Chopin Études Beethoven Piano Trios
author: Andrew McGregor

text: To say that Nasir Jones is back, would imply a distinct absence from the game, but with 3 albums released in little more than a year this is, undoubtedly, not the case.
author: Buki Bakare

text: Following Stillmatic and The Lost Tapes (an album made up of previously un-released B side tracks) the 'King of New York'now brings his 6th studio album to the hip-hop table and it certainly doesn't disappoint.
author: Buki Bakare

text: The first single from the album "Made You Look" does the job it professes to do.
author: Buki Bakare

text: This is raw hip-hop at its best with an uncompromising, head-nodding beat and ruthless hook.
author: Buki Bakare

text: Definitely one for the clubs and car stereos.
author: Buki Bakare

text: With "The Last Real N**** Alive", our narrator breaks down his entire career history, including his relationship with Biggie, and of course the famous but somewhat over-hyped beef with Jay-Z.
author: Buki Bakare

text: "I Can" is a positive, inspirational track that assures kids that they can achieve their dreams.
author: Buki Bakare

text: Uncharacteristically, he's added a few star names to the roster, including current girlfriend Kelis on "Hey Nas".
author: Buki Bakare

text: Alicia Keys also climbs on board for "Warrior Song" andman-of-the-moment Eminem contributeson "The Cross", although regrettably it falls short of his usual standard.
author: Buki Bakare

text: Having gained the respect from hip-hop heads Nas refuses to follow that well trodden road too many popular rappers inevitably end up taking (no names mentioned here!).
author: Buki Bakare

text: Instead, God's Son takes us on a very different journey, one that's lyrically insightful, honest and reflective.
author: Buki Bakare

text: Signifying personal growth and maturity as an artist, this 29 year old, Queensbridge rapper paints a vivid portrait.
author: Buki Bakare

text: You get the feeling a distinct metamorphosis has taken place.
author: Buki Bakare

text: It would appear Nasty Nas has long gone and now been replaced with a more philosophical and spiritual God's Son.
author: Buki Bakare

text: Mr Jones is going all out to return to his throne and reclaim his title.
author: Buki Bakare

text: If his last three efforts are anything to judge by, I think we can say he's well on his way.
author: Buki Bakare

text: Any competitors out there need to make sure they're keeping up with this Jones!
author: Buki Bakare

text: Chick's career (sorry) has been marked by flashes of brilliance and rather more frequent lapses of taste (check the cover of Friends if you don't believe me).
author: Peter Marsh

text: In spite of his undoubted skills as an improviser, he's never quite achieved the scale of commercial or (especially) critical success awarded to fellow ivory tinklers and Miles alumni Hancock, Jarrett or Zawinul.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Corea first teamed up with bassist Miroslav Vitous (later to join Weather Report) and drummer Roy Haynes in 1968 for Now He Sings, Now He Sobs.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Trio Music (originally issued as a double CD) is drawn from their second meeting in 1981.
author: Peter Marsh

text: ECM has always brought out the best in Corea, with the label's tendency towards introspection stripping away most of the fussiness and bombast that makes some of his other recordings a bit hard to stomach.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The trio setting is a sympathetic frame for Corea's pianistic talents for much the same reasons.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The set is split between free-ish improvisations (sometimes based round tiny predetermined themes) and some Monk tunes.
author: Peter Marsh

text: As Steve Lacy's proved, interpreting Monk is best treated as the work of a lifetime and probably best done without a piano in sight, and these knotty, sparse tunes aren't an obvious fit with Corea's Bud Powell derived bop stylings.
author: Peter Marsh

text: But there are plenty of instances where the idea pays off; "Rhythm-ning" and "Little Rootie Tootie" feature playful, splashy piano solos and some nifty comments from the rhythm section.
author: Peter Marsh

text: On the downside, "Reflections" falls victim to Corea's decorative flourishes which effectively bury Monk's delicate, quizzical melody.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The improvisations are spikier affairs; "No 3" is dense, episodic and the effect is often more likeStravinsky than anything else.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Vitous uses a bow much of the time, which is a shame as his reedy, thin tone is nowhere near as engaging as his meaty pizzicato playing.
author: Peter Marsh

text: "No1" and the desperately exciting "Slippery When Wet" are kicked into a bebop-driven orbit by Vitous' nimble drive and the unstoppable Haynes.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Personally I'd pay money to hear Mr Haynes tap his fingers on a table, but his performances here are really something else and bring out the best in all involved.
author: Peter Marsh

text: 'From the day you were born there was a gleam in your eye', 'I told him as a youngster he'd be the greatest man alive'; so speaks Jazz veteran and father of Nas, Olu Dara, who features on several tracks on this album.It's the sort of quasi-religious talk that typifies the more pompous end of hip-hop, but hey - Nas deserves that respect than most.
author: Ruth Jamieson

text: In his latest incarnation our saviour shows a more grown-up, more thoughtful side to his character.
author: Ruth Jamieson

text: Perhaps love, for new beau Kelis, has mellowed Nas.
author: Ruth Jamieson

text: The over-riding theme on Street Disciple is one of imparting the wisdom he has come by on his journey through life and hip hop.
author: Ruth Jamieson

text: Holier-than-y'all-Nas calls out false idols on "Coon's Picnic".
author: Ruth Jamieson

text: The black role models of the NBA, 'UPN9 and WB who "yes master" on TV' are criticised and Kobe Bryant, Cuba Gooding Jr and Tiger Woods are asked 'what you doing for the hood?' The album has sermons on war, AIDS, and Black on Black violence.
author: Ruth Jamieson

text: When it comes to American politics his 'Who you gonna elect, Satan or Satan?' attitude is at odds with Puffy's recent 'vote or die' campaign.
author: Ruth Jamieson

text: It's clear he wants to cure not just the ghetto, but the whole world.
author: Ruth Jamieson

text: The Gangster/HolyManeven anoints the dead on "Just a Moment".
author: Ruth Jamieson

text: Happily there's still room on this double album to turn out a handful of dance floor fillers; the creepy bassy number "Suicide Bounce" where Busta Rhymes guests, and the infectious boing of "Virgo" where Ludacris joins him to Doug E.
author: Ruth Jamieson

text: And he squeezes in the occasional pop at Jay-Z, natch.
author: Ruth Jamieson

text: With star producers DJ Premier and Dr Dre missing, Streets Disciple may not be the sit-up-and-pay-attention album that God's Son was.
author: Ruth Jamieson

text: But it does deliver Nas trademark package of multi-various flows, arresting narrative and hookless, lyric-focussed rhymes.
author: Ruth Jamieson

text: No one's going to be complaining.
author: Ruth Jamieson

text: I first heard John Taylor more than ten years ago at London's Jazz Cafe (in those days you used to be able to hear jazz there).
author: Ian Latham

text: After an incredible solo, a musician friend sitting next to me asked me to name a better pianist.
author: Ian Latham

text: Here was a British player with a highly developed individual style, an astonishing harmonic sense, a frightening mastery of rhythm and a highly sophisticated composer.
author: Ian Latham

text: The great jazz musicians have in some way pushed the boundaries of the music, some technically, others emotionally.
author: Ian Latham

text: This man was really taking many things forward.
author: Ian Latham

text: With his modernist style and distinctive harmonic language, John Taylor stands alongside players like Keith Jarrett, Bill Evans and McCoy Tyner as one of the major jazz keyboard stylists.
author: Ian Latham

text: Long gone are the days when British musicians could only be pale imitations of the American jazz deities.
author: Ian Latham

text: For a man that has recorded over seventy albums with an impressive array of contemporary jazz luminaries, it is remarkable that Rosslyn is Taylor's first recording under his own name for over ten years.
author: Ian Latham

text: Perhaps too, it is an indictment on the UK's shocking neglect of this living national treasure.
author: Ian Latham

text: This latest recording picks up on the legacy of his four trio albums with ex-Weather Report drummer Peter Erskine, further refining his artfully thoughtful and delicate piano trio music.
author: Ian Latham

text: For this session he chooses the American company of Marc Johnson, Bill Evans' last bass player, and drummer Joey Baron.
author: Ian Latham

text: There is a distinct sense of telepathy between these musicians, and more so than in the Erskine band.
author: Ian Latham

text: The title track Rosslyn is typical of a Taylor composition.
author: Ian Latham

text: It opens with a deceptively simple chant that repeats meditatively over a static pedal bass note.
author: Ian Latham

text: On closer examination, the chant reveals itself to be a two bar phrase in 15/8.
author: Ian Latham

text: The bass and drums soon enter, enhancing the hypnotic mood.
author: Ian Latham

text: Gradually, Taylor weaves a melodic and harmonic counterpoint through the chant as the track builds in intensity.
author: Ian Latham

text: Too much jazz these days suffers from being technical for the sake of being technical, and at the expense of many more important ingredients.
author: Ian Latham

text: With Taylor, the sophistication is that he conceals the technique and allows the music to shine through.
author: Ian Latham

text: Field Day is a real masterpiece.
author: Ian Latham

text: The track opens with a mysterious out-of-time Messaien bird-song like introduction.
author: Ian Latham

text: The mood changes for the main theme that is constructed from a falling sequence of a minor third and semitone one of Messaien's modes of limited transposition.
author: Ian Latham

text: Taylor's harmonies transform this symmetrical geometric line into beautiful singing melody.
author: Ian Latham

text: The piece moves through several sections of improvisation and composition before returning to the peaceful birdsong.
author: Ian Latham

text: These days, the jazz world is increasingly dominated by individuals who are more skilled in the art of self-promotion than in musicianship.
author: Ian Latham

text: Players like John Taylor, more interested in their art than being rich or famous, largely escape the notice of the mainstream audience.
author: Ian Latham

text: But deeper things take longer to spread their roots before coming into bloom.
author: Ian Latham

text: In time, John Taylor will be remembered as one of the greatest musicians this country has ever produced.
author: Ian Latham

text: I hope that this album helps speed up that process.
author: Ian Latham

text: In English: divinely decadent music which works wonders on your imagination.
author: Helene Rammant

text: Au Cabaret Sauvage will grab you, throw you up in the air, till you eventually find yourself floating in the dark world of singer Pean's poetic and musical galaxy.
author: Helene Rammant

text: This is the third album by Pean and his tribe Lo Jo who are more then just a band.
author: Helene Rammant

text: They are a multi-ethnic collective of music-making poets, street and circus performers, film-activists: cultural militants who have been operating communally from a house in Anger, France since 1982.
author: Helene Rammant

text: Their musical style?
author: Helene Rammant

text: A fascinating mixture of languages, instruments and cultures, that draws on the legacy of les Negresses Vertes and Mano Negra.
author: Helene Rammant

text: The musical ingredients are North African, cabaret style, on a bed of French chanson, with a dash of dub.
author: Helene Rammant

text: Verrrry tasty, and certainly food for thought.
author: Helene Rammant

text: Pean, a French Tom Waits, sings with the cynical charm of Gainsbourg about the blood dancing in the veins of our slumbering sisters.
author: Helene Rammant

text: His lyrics (in Esperanto!) combine humour and pathos to present insights about a world we did not create and may never hope to completely understand.
author: Helene Rammant

text: This must be the vision you get from up-there, as a trapeze artist.
author: Helene Rammant

text: 'Les Humains' kicks off with a dreamy 6/8 on kora, soon joined byPean's "miles of petals" which mingle beautifully with the Berber singing of sisters Nadia and Yamina.
author: Helene Rammant

text: Their voices are also finely demonstrated on 'Tangito', a gloomy tango number with lots of Bohemian violin.
author: Helene Rammant

text: 'Le Poeme de Japonais 'displays a trance-inducing, ululating feast of catchy balafon and ngoni (harp) playing, clearly inspired by the music of Lo Jo's southern neighbours, and personal friends, the Touaregs.
author: Helene Rammant

text: Vive la world!
author: Helene Rammant

text: This is a group with a joie de vivre and voice of its own, a delicious blend of good music with worldly philosophy.
author: Helene Rammant

text: Au Cabaret Sauvage is truly a breath of fresh air.
author: Helene Rammant

text: Showbiz deity Liza Minnelli bounces back from drug and drink dependence, obesity and brain disease with a live recording of her recent Broadway show devised by svengali-esque husband David Gest.
author: Morag Reavley

text: Minnelli opens proceedings in roistering form with a new gem, 'Liza's Back', by Kander and Ebb of Chicago and Cabaret fame.
author: Morag Reavley

text: The opening lines say it all: "I've took my bottle of pills and tossed them away.
author: Morag Reavley

text: I emptied the booze, went back to AA.
author: Morag Reavley

text: Hey, Broadway, Liza's back!" This is a self-mocking, good-natured parody of the showbiz comeback.
author: Morag Reavley

text: How many other stars would be in anything but denial?
author: Morag Reavley

text: It sets the tone for the album.
author: Morag Reavley

text: Her singing is suffused by an infectious sense of joy in her enhanced vocal powers, even more textured and boisterous than before, while her audience banter is alternately mischievous and tender.
author: Morag Reavley

text: The audience themselves are clearly finely attuned to the show's comic and ironic nuances.
author: Morag Reavley

text: These are most evident in a romp through Liza's classics, invested with new significance.
author: Morag Reavley

text: In a raft of songs from Cabaret, Minnelli fully explores the vagaries of showbiz ambitions after 40 up-and-down years.
author: Morag Reavley

text: The tale in Cabaret of Elsie-from-Chelsea, who takes too many pills and too much liquor and ends as the happiest corpse you've ever seen, is sung with wry cadences and knowing pauses.
author: Morag Reavley

text: New material includes 'Don't Smoke In Bed', specially penned by Kander and Ebb.
author: Morag Reavley

text: This is a smouldering, beautifully controlled farewell, to a partner, to a way of life, that one is not totally able to surrender.
author: Morag Reavley

text: 'Something Wonderful', dedicated to Mr.
author: Morag Reavley

text: Minnelli, is expansive and refreshingly unsentimental.
author: Morag Reavley

text: It, and Liza's between-song comments, suggest that this marriage is not without turbulence, though whatever Gest does for Liza, it's working a treat.
author: Morag Reavley

text: "You either got it, or you've had it", Minnelli throbs on 'Rose's Turn'.
author: Morag Reavley

text: On the evidence of this recording, Liza definitely still has it.
author: Morag Reavley

text: Listening to anything by Tosca - indeed anything with Richard Dorfmeister's name on -is always a gloriously self-indulgent experience.
author: Jack Smith

text: Dehli 9 - named after the band in which Rupert Huber and Richard Dorfmeister started their musical experimentation back in their schooldays - is certainly no exception.
author: Jack Smith

text: The bonus CD is a particular treat; more of that later.
author: Jack Smith

text: It's 15 Feb 2003, and Waterloo is seething with anti-war protesters heading for Britain's biggest ever peace-time demonstration.
author: Jack Smith

text: Yet on the train, headphones on, I press play, and within seconds there is no demonstration, no London - no war even - just sunshine on my eyelids and the lush production and laid-back, optimistic grooves of Tosca's3rd album.
author: Jack Smith

text: This is instantly recognisable, on-form Tosca.
author: Jack Smith

text: Not as off-the-wall as Chocolate Elvis, not as irresistibly funky as Opera, but rhythmically unmistakeable.
author: Jack Smith

text: On this album you won't find their trademark repetition of musical ideas; rather a new theme per song.
author: Jack Smith

text: If anything, Delhi 9 is reminiscent of the K&D Sessions, Dorfmeister's superb collaboration with Peter Kruder.
author: Jack Smith

text: What appeals most on this album is the instrumentation.
author: Jack Smith

text: Shining clearly through programmed rhythms and those lovely repeated syncopated echoes, are the sounds of real guitars, bass, vocals, drums.
author: Jack Smith

text: Dorfmeister plays flute on the upbeat and out-there "Wonderful"; Anna Clementis' vocals are understated and gorgeous on "Me and Yoko Ono" and "Oscar" (never has "Diddy dum dum dum da dum" sounded so sexy) and the bass on "Rolf Royce" is fat, dry and earthy.
author: Jack Smith

text: As if all this weren't enough of a treat for Tosca fans, there's the bonus CD.
author: Jack Smith

text: Huber's contemplative, spacious piano compositions are beautifully reworked by Dorfmeister.
author: Jack Smith

text: If you're an Eno fan you might be reminded of his collaboration with Harold Budd, Ambient 2/Plateaux of Mirrors.
author: Jack Smith

text: If you're not, enjoy this bonus CD just for its simplicity and beauty.
author: Jack Smith

text: But dance music it ain't!
author: Jack Smith

text: So, there you have it.
author: Jack Smith

text: A Tosca album so recognisable you may feel you've heard it before, but all the more delightful for being familiar and a bonus CD with 30 minutes of ambient experimental piano music.
author: Jack Smith

text: What are you waiting for?
author: Jack Smith

text: Any album which describes itself with the phrase "classic love songs" is almost certainly doomed before the CD case is even opened.
author: Morag Reavley

text: The omen turns out to be only too accurate in the case of Donny Osmond's latest release.
author: Morag Reavley

text: The album may be Somewhere in Time but its heart is firmly in the 1970s.
author: Morag Reavley

text: "I Can't Go For That", "After The Love Has Gone" and "Would I Lie To You" are off-vintage disco tracks, all high-pitched vocals, homogenised backing groups and saxophone swirls.
author: Morag Reavley

text: A nod is made to the 1980s in a cover of Crowded House's "Don't Dream It's Over".
author: Morag Reavley

text: This is a big ballad number, recorded with the engineer's finger firmly on the echo-effect button.
author: Morag Reavley

text: As rendered by Donny's pleasant-but-bland voice, however, it is but a pale imitation of a pallid original.
author: Morag Reavley

text: Peculiar for an album of classic love songs is the inclusion of "Crazy Horses".
author: Morag Reavley

text: An original Osmond Brothers' number, this is re-recorded as a heavy-soul track with scary feedback and funky drums designed to show that Donny can still rock.
author: Morag Reavley

text: The album concludes with "Puppy Love", first recorded when Donny was a callow 14-year-old, and the leaden weight to which his career will forever be shackled.
author: Morag Reavley

text: Produced here in a stripped-down format with simple guitar accompaniment by none other than Phil Ramone, it nevertheless loses any charm it ever had as an expression of teenage frustration when sung by a man of 45.
author: Morag Reavley

text: With a television career now well-established, it seems perverse for Donny to return to the past with what can only be described as a vanity recording project.
author: Morag Reavley

text: Perhaps it gives him the chance to record the songs he wishes hed been offered during his singing heyday.
author: Morag Reavley

text: A puppy no longer, Donny's closing assertion that "This is not a puppy love" seems only too sadly true.
author: Morag Reavley

text: If only it were then there might be some excuse for this album.
author: Morag Reavley

text: Trapist's debut album became one of my most played records of last year.At best a minimal experience,it was a bit like Charlie Haden, Paul Motian and Ry Cooder free improvising in a roomful of faulty electronic equipment while under mild sedation.This time round, they're signed up to the consistently interesting Thrill Jockey imprint - a move which might win them more of an audience.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Let's hope so, because this trio (are for my money) one of the most individual and rewarding bands around at the moment.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Ballroom is a more expansive beast than its predecessor; the core guitar/bass/drums line up has been augmented with lashings of plaintive analogue synths, gobs of dirty digital distortions and unobtrusive studio trickery.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The result is aluscious, mobile soundscape, capable of ambient purr or abrasive noisebursts.They groove more too, with drummer Martin Brandlmayr and double bassist Joe Williamson locking into spare, insistent pulses.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The feel is more compositional, more structured than before.Whether that's a result of predetermined structures or editing and overdubbing is neither here nor there, but what Trapist have managed is the trick of sounding not really like anyone else but themselves.
author: Peter Marsh

text: This is pretty much entirely down to the trio's feel for texture.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Even at their most frenetic, there's a real sense that every sound is worked on and thought about before it's allowed to escape the instrument.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Brandlmayr's gift for teasinga huge range of textures from his kit is augmented by subtle electronic shadings.Meanwhile Martin Siewert's deliberate, poised guitars (including some delicious lap and pedal steel work) weave resonant, slightly mournful lines, sometimes looped or fed through unstable treatments that threaten to rip his thoughtful melodics apart.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Ballroom may be a cerebral experience, but there's a deep (but ungraspable) emotional undertow beneath its shifting sonics.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Poignant, confrontational, blissful and at 48 minutes, too short...
author: Peter Marsh

text: This trio chose their name well; although they haven't quite taken a vow of silence, they get pretty close to it at times.
author: Peter Marsh

text: If Trapist are a power trio (and a casual glance at the guitar, bass, drums lineup might lead you to think so), they're running on an ancient car battery rather than the national grid.
author: Peter Marsh

text: This deliberate, sparse improv is about what isn't played as much as anything else.
author: Peter Marsh

text: If Morton Feldman, John Cage and David Tudor had formed a rock band, they might have sounded a bit like this.
author: Peter Marsh

text: On the opening tracks, Martin Siewert's minimalist guitar is hardly there; faint pencil strokes of melody or resonant drones are framed by clicks, buzzes and static.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Martin Brandlmayr's drumming is as much about texture as rhythm, while Joe Williamson's bass adds a warm, dark throb.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Williamson is also credited with 'trackball'.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Whether this is connected to a laptop or not isn't made clear, but occasionally more obviously electronic elements creep in, though what generates them isn't clear either.
author: Peter Marsh

text: "Impex" appears to feature a modem undergoing torture, and many of the sounds here resemble equipment malfunction as much as anything else.
author: Peter Marsh

text: As the album goes on Trapist get progressively less interested in silence, engaging in comparatively hyperactive exchanges which hum with a repressed, focussed energy, sometimes settling into spare, sinewy grooves.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Siewert's guitar is alternately abstract scrabble or desolate, almost bluesy in best John Fahey mode.
author: Peter Marsh

text: This is best heard on the fragile "Mine Was The Shoulder You Cried On That Day", where he carefully places long, mournful notes over a soft, tumbling bed of drums and bass.
author: Peter Marsh

text: It's the most conventionally beautiful moment on a CD stuffed with moments of stranger, alien beauties.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Kelly Osbourne is the crown princess of Satan's jukebox.
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: Her breakout debut will appease fans of this scowling pro-shopper while reloading the ammo holster for those eager to take aim, fire, and watch her plummet back to earth.
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: Shut Up (which was to have been titled 'Buy Me') smacks of multiple collaborations and producer credits.
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: It veers wildly between Skate-Lite, Pop Metal and requisite Rrriot Girl.
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: Strangely, a cohesive sound of sorts bleeds through the tough-as-nails façade, marred only by the startling misjudgment of an awkward and ill-suited ballad to mommy dearest ("More Than Life Itself").
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: Yet even knee deep in slush, Kelly soldiers on, bashing errant boyfriends, railing against the media machine and tapping an expansive geyser of teenage venom.
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: Aided by her pre-packaged band members, Kelly belly-flops into a reliable bitch sista's soundscape - the likes of Veruca Salt, Bikini Kill, and Hole spring to mind - but without the sloganeering.
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: Opening track "Disconnected" bursts the cork on a veritable magnum of spite, with forthright if deliciously daft lyrics; 'Hope you're drowning in a pool you've fallen in...'Cos you can't swim'.
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: Her anger gathers pace with the likes of "Contradiction" and "On Your Own", only stopping for the fantastically derivative "Coolhead", a bastard cousin of The B52s "Rock Lobster".
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: Whereas other tracks recycle a pleasant if not particularly original Foo Fighter-ish vibe, this tackles a sixties beach boogie hook.
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: It's a fusion cookery dish that shouldn't work yet still tickles the palette.
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: Second single release "Shut Up" seems closest to Kelly's petulant self, throwing her tantrum-in-a-mansion.
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: The album's final track is a cover of Madonna's "Papa Don't Preach".
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: More than any other, this track captures the zeitgeist rise of The Osbournes MTV show and Kelly's infamous potty mouth in three minutes of raucous, strangled verse.
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: Her voice ain't no Aguilera, but what Kelly lacks in vocal range she claws back in vitriol.
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: Still not a fan?
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: You tell her then.
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: I'm keeping well out of it...
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: Bent's debut album Programmed To Love came bursting out into our living rooms three years ago.
author: Jack Smith

text: With choice tunes like "I Love My Man", "Always" and "Swollen", it heralded a new direction in leftfield dance, and in turn welcomed a new addition to the coffee table CD collection.
author: Jack Smith

text: Those Sunday Best tracks are now considered classics thanks to their over exposure on the latest All-Back-To-Mine-For-The-Greatest-Chillout-Album-In-The-World-Ever collection.
author: Jack Smith

text: The Nottingham duo's new album, The Everlasting Blink, is by Simon Mills and Nail Tolliday's own admission their first album proper; their aforementioned debut to their minds more a collection of tracks.
author: Jack Smith

text: Regardless, the culmination of years of trawling second-hand record shops and car boot sales in search of the ultimate sample have produced a record that is firmly tongue-in-cheek and full of surprises.
author: Jack Smith

text: Whilst the band are keen to stress this is not a concept album, there is a distinct theme with eerie soundtrack beds, kitsch sci-fi flavours and loved-up, down tempo beats en masse.
author: Jack Smith

text: Similarly, collaborations are aplenty: 1970s icon David Essex adds his two-pennys-worth to the Spanish guitar-kissed "Stay The Same", and country star Billie Jo Spears is to "So Long Without You" what Tammy Wynette was to the KLF's hoedown "Justified And Ancient".
author: Jack Smith

text: The ethereal tones of the Beloved's Jon Marsh makes an appearance on the drifting string-soaked "Beautiful Otherness", while Captain & Tennille are expertly sampled to provide the musical inspiration on the beautifully lush 'n' dreamy lead-single "Magic Love".
author: Jack Smith

text: This is by far the album's standout track and with Ashley Beedle's remix makes the song an early contender for single of the year.
author: Jack Smith

text: As a whole the chill beats and blissed out musicianship work well together and further highlight why Bent are the dons of eclectic cool and a slightly less pretentious alternative to, say, Air.
author: Jack Smith

text: Well worth getting your hands on.
author: Jack Smith

text: Aah, the difficult, yet all important third album: the first could go either way, but having proven themselves the second was a test to show if the first wasn't a fluke; but the third, well that's a whole different story...
author: Jack Smith

text: Thankfully for Bent, in Ariels they've nothing to worry about.
author: Jack Smith

text: Joining Programmed To Love and The Everlasting Blink on the coffee table is another worthy companion full of surprises and enriched by beautifully lush 'n' dreamy numbers, like the Carpenters-esque "Sunday 29th" sung by longstanding cohort Kathy Heath.
author: Jack Smith

text: Less overtly electronic than what's gone before, here songs and acoustic instruments replace synths and samples, along with some quite captivating vocals.
author: Jack Smith

text: This time out the Nottingham duo - Simon Mills and Nail Tolliday - have enlisted the services of a handful of accomplished singers to add a variety of contrasting layers to their productions.
author: Jack Smith

text: Notably Rachel Foster from the Weekend Players who adds her lush larynx to the distinctly Air-sounding first single, "Comin' Back"; she also sounds uncannily like Enya on the ethereal "Sing Me".
author: Jack Smith

text: Kosheen's Sian Evans sounds equally at home on the seductively rich "I Can't Believe It's Over"; and X-press 2 and Cassius sessioner Steve Edwards offers a strong male lead on the slow burning toe-tapping optimistically upbeat "Silent Life".
author: Jack Smith

text: Bent closed their Big Chill headline set this year with a sublime cover version/remix of Hall and Oates' "I Can't Go For That".
author: Jack Smith

text: Regrettably, Ariels doesn'tprovide a home for this welcome return to 1981.
author: Jack Smith

text: However you will be able to find it as the closing track ona new compilation called Flowers In The Attic which is out on Mint Source Recordings.
author: Jack Smith

text: As a whole the chill beats and multi-layered musicianship work well together and certainly wouldn't sound out of place on the Six Feet Under soundtrack; all of which conspire to make Bent one of the most happening bands in the living room.
author: Jack Smith

text: Traditional Malian, or Mande music, has captured the imagination of Western music lovers like almost no other African music.
author: John Armstrong

text: It possesses a translucent purity both in sound and delivery, such that an understanding of the songs meanings become almost secondary to the atmosphere they generate.
author: John Armstrong

text: Kasse Mady Foday Diabate is as well-qualified as any Malian musician to take us on this wonderful reconnaissance tour of Mande music's many facets.
author: John Armstrong

text: The instrumentation throughout is traditional but robust.
author: John Armstrong

text: One composition may highlight the possibilities of the balafon (xylophone) whilst another concentrates on the ngoni (lute) or Kora(21-string harp).
author: John Armstrong

text: There are also two Cuban style charanga pieces, led by the flute of Dramane Coulibaly who formed part of the famous 70s Malian charanga band Las Maravillas De Mali.
author: John Armstrong

text: These are underpinned by the surprising but welcome guest appearance of renowned Cuban bassist Orlando Cachaito Lopez.
author: John Armstrong

text: Producer Lucy Duran arranged for these recordings to be made largely on site, in a hastily converted hut in Kela, the village home of many of Mali's finest jelis, or praise singers.
author: John Armstrong

text: The sense of midday heat and rural tranquillity are almost palpable as the musicians work their way unhurriedly through tracks like 'Eh Ya Ye', a cautionary tale about not exaggerating one's abilities.
author: John Armstrong

text: There's a traditional reworking of Kasse Mady's 80s Paris dancefloor hit 'Kaba Mansa' and the beautiful Jembe dance song 'Danya'.
author: John Armstrong

text: The lovely Cuban-style dance tune, 'Balomina Mwanga', is sung in Spanish but the main languages used here are Maninka and Bamana.
author: John Armstrong

text: Duran's fascinating liner notes do justice to her profound knowledge of, and love for Malian culture.
author: John Armstrong

text: The painstaking preparation that clearly went into the making of this record is an object lesson for those sceptics who claim that music sounds the same wherever it's recorded.
author: John Armstrong

text: It doesn't, and here's the living proof.
author: John Armstrong

text: The undisputed heavyweight champion of the 'Dancehall' world most commonly known as Beenie Man unleashes his second output under the Virgin Records banner entitled 'Tropical Storm'.
author: Keysha Davis

text: A few years sovereignty at the top of the trend-ridden and competitive world of deejaying is worthy of a pat on the back.
author: Keysha Davis

text: Beenie's 10 year reign marks an unprecedented onslaught, which has calmlyweathered the storm due to his chameleon instinct.
author: Keysha Davis

text: How many other artists in the genre of dancehall can successfully flirt with varying musical styles such as country and western, gospel and soca and still remain credible?
author: Keysha Davis

text: Seemingly bored with defending his title, Beenie has now set his sights on becoming a global entertainer; Tropical Storm covers a broad spectrum of styles, for the most part, reeking of commerciality.
author: Keysha Davis

text: The happy-clappy, hip-pop feel filters throughout, with Kingston's finest enlisting today's connoisseurs of crossover such as Janet Jackson and The Neptunes for guaranteed mass appeal.
author: Keysha Davis

text: Ironically, the most interesting tracks come courtesy of the guest appearances.s 'Fresh From Yard' enigmatically pairs Beenie with Brooklyn bad gyal 'Lil Kim'.
author: Keysha Davis

text: The two trade boastful couplets; Beenie's pointing towards his sexual prowess, while Kim's surprisingly steers away from sexual subject matters and more towards material wealth.
author: Keysha Davis

text: The track is produced by seasoned NY board controller DJ Clue, and will definitely appeal to ragga heads and hip-hoppers alike.
author: Keysha Davis

text: Similarly 'Yagga Yagga Yo' featuring So Solid Crew is quintessential UK Garage - moody bass lines, frantic keyboards and the over-excitable deejay screaming nonsensical yelps in his trademark style.
author: Keysha Davis

text: The 13 track CD is an overall mixed-bag which will further seal Beenie's status as 'Man of the People'.
author: Keysha Davis

text: Ragga purists might be a tad perturbed though; the tepid output translates into more of a tropical drizzle than a fully-fledged storm.
author: Keysha Davis

text: Dancehall has burst the doors of the Urban scene wide open in the last few years.
author: Jack Smith

text: With artists like Sean Paul and Elephant Man leading the charge, ' Beenie Man- the 'Gal dem Sugar - is back to reclaim his crown.
author: Jack Smith

text: Back To Basics is just what it claims to be.
author: Jack Smith

text: Beenie has shunned the genre's acceptanceby the mainstream market for an old skool sound which could easily have been produced in the nineties.
author: Jack Smith

text: There's not a Neptunes' collaboration in sight.
author: Jack Smith

text: And what's on the menu?
author: Jack Smith

text: Sex, sex and more sex!
author: Jack Smith

text: Not that this raw approach has got in the way of Beenie's appeal; nobody could ignore the phenomenal worldwide success of "Dude", a song that praised the virtue of men with stamina; 'I want a man with the wickedest slam'.
author: Jack Smith

text: Don't we all, darling!
author: Jack Smith

text: "King of the Dancehall", the second single from the album, is aptly named for the man who made the difficult transition from childhood deejay (at the ripe old age of 5) to reggae superstar.
author: Jack Smith

text: Beenie celebrates his prowess in more places than the dancehall, though I fear this track will prove far too sexually explicit for the mainstream audience.
author: Jack Smith

text: And let's make it clear, this is a hardcore album.
author: Jack Smith

text: If tales of Beenie's prowess aren't your cup of tea, you may find Back To Basics hard to swallow.
author: Jack Smith

text: There are a few quieter moments, including the gospel inspired "If A Neva God", but these serve only to highlight the libidinous content of the whole.
author: Jack Smith

text: However, for the Beenie Man fan base and lovers of dancehall in its truest form, this disc will slot easily into their collection and reconfirm his status as an institution on the scene.
author: Jack Smith

text: Beenie brings it 'Back To Basics', as only he can.
author: Jack Smith

text: With stars like Youssou N'Dour, Baaba Maal, Salif Keita and Orchestre Baobab, West Africa is certainly not short of talent.
author: John Armstrong

text: But every so often, a new act appears from that musically abundant region to prick up the ears.
author: John Armstrong

text: Pape Amadou Fall and Cheikhou Coulibaly are being promoted as a sort of folk protest group, and Real World's website makes much reference to the Dylans and Baezes of this world.
author: John Armstrong

text: But do yourself a favour by listening to the music first, without the benefit of the sleevenote's lyric translation.
author: John Armstrong

text: The title track is one of those luscious, melancholy airs that one associates with Afro-Parisian star Lokua Kanza.
author: John Armstrong

text: Afro-Celt James McNally'saccordion is a natural accompaniment to the swirling melody line.
author: John Armstrong

text: The mood is revisited in the upbeat 'Kekilo' and the more reflective 'Ma Ansou'.
author: John Armstrong

text: 'Yaay' ups the tempo and features a dark organ riff and wah wah guitar figure against traditional percussion.
author: John Armstrong

text: Then there's a wonderful moment where the minor key slips into a major, then back to the minor key: this track must be the natural choice for a few dance floor remixes.
author: John Armstrong

text: 'Kokoliko' and 'Jello': are just acoustic guitar and voice.
author: John Armstrong

text: Here is where the western protest/folk comparisons do make sense.
author: John Armstrong

text: This reviewer detected shades of early Bert Jansch/John Renbourn/Davy Graham in atmosphere and style if not content.
author: John Armstrong

text: 'Kamalemba' and 'Yatal Gueew' take us deep into Youssou N'Dour territory, the former featuring that unmistakable skipping 6/8 beat of traditional Wolof percussion and handclapping, the latter bringing to mind Youssou's massive 1985 hit 'Immigres'.
author: John Armstrong

text: 'Lonkotina', with its forbidding electric guitar line, has something of Neil Young circa 'Cowgirl In The Sand' about it!
author: John Armstrong

text: The album tapes, originally recorded in Youssou N'Dour's studio in Dakar and released domestically a couple of years ago as a cassette-only album, have been judiciously 'cleaned up' for this international release.
author: John Armstrong

text: But original Canadian producer Mac Fallows' deliberately understated feel still shines through.
author: John Armstrong

text: Pape and Cheikh are currently touring Europe with Tracy Chapman.
author: John Armstrong

text: We'll be lucky if we hear a more interesting Senegalese debut release this year.
author: John Armstrong

text: Charles Pierce (the man behind end) has crafted this album of modern electronica as a kind of concept.
author: Marcus Scott

text: Like science fiction at its best, he wants to capture the un-mastered realm of our imaginative experience.
author: Marcus Scott

text: In the press release Hymen make a big deal of the processes this music is made from, as it is made entirely from the complex overlay of samples via digital computer processing.
author: Marcus Scott

text: However with the use of commercially available sample CDs,music software and computers replacing the use of keyboards and drum machines, it's hard to see what they're trying to prove here.
