author: Marcus Scott

text: This is his first full length album and it comes complete with a lot of theoretical baggage.
author: Marcus Scott

text: From the academic jargon of the press release through to the titles, "simulacra and simulations", "society of the spectacle" etc which sound like lifts from post-modern philosophy books, Pierce seems to want to make a grand statement.
author: Marcus Scott

text: The titles could be thereto make the listener aware of the de-contextualising the samples made to make this music, as well as giving some pointers about Pierce's reading habits and interests, but whatever, the music itself is good.
author: Marcus Scott

text: Opener "eclipse of reason" is all complex drums, clicks and grainy whooshes over baleful strings, breaking down into unrecognisable washes of noise and up again into more complex seemingly random drum patterns.
author: Marcus Scott

text: end'screaky, grainy drums and cinema-for-the-ear pretensions are at their best on "Global media engine" with solid drums, a noise like a b-52 bomber, dark dissonant chords and sub bass adding up to one of the albums most epic moments..
author: Marcus Scott

text: "An elaborate accounting hoax" has an almost digi-dub feel to it, with off kilter chords, bleepy stabs and a shuffling drum break that make the track sound like some alien hybrid of '93 breakbeat hardcore.
author: Marcus Scott

text: What's more the incredibly creepy "The culture industry" is constructed from a glitchyhip hop drumgroove and a needle sharp melody, underpinned by deep bass drones.
author: Marcus Scott

text: It's this kind of gear change that keeps the listener's interest level up.
author: Marcus Scott

text: Overall the album owes as much to Squarepusher as the processed glitchscapes of Oval, but is best described as a richer, more sophisticated take on Ed Rush and Nico's genre-breaking dystopian drum and bass on early No-U turn records.
author: Marcus Scott

text: The soundtrack like elementswork too;the strange alien clicks and drones add a level of oddity that engages the listeners imagination and takes them deeper into the music.
author: Marcus Scott

text: ...or, more accurately, the best of the post Island Records years, because none of Baaba Maal's early 80s Senegalese cassette-only material is here.
author: John Armstrong

text: But what the heck, it's still better than almost all the competition rolled into one.
author: John Armstrong

text: Remember the majestic 'Yero Mama'?
author: John Armstrong

text: or the princely original version of'African Woman', now remixed out of our collective consciousness?
author: John Armstrong

text: Or the song that gave his band their name (or vice versa) 'Dande Lenol'?
author: John Armstrong

text: Well, they're all here, and you'd be wise to snap up this careful compilation even if you do have the original three or four albums from which its culled.
author: John Armstrong

text: Baaba's childhood in a small fishing village showed little promise of his musical future until he persuaded the powers that be to allow him to call the worshippers to the mosque each day.
author: John Armstrong

text: His musician mother encouraged him to follow a career in music and, after moving to Dakar and winning a scholarship he joined a 70-piece orchestra, Asly Fouta.
author: John Armstrong

text: After touring West Africa with his guitarist friend Mansour Seck, the two decamped to Paris and the Conservatoire des Beaux Arts, returning to Senegal with a mass of new ideas for incorporating pop and reggae with traditional Senegalese music.
author: John Armstrong

text: Enter the ubiquitous Afro-Parisian producer Ibrahim Sylla, who launched Baaba Maal onto an international stage with the 1988 album Wango.
author: John Armstrong

text: The main feature of all Baaba Maal's music both then and now, is a strict adherence to a Senegalese feel, no matter what technology is used to ease its passage.
author: John Armstrong

text: Baaba is unwavering loyal to Senegalese culture.
author: John Armstrong

text: When interviewed, he never defers to the sort of preening self-promotion that some African artists resort to: when asked about his influences, he doesn't say John Coltrane, or Otis Redding or The Beatles, as many do.
author: John Armstrong

text: He replies: traditional Senegalese music.
author: John Armstrong

text: And traditional Senegalese music is certainly what he plays.
author: John Armstrong

text: 'To Josquin we owe the delectable art of song in several voices; to Mouton, the true art of contrapuntal variation, and to Willaert, the art of sweet harmonies.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: But to Cipriano the unique, heaven granted gift of blending all three in one'.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Cipriano was the great 16th century Flemish composer Cipriano de Rore, who spent more-or-less his entire career working in Italy.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: You might expect his collaborator and publisher Gardano to have nothing but praise for Rore only a year after his death in 1565; but even the great Monteverdi admired him, and praised by name two of the madrigals that appear on this new cd.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: So what made Rore's music so special to his contemporaries?
author: Andrew McGregor

text: It seems to have been a rare combination of contrapuntal skill and expressive genius - the intellect blending seamlessly with the emotional.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: So why isn't he better known?
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Perhaps that's because recordings as good as this one are rarer than hens' teeth.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: The opening item is a simple eight voice chanson...
author: Andrew McGregor

text: or at least it feels simple enough, until Rore unwraps cascades of suspensions, swiftly resolved discords that encapsulate the emotional upheaval of the poet in love.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: The main meat of the disc though is an astonishing mass setting, famous as a technical tour de force even in Rore's lifetime.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: It's a parody mass, based on the Christmas motet Praeter rerum seriem by Josquin...but that's not the whole story.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: It also manages to qualify as a cantus firmus mass, where the tenor part of every movement sings the praises of Rore's employer, by slowly unfolding a tune he'd used before with a text praising his boss.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Tricky stuff - but the real miracle of this mass is that despite the technical sophistication, your nose is never rubbed in it: the music speaks clearly, emotionally and expressively.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Paul van Nevel calls the Missa Praeter rerum seriem 'perhaps the most monumental mass of the 16th century' - and performed like this by his Huelgas Ensemble, I dont feel like taking issue with him.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: The unaccompanied voices are crystal clear, the texture unfolds easily in front of you, and yet there's no feeling of fussiness - despite the accuracy and cleanness of the singing and the almost vibrato-less voices, never for a moment does this feel sterile.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: The acoustic has been captured superbly, and the way the soaring sopranos set the stonework ringing can make you catch your breath.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: This is one of those rare discs it's almost impossible to criticise.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Even if we're unlikely ever to see cds of Rore stacked high and sold cheap in our local non-specialist record shops, I suspect this is an important, and necessary, recording.
author: Andrew McGregor

text: I must go listen to it one more time...
author: Andrew McGregor

text: Try These: Lalande: Music for the Sun King A Venetian Christmas: Gabrieli Consort Pergolesi: Marian Vespers
author: Andrew McGregor

text: The piano/guitar duet is a rare beast in jazz, and one that imediately brings to mind the classic Bill Evans and Jim Hall sessions that produced Intermodulation and Undercurrent.
author: Peter Marsh

text: It would be unfair to expect messrs Zoffer and Larrabee to match that, but at times on this unpretentious and often quite lovely CD they come close enough.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Zoffer and Larabee are very different players from Evans, Hall or indeed each other.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Larrabee's guitar is straight out of the lineage of players like John Abercrombie or John Scofield; though there's the rich harmonic language of Hall's post bop approach, it's tinged with a bluesier, rockier edge.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Zoffer meanwhile is a straighahead, funky pianist with a boisterous, playful touch, but capable of passages of hushed delicacy.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The opening "Talk to Me" is a fragile, crystalline piece that recalls the impressionist wanderings of Ralph Towner and John Abercrombie's Sargasso Sea.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Larrabee shines here with a thoughtful, cascading improvisation that threads through Zoffer's carefully placed, wide open chords.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The duo seem to work best on the ballads; "Escape Artist" is similarly resonant, while they even pull off the oft attempted 'jazzmen play the classics' trick with a reworking of Chopin's Nocturne no 12.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Despite the cringeworthy title ("Chopin Noc-turned"), Zoffer's rearrangement finds new beauties in an old chestnut, though purists may disagree.
author: Peter Marsh

text: It's on the uptempo numbers that the going can get a little tough; while Zoffer's joyful "Need you So" (a distant cousin of John Scofield's "Still Warm") packs a joyful punch, sometimes the lack of a rhythm section is felt quite keenly.
author: Peter Marsh

text: It's here that the diversity of the players' approaches counts against them.; Larabee sounds much less comfortable with straightahead swing, something that Zoffer excels at.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The guitarists's use of occasional effects can be a bit jarring too, withwah wah and touches of distortion putting too much textural distance between guitar and piano.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Still, the two men's obvious empathy makes this a pretty enjoyable listening experience for the most part, and if Paul Bley likes them (as he apparently does), that should be enough for the likes of us.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Roisin Murphy and Mark Brydonare back with the unmistakable sound of Moloko.
author: Lucy Davies

text: Following 2000's Things to Make and Do,they return with an album that is fresh, keeping all the things that are good, buttoning down their darker side,and adding a more mature element, encompassing upset and sadness.
author: Lucy Davies

text: The quality of Roisin's voice, recorded intimately close to the mic, carries off the trademark posturing dramatics of the music.
author: Lucy Davies

text: Sometimes this expresses unrequited love, as in "I Want You", and "Blow X Blow".
author: Lucy Davies

text: Never before has heartbreak sounded so glamorous: many a jilted soul will find comfort in the vamped up confessions, backed always by contradictory cheerful latin inspired beats.
author: Lucy Davies

text: The opening floor filler "Familiar Feeling" has one to the best introductions heard for a long time: starting with Hammond noodlings,latin guitar and beats, flourishes of fiddles build up tension to an impossible level.
author: Lucy Davies

text: The track appears to halt, then start afresh, with Roisin expressing a laid back philosophy: " I never doubted it: What's for you, won't pass you by".
author: Lucy Davies

text: Self assured and going with the flow, the oncoming chorus is big enough to justify all that building up and knocking down.
author: Lucy Davies

text: Butin "Come on", they're back in that slightly dementeddark side, melodies leaping all over the place with snapping rhythms, outlined by electronic sounds singing along.
author: Lucy Davies

text: Witha refrain of "ha ha ha" - you have the feeling that even though they might know that they're not quite all there, they're going to enjoy themselves.
author: Lucy Davies

text: One of the things that sets Moloko apart from other dance duos is their handling of instrumentation, often with simply structuredsongs renewing themselves time and time again, as they find new ways to say the same thing.In Statues this is something that they've excelled in once again.
author: Lucy Davies

text: "Over and Over", the final track, conveys the ending of a relationship with eloquence and grace.
author: Lucy Davies

text: Areal feeling of spaciousness has been achieved dramatic and beautifully produced strings, harmonised vocals repeating "over and over" rising and rising.
author: Lucy Davies

text: Combining string glissandos with electric guitar, and death knells of huge orchestral chimes, the album closes as dramatically as it began.
author: Lucy Davies

text: These are real artists, and they know their medium as well as they know the craft of writinga song: beautifully.
author: Lucy Davies

text: Sangam is Michael Nyman's latest and boldest attempt to fuse two diametrically opposed musical worlds, the improvisatory world of Indian classical music and the pre-composed world of Nyman.
author: Helene Rammant

text: Indeed, 'sangam' is a Hindi word meaning a coming together.
author: Helene Rammant

text: But is this venture really a match made in heaven, as the CD's sleeve notes seem to suggest?
author: Helene Rammant

text: Sangam is the result of an artistic partnership between Nyman and the Asian Music Circuit who took Michael on an extensive trip to India in search of suitable musical collaborators.
author: Helene Rammant

text: "When I set out for India on this project I didn't know what it was I was looking for", says Michael.
author: Helene Rammant

text: Until he reached Benares in India, that is, where he had his revelation.
author: Helene Rammant

text: The dry and mysterious Vedic chants he heard at the house of Rajan and Sajan Misra struck his minimalist chord.
author: Helene Rammant

text: Nonetheless, it is khyal singing we hear on this record, as performed by the Misra brothers.
author: Helene Rammant

text: In 'Three Ways of Describing Rain' Michael's aim is to present "a velvet cushion on which these jewels could sit".
author: Helene Rammant

text: Nyman's harmonic cushion (in D major predominantly) is woven out of a chord progression set at random against the vocals of the Indian singers.
author: Helene Rammant

text: The stylistic effect is ...
author: Helene Rammant

text: minimalist, very Nymanesque.
author: Helene Rammant

text: Not very Indian.
author: Helene Rammant

text: On 'Compiling The Colours', Michael and his band are joined by South India's mandolin star Shrinivas.
author: Helene Rammant

text: Shrivanas virtusosi tans (or compositions), are injected by Nyman with pentatonic steroids on piano, everlasting sawing strings and mechanical cross-rhythms reminiscent of Phillip Glass' music in 12 parts.
author: Helene Rammant

text: The composer's old ideas and concepts are seemingly unaffected by his immersion in Karnatic music.
author: Helene Rammant

text: Not very dialectical.
author: Helene Rammant

text: I wondered what the project would sound like as a live performance, and therefore headed to the Festival Hall on Thursday to listen to its London premiere.
author: Helene Rammant

text: The piece sounded chaotic, at times out of sync, despite Nyman's gesticulating and conducting throughout.
author: Helene Rammant

text: This is not a record which achieves true stylistic integration.
author: Helene Rammant

text: More a collision of worlds, to use Nyman's vocabulary, then a melding and mutual nourishment of sound.
author: Helene Rammant

text: Less is not always more.
author: Helene Rammant

text: Rimsky-Korsakov's Sheherezade is loosely based on the Persian fairy tales of A Thousand and One Nights, famously related by the Sultana Sheherazade to her despotic Sultan husband in a two-and-a-half year series of cliffhangers designed to postpone the ever-present threat of execution.
author: Matthew Shorter

text: Like all good bedtime stories, it thrives on repetition.
author: Matthew Shorter

text: The opening musical phrase representing alternately the Sultan and the stormy sea occurs 38 times (complete or truncated) in the first movement alone, before appearing in altered forms later in the work.
author: Matthew Shorter

text: The repetition is no accident - it's ingenious both as a vehicle for Rimsky's fabulous inventiveness in harmony and orchestration, and as a depiction of the simultaneous sameness and unpredictability of the sea, in a movement subtitled The Sea and Sinbad's Ship.
author: Matthew Shorter

text: But Valery Gergiev's slow and somewhat rigid tempos tend to emphasise the movement's monotony at the expense of its colour - a rather wooden ship on a wooden sea.
author: Matthew Shorter

text: There's a similar knowingness to the storytelling in the second movement, where slow tempos, and a mannered approach in the wind solos which punctuate the movement, underline the episodic nature of the music in thick felt-tip pen.
author: Matthew Shorter

text: The solo violin part throughout the work also feels more studied than deeply felt, as do the romantic climaxes in the love-scene third movement.
author: Matthew Shorter

text: All credit, however, to orchestra and conductor for the quality of playing in general, and to the producers for the balance, both in the tuttis, and in bringing out Rimsky's crystalline solo textures, such as the passages for solo cello, horn and woodwinds in the first movement.
author: Matthew Shorter

text: And if tempos are slow in the first three movements, Gergiev makes up for lost time in the fiery, bristling fourth, which becomes a tour-de-force for an orchestra clearly at the height of its powers (featuring some breathtaking display from trumpet and piccolo in particular).
author: Matthew Shorter

text: Two contemporary works complete the disc, Borodin's In the Steppes of Central Asia and Balakirev's Islamey.
author: Matthew Shorter

text: If the latter feels like an overgrown encore to a Warner Brothers cartoon, the former turns out to be the perfect vehicle for Gergiev's gifts.
author: Matthew Shorter

text: Borodin's musical picture evokes a relationship of sweetness and light between the Russian conquerors and Caucasian conquered - probably as unlikely then as now, through folk-inspired music which is gentle and measured throughout, and which Gergiev handles with real sensitivity.
author: Matthew Shorter

text: Try These: Shchedrin: Carmen Suite Sibelius: Tone Poems Stravinsky: The Rite of Spring
author: Matthew Shorter

text: New York based trio The Hub are out to defy jazz conventions.
author: Ian Latham

text: They thrust their thrash metal and long hair into a scene which is ripe for a shake up.
author: Ian Latham

text: It's a band at the very fringes of what we accept as jazz; indeed, it's only really alto player Dan Magaywho provides any jazz substance with his free form soloing.
author: Ian Latham

text: Electric bass player Tim Dahl alternates between pure and distorted tones as he lays down lines that draw from funk and punk.
author: Ian Latham

text: Drummer Sean Noonan seems most content when he's making a lot of noise, thumping on his kick drum and imitating machine guns on his snare.
author: Ian Latham

text: This band shows that it's quite easy to challenge jazz norms, but much more difficult to do it with intelligence and sophistication.
author: Ian Latham

text: The Hub might succeed with the former, but they fall short of the latter.
author: Ian Latham

text: The Hub are strongly reminiscent of the cult Belgian band Aka Moon.
author: Ian Latham

text: They share the same line-up, and both alto players are reminiscent of Steve Coleman.
author: Ian Latham

text: Although The Hub are tight and confident, they are technically light years behind Aka Moon's advanced polymetric concept and extraordinary range of influence.
author: Ian Latham

text: Curiously, both bands also play with an arrogance which insists that they are somehow 'future of the music'.
author: Ian Latham

text: It's an attitude which is at best naive.
author: Ian Latham

text: Both bands, in their own way, lead the way to a dead end, a path of narrow appeal and ultimate obscurity.
author: Ian Latham

text: Trucker is an album of original compositions by Dahl and Noon, which typically juxtapose deliberately simple, inane melodies with aggressively thrashy sections.
author: Ian Latham

text: The writing is certainly the weakest link in this music; after listening to the album a few times, you start to dread the annoying tunes.
author: Ian Latham

text: All of the compositions are in four and the phrases are clumsily square.
author: Ian Latham

text: There is an overdependence on unison writing between the alto and bass, and most of the drum lines are unimaginative and monotonous.
author: Ian Latham

text: It's curious that sax man Magay hasn't contributed any compositions for the album, as he demonstrates a more highly developed sense of phrasing in his soloing.
author: Ian Latham

text: The band are strongest in the improvised sections, with the players complementing each others maniacal energy with genuine communication and empathy.
author: Ian Latham

text: It's always welcome to find a band that are not following the crowd and really doing their own thing.
author: Ian Latham

text: There's no denying that The Hub have developed a distinctive band sound.
author: Ian Latham

text: The trouble is, the quality of their music really isn't high enough to lift them above being anything other than a novelty and a curiosity.
author: Ian Latham

text: For those of you not familiar with Tadd Mullinix, the man behind James Cotton and Dabrye, this is a name that should be at the top of your shopping list, no matter what styles of music you're currently grooving to.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Based in Ann Arbor, Michigan, this talented 22 year old has been lurking around the American music scene for a few years now.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Getting his start as a techno dj and then moving on to more experimental sounds, Mullinix has been impressing audiences across the US and Europe with his beautifully baroque influenced debut CD and of course, his booty shakin', head boppin debut as Dabrye.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Literally blowing the roof of BBC HQ, Mullinix's Dabrye cds hit us like a ton of bricks and now the man is back, giving us another taste into his multifaceted persona with Panes.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Firing off in a completely different direction for this outing, Panes strips away the funk and instead replaces it with a grinding industrial feel.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Dark, deep factory noises grind away under plate reverbs and thudding warehouse beats all enshrouded in a thick aura of dub.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Panes lurches through the soundscapes, its sounds crawling and leering across the stereo spectrum.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Tracks like "Shaven Glass" and "Alternating Currents" live up to their names, offering repetitive melodies interlaced with dissonant noise offering only a hint of song.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Mullinix rips apart his DJ past in "Sealed" and "Exchanging Modes" where a distorted and mutant bass rhythm slips and slides across something that tries very hard to approach an old school Detroit techno track, but never quite makes it.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Mullinix has a great knack for taking traditional styles of electronic music, be it Detroit techno or Chicago Hip-Hop and painting his unique style over it, much like a graffitti artist would spray paint over a particularly vibrant subway ad.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: For those into more industrial sounds or those searching for the sounds of a warehouse party gone wrong, this is a great place to start.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: Fans of Mullinix's previous work should enjoy this release, even though it is a far cry from his earlier works of beauty.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: "Panes" is dissonant, dark, dubby and deeply, deeply enjoyable; another winner from one of our favourite up and coming artists.
author: Olli Siebelt

text: We've been spoilt in recent years with quality neo-soul female singers since Erykah Badu first exploded onto the scene back in 1997 (yes, it was that long ago).
author: Jack Smith

text: We've embraced Macy Gray, Jill Scott, India Arie and most recently, Alicia Keys.
author: Jack Smith

text: The latest to join the sisterhood is Philadelphia starlet Vivian Green who's debut album, A Love Story, must surely earn her an early entry in the end of year Best Newcomer shortlist.
author: Jack Smith

text: "Fanatic" oozes Badu-isms; "Superwoman" smacks of a bygone folk age, and "What Is Love?" echoes of Alicia's "Falling".
author: Jack Smith

text: While "Emotional Rollercoaster", the first single, goes some way to show her true worth.
author: Jack Smith

text: But for me the trio, "24 Hour Blue (Just One Of Those Days)", "Be Good To You" and "Keep On Going" are by far the strongest outings from the Philly singer-songwriter who co-wrote all fourteen tracks on her debut opus.
author: Jack Smith

text: Spotted as a major talent while singing back-up for Jill Scott and Maxwell three years ago, it's reported that Columbia paid seven figures to secure Green's services.
author: Jack Smith

text: Money well spent if you look at the sales (particularly in America) of her aforementioned nubile Nubian goddess peers.
author: Jack Smith

text: A Love Story is an inspired blend of seductive neo-soul coupled with a vocal maturity and emotional range of a young woman who's seen lifes up-and-downs.
author: Jack Smith

text: "The album actually is a love story",says Green.
author: Jack Smith

text: "I wear my heart on my sleeve".
author: Jack Smith

text: But it's far from a cliched boy-meets-girl plot, rather a sophisticated, autobiographical rumination on a relationship gone wrong, learning to love yourself and then finding true love.
author: Jack Smith

text: Aah, we all like a happy ending!
author: Jack Smith

text: Mature beyond her tender years (hard to believe she's still only 23), cuts like the slow jazz refinement of "No Sittin By The Phone" exudes a Billie Holiday quality, while on the lyrically identifiable "Complete", her vocal is appropriately soft but never soppy.
author: Jack Smith

text: Major stardom seems assured for Vivian Green whose blend of musical styles and lyrical messages is diverse enough to satisfy every listeners aural taste buds.
author: Jack Smith

text: In a word - sublime.
author: Jack Smith

text: Colin MacIntyre, the creative force behind Mull Historical Society, has been jotting lyrics and blunting thumb tips since the age of six.
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: Growing up on the Scottish island of the same name, the influence of his uncles touring tribute band led to a propensity for ego-free pop; music for the sake of shared enjoyment, instead of sucking in cheek cavities for the camera.
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: Years later, the result is a subtle, often mesmerising lyricism and playing style.
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: 2001's Loss was a sunny, feel good, rabble rousing debut album.
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: Us, however, is full of breezy melancholia and expands upon his outsider aesthetic to conjure a sense of magical otherness.
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: "The Final Arrears" creates an indie-lullaby with shades of Christmas carol, "Am I Wrong" treads a similar path; giving post break-up analysis an unreal calm.
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: Shades of earlier, bouncy chart single "Xanadu" return for "Live Like The Automatics", which is perhaps the most commercial of the current bunch.
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: It's certainly a much-needed antidote to the likes of "Asylum", which slides a little too close to Coldplay's excessive introspection for comfort.
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: Part Royston-Vasey, part Peter Kay, it's the minutiae of life on the fringes, of small town whimsy and wry observations that prove to be MacIntyre's currency.
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: Up one minute, down the next, if Us were a mental condition it would be manic-optimistic.
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: Fellow Scots Belle & Sebastian potter in similar kooky territory, while the occasional skirmish in the percussion cupboard recalls the trimmings of Super Furry Animals.
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: The likes of "5 More Minutes", "Can" and "Us" peel back the production even further; exposing the accomplished singer songwriter by virtue of an almost solely acoustic delivery.
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: In fact his closest musical kin would seem to be Ben Folds (formerly of the Ben Folds Five).
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: Both being unassuming masters of their trade (Folds of the piano, MacIntryre of the guitar), elevated to the position of bedroom evangelists.
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: If the meek shall inherit the Earth, Mull Historical Society shall provide a template for the new world order.
author: Bren O'Callaghan

text: Three riders galloping abreast of each other, each fully aware of the other.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: All aiming for a single destination.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Splash of cymbals like the dust raised by hooves.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Their destination is reached 6 minutes 3 seconds after they set out.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Not a race in a fusion sense of piling on the notes, but rather of a serious but joyful vigour in pursuit of something or - come to think of it joy in the race itself, rather than the goal.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: "In Media Res" makes for an invigorating beginning.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: "Accumulated Gestures" continues without pause for breath.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: It pushes, pulls and worries at a motif which conveys the impression of a movement of the hand, a toss of the head, each successive pattern piling up in the corner in a heap.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: "Generations" is the first track to let up the pace a little.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: It's a slow spooky number: rolling piano figures played on the left hand are echoed by tenor and cymbal work.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: The mournful undertones of this track conjure a sense of loss, perhaps for ancestors, perhaps for all passing.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Fieldwork are a trio comprising Elliot Humberto Kavee on drums, Aaron Stewart on tenor and Vijay Iyer on piano.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: The absence of a bass creates a particular tension, the lack of traditional resolution throws the three instruments into particular relief.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Rhythm is mutable; it seems to speed up and slow down at will.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: From moment to moment you don't know what it's going to do next.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: "Step Lively" is particularly noteworthy in this respect: it does the opposite of what it says by running slowly but surely out of steam, exhausted.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: I can't help but detect a likeable humour in this.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: On other pieces, each instrument appears to play catch with the rhythm - throwing it from one to the other to the other, sometimes it almost feels like it can be spied momentarily in mid-air.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Fieldwork evince seriousness, displaying a music full of change and vigour.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Serious, even perhaps a little forbidding, this music repays concentration.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: The mood of each piece gradually takes shape with each listen, like the eye will assemble and eventually make sense of an object seen through gauze.
author: Colin Buttimer

text: Terry Riley's minimalist classic In C is one of those pieces that'sinstantly recognisable, despite the fact that no two performances of it can ever quantitatively be very similar.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Each musician is given a sequence of 53 musical phrases.
author: Peter Marsh

text: He or she repeats each phrase for as long as they like (though Riley suggests that as the piece should last around forty minutes, anything between 45 and 90 seconds is best) before playing the next one.
author: Peter Marsh

text: If the musician can't play a phrase, they just skip it.
author: Peter Marsh

text: There are no guides as to instrumentation, though the usual number of performers is around 30.
author: Peter Marsh

text: As Riley's simple phrases drift in and out of sync with each other, complex, hypnotic patterns emerge and dissolve, making concentration a tricky business for the performers, but an experience of potentially psychedelic proportions for the listener.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Though Riley's music was undoubtedly a big influence on a generation of drone-rockers, it's only recently thatIn C's been visited recently by the likes of Acid Mothers Temple, and now by New York band The Styrenes.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Riley's emphasis on group listening and relaxed approach to technique makethe piece an obvious fit with the dynamics of ye olde rocke group, and this album's proof.
author: Peter Marsh

text: The Styrenes were formed by Paul Marotta, previously of Cleveland art punkers The Electric Eels, back in 1975.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Having met Riley, he'd become convinced of the possibilities of an In C played with rock instrumentation (previous recorded versions have usually featured tuned percussion and wind instruments), though held off actually doing it for some years.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Here appearing asa septet, the bandmanage 20 instruments through a spot of studio magic, playing the whole thing through twice through plus a few overdubs.
author: Peter Marsh

text: And it's a beautiful noise.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Props go to drummer Mike Hoffman, whose sensitive deployment of various elements of his kit provides propulsion and texture in equal measure.
author: Peter Marsh

text: Guitars, keys and marimba provide the melodic wonderment that generally arises during a performance of the piece, and the Styrenes infuse the proceedings with a scratchy, raw energy that's immediate and infectious.
author: Peter Marsh
